“Kauśika! It is because the intrinsic nature of the perfection of generosity cannot be dedicated; it is because the intrinsic natures of the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom cannot be dedicated;

it is because the intrinsic nature of internal emptiness cannot be dedicated; and it is because the intrinsic natures of external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, endless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, non-alteration emptiness, essential emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common-characteristic emptiness, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature cannot be dedicated.”

It is because the nature of true suchness cannot be dedicated; it is because the natures of the dharma-realm, the dharma-nature, non-illusory nature, unchanging nature, equality, the state beyond birth, the fixed nature of dharmas, the stability of dharmas, the limit of reality, the realm of space, and the inconceivable realm cannot be dedicated;
it is because the nature of the noble truth of suffering cannot be dedicated, nor can the natures of the noble truths of origination, cessation, and the path be dedicated;
it is because the nature of the four dhyānas cannot be dedicated, nor can the natures of the four immeasurables and the four formless absorptions be dedicated.

It is because the intrinsic nature of the eight liberations cannot be dedicated; it is because the intrinsic nature of the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive absorptions, and the ten totalities cannot be dedicated;

it is because the intrinsic nature of the four foundations of mindfulness cannot be dedicated; it is because the intrinsic nature of the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path cannot be dedicated;

it is because the intrinsic nature of the liberation door of emptiness cannot be dedicated; and it is because the intrinsic nature of the liberation doors of signlessness and wishlessness cannot be dedicated.
It is because the intrinsic nature of the ten stages of a bodhisattva cannot be dedicated;
it is because the intrinsic nature of the five eyes cannot be dedicated, nor can the intrinsic nature of the six supernormal powers be dedicated;

it is because the intrinsic nature of the ten powers of a Buddha cannot be dedicated, nor can the intrinsic nature of the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, or the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha be dedicated.
The nature of the quality of non-forgetfulness cannot be dedicated, nor can the nature of the constant abiding in equanimity be dedicated;
the nature of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) cannot be dedicated, nor can the natures of the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*) and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) be dedicated;
the natures of all dhāraṇī-doors cannot be dedicated, nor can the natures of all samādhi-doors be dedicated.
The intrinsic nature of the fruit of stream-entry cannot be redirected; the intrinsic nature of the fruits of once-returner, non-returner, and arhatship cannot be redirected;
the intrinsic nature of pratyekabuddha enlightenment cannot be redirected;
and the intrinsic nature of all the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cannot be redirected.
It is because the intrinsic nature of the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas cannot be redirected through dedication. "Furthermore, Kausika,

if a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to demonstrate, instruct, encourage, and gladden other sentient beings regarding unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they should do so with a mind that accords with the true nature of reality."

Furthermore, one should likewise manifest, instruct, exhort, and gladden them with praise as follows: when practicing the perfection of generosity, one should not discriminate, thinking "I am able to give";
when practicing the perfection of ethical discipline, one should not discriminate, thinking "I am able to protect my precepts";
and when practicing the perfection of patience, one should not discriminate, thinking "I am able to cultivate patience."
When practicing the perfection of diligence, one should not discriminate, thinking, "I am able to be diligent";
when practicing the perfection of meditative concentration, one should not discriminate, thinking, "I am able to enter samādhi";
and when practicing the perfection of wisdom, one should not discriminate, thinking, "I am able to cultivate insight."
When practicing inner emptiness, one should not discriminate, thinking, "I am able to abide in inner emptiness.

When practicing outer emptiness, inner-and-outer emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, non-altering emptiness, essential emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common-characteristic emptiness, the emptiness of all dharmas, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature, one should not discriminate, thinking, "I am able to abide in outer emptiness," up to and including "the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature."
When practicing in accordance with suchness, one should not discriminate, thinking, "I am able to abide in suchness.

When practicing in accordance with the dharma-realm, the nature of phenomena, non-falsity, immutability, equality, the state beyond birth, the fixed nature of phenomena, the stability of phenomena, the limit of reality, the realm of space, or the inconceivable realm, one should not discriminate, thinking, "I am able to abide in the dharma-realm" up to "the inconceivable realm."
When practicing the Noble Truth of Suffering, one should not discriminate, thinking, "I am able to abide in the Noble Truth of Suffering";
when practicing the Noble Truths of Origination, Cessation, and the Path, one should not discriminate, thinking, "I am able to abide in the Noble Truths of Origination, Cessation, and the Path."
When practicing the four dhyānas, one should not discriminate, thinking, "I am able to cultivate the four dhyānas";
when practicing the four immeasurables or the four formless attainments, one should not discriminate, thinking, "I am able to cultivate the four immeasurables or the four formless attainments."
When practicing the eight liberations, one should not discriminate, thinking, "I am able to cultivate the eight liberations.

When practicing the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, or the ten totalities, one should not discriminate, thinking, "I am able to cultivate the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, or the ten totalities."
When practicing the four foundations of mindfulness, one should not discriminate, thinking, "I am able to cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness.

When practicing the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, or the eightfold noble path, one should not discriminate, thinking, "I am able to cultivate the four right efforts" up to "the eightfold noble path."
When practicing the gate of liberation of emptiness, one should not discriminate, thinking, "I am able to cultivate the gate of liberation of emptiness";
when practicing the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness, one should not discriminate, thinking, "I am able to cultivate the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness."
When practicing the ten stages of a bodhisattva, one should not discriminate, thinking, "I am able to cultivate the ten stages of a bodhisattva";
when practicing the five eyes, one should not discriminate, thinking, "I am able to cultivate the five eyes";
and when practicing the six supernormal powers, one should not discriminate, thinking, "I am able to cultivate the six supernormal powers."
When practicing the ten powers of a Buddha, one should not discriminate, thinking, "I am able to cultivate the ten powers of a Buddha.

When practicing the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, one should not discriminate, thinking, "I am able to cultivate the four fearlessnesses up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha."
When practicing the quality of non-forgetfulness, one should not discriminate, thinking, "I am able to cultivate non-forgetfulness";
when practicing the state of constant equanimity, one should not discriminate, thinking, "I am able to cultivate constant equanimity."
When practicing for the sake of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), one should not discriminate, thinking, "I am able to cultivate all-knowledge";

when practicing for the sake of the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*) and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), one should not discriminate, thinking, "I am able to cultivate the knowledge of the paths and the knowledge of all aspects."
When practicing all the gateways of dhāraṇī, one should not discriminate, thinking, "I am able to cultivate all the gateways of dhāraṇī";
when practicing all the gateways of samādhi, one should not discriminate, thinking, "I am able to cultivate all the gateways of samādhi."
When practicing the dharmas that resemble the fruit of stream-entry, one should not discriminate, thinking, "I am able to cultivate the dharmas resembling the fruit of stream-entry";

when practicing the dharmas that resemble the fruits of once-returning, non-returning, or arhatship, one should not discriminate, thinking, "I am able to cultivate the dharmas resembling the fruits of once-returning, non-returning, or arhatship."
When practicing the dharmas that resemble the awakening of a pratyekabuddha, one should not discriminate, thinking, "I am able to cultivate the dharmas resembling the awakening of a pratyekabuddha.
When practicing all the practices of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, one should not discriminate, thinking, "I am able to cultivate all the practices of a bodhisattva mahāsattva."

When practicing for the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas, one should not discriminate, thinking, "I am able to cultivate the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas. Kausika!

All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should thus demonstrate, instruct, exhort, and gladden other sentient beings regarding unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva can thus demonstrate, instruct, exhort, and gladden other sentient beings regarding unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they will neither harm themselves nor harm others, for they are demonstrating, instructing, exhorting, and gladdening sentient beings in accordance with what is permitted by all the Tathāgatas.

“Kauśika! If sons and daughters of good family who abide in the Bodhisattva vehicle can thus manifest, instruct, exhort, encourage, and gladden sentient beings who are proceeding toward the Bodhisattva vehicle, they will be able to remain far removed from all conceptual attachments.”
At that time, the Blessed One praised the Venerable Subhūti, saying:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
It is as you have said.
Subhūti, you have now skillfully explained the characteristics of attachment for the sake of all bodhisattvas. Subhūti!
"Furthermore, there are other subtle points of attachment that I shall explain to you; you should listen attentively and reflect upon them most thoroughly.
Subhūti replied, "So be it!"
"Please speak!
We wish to hear it.
The Buddha said:

“Subhūti! If sons of good family or daughters of good family who have set out upon the bodhisattva vehicle and wish to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment should apprehend signs and dwell upon the recollection of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, all such acts are attachments.

If they should apprehend signs and dwell upon the recollection of the unattached merits of all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the past, future, and present—from their first production of the thought of enlightenment until the endurance of the Dharma—and having so recollected them, dedicate them toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, all such apprehension of signs and dwelling upon recollection is termed attachment.”

If one takes up signs, recollects, and dedicates the wholesome dharmas cultivated toward all disciples of the Tathāgatas and other sentient beings toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment—all such acts are likewise called attachment.

Why is this? Because one should not recollect the unattached merits and roots of virtue of all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas by grasping at signs; nor should one recollect the wholesome dharmas of the Buddha’s disciples and other sentient beings by grasping at signs, for all who grasp at signs are deluded.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This Prajñāpāramitā is most profound.”
The Buddha said: "It is so!
Because all dharmas are by their very nature detached."
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
This Prajñāpāramitā should be paid homage in this way."
The Buddha said: "It is so!
Because its merit is vast, yet this Prajñāpāramitā is without creation or fabrication, and there is no one who can awaken to it."
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The nature of all dharmas is difficult to awaken to.”
The Buddha said: "It is so!
Because all dharmas are of a single nature and not two."

“Subhūti! You should know that the single nature of all phenomena is itself the absence of nature; the absence of nature in all phenomena is itself their single nature. Thus, these phenomena—being of a single nature and devoid of nature—are without creation and without action. If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can truly know that all phenomena are of a single nature and devoid of nature, and are without creation or action, they will be able to remain far removed from all attachments.”
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
this Prajñāpāramitā is difficult to realize.”
The Buddha said: "It is so!
Because this prajñāpāramitā is devoid of the characteristics of realization, there is no one who can see it, no one who can hear it, no one who can perceive it, and no one who can know it."
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
This Prajñāpāramitā is inconceivable."
The Buddha said: “So it is! Why is this? Because...”
Thus, this perfection of wisdom cannot be known by means of the mind, because it is free from the characteristics of the mind.
Thus, this perfection of wisdom cannot be known by means of form, because it is free from the characteristics of form;
it cannot be known by means of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, because it is free from the characteristics of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
In this way, the perfection of wisdom cannot be known by means of the sense-base of the eye, because it is devoid of the characteristics of the sense-base of the eye;
nor can it be known by means of the sense-bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind, because it is devoid of the characteristics of the sense-bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
In this way, the perfection of wisdom cannot be known through the sense-base of form, because it is free from the characteristics of the sense-base of form;

it cannot be known through the sense-bases of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, or mental phenomena, because it is free from the characteristics of the sense-bases of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena.
Thus, this *prajñāpāramitā* cannot be known by means of the eye-element (*cakṣurdhātu*), because it is free from the characteristics of the eye-element;

nor can it be known by means of the form-element (*rūpadhātu*), the eye-consciousness-element (*cakṣurvijñānadhātu*), eye-contact (*cakṣuḥsaṃsparśa*), or the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition (*cakṣuḥsaṃsparśapratyayaja-vedanā*), because it is free from the characteristics of the form-element up to the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition.
In this way, the perfection of wisdom cannot be known by means of the ear-element, because it is free from the characteristics of the ear-element;

nor can it be known by means of the sound-element, the ear-consciousness-element, ear-contact, or the various feelings produced with ear-contact as a condition, because it is free from the characteristics of the sound-element up to the various feelings produced with ear-contact as a condition.
Thus, this perfection of wisdom cannot be known by means of the nose-element, because it is free from the characteristics of the nose-element;

nor can it be known by means of the odor-element, the nose-consciousness-element, nose-contact, or the various feelings produced with nose-contact as a condition, because it is free from the characteristics of the odor-element up to the various feelings produced with nose-contact as a condition.
In this way, the perfection of wisdom cannot be known by means of the tongue-element, because it is devoid of the characteristics of the tongue-element;

nor can it be known by means of the taste-element, the tongue-consciousness-element, tongue-contact, or the various sensations produced with tongue-contact as a condition, because it is devoid of the characteristics of the taste-element up to and including the various sensations produced with tongue-contact as a condition.
In this way, the perfection of wisdom cannot be known by means of the body-element (*kāyadhātu*), because it is free from the characteristics of the body-element;

nor can it be known by means of the touch-element (*spraṣṭavyadhātu*), the body-consciousness-element (*kāyavijñānadhātu*), body-contact (*kāyasparśa*), or the various feelings (*vedanā*) produced with body-contact as a condition, because it is free from the characteristics of the touch-element up to the various feelings produced with body-contact as a condition.
In this way, the perfection of wisdom cannot be known by means of the mental faculty element (*manodhātu*), because it is free from the characteristics of the mental faculty element;

nor can it be known by means of the phenomena element (*dharmadhātu*), the mental consciousness element (*manovijñānadhātu*), mental contact (*manaḥsaṃsparśa*), or the various feelings (*vedanā*) produced with mental contact as a condition, because it is free from the characteristics of the phenomena element up to the various feelings produced with mental contact as a condition.
In this way, the perfection of wisdom cannot be known through the earth element, because it is free from the characteristics of the earth element;
it cannot be known through the water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness elements, because it is free from the characteristics of the water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness elements.
Thus, this perfection of wisdom cannot be known through ignorance, because it is free from the characteristics of ignorance;

nor can it be known through volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, or old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair, because it is free from the characteristics of volitional formations up to old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair.
Thus, this perfection of wisdom cannot be known by means of the perfection of generosity, because it is devoid of the characteristics of the perfection of generosity;

nor can it be known by means of the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, or wisdom, because it is devoid of the characteristics of the perfections from ethical discipline up to wisdom.
In this way, the perfection of wisdom cannot be known through internal emptiness, because it is devoid of the characteristics of internal emptiness;

nor can it be known through external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, endless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, non-alteration emptiness, essential nature emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common characteristic emptiness, the emptiness of all dharmas, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, or the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature, because it is devoid of the characteristics of external emptiness up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature.
Thus, this *prajñāpāramitā* cannot be known by means of *tathatā*, because it is free from the characteristics of *tathatā*;

nor can it be known by means of the *dharmadhātu*, *dharmatā*, the nature of non-falsity, the nature of immutability, equality, the nature of freedom from arising, the fixedness of phenomena, the stability of phenomena, the limit of reality, the realm of space, or the inconceivable realm, because it is free from the characteristics of the *dharmadhātu* up to the inconceivable realm.
Thus, this perfection of wisdom cannot be known through the noble truth of suffering, because it is free from the characteristics of the noble truth of suffering;
nor can it be known through the noble truths of origination, cessation, or the path, because it is free from the characteristics of the noble truths of origination, cessation, or the path.
In this way, the perfection of wisdom cannot be known by means of the four dhyānas, because it is free from the characteristics of the four dhyānas;
nor can it be known by means of the four immeasurables or the four formless attainments, because it is free from the characteristics of the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments.
Thus, this perfection of wisdom cannot be known by means of the eight liberations, because it is free from the characteristics of the eight liberations;

nor can it be known by means of the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative attainments, or the ten totalities, because it is free from the characteristics of the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative attainments, and the ten totalities.
In this way, the perfection of wisdom cannot be known by means of the four foundations of mindfulness, because it is free from the characteristics of the four foundations of mindfulness;

nor can it be known by means of the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, or the eightfold noble path, because it is free from the characteristics of the four right efforts up to and including the eightfold noble path.
Thus, this perfection of wisdom cannot be known through the gate of liberation of emptiness, because it is free from the characteristics of the gate of liberation of emptiness;
nor can it be known through the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness, because it is free from the characteristics of the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness.
In this way, the perfection of wisdom cannot be known by means of the ten stages of a bodhisattva, because it is free from the characteristics of the ten stages of a bodhisattva.
In this way, the perfection of wisdom cannot be known by means of the five eyes, because it is free from the characteristics of the five eyes;
nor can it be known by means of the six supernormal powers, because it is free from the characteristics of the six supernormal powers.
In this way, the perfection of wisdom cannot be known by means of the ten powers of a Buddha, because it is free from the characteristics of the ten powers of a Buddha;

nor can it be known by means of the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great joy, great equanimity, or the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, because it is free from the characteristics of the four fearlessnesses up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
In this way, the perfection of wisdom cannot be known by means of the quality of non-forgetfulness, because it is devoid of the characteristics of non-forgetfulness;
nor can it be known by means of the state of constant equanimity, because it is devoid of the characteristics of constant equanimity.
Thus, this perfection of wisdom cannot be known by means of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), because it is free from the characteristics of all-knowledge;

nor can it be known by means of the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*) or the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), because it is free from the characteristics of the knowledge of the paths and the knowledge of all aspects.
Thus, this prajñāpāramitā cannot be known by means of any of the dhāraṇī-doors, because it is free from the characteristics of all dhāraṇī-doors;
nor can it be known by means of any of the samādhi-doors, because it is free from the characteristics of all samādhi-doors.
Thus, this perfection of wisdom cannot be known by means of the fruit of stream-entry, because it is devoid of the characteristics of the fruit of stream-entry;
it cannot be known by means of the fruits of once-returner, non-returner, or arhatship, because it is devoid of the characteristics of the fruits of once-returner, non-returner, or arhatship.
In this way, the perfection of wisdom cannot be known by means of the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, because it is free from the characteristics of the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha.

In this way, the perfection of wisdom cannot be known by means of the practices of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, because it is free from the characteristics of the practices of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.

In this way, the perfection of wisdom cannot be known by means of the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas, because it is devoid of the characteristics of the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
this Prajñāpāramitā is without any conditioned activity.”
The Buddha said: “It is so! For all agents are unattainable.”
“Subhūti! Because form cannot be apprehended, an agent cannot be apprehended; because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness cannot be apprehended, an agent cannot be apprehended.”

“Subhūti! Because the sense-base of the eye is unapprehendable, the agent is unapprehendable; because the sense-bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are unapprehendable, the agent is unapprehendable.”

“Subhūti! Because the sphere of form (rūpāyatana) is unapprehendable, an agent is unapprehendable; because the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena (dharmāyatana) are unapprehendable, an agent is unapprehendable.”

“Subhūti! Because the eye-element is unapprehendable, an agent is unapprehendable; because the form-element, the eye-consciousness-element, and eye-contact, as well as all feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition, are unapprehendable, an agent is unapprehendable.”

“Subhūti! Because the ear-element is unapprehendable, the agent is unapprehendable. Because the sound-element, the ear-consciousness-element, ear-contact, and all feelings produced with ear-contact as a condition are unapprehendable, the agent is unapprehendable.”

"Subhūti! Because the nose-element (*ghrāṇadhātu*) is unapprehendable, an agent is unapprehendable. Because the odor-element (*gandhadhātu*), the nose-consciousness-element (*ghrāṇavijñānadhātu*), nose-contact (*ghrāṇasamsparśa*), and all feelings produced with nose-contact as a condition are unapprehendable, an agent is unapprehendable."

“Subhūti! Because the tongue element is unapprehendable, the agent is unapprehendable; because the taste element, the tongue-consciousness element, tongue-contact, and all feelings produced with tongue-contact as a condition are unapprehendable, the agent is unapprehendable.”

"Subhūti! Because the body-element (*kāyadhātu*) is unapprehendable, the agent is unapprehendable; because the touch-element (*spraṣṭavyadhātu*), the body-consciousness-element (*kāyavijñānadhātu*), body-contact (*kāyasparśa*), and all feelings produced with body-contact as a condition are unapprehendable, the agent is unapprehendable."

"Subhūti! Because the mind-element (*manodhātu*) cannot be apprehended, an agent cannot be apprehended; because the dharma-element, the mind-consciousness-element (*manovijñānadhātu*), as well as mind-contact (*manaḥsaṃsparśa*) and the various feelings produced with mind-contact as a condition cannot be apprehended, an agent cannot be apprehended."

“Subhūti! Because the earth element cannot be apprehended, an agent cannot be apprehended; because the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements cannot be apprehended, an agent cannot be apprehended.”

"Subhūti! Because ignorance cannot be apprehended, an agent cannot be apprehended; because formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, existence, birth, and old age, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair cannot be apprehended, an agent cannot be apprehended."

“Subhūti! Because the perfection of generosity cannot be apprehended, an agent cannot be apprehended; because the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom cannot be apprehended, an agent cannot be apprehended.”

“Subhūti! Because internal emptiness is unapprehendable, an agent is unapprehendable; because external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, the emptiness of the ultimate, the emptiness of the conditioned, the emptiness of the unconditioned, absolute emptiness, the emptiness of the limitless, the emptiness of dispersion, the emptiness of non-alteration, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, the emptiness of self-characteristic, the emptiness of common characteristic, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence are unapprehendable, an agent is unapprehendable.”

“Subhūti! Because true suchness (tathatā) cannot be apprehended, an agent cannot be apprehended. Because the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), the dharma-nature (dharmatā), non-illusory nature, non-alteration, equality, the nature of being free from birth, the fixedness of dharmas (dharmaniyāmatā), the stability of dharmas (dharmasthititā), the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi), the realm of space (ākāśadhātu), and the inconceivable realm (acintyadhātu) cannot be apprehended, an agent cannot be apprehended.”

“Subhūti! Because the four dhyānas are unapprehendable, an agent is unapprehendable; because the four immeasurables and the four formless absorptions are unapprehendable, an agent is unapprehendable.”

“Subhūti! Because the eight liberations are unapprehendable, an agent is unapprehendable; because the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities are unapprehendable, an agent is unapprehendable.”

“Subhūti! Because the four foundations of mindfulness cannot be apprehended, an agent cannot be apprehended; because the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of awakening, and the eightfold noble path cannot be apprehended, an agent cannot be apprehended.”

“Subhūti! Because the gate of liberation of emptiness cannot be apprehended, an agent cannot be apprehended; because the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness cannot be apprehended, an agent cannot be apprehended.”
“Subhūti! Because the ten stages of a bodhisattva cannot be apprehended, an agent cannot be apprehended. Subhūti!”
Because the five eyes are unapprehendable, the agent is unapprehendable; because the six supernormal powers are unapprehendable, the agent is unapprehendable. "Subhūti!

Because the ten powers of a Buddha are unapprehendable, the agent is unapprehendable; because the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are unapprehendable, the agent is unapprehendable."
“Subhūti! Because the quality of non-forgetfulness is unapprehendable, an agent is unapprehendable; because the state of constant equanimity is unapprehendable, an agent is unapprehendable.”

“Subhūti! Because omniscience (sarvajñatā) is unapprehendable, the agent is unapprehendable; because the knowledge of the paths (mārgākārajñatā) and the knowledge of all aspects (sarvākārajñatā) are unapprehendable, the agent is unapprehendable.”
"Subhūti! Because all dharanī-doors are unapprehendable, an agent is unapprehendable; because all samādhi-doors are unapprehendable, an agent is unapprehendable."

“Subhūti! Because the fruit of stream-entry cannot be apprehended, an agent cannot be apprehended; because the fruits of once-returning, non-returning, and arhatship cannot be apprehended, an agent cannot be apprehended.”
“Subhūti! Because solitary awakening (pratyekabodhi) cannot be apprehended, an agent cannot be apprehended. Subhūti!”
Because all the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are unapprehendable, the agent is unapprehendable. "Subhūti!
Because the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas is unapprehendable, the agent is unapprehendable."
“Subhūti! Because an agent and phenomena such as form cannot be apprehended, this perfection of wisdom is without any purposeful activity.”

The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle 288. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Part One: Chapter Thirty-Six, Part Three, "The Characteristics of Attachment and Non-attachment. The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
“How should a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice the perfection of wisdom?
The Buddha said,
“Suvikrāntavikrāmin!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, if they do not practice by way of form, that is practicing the perfection of wisdom; if they do not practice by way of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, that is practicing the perfection of wisdom.

If they do not practice by way of form being permanent or impermanent, that is practicing the perfection of wisdom; if they do not practice by way of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness being permanent or impermanent, that is practicing the perfection of wisdom.

If they do not practice by way of form being pleasant or painful, that is practicing the perfection of wisdom; if they do not practice by way of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness being pleasant or painful, that is practicing the perfection of wisdom.

Not practicing with regard to form as being either self or non-self is practicing the perfection of wisdom; not practicing with regard to feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as being either self or non-self is practicing the perfection of wisdom.

Not practicing with regard to form as being either pure or impure is practicing the perfection of wisdom; not practicing with regard to feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as being either pure or impure is practicing the perfection of wisdom.
Why is this? Subhūti!
Since even the intrinsic nature of form does not exist, how much less can there be form that is either permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, pure or impure!

Since the very nature of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness does not exist at all, how much less could there be feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness that are either permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, pure or impure!

“Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, if they do not practice by way of the sense-base of the eye, they are practicing the perfection of wisdom; if they do not practice by way of the sense-bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind, they are practicing the perfection of wisdom.

If they do not practice by way of the sense-base of the eye as being either permanent or impermanent, they are practicing the perfection of wisdom; if they do not practice by way of the sense-bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as being either permanent or impermanent, they are practicing the perfection of wisdom.”

Not practicing with regard to whether the eye-base is pleasant or painful is practicing the perfection of wisdom; not practicing with regard to whether the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind-base is pleasant or painful is practicing the perfection of wisdom.

Not practicing with regard to whether the eye-base is self or non-self is practicing the perfection of wisdom; not practicing with regard to whether the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind-base is self or non-self is practicing the perfection of wisdom.

Not practicing with regard to whether the eye-base is pure or impure is practicing the perfection of wisdom; not practicing with regard to whether the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind-base is pure or impure is practicing the perfection of wisdom.
Why is this? Subhūti!

Since the intrinsic nature of the eye-base does not exist at all, how much less could there be an eye-base that is either permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, pure or impure!

Since the intrinsic nature of the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind does not even exist, how could there be an ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind that is either permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, pure or impure?

“Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, if they do not practice by way of the sphere of form, they are practicing the perfection of wisdom; if they do not practice by way of the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, or mental phenomena, they are practicing the perfection of wisdom.

If they do not practice by way of the sphere of form as being permanent or impermanent, they are practicing the perfection of wisdom; if they do not practice by way of the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, or mental phenomena as being permanent or impermanent, they are practicing the perfection of wisdom.”

Not practicing with regard to the sphere of form as being either pleasant or painful is practicing the perfection of wisdom; not practicing with regard to the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, or mental phenomena as being either pleasant or painful is practicing the perfection of wisdom.

Not practicing with regard to the sphere of form as being either self or non-self is practicing the perfection of wisdom; not practicing with regard to the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, or mental phenomena as being either self or non-self is practicing the perfection of wisdom.

Not practicing with regard to the sphere of form as being either pure or impure is practicing the perfection of wisdom; not practicing with regard to the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, or mental phenomena as being either pure or impure is practicing the perfection of wisdom.
Why is this? Subhūti!

Since the intrinsic nature of the sense-sphere of form does not even exist, how much less could there be a sense-sphere of form that is either permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, pure or impure?

Since the intrinsic nature of the bases of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena does not even exist, how could there be sound, odor, taste, tangibility, or mental phenomena that are either permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, pure or impure?

“Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, if they do not practice by way of the eye-element, they are practicing the perfection of wisdom; if they do not practice by way of the form-element, the eye-consciousness-element, eye-contact, or the various feelings produced with eye-contact as condition, they are practicing the perfection of wisdom;

if they do not practice by way of the eye-element being either permanent or impermanent, they are practicing the perfection of wisdom; and if they do not practice by way of the form-element, up to the various feelings produced with eye-contact as condition, being either permanent or impermanent, they are practicing the perfection of wisdom.”

Not practicing with the notion that the eye-element is either pleasant or painful is practicing the perfection of wisdom; not practicing with the notion that the form-element, up to and including those feelings produced with eye-contact as condition, are either pleasant or painful is practicing the perfection of wisdom.

Not practicing with the notion that the eye-element is either self or non-self is practicing the perfection of wisdom; not practicing with the notion that the form-element, up to and including those feelings produced with eye-contact as condition, are either self or non-self is practicing the perfection of wisdom.

Not practicing with the notion that the eye-element is either pure or impure is practicing the perfection of wisdom; not practicing with the notion that the form-element, up to and including those feelings produced with eye-contact as condition, are either pure or impure is practicing the perfection of wisdom.
Why is this? Subhūti!
Since the nature of the eye-element does not even exist, how could there be an eye-element that is either permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, pure or impure?

Since even the nature of the form realm, up to and including the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition, does not exist, how much less could there be anything in the form realm, up to and including the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition, that is either permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, pure or impure!

“Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, if they do not practice by way of the ear element, they are practicing the perfection of wisdom; if they do not practice by way of the sound element, the ear-consciousness element, ear-contact, or the various feelings produced with ear-contact as a condition, they are practicing the perfection of wisdom;

if they do not practice by way of the ear element being either permanent or impermanent, they are practicing the perfection of wisdom; if they do not practice by way of the sound element, up to the various feelings produced with ear-contact as a condition, being either permanent or impermanent, they are practicing the perfection of wisdom.”

Not practicing with the notion that the ear-element is either pleasant or painful is practicing the perfection of wisdom; not practicing with the notion that the sound-element, up to and including the various feelings produced with ear-contact as a condition, are either pleasant or painful is practicing the perfection of wisdom.

Not practicing with the notion that the ear-element is either self or non-self is practicing the perfection of wisdom; not practicing with the notion that the sound-element, up to and including the various feelings produced with ear-contact as a condition, are either self or non-self is practicing the perfection of wisdom.

Not practicing with the notion that the ear-element is either pure or impure is practicing the perfection of wisdom; not practicing with the notion that the sound-element, up to and including the various feelings produced with ear-contact as a condition, are either pure or impure is practicing the perfection of wisdom.
Why is this? Subhūti!
Since the very nature of the ear-element does not exist, how much less could there be an ear-element that is either permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, pure or impure!

Since even the nature of the sphere of sound, up to and including the various feelings produced with ear-contact as a condition, does not exist, how much less could there be anything—whether the sphere of sound up to the various feelings produced with ear-contact as a condition—that is permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, pure or impure!

“Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, if they do not practice by way of the nose element, they are practicing the perfection of wisdom; if they do not practice by way of the odor element, the nose-consciousness element, nose-contact, or the various feelings produced with nose-contact as a condition, they are practicing the perfection of wisdom;

if they do not practice by way of the nose element being either permanent or impermanent, they are practicing the perfection of wisdom; if they do not practice by way of the odor element, up to and including the various feelings produced with nose-contact as a condition, being either permanent or impermanent, they are practicing the perfection of wisdom.”

Not practicing with regard to the nose-element as being either pleasant or painful is practicing the perfection of wisdom; not practicing with regard to the odor-element, up to and including the various feelings produced with nose-contact as condition, as being either pleasant or painful is practicing the perfection of wisdom.

Not practicing with regard to the nose-element as being either self or non-self is practicing the perfection of wisdom; not practicing with regard to the odor-element, up to and including the various feelings produced with nose-contact as condition, as being either self or non-self is practicing the perfection of wisdom.

Not practicing with regard to the nose-element as being either pure or impure is practicing the perfection of wisdom; not practicing with regard to the odor-element, up to and including the various feelings produced with nose-contact as condition, as being either pure or impure is practicing the perfection of wisdom.
Why is this? Subhūti!
Since the very nature of the nose-element does not exist, how much less could there be a nose-element that is either permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, pure or impure!

Since even the nature of the fragrance element, up to and including the various feelings produced with nose-contact as a condition, does not exist, how much less could there be anything—whether permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, pure or impure—within the fragrance element, up to and including the various feelings produced with nose-contact as a condition!

“Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, if they do not practice by way of the tongue element, that is practicing the perfection of wisdom; if they do not practice by way of the taste element, the tongue-consciousness element, tongue-contact, or the various feelings produced with tongue-contact as a condition, that is practicing the perfection of wisdom;

if they do not practice by way of the tongue element being either permanent or impermanent, that is practicing the perfection of wisdom; and if they do not practice by way of the taste element, up to the various feelings produced with tongue-contact as a condition, being either permanent or impermanent, that is practicing the perfection of wisdom.”

To not practice with the notion that the tongue-element is pleasant or painful is to practice the perfection of wisdom; to not practice with the notion that the taste-element, up to and including the feelings produced with tongue-contact as condition, are pleasant or painful is to practice the perfection of wisdom.

To not practice with the notion that the tongue-element is self or non-self is to practice the perfection of wisdom; to not practice with the notion that the taste-element, up to and including the feelings produced with tongue-contact as condition, are self or non-self is to practice the perfection of wisdom.

To not practice with the notion that the tongue-element is pure or impure is to practice the perfection of wisdom; to not practice with the notion that the taste-element, up to and including the feelings produced with tongue-contact as condition, are pure or impure is to practice the perfection of wisdom.
Why is that? Subhūti!

Since the intrinsic nature of the tongue-element does not even exist, how could there be a tongue-element that is either permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, pure or impure?

Since the nature of the taste element, up to and including the various feelings produced with tongue-contact as a condition, does not even exist, how much less could there be anything—whether permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, pure or impure—within the taste element, up to and including the various feelings produced with tongue-contact as a condition!

“Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, if they do not practice by way of the body-element, they are practicing the perfection of wisdom; if they do not practice by way of the contact-element, the body-consciousness-element, body-contact, or the various feelings produced with body-contact as a condition, they are practicing the perfection of wisdom.

If they do not practice by way of whether the body-element is permanent or impermanent, they are practicing the perfection of wisdom; if they do not practice by way of whether the contact-element, up to and including the various feelings produced with body-contact as a condition, are permanent or impermanent, they are practicing the perfection of wisdom.”

Not practicing with the thought that the body-element is either pleasant or painful is practicing the perfection of wisdom; not practicing with the thought that the object-contact-element, up to and including the various feelings produced with body-contact as a condition, are either pleasant or painful is practicing the perfection of wisdom.

Not practicing with the thought that the body-element is either self or non-self is practicing the perfection of wisdom; not practicing with the thought that the object-contact-element, up to and including the various feelings produced with body-contact as a condition, are either self or non-self is practicing the perfection of wisdom.

Not practicing with the thought that the body-element is either pure or impure is practicing the perfection of wisdom; not practicing with the thought that the object-contact-element, up to and including the various feelings produced with body-contact as a condition, are either pure or impure is practicing the perfection of wisdom.
Why is this? Subhūti!
Since the very nature of the body-element does not exist, how could there be a body-element that is either permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, pure or impure?

Since even the nature of the feeling produced with the tangible element as condition, up to the body-contact as condition, does not exist at all, how much less could there be such a thing as the feeling produced with the tangible element as condition, up to the body-contact as condition, that is either permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, pure or impure!

“Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, if they do not practice by way of the mind-element, they are practicing the perfection of wisdom; if they do not practice by way of the dharma-element, the mind-consciousness-element, or mental contact and the various feelings produced with mental contact as a condition, they are practicing the perfection of wisdom.

If they do not practice by way of whether the mind-element is permanent or impermanent, they are practicing the perfection of wisdom; if they do not practice by way of whether the dharma-element, up to and including the various feelings produced with mental contact as a condition, is permanent or impermanent, they are practicing the perfection of wisdom.”

Not practicing whether the mind-element (*manodhātu*) is pleasant or painful is practicing the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*); not practicing whether the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*), up to and including the various sensations produced with mind-contact as condition, are pleasant or painful is practicing the perfection of wisdom.

Not practicing whether the mind-element is self or non-self is practicing the perfection of wisdom; not practicing whether the dharma-element, up to and including the various sensations produced with mind-contact as condition, are self or non-self is practicing the perfection of wisdom.

Not practicing whether the mind-element is pure or impure is practicing the perfection of wisdom; not practicing whether the dharma-element, up to and including the various sensations produced with mind-contact as condition, are pure or impure is practicing the perfection of wisdom.
Why is this? Subhūti!
Since the very nature of the mind-element does not exist, how could there be a mind-element that is either permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, pure or impure?

Since even the nature of the dharma-realm, up to and including all feelings produced with mental contact as a condition, does not exist, how much less could there be a dharma-realm, up to and including all feelings produced with mental contact as a condition, that is either permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, pure or impure!

“Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, if they do not practice the earth element, that is practicing the perfection of wisdom; if they do not practice the water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness elements, that is practicing the perfection of wisdom.

If they do not practice the earth element as permanent or impermanent, that is practicing the perfection of wisdom; if they do not practice the water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness elements as permanent or impermanent, that is practicing the perfection of wisdom.”

Not practicing with regard to the earth element as being either pleasant or painful is practicing the perfection of wisdom; not practicing with regard to the water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness elements as being either pleasant or painful is practicing the perfection of wisdom.

Not practicing with regard to the earth element as being either self or non-self is practicing the perfection of wisdom; not practicing with regard to the water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness elements as being either self or non-self is practicing the perfection of wisdom.

Not practicing with regard to the earth element as being either pure or impure is practicing the perfection of wisdom; not practicing with regard to the water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness elements as being either pure or impure is practicing the perfection of wisdom.
Why is this? Subhūti!

Since the intrinsic nature of the earth element does not exist at all, how much less could there be a earth element that is either permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, pure or impure!

Since the intrinsic nature of the elements of water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness does not even exist, how much less could there be anything regarding these elements of water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness that is either permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, pure or impure!

"Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, if they do not practice [the notion that] ignorance is practicing the perfection of wisdom; if they do not practice [the notions that] volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, or old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are practicing the perfection of wisdom;

if they do not practice [the notion that] ignorance is either permanent or impermanent as practicing the perfection of wisdom; and if they do not practice [the notion that] volitional formations up to old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are either permanent or impermanent as practicing the perfection of wisdom—[then they are indeed practicing the perfection of wisdom]."

Not practicing with regard to whether ignorance is pleasant or painful is practicing the perfection of wisdom; not practicing with regard to whether the formative forces up to old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair are pleasant or painful is practicing the perfection of wisdom;

not practicing with regard to whether ignorance is self or non-self is practicing the perfection of wisdom; not practicing with regard to whether the formative forces up to old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair are self or non-self is practicing the perfection of wisdom;

not practicing with regard to whether ignorance is pure or impure is practicing the perfection of wisdom; not practicing with regard to whether the formative forces up to old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair are pure or impure is practicing the perfection of wisdom.
Why is this? Subhūti!
Since even the nature of ignorance does not exist, how much less could there be an ignorance that is either permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, pure or impure!

Since even the nature of volitional formations up to old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair does not exist, how much less could there be volitional formations up to old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair that are either permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, pure or impure!

“Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, if they do not practice the perfection of generosity, this is practicing the perfection of wisdom; if they do not practice the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, or wisdom, this is practicing the perfection of wisdom.

If they do not practice the perfection of generosity as either permanent or impermanent, this is practicing the perfection of wisdom; if they do not practice the perfections from ethical discipline up to wisdom as either permanent or impermanent, this is practicing the perfection of wisdom.”

Not practicing the perfection of generosity as either pleasant or painful is practicing the perfection of wisdom; not practicing the perfections from ethical discipline up to wisdom as either pleasant or painful is practicing the perfection of wisdom.

Not practicing the perfection of generosity as either self or non-self is practicing the perfection of wisdom; not practicing the perfections from ethical discipline up to wisdom as either self or non-self is practicing the perfection of wisdom.

Not practicing the perfection of generosity as either pure or impure is practicing the perfection of wisdom; not practicing the perfections from ethical discipline up to wisdom as either pure or impure is practicing the perfection of wisdom.
Why is this? Subhūti!

Since even the intrinsic nature of the perfection of giving does not exist, how much less could there be a perfection of giving that is either permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, pure or impure!

Since even the nature of the perfection of ethical discipline up to the perfection of wisdom does not exist, how much less could there be a perfection of ethical discipline up to the perfection of wisdom that is either permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, pure or impure!

“Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, if they do not practice inner emptiness, that is practicing the perfection of wisdom; if they do not practice outer emptiness, inner-and-outer emptiness, emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, endless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, non-altering emptiness, essential emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common-characteristic emptiness, emptiness of all phenomena, emptiness of the unapprehendable, emptiness of non-existence, emptiness of intrinsic nature, or emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature, that is practicing the perfection of wisdom.”

Not practicing that inner emptiness is either permanent or impermanent is practicing the perfection of wisdom; not practicing that outer emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of the essential nature of non-entities, is either permanent or impermanent is practicing the perfection of wisdom;

not practicing that inner emptiness is either pleasant or painful is practicing the perfection of wisdom; not practicing that outer emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of the essential nature of non-entities, is either pleasant or painful is practicing the perfection of wisdom;

not practicing that inner emptiness is either self or non-self is practicing the perfection of wisdom; not practicing that outer emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of the essential nature of non-entities, is either self or non-self is practicing the perfection of wisdom.

Not practicing inner emptiness as either pure or impure is practicing the perfection of wisdom; not practicing outer emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of non-existence and self-nature, as either pure or impure is practicing the perfection of wisdom.
Why is this? Subhūti!

Even the nature of internal emptiness does not exist; how much less could there be an internal emptiness that is either permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, pure or impure!

Since even the emptiness of the external up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature do not exist at all, how much less could there be an emptiness of the external up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature that is either permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, or pure or impure!

"Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, if they do not practice by way of practicing suchness, they are practicing the perfection of wisdom; if they do not practice by way of practicing the dharma-realm, the dharma-nature, non-falsity, non-alteration, equality, the nature of being free from birth, the fixedness of dharmas, the stability of dharmas, the limit of reality, the realm of space, or the inconceivable realm, they are practicing the perfection of wisdom;

if they do not practice by way of whether suchness is permanent or impermanent, they are practicing the perfection of wisdom; if they do not practice by way of whether the dharma-realm, up to and including the inconceivable realm, is permanent or impermanent, they are practicing the perfection of wisdom."

Not practicing whether true suchness is pleasant or painful is practicing the perfection of wisdom; not practicing whether the dharma-realm, up to the inconceivable realm, is pleasant or painful is practicing the perfection of wisdom.

Not practicing whether true suchness is self or non-self is practicing the perfection of wisdom; not practicing whether the dharma-realm, up to the inconceivable realm, is self or non-self is practicing the perfection of wisdom.

Not practicing whether true suchness is pure or impure is practicing the perfection of wisdom; not practicing whether the dharma-realm, up to the inconceivable realm, is pure or impure is practicing the perfection of wisdom.
Why is this? Subhūti!
Since even the nature of suchness does not exist, how much less could there be a suchness that is either permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, pure or impure!

Since even the nature of the dharma-realm up to the inconceivable realm does not exist, how much less could there be a dharma-realm up to an inconceivable realm that is either permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, pure or impure!

“Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, if they do not practice the noble truth of suffering, that is practicing the perfection of wisdom; if they do not practice the noble truths of origin, cessation, or the path, that is practicing the perfection of wisdom.

If they do not practice the noble truth of suffering as either permanent or impermanent, that is practicing the perfection of wisdom; if they do not practice the noble truths of origin, cessation, or the path as either permanent or impermanent, that is practicing the perfection of wisdom.”

Not practicing the noble truth of suffering as either pleasant or painful is practicing the perfection of wisdom; not practicing the noble truths of origin, cessation, and the path as either pleasant or painful is practicing the perfection of wisdom.

Not practicing the noble truth of suffering as either self or non-self is practicing the perfection of wisdom; not practicing the noble truths of origin, cessation, and the path as either self or non-self is practicing the perfection of wisdom.

Not practicing the noble truth of suffering as either pure or impure is practicing the perfection of wisdom; not practicing the noble truths of origin, cessation, and the path as either pure or impure is practicing the perfection of wisdom.
Why is this? Subhūti!

Since even the intrinsic nature of the noble truth of suffering does not exist, how much less could there be a noble truth of suffering that is either permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, pure or impure!

Since even the intrinsic nature of the noble truths of suffering, origination, cessation, and the path does not exist, how much less could there be any noble truth of origination, cessation, or the path that is either permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, pure or impure!

“Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, if they do not practice the four dhyānas, that is practicing the perfection of wisdom; if they do not practice the four immeasurables or the four formless attainments, that is practicing the perfection of wisdom;

if they do not practice the four dhyānas as either permanent or impermanent, that is practicing the perfection of wisdom; if they do not practice the four immeasurables or the four formless attainments as either permanent or impermanent, that is practicing the perfection of wisdom.”

Not practicing the four dhyānas as either pleasant or painful is practicing the perfection of wisdom; not practicing the four immeasurables or the four formless attainments as either pleasant or painful is practicing the perfection of wisdom.

Not practicing the four dhyānas as either self or non-self is practicing the perfection of wisdom; not practicing the four immeasurables or the four formless attainments as either self or non-self is practicing the perfection of wisdom.

Not practicing the four dhyānas as either pure or impure is practicing the perfection of wisdom; not practicing the four immeasurables or the four formless attainments as either pure or impure is practicing the perfection of wisdom.
Why is this? Subhūti!
Since the very nature of the four dhyānas does not exist, how much less could there be four dhyānas that are either permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, pure or impure!

Since even the four immeasurables and the four formless absorptions have no fixed nature whatsoever, how much less could the four immeasurables and the four formless absorptions be permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, pure or impure!

“Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, if they do not practice the eight liberations, that is practicing the perfection of wisdom; if they do not practice the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, or the ten totalities, that is practicing the perfection of wisdom;

if they do not practice the eight liberations as permanent or impermanent, that is practicing the perfection of wisdom; if they do not practice the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, or the ten totalities as permanent or impermanent, that is practicing the perfection of wisdom.”

Not practicing the eight liberations as either pleasant or painful is practicing the perfection of wisdom; not practicing the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, or the ten totalities as either pleasant or painful is practicing the perfection of wisdom.

Not practicing the eight liberations as either self or non-self is practicing the perfection of wisdom; not practicing the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, or the ten totalities as either self or non-self is practicing the perfection of wisdom.

Not practicing the eight liberations as either pure or impure is practicing the perfection of wisdom; not practicing the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, or the ten totalities as either pure or impure is practicing the perfection of wisdom.
Why is this? Subhūti!

Since even the nature of the eight liberations does not exist, how much less could there be eight liberations that are either permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, pure or impure!

Since even the nature of the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten universal bases does not exist, how much less could there be anything regarding the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, or the ten universal bases that is either permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, pure or impure!

“Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, if they do not practice the four foundations of mindfulness, that is practicing the perfection of wisdom; if they do not practice the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of awakening, or the eightfold noble path, that is practicing the perfection of wisdom;

if they do not practice the four foundations of mindfulness as permanent or impermanent, that is practicing the perfection of wisdom; if they do not practice the four right efforts up to the eightfold noble path as permanent or impermanent, that is practicing the perfection of wisdom.”

Not practicing the four foundations of mindfulness as either pleasant or painful is practicing the perfection of wisdom; not practicing the four right efforts, up to and including the eightfold noble path, as either pleasant or painful is practicing the perfection of wisdom.

Not practicing the four foundations of mindfulness as either self or non-self is practicing the perfection of wisdom; not practicing the four right efforts, up to and including the eightfold noble path, as either self or non-self is practicing the perfection of wisdom.

Not practicing the four foundations of mindfulness as either pure or impure is practicing the perfection of wisdom; not practicing the four right efforts, up to and including the eightfold noble path, as either pure or impure is practicing the perfection of wisdom.
Why is this? Subhūti!

Since the intrinsic nature of the four foundations of mindfulness does not even exist, how much less could there be four foundations of mindfulness that are either permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, pure or impure!

Since even the nature of the four right efforts up to the eightfold noble path does not exist, how much less could there be four right efforts up to the eightfold noble path that are either permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, pure or impure?

“Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, if they do not practice the liberation door of emptiness, that is practicing the perfection of wisdom; if they do not practice the liberation doors of signlessness and wishlessness, that is practicing the perfection of wisdom.

If they do not practice the liberation door of emptiness as either permanent or impermanent, that is practicing the perfection of wisdom; if they do not practice the liberation doors of signlessness and wishlessness as either permanent or impermanent, that is practicing the perfection of wisdom.”

Not practicing the gate of liberation of emptiness as either pleasant or painful is practicing the perfection of wisdom; not practicing the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness as either pleasant or painful is practicing the perfection of wisdom.

Not practicing the gate of liberation of emptiness as either self or non-self is practicing the perfection of wisdom; not practicing the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness as either self or non-self is practicing the perfection of wisdom.

Not practicing the gate of liberation of emptiness as either pure or impure is practicing the perfection of wisdom; not practicing the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness as either pure or impure is practicing the perfection of wisdom.
Why is this? Subhūti!

Since even the intrinsic nature of the gate of liberation of emptiness does not exist, how much less could there be a gate of liberation of emptiness that is either permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, pure or impure!

Since even the intrinsic nature of the gateways to liberation of signlessness and wishlessness does not exist, how could there be anything regarding the gateways to liberation of signlessness and wishlessness that is either permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, pure or impure?

“Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, if they do not practice the ten stages of a bodhisattva, this is practicing the perfection of wisdom; if they do not practice the ten stages of a bodhisattva as either permanent or impermanent, this is practicing the perfection of wisdom; if they do not practice the ten stages of a bodhisattva as either pleasant or painful, this is practicing the perfection of wisdom; if they do not practice the ten stages of a bodhisattva as either self or non-self, this is practicing the perfection of wisdom; if they do not practice the ten stages of a bodhisattva as either pure or impure, this is practicing the perfection of wisdom.”
Why is this? Subhūti!

Since even the nature of the ten stages of a bodhisattva does not exist, how much less could there be a bodhisattva’s ten stages that are either permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, pure or impure!

“Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, if they do not practice the five eyes, that is practicing the perfection of wisdom; if they do not practice the six superknowledges, that is practicing the perfection of wisdom.

If they do not practice the five eyes as permanent or impermanent, that is practicing the perfection of wisdom; if they do not practice the six superknowledges as permanent or impermanent, that is practicing the perfection of wisdom.”

Not practicing with regard to the five eyes as either pleasant or painful is practicing the perfection of wisdom; not practicing with regard to the six superknowledges as either pleasant or painful is practicing the perfection of wisdom.

Not practicing with regard to the five eyes as either self or non-self is practicing the perfection of wisdom; not practicing with regard to the six superknowledges as either self or non-self is practicing the perfection of wisdom.

Not practicing with regard to the five eyes as either pure or impure is practicing the perfection of wisdom; not practicing with regard to the six superknowledges as either pure or impure is practicing the perfection of wisdom.
Why is this? Subhūti!
Since the very nature of the five eyes does not exist, how much less could there be five eyes that are either permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, pure or impure!

If even the nature of the six supernormal powers does not exist, how much less could there be six supernormal powers that are either permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, pure or impure!

“Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, if they do not practice the ten powers of a buddha, that is practicing the perfection of wisdom; if they do not practice the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, or the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha, that is practicing the perfection of wisdom.

If they do not practice whether the ten powers of a buddha are permanent or impermanent, that is practicing the perfection of wisdom; if they do not practice whether the four fearlessnesses up to the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha are permanent or impermanent, that is practicing the perfection of wisdom.”

Not practicing whether the ten powers of a Buddha are pleasant or painful is practicing the perfection of wisdom; not practicing whether the four fearlessnesses up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are pleasant or painful is practicing the perfection of wisdom.

Not practicing whether the ten powers of a Buddha are self or non-self is practicing the perfection of wisdom; not practicing whether the four fearlessnesses up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are self or non-self is practicing the perfection of wisdom.

Not practicing whether the ten powers of a Buddha are pure or impure is practicing the perfection of wisdom; not practicing whether the four fearlessnesses up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are pure or impure is practicing the perfection of wisdom.
Why is this? Subhūti,

since even the nature of the Buddha’s ten powers does not exist, how could there be any Buddha’s ten powers that are either permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, pure or impure?

Since even the nature of the four fearlessnesses up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha does not exist, how much less could the four fearlessnesses up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha be permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, pure or impure!

“Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, if they do not practice the dharma of non-forgetfulness, that is practicing the perfection of wisdom; if they do not practice the nature of constant equanimity, that is practicing the perfection of wisdom.
