"World-Honored One!"
"In this way, this perfection of wisdom is the perfection of the four dhyānas.
The Buddha said, "So it is!"
“Because the entities of the four dhyānas cannot be apprehended.
“World-Honored One!
This perfection of wisdom is the perfection of the four immeasurables.”
The Buddha said: "It is so!
Because the four immeasurables are unattainable."
“World-Honored One!
This perfection of prajñā is the perfection of the four formless absorptions.
The Buddha said:
"So it is! Because the objective basis for the four formless absorptions cannot be apprehended.
"World-Honored One!"
"In this way, this perfection of wisdom is the perfection of the five eyes.
The Buddha said, "So it is!"
"Because the objects of the five eyes cannot be apprehended.
"World-Honored One!
This Prajñāpāramitā is the Ṣaḍabhijñāpāramitā (the perfection of the six superknowledges)."
The Buddha said: “It is so!
Because the phenomena of the six supernormal powers are unattainable.”

The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle 296. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Part One, Chapter on the Perfections, Number Thirty-Eight, Part Two. "World-Honored One!..."
"In this way, this perfection of wisdom is the perfection of the ten powers of a Buddha. The Buddha said, "So it is!"
"Because it penetrates all dharmas and is difficult to subdue.
"World-Honored One!
This perfection of prajñāpāramitā is the perfection of the four fearlessnesses."
The Buddha said: "It is so!
Because the wisdom of the marks of attaining the Way does not decline or disappear."
“World-Honored One!
This Prajñāpāramitā is the Pāramitā of the four kinds of unimpeded analytical knowledge.
The Buddha said:
"So it is! Because one attains the knowledge of all aspects (sarvākārajñatā) without obstruction.
"World-Honored One!"
"In this way, the perfection of wisdom is the perfection of great loving-kindness.
The Buddha said, "So it is!"
“Because it brings peace and happiness to all sentient beings.
“World-Honored One!
Thus, this perfection of wisdom is the perfection of great compassion.”
The Buddha said: "It is so!
It is for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings."
“World-Honored One!
This perfection of wisdom is the perfection of great joy.
The Buddha said:
"So it is! Because one does not abandon any sentient being.
"World-Honored One!"
"In this way, the perfection of wisdom is the great perfection of relinquishment.
The Buddha said, "It is so!"
"Because their minds are equal toward all sentient beings.
"World-Honored One!
This perfection of wisdom is the perfection of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha."
The Buddha said: “It is so!
Because it transcends all the dharmas of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.”
“World-Honored One!
This Prajñāpāramitā is the pāramitā of the dharma of non-forgetfulness.
The Buddha said:
"So it is! For the occurrence of forgetfulness cannot be found.
"World-Honored One!"
"In this way, this perfection of wisdom is the perfection of the nature of constant equanimity.
The Buddha said: "So it is!"
“Because the phenomenon of the state of constant equanimity cannot be apprehended.
“World-Honored One!
This Prajñāpāramitā is the perfection of all dhāraṇī-doors.”
The Buddha said:
"It is so! For the phenomena of all dhāraṇīs are unattainable."
“World-Honored One!
This perfection of prajñāpāramitā is the perfection of all doors of samādhi.
The Buddha said:
"So it is! Because the objective referents of all meditative concentrations (*samādhi*) are unapprehendable.
"World-Honored One!"
"In this way, the perfection of wisdom is the perfection of omniscience.
The Buddha said, "So it is!"
"Because all matters of omniscience are unapprehendable.
"World-Honored One!
Thus, this perfection of wisdom is the perfection of the knowledge of the aspects of the path."
The Buddha said: "It is so!
Because the phenomena of the knowledge of the aspects of the path cannot be apprehended."
“World-Honored One!
This perfection of prajñā is the perfection of all-aspect omniscience.

"So it is! Because the activities of the knowledge of all aspects are unapprehendable.
"World-Honored One!"
"In this way, the perfection of wisdom is the practice of all perfections for all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.

“Because the activities of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cannot be apprehended.

This perfection of wisdom is the perfection of the unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas.”

“World-Honored One!
This Prajñāpāramitā is the Tathāgata-pāramitā.
The Buddha said:
"So it is! For you are able to speak of all phenomena exactly as they are.
"World-Honored One!"
"In this way, this perfection of wisdom is the perfection of spontaneity.
The Buddha said, "So it is!"
"Because one attains mastery over all phenomena.
"World-Honored One!
This perfection of wisdom is the perfection of perfect enlightenment."
The Buddha said: "It is so!

Chapter 39: The Merit of Hearing What Is Difficult to Hear, Part One, Section One. At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, had this thought:

"If good sons and good daughters have, in the past, approached and made offerings to immeasurable Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas; if they have generated great vows and planted various roots of goodness; and if they have been sustained by many spiritual friends—only then do they now hear the names and merits of such a Prajñāpāramitā, let alone being able to write it down, recite it, uphold it, contemplate it according to principle, explain it to others, or practice according to the teachings as best they can!"

It should be known that this person has, in the past, approached, served, made offerings to, honored, respected, and praised immeasurable Buddhas; they have planted many roots of virtue, heard the *prajñāpāramitā*, and having heard it, have upheld, contemplated, recited, and explained it to others, practicing according to the teaching, or were able to question and answer regarding this sutra. By the power of such merit, they have now accomplished this matter.

If good sons or good daughters have already made offerings to immeasurable Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, and their merit is pure, then upon hearing this Prajñāpāramitā, their minds will not be startled, terrified, or afraid; having heard it, they will believe and rejoice, practicing according to the teaching. It should be known that such persons, because they have practiced the pāramitās of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom for many koṭis of kalpas, are able to accomplish this matter in their present life.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!

If sons and daughters of good family, upon hearing this profound meaning and intent of the *Prajñāpāramitā*, their minds are not startled, not terrified, and not afraid; and having heard it, they copy it, read and recite it, receive and uphold it, contemplate it according to principle, explain it to others, or further practice according to the teaching as far as their strength allows—then one should know that such persons are like Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have reached the stage of non-retrogression."
Why is this? World-Honored One!

The meaning and purport of this *prajñāpāramitā* are so profound that they are extremely difficult to believe and understand. If one has not practiced the *pāramitās* of giving, pure morality, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom for a long time in previous lives, how could one possibly believe and understand them upon merely hearing them briefly?
“World-Honored One!

If good sons or good daughters hear this teaching of the *prajñāpāramitā* and disparage or slander it, one should know that these persons also previously, in past lives, disparaged this profound *prajñāpāramitā*.
Why is this? World-Honored One!

Because these sons and daughters of good family, upon hearing such a profound exposition of the *prajñāpāramitā*, do not believe or rejoice in it due to the power of their past habits, and their minds are not pure.
“World-Honored One!
These sons and daughters of good family have never approached the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, or the assembly of disciples, nor have they ever inquired:
‘How should one practice the perfection of giving?’”
How should one practice the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom?
How should one abide in internal emptiness?

How should one abide in external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, non-altering emptiness, essential emptiness, the emptiness of self-characteristics, the emptiness of common characteristics, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of non-apprehensibility, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence?
How should one abide in suchness?

How should one abide in the dharma-realm, the nature of phenomena, the non-falsity of phenomena, the immutability of phenomena, the equality of phenomena, the state beyond birth, the fixed nature of phenomena, the stability of phenomena, the limit of reality, the realm of empty space, and the inconceivable realm?
How should one abide in the noble truth of suffering?
How should one abide in the noble truths of the origin, cessation, and the path?
How should one cultivate the four dhyānas?
How should one cultivate the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments?
How should one cultivate the eight liberations?
How should one cultivate the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities?
How should one cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness?
How should one cultivate the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path?
How should one cultivate the gate of liberation of emptiness?
How should one cultivate the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness?
How should one cultivate the five eyes?
How should one cultivate the six supernormal powers?
How should one cultivate the ten powers of a Buddha?

How should one cultivate the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha?
How should one cultivate the quality of non-forgetfulness?
How should one cultivate the state of constant equanimity?
How should one cultivate omniscience?
How should one cultivate the knowledge of the characteristics of the path and the knowledge of all characteristics?
How should one cultivate all the doors of dhāraṇī?
How should one cultivate all the doors of samādhi?
"How should one cultivate all the practices of a bodhisattva mahāsattva?
How should one cultivate the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas?
Because they have heard this teaching of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they disparage and revile it, neither believing nor delighting in it, and their minds are not pure.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, said to Śāriputra:
"Venerable One!

The meaning and purport of this Prajñāpāramitā are so profound and extremely difficult to believe and understand. It is not at all surprising if sons and daughters of good family, who have not long since gained faith and understanding in the perfections of giving, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, and have not long practiced them, fail to believe and understand upon hearing the teaching of the Prajñāpāramitā, or even give rise to slander."

If sons or daughters of good family have not long since gained faith and understanding in, nor long since dwelt securely in, internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, non-altering emptiness, essential emptiness, emptiness of own-marks, common emptiness, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of self-nature, and the emptiness of the self-nature of non-existence—then it is not surprising if, upon hearing the teaching of the *prajñāpāramitā*, they are unable to gain faith and understanding or even give rise to slander.

If good sons or good daughters, having not long since gained faith and understanding in, nor long since dwelt securely in, suchness (*tathatā*), the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), the non-illusory nature, the unchanging nature, equality, the nature free from birth, the fixed nature of dharmas, the stability of dharmas, the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), the realm of space, and the inconceivable realm, should upon hearing the teaching of the *prajñāpāramitā* fail to gain faith and understanding or even give rise to slander, this would not be considered rare.

If good sons or good daughters, having not long since gained faith and understanding in the Four Noble Truths and not yet long since dwelt securely therein, hear the teaching of the Prajñāpāramitā and are unable to believe and understand it, or even give rise to slander, this is not yet considered extraordinary.

If good sons or good daughters, regarding the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments; or the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities; or the four applications of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path; or the gateways to liberation of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; or having not long since gained faith and understanding in, nor long practiced, the ten stages of a bodhisattva—should, upon hearing the teaching of the *prajñāpāramitā*, be unable to gain faith and understanding, or should even give rise to slander, this is not yet considered rare.

If good sons or good daughters, having not long since gained faith and understanding in, nor long practiced, the five eyes, the six supernormal powers; or the ten powers of a Buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; or the quality of non-forgetfulness, the state of constant abiding in equanimity; or all-knowledge, the knowledge of the paths, and the knowledge of all aspects; or all the doors of dhāraṇī and all the doors of samādhi—then it is not yet considered rare if, upon hearing the teaching of the *prajñāpāramitā*, they cannot gain faith and understanding or even give rise to slander.

If sons or daughters of good family, having not long since gained faith and understanding in the practices of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas or in the Buddha’s unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and having not long practiced them, are unable to believe and understand upon hearing the teaching of the *prajñāpāramitā*, or even give rise to slander, this is not yet considered rare.
"Venerable One!
I now pay homage to the profound Prajñāpāramitā; to pay homage to the Prajñāpāramitā is to pay homage to the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna)."
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śakra, the Lord of the Devas, saying:
“Kauśika, it is so! It is thus!”
So it is! It is just as you have said.
To pay homage to the Prajñāpāramitā is to pay homage to the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna).
Why is this? Kauśika!
It is because the omniscient wisdom of all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, is born from the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
“Kauśika! If good sons and good daughters wish to abide in the all-knowledge of all Buddhas, they should abide in the perfection of wisdom;
if they wish to give rise to all-knowledge, the knowledge of the paths, and the knowledge of all aspects, they should study the perfection of wisdom.”
Those who wish to sever all habitual tendencies of the afflictions should study the Prajñāpāramitā;
those who wish to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, turn the wondrous wheel of Dharma, and deliver immeasurable multitudes should study the Prajñāpāramitā.

If good sons or good daughters wish to skillfully establish sentient beings in the fruit of a stream-enterer, or the fruit of a once-returner, or the fruit of a non-returner, or the fruit of an arhat, or in the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha; or if they themselves wish to train, they should train in the perfection of wisdom.
If sons or daughters of good family wish to skillfully establish sentient beings in the Buddha’s unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they should study the perfection of wisdom.

If good sons or good daughters, wishing to skillfully establish sentient beings in the practices of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas so that they do not regress, or wishing to practice them themselves, should study the *prajñāpāramitā*.
If bodhisattva-mahāsattvas wish to subdue all māras and crush all non-Buddhists, they should study the perfection of wisdom;
if bodhisattva-mahāsattvas wish to skillfully sustain the community of bhikṣus, they should study the perfection of wisdom.
At that time, Śakra, the Lord of Devas, addressed the Buddha,
saying: “World-Honored One,
when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom, how do they abide in form?”
How does one dwell upon feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness?
How does one cultivate form?
How does one cultivate feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness?
How does one dwell in the sense base of the eye?
How does one dwell in the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind?
How does one practice with regard to the sense base of the eye?
How does one practice with regard to the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind?
How does one abide with regard to the sense base of forms?
How does one abide with regard to the sense bases of sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena?
What is the cultivation of the sense-base of form?
What is the cultivation of the sense-bases of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena?
What is abiding in the eye-element?
How does one dwell in the eye-consciousness element, the eye-contact, and the various feelings produced with eye-contact as condition?
How does one cultivate the eye-element?
How does one cultivate the form-element, and so forth, up to the various feelings produced with eye-contact as condition?
How does one abide in the ear-element?
How does one abide in the sound-element, the ear-consciousness-element, ear-contact, and the various feelings produced with ear-contact as condition?
How does one cultivate the ear-element?
How does one practice regarding the sphere of sound, up to the various feelings produced with ear-contact as condition?
How does one abide in the sphere of the nose?
How does one abide in the sphere of odors, the sphere of nose-consciousness, nose-contact, and the various feelings produced with nose-contact as condition?
How does one cultivate the nose element?
How does one cultivate the odor element, and so forth, up to the various feelings produced with nose-contact as their condition?
How does one abide in the tongue element?
How does one dwell upon the element of taste, the element of tongue-consciousness, and tongue-contact, as well as the various feelings produced with tongue-contact as their condition?
How does one cultivate the element of the tongue?
How does one cultivate the element of taste, and so forth, up to the various feelings produced with tongue-contact as their condition?
How does one dwell in the body element?
How does one dwell in the tangible-object element, the body-consciousness element, as well as body-contact and the various feelings arising with body-contact as their condition?
How does one cultivate the body element?
What is the cultivation of the sphere of tangibles, up to the various feelings produced with body-tangibles as condition?
What is dwelling in the sphere of mind?
What is dwelling in the sphere of mental phenomena, the sphere of mental consciousness, and mental contact, as well as the various feelings produced with mental contact as condition?
What is the cultivation of the mind-element (*manodhātu*)?
What is the cultivation of the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*), up to the various feelings produced with mind-contact as condition?
And what is the abiding in the earth-element (*pṛthivīdhātu*)?
How does one abide in the elements of water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness?
How does one practice with the earth element?
How does one practice with the elements of water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness?
How does one abide in ignorance?

How does one abide in volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, existence, birth, and old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair?
How does one cultivate ignorance?
How does one cultivate volitional formations, up to and including old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair?
And how does one abide in the perfection of generosity?
How does one abide in the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom?
How does one practice the perfection of generosity?
How does one practice the pure precepts up to the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*)?
How does one abide in internal emptiness (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*)?

How does one abide in external emptiness (*bahirdhā-śūnyatā*), internal-and-external emptiness (*adhyātma-bahirdhā-śūnyatā*), the emptiness of emptiness (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*), great emptiness (*mahā-śūnyatā*), ultimate emptiness (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*), conditioned emptiness (*saṃskṛta-śūnyatā*), unconditioned emptiness (*asaṃskṛta-śūnyatā*), absolute emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*), boundless emptiness (*anavarāgra-śūnyatā*), dispersed emptiness (*anavakāra-śūnyatā*), non-alteration emptiness (*anavakāra-śūnyatā*), essential nature emptiness (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*), self-characteristic emptiness (*svalakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*), common characteristic emptiness (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*), the emptiness of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-śūnyatā*), the emptiness of the unapprehendable (*anupalambha-śūnyatā*), the emptiness of non-existence (*abhāva-śūnyatā*), the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*), and the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature (*abhāvasvabhāva-śūnyatā*)?
How does one practice internal emptiness?
How does one practice external emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence?
How does one abide in suchness?

How does one abide in the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), non-falsity (avitathatā), non-alteration (ananyathābhāva), equality (samatā), the state beyond birth (anirodhatā), the fixedness of phenomena (dharmaniyāmatā), the stability of phenomena (dharmasthititā), the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi), the realm of space (ākāśadhātu), and the inconceivable realm (acintyadhātu)?
What is the cultivation of true thusness?
What is the cultivation of the dharma-realm, up to and including the inconceivable realm?
How does one abide in the noble truth of suffering?
How does one abide in the noble truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path?
How does one cultivate the noble truth of suffering?
How does one cultivate the noble truths of its origin, its cessation, and the path?
How does one abide in the four dhyānas?
How does one abide in the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments?
How does one practice the four dhyānas?
How does one practice the four immeasurables and the four formless absorptions?
How does one dwell in the eight liberations?
How does one dwell in the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities?
How does one practice the eight liberations?
How does one practice the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative attainments, and the ten totalities?
How does one abide in the four foundations of mindfulness?
How does one abide in the four right endeavors, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path?
How does one practice the four foundations of mindfulness?
How does one practice the four right efforts, up to and including the eightfold noble path?
How does one dwell in the gate of liberation of emptiness?
How does one dwell in the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness?
How does one practice the gate of liberation of emptiness?
How does one practice the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness?
How does one abide in the ten stages of a bodhisattva?
How does one practice the ten stages of a bodhisattva?
How does one abide in the five eyes?
How does one abide in the six supernormal powers?
How does one practice the five eyes?
How does one practice the six supernormal powers?
How does one abide in the ten powers of a Buddha?

How does one abide in the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha?
How does one practice the ten powers of a Buddha?
How does one practice the four fearlessnesses up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha?
How does one abide in the quality of non-forgetfulness?
How does one abide in the nature of constant equanimity?
How does one cultivate the quality of non-forgetfulness?
How does one cultivate the nature of constant equanimity?
How does one abide in all-knowledge?
How does one abide in the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects?
How does one cultivate all-knowledge?
How does one practice the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects?
How does one abide in all dharani-doors? How does one abide in all samadhi-doors?
How does one practice all the gateways of dhāraṇī?
How does one practice all the gateways of samādhi?
How does one abide in the fruit of stream-entry?
How does one abide in the fruit of a once-returner, a non-returner, or an arhat?
How does one cultivate the fruit of stream-entry?
How does one cultivate the fruits of a once-returner, a non-returner, or an arhat?
How does one abide in the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha?
How does one cultivate the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha?
How does one abide in all the practices of a bodhisattva mahāsattva?
How does one practice all the conducts of a bodhisattva mahāsattva?
How does one abide in the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas?
How does one practice the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas?
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śakra, the Lord of the Devas, saying:
“Kauśika, excellent! Excellent!”
Excellent! Now, sustained by the Buddha’s spiritual power, you are able to inquire of the Tathāgata regarding such a profound meaning.
Listen attentively!
Listen attentively!
Reflect upon it well; I shall speak for you, Kausika!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, if they do not dwell upon or cultivate form, this is dwelling upon and cultivating form;
if they do not dwell upon or cultivate feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, this is dwelling upon and cultivating feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
Why is this? Kauśika!
It is because the forms through which one dwells and practices, up to and including consciousness, are unapprehendable.

“Kauśika! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, if they do not dwell upon nor cultivate the sense base of the eye, this is dwelling upon and cultivating the sense base of the eye;
if they do not dwell upon nor cultivate the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, this is dwelling upon and cultivating the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.”
Why is this? Kauśika,
it is because the bases of practice from the sphere of the eye up to the sphere of the mind cannot be apprehended.
“Kauśika! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, if they do not dwell upon nor cultivate the sphere of form, this is dwelling upon and cultivating the sphere of form;

if they do not dwell upon nor cultivate the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, or mental phenomena, this is dwelling upon and cultivating the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena.”
Why is this? Kauśika!
It is because the bases of practice, from the sphere of form up to the sphere of mental phenomena, are unattainable.
“Kauśika! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, if they do not dwell upon nor cultivate the eye-element, this is dwelling upon and cultivating the eye-element;

if they do not dwell upon nor cultivate the form-element, the eye-consciousness-element, eye-contact, and the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition, this is dwelling upon and cultivating the form-element up to the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition.”
Why is this? Kauśika,
it is because the eye-element in which one dwells and practices, up to and including the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition, are all unapprehendable.

“Kauśika! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, if they do not dwell upon nor cultivate the sphere of the ear (*śrotra-dhātu*), this is precisely what it means to dwell upon and cultivate the sphere of the ear.

If they do not dwell upon nor cultivate the sphere of sounds (*śabda-dhātu*), the sphere of auditory consciousness (*śrotra-vijñāna-dhātu*), as well as auditory contact (*śrotra-saṃsparśa*) and the various feelings (*vedanā*) produced with auditory contact as a condition, this is precisely what it means to dwell upon and cultivate the sphere of sounds up to the various feelings produced with auditory contact as a condition.”
Why is this? Kauśika!
Because the ear-element in which one dwells and practices, up to and including the various feelings produced with ear-contact as a condition, are all unattainable.

“Kauśika! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, if they do not dwell upon nor cultivate the sphere of the nose (*ghrāṇadhātu*), this is dwelling upon and cultivating the sphere of the nose;

if they do not dwell upon nor cultivate the sphere of odors (*gandhadhātu*), the sphere of nose-consciousness (*ghrāṇavijñānadhātu*), nose-contact (*ghrāṇasparśa*), and the various feelings produced with nose-contact as a condition, this is dwelling upon and cultivating the sphere of odors up to the various feelings produced with nose-contact as a condition.”
Why is this? Kauśika!
It is because the nose element in which one dwells and practices, up to and including the various feelings produced with nose-contact as a condition, are all unattainable.
“Kauśika! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, if they do not dwell upon nor cultivate the tongue-element, this is dwelling upon and cultivating the tongue-element;

if they do not dwell upon nor cultivate the taste-element, the tongue-consciousness-element, tongue-contact, or the various feelings produced with tongue-contact as a condition, this is dwelling upon and cultivating the taste-element up to the various feelings produced with tongue-contact as a condition.”
Why is this? Kauśika!
It is because the tongue-element in which one dwells and practices, up to and including the various sensations produced with tongue-contact as a condition, are all unapprehendable.

“Kauśika! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, if he does not dwell upon nor cultivate the element of the body, this is his dwelling upon and cultivation of the element of the body;

if he does not dwell upon nor cultivate the element of tangibles, the element of body-consciousness, as well as body-contact and the various feelings produced with body-contact as a condition, this is his dwelling upon and cultivation of the element of tangibles up to the various feelings produced with body-contact as a condition.”
Why is this? Kauśika!
It is because the body element in which one dwells and practices, up to and including the various feelings produced with body-contact as a condition, are all unapprehendable.

“Kauśika! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, if they do not abide in and do not cultivate the mind-element (*manodhātu*), this is abiding in and cultivating the mind-element;

if they do not abide in and do not cultivate the dharma-element, the mind-consciousness-element (*manovijñānadhātu*), mental contact (*manaḥsaṃsparśa*), and the various feelings (*vedanā*) produced with mental contact as a condition, this is abiding in and cultivating the dharma-element up to the various feelings produced with mental contact as a condition.”
Why is this? Kauśika!

Because the mental faculty (*manodhātu*) in which one dwells and practices, up to and including the various feelings produced with mental contact (*manaḥsaṃsparśa*) as a condition, are unapprehendable.
“Kauśika! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, if they do not dwell upon nor cultivate the earth element, this is dwelling upon and cultivating the earth element;
if they do not dwell upon nor cultivate the water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness elements, this is dwelling upon and cultivating the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements.”
Why is this? Kauśika!
It is because the earth element, up to and including the consciousness element, as they are practiced and dwelled upon, cannot be apprehended.
“Kauśika! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, if he does not dwell upon nor cultivate ignorance, this is his dwelling upon and cultivation of ignorance.

If he does not dwell upon nor cultivate volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, or old age, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair, this is his dwelling upon and cultivation of volitional formations through to old age, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair.”
Why is this? Kausika!
It is because that which is practiced while dwelling [in samsara]—from ignorance through to old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair—is unapprehendable.

“Kauśika! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, if they do not dwell upon nor cultivate the perfection of giving, this is their dwelling upon and cultivation of the perfection of giving;

if they do not dwell upon nor cultivate the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, this is their dwelling upon and cultivation of the perfections from ethical discipline up to wisdom.”
Why is this? Kauśika,
it is because that which abides in and practices the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom cannot be apprehended.

“Kauśika! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, if they do not dwell upon or cultivate internal emptiness, this is precisely dwelling upon and cultivating internal emptiness.

If they do not dwell upon or cultivate external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, non-altering emptiness, essential emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common-characteristic emptiness, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature—this is precisely dwelling upon and cultivating external emptiness up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature.”
Why is this? Kauśika!
It is because that which dwells in and practices the emptiness of the internal, up to the emptiness of the nature of non-nature, is unapprehendable.

“Kauśika! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, if they do not dwell upon nor cultivate true suchness (*tathatā*), this is precisely dwelling upon and cultivating true suchness.

If they do not dwell upon nor cultivate the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), non-falsity, immutability, equality, the state beyond birth, the fixed nature of phenomena, the stability of phenomena, the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), the realm of space, or the inconceivable realm, this is precisely dwelling upon and cultivating the realm of phenomena up to the inconceivable realm.”
Why is this? Kauśika!
Because that which is dwelled upon and practiced—the suchness (tathatā) up to the inconceivable realm (acintyadhātu)—is unapprehendable.

“Kauśika! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, if he does not dwell upon nor cultivate the noble truth of suffering, this is his dwelling upon and cultivation of the noble truth of suffering;

if he does not dwell upon nor cultivate the noble truths of origination, cessation, and the path, this is his dwelling upon and cultivation of the noble truths of origination, cessation, and the path.”
Why is this? Kauśika!
It is because the Noble Truths of Suffering, Origination, Cessation, and the Path, as they are practiced and dwelt upon, are unattainable.
“Kauśika! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, if they do not dwell in nor cultivate the four dhyānas, this is their dwelling in and cultivation of the four dhyānas;
if they do not dwell in nor cultivate the four immeasurables or the four formless absorptions, this is their dwelling in and cultivation of the four immeasurables and the four formless absorptions.”
Why is this? Kauśika,
it is because the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments in which one dwells and practices are unapprehendable.

“Kauśika! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, if they do not dwell upon nor cultivate the eight liberations, this is their dwelling upon and cultivation of the eight liberations;

if they do not dwell upon nor cultivate the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative attainments, or the ten totalities, this is their dwelling upon and cultivation of the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative attainments, and the ten totalities.”
Why is this? Kauśika!
It is because that which is practiced while dwelling in the eight liberations up to the ten spheres of totality cannot be apprehended.

“Kauśika! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, if they do not dwell upon nor cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness, this constitutes dwelling upon and cultivating the four foundations of mindfulness;

if they do not dwell upon nor cultivate the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, or the eightfold noble path, this constitutes dwelling upon and cultivating the four right efforts up to the eightfold noble path.”
Why is this? Kauśika,
it is because that which is practiced while abiding in the four foundations of mindfulness, up to and including the eightfold noble path, is unapprehendable.

“Kauśika! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, if they do not dwell upon nor cultivate the gate of liberation of emptiness, this is dwelling in and cultivating the gate of liberation of emptiness;
if they do not dwell upon nor cultivate the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness, this is dwelling in and cultivating the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness.”
Why is this? Kauśika,
it is because the dwelling in the practice of the gate of liberation of emptiness, the gate of liberation of signlessness, and the gate of liberation of wishlessness cannot be apprehended.

“Kauśika! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), if they neither abide in nor cultivate the ten stages of a bodhisattva, this is precisely how they abide in and cultivate the ten stages of a bodhisattva.”
Why is this? Kauśika!
It is because the ten stages of a bodhisattva, in which one dwells and practices, are unattainable.
“Kauśika! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, if they do not dwell upon nor cultivate the five eyes, this is what it means to dwell upon and cultivate the five eyes;
if they do not dwell upon nor cultivate the six supernormal powers, this is what it means to dwell upon and cultivate the six supernormal powers.”
Why is this? Kauśika!
It is because that which dwells upon and practices the five eyes and the six supernormal powers is unattainable.

“Kauśika! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), if they do not dwell upon nor cultivate the ten powers (daśabala) of a Buddha, this is precisely how they dwell upon and cultivate the ten powers of a Buddha;

if they do not dwell upon nor cultivate the four fearlessnesses (catur-vaiśāradya), the four analytical knowledges (catasraḥ pratisamvidah), great loving-kindness (mahāmaitrī), great compassion (mahākaruṇā), great sympathetic joy (mahāmuditā), great equanimity (mahopekṣā), and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (āveṇika-buddhadharma), this is precisely how they dwell upon and cultivate the four fearlessnesses up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.”
Why is this? Kauśika!
It is because that which abides in and practices the ten powers of a Buddha, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, is unattainable.

“Kauśika! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, if they do not dwell upon nor cultivate the quality of non-forgetfulness, this is precisely how they dwell upon and cultivate non-forgetfulness;
if they do not dwell upon nor cultivate the nature of constant equanimity, this is precisely how they dwell upon and cultivate constant equanimity.”
Why is this? Kauśika!
It is because the state of dwelling in the practice of the dharma of non-forgetfulness and the nature of constant abiding in equanimity are ungraspable.
“Kauśika! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, if they do not dwell upon nor cultivate omniscience, this is dwelling upon and cultivating omniscience;

if they do not dwell upon nor cultivate the knowledge of the aspects of the path or the knowledge of all aspects, this is dwelling upon and cultivating the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects.”
Why is this? Kauśika!

It is because that which dwells upon and practices all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) is unattainable.

“Kauśika! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, if they do not dwell upon nor cultivate any of the dhāraṇī-doors, this is called dwelling upon and cultivating all the dhāraṇī-doors;
if they do not dwell upon nor cultivate any of the samādhi-doors, this is called dwelling upon and cultivating all the samādhi-doors.”
Why is this? Kauśika!
It is because the practice of all the gateways of dhāraṇī and all the gateways of samādhi in which one dwells cannot be apprehended.

“Kauśika! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, if they neither dwell upon nor cultivate the fruit of a stream-enterer, this is their dwelling in and cultivation of the fruit of a stream-enterer;

if they neither dwell upon nor cultivate the fruits of a once-returner, a non-returner, or an arhat, this is their dwelling in and cultivation of the fruits of a once-returner, a non-returner, and an arhat.”
Why is this? Kauśika!
It is because the states of abiding and training—the fruits of stream-entry, once-returning, non-returning, and arhatship—are unattainable.

“Kauśika! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, if they do not dwell upon nor cultivate pratyekabuddha-enlightenment, this is what constitutes dwelling upon and cultivating pratyekabuddha-enlightenment.”
Why is this? Kauśika,
it is because the solitary awakening (pratyekabodhi) in which one dwells and practices cannot be apprehended.

“Kauśika! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, if they do not dwell upon nor cultivate any of the practices of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, this is precisely what it means to dwell upon and cultivate all the practices of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.”
Why is this? Kauśika!
It is because the practices of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, as they are cultivated while dwelling therein, are unapprehendable.

“Kauśika! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, if they do not dwell upon nor cultivate the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas, this is precisely how they dwell upon and cultivate the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas.”
Why is this? Kauśika!
It is because the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas, which they have dwelled upon and practiced, is unattainable.

"Furthermore, Kauśika, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, if they neither abide nor do not abide in form, neither practice nor do not practice it, this is called abiding in and practicing form.

If they neither abide nor do not abide in feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, neither practice nor do not practice them, this is called abiding in and practicing feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness."
Why is this? Kauśika!
It is because this bodhisattva mahāsattva perceives that form, up to and including consciousness, cannot be apprehended in its prior, subsequent, or intermediate limits.

“Kauśika! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, if they neither abide nor do not abide in the sense-field of the eye, and neither practice nor do not practice it, this is called abiding in and practicing the sense-field of the eye.

If they neither abide nor do not abide in the sense-fields of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, and neither practice nor do not practice them, this is called abiding in and practicing the sense-fields of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.”
Why is this? Kauśika,
it is because this bodhisattva mahāsattva observes that the eye base, up to and including the mind base, cannot be apprehended in the past, future, or present limits.

“Kauśika! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, if they neither abide nor do not abide in the sphere of form, neither practice nor do not practice it, this is what is meant by abiding in and practicing the sphere of form.

If they neither abide nor do not abide in the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena, neither practice nor do not practice them, this is what is meant by abiding in and practicing the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena.”
Why is this? Kauśika!

It is because this bodhisattva mahāsattva observes that the past, future, and present limits of the sphere of form (rūpāyatana) up to the sphere of mental phenomena (dharmāyatana) are unapprehendable.

“Kauśika! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, if they neither abide nor do not abide in the eye-element, neither cultivate nor do not cultivate it, this is called abiding in and cultivating the eye-element.

If they neither abide nor do not abide in the form-element, the eye-consciousness-element, eye-contact, and the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition, neither cultivating nor not cultivating them, this is called abiding in and cultivating the form-element up to the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition.”
Why is this so? Kauśika!

It is because this bodhisattva mahāsattva perceives that the eye-element, and so forth up to the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition, cannot be apprehended in the past, future, or present limits.

“Kauśika! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, if they neither dwell nor do not dwell in the ear-element, neither practice nor do not practice it, this is called dwelling in and practicing the ear-element.

If they neither dwell nor do not dwell in the sound-element, the ear-consciousness-element, ear-contact, and the various feelings produced with ear-contact as a condition, neither practicing nor not practicing them, this is called dwelling in and practicing the sound-element up to the various feelings produced with ear-contact as a condition.”
Why is this? Kauśika!

It is because this bodhisattva mahāsattva perceives that the ear-element, and even the various feelings produced with ear-contact as a condition, cannot be apprehended in the past, the future, or the present.

“Kauśika! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, if they neither abide nor do not abide in the nose element (*ghrāṇadhātu*), and neither cultivate nor do not cultivate it, this is called abiding in and cultivating the nose element.

If they neither abide nor do not abide in the odor element (*gandhadhātu*), the nose-consciousness element (*ghrāṇavijñānadhātu*), nose-contact (*ghrāṇasparśa*), and the various feelings (*vedanā*) produced with nose-contact as a condition, and neither cultivate nor do not cultivate them, this is called abiding in and cultivating the odor element up to the various feelings produced with nose-contact as a condition.”
Why is this? Kauśika!

It is because this bodhisattva mahāsattva observes that the nose element, and even the various feelings produced with nose-contact as a condition, cannot be apprehended in the past, future, or present limits.

“Kauśika! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, if they neither abide nor do not abide in the tongue element, neither practice nor do not practice it, this is called abiding in and practicing the tongue element.

If they neither abide nor do not abide in the taste element, the tongue-consciousness element, tongue-contact, and the various feelings produced with tongue-contact as a condition, neither practicing nor not practicing them, this is called abiding in and practicing the taste element up to the various feelings produced with tongue-contact as a condition.”
Why is that? Kauśika!

It is because this bodhisattva mahāsattva observes that the tongue-element, up to and including the various feelings produced with tongue-contact as a condition, cannot be apprehended in the past, future, or present limits.

“Kauśika! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, if they neither abide nor do not abide in the body element, and neither practice nor do not practice it, this is called abiding in and practicing the body element.

If they neither abide nor do not abide in the contact element, the body-consciousness element, as well as body-contact and the various feelings produced with body-contact as a condition, and neither practice nor do not practice them, this is called abiding in and practicing the contact element up to the various feelings produced with body-contact as a condition.”
Why is this? Kauśika!

It is because this bodhisattva mahāsattva observes that the body element, up to and including the various feelings produced with body-contact as a condition, cannot be apprehended in the past, the future, or the present.

“Kauśika! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, if they neither abide nor do not abide in the mental element (*manodhātu*), and neither cultivate nor do not cultivate it, this is called abiding in and cultivating the mental element.

If they neither abide nor do not abide in the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*), the mental-consciousness element (*manovijñānadhātu*), mental contact (*manaḥsaṃsparśa*), and the various feelings (*vedanā*) produced with mental contact as a condition, and neither cultivate nor do not cultivate them, this is called abiding in and cultivating the dharma-element up to the various feelings produced with mental contact as a condition.”
Why is this? Kauśika!

It is because this bodhisattva mahāsattva observes that the mental faculty (*manodhātu*), and even the various feelings produced with mental contact as a condition, cannot be apprehended in the past, future, or present limits.

“Kauśika! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, if they neither abide nor do not abide in the earth element, and neither practice nor do not practice it, this is called abiding in and practicing the earth element.

If they neither abide nor do not abide in the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements, and neither practice nor do not practice them, this is called abiding in and practicing the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements.”
Why is this? Kauśika!
It is because this bodhisattva mahāsattva perceives that the element of earth, up to and including the element of consciousness, cannot be apprehended in its prior, posterior, or middle limits.

“Kauśika! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, if they neither abide in nor do not abide in ignorance, neither cultivate nor do not cultivate it, this is called abiding in and cultivating ignorance.

If they neither abide in nor do not abide in volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, and old age, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair; neither cultivate nor do not cultivate them, this is called abiding in and cultivating volitional formations up to old age, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair.”
Why is this? Kauśika!

It is because this bodhisattva mahāsattva observes that ignorance, up to and including old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair, cannot be apprehended in their prior, posterior, or intermediate limits.

“Kauśika! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, if they neither abide nor do not abide in the perfection of generosity, neither practice nor do not practice it, this is abiding in and practicing the perfection of generosity;

if they neither abide nor do not abide in the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, neither practice nor do not practice them, this is abiding in and practicing the perfections from ethical discipline up to wisdom.”
Why is this? Kauśika!
It is because this bodhisattva mahāsattva observes that the beginning, middle, and end of the perfection of giving, up to and including the perfection of wisdom, are unapprehendable.

“Kauśika! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, if they neither abide nor do not abide in internal emptiness, neither practice nor do not practice it, this is called abiding in and practicing internal emptiness.

If they neither abide nor do not abide in external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, endless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, non-alteration emptiness, essential nature emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common characteristic emptiness, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature; neither practicing nor not practicing them—this is called abiding in and practicing external emptiness, up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature.”
Why is this? Kauśika!

Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates that from the emptiness of the internal up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature, the prior, posterior, and middle limits are unapprehendable.

The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle 297. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Part One: Chapter Thirty-nine, Part Two, "The Merit of Hearing What is Difficult to Hear. "Kauśika!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, if they neither abide nor do not abide in suchness, and neither practice nor do not practice it, this is called abiding in and practicing suchness.

If they neither abide nor do not abide in the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu), the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), the non-falsity, the unchanging nature, equality, the state beyond birth, the fixed nature of phenomena, the stability of phenomena, the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi), the realm of empty space, and the inconceivable realm, and neither practice nor do not practice them, this is called abiding in and practicing the realm of phenomena up to the inconceivable realm.
Why is this? Kauśika!
It is because this bodhisattva mahāsattva observes that from the beginning, middle, and end of true suchness (tathatā) up to the inconceivable realm (acintyadhātu), nothing can be apprehended.

“Kauśika! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), if they neither abide nor do not abide in the noble truth of suffering, neither practice nor do not practice it, this is called abiding in and practicing the noble truth of suffering.

If they neither abide nor do not abide in the noble truths of origin, cessation, and the path, neither practice nor do not practice them, this is called abiding in and practicing the noble truths of origin, cessation, and the path.”
Why is this? Kauśika!
It is because for this bodhisattva mahāsattva, the noble truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path cannot be apprehended in terms of past, future, or middle limits.

“Kauśika! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, if they neither abide nor do not abide in the four dhyānas, and neither practice nor do not practice them, this is called abiding in and practicing the four dhyānas.

If they neither abide nor do not abide in the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments, and neither practice nor do not practice them, this is called abiding in and practicing the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments.”
Why is this? Kauśika!
It is because this bodhisattva mahāsattva perceives that the past, future, and present limits of the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments are unapprehendable.

“Kauśika! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, if they neither abide nor do not abide in the eight liberations, and neither practice nor do not practice them, this is called abiding in and practicing the eight liberations.

If they neither abide nor do not abide in the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities, and neither practice nor do not practice them, this is called abiding in and practicing the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities.”
Why is this? Kauśika!
It is because this bodhisattva mahāsattva observes that the eight liberations, up to and including the ten totalities, cannot be apprehended in their prior, posterior, or intermediate limits.

“Kauśika! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, if they neither abide nor do not abide in the four foundations of mindfulness, and neither practice nor do not practice them, this is called abiding in and practicing the four foundations of mindfulness.

If they neither abide nor do not abide in the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of awakening, and the eightfold noble path, and neither practice nor do not practice them, this is called abiding in and practicing the four right efforts up to the eightfold noble path.”
Why is this? Kauśika!

It is because this bodhisattva mahāsattva perceives that the four foundations of mindfulness, up to and including the eightfold noble path, cannot be apprehended in terms of their prior, subsequent, or intermediate limits.

“Kauśika! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, if they neither abide nor do not abide in the gate of liberation of emptiness, and neither practice nor do not practice it, this is called abiding in and practicing the gate of liberation of emptiness;

if they neither abide nor do not abide in the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness, and neither practice nor do not practice them, this is called abiding in and practicing the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness.”
Why is this? Kausika!
Because for this bodhisattva mahāsattva, the past, future, and present limits of the gateways to liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—are unapprehendable.

“Kauśika! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, if they neither abide nor do not abide in the ten stages of a bodhisattva, and neither cultivate nor do not cultivate them, this is what it means to abide in and cultivate the ten stages of a bodhisattva.”
Why is this? Kauśika!
It is because this bodhisattva mahāsattva perceives that the prior, posterior, and intermediate limits of the ten stages of a bodhisattva are unobtainable.

“Kauśika! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, if they neither abide nor do not abide in the five eyes, and neither practice nor do not practice them, this is called abiding in and practicing the five eyes;
if they neither abide nor do not abide in the six supernormal powers, and neither practice nor do not practice them, this is called abiding in and practicing the six supernormal powers.”
Why is this? Kauśika!
It is because this bodhisattva mahāsattva observes that the five eyes and the six supernormal powers cannot be apprehended in terms of their prior, posterior, or intermediate limits.

“Kauśika! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, if they neither abide nor do not abide in the ten powers of a buddha, and neither cultivate nor do not cultivate them, this is called abiding in and cultivating the ten powers of a buddha.

If they neither abide nor do not abide in the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha, and neither cultivate nor do not cultivate them, this is called abiding in and cultivating the four fearlessnesses up to the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha.”
Why is this? Kausika!
It is because for these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, the ten powers of a Buddha up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha cannot be apprehended in the past, future, or present limits.

“Kauśika! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, if they neither abide nor do not abide in the quality of non-forgetfulness, and neither practice nor do not practice it, this is called abiding in and practicing the quality of non-forgetfulness.
If they neither abide nor do not abide in the state of constant equanimity, and neither practice nor do not practice it, this is called abiding in and practicing the state of constant equanimity.”
Why is this? Kauśika!
It is because for this bodhisattva mahāsattva, the dharma of non-forgetfulness and the nature of constant equanimity cannot be apprehended in the past, future, or present limits.

“Kauśika! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, if they neither abide nor do not abide in all-knowledge, and neither cultivate nor do not cultivate it, this is called abiding in and cultivating all-knowledge.

If they neither abide nor do not abide in the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects, and neither cultivate nor do not cultivate them, this is called abiding in and cultivating the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects.”
Why is this? Kauśika!

It is because this bodhisattva mahāsattva perceives that the prior, posterior, and middle limits of all-knowledge (sarvajñatā), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (mārgākārajñatā), and the knowledge of all aspects (sarvākārajñatā) are unapprehendable.

“Kauśika! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, if they neither abide nor do not abide in any dhāraṇī doors, and neither practice nor do not practice them, this is called abiding in and practicing all dhāraṇī doors;
if they neither abide nor do not abide in any samādhi doors, and neither practice nor do not practice them, this is called abiding in and practicing all samādhi doors.”
Why is this? Kauśika!
It is because this bodhisattva mahāsattva perceives that the beginning, middle, and end of all dhāraṇī-doors and all samādhi-doors are unapprehendable.

“Kauśika! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, if they neither abide nor do not abide in the fruit of a stream-enterer, and neither practice nor do not practice it, this is called abiding in and practicing the fruit of a stream-enterer.

If they neither abide nor do not abide in the fruits of a once-returner, a non-returner, or an arhat, and neither practice nor do not practice them, this is called abiding in and practicing the fruits of a once-returner, a non-returner, or an arhat.”
Why is this? Kausika!

It is because this bodhisattva mahasattva observes that the prior, posterior, and intermediate limits of the fruit of stream-entry, the once-returner, the non-returner, and the fruit of arhatship are unapprehendable.

“Kauśika! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, if they neither abide nor do not abide in the awakening of a pratyekabuddha, and neither cultivate nor do not cultivate it, this is what is meant by abiding in and cultivating the awakening of a pratyekabuddha.”
Why is this? Kauśika!
It is because this bodhisattva mahāsattva perceives that the past, future, and middle limits of pratyekabuddha-bodhi are unapprehendable.

“Kauśika! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, if they neither abide nor do not abide in any bodhisattva mahāsattva practice, and neither cultivate nor do not cultivate them, this is what it means to abide in and cultivate all bodhisattva mahāsattva practices.”
Why is this? Kauśika!
It is because this bodhisattva mahāsattva perceives that the past, future, and present limits of all bodhisattva mahāsattva practices are unapprehendable.

“Kauśika! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, if they neither abide nor do not abide in the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas, and neither cultivate nor do not cultivate it, this is what constitutes abiding in and cultivating the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas.”
Why is this so? Kauśika!

It is because when these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas contemplate the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas, they find that its past, future, and middle limits are unapprehendable.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This Prajñāpāramitā is most profound.”
The Buddha said, “So it is, Śāriputra!”

Because the suchness of form is profound, the perfection of wisdom is profound; because the suchness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is profound, the perfection of wisdom is profound.

“Śāriputra! Because the suchness of the eye-base is profound, the perfection of wisdom is profound; because the suchness of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-bases is profound, the perfection of wisdom is profound.”

“Śāriputra! Because the suchness of the sphere of form is profound, the perfection of wisdom is profound; because the suchness of the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena is profound, the perfection of wisdom is profound.”

“Śāriputra! Because the suchness of the eye-element is profound, the perfection of wisdom is profound; because the suchness of the form-element, the eye-consciousness-element, eye-contact, and the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition is profound, the perfection of wisdom is profound.”

“Śāriputra! Because the suchness of the ear-element is profound, the perfection of wisdom is profound; because the suchness of the sound-element, the ear-consciousness-element, ear-contact, and all feelings produced with ear-contact as a condition is profound, the perfection of wisdom is profound.”

“Śāriputra! Because the suchness of the nose element is profound, the perfection of wisdom is profound; because the suchness of the odor element, the nose-consciousness element, nose-contact, and all sensations produced with nose-contact as a condition is profound, the perfection of wisdom is profound.”

“Śāriputra! Because the *tathatā* (suchness) of the tongue element is profound, the *prajñāpāramitā* is profound; because the *tathatā* of the taste element, the tongue-consciousness element, as well as tongue-contact and the various feelings produced with tongue-contact as a condition, are profound, the *prajñāpāramitā* is profound.”

“Śāriputra! Because the suchness of the body element is profound, the perfection of wisdom is profound; because the suchness of the tangible element, the body-consciousness element, body-contact, and all feelings produced with body-contact as a condition is profound, the perfection of wisdom is profound.”

“Śāriputra! Because the suchness of the mind-element (*manodhātu*) is profound, the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) is profound. Because the suchness of the dharma-element, the mind-consciousness-element (*manovijñānadhātu*), as well as mental contact (*manaḥsaṃsparśa*) and the various feelings produced with mental contact as a condition are profound, the perfection of wisdom is profound.”

“Śāriputra! Because the suchness of the earth element is profound, the perfection of wisdom is profound; because the suchness of the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements is profound, the perfection of wisdom is profound.”

“Śāriputra! Because the suchness of ignorance is profound, the perfection of wisdom is profound; because the suchness of volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, and old age, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair is profound, the perfection of wisdom is profound.”

“Śāriputra! Because the suchness of the perfection of generosity is profound, the perfection of wisdom is profound; because the suchness of the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom is profound, the perfection of wisdom is profound.”

“Śāriputra! Because the suchness (*tathatā*) of internal emptiness is profound, the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) is profound. Because the suchness of external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, non-alteration emptiness, essential nature emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common characteristic emptiness, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature is profound, the perfection of wisdom is profound.”

“Śāriputra! Because the suchness of suchness is profound, the perfection of wisdom is profound. Because the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu), the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), the non-erroneous nature, the unchanging nature, the state of equality, the nature free from birth, the fixedness of phenomena (dharmaniyāmatā), the stability of phenomena (dharmasthititā), the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi), the realm of space (ākāśadhātu), and the inconceivable realm are the suchness of suchness and are profound, the perfection of wisdom is profound.”

“Śāriputra! Because the suchness of the noble truth of suffering is profound, the perfection of wisdom is profound; because the suchness of the noble truths of origination, cessation, and the path is profound, the perfection of wisdom is profound.”

“Śāriputra! Because the suchness of the four dhyānas is profound, the perfection of wisdom is profound; because the suchness of the four immeasurables and the four formless absorptions is profound, the perfection of wisdom is profound.”

“Śāriputra! Because the suchness of the eight liberations is profound, the perfection of wisdom is profound; because the suchness of the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive absorptions, and the ten totalities is profound, the perfection of wisdom is profound.”

“Śāriputra! Because the suchness of the four foundations of mindfulness is profound, the perfection of wisdom is profound; because the suchness of the four right endeavors, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path is profound, the perfection of wisdom is profound.”

“Śāriputra! Because the suchness of the gate of liberation of emptiness is profound, the perfection of wisdom is profound; because the suchness of the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness is profound, the perfection of wisdom is profound.”
“Śāriputra, because the suchness of the ten stages of a bodhisattva is profound, the perfection of wisdom is profound.
Śāriputra, [it is thus.]”
Because the suchness of the five eyes is profound, the perfection of wisdom is profound; because the suchness of the six supernormal powers is profound, the perfection of wisdom is profound.

“Śāriputra! Because the suchness of the ten powers of a Buddha is profound, the perfection of wisdom is profound; because the suchness of the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha is profound, the perfection of wisdom is profound.”

“Śāriputra! Because the suchness of the quality of non-forgetfulness is profound, the perfection of wisdom is profound; because the suchness of the state of constant equanimity is profound, the perfection of wisdom is profound.”

“Śāriputra! Because the *tathatā* of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) is profound, the *prajñāpāramitā* is profound; because the *tathatā* of the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*) and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) is profound, the *prajñāpāramitā* is profound.”
“Śāriputra, because the suchness of all dhāraṇī-doors is profound, the perfection of wisdom is profound; because the suchness of all samādhi-doors is profound, the perfection of wisdom is profound.”

“Śāriputra! Because the reality-limit (tathatā) of the fruit of stream-entry is profound, the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) is profound; because the reality-limit of the fruits of once-returner, non-returner, and arhatship is profound, the perfection of wisdom is profound.”
“Śāriputra! Because the suchness of pratyekabuddha-enlightenment is profound, the perfection of wisdom is profound. Śāriputra!”
Because the suchness of the practices of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas is profound, the perfection of wisdom is profound.
"Śāriputra! Because the suchness of the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas is profound, the perfection of wisdom is profound."
At that time, Śāriputra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This Prajñāpāramitā is difficult to fathom.”
The Buddha said, “So it is, Śāriputra!”

Because the suchness of form is difficult to measure, the perfection of wisdom is difficult to measure; because the suchness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is difficult to measure, the perfection of wisdom is difficult to measure.

“Śāriputra! Because the suchness of the eye-base is difficult to fathom, the perfection of wisdom is difficult to fathom; because the suchness of the ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-bases is difficult to fathom, the perfection of wisdom is difficult to fathom.”

“Śāriputra! Because the suchness (*tathatā*) of the form base (*rūpāyatana*) is difficult to fathom, the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) is difficult to fathom; because the suchness of the sound, odor, taste, tangible, and mental-object bases is difficult to fathom, the perfection of wisdom is difficult to fathom.”

“Śāriputra! Because the *tathatā* (suchness) of the eye-element is difficult to fathom, the *prajñāpāramitā* is difficult to fathom. Because the *tathatā* of the form-element, the eye-consciousness-element, eye-contact, and all feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition is difficult to fathom, the *prajñāpāramitā* is difficult to fathom.”

“Śāriputra! Because the suchness of the ear-element is difficult to fathom, the perfection of wisdom is difficult to fathom. Because the suchness of the sound-element, the ear-consciousness-element, ear-contact, and all feelings produced with ear-contact as a condition is difficult to fathom, the perfection of wisdom is difficult to fathom.”

“Śāriputra! Because the suchness of the nose element is difficult to fathom, the perfection of wisdom is difficult to fathom. Because the suchness of the odor element, the nose-consciousness element, nose-contact, and all feelings produced with nose-contact as a condition is difficult to fathom, the perfection of wisdom is difficult to fathom.”

“Śāriputra! Because the suchness of the tongue element is difficult to fathom, the perfection of wisdom is difficult to fathom. Because the suchness of the taste element, the tongue-consciousness element, tongue-contact, and all feelings produced with tongue-contact as a condition is difficult to fathom, the perfection of wisdom is difficult to fathom.”

“Śāriputra! Because the *tathatā* (suchness) of the body element is difficult to fathom, the *prajñāpāramitā* is difficult to fathom. Because the *tathatā* of the tangible object element, the body-consciousness element, body-contact, and all sensations produced with body-contact as a condition is difficult to fathom, the *prajñāpāramitā* is difficult to fathom.”

“Śāriputra! Because the suchness of the mind-element (manodhātu) is difficult to fathom, the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) is difficult to fathom. Because the suchness of the dharma-element, the mind-consciousness-element, and the feeling produced with mind-contact as its condition is difficult to fathom, the perfection of wisdom is difficult to fathom.”

“Śāriputra! Because the suchness of the earth element is difficult to measure, the perfection of wisdom is difficult to measure. Because the suchness of the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements is difficult to measure, the perfection of wisdom is difficult to measure.”
