In a future age, there will be sons of good family and daughters of good family belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle who abandon the profound sūtras of the Great Prajñāpāramitā and seek instead to study sūtras associated with the two vehicles; their desire to seek the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna) therein shall be just like this.”
"What do you think?
Are these sons and daughters of good family wise? Subhūti replied:
"They are of a foolish nature," the Buddha said, "Subhūti!"
"So it is! So it is! You should know that this constitutes a Māra-activity of a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When sons and daughters of good family who abide in the Bodhisattva vehicle are transcribing this profound *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, various forms of eloquence may arise, and they may take delight in expounding various distinct Dharma-gates, thereby preventing the transcription of this profound *Prajñāpāramitā* from reaching completion. You should know that this is a demonic deed of a bodhisattva."

That is to say: delighting in eloquent discourse on generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom; delighting in eloquent discourse on the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm; delighting in eloquent discourse on upholding, reciting, and proclaiming [the Dharma]; delighting in eloquent discourse on tending to the sick and cultivating other meritorious deeds; delighting in eloquent discourse on form; delighting in eloquent discourse on feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness;
delighting in eloquent discourse on the sense base of the eye; delighting in eloquent discourse on the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind;
and delighting in eloquent discourse on the sense base of forms, and the sense bases of sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena.

He delights in explaining the eye-element, and delights in explaining the form-element, the eye-consciousness-element, and the contact of the eye, as well as all feelings produced with eye-contact as their condition;

he delights in explaining the ear-element, and delights in explaining the sound-element, the ear-consciousness-element, and the contact of the ear, as well as all feelings produced with ear-contact as their condition;

he delights in explaining the nose-element, and delights in explaining the odor-element, the nose-consciousness-element, and the contact of the nose, as well as all feelings produced with nose-contact as their condition.

They delight in eloquently expounding the tongue element, the taste element, the tongue-consciousness element, as well as tongue-contact and all sensations produced with tongue-contact as a condition;

they delight in eloquently expounding the body element, the tangible-object element, the body-consciousness element, as well as body-contact and all sensations produced with body-contact as a condition;

they delight in eloquently expounding the mind element, the mental-object element, the mind-consciousness element, as well as mind-contact and all sensations produced with mind-contact as a condition.
He delights in expounding the element of earth; he delights in expounding the elements of water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness.

He delights in expounding ignorance; he delights in expounding volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, existence, birth, and old age, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair.
He delights in expounding the perfection of generosity; he delights in expounding the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom.

He delights in eloquently expounding internal emptiness; he delights in eloquently expounding external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersal emptiness, non-alteration emptiness, essential nature emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common characteristic emptiness, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature.

He delights in eloquently expounding suchness; he delights in eloquently expounding the dharma-realm, the dharma-nature, non-falsity, non-alteration, equality, the state beyond birth, the fixedness of phenomena, the stability of phenomena, the reality-limit, the realm of space, and the inconceivable realm.
He delights in eloquently expounding the noble truth of suffering; he delights in eloquently expounding the noble truths of origin, cessation, and the path.
He delights in expounding the four dhyānas; he delights in expounding the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments;
he delights in expounding the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities;

he delights in expounding the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path.
They delight in expounding the liberation door of emptiness; they delight in expounding the liberation doors of signlessness and wishlessness;
they delight in expounding the ten stages of the bodhisattva;
they delight in expounding the five eyes, and they delight in expounding the six supernormal powers.

He delights in expounding the ten powers of a Buddha; he delights in expounding the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
he delights in expounding the quality of non-forgetfulness, and he delights in expounding the nature of constant abiding in equanimity;
he delights in expounding all-knowledge, the knowledge of the paths, and the knowledge of all aspects.
They delight in expounding all dharani-gates; they delight in expounding all samadhi-gates;
they delight in expounding the fruit of stream-entry; they delight in expounding the fruits of once-returning, non-returning, and arhatship;
they delight in expounding the enlightenment of the pratyekabuddhas.
They delight in expounding all the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas;
they delight in expounding the anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi of all buddhas.
"For what reason?"

"Subhūti! Because the profound *prajñāpāramitā* lacks the characteristic of eloquence; because the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is inconceivable; because the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is beyond deliberation; because the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is without arising or ceasing; because the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is without defilement or purity; because the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is without stability or distraction; because the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is free from names and words; because the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is ineffable; and because the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is unattainable."
Why is this so? Subhūti!
Within the profound perfection of wisdom, all those phenomena previously mentioned are non-existent and entirely unapprehendable.

When sons and daughters of good family who abide in the Bodhisattva vehicle are transcribing this profound *Prajñāpāramitā* sūtra, if such phenomena disturb their minds and prevent them from reaching completion, you should know that these are the deeds of Māra for a bodhisattva.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
can this profound prajñāpāramitā be written down?”
The Buddha said,
“Suvikrāntavikrāmin!
The profound perfection of wisdom cannot be written down.”
Why is this? Subhūti!

Within this profound *prajñāpāramitā* sūtra, the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of form is non-existent and unapprehendable; the intrinsic nature of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is non-existent and unapprehendable.
The intrinsic nature of the eye-base is non-existent and unapprehendable; the intrinsic natures of the ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-bases are non-existent and unapprehendable.
The intrinsic nature of the form-base is non-existent and unapprehendable; the intrinsic natures of the sound-, odor-, taste-, tangible-, and phenomena-bases are non-existent and unapprehendable.

The intrinsic nature of the eye-element is non-existent and unapprehendable; the intrinsic natures of the form-element, the eye-consciousness-element, and eye-contact, as well as all feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition, are non-existent and unapprehendable.

The nature of the ear-element is non-existent and unapprehendable; the nature of the sound-element, the ear-consciousness-element, ear-contact, and all feelings produced with ear-contact as a condition is non-existent and unapprehendable.

The nature of the nose-element is non-existent and unapprehendable; the nature of the odor-element, the nose-consciousness-element, nose-contact, and all feelings produced with nose-contact as a condition is non-existent and unapprehendable.

The nature of the tongue-element is non-existent and unapprehendable; the nature of the taste-element, the tongue-consciousness-element, tongue-contact, and all feelings produced with tongue-contact as a condition is non-existent and unapprehendable.

The intrinsic nature of the body element is non-existent and unapprehendable; the intrinsic nature of the tangible object element, the body-consciousness element, body-contact, and all sensations produced with body-contact as a condition is non-existent and unapprehendable.

The intrinsic nature of the mind element is non-existent and unapprehendable; the intrinsic nature of the mental-object element, the mind-consciousness element, mind-contact, and all sensations produced with mind-contact as a condition is non-existent and unapprehendable.
The intrinsic nature of the earth element is non-existent and unapprehendable; the intrinsic nature of the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements is non-existent and unapprehendable.

The intrinsic nature of ignorance is non-existent and unapprehendable; the intrinsic nature of volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, and old age, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair is non-existent and unapprehendable.

The intrinsic nature of the perfection of generosity is non-existent and unapprehendable; the intrinsic nature of the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom is non-existent and unapprehendable.

The intrinsic nature of internal emptiness is non-existent and unapprehendable; likewise, the intrinsic nature of external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, unchanging emptiness, essential emptiness, the emptiness of own-marks, the emptiness of common marks, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence is non-existent and unapprehendable.

The intrinsic nature of *tathatā* (suchness) is non-existent and unapprehendable; the intrinsic nature of the *dharmadhātu*, *dharmatā*, non-illusory nature, non-alteration, equality, nature free from birth, the fixed nature of phenomena (*dharma-sthititā*), the stability of phenomena (*dharma-vyavasthāna*), the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), the realm of space (*ākāśa-dhātu*), and the inconceivable realm is non-existent and unapprehendable.

The intrinsic nature of the noble truth of suffering is non-existent and unapprehendable; the intrinsic nature of the noble truths of origination, cessation, and the path is non-existent and unapprehendable.
The intrinsic nature of the four dhyānas is non-existent and unapprehendable; the intrinsic nature of the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments is non-existent and unapprehendable.

The intrinsic nature of the eight liberations is non-existent and unapprehendable; the intrinsic nature of the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities is non-existent and unapprehendable.

The intrinsic nature of the four foundations of mindfulness is non-existent and unapprehendable; the intrinsic nature of the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eight branches of the noble path is non-existent and unapprehendable.

The intrinsic nature of the gate of liberation of emptiness is non-existent and unapprehendable; the intrinsic nature of the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness is non-existent and unapprehendable.
The intrinsic nature of the ten stages of a bodhisattva is non-existent and unapprehendable;
the intrinsic nature of the five eyes is non-existent and unapprehendable; the intrinsic nature of the six supernormal powers is non-existent and unapprehendable;

the intrinsic nature of the ten powers of a buddha is non-existent and unapprehendable; and the intrinsic nature of the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha is non-existent and unapprehendable.
The nature of the quality of non-forgetfulness is non-existent and unapprehendable; the nature of the state of constant equanimity is non-existent and unapprehendable.

The nature of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) is non-existent and unapprehendable; the nature of the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*) and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) is non-existent and unapprehendable.
The nature of all dharani-doors is non-existent and unapprehendable; the nature of all samadhi-doors is non-existent and unapprehendable.

The intrinsic nature of the fruit of stream-entry is non-existent and unapprehendable; the intrinsic nature of the fruits of once-returning, non-returning, and arhatship is non-existent and unapprehendable;
the intrinsic nature of pratyekabuddha-enlightenment is non-existent and unapprehendable;
and the intrinsic nature of all the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas is non-existent and unapprehendable.
The unexcelled, perfect enlightenment of all Buddhas has no intrinsic nature and is unapprehendable. "Subhūti!
Because the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is entirely non-existent and unapprehendable, it is 'non-nature' (niḥsvabhāva); this very non-nature is the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā)."
It is not that a dharma devoid of intrinsic nature can write down that which is devoid of intrinsic nature; therefore, the Prajñāpāramitā cannot be written down. "Subhūti!
If sons or daughters of good family belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle should form such a thought as this:"
"In this profound *Prajñāpāramitā* sūtra, non-nature is form; non-nature is feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness;
non-nature is the eye-base; non-nature is the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-bases;
non-nature is the form-base; and non-nature is the sound, odor, taste, tangible, and mental-object bases."

The absence of intrinsic nature is the eye-element; the absence of intrinsic nature is the form-element, the eye-consciousness-element, and the sensations produced with eye-contact as their condition.

The absence of intrinsic nature is the ear-element; the absence of intrinsic nature is the sound-element, the ear-consciousness-element, and the sensations produced with ear-contact as their condition.

The absence of intrinsic nature is the nose-element; the absence of intrinsic nature is the odor-element, the nose-consciousness-element, and the sensations produced with nose-contact as their condition.

The absence of intrinsic nature is the tongue element; the absence of intrinsic nature is the taste element, the tongue-consciousness element, tongue-contact, and all sensations produced with tongue-contact as a condition.

The absence of intrinsic nature is the body element; the absence of intrinsic nature is the tangible-object element, the body-consciousness element, body-contact, and all sensations produced with body-contact as a condition.

The absence of intrinsic nature is the mind element; the absence of intrinsic nature is the mental-object element, the mind-consciousness element, mind-contact, and all sensations produced with mind-contact as a condition.
The absence of intrinsic nature is the earth element; the absence of intrinsic nature is the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements.

The absence of intrinsic nature is ignorance; the absence of intrinsic nature is volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, and old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair.
The absence of intrinsic nature is the perfection of generosity; the absence of intrinsic nature is the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom.

The absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) is internal emptiness; the absence of intrinsic nature is external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, non-alteration emptiness, essential emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common-characteristic emptiness, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of the absence of intrinsic nature, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the absence of intrinsic nature in intrinsic nature.

The absence of intrinsic nature is suchness (*tathatā*); the absence of intrinsic nature is the dharma-sphere (*dharmadhātu*), the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*), the non-falsity, the non-alteration, the equality, the state beyond birth, the fixedness of dharma, the stability of dharma, the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*), the realm of space, and the inconceivable realm.
The absence of intrinsic nature is the noble truth of suffering; the absence of intrinsic nature is the noble truths of origin, cessation, and the path.
The absence of intrinsic nature is the four dhyānas; the absence of intrinsic nature is the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments.
The absence of intrinsic nature is the eight liberations; the absence of intrinsic nature is the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities.

The absence of intrinsic nature is the four foundations of mindfulness; the absence of intrinsic nature is the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path;
the absence of intrinsic nature is the gateway of liberation of emptiness; the absence of intrinsic nature is the gateways of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness;
the absence of intrinsic nature is the ten stages of the bodhisattva.
The absence of intrinsic nature is the five eyes; the absence of intrinsic nature is the six supernormal powers;

the absence of intrinsic nature is the ten powers of a Buddha; the absence of intrinsic nature is the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
the absence of intrinsic nature is the quality of non-forgetfulness; the absence of intrinsic nature is the state of constant abiding in equanimity.
Non-substantiality is omniscience; non-substantiality is the knowledge of the paths and the knowledge of all aspects;
non-substantiality is all the doors of dhāraṇī, and non-substantiality is all the doors of samādhi;
non-substantiality is the fruit of stream-entry, and non-substantiality is the fruits of once-returning, non-returning, and arhatship.
The absence of intrinsic nature is the enlightenment of the pratyekabuddhas;
the absence of intrinsic nature is the practice of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas;
the absence of intrinsic nature is the unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas.
"You should know that this is a deed of Māra for a bodhisattva.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
If sons or daughters of good family belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle were to write down this profound perfection of wisdom and think:
"I am writing down the perfection of wisdom with letters."
“If one clings to written characters as being able to transcribe the *prajñāpāramitā*, you should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva.
Why is this? ‘O Bhagavān!...’”

In this profound *Prajñāpāramitā* sūtra, form (*rūpa*) is without letters; feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) are without letters.
The eye-base (*cakṣur-āyatana*) is without letters; the ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-bases (*śrotra-ghrāṇa-jihvā-kāya-manas-āyatana*) are without letters.
The form-base (*rūpa-āyatana*) is without letters; the sound-, odor-, taste-, tangible-, and phenomena-bases (*śabda-gandha-rasa-spraṣṭavya-dharma-āyatana*) are without letters.
The eye-element is without letters; the form-element, the eye-consciousness-element, eye-contact, and all feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition are without letters.
The ear-element is without letters; the sound-element, the ear-consciousness-element, ear-contact, and all feelings produced with ear-contact as a condition are without letters.
The nose-element is without letters; the odor-element, the nose-consciousness-element, nose-contact, and all feelings produced with nose-contact as a condition are without letters.
The tongue element has no letters; the taste element, the tongue-consciousness element, tongue-contact, and all feelings produced with tongue-contact as a condition have no letters.
The body element has no letters; the tangible object element, the body-consciousness element, body-contact, and all feelings produced with body-contact as a condition have no letters.
The mind element has no letters; the mental-object element, the mind-consciousness element, mind-contact, and all feelings produced with mind-contact as a condition have no letters.
The earth element is without letters; the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements are without letters.

Ignorance is without letters; volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, existence, birth, and old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are without letters.
The perfection of generosity is without letters; the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom are without letters.

Inner emptiness is without syllables; outer emptiness, inner-and-outer emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, the emptiness of the ultimate meaning, the emptiness of conditioned phenomena, the emptiness of unconditioned phenomena, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, the emptiness of dispersion, the emptiness of non-alteration, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, the emptiness of self-characteristics, the emptiness of common characteristics, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature are without syllables.

True suchness is without syllables; the dharma-realm, the dharma-nature, the non-falsity, the non-alteration, the equality, the state beyond birth, the fixed nature of dharmas, the stability of dharmas, the limit of reality, the realm of space, and the inconceivable realm are without syllables.
The noble truth of suffering is without words; the noble truths of origin, cessation, and the path are without words.
The four dhyānas are without words; the four immeasurables and the four formless absorptions are without words.
The eight liberations are without words; the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive absorptions, and the ten totalities are without words.

The four foundations of mindfulness are without letters; the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path are without letters;
the gate of liberation of emptiness is without letters; the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness are without letters;
and the ten stages of the bodhisattva are without letters.
The five eyes are without letters; the six supernormal powers are without letters;

the ten powers of a Buddha are without letters; the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are without letters;
the quality of non-forgetfulness is without letters; and the state of constant abiding in equanimity is without letters.
All-knowledge is without letters; the knowledge of the paths and the knowledge of all aspects are without letters;
all dharani-doors are without letters; all samadhi-doors are without letters;
the fruit of stream-entry is without letters; the fruits of once-returning, non-returning, and arhatship are without letters.
The enlightenment of the pratyekabuddhas is without words;
the practices of all bodhisattva mahāsattvas are without words;
and the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas is without words.
Therefore, one should not cling to the notion that there are syllables capable of writing down the *prajñāpāramitā*.
"World-Honored One,
if sons and daughters of good family belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle should form such a clinging as this:"
"In this profound *Prajñāpāramitā* sūtra, there are no syllables that constitute form; there are no syllables that constitute feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
There are no syllables that constitute the eye-base; there are no syllables that constitute the bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind.
There are no syllables that constitute the form-base; there are no syllables that constitute the bases of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, or mental phenomena."

The absence of letters is the eye-element; the absence of letters is the form-element, the eye-consciousness-element, and eye-contact, as well as all feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition.

The absence of letters is the ear-element; the absence of letters is the sound-element, the ear-consciousness-element, and ear-contact, as well as all feelings produced with ear-contact as a condition.

The absence of letters is the nose-element; the absence of letters is the odor-element, the nose-consciousness-element, and nose-contact, as well as all feelings produced with nose-contact as a condition.
The tongue element is without letters; the taste element, the tongue-consciousness element, tongue-contact, and all sensations produced with tongue-contact as a condition are without letters.
The body element is without letters; the tangible-object element, the body-consciousness element, body-contact, and all sensations produced with body-contact as a condition are without letters.
The mind element is without letters; the mental-phenomena element, the mind-consciousness element, mind-contact, and all sensations produced with mind-contact as a condition are without letters.
The absence of letters is the earth element; the absence of letters is the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements.

The absence of letters is ignorance; the absence of letters is volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, and old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair.
The absence of letters is the perfection of generosity; the absence of letters is the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom.

The absence of words is inner emptiness; the absence of words is outer emptiness, inner-and-outer emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, non-alteration emptiness, essential nature emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common characteristic emptiness, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of non-apprehensibility, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature.

The absence of words is suchness; the absence of words is the dharma-realm, the dharma-nature, the non-falsehood, the non-alteration, the equality, the state beyond birth, the fixedness of dharma, the stability of dharma, the limit of reality, the realm of space, and the inconceivable realm.
The noble truth of suffering is without letters; the noble truths of origination, cessation, and the path are without letters.
The four dhyānas are without letters; the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments are without letters.
The eight liberations are without letters; the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities are without letters.

The absence of letters is the four foundations of mindfulness; the absence of letters is the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path;
the absence of letters is the gate of liberation of emptiness; the absence of letters is the gate of liberation of signlessness and the gate of liberation of wishlessness;
the absence of letters is the ten stages of the bodhisattva.
The absence of words is the five eyes; the absence of words is the six supernormal powers;

the absence of words is the ten powers of a Buddha; the absence of words is the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
the absence of words is the quality of non-forgetfulness; the absence of words is the state of constant abiding in equanimity.
The absence of letters is omniscience; the absence of letters is the knowledge of the paths and the knowledge of all aspects;
the absence of letters is all doors of dhāraṇī, and the absence of letters is all doors of samādhi;
the absence of letters is the fruit of stream-entry, and the absence of letters is the fruits of once-returning, non-returning, and arhatship.
The absence of words is the enlightenment of the pratyekabuddhas;
the absence of words is the practice of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas;
the absence of words is the unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas.
"You should know that this is a deed of Māra for a bodhisattva.
The Buddha said,
"Suvikrāntavikrāmin!..."
So it is! So it is! It is just as you have said.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When sons of good family or daughters of good family who abide in the Bodhisattva vehicle write down, uphold, read, recite, cultivate, contemplate, and explain this profound *prajñāpāramitā* sūtra, if they give rise to thoughts of countries, thoughts of towns and cities, thoughts of royal capitals, or thoughts of specific regions, you should know that these are the deeds of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When sons or daughters of good family who have set out in the bodhisattva vehicle write down, uphold, read, recite, cultivate, contemplate, and explain this profound *prajñāpāramitā* sūtra, if they give rise to thoughts of their teachers and preceptors, or thoughts of their fellow students and virtuous friends, or thoughts of their parents, wives, and children, or thoughts of their brothers and sisters, or thoughts of their kinsmen and companions, you should know that these are the deeds of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When sons and daughters of good family who abide in the Bodhisattva vehicle write down, uphold, read, recite, practice, contemplate, and expound this profound *Prajñāpāramitā* Sūtra, if they give rise to thoughts of wicked bandits or ferocious beasts; or thoughts of wicked people or malevolent spirits; or thoughts of social gatherings and amusements; or thoughts of pleasure with courtesans; or thoughts of repaying kindness or resentment; or any other immeasurable and diverse thoughts—these are all instigated by Māra to create obstacles for the *Prajñāpāramitā*. You should know that these are the deeds of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When sons and daughters of good family who abide in the Bodhisattva vehicle write down, uphold, read, recite, cultivate, contemplate, and explain this profound *prajñāpāramitā* sūtra, they may receive great fame, honor, and offerings—namely, clothing, food and drink, bedding, medicine, and material wealth. If these sons and daughters of good family become attached to such things and neglect their spiritual practice, you should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When sons and daughters of good family who abide in the Bodhisattva vehicle are copying, upholding, reading, reciting, practicing, contemplating, and expounding this profound *Prajñāpāramitā* sūtra, there will be various evil Māras who take hold of various worldly treatises or even scriptures associated with the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), and falsely manifesting as friends, they will offer them to the Bodhisattvas. These [treatises] extensively explain worldly superior matters, or else they extensively explain the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), sense bases (*āyatana*), truths (*satya*), dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣikadharma*), the three gates of liberation (*vimokṣamukha*), the four meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), and so forth, claiming: 'The meaning and intent of these scriptures are profound; you should diligently practice and study them, and abandon the scriptures you have previously practiced.'"

These sons and daughters of good family who belong to the Bodhisattva vehicle, through their skillful means, should not become attached to the worldly treatises given by evil Māras, nor to the sūtras of the two vehicles.

Why is this? Because worldly treatises and the scriptures of the two vehicles cannot give rise to the knowledge of all modes; they are not skillful means for proceeding toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

"Subhūti! Within this profound sūtra of the Perfection of Wisdom, I have extensively explained the skillful means of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas' path; if one diligently trains in this, one will swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

If sons or daughters of good family belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle should abandon the profound sūtras of the *prajñāpāramitā* and instead study the worldly treatises of Māra or the sūtras of the two vehicles, one should know that this constitutes a work of Māra for a bodhisattva.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If those who are able to listen to the Dharma take delight in hearing, copying, upholding, reciting, and practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, yet those who are able to preach the Dharma are attached to pleasure and indolence, unwilling to preach it, you should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If the one who preaches the Dharma has a mind that is neither attached to pleasure nor indolent, and delights in preaching the profound *prajñāpāramitā* to others, skillfully encouraging them to copy, uphold, read, recite, and cultivate it; yet the one who listens to the Dharma is indolent and attached to pleasure, having no desire to listen or receive it—you should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If those who are able to hear the Dharma delight in hearing, copying, receiving, upholding, reciting, and practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, yet the one who is able to preach it desires to go elsewhere and is unable to preach it for them, you should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If a teacher of the Dharma delights in expounding the profound *prajñāpāramitā* to others and skillfully encourages them to copy, uphold, recite, and cultivate it, yet a listener of the Dharma wishes to travel to another region and thus fails to receive and hear it, you should know that this is an act of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If the one who preaches the Dharma possesses great evil desires, being deeply attached to fame, profit, clothing, food and drink, bedding, medicine, offerings, and material wealth; while the one who listens to the Dharma has few desires, is easily contented, practices the life of seclusion, is courageous and diligent, is endowed with mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom, and feels weary of and fears gain, honor, and reputation—then these two will not be in harmony. They shall fail to obtain the preaching and listening, the copying, receiving and upholding, reading and reciting, or the cultivation of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. You should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."

"Furthermore, Subhūti! Suppose the one who preaches the Dharma has few desires, is easily contented, practices seclusion, exerts himself with courageous diligence, and is endowed with mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom; he detests and fears gain, honor, and fame. Yet the one who listens to the Dharma possesses great evil desires, craving and valuing reputation, profit, clothing, food and drink, bedding, medicine, offerings, and material wealth. Because these two are not in harmony, they fail to obtain the opportunity to preach and listen to, write down, receive and uphold, read and recite, or practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. You should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti! A preacher of the Dharma should practice and undertake the twelve dhūta-guṇas:

first, dwelling in an araṇya; second, always begging for food; third, wearing robes of discarded rags; fourth, eating at a single session; fifth, eating from a single sitting; sixth, accepting whatever food is obtained; seventh, dwelling among tombs; eighth, dwelling in the open air; ninth, dwelling at the foot of a tree; tenth, always sitting and not lying down; eleventh, using whatever bedding is obtained; and twelfth, possessing only the three robes."

If those who listen to the Dharma do not accept the twelve dhūta qualities—meaning they do not dwell in forest hermitages, and so forth, up to not accepting the practice of wearing only three robes—and if the two parties do not harmonize such that they fail to engage in the exposition and listening, the copying, receiving and upholding, reading and reciting, and the cultivation of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, you should know that this constitutes a demonic deed (*mārakarman*) for the bodhisattva.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

Suppose the one who listens to the Dharma observes and practices the twelve dhūta-qualities—namely, dwelling in an araṇya, up to and including accepting only three robes—while the one who preaches the Dharma does not observe the twelve dhūta-qualities—namely, not dwelling in an araṇya, up to and including not accepting only three robes—and thus the two are not in harmony, they will fail to achieve the preaching and listening, the copying, receiving, upholding, reciting, and practicing of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. You should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."

"Furthermore, Subhūti, suppose the one who can preach the Dharma possesses faith, ethical discipline, and a noble intention, and desires to explain the profound *prajñāpāramitā* to others, encouraging them through skillful means to copy, uphold, read, recite, and cultivate it; yet the one who listens to the Dharma lacks faith, lacks ethical discipline, and lacks a noble intention, and does not delight in hearing or receiving it. Because these two are not in harmony, they fail to achieve the preaching and listening, the copying, upholding, reading, reciting, and cultivation of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. You should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

Suppose the one who listens to the Dharma possesses faith, ethical discipline, and a noble intention, and seeks to hear, write down, receive, uphold, recite, and cultivate the profound *prajñāpāramitā*; yet the one who preaches the Dharma lacks faith, lacks ethical discipline, lacks a noble intention, and has no desire to preach it. Because these two are not in harmony, they fail to achieve the hearing and preaching, the writing, receiving, upholding, reciting, and cultivation of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. You should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If the one who preaches the Dharma has a mind free from stinginess and is able to relinquish everything, while the one who listens to the Dharma has a mind possessed by stinginess and is unable to renounce anything, these two will not be in harmony. They shall fail to obtain the preaching and listening, the copying, the upholding, the reading and reciting, and the cultivation of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. You should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If the one who listens to the Dharma has a mind free from stinginess and is able to relinquish everything, while the one who preaches the Dharma has a mind possessed by stinginess and is unable to renounce anything, these two will not be in harmony. They shall fail to obtain the preaching and listening, the copying, the upholding, the reciting, and the cultivation of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. You should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If those who wish to hear the Dharma seek to provide offerings of robes, food and drink, bedding, medicine, and other necessities to those who preach the Dharma, yet the preachers do not wish to accept them, and because of this lack of harmony, they fail to engage in the preaching and hearing, copying, upholding, reading, reciting, and practicing of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, you should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If the one who preaches the Dharma seeks to provide the listener with clothing, food and drink, bedding, medicine, and other necessities, yet the listener does not wish to accept them, and because of this lack of harmony between the two, they fail to engage in the preaching and listening, the copying, upholding, reciting, and cultivation of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, you should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If the one who preaches the Dharma possesses the wisdom of opening [the meaning] yet does not delight in extensive explanation, and the one who listens to the Dharma possesses the wisdom of unfolding [the words] yet does not delight in concise explanation, and the two do not harmonize, such that they fail to achieve the preaching and listening, the copying, the upholding, the reciting, and the cultivation of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, you should know that this is a deed of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If the listener possesses the wisdom of opening [the meaning] and desires only a brief explanation, while the speaker possesses the wisdom of exposition and desires only a detailed explanation, and the two do not harmonize, such that they fail to obtain the teaching, listening, copying, upholding, reciting, and practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, you should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."

"Furthermore, Subhūti, it may be that the one who preaches the Dharma takes exclusive delight in extensively knowing the sequential meanings of the twelve branches of the teaching—namely, the sūtras, geyas, vyākaraṇas, gāthās, udānas, nidānas, avadānas, vṛttakas, jātakas, vaipulyas, adbhutadharmas, and upadeśas—whereas the one who listens to the Dharma does not take delight in extensively knowing the sequential meanings of the twelve branches of the teaching, from the sūtras up to the upadeśas. When these two are not in harmony, they will fail to obtain the preaching and listening, the copying, receiving and upholding, reading and reciting, and the cultivation of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. You should know that this is an act of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

Suppose the listener is intent on and delights in extensively knowing the sequential meaning of the twelvefold teaching—namely, from the *sūtra* up to the *upadeśa*—while the speaker does not delight in extensively knowing the sequential meaning of the twelvefold teaching—namely, from the *sūtra* up to the *upadeśa*. Because these two are not in harmony, they fail to achieve the preaching and listening, the copying, receiving and maintaining, reading and reciting, and the cultivation of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. You should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If the one who preaches the Dharma has already accomplished the six pāramitās, while the one who listens to the Dharma has not yet accomplished the six pāramitās, they will not be in harmony. They shall fail to obtain the preaching and listening, the copying, upholding, reciting, and cultivation of the profound Prajñāpāramitā; you should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If the one who listens to the Dharma has already accomplished the six pāramitās, while the one who preaches the Dharma has not yet accomplished the six pāramitās, and the two are thus not in harmony, they will fail to obtain the preaching and listening, the copying, the upholding, the reciting, and the cultivation of the profound Prajñāpāramitā. You should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle Three Hundred and Three;
The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle Three Hundred and Four.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.
The First Part of the Chapter on the Deeds of Māra, Forty: Part Two.

"Furthermore, Subhūti, if the one who preaches the Dharma possesses skillful means regarding the six pāramitās, while the one who listens to the Dharma lacks skillful means regarding the six pāramitās, these two will not be in harmony. They shall fail to obtain the preaching and listening, the copying, the upholding, the reciting, and the cultivation of the profound Prajñāpāramitā; you should know that this is a deed of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If the one who listens to the Dharma possesses skillful means regarding the six perfections, while the one who preaches the Dharma lacks skillful means regarding the six perfections, these two will not be in harmony. They shall fail to obtain the preaching and listening, the copying, the upholding, the reading and reciting, and the cultivation of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. You should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If the one who preaches the Dharma has attained dhāraṇī, while the one who listens to the Dharma has not attained dhāraṇī, the two will not be in harmony. They will fail to achieve the preaching and listening, the copying, receiving and upholding, reading and reciting, and the cultivation of the profound Prajñāpāramitā; you should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If the one who listens to the Dharma has attained dhāraṇī, while the one who preaches the Dharma has not attained dhāraṇī, these two will not be in harmony. They shall fail to obtain the preaching and listening, the copying, the upholding, the reciting, and the cultivation of the profound Prajñāpāramitā; you should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."

"Furthermore, Subhūti, if the one who preaches the Dharma desires that others respectfully copy, receive, uphold, read, recite, and practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, while the one who listens to the Dharma does not desire to respectfully copy, receive, uphold, read, recite, and practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, then because these two are not in harmony, they will fail to achieve the preaching and listening, the copying, receiving, upholding, reading, reciting, and practicing of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. You should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If the listener desires to respectfully copy, receive, uphold, recite, and cultivate the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, while the speaker does not desire to respectfully copy, receive, uphold, recite, and cultivate the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, and the two do not reach harmony, such that they fail to engage in the speaking, listening, copying, receiving, upholding, reciting, and cultivating of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, you should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If the one who preaches the Dharma has already abandoned the hindrances of sensual desire, ill will, sloth-and-torpor, restlessness-and-remorse, and doubt, while the one who listens to the Dharma has not yet abandoned the hindrances of sensual desire, ill will, sloth-and-torpor, restlessness-and-remorse, and doubt, and thus the two are not in harmony, they will fail to obtain the preaching and listening, the copying, receiving, upholding, reading, reciting, and cultivation of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. You should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If the one who listens to the Dharma has already abandoned the hindrances of sensual desire, ill will, sloth and torpor, restlessness and remorse, and doubt, while the one who preaches the Dharma has not yet abandoned the hindrances of sensual desire, ill will, sloth and torpor, restlessness and remorse, and doubt, and thus the two are not in harmony, they will fail to obtain the opportunity for preaching and listening, copying, receiving and upholding, reading and reciting, or practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. You should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When someone is copying, upholding, reading, reciting, practicing, contemplating, or expounding this profound *Prajñāpāramitā* Sūtra, if someone should come and speak of the various sufferings of the three miserable realms, saying further:

'You should exert yourself with diligence in this very body to quickly reach the end of suffering and enter parinirvāṇa; why do you linger in the great ocean of birth and death to undergo hundreds of thousands of kinds of unbearable sufferings in pursuit of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment? "

"Because of these words, they will fail to reach the ultimate goal regarding the profound sūtras of the *prajñāpāramitā*—whether in writing them down, receiving and upholding them, reciting and chanting them, practicing and cultivating them, contemplating them, or explaining them. You should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti! When someone is writing down,
receiving, upholding, reading, reciting, practicing, contemplating, or expounding this profound *prajñāpāramitā* sūtra,
if there should come someone who praises and describes the various [attributes] of the human realm..."
Regarding superior matters, he praises and describes the various excellent and sublime things of the Cāturmahārājakāyika, Trāyastriṃśa, Yāma, Tuṣita, Nirmāṇarati, and Paranirmitavaśavartin heavens;
and he praises and describes the various excellent and sublime things of the Brahmakāyika, Brahmapurohita, Brahmakāyika (Brahmapārṣadya), and Mahābrahmā heavens.
He spoke in praise of the sublime and wondrous qualities of the Ābhāsvara, Parīttābhā, Apramāṇābhā, and Ābhāsvara-svabhāva devas;
he spoke in praise of the sublime and wondrous qualities of the Śubha, Parīttaśubha, Apramāṇaśubha, and Śubhakṛtsna devas;
and he spoke in praise of the Bṛhatphala, Parīttabṛhatphala, and Apramāṇabṛhatphala devas.

...the various sublime and wondrous matters of the Bṛhatphala Heaven; he praised and described the various sublime and wondrous matters of the Avṛha Heaven, the Atapa Heaven, the Sudṛśa Heaven, the Sudarśana Heaven, and the Akaniṣṭha Heaven;

and he praised and described the [attainments of] the Sphere of Infinite Space, the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness, the Sphere of Nothingness, and the Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-Perception.
Regarding these most excellent matters, he further addressed him, saying:

"Although you may experience the pleasures of desire in the desire realm, the bliss of meditative concentration in the form realm, and the bliss of tranquil absorption in the formless realm, all of these are impermanent, suffering, empty, selfless, impure, and subject to decay; they are phenomena that end, fade away, depart, and cease. Why do you not apply yourself with diligence to this very body to attain the fruit of a stream-enterer, or the fruit of a once-returner, or the fruit of a non-returner, or the fruit of an arhat, or the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, thereby entering parinirvāṇa for ultimate peace and happiness? Why remain for so long in the cycle of birth and death, needlessly undergoing various sufferings for the sake of others, while seeking to proceed toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?"

"Because of those words, one will fail to reach the ultimate goal regarding the profound sūtras of the *prajñāpāramitā*—whether in their transcription, reception and retention, recitation, cultivation, contemplation, or exposition; know that this is an act of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When the one who preaches the Dharma is free from worldly entanglements and possesses unimpeded mastery, yet the one who listens to the Dharma brings along a large multitude of people who cause disturbance and bondage, so that the two are not in harmony and fail to obtain the preaching and listening, the copying, upholding, reading, reciting, and cultivation of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, you should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

Suppose the one who listens to the Dharma is alone, free from burdens, unimpeded, and at ease, while the one who expounds the Dharma is accompanied by a large multitude, entangled and bound by them. Because these two are not in harmony, they fail to engage in the exposition and listening, the copying, receiving and upholding, reading and reciting, or the cultivation of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. You should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If the one who preaches the Dharma does not delight in being among a crowd, while the one who listens to the Dharma delights in being among a crowd, and the two are thus not in harmony, they will fail to obtain the opportunity for preaching and listening, copying, upholding, reciting, and practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. You should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If those who listen to the Dharma do not delight in the company of the multitude, while those who preach the Dharma delight in dwelling among the multitude, these two will not be in harmony. Consequently, they shall fail to obtain the opportunity for the preaching and listening, the copying, the upholding, the reciting, and the cultivation of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. You should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If the one who preaches the Dharma desires that the listener provide full assistance in what I have done, yet the listener does not comply with that desire, and the two do not reach harmony, such that they fail to obtain the preaching and listening, the copying, receiving and upholding, reciting, and practicing of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, you should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If those who wish to listen to the Dharma desire to assist the speaker in all their undertakings, yet the speaker does not comply with their wishes, and because the two are not in harmony, they fail to obtain the teaching and listening, the copying, the upholding, the reciting, and the cultivation of the profound Prajñāpāramitā—know that this is a deed of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

Suppose a teacher of the Dharma, for the sake of material gain, desires to explain the profound *prajñāpāramitā* to others and further wishes to cause them to write it down, receive and uphold it, recite it, and cultivate it; yet the listener, understanding his motive, does not wish to receive it from him. Because these two do not harmonize, they fail to obtain the explanation and listening, the writing, receiving and upholding, reciting, and cultivation of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. You should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."

"Furthermore, Subhūti! Suppose there is one who listens to the Dharma for the sake of material gain, desiring to request another to preach the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, and further wishing to employ skillful means to copy, receive, uphold, recite, and cultivate it; yet the one who preaches the Dharma, knowing their motive, does not comply with the request. Because these two are not in harmony, they fail to obtain the preaching and listening, the copying, receiving, upholding, reciting, and cultivation of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. You should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If the one who can preach the Dharma wishes to travel to another region where life and limb are in danger, while the one who can listen to the Dharma fears for their life and does not wish to go along with them, and thus the two do not harmonize, failing to obtain the opportunity to preach and listen, to copy, receive and uphold, read and recite, or practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, you should know that this is an affair of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

Suppose the one who wishes to hear the Dharma intends to travel to another region where life and limb are in danger, while the one who wishes to preach the Dharma fears for their own life and does not wish to go with them. Because these two do not harmonize, they fail to engage in the preaching and hearing, copying, receiving and upholding, reading and reciting, or practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. You should know that this is the work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If the one who can preach the Dharma wishes to travel to another region where food and water are scarce, and the one who can listen to the Dharma fears such hardships and does not wish to go along with them, and because these two are not in harmony, they fail to obtain the opportunity to preach and listen, to copy, receive and uphold, read and recite, or practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, you should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If those who wish to hear the Dharma intend to travel to another region where food and water are scarce, and the one who wishes to preach the Dharma, fearing their hardships, does not go with them, then because the two are not in harmony, they will fail to explain, listen to, write down, receive, uphold, read, recite, or practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. You should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."

"Furthermore, Subhūti! Suppose a teacher of the Dharma wishes to go to another region that is prosperous and joyful, and a listener of the Dharma wishes to follow him. At that time, the teacher of the Dharma should skillfully admonish him, saying:

'Although you wish to follow me for the sake of gain, will you necessarily achieve your heart's desire upon reaching that place? You should reflect well and carefully; do not later feel sorrow or regret.'"
At that time, those listening to the Dharma, having heard this, thought to themselves:
"This is his sign of not wishing for me to leave; even if I were to follow him persistently, would I necessarily hear the Dharma?"

For this reason, he does not follow him; thus, the two do not reach harmony, and they fail to obtain the opportunity to explain or listen to, write down, receive and uphold, read and recite, or practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. You should know that this constitutes a work of Māra for a bodhisattva.

"Furthermore, Subhūti! Suppose a teacher of the Dharma wishes to travel to another region, and the road he must traverse passes through a vast wilderness that is perilous and difficult, where there are many fears of bandits, fears of *caṇḍālas*, fears of hunters, wild beasts, venomous snakes, and the like. When a listener wishes to follow him on his journey, the teacher of the Dharma should use skillful means to admonish him, saying:
'For what reason do you now follow me without any business of your own, intending to pass through such places of peril? You should reflect upon this well so as not to cause regret later.'"
At that time, the listeners, having heard this, thought to themselves:
"This person likely does not wish for us to follow him; even if we were to insist on following, why would we hear the Dharma?"

"Because of these causes and conditions, he does not follow him; thus, the two do not harmonize, and they fail to obtain the opportunity to explain, listen to, write down, receive, uphold, read, recite, or practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. You should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

There may be many donors who frequently follow after a Dharma-preacher. When a listener comes to request that he preach the *prajñāpāramitā*, if the preacher is hindered by circumstances and lacks the leisure to speak immediately, and the listener consequently conceives resentment and refuses to listen when the preaching occurs later, such that the two are not in harmony and fail to engage in the profound *prajñāpāramitā*—neither preaching nor listening, neither copying, upholding, reading, reciting, nor practicing it—one should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

There are certain evil Māras who, assuming the form of bhikṣus, approach the Bodhisattva with skillful means to destroy him, so that he may not copy, uphold, recite, practice, contemplate, or explain to others the profound sūtras of the Prajñāpāramitā."
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha,

saying: “World-Honored One, how does Māra, the Evil One, assuming the guise of a bhikṣu, approach a bodhisattva and employ skillful means to destroy them, so that they do not write down, receive and uphold, read and recite, practice, contemplate, or explain to others this profound sūtra of the Prajñāpāramitā?”
The Buddha said, “Subhūti!

There are certain evil Māras who take the form of bhikṣus and approach the bodhisattvas with skillful means to destroy them, causing them to disparage and become weary of the profound Prajñāpāramitā, saying these words:”
"The markless sūtras you have studied and recited are not the true Prajñāpāramitā; the sūtras with marks that I have studied and recited are the true Prajñāpāramitā."

When these words were spoken, there were bodhisattvas who had not yet received their prediction of enlightenment and consequently gave rise to doubt regarding the *prajñāpāramitā*. Because of this doubt, they developed a sense of revulsion toward the *prajñāpāramitā*; because of this revulsion, they failed to transcribe, uphold, read, recite, cultivate, contemplate, or explain to others the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. One should know that this constitutes a work of Māra for a bodhisattva.
"Furthermore, Subhūti! There are certain evil Māras who take the form of bhikṣus and approach a bodhisattva, saying to that bodhisattva:

'If a bodhisattva practices this perfection of wisdom, they will only realize the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) and attain the fruit of a stream-enterer, or the fruit of a once-returner, or the fruit of a non-returner, or the fruit of an arhat, or the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha; they will never be able to attain the unsurpassed fruit of Buddhahood. For what reason should you exert yourself in vain upon this?'"

When a bodhisattva, having heard this, does not write down, receive and uphold, read and recite, practice, contemplate, or explain to others the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, you should know that this is a work of Māra for the bodhisattva.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
When this profound *prajñāpāramitā* is being explained or heard, many demonic obstacles (*mārakarman*) will arise as hindrances; the bodhisattva should recognize them and keep far away from them."
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What are called the deeds of Māra and obstacles, which a bodhisattva should recognize and distance himself from?”
The Buddha said, “Suvikrāntavikrāmin!

When this profound *prajñāpāramitā* is being taught or heard, there will be many demonic obstacles (*mārakarman*) resembling the *prajñā*, *dhyāna*, *vīrya*, *kṣānti*, *śīla*, and *dāna* pāramitās; bodhisattvas should recognize and remain far removed from them.”
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When this profound *prajñāpāramitā* is being explained or heard, there will be many demonic obstacles (*mārakarman*) resembling the emptinesses—namely: internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, non-alteration emptiness, essential emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common-characteristic emptiness, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of non-apprehensibility, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence. A bodhisattva should recognize these and remain far removed from them."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When this profound *prajñāpāramitā* is being explained or heard, there will be many demonic obstacles (*mārakarman*) resembling true suchness (*tathatā*), the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), non-falsity, non-alteration, equality, the state beyond birth, the fixed nature of phenomena (*dharmaniyāmatā*), the stability of phenomena (*dharmaniyāmatā*), the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), the realm of space (*ākāśadhātu*), and the inconceivable realm (*acintyadhātu*). A bodhisattva should recognize these and remain far removed from them."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When this profound *prajñāpāramitā* is being explained or heard, there may be evil Māras who, assuming the guise of bhikṣus, come to where the bodhisattva is and proclaim teachings associated with the two vehicles—namely, the four noble truths, the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative concentrations, the ten totalities, the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, the eightfold noble path, the three doors of liberation, the six superknowledges, and so forth. Having taught these dharmas, they say to the bodhisattva:
'Great Being, you should know this!'"

Furthermore, if by diligently training in this Dharma one can attain the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, or the fruit of arhatship, or even the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha—thereby becoming far removed from all birth, old age, sickness, and death—what need is there for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?
"This is an obstacle and hindrance caused by Māra regarding the *prajñā*; a bodhisattva should recognize it and remain far removed from it.

Furthermore, Subhūti, there are evil Māras who take the form of bhikṣus, with dignified deportment and a handsome appearance. When a bodhisattva sees them, he develops deep attachment; because of this, his omniscience (*sarvajñājñāna*) is diminished, and he fails to hear, write down, uphold, recite, practice, contemplate, or explain the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. You should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

There are certain evil Māras who manifest in the form of a Buddha, their bodies pure golden in color, with a constant radiance extending one fathom, fully endowed with the thirty-two marks of a great man and adorned by the eighty secondary signs. When a bodhisattva sees them, they develop deep attachment; because of this, they diminish their omniscient wisdom (*sarvajñajñāna*) and fail to hear, write down, receive, uphold, recite, cultivate, contemplate, or explain the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. You should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
There may be evil Māras who manifest in the form of a Buddha, surrounded by bhikṣus proclaiming the essentials of the Dharma. When a bodhisattva sees this, they develop a deep attachment and think:
'May I also be like this in the future.'"

"Because of this, they diminish the wisdom of all-knowledge (sarvajñajñāna) and fail to hear, write down, receive and uphold, read and recite, practice, contemplate, or explain the profound Prajñāpāramitā; you should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

There are evil Māras who manifest in the forms of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas—whether numbering a hundred, a thousand, or even immeasurably many—and they may practice the perfection of giving, or practice the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom. When a bodhisattva sees them, he develops deep attachment; because of this, his omniscience is diminished, and he fails to hear, write down, receive, uphold, recite, cultivate, contemplate, or explain the profound perfection of wisdom. You should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Why is that? Subhūti!
Within this profound perfection of wisdom, form does not exist; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness do not exist."

If, in this place, form does not exist, and feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness do not exist, then in this place the Buddha does not exist, nor do bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, or pratyekabuddhas exist.
Why is this? Because all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature.
"Suvikrāntavikrāmin!
Within this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, the sense-base of the eye does not exist; the sense-bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind do not exist.

If, in this place, the sense-base of the eye does not exist, and the sense-bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind do not exist, then in this place the Buddha does not exist, nor do the bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas exist.
Why is this? Because all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature.
"Suvikrāntavikrāmin!
Within this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, the sphere of form does not exist; the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena do not exist.

If, in this place, the sphere of form does not exist, and the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena do not exist, then in this place the Buddha does not exist, nor do bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, or pratyekabuddhas exist.
Why is this? Because all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature.
"Suvikrāntavikrāmin!..."

Within this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, the eye-element does not exist; the form-element, the eye-consciousness-element, as well as eye-contact and the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition do not exist.

If, in a certain place, the eye-element is non-existent, and the form-element up to the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition are non-existent, then in that place the Buddha is non-existent, and the bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas are also non-existent.
Why is this? Because all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature.
"Suvikrāntavikrāmin! [It is thus.]”

Within this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, the ear-element does not exist; the sound-element, the ear-consciousness-element, as well as ear-contact and the various sensations produced with ear-contact as a condition, do not exist.

If, in this place, the ear-element does not exist, and the sound-element up to the various feelings produced with ear-contact as a condition do not exist, then in this place the Buddha does not exist, nor do the bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, or pratyekabuddhas exist.
Why is this? Because all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature.
"Suvikrāntavikrāmin! [It is thus.]”

Within this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, the nose-element (*ghrāṇadhātu*) does not exist; the odor-element (*gandhadhātu*), the nose-consciousness-element (*ghrāṇavijñānadhātu*), as well as nose-contact (*ghrāṇasparśa*) and the various feelings (*vedanā*) produced with nose-contact as a condition, do not exist.

If, in this place, the nose-element is non-existent, and the odor-element up to the various feelings produced with nose-contact as a condition are non-existent, then in this place the Buddha is non-existent, and bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas are also non-existent.
Why is this? Because all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature.
"Suvikrāntavikrāmin!

Within this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, the tongue element (*jihvādhātu*) does not exist; the taste element (*rasadhātu*), the tongue-consciousness element (*jihvāvijñānadhātu*), tongue-contact (*jihvāsaṃsparśa*), and all sensations (*vedanā*) produced with tongue-contact as a condition do not exist.

If, in a certain place, the tongue-element is non-existent, and the taste-element up to the various feelings produced with tongue-contact as a condition are non-existent, then in that place the Buddha is non-existent, and Bodhisattvas, Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas are also non-existent.
Why is this? Because all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature. "Subhūti!

Within this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, the body element (*kāyadhātu*) does not exist; the tangible object element (*spraṣṭavyadhātu*), the body-consciousness element (*kāyavijñānadhātu*), as well as body-contact (*kāyasparśa*) and all feelings (*vedanā*) produced with body-contact as a condition, do not exist.

If, in this place, the body-element is non-existent, and the touch-element up to the various feelings produced with body-contact as a condition are non-existent, then in that place the Buddha is non-existent, and bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas are also non-existent.
Why is this? Because all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature. "Subhūti!..."

Within this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, the mind-element (*manodhātu*) does not exist; the dharma-element, the mind-consciousness-element, as well as mental contact (*manaḥsaṃsparśa*) and the various feelings produced with mental contact as a condition do not exist.

If, in a certain place, the mind-element (*manodhātu*) is non-existent, and the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*) up to the various feelings produced with mind-contact as condition are non-existent, then in that place the Buddha is non-existent, and bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas are also non-existent.
Why is this? Because all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature.
"Suvikrāntavikrāmin!
Within this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, the earth element does not exist; the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements do not exist.

If, in a certain place, the earth element does not exist, and the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements do not exist, then in that place the Buddha does not exist, nor do bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, or pratyekabuddhas exist.
Why is this? Because all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature. "Subhūti!..."

Within this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, ignorance does not exist; volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, sensation, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, and old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair do not exist.

If, in this place, ignorance is non-existent, and formations up to old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair are non-existent, then in this place the Buddha is non-existent, and bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas are likewise non-existent.
Why is this? Because all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature.
"Suvikrāntavikrāmin!..."
Within this profound perfection of wisdom, the perfection of generosity does not exist; the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom do not exist.

If, in this regard, the perfection of generosity is non-existent, and from the perfection of ethical discipline up to the perfection of wisdom are non-existent, then in this regard the Buddha is non-existent, and bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas are likewise non-existent.
Why is this? Because all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature.
"Suvikrāntavikrāmin!

Within this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, internal emptiness (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*) is non-existent; external emptiness (*bahirdhā-śūnyatā*), internal-and-external emptiness (*adhyātma-bahirdhā-śūnyatā*), emptiness of emptiness (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*), great emptiness (*mahā-śūnyatā*), ultimate emptiness (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*), conditioned emptiness (*saṃskṛta-śūnyatā*), unconditioned emptiness (*asaṃskṛta-śūnyatā*), absolute emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*), boundless emptiness (*anavara-agra-śūnyatā*), dispersal emptiness (*anavakāra-śūnyatā*), non-alteration emptiness (*anavakāra-śūnyatā*), essential nature emptiness (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*), self-characteristic emptiness (*svalakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*), common characteristic emptiness (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*), emptiness of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-śūnyatā*), emptiness of the unapprehendable (*anupalambha-śūnyatā*), emptiness of non-existence (*abhāva-śūnyatā*), emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*), and emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence (*abhāva-svabhāva-śūnyatā*) are all non-existent.

If, in this regard, internal emptiness is non-existent, and external emptiness up to the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-entities is non-existent, then in that place the Buddha is non-existent, and bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas are likewise non-existent.
Why is this? Because all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature. "Subhūti!..."
