Furthermore, they are able to embrace all-knowledge; furthermore, they are able to embrace the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects;
furthermore, they are able to embrace all dharani-doors and all samadhi-doors;
furthermore, they are able to embrace all the practices of bodhisattva-mahasattvas.
Furthermore, they are able to embrace the unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment of all Buddhas.

Subhūti, you should know that such sons and daughters of good family who abide in the Bodhisattva vehicle will never suffer decline or regression along the way; they will transcend the stages of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, bring sentient beings to maturity, purify Buddha-fields, and realize unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
Why is this? Because they possess skillful means capable of embracing the profound *prajñāpāramitā* up to the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening of all Buddhas.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha,
saying: “World-Honored One,

how is it that sons and daughters of good family who belong to the bodhisattva vehicle, by not embracing the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and also by not embracing skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), fall back and descend into the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas?”
The Buddha said:
"Excellent, Excellent, Subhūti!"

Excellent! For the sake of benefiting and bringing happiness to those sons and daughters of good family who abide in the Bodhisattva vehicle, you have asked the Tathāgata about such a vital matter. Listen attentively now, and I shall explain it to you.

“Subhūti! There are sons and daughters of good family belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle who, from the first production of the thought of enlightenment, dwell in the grasping of ‘I’ and ‘mine’ while practicing the perfection of generosity; they dwell in the grasping of ‘I’ and ‘mine’ while practicing the perfection of ethical discipline; they dwell in the grasping of ‘I’ and ‘mine’ while practicing the perfection of patience; they dwell in the grasping of ‘I’ and ‘mine’ while practicing the perfection of diligence; they dwell in the grasping of ‘I’ and ‘mine’ while practicing the perfection of meditative concentration; and they dwell in the grasping of ‘I’ and ‘mine’ while practicing the perfection of wisdom.”
“Subhūti! When these sons and daughters of good family practice generosity, they form this thought:
‘I am able to give; that person receives what I have given; I am giving such an object.’”
When practicing pure ethical discipline, one forms this thought:
"I am able to uphold the precepts; the precepts are what I uphold; I have accomplished these precepts.
When practicing patience, one forms this thought:
"I am able to cultivate patience; that is what I endure; I have accomplished this patience.
When cultivating diligence, one forms this thought:
"I am able to be diligent; I am for the sake of this diligence; I am endowed with this diligence."
When practicing meditative concentration, one forms this thought:
"I am able to practice concentration; I practice concentration for this purpose; I have accomplished this concentration.
When practicing wisdom, one forms this thought:
"I am able to cultivate wisdom; I cultivate this wisdom for this purpose; I have accomplished this wisdom.

Furthermore, Subhūti, when these sons and daughters of good family belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle practice generosity, they grasp at this generosity as existing, they grasp at it as arising from this [agent], and they grasp at generosity as "mine."

When practicing pure ethical discipline, they grasp at the existence of this pure ethical discipline, grasp at it as arising from this pure ethical discipline, and grasp at pure ethical discipline as "mine";
when practicing patience, they grasp at the existence of this patience, grasp at it as arising from this patience, and grasp at patience as "mine";
when practicing diligence, they grasp at the existence of this diligence, grasp at it as arising from this diligence, and grasp at diligence as "mine."

When practicing meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), one clings to the existence of this concentration, clings to it as being derived from this concentration, and clings to the concentration as "mine.
When practicing wisdom (*prajñā*), one clings to the existence of this wisdom, clings to it as being derived from this wisdom, and clings to the wisdom as "mine."
Why is this so? Because within the perfection of generosity (dānapāramitā), such conceptual discrimination does not exist.
For what reason?
Because the characteristic of the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*) consists in being far removed from this shore and the other shore,
such conceptual discrimination does not exist within the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*). Why is this?
Because distancing oneself from this shore and the other shore is the characteristic of the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*),
whereas such conceptual discrimination does not exist within the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*). Why is this?
Because distancing oneself from this shore and the other shore is the characteristic of the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*).
Within the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*), such conceptual differentiation does not exist. Why is that?
Because the perfection of vigor has the characteristic of being far removed from this shore and the other shore,
such conceptual discrimination does not exist within the perfection of meditative concentration. Why is this?
Because the characteristic of the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*) is the transcendence of this shore and that shore;
within the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), such conceptual discrimination does not exist. Why is this?
Because being far removed from both this shore and the other shore is the characteristic of the *prajñāpāramitā*. "Subhūti!

Because these sons and daughters of good family belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle do not know the characteristics of this shore and the other shore, they are unable to embrace the *dānapāramitā*, and they are unable to embrace the *śīla*, *kṣānti*, *vīrya*, *dhyāna*, and *prajñāpāramitā*."

They cannot embrace internal emptiness; they cannot embrace external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, non-alteration emptiness, essential nature emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common characteristic emptiness, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of non-apprehensibility, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature.

They cannot embrace suchness; they cannot embrace the dharma-realm, the dharma-nature, non-falsity, non-alteration, equality, the state beyond birth, the fixed nature of dharmas, the stability of dharmas, the limit of reality, the realm of space, and the inconceivable realm.
They cannot embrace the noble truth of suffering, nor can they embrace the noble truths of its origin, its cessation, and the path;
they cannot embrace the four dhyānas, nor can they embrace the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments;
they cannot embrace the eight liberations, nor can they embrace the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative attainments, or the ten totalities.

They cannot embrace the four foundations of mindfulness; they cannot embrace the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path;
they cannot embrace the liberation door of emptiness, nor the liberation doors of signlessness and wishlessness;
and they cannot embrace the ten stages of the bodhisattva.
They cannot encompass the five eyes, nor can they encompass the six supernormal powers;

they cannot encompass the ten powers of a Buddha, nor can they encompass the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
they cannot encompass the quality of non-forgetfulness, nor can they encompass the state of constant abiding in equanimity.
They cannot encompass all-knowledge; they cannot encompass the knowledge of the aspects of the path or the knowledge of all aspects;
they cannot encompass all doors of dhāraṇī, nor can they encompass all doors of samādhi;
they cannot encompass the practices of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
They will be unable to take hold of the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas. Subhūti!

For this reason, these sons and daughters of good family belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle will fall to the level of a śrāvaka or the level of a pratyekabuddha, and will not realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle 312. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Part One, Chapter Forty-Four, "Various Similes," Section Three. The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
“What is meant by a person who has set out in the Bodhisattva vehicle lacking skillful means?
The Buddha said,
“Suvikrāntavikrāmin!

If a person belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle, from the first generation of the mind of awakening, practices the perfection of generosity without skillful means; practices the perfection of ethical discipline without skillful means; practices the perfection of patience without skillful means; practices the perfection of diligence without skillful means; practices the perfection of meditative concentration without skillful means; and practices the perfection of wisdom without skillful means.
"Subhūti! When this person belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle practices generosity, they form this thought:
'I am able to practice giving; that person receives what I give; I give such an object.'"
When practicing pure ethical discipline, one forms this thought:
"I am able to maintain the precepts; the precepts are what I maintain; I have accomplished these precepts.
When practicing patience, one forms this thought:
"I am able to practice patience; that is what I endure; I have accomplished this patience.
When practicing diligence, one forms this thought:
"I am able to be diligent; I am for the sake of this diligence; I am endowed with this diligence."
When practicing meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), one forms this thought:
"I am able to practice concentration; I practice concentration for this purpose; I have accomplished this concentration.
When practicing wisdom (*prajñā*), one forms this thought:
"I am able to cultivate wisdom; I cultivate this wisdom for this purpose; I have accomplished this wisdom.

Furthermore, Subhūti, when such a person belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle practices generosity, they grasp at the existence of this generosity, grasp at that from which this generosity arises, and grasp at generosity as "mine," thereby giving rise to conceit.

When practicing pure ethical discipline (*śīla*), one clings to the existence of this pure ethical discipline, clings to it as being derived from this pure ethical discipline, and clings to pure ethical discipline as "mine," thereby giving rise to conceit;
when practicing patience (*kṣānti*), one clings to the existence of this patience, clings to it as being derived from this patience, and clings to patience as "mine," thereby giving rise to conceit;

when practicing diligence (*vīrya*), one clings to the existence of this diligence, clings to it as being derived from this diligence, and clings to diligence as "mine," thereby giving rise to conceit.

When practicing meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), one conceives of this concentration as existing, conceives of it as being derived from this concentration, and conceives of concentration as "mine," thereby giving rise to arrogance;
when practicing wisdom (*prajñā*), one conceives of this wisdom as existing, conceives of it as being derived from this wisdom, and conceives of wisdom as "mine," thereby giving rise to arrogance.

Why is this? Within the perfection of generosity (dānapāramitā), there is no such conceptual differentiation, nor does it exist in the manner in which it is conceptually differentiated. Why is this so?
Because the characteristic of the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*) is not the reaching of this shore or the other shore;
within the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*), there is no such conceptual differentiation, nor is it as it is conceptually differentiated by them.
Why is this? Because it is not the case that reaching the further shore constitutes the characteristic of the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*).
Within the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*), there is no such conceptual differentiation, nor does it accord with what is conceptually differentiated by others.
Why is this? Because reaching the further shore is not the defining characteristic of the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*).
Within the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*), there is no such conceptual differentiation, nor does it accord with that which is so differentiated.
Why is this? Because reaching the further shore is not the defining characteristic of the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*).
Within the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-pāramitā*), there is no such conceptual differentiation, nor does it accord with that which is so differentiated.
Why is this? Because reaching the further shore is not the defining characteristic of the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*).
Within the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), there is no such conceptual differentiation, nor does it accord with that which is so differentiated.
Why is this? Because reaching the further shore is not the characteristic of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
"Suvikrāntavikrāmin!..."

Because these individuals belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle do not understand the characteristics of this shore and the other shore, they are unable to embrace the perfection of generosity; they are unable to embrace the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom;
they are unable to embrace skillful means;

they are unable to embrace internal emptiness, nor can they embrace external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, non-altering emptiness, essential emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common-characteristic emptiness, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature.

They cannot embrace suchness; they cannot embrace the dharma-realm, the nature of phenomena, non-falsity, immutability, equality, the state beyond birth, the fixed nature of phenomena, the stability of phenomena, the limit of reality, the realm of space, or the inconceivable realm.
They cannot embrace the noble truth of suffering; they cannot embrace the noble truths of the origin, cessation, and the path.
They cannot embrace the four dhyānas; they cannot embrace the four immeasurables or the four formless attainments.
They are unable to embrace the eight liberations; they are unable to embrace the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities;

they are unable to embrace the four foundations of mindfulness; they are unable to embrace the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path;
they are unable to embrace the gate of liberation of emptiness; and they are unable to embrace the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness.
They cannot encompass the ten stages of a bodhisattva;
they cannot encompass the five eyes, nor the six supernormal powers;

they cannot encompass the ten powers of a Buddha, nor the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
They cannot embrace the quality of non-forgetfulness; they cannot embrace the state of constant equanimity.
They cannot embrace all-knowledge; they cannot embrace the knowledge of the paths and the knowledge of all aspects.
They cannot embrace all doors of dhāraṇī; they cannot embrace all doors of samādhi.
One cannot encompass all the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas;
one cannot encompass the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas. Subhūti!

Due to these causes and conditions, this person belonging to the vehicle of the bodhisattvas falls to the level of a śrāvaka or the level of a pratyekabuddha, and does not realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

"In this way, Subhūti, those sons and daughters of good family who have set out in the vehicle of the bodhisattvas, because they do not embrace the profound perfection of wisdom and also do not embrace skillful means, fall back into the levels of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and do not realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha,
saying: "World-Honored One,

how is it that sons and daughters of good family who have set out upon the bodhisattva vehicle, by virtue of being able to embrace the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and also being able to embrace skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), do not fall into the stages of the śrāvaka or the pratyekabuddha, but swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?"
The Buddha said, “Subhūti!

There are sons of good family and daughters of good family belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle who, from the first production of the thought of enlightenment, practice the perfection of generosity while remaining free from attachment to ‘I’ and ‘mine’; they practice the perfection of ethical discipline while remaining free from attachment to ‘I’ and ‘mine’; they practice the perfection of patience while remaining free from attachment to ‘I’ and ‘mine’; they practice the perfection of diligence while remaining free from attachment to ‘I’ and ‘mine’; they practice the perfection of meditative concentration while remaining free from attachment to ‘I’ and ‘mine’; and they practice the perfection of wisdom while remaining free from attachment to ‘I’ and ‘mine.’”
"Subhūti! When these sons and daughters of good family practice generosity, they do not form such thoughts as:
'I am able to give; that person receives what I have given; I am giving such an object.'"
When practicing pure ethical discipline, one does not form such thoughts as:
"I am able to uphold the precepts; these precepts are what I uphold; I have accomplished this ethical discipline.
When practicing patience, one does not form such thoughts:
"I am able to practice patience; that is what I endure; I have accomplished this patience.
When practicing diligence, one does not form such thoughts:
"I am able to be diligent; I am performing this diligence; I am endowed with this diligence."
When practicing meditative concentration, one does not form such thoughts as:
"I am able to practice concentration," "I am practicing concentration for this purpose," or "I have accomplished this concentration.
When practicing wisdom, one does not form such thoughts:
“I am able to cultivate wisdom; I cultivate this wisdom for this purpose; I have accomplished this wisdom.

Furthermore, Subhūti, when these sons and daughters of good family belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle practice generosity, they do not grasp at the existence of generosity, they do not grasp at that by which they give, and they do not grasp at generosity as being "mine."

When practicing pure ethical discipline, one does not grasp at the existence of pure ethical discipline, does not grasp at it as being "by means of" this pure ethical discipline, and does not grasp at pure ethical discipline as "mine.
When practicing patience, one does not grasp at the existence of patience, does not grasp at it as being "by means of" this patience, and does not grasp at patience as "mine.
When practicing diligence, one does not grasp at the existence of diligence, does not grasp at it as being "by means of" this diligence, and does not grasp at diligence as "mine."

When practicing meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), one does not grasp at the existence of meditative concentration, does not grasp at being [defined] by this meditative concentration, and does not grasp at meditative concentration as "mine.
When practicing wisdom (*prajñā*), one does not grasp at the existence of wisdom, does not grasp at being [defined] by this wisdom, and does not grasp at wisdom as "mine."
Why is this? Within the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*), there is no such conceptual differentiation that could give rise to this attachment. Why is that?
Because the characteristic of the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*) is the transcendence of this shore and the other shore,
such conceptual discrimination as could give rise to this attachment does not exist within the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*).
Why is this? Because the characteristic of the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*) is the transcendence of both this shore and the other shore.
Within the perfection of patience (*kṣāntipāramitā*), such conceptual distinctions that could give rise to this attachment do not exist.
Why is this? Because the characteristic of the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*) is the transcendence of both this shore and the other shore.
Within the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*), there is no such conceptual differentiation that could give rise to this attachment.
Why is this? Because the characteristic of the perfection of diligence (*vīryapāramitā*) is the transcendence of both this shore and the other shore;
within the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*), such conceptual distinctions that could give rise to this attachment do not exist.
Why is this? Because the characteristic of the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*) is the transcendence of both this shore and the other shore.
Within the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), there is no such conceptual differentiation that could give rise to this attachment.
Why is this? Because being far removed from both this shore and the other shore is the characteristic of the *prajñāpāramitā*.
"Suvikrāntavikrāmin!..."

These sons and daughters of good family who belong to the bodhisattva vehicle, because they thoroughly understand the characteristics of this shore and the other shore, are able to embrace the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom; they do not fall into the levels of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, but swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Furthermore, they are able to embrace internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, non-alteration emptiness, essential nature emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common characteristic emptiness, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of non-apprehensibility, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence; thus they do not fall into the levels of Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas, but swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Furthermore, they are able to embrace *tathatā* (suchness), the *dharmadhātu* (dharma-realm), the *dharmatā* (dharma-nature), non-illusory nature, unchanging nature, equality, the nature of being free from birth, the fixed nature of dharmas, the stability of dharmas, the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), the realm of space, and the inconceivable realm; thereby not falling into the stages of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, they swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Furthermore, they are able to embrace the noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the origin [of suffering], the noble truth of cessation, and the noble truth of the path; thereby not falling into the stages of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, they swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Furthermore, they are able to embrace the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless absorptions; thereby not falling into the stages of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, they swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Furthermore, they are able to embrace the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative attainments, and the ten totalities, without falling into the levels of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, swiftly realizing unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment;

furthermore, they are able to embrace the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of miraculous power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of awakening, and the eightfold noble path, without falling into the levels of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, swiftly realizing unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment;

furthermore, they are able to embrace the gate of liberation of emptiness, the gate of liberation of signlessness, and the gate of liberation of wishlessness, without falling into the levels of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, swiftly realizing unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Furthermore, they are able to embrace the ten stages of a bodhisattva (*daśabhūmi*), not falling into the stages of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, and swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment;

furthermore, they are able to embrace the five eyes and the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*), not falling into the stages of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, and swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment;

furthermore, they are able to embrace the ten powers of a buddha (*daśabala*), the four fearlessnesses (*caturvaiśāradya*), the four analytical knowledges (*catasraḥ pratisamvid*), great loving-kindness, great compassion, great joy, and great equanimity, as well as the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha (*āveṇikabuddhadharma*), not falling into the stages of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, and swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Furthermore, they are able to embrace the quality of non-forgetfulness and the state of constant equanimity, not falling into the stages of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, but swiftly realizing unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment;

furthermore, they are able to embrace all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*), and knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), not falling into the stages of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, but swiftly realizing unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment;

furthermore, they are able to embrace all doors of dhāraṇī and all doors of samādhi, not falling into the stages of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, but swiftly realizing unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Furthermore, they are able to embrace all the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, not falling into the stages of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, and swiftly realizing unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment;

furthermore, they are able to embrace the unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas, not falling into the stages of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, and swiftly realizing unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,
how does a person belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle possess skillful means?"
The Buddha said, “Subhūti!

If a person belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle, from the first generation of the mind of awakening, practices the perfection of generosity with skillful means; practices the perfection of ethical discipline with skillful means; practices the perfection of patience with skillful means; practices the perfection of diligence with skillful means; practices the perfection of meditative concentration with skillful means; and practices the perfection of wisdom with skillful means.”
"Subhūti! When this person belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle practices generosity, they do not form such thoughts as:
'I am able to practice giving; that other receives what I give; I am giving such-and-such an object.'"
When practicing pure ethical discipline, one does not form this thought:
"I am able to uphold the precepts; these precepts are what I uphold; I have accomplished this ethical discipline.
When practicing patience, one does not form this thought:
"I am able to practice patience; that is what I endure; I have accomplished this patience.
When practicing diligence, one does not form such thoughts:
"I am able to be diligent; I am practicing this diligence; I am endowed with this diligence."
When practicing meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), one does not form such thoughts as:
"I am able to practice concentration," "I am practicing concentration for this purpose," or "I have accomplished this concentration.
When practicing wisdom (*prajñā*), one does not form such thoughts:
“I am able to cultivate wisdom; I cultivate this wisdom for this purpose; I have accomplished this wisdom.

Furthermore, Subhūti, when a person belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle practices generosity, they do not grasp at the existence of generosity, they do not grasp at that by which one gives, nor do they grasp at generosity as "mine," nor do they become conceited.

When practicing pure ethical discipline, one does not grasp at the existence of pure ethical discipline, does not grasp at it as being "by means of" this pure ethical discipline, does not grasp at pure ethical discipline as "mine," and is not conceited;
when practicing patience, one does not grasp at the existence of patience, does not grasp at it as being "by means of" this patience, does not grasp at patience as "mine," and is not conceited;
when practicing diligence, one does not grasp at the existence of diligence, does not grasp at it as being "by means of" this diligence, does not grasp at diligence as "mine," and is not conceited.

When practicing meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), one does not grasp at the existence of concentration, does not grasp at it as being "by means of" this concentration, does not grasp at concentration as "mine," nor does one become conceited;

when practicing wisdom (*prajñā*), one does not grasp at the existence of wisdom, does not grasp at it as being "by means of" this wisdom, does not grasp at wisdom as "mine," nor does one become conceited.
Why is this so? Within the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*), there is no such conceptual differentiation, nor does it exist in the manner that it is conceptually differentiated. Why is this?
Because neither this shore nor the other shore constitutes the defining characteristic of the perfection of generosity.
Within the perfection of ethical discipline, there is no such conceptual differentiation, nor does it exist in the manner that it is conceptually differentiated.
Why is this? Because the perfection of ethical discipline (śīla-pāramitā) does not have the characteristic of reaching from this shore to the other shore.
Within the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā), there is no such conceptual differentiation, nor is it as it is conceptually differentiated by others.
Why is this? Because the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*) does not have the characteristic of reaching from this shore to the other shore.
Within the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*), there is no such conceptual differentiation, nor is it as it is conceptually differentiated by them.
Why is this? Because the perfection of diligence does not have as its characteristic the reaching of this shore or the other shore.
Within the perfection of meditative concentration, there is no such conceptual differentiation, nor is it as it is conceptually differentiated by others.
Why is this? Because the characteristic of the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*) does not consist in reaching this shore or the other shore.
Within the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), there is no such conceptual discrimination, nor is it as it is conceptually discriminated by others.
Why is this? Because neither reaching this shore nor reaching the other shore is the characteristic of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), Subhūti!

Because these individuals belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle understand the characteristics of this shore and the other shore, they are able to embrace the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom; they do not fall into the levels of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, but swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Furthermore, they are able to embrace skillful means and do not fall into the levels of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, but swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Furthermore, they are able to embrace internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, non-alteration emptiness, essential nature emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common characteristic emptiness, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of non-apprehensibility, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence; thereby they do not fall into the stages of Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas, but swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Furthermore, they are able to embrace suchness, the dharma-realm, the nature of phenomena, non-falsity, immutability, equality, the state beyond birth, the fixed nature of phenomena, the stability of phenomena, the limit of reality, the realm of space, and the inconceivable realm; without falling into the stages of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, they swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Furthermore, they are able to embrace the noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the origin [of suffering], the noble truth of cessation, and the noble truth of the path; without falling into the stages of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, they swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Furthermore, they are able to embrace the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments; without falling into the stages of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, they swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Furthermore, they are able to embrace the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative attainments, and the ten totalities, without falling into the stages of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, swiftly realizing unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment;

furthermore, they are able to embrace the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of awakening, and the eightfold noble path, without falling into the stages of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, swiftly realizing unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment;

furthermore, they are able to embrace the gate of liberation of emptiness, the gate of liberation of signlessness, and the gate of liberation of wishlessness, without falling into the stages of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, swiftly realizing unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Furthermore, they are able to embrace the ten stages of a bodhisattva (*daśabhūmi*), not falling into the stages of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, and swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*);

furthermore, they are able to embrace the five eyes (*pañcacakṣus*) and the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*), not falling into the stages of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, and swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment;

furthermore, they are able to embrace the ten powers of a buddha (*daśabala*), the four fearlessnesses (*catvāri vaiśāradyāni*), the four analytical knowledges (*catasraḥ pratisaṃvidah*), great loving-kindness (*mahāmaitrī*), great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), great sympathetic joy (*mahāmuditā*), great equanimity (*mahopekṣā*), and the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*), not falling into the stages of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, and swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Furthermore, they are able to embrace the quality of non-forgetfulness and the state of constant equanimity, thereby not falling into the levels of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, but swiftly realizing unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening;

furthermore, they are able to embrace all-knowledge, the knowledge of the paths, and the knowledge of all aspects, thereby not falling into the levels of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, but swiftly realizing unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening;

furthermore, they are able to embrace all doors of dhāraṇī and all doors of samādhi, thereby not falling into the levels of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, but swiftly realizing unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.

Furthermore, they are able to embrace all the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, not falling into the stages of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, and swiftly realizing unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment;

furthermore, they are able to embrace the unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas, not falling into the stages of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, and swiftly realizing unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Thus it is, Subhūti!

Those sons and daughters of good family who abide in the vehicle of the bodhisattvas, by virtue of being able to embrace the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and also being able to embrace skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), do not fall into the stages of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, but swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Chapter 45: The Chapter on the True and Good Friend, Part One. At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How should a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is a beginner train in the perfection of wisdom?
How should they train in the perfection of meditative concentration?
How should one train in the perfection of diligence?
How should one train in the perfection of patience?
How should one train in the perfection of ethical discipline?
"How should one train in the perfection of generosity?
The Buddha said,
"Suvikrāntavikrāmin!..."

A bodhisattva mahāsattva who is a beginner, if they wish to practice and study the perfection of wisdom, meditative concentration, diligence, patience, ethical discipline, and generosity, should first approach, serve, and honor a true spiritual friend who is skilled at explaining the perfections of wisdom, meditative concentration, diligence, patience, ethical discipline, and generosity—that is, one who, when teaching the profound sūtras on the perfection of wisdom, speaks as follows: "Come!..."
"Good son! When you practice giving, you should form this thought:
'The gift I have cultivated is bestowed universally upon all sentient beings, and together we dedicate it toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.'"
"When you uphold the precepts, you should form this thought:
'The pure ethical discipline I cultivate is universally bestowed upon all sentient beings, and together we dedicate it toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.'"
"When you practice patience, you should form this thought:
'The patience I am practicing is universally bestowed upon all sentient beings, and together we dedicate it toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.'"
"When you practice diligence, you should form this thought:
'The diligence I cultivate is universally bestowed upon all sentient beings, and together we dedicate it toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.'"
"When you practice meditative concentration, you should form this thought:
'The dhyāna that I practice shall be universally bestowed upon all sentient beings, and together we shall dedicate it toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.'"
"When you cultivate wisdom, you should form this thought:
'The prajñā being cultivated shall be universally bestowed upon all sentient beings, and together we shall dedicate it toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.'"

“‘Good son! You should not apprehend unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of form; nor should you apprehend unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.’”

Why is this? Because if one does not grasp at form, one attains unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; and because if one does not grasp at feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, one attains unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

“Good son! You should not apprehend unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the sense base of the eye; nor should you apprehend unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind.”

Why is this? Because if one does not grasp at the sense base of the eye, one attains unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; and because if one does not grasp at the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind, one attains unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

“Good son! You should not apprehend unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the sense-base of form; nor should you apprehend unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the sense-bases of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, or mental phenomena.”

Why is this? Because if one does not grasp at the sphere of form, one attains unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening; and because if one does not grasp at the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, or mental phenomena, one attains unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.
“‘O son of good family!

You should not grasp unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the eye-element; nor should you grasp unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the form-element, the eye-consciousness-element, eye-contact, or the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition.’”

Why is this? Because if one does not grasp at the eye-element, one attains unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; and because if one does not grasp at the form-element, up to and including the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition, one attains unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

“‘Good son! You should not apprehend unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the ear element; nor should you apprehend unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the sound element, the ear-consciousness element, ear-contact, or the various feelings produced with ear-contact as their condition.

Why is this? Because if one does not grasp at the ear element, one attains unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening; and because if one does not grasp at the sound element, up to the various feelings produced with ear-contact as a condition, one attains unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.

“‘Good son! You should not apprehend unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the nose element; nor should you apprehend unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the odor element, the nose-consciousness element, nose-contact, or the various feelings produced with nose-contact as a condition.

Why is this? Because if one does not grasp at the nose element, one attains unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening; and because if one does not grasp at the odor element, up to and including the various feelings produced with nose-contact as a condition, one attains unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.

“Good son! You should not apprehend unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the tongue element; nor should you apprehend unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the taste element, the tongue-consciousness element, tongue-contact, or the various feelings produced with tongue-contact as a condition.”

Why is this? Because if one does not grasp at the tongue element, one attains unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; and because if one does not grasp at the taste element, up to and including the various feelings produced with tongue-contact as a condition, one attains unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

“Good son! You should not take hold of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening by means of the body-element (*kāya-dhātu*); nor should you take hold of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening by means of the touch-element (*spraṣṭavya-dhātu*), the body-consciousness-element (*kāya-vijñāna-dhātu*), body-contact (*kāya-saṃsparśa*), or the various feelings (*vedanā*) produced with body-contact as their condition.”

Why is this? Because if one does not grasp the body element, one attains unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; and because if one does not grasp the contact element, nor even the various feelings produced with body-contact as a condition, one attains unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

“Good son! You should not apprehend unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the mind element (*manodhātu*); nor should you apprehend unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the phenomena element (*dharmadhātu*), the mind-consciousness element (*manovijñānadhātu*), mind-contact (*manaḥsaṃsparśa*), or the various feelings (*vedanā*) produced with mind-contact as their condition.”

Why is this? Because if one does not grasp at the mind-element, one attains unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; and because if one does not grasp at the dharma-element, up to and including those sensations produced with mind-contact as a condition, one attains unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

“‘Good son! You should not apprehend unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the earth element; nor should you apprehend unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness elements.’”

Why is this? Because if one does not grasp at the earth element, one attains unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening; and because if one does not grasp at the water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness elements, one attains unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.

“Good son! You should not grasp at unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of ignorance; nor should you grasp at unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, existence, birth, or old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair.”

Why is this? Because if one does not grasp at ignorance, one attains unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; and because if one does not grasp at formative forces, up to and including old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair, one attains unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

“‘Good son! You should not take hold of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the perfection of generosity; nor should you take hold of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, or wisdom.’”

Why is this? Because one attains unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment without grasping at the perfection of generosity, and one attains unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment without grasping at the perfections from ethical discipline up to wisdom.
“‘O son of good family!

You should not apprehend unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of internal emptiness; nor should you apprehend unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, the emptiness of the ultimate truth, the emptiness of conditioned phenomena, the emptiness of unconditioned phenomena, absolute emptiness, the emptiness of the limitless, the emptiness of dispersion, the emptiness of non-alteration, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, the emptiness of self-characteristics, the emptiness of common characteristics, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of non-apprehensibility, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of self-nature, or the emptiness of the self-nature of non-existence.’”

Why is this? Because if one does not grasp at internal emptiness, one attains unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; and because if one does not grasp at external emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence, one attains unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

“‘Good son! You should not apprehend unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of suchness; nor should you apprehend unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu), the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), non-falsity, immutability, equality, the nature of being free from birth, the fixed nature of phenomena (dharmaniyāmatā), the stability of phenomena (dharmasthititā), the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi), the realm of space (ākāśadhātu), or the inconceivable realm.’”

Why is this? Because if one does not grasp at suchness, one attains unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; and because if one does not grasp at the dharma-realm, up to and including the inconceivable realm, one attains unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

“Good son! You should not apprehend unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the noble truth of suffering; nor should you apprehend unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the noble truths of origin, cessation, or the path.”

Why is this? Because one attains unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment without grasping at the noble truth of suffering, and one attains unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment without grasping at the noble truths of origin, cessation, or the path.
“‘O son of good family!

You should not attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the four dhyānas, nor should you attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the four immeasurables or the four formless absorptions.’”

Why is this? Because one attains unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment without grasping at the four dhyānas, and because one attains unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment without grasping at the four immeasurables or the four formless absorptions.

“Good son! You should not take hold of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the eight liberations; nor should you take hold of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, or the ten totalities.”

Why is this? Because one attains unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment without grasping at the eight liberations, and because one attains unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment without grasping at the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, or the ten totalities.

“‘Good son! You should not apprehend unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the four applications of mindfulness; nor should you apprehend unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of awakening, or the eightfold noble path.’”

Why is this? Because one attains unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment without grasping at the four foundations of mindfulness, and because one attains unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment without grasping at the four right endeavors, up to and including the eightfold noble path.

“‘Good son! You should not take up unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the liberation door of emptiness; nor should you take up unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the liberation doors of signlessness or wishlessness.’”

Why is this? Because one attains unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment without grasping at the gate of liberation of emptiness, and one attains unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment without grasping at the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness.
“‘Good son! You should not attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the ten stages of a bodhisattva. Why is that?’”
"If one does not grasp at the ten stages of a bodhisattva, one will then attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. "Good son!

You should not grasp at unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the five eyes, nor should you grasp at unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the six supernormal powers."

Why is this? Because one attains unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment without grasping at the five eyes, and one attains unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment without grasping at the six supernormal powers.

“‘Good son! You should not take up unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the ten powers of a Buddha; nor should you take up unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, or the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.’”

Why is this? Because one attains unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment without grasping at the ten powers of a Buddha, and because one attains unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment without grasping at the four fearlessnesses, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.

“‘Good son! You should not grasp at unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the quality of non-forgetfulness, nor should you grasp at unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the nature of constant equanimity.’”

Why is this? Because if one does not grasp at the quality of non-forgetfulness, one attains unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; and because if one does not grasp at the state of constant dwelling in equanimity, one attains unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

“‘Good son! You should not grasp at unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of all-knowledge; nor should you grasp at unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the knowledge of the aspects of the path or the knowledge of all aspects.’”

Why is this? Because one attains unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment without grasping at all-knowledge, and because one attains unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment without grasping at the knowledge of the paths or the knowledge of all aspects.

“‘Good son! You should not grasp unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening by means of any of the gateways of dhāraṇī, nor should you grasp unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening by means of any of the gateways of samādhi.’”

Why is this? Because one attains unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment without grasping at any of the gateways of dhāraṇī, and one attains unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment without grasping at any of the gateways of samādhi.

“‘Good son! You should not realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening by means of the fruit of stream-entry; nor should you realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening by means of the fruits of once-returner, non-returner, or arhatship.’”

Why is this? Because one attains unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment without having taken up the fruit of stream-entry; and because one attains unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment without having taken up the fruits of once-returner, non-returner, or arhatship.
“Good son! You should not take up unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha. Why is that?
"If one does not grasp at the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, one will attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. "Good son!
You should not grasp at unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of any of the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas."
Why is this? Because if one does not grasp at any of the practices of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, one will attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
"O son of good family!
You should not grasp at unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas. Why is that?
Because if one does not grasp at the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas, one then attains unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
“‘Good son! Do not give rise to craving for form, nor do you give rise to craving for feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.’”
Why is this so? Because form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are not objects for craving.
For what reason?
Because all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature. "Good son!
Do not give rise to craving for the sense base of the eye, nor do you give rise to craving for the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind."
Why is this so? Because the sense bases of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are not objects of craving.
For what reason?
Because all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature. "Good son!
Do not give rise to craving for the sphere of form, nor do you give rise to craving for the spheres of sound, odor, taste, touch, or mental phenomena."
Why is this? Because the sense bases of form, sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena are not objects of craving.
For what reason?
Because all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature. "Good son!

Do not give rise to craving for the eye-element; nor do you give rise to craving for the form-element, the eye-consciousness-element, eye-contact, or the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition."
Why is this? Because the various feelings produced with conditions ranging from the eye-faculty to eye-contact are not objects of craving. Why is that?
Because all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature. "Good son!

You should not give rise to craving for the ear element, nor should you give rise to craving for the sound element, the ear-consciousness element, ear-contact, or the various feelings produced with ear-contact as a condition."
Why is this? Because the various feelings produced with conditions ranging from the ear-element up to auditory contact are not objects of craving. Why is that?
Because all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature. "Good son!

Do not give rise to craving for the nose element; nor do you give rise to craving for the fragrance element, the nose-consciousness element, nose-contact, or the various sensations produced with nose-contact as a condition."
Why is this? Because the various feelings produced with the nose element, up to and including those produced with nose-contact as condition, are not objects of craving. Why is that?
Because all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature. "Good son!

Do not give rise to craving for the tongue element; nor do you give rise to craving for the taste element, the tongue-consciousness element, tongue-contact, or the various sensations produced with tongue-contact as a condition."
Why is this? Because the various sensations produced with the tongue-element and even tongue-contact as conditions are not objects of craving. Why is that?
Because all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature. "Good son!

You should not give rise to craving for the body element, nor should you give rise to craving for the contact element, the body-consciousness element, body-contact, or the various feelings produced with body-contact as their condition."
Why is this so? Because the various feelings produced with the body-element and even body-contact as conditions are not objects for craving. Why is that?
Because all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature. "Good son!

Do not give rise to craving for the mind-element (*manodhātu*), nor do you give rise to craving for the dharma-element, the mind-consciousness-element, mental contact (*manaḥsaṃsparśa*), or the various feelings produced with mental contact as a condition."
Why is this? Because the various feelings produced with the mind-element and even with mind-contact as conditions are not objects of craving. Why is that?
Because all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature. "Good son!
You should not give rise to craving for the earth element, nor should you give rise to craving for the water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness elements."
Why is this so? Because the elements of earth, water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness are not objects of craving.
For what reason?
Because all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature. "Good son!

Do not give rise to craving for ignorance; nor do you give rise to craving for volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, existence, birth, or old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair."
Why is this? Because ignorance up to old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair are not objects of craving.
For what reason?
Because all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature. "Good son!

You should not give rise to craving or attachment toward the perfection of generosity, nor should you give rise to craving or attachment toward the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, or wisdom."
Why is this so? Because from generosity up to the perfection of wisdom, these are not objects of craving.
For what reason?
Because all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature. "Good son! Do not give rise to craving for internal emptiness;

nor do you give rise to craving for external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, non-altering emptiness, essential emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common-characteristic emptiness, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, or the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence."
Why is this? Because inner emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence, is not something to be craved.
For what reason?
Because all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature.
"Good son! Do not give rise to craving for suchness;

nor do you give rise to craving for the dharma-realm, the dharma-nature, the non-illusory nature, the unchanging nature, the equality, the nature free from birth, the fixedness of dharma, the stability of dharma, the reality-limit, the realm of space, or the inconceivable realm."
Why is this so? Because from suchness up to the inconceivable realm, these are not objects of craving.
For what reason?
Because all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature.
"Good son! You should not give rise to craving for the Noble Truth of Suffering, nor should you give rise to craving for the Noble Truths of Origination, Cessation, or the Path."
Why is this? Because the Noble Truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path are not objects of craving.
For what reason?
Because all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature. "Good son!
You should not give rise to craving for the four dhyānas, nor should you give rise to craving for the four immeasurables or the four formless attainments."
Why is this? Because the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments are not objects of craving.
For what reason?
Because all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature. "Good son!

Do not give rise to craving or attachment toward the eight liberations, nor do you give rise to craving or attachment toward the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, or the ten pervasive bases."
Why is this? Because the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten universal bases are not objects of craving. Why is that?
Because all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature. "Good son!

Do not give rise to craving for the four foundations of mindfulness; nor do you give rise to craving for the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, or the eightfold noble path."
Why is this so? Because the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path cannot be objects of craving.
For what reason?
Because all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature.

"Good son! You should not give rise to craving or attachment toward the gate of liberation of emptiness, nor should you give rise to craving or attachment toward the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness."
Why is this? Because the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—are not objects of craving.
For what reason?
Because all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature.
"Good son! You should not give rise to craving or attachment toward the ten stages of a bodhisattva."
Why is this? Because the ten stages of a bodhisattva are not objects to be craved.
For what reason?
Because all dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature.
"Good son! You should not give rise to craving for the five eyes, nor should you give rise to craving for the six supernormal powers."
Why is this? Because the five eyes and the six supernormal powers are not objects of craving.
For what reason?
Because all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature. "Good son!

You should not give rise to craving or attachment toward the ten powers of a Buddha, nor should you give rise to craving or attachment toward the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great joy, great equanimity, or the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha."
Why is this? Because the ten powers of a Buddha, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, are not objects of craving. Why is that?
Because all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature. "Good son!
Do not give rise to craving for the quality of non-forgetfulness, nor do you give rise to craving for the state of constant abiding in equanimity."
Why is this? Because the quality of non-forgetfulness and the state of constant abiding in equanimity are not objects of craving. Why is that?
Because all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature. "Good son!
You should not give rise to craving or attachment toward omniscience, nor should you give rise to craving or attachment toward the knowledge of the paths or the knowledge of all aspects."

Why is this? Because omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) are not objects of craving. Why is that?
Because all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature.
"Good son! You should not give rise to craving or attachment toward any of the gateways of dhāraṇī, nor should you give rise to craving or attachment toward any of the gateways of samādhi."
Why is this? Because all doors of dhāraṇī and all doors of samādhi are not objects of craving.
For what reason?
Because all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature.

"Good son! You should not give rise to craving and attachment for the fruit of a stream-enterer, nor should you give rise to craving and attachment for the fruits of a once-returner, a non-returner, or an arhat."
Why is this? Because the fruits of stream-entry, once-returning, non-returning, and arhatship are not objects of craving.
For what reason?
Because all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature.
"Good son! Do not give rise to craving or attachment toward the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha."
Why is this? Because the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha is not something to be craved.
For what reason?
Because all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature.
"Good son! You must not give rise to craving or attachment toward any of the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas."
Why is this? Because the practices of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are not objects of craving.
For what reason?
Because all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature.
"Good son! You should not give rise to craving or attachment toward the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas."
Why is this? Because the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas is not something to be craved or attached to.
For what reason?
"Because all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature.

Thus ends the three hundred and thirteenth fascicle of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by imperial decree, Part One, Chapter Forty-five, "The True Spiritual Friend," Section Two. At that time, the Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

These bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are able to perform what is difficult: within the emptiness of intrinsic nature of all phenomena, they aspire for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, desiring to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
The Buddha said, "So it is, Subhūti!"
"So it is! It is just as you have said.

These bodhisattva-mahāsattvas perform what is difficult to do, for while all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature, they aspire to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, desiring to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

"Subhūti! Although bodhisattva mahāsattvas know that all phenomena are like illusions, like dreams, like echoes, like images, like reflections, like mirages, like magical transformations, and like cities of the gandharvas—all being empty of intrinsic nature—they nevertheless set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment for the sake of attaining benefit for the world;
they set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment for the sake of bringing about the welfare of the world."
They set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment in order to bring peace and happiness to the world;
they set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment out of a desire to rescue all the world;
they set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment in order to serve as a refuge for the world.
They set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment in order to act as a dwelling place for the world;
they set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment because they desire to act as the ultimate path for the world;
they set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment in order to act as an island for the world.
They set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment in order to act as a light for the world;
they set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment in order to act as a lamp for the world;
they set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment in order to act as a guide for the world.
They set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment in order to act as generals for the world;
they set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment in order to act as the destination for the world.
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening in order to bring about the benefit and welfare of the world?”
The Buddha said, “Subhūti!

A bodhisattva mahāsattva practices generosity and sets out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment because he desires to liberate all sentient beings from their manifold sufferings and afflictions.”
To liberate all sentient beings from their manifold sufferings and afflictions, they practice pure ethical discipline and set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment;
to liberate all sentient beings from their manifold sufferings and afflictions, they practice patience and set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment;
to liberate all sentient beings from their manifold sufferings and afflictions, they practice diligence and set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
In order to liberate all sentient beings from their manifold sufferings and afflictions, they practice meditative concentration and set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment;
in order to liberate all sentient beings from their manifold sufferings and afflictions, they practice wisdom and set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
“Subhūti! This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva sets out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening in order to bring benefit and profit to the world.
The venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening in order to bring benefit to the world?
The Buddha said:

“Subhūti! Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening in order to extract sentient beings from the terrors of the five destinies and establish them on the fearless further shore of nirvāṇa.”
“Subhūti! It is for the sake of bringing benefit to the world that bodhisattva mahāsattvas set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening in order to bring peace and happiness to the world?
The Buddha said:

“Subhūti! A bodhisattva mahāsattva sets out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening in order to uproot the sorrow, suffering, grief, and affliction of sentient beings and establish them on the secure and peaceful further shore of nirvāṇa.”
"Subhūti! It is for the sake of bringing peace and happiness to the world that bodhisattva-mahāsattvas set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment in order to rescue and deliver all the worlds?
The Buddha said:

“Subhūti! It is for the sake of uprooting the manifold sufferings of birth and death for sentient beings that bodhisattva-mahāsattvas set out toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; when they attain enlightenment, they are then able to teach the Dharma for the cessation of suffering as it truly is, and sentient beings, having heard it, gradually practice according to the teachings of the three vehicles and thereby attain liberation.”
"Subhūti! This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, desiring to rescue and deliver all the world, sets out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment in order to serve as a refuge for the world?
The Buddha said:

“Subhūti! Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment in order to bring all sentient beings—who are subject to the conditions of birth, aging, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair—to liberation from these conditions of birth, aging, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair, so that they may abide in the realm of nirvāṇa without remainder.”
"Subhūti! It is for this reason that bodhisattva mahāsattvas set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment in order to act as a refuge for the world.
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening in order to act as a dwelling place for the world?
The Buddha said:
"Subhūti! A bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to teach all phenomena to sentient beings as being entirely non-composite should set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
"Subhūti! This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva sets out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment in order to act as a dwelling place for the world.
Subhūti spoke again:
“World-Honored One!
Why are all dharmas entirely non-composite?
The Buddha said:

“Subhūti! The non-combination of form is the non-attachment of form; the non-attachment of form is the non-arising of form; the non-arising of form is the non-ceasing of form; and the non-ceasing of form is the non-combination of form.

The non-combination of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is the non-attachment of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; the non-attachment of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is the non-arising of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; the non-arising of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is the non-ceasing of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; and the non-ceasing of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is the non-combination of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.”

“Subhūti! The non-conjunction of the eye-base is the non-attachment of the eye-base; the non-attachment of the eye-base is the non-arising of the eye-base; the non-arising of the eye-base is the non-ceasing of the eye-base; and the non-ceasing of the eye-base is the non-conjunction of the eye-base.”
