When this characteristic of suchness was being taught, twelve thousand bhikṣus among the assembly had their outflows forever exhausted, their minds attained liberation, and they became arhats; five hundred bhikṣuṇīs were distanced from dust and free from defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena; five thousand bodhisattva-mahāsattvas attained the forbearance of the non-arising of dharmas; and sixty thousand bodhisattvas had their outflows forever exhausted, their minds attained liberation, and they became arhats.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra, saying:

"These sixty thousand bodhisattvas have, in the past, personally attended upon and made offerings to five hundred buddhas. At the site of each buddha, they gave rise to great vows and left the household life with right faith; yet, although they cultivated generosity, pure ethical discipline, patience, diligence, and meditative concentration, they did not embrace the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), nor did they embrace the power of skillful means (upāyakauśalya). Consequently, they gave rise to divergent conceptions and engaged in divergent practices."
When practicing generosity, one forms this thought:
"This is the act of giving; these are the material goods; this is the recipient; I am the one who can practice giving."
When practicing pure ethical discipline, one forms this thought:
"This is pure ethical discipline; this is sinful karma; this is the object to be guarded; I am able to maintain the precepts."
When practicing patience, one should form this thought:
"This is patience; this is an obstacle to patience; this is the object of patience; I am capable of being patient."
When practicing diligence, one forms this thought:
"This is diligence; this is laziness; this is that which is to be done; I am capable of being diligent."
When practicing meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), one forms this thought:
"This is meditative concentration; this is distraction; this is that which is to be accomplished; I am able to cultivate concentration."

Because they are devoid of the perfection of wisdom and lack the power of skillful means, they practice the distinct practices of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, and meditative concentration based on the perception of diversity.

Because of their divergent perceptions and divergent practices, they cannot enter the Bodhisattva’s stage of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*). Because they do not enter the Bodhisattva’s stage of right determination, they attain the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*) and proceed gradually through the stages up to the fruit of arhatship.

Śāriputra! Although these bodhisattvas possess the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—of the bodhisattva path, because they are far removed from the perfection of wisdom and the power of skillful means, they realize the limit of reality and attain the fruit of a śrāvaka.

The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle 320–322. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Part One: Chapter Forty-seven on Suchness (Tathatā), Section Six. At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”

For what reason do some bodhisattvas practice the gates of liberation of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, yet fail to embrace the perfection of wisdom and, lacking the power of skillful means, realize the limit of reality and attain the fruit of a śrāvaka or the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha;

while other bodhisattvas practice the gates of liberation of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, embrace the perfection of wisdom, and, possessing the power of skillful means, do not realize the limit of reality but proceed toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?
The Buddha said, “Śāriputra!

If bodhisattvas distance themselves from the mind of omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*) while cultivating the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—those bodhisattvas do not embrace the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*). Due to the lack of skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), they then realize the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) and attain the fruit of a śrāvaka or the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha.”

If bodhisattvas, without departing from the mind of omniscience, cultivate the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—these bodhisattvas embrace the perfection of wisdom; by virtue of their skillful means, they are able to enter the stage of the bodhisattva’s correct nature free from birth and attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
“Śāriputra! It is as if there were a bird whose body was one hundred yojanas in length, or perhaps two hundred, even up to five hundred yojanas, yet it had no wings.”
This bird, having leaped down from the Heaven of the Thirty-three and heading toward Jambudvīpa, while on its way, thinks to itself:
"I wish to return up to the Heaven of the Thirty-three."
"Śāriputra! What do you think? Would this bird be able to return to the Heaven of the Thirty-three?"
Śāriputra said: “No, World-Honored One!”
The Buddha said,
“Śāriputra! Suppose this bird,
midway along its path, were to make this aspiration:”
"May my body reach Jambudvīpa without injury or affliction. Śāriputra, what do you think?
"Can this bird's wish be fulfilled? Śāriputra replied, "No!"
World-Honored One!
When this bird reaches this Jambudvīpa, its body will certainly suffer injury and affliction; it will either meet its end or experience suffering close to death.
For what reason?
World-Honored One!
This bird’s body is large, yet it falls from afar because it has no wings.
The Buddha said:
“Śāriputra, it is so! It is thus!”
"So it is! It is just as you have said, Śāriputra."

There are likewise some bodhisattvas who, although they have diligently practiced generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, and meditative concentration for as many great eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, and have also cultivated the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—performing vast deeds and generating a vast mind desiring to realize the immeasurable, ungraspable, subtle, and unsurpassed perfect enlightenment, nevertheless fall into the level of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha because they lack the perfection of wisdom and are far removed from the power of skillful means.

Why is this? Śāriputra, because these bodhisattvas have distanced themselves from the mind of omniscient wisdom (*sarvajñajñāna*), even though they have diligently practiced generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, and meditative concentration for many eons, and have also cultivated the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—they lack the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) and the power of skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*). Consequently, they fall into the level of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha.

“Śāriputra! Although these bodhisattvas recollect the aggregates of ethical discipline, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation of all the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the past, future, and present—and though they honor, make offerings to, and practice in accordance with them—they are unable to correctly understand the true merits of these aggregates of ethical discipline, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation of those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas because they grasp at signs within them.”

Śāriputra! Because these bodhisattvas cannot correctly understand the qualities of the Buddha, although they hear the sounds of the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—of the bodhisattva path, they grasp at their signs based on those sounds; having grasped at these signs, they dedicate [their merit] toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
If these bodhisattvas dedicate in this manner and do not attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they will abide on the level of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha. Why is that?

Śāriputra! Because these bodhisattvas are far removed from the perfection of wisdom and lack the power of skillful means, although they dedicate their various cultivated roots of goodness toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, they nevertheless abide on the level of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha.

“Śāriputra! There are bodhisattvas who, from their first generation of the mind of awakening, never depart from the mind of omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*), diligently cultivating generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, and meditative concentration, and never being separated from the skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*) of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*). Although they recollect the aggregates of morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation of all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksambuddhas of the past, future, and present, they do not grasp at their signs. Although they cultivate all the doors of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—they do not grasp at their signs. Although they recollect the various merits and roots of goodness of themselves and others, they dedicate them together with all sentient beings toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, yet they do not grasp at their signs.”

Śāriputra! You should know that this bodhisattva mahāsattva does not abide in the stages of the śrāvaka or the pratyekabuddha, but proceeds directly toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Why is this? Śāriputra, from the first generation of the mind of awakening until its ultimate consummation, this bodhisattva mahāsattva is always able to remain never apart from the mind of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*). Although they practice generosity, they do not grasp at signs; although they practice ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, they likewise do not grasp at signs. Although they recollect the aggregates of morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation belonging to all the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the past, future, and present, they likewise do not grasp at signs. Although they cultivate all the bodhisattva paths—the gates of liberation of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—they likewise do not grasp at signs.

“Śāriputra! Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva possesses skillful means, they practice the perfection of generosity with a mind free from signs; they practice the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom with a mind free from signs.”

“Śāriputra! Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva possesses skillful means, he dwells with a mind free from signs in internal emptiness; he dwells with a mind free from signs in external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersion emptiness, non-alteration emptiness, essential nature emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common characteristic emptiness, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence.”

“Śāriputra! Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva possesses skillful means, he dwells with a mind free from signs in suchness; he dwells with a mind free from signs in the dharma-realm, the dharma-nature, non-falsity, immutability, equality, the nature of being free from birth, the fixedness of phenomena, the stability of phenomena, the limit of reality, the realm of space, and the inconceivable realm.”

"Śāriputra! Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva possesses skillful means, they practice the four foundations of mindfulness with a mind free from signs; they practice the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path with a mind free from signs."

“Śāriputra! Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva possesses skillful means, he dwells with a mind free from signs in the noble truth of suffering, and dwells with a mind free from signs in the noble truths of origin, cessation, and the path.”

“Śāriputra! Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva possesses skillful means, he practices the four dhyānas with a mind free from signs, and he practices the four immeasurables and the four formless absorptions with a mind free from signs.”

“Śāriputra! Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva possesses skillful means, he practices the eight liberations with a mind free from signs; he practices the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities with a mind free from signs.”

“Śāriputra! Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva possesses skillful means, he practices the gate of liberation of emptiness with a mind free from signs; he practices the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness with a mind free from signs.”

“Śāriputra! Because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas possess skillful means, they cultivate the five eyes with a mind free from signs, and they cultivate the six supernormal powers with a mind free from signs.”

“Śāriputra! Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva possesses skillful means, he practices the gates of samādhi with a mind free from signs, and he practices the gates of dhāraṇī with a mind free from signs.”

“Śāriputra! Because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas possess skillful means, they cultivate the ten powers of a buddha with a mind free from signs; they cultivate the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha with a mind free from signs.”

“Śāriputra! Because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas possess skillful means, they cultivate all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) with a mind free from signs, and they cultivate the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*) and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) with a mind free from signs.”
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva, from the first generation of the mind of awakening until the ultimate end, embraces the perfection of wisdom and does not depart from the power of skillful means, this bodhisattva mahāsattva will certainly draw near to unexcelled, perfect, and complete awakening.”
Why is this? "World-Honored One!

From the first production of the thought of enlightenment until its ultimate consummation, this bodhisattva mahāsattva does not perceive even the slightest dharma that can be apprehended—whether it be that which realizes, that which is realized, the place of realization, the time of realization, or that by means of which one realizes; none of these can be apprehended."
Whether it be form, or feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, none of these can be apprehended;
whether it be the eye-base, or the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind-base, none of these can be apprehended;
whether it be the form-base, or the sound, odor, taste, tangible object, or mental-object base, none of these can be apprehended.

Whether it be the eye-element, or the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-elements, none are to be apprehended; whether it be the form-element, or the sound, odor, taste, tangible-object, and mental-phenomena elements, none are to be apprehended;
whether it be the eye-consciousness-element, or the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-consciousness-elements, none are to be apprehended;
whether it be eye-contact, or ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-contact, none are to be apprehended.
Whether it be the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition, or those produced with ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-contact as conditions, none are to be apprehended;
whether it be the earth element, or the water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness elements, none are to be apprehended;

whether it be ignorance, or volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, existence, birth, or old age and death, none are to be apprehended.
Whether it be the perfection of generosity, or the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom—none of these can be apprehended.

Whether it be internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, the emptiness of the ultimate, the emptiness of conditioned phenomena, the emptiness of unconditioned phenomena, absolute emptiness, the emptiness of the limitless, the emptiness of dispersion, the emptiness of non-alteration, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, the emptiness of specific characteristics, the emptiness of common characteristics, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of non-apprehension, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, or the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature—none of these can be apprehended.

Whether it be suchness, the dharma-realm, the nature of phenomena, non-falsity, immutability, equality, the state beyond birth, the fixedness of phenomena, the stability of phenomena, the limit of reality, the realm of space, or the inconceivable realm—all these are unapprehendable;

whether it be the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, or the eightfold noble path—all these are unapprehendable;
whether it be the noble truth of suffering, or the noble truths of origin, cessation, and the path—all these are unapprehendable.
Whether it be the four dhyānas, or the four immeasurables, or the four formless attainments, none of these can be apprehended;
whether it be the eight liberations, or the eight bases of mastery, or the nine successive attainments, or the ten totalities, none of these can be apprehended;
whether it be the gate of liberation of emptiness, or the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness, none of these can be apprehended.
Whether it be the five eyes or the six supernormal powers, none are to be apprehended;
whether it be the gateways of samādhi or the gateways of dhāraṇī, none are to be apprehended;

whether it be the ten powers of a Buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, or the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, none are to be apprehended.
Whether it be the fruit of stream-entry, or the fruits of once-returning, non-returning, or arhatship, none are to be apprehended;
whether it be the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, none is to be apprehended;
whether it be all-knowledge, the knowledge of the aspects of the path, or the knowledge of all aspects, none are to be apprehended.

“Bhagavān, there are sons and daughters of good family belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle who, being far removed from the skillful means of the perfection of wisdom, seek unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; it should be known that they may or may not attain the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment they seek.”
Why is this? World-Honored One!
Because these sons and daughters of good family belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle have distanced themselves from the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Because they employ skillful means regarding the *Prajñāpāramitā*, they grasp at signs in the practices of the perfections of generosity,
ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom; and likewise in the internal emptiness,
external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, and the emptiness of the ultimate.
The emptiness of the conditioned, the emptiness of the unconditioned, ultimate emptiness, boundless emptiness, emptiness of dispersion, emptiness of non-alteration,
emptiness of intrinsic nature, emptiness of self-characteristics, emptiness of common characteristics, emptiness of all phenomena, emptiness of the unapprehendable,
emptiness of non-existence, emptiness of intrinsic nature, and emptiness of the non-existent intrinsic nature.

Because they all grasp at signs; because they grasp at signs regarding the true suchness (*tathatā*), the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), the non-erroneous nature, the unchanging nature, equality, the state beyond birth, the fixed nature of phenomena (*dharmaniyāmatā*), the stability of phenomena (*dharmaniyāmatā*), the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), the realm of space (*ākāśadhātu*), and the inconceivable realm; regarding that which is...

Because one practices the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path by grasping at their signs;
because one grasps at the signs of the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path in which one abides; and because one grasps at the signs of the four dhyānas that one practices...
Because they grasp at signs regarding the four immeasurables and the four formless absorptions;
because they grasp at signs regarding the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative attainments, and the ten universal bases that they practice;
and because they grasp at signs regarding the doors of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—that they practice. Regarding what is practiced...
Because they grasp at signs while practicing the five eyes and the six supernormal powers; because they grasp at signs regarding the samādhi doors and dhāraṇī doors they practice;

and because they grasp at signs regarding the Buddha’s ten powers, four fearlessnesses, four unhindered understandings, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity that they practice—
Because they grasp at signs regarding all eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, they grasp at signs regarding all-knowledge,
the knowledge of the paths, and the knowledge of all aspects in all their practices.
“World-Honored One!
For this reason, these sons and daughters of good family belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle will all either attain or fail to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.”
“World-Honored One!

For this reason, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they must certainly not distance themselves from the skillful means of the perfection of wisdom.”
“World-Honored One!

This bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling securely in the perfection of wisdom through skillful means, employing non-apprehension as the means, should cultivate the perfection of giving with a mind accompanied by the signless; they should likewise cultivate the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom.”
“World-Honored One!

This bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling securely in the perfection of wisdom through skillful means, employing the method of non-apprehension, and with a mind accompanied by the signless, should dwell in internal emptiness; they should dwell in external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, unchanging emptiness, essential emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common-characteristic emptiness, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of non-apprehension, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature.”
“World-Honored One!

This bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling securely in the perfection of wisdom through skillful means, employing the method of non-apprehension, should abide in suchness with a mind accompanied by the signless; they should abide in the dharma-realm, the dharma-nature, the non-erroneous nature, the unchanging nature, the nature of equality, the nature of freedom from birth, the fixedness of dharmas, the stability of dharmas, the limit of reality, the realm of empty space, and the inconceivable realm.”

“Bhagavān! This bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling securely in the perfection of wisdom through skillful means, employing the method of non-apprehension, should cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness with a mind accompanied by the signless; they should likewise cultivate the four right endeavors, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path.”
“World-Honored One!

This bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling securely in the perfection of wisdom through skillful means, employing the method of non-apprehension, should dwell in the noble truth of suffering with a mind accompanied by the signless; they should likewise dwell in the noble truths of origin, cessation, and the path.”
“World-Honored One!

This bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling securely in the perfection of wisdom through skillful means, employing the method of non-apprehension, should cultivate the four dhyānas and the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments with a mind accompanied by signlessness.”
“World-Honored One!

This bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling securely in the perfection of wisdom through skillful means, employing the method of non-apprehension, should cultivate the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities with a mind accompanied by the signless.”
“World-Honored One!

This bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling securely in the skillful means of the perfection of wisdom, employing the method of non-apprehension, should cultivate the gate of liberation of emptiness with a mind accompanied by signlessness; they should likewise cultivate the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness.”
“World-Honored One!

This bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling securely in the perfection of wisdom through skillful means, employing the method of non-apprehension and with a mind accompanied by the signless, should cultivate the five eyes and should cultivate the six supernormal powers.”
“World-Honored One!

This bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling securely in the perfection of wisdom through skillful means, employing the method of non-apprehension, should cultivate the gates of samādhi and the gates of dhāraṇī with a mind accompanied by the signless.”
“World-Honored One!

This bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling securely in the perfection of wisdom through skillful means, employing the method of non-apprehension, should cultivate the ten powers of a Buddha with a mind accompanied by the signless; they should cultivate the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.”
“World-Honored One!

This bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling securely in the perfection of wisdom through skillful means, employing the method of non-apprehension and with a mind accompanied by the signless, should cultivate all-knowledge (sarvajñatā), should cultivate the knowledge of the aspects of the path (mārgākārajñatā), and should cultivate the knowledge of all aspects (sarvākārajñatā).”
“World-Honored One!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva abides in the perfection of wisdom through skillful means, employing the method of non-apprehension and with a mind accompanied by the signless, they will abide in all such buddha-dharmas and will certainly attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.”
At that time, the devaputras of the desire and form realms addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas is extremely difficult to believe and understand, and exceedingly difficult to realize.”

Why is this? Because all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas must realize and know both the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) and the general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena (*dharma*) before they can attain the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*) they seek; yet, the characteristics of phenomena as known by bodhisattvas are entirely non-existent and unapprehendable.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the sons of the gods, saying: "So it is! So it is!"
It is as you have said.
The unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas is extremely difficult to believe and understand, and exceedingly difficult to attain.
O Son of Heaven, you should know this!

I too have directly awakened to the characteristics of all phenomena and realized unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, yet I have not apprehended any ultimate characteristic of phenomena that could be said to be "this is the means of realization," "this is the object of realization," "this is the place of realization," "this is the time of realization," or "it is by means of this that one realizes."
Why is this? O sons of the gods!
Because all dharmas are ultimately pure, and because the conditioned and the unconditioned are ultimately empty.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

As the Buddha has taught, the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas is extremely difficult to believe and understand, and exceedingly difficult to realize. Yet, as I contemplate the meaning of what the Buddha has said, the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas is extremely easy to believe and understand, and exceedingly easy to realize.”

Why is this? If one can believe and understand that there is no dharma that can realize, no dharma that is realized, no place of realization, no time of realization, and furthermore, nothing by means of which realization occurs, then one can believe and understand the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas.

If one realizes that there is no dharma that can realize, no dharma that is realized, no place of realization, no time of realization, and nothing by means of which realization occurs, then one will be able to realize the sought-after unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Why is this? World-Honored One!

Because all dharmas are ultimately empty; within ultimate emptiness, there is no dharma that can be called the "realizer," no dharma that can be called the "object realized," no dharma that can be called the "place of realization," no dharma that can be called the "time of realization," and no dharma by which anything is realized.
Why is this? All phenomena are empty; whether increasing or decreasing, they possess nothing whatsoever and are entirely unattainable.
"World-Honored One!..."
The giving, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom perfections practiced by the bodhisattva mahāsattvas are all non-existent and entirely unapprehendable.

“Bhagavān! The inner emptiness, outer emptiness, inner-and-outer emptiness, emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, non-alteration emptiness, essential nature emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common characteristic emptiness, emptiness of all phenomena, unapprehendable emptiness, emptiness of non-existence, emptiness of intrinsic nature, and emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence—all these in which the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas abide are entirely non-existent and cannot be apprehended.”
“World-Honored One!

The suchness, the dharma-realm, the dharma-nature, the non-falsity, the non-alteration, the equality, the state beyond birth, the fixedness of dharma, the stability of dharma, the limit of reality, the realm of empty space, and the inconceivable realm in which all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas abide are entirely non-existent and cannot be apprehended.”
“World-Honored One!

The four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of awakening, and the eightfold noble path cultivated by bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are entirely non-existent and utterly unapprehendable.”
“World-Honored One!
The noble truths of suffering, origination, cessation, and the path, in which all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas abide, are entirely non-existent and utterly unapprehendable.”
“World-Honored One!
The four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments cultivated by bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are all non-existent and entirely unapprehendable.”
“World-Honored One!
The eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities cultivated by bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are all non-existent and entirely unobtainable.”
“World-Honored One!
The gateways to liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—cultivated by all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are entirely non-existent and utterly unapprehendable.”
“World-Honored One!

Because all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas contemplate all phenomena as being entirely devoid of intrinsic nature and identical to space; for example, space does not form such a thought:
"I shall believe, understand, and swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Likewise, all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should not form such a thought as:
"I shall believe, understand, and swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
Why is this? Subhūti! All phenomena are empty and equal to space;

At that time, the Venerable Subhūti said to Śāriputra:

"If all dharmas, by virtue of their truth and their abiding nature, are entirely non-existent and cannot be apprehended, what dharma could be said to regress from unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?"
Then, Śāriputra said to Subhūti:

"According to what you have said, within the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), there is no phenomenon whatsoever, nor is there any bodhisattva who could be said to experience retreat from unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. If that is so, for what reason did the Buddha speak of three types of individuals who abide in the vehicle of the bodhisattvas, rather than speaking of only one?"
"Furthermore, as you have said, there should be no distinction between the three vehicles of bodhisattvas; there should be only one vehicle of the perfectly awakened ones.
Then, the Venerable Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra said to Śāriputra, "You should ask Subhūti:"
Do you admit that there exists a single Bodhisattvayāna?
Only then may one raise the objection:
"There should be no establishment of distinctions among three vehicles; rather, there should be only a single vehicle of Perfectly Complete Enlightenment."
Then, Śāriputra asked Subhūti: "Is it admitted that there is such a thing as a bodhisattva vehicle?
At that time, Subhūti said to Śāriputra:
“Śāriputra, what do you think? Within the suchness of all phenomena,
are there three distinct characteristics of individuals who abide in the vehicle of the bodhisattvas?”
"Does one definitely experience regression from unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, or does one definitely not experience regression,
or is it indefinite? Śāriputra replied, "No!"
"Subhūti! Śāriputra! What do you think?"
Within the suchness (*tathatā*) of all phenomena, are there distinctions among the bodhisattvas of the three vehicles—
namely, the bodhisattvas of the śrāvaka vehicle, the bodhisattvas of the pratyekabuddha vehicle, and the bodhisattvas of the samyaksambuddha vehicle?
Śāriputra said: “No, Subhūti!”
“Śāriputra, what do you think? Within the true suchness (tathatā) of all phenomena, is there truly any fixed bodhisattva vehicle that does not regress?”
Śāriputra said: “No, Subhūti!”
“Śāriputra, what do you think? Within the suchness of all phenomena,
does there truly exist a vehicle of the perfectly awakened ones for bodhisattvas?”
Śāriputra said: "No, Subhūti!"
“Śāriputra, what do you think? Does the suchness of all phenomena possess the characteristics of being one, two, or three?”
Śāriputra said: “No, Subhūti!”
“Śāriputra, what do you think? Within the suchness of all phenomena, can any phenomenon or any bodhisattva be apprehended?”
Śāriputra said: "No, Subhūti!"

At that time, Subhūti said to Śāriputra: "If all phenomena, by virtue of their truth and their abiding nature, are entirely non-existent and cannot be apprehended, how can you, Śāriputra, conceive such thoughts as:

'This bodhisattva will certainly experience retreat from the Buddha’s unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment'; 'this bodhisattva will certainly not experience retreat from the Buddha’s unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment'; 'this bodhisattva is indeterminate regarding the Buddha’s unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment'; 'this bodhisattva belongs to the vehicle of the śrāvakas'; 'this bodhisattva belongs to the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas'; 'this bodhisattva belongs to the vehicle of the perfectly enlightened ones'—thus making three, or thus making one?"

Śāriputra! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva finds nothing at all to be apprehended among all phenomena, and is likewise well able to have faith and understanding that even the suchness of all phenomena is entirely unapprehendable, and finds nothing to be apprehended regarding other bodhisattvas, and finds nothing to be apprehended regarding the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of a Buddha, you should know that this one is a true bodhisattva mahāsattva.

Śāriputra! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, upon hearing it said that such true thusness (tathatā) of all phenomena is characterized by non-apprehensibility, their mind is not startled, not terrified, not afraid, does not doubt, does not regret, does not retreat, and does not sink; this bodhisattva mahāsattva will swiftly attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Venerable Subhūti, saying:
“Subhūti, excellent! Excellent!”

Excellent! You are now able to skillfully expound the essential Dharma for the sake of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; everything you have spoken is due to the majestic empowerment of the Tathāgata’s spiritual power, not through your own personal strength.

"Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva develops deep faith and understanding regarding the signless unapprehensibility of the true nature (*tathatā*) of phenomena, and knows that all phenomena are without differentiated characteristics; and upon hearing it said that such true nature of all phenomena is signless and unapprehensible, his mind is not startled, not terrified, not afraid, does not doubt, does not regret, does not retreat, and does not sink—this bodhisattva mahāsattva will swiftly attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes this dharma, will they swiftly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?”
The Buddha said,
“Śāriputra, it is so! It is thus!”

It is so! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes these dharmas, they will swiftly attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and shall not fall into the stages of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
Chapter 48: The Stages of the Bodhisattva, Part One. At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, in what should he dwell?
How should he dwell?
The Buddha said:

“Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they should abide in a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings and should not abide in a mind of inequality;
they should give rise to a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings and should not give rise to a mind of inequality.”
One should address all sentient beings with an impartial mind, and not with a partial mind;
one should give rise to a mind of great loving-kindness toward all sentient beings, and not give rise to a mind of malice;
one should address all sentient beings with a mind of great loving-kindness, and not with a mind of malice.
One should give rise to great compassion toward all sentient beings and should not give rise to a mind of malice or harm;
one should address all sentient beings with a mind of great compassion and should not address them with a mind of malice or harm;
one should give rise to great sympathetic joy toward all sentient beings and should not give rise to a mind of envy.
One should address all sentient beings with a mind of great joy, and not with a mind of envy;
one should give rise to a mind of great equanimity toward all sentient beings, and not give rise to a mind of partiality;
one should address all sentient beings with a mind of great equanimity, and not with a mind of partiality.
One should give rise to a mind of reverence toward all sentient beings and should not give rise to a mind of arrogance;
one should address all sentient beings with a mind of reverence and should not address them with a mind of arrogance;
one should give rise to a mind of straightforwardness toward all sentient beings and should not give rise to a mind of flattery or deceit.
One should speak to all sentient beings with a straightforward mind and not with a deceitful or fraudulent mind;
one should give rise to a mind of gentleness toward all sentient beings and not give rise to a harsh or rigid mind;
one should speak to all sentient beings with a gentle mind and not with a harsh or rigid mind.
One should give rise to a mind of benefit toward all sentient beings and should not give rise to a mind of non-benefit;
one should address all sentient beings with a mind of benefit and should not address them with a mind of non-benefit;
one should give rise to a mind of happiness toward all sentient beings and should not give rise to a mind of unhappiness.
One should address all sentient beings with a mind of peace and happiness, and not with a mind of unhappiness;
one should give rise to an unobstructed mind toward all sentient beings, and not give rise to an obstructed mind;
one should address all sentient beings with an unobstructed mind, and not with an obstructed mind.

One should regard all sentient beings with a mind as toward one’s parents, as toward brothers, as toward sisters, as toward sons and daughters, and as toward kinsmen; one should also speak to them with that same mind.
One should regard all sentient beings with a mind as toward friends, and one should also speak to them with that same mind.

One should regard all sentient beings with a mind as toward one’s preceptors, as toward one’s instructors, as toward disciples, and as toward fellow students; one should also speak to them with that same mind.
One should give rise to a mind toward all sentient beings as one would toward a stream-enterer, a once-returner, a non-returner, or an arhat, and one should address them with that very same mind;
one should give rise to a mind toward all sentient beings as one would toward a pratyekabuddha, and one should address them with that very same mind;
one should give rise to a mind toward all sentient beings as one would toward a bodhisattva mahāsattva, and one should address them with that very same mind.
One should give rise to a mind toward all sentient beings that is like that of a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, and should speak to them with that very same mind;
one should give rise to a mind toward all sentient beings that regards them as worthy of offerings, reverence, respect, and praise, and should speak to them with that very same mind;
one should give rise to a mind toward all sentient beings that seeks to rescue, pity, and protect them, and should speak to them with that very same mind.
One should give rise to a mind of ultimate emptiness, non-existence, and ungraspability toward all sentient beings, and with that very mind, one should speak to them;
one should give rise to a mind of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness toward all sentient beings, and with that very mind, one should speak to them.
"Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they should abide in this state by means of non-apprehension as their skillful method."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they should personally abstain from taking life and also encourage others to abstain from taking life; they should constantly and correctly praise the practice of abstaining from taking life and joyfully extol those who abstain from taking life.

They should personally abstain from taking what is not given and sexual misconduct, and also encourage others to abstain from taking what is not given and sexual misconduct; they should constantly and correctly praise the practices of abstaining from taking what is not given and sexual misconduct, and joyfully extol those who abstain from taking what is not given and sexual misconduct."

“Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they should personally abstain from false speech, and also exhort others to abstain from false speech; they should constantly and correctly praise the dharma of abstaining from false speech, and joyfully laud those who abstain from false speech.

They should personally abstain from harsh speech, divisive speech, and frivolous chatter, and also exhort others to abstain from harsh speech, divisive speech, and frivolous chatter; they should constantly and correctly praise the dharma of abstaining from harsh speech, divisive speech, and frivolous chatter, and joyfully laud those who abstain from harsh speech, divisive speech, and frivolous chatter.”

“Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they should personally distance themselves from sensual desire, and also exhort others to distance themselves from sensual desire; they should constantly and correctly praise the dharma of distancing oneself from sensual desire, and joyfully extol those who have distanced themselves from it.

They should personally distance themselves from ill will and wrong views, and also exhort others to distance themselves from ill will and wrong views; they should constantly and correctly praise the dharma of distancing oneself from ill will and wrong views, and joyfully extol those who have distanced themselves from them.”

“Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they should personally cultivate the first dhyāna, and also encourage others to cultivate the first dhyāna; they should constantly and correctly praise the practice of the first dhyāna, and joyfully extol those who cultivate the first dhyāna.

They should personally cultivate the second, third, and fourth dhyānas, and also encourage others to cultivate the second, third, and fourth dhyānas; they should constantly and correctly praise the practice of the second, third, and fourth dhyānas, and joyfully extol those who cultivate the second, third, and fourth dhyānas.”

"Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to attain unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, they should personally cultivate immeasurable loving-kindness and also exhort others to cultivate immeasurable loving-kindness; they should always correctly praise the practice of immeasurable loving-kindness and joyfully extol those who cultivate immeasurable loving-kindness.

They should personally cultivate immeasurable compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity, and also exhort others to cultivate immeasurable compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity; they should always correctly praise the practice of immeasurable compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity, and joyfully extol those who cultivate immeasurable compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity."

“Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, they should personally cultivate the meditative absorption of the sphere of infinite space, and also encourage others to cultivate the meditative absorption of the sphere of infinite space; they should constantly and correctly praise the method of cultivating the meditative absorption of the sphere of infinite space, and joyfully extol those who cultivate the meditative absorption of the sphere of infinite space.

One should personally cultivate the meditative attainments of the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; one should also encourage others to cultivate the meditative attainments of the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; one should constantly and correctly praise the practice of these meditative attainments of the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; and one should rejoice in and extol those who cultivate the meditative attainments of the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

“Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they should personally fulfill the perfection of generosity, encourage others to fulfill the perfection of generosity, constantly and correctly praise the dharma of fulfilling the perfection of generosity, and joyfully extol those who fulfill the perfection of generosity;

One should personally fulfill the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom; likewise, one should encourage others to fulfill the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom; one should constantly and correctly praise the dharmas of fulfilling the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom; and one should joyfully extol those who have fulfilled the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom.

“Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they should themselves abide in internal emptiness, also encourage others to abide in internal emptiness, constantly and correctly praise the dharma of abiding in internal emptiness, and joyfully extol those who abide in internal emptiness;”

One should personally abide in external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, unchanging emptiness, essential emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common-characteristic emptiness, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of non-apprehensibility, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence; one should also exhort others to abide in external emptiness up to the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence, constantly and correctly extol the practice of abiding in external emptiness up to the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence, and joyfully praise those who abide in external emptiness up to the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence.

“Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they should themselves abide in suchness (*tathatā*), and also encourage others to abide in suchness; they should constantly and correctly praise the dharma of abiding in suchness, and joyfully extol those who abide in suchness.

They should themselves abide in the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), non-falsity, immutability, equality, the state beyond birth, the fixed nature of phenomena (*dharmaniyāmatā*), the stability of phenomena (*dharmaniyāmatā*), the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), the realm of space (*ākāśadhātu*), and the inconceivable realm; they should also encourage others to abide in the realm of phenomena up to the inconceivable realm, constantly and correctly praise the dharmas of abiding in the realm of phenomena up to the inconceivable realm, and joyfully extol those who abide in the realm of phenomena up to the inconceivable realm.”

“Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they should personally cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness and also encourage others to cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness; they should constantly and correctly praise the practice of the four foundations of mindfulness and joyfully extol those who cultivate them.

They should personally cultivate the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path, and also encourage others to cultivate the four right efforts up to the eightfold noble path; they should constantly and correctly praise the practice of the four right efforts up to the eightfold noble path and joyfully extol those who cultivate the four right efforts up to the eightfold noble path.”

“Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they should themselves abide in the noble truth of suffering, and also encourage others to abide in the noble truth of suffering; they should constantly and correctly praise the dharma of abiding in the noble truth of suffering, and joyfully extol those who abide in the noble truth of suffering.

They should themselves abide in the noble truths of origin, cessation, and the path, and also encourage others to abide in the noble truths of origin, cessation, and the path; they should constantly and correctly praise the dharma of abiding in the noble truths of origin, cessation, and the path, and joyfully extol those who abide in the noble truths of origin, cessation, and the path.”

“Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they should personally cultivate the eight liberations and also encourage others to cultivate the eight liberations; they should constantly and correctly praise the practice of the eight liberations and joyfully extol those who cultivate them.

They should personally cultivate the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative attainments, and the ten totalities, and also encourage others to cultivate the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative attainments, and the ten totalities; they should constantly and correctly praise the practice of the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative attainments, and the ten totalities, and joyfully extol those who cultivate them.”

“Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they should personally cultivate the gate of liberation of emptiness, and also encourage others to cultivate the gate of liberation of emptiness; they should constantly and correctly praise the dharma of cultivating the gate of liberation of emptiness, and joyfully extol those who cultivate the gate of liberation of emptiness.

They should personally cultivate the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness, and also encourage others to cultivate the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness; they should constantly and correctly praise the dharma of cultivating the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness, and joyfully extol those who cultivate the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness.”

“Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they should personally fulfill the Ground of Extreme Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), and also encourage others to fulfill the Ground of Extreme Joy; they should constantly and correctly praise the qualities of fulfilling the Ground of Extreme Joy, and joyfully extol those who have fulfilled the Ground of Extreme Joy.

They should personally fulfill the Ground of Purity (*vimalā-bhūmi*), the Ground of Radiance (*prabhākārī-bhūmi*), the Ground of Blazing Wisdom (*arciṣmatī-bhūmi*), the Ground Difficult to Conquer (*sudurjayā-bhūmi*), the Ground of Presence (*abhimukhī-bhūmi*), the Ground of Far-Going (*dūraṅgamā-bhūmi*), the Ground of Immovability (*acalā-bhūmi*), the Ground of Good Intelligence (*sādhumatī-bhūmi*), and the Ground of the Dharma Cloud (*dharmameghā-bhūmi*); they should also encourage others to fulfill these grounds from the Ground of Purity up to the Ground of the Dharma Cloud; they should constantly and correctly praise the qualities of fulfilling these grounds from the Ground of Purity up to the Ground of the Dharma Cloud, and joyfully extol those who have fulfilled them.”

“Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they should themselves fulfill the five eyes and also encourage others to fulfill the five eyes; they should constantly and correctly praise the dharma of fulfilling the five eyes and joyfully extol those who have fulfilled the five eyes.

They should themselves fulfill the six supernormal powers and also encourage others to fulfill the six supernormal powers; they should constantly and correctly praise the dharma of fulfilling the six supernormal powers and joyfully extol those who have fulfilled the six supernormal powers.”

“Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they should personally fulfill the gateways of samādhi, and also exhort others to fulfill the gateways of samādhi; they should constantly and correctly praise the dharma of fulfilling the gateways of samādhi, and joyfully extol those who have fulfilled the gateways of samādhi.

They should personally fulfill the gateways of dhāraṇī, and also exhort others to fulfill the gateways of dhāraṇī; they should constantly and correctly praise the dharma of fulfilling the gateways of dhāraṇī, and joyfully extol those who have fulfilled the gateways of dhāraṇī.”

“Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they should personally fulfill the ten powers of a buddha, and also encourage others to fulfill the ten powers of a buddha; they should constantly and correctly praise the dharma of fulfilling the ten powers of a buddha, and joyfully extol those who have fulfilled the ten powers of a buddha.

They should personally fulfill the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha; they should also encourage others to fulfill the four fearlessnesses up to the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha; they should constantly and correctly praise the fulfillment of the four fearlessnesses up to the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha, and joyfully extol those who have fulfilled the four fearlessnesses up to the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha.”

“Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they should personally contemplate the twelve links of dependent origination in both forward and reverse order; they should also exhort others to contemplate the twelve links of dependent origination in both forward and reverse order; they should constantly and correctly praise the method of contemplating the twelve links of dependent origination in both forward and reverse order; and they should joyfully laud those who contemplate the twelve links of dependent origination in both forward and reverse order.”

“Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they should personally know suffering, abandon its origin, realize its cessation, and cultivate the path; they should also encourage others to know suffering, abandon its origin, realize its cessation, and cultivate the path; they should constantly and correctly praise the dharma of knowing suffering, abandoning its origin, realizing its cessation, and cultivating the path; and they should joyfully extol those who know suffering, abandon its origin, realize its cessation, and cultivate the path.”

“Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to attain unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, they should personally give rise to the wisdom that realizes the fruit of stream-entry, yet without realizing the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) while attaining the fruit of stream-entry; they should also exhort others to give rise to the wisdom that realizes the fruit of stream-entry and to realize the limit of reality while attaining the fruit of stream-entry; they should constantly and correctly praise the dharma of giving rise to the wisdom that realizes the fruit of stream-entry and realizing the limit of reality while attaining the fruit of stream-entry; and they should joyfully extol those who have given rise to the wisdom that realizes the fruit of stream-entry and realized the limit of reality while attaining the fruit of stream-entry.”

One should personally give rise to the knowledge of the fruit of once-returner, non-returner, and arhatship, yet without realizing the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi), one attains the fruit of once-returner, non-returner, and arhatship; one also encourages others to give rise to the knowledge of the fruit of once-returner, non-returner, and arhatship and to realize the limit of reality to attain the fruit of once-returner, non-returner, and arhatship; one constantly and correctly extols the dharma of giving rise to the knowledge of the fruit of once-returner, non-returner, and arhatship and realizing the limit of reality to attain the fruit of once-returner, non-returner, and arhatship; and one joyfully praises those who give rise to the knowledge of the fruit of once-returner, non-returner, and arhatship and realize the limit of reality to attain the fruit of once-returner, non-returner, and arhatship.

“Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they should personally give rise to the wisdom that realizes the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, yet without realizing the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) to attain the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha; they should also exhort others to give rise to the wisdom that realizes the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha and to realize the limit of reality to attain the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha; they should constantly and correctly praise the method of giving rise to the wisdom that realizes the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha and realizing the limit of reality to attain the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha; and they should joyfully extol those who give rise to the wisdom that realizes the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha and realize the limit of reality to attain the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha.”

“Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they should personally enter the bodhisattva’s stage of certainty and departure from error, and likewise encourage others to enter the bodhisattva’s stage of certainty and departure from error; they should constantly and correctly extol the dharma of entering the bodhisattva’s stage of certainty and departure from error, and joyfully praise those who have entered the bodhisattva’s stage of certainty and departure from error.”

“Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they should personally purify a buddha-field, and also encourage others to purify a buddha-field; they should constantly and correctly extol the methods for purifying a buddha-field, and joyfully praise those who purify a buddha-field.”

"Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they should personally bring sentient beings to maturity, and also instruct others to bring sentient beings to maturity; they should constantly and correctly praise the method of bringing sentient beings to maturity, and joyfully extol those who do so."

“Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they should personally give rise to the supernormal powers of a bodhisattva, and also teach others to give rise to the supernormal powers of a bodhisattva; they should constantly and correctly praise the method of giving rise to the supernormal powers of a bodhisattva, and joyfully extol those who have given rise to them.”

“Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they should personally give rise to the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñatā*), and also teach others to give rise to the knowledge of all modes; they should constantly and correctly praise the dharma of giving rise to the knowledge of all modes, and joyfully extol those who have given rise to the knowledge of all modes.

They should personally give rise to the knowledge of the paths (*mārgākārajñatā*) and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), and also exhort others to give rise to the knowledge of the paths and the knowledge of all aspects; they should constantly and correctly praise the dharma of giving rise to the knowledge of the paths and the knowledge of all aspects, and joyfully extol those who have given rise to the knowledge of the paths and the knowledge of all aspects.”

“Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they should personally sever all afflictions along with their continuities and habitual tendencies; they should also exhort others to sever all afflictions along with their continuities and habitual tendencies; they should constantly and correctly praise the method of severing all afflictions along with their continuities and habitual tendencies; and they should joyfully extol those who have severed all afflictions along with their continuities and habitual tendencies.”

The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle Three Hundred and Twenty-four. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Part One: Chapter Forty-eight, "The Bodhisattva’s Dwelling," Section Two. "Subhūti!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they should personally give rise to the quality of non-forgetfulness (*asaṃpramoṣadharma*), and also encourage others to give rise to the quality of non-forgetfulness; they should constantly and correctly praise the dharma of giving rise to non-forgetfulness, and joyfully extol those who have given rise to non-forgetfulness.

They should personally give rise to the state of constant equanimity (*upekṣā*), and also encourage others to give rise to the state of constant equanimity; they should constantly and correctly praise the dharma of giving rise to constant equanimity, and joyfully extol those who have given rise to constant equanimity.

“Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they should themselves embrace the perfection of lifespan, and also encourage others to embrace the perfection of lifespan; they should constantly and correctly praise the dharma of embracing the perfection of lifespan, and joyfully extol those who embrace the perfection of lifespan.”

“Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they should personally turn the wheel of Dharma, encourage others to turn the wheel of Dharma, constantly and correctly praise the method of turning the wheel of Dharma, and joyfully extol those who turn the wheel of Dharma.”

“Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, they should themselves uphold and protect the true Dharma so that it remains, and likewise encourage others to uphold and protect the true Dharma so that it remains; they should constantly and correctly praise the practice of upholding and protecting the true Dharma, and joyfully extol those who uphold and protect the true Dharma.”
“Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, they should abide in this manner, employing non-apprehension as the means.”

“Subhūti! A bodhisattva mahāsattva should train in the skillful means of this profound *prajñāpāramitā* in this way; if they train in this way, they will be able to abide securely in the state of abiding. If they train in this way and abide thus, they will attain non-obstruction regarding form (*rūpa*), and attain non-obstruction regarding feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*);

Chapter 49: On Irreversibility, Part One, Section 49-1. At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What are the practices, what are the signs, and what are the characteristics of a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who is non-retrogressive?
How may we know that one is a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who is non-retrogressive?

The Buddha said, “Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can know, as they truly are, the stage of ordinary beings, the stage of śrāvakas, the stage of pratyekabuddhas, the stage of bodhisattvas, and the stage of tathāgatas— and if these stages are, within the suchness of all phenomena, without change, without differentiation, and entirely non-dual and indivisible— then although this bodhisattva mahāsattva has realized the suchness of all phenomena as it truly is, they do not engage in conceptual discrimination regarding that suchness, because they employ the method of non-apprehension.”

Once this bodhisattva mahāsattva has thus entered into the true suchness (tathatā) of all phenomena as they truly are, although they hear that true suchness and all phenomena are non-dual and indistinguishable, they remain free from doubt or obstruction.
Why is this? Because *tathatā* (suchness) and all phenomena cannot be described as being either identical or different, nor both, nor neither.
This bodhisattva-mahāsattva never utters speech frivolously; all the speech he utters leads to meaningful benefit, and if it lacks such benefit, he never speaks at all.
This bodhisattva mahāsattva does not observe the likes and dislikes, or the strengths and weaknesses of others; rather, with impartial compassion, he teaches them the Dharma. Subhūti!

A non-retrogressive bodhisattva mahāsattva possesses such practices, tokens, and signs; by means of these practices, tokens, and signs, one should know him to be a non-retrogressive bodhisattva mahāsattva.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
By what conduct, what characteristics, and what signs is one to know that this is a non-retrogressive bodhisattva mahāsattva?"
The Buddha said,
“Suvikrāntavikrāmin!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to contemplate all dharmas as being without activity, without characteristics, and without marks, you should know that this is a non-retrogressive bodhisattva mahāsattva.”
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha again, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If all dharmas are without activity, without characteristics, and without marks, from what dharma does a bodhisattva mahāsattva regress that he is therefore called ‘non-regressive’?”
The Buddha said, “Suvikrāntavikrāmin!

This bodhisattva mahāsattva is called ‘non-retrogressive’ because he retrogresses from form; he is called ‘non-retrogressive’ because he retrogresses from feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.”
Why is this? Subhūti!

The intrinsic nature of form does not exist; the intrinsic nature of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness also does not exist. Because a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not abide therein, it is called "regression."

“Subhūti! This bodhisattva mahāsattva is called ‘non-retrogressive’ because they have turned back from the sphere of the eye; they are called ‘non-retrogressive’ because they have turned back from the spheres of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.”
Why is this? Subhūti!

The intrinsic nature of the sense base of the eye does not exist; the intrinsic natures of the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind also do not exist. Because a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not abide therein, he is said to be "regressing."

“Subhūti! This bodhisattva mahāsattva is called ‘non-retrogressive’ because they retrogress from the sphere of form; they are called ‘non-retrogressive’ because they retrogress from the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena.”
Why is this? Subhūti!

The intrinsic nature of the sphere of form does not exist; the intrinsic natures of the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena likewise do not exist. Because a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not dwell within these, they are said to be "receding."

“Subhūti! This bodhisattva mahāsattva is called ‘non-retrogressive’ because they have turned back from the eye-element; they are called ‘non-retrogressive’ because they have turned back from the ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-elements.”
Why is this? Subhūti!

Because the intrinsic nature of the eye-element (*cakṣurdhātu*) does not exist, and the intrinsic natures of the ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-elements (*śrotra-, ghrāṇa-, jihvā-, kāya-, manodhātu*) likewise do not exist; because a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not abide therein, he is said to be "regressing."

“Subhūti! This bodhisattva mahāsattva is called ‘non-retrogressive’ because he has turned back from the realm of form; he is called ‘non-retrogressive’ because he has turned back from the realms of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena.”
Why is this? Subhūti!

The intrinsic nature of the realm of form does not exist; the intrinsic natures of the realms of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena likewise do not exist. Because a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not abide within these, they are said to be "receding."

"Subhūti! This bodhisattva mahāsattva is called 'non-retrogressive' because they have turned back from the sphere of visual consciousness; they are called 'non-retrogressive' because they have turned back from the spheres of auditory, olfactory, gustatory, tactile, and mental consciousness."
Why is this? Subhūti!

The intrinsic nature of the eye-consciousness element does not exist; the intrinsic natures of the ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-consciousness elements likewise do not exist. Because a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not abide within these, they are said to be "regressed."

“Subhūti! This bodhisattva mahāsattva is called ‘non-regressive’ because they have turned back from eye-contact; they are called ‘non-regressive’ because they have turned back from ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-contact.”
Why is this? Subhūti!

The intrinsic nature of eye-contact does not exist; the intrinsic nature of ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact likewise does not exist. Because a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not abide within these, they are said to be "regressing."

“Subhūti! This bodhisattva mahāsattva is called ‘non-retrogressive’ because they have turned back from all feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition; they are called ‘non-retrogressive’ because they have turned back from all feelings produced with ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact as conditions.”
Why is this? Subhūti!

The intrinsic nature of all feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition does not exist; the intrinsic nature of all feelings produced with ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-contact as conditions likewise does not exist. Because a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not abide therein, he is said to be "receding."

“Subhūti! This bodhisattva mahāsattva is called ‘non-retrogressive’ because they have turned back from the earth element; they are called ‘non-retrogressive’ because they have turned back from the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements.”
Why is this? Subhūti!

The intrinsic nature of the earth element does not exist; the intrinsic natures of the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements also do not exist. Because a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not abide within these, they are said to be "regressing."

“Subhūti! This bodhisattva mahāsattva is called ‘non-retrogressive’ because they have turned back from ignorance; they are called ‘non-retrogressive’ because they have turned back from volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, and old age and death.”
Why is this? Subhūti!

The intrinsic nature of ignorance does not exist, and the intrinsic nature of everything from volitional formations up to old age and death also does not exist; because a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not abide therein, he is said to be "regressing."

“Subhūti! This bodhisattva mahāsattva is called ‘non-retrogressive’ because he does not regress from the perfection of generosity; he is called ‘non-retrogressive’ because he does not regress from the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom.”
Why is this? Subhūti!

The intrinsic nature of the perfection of giving does not exist; the intrinsic natures of the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom also do not exist. Because a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not abide within these, they are said to be "regressing."

“Subhūti! This bodhisattva mahāsattva is called ‘non-retrogressive’ because they do not regress from internal emptiness; they are called ‘non-retrogressive’ because they do not regress from external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, non-altering emptiness, essential emptiness, emptiness of self-characteristic, emptiness of common characteristic, emptiness of all phenomena, emptiness of the unapprehendable, emptiness of non-existence, emptiness of intrinsic nature, and emptiness of the non-existent intrinsic nature.”
Why is this? Subhūti!

The intrinsic nature of internal emptiness does not exist; the intrinsic nature of external emptiness, up to and including the intrinsic nature of the emptiness of non-existence and intrinsic nature, also does not exist. Because a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not abide therein, they are said to be "regressing."
