If the ineffable meaning neither increases nor decreases, then the Stage of Extreme Joy (Pramuditā-bhūmi) should likewise neither increase nor decrease; and the Stage Free from Defilement (Vimalā-bhūmi), the Radiant Stage (Prabhākari-bhūmi), the Stage of Blazing Wisdom (Arciṣmatī-bhūmi), the Stage Difficult to Conquer (Sudurjayā-bhūmi), the Manifest Stage (Abhimukhi-bhūmi), the Far-Reaching Stage (Dūraṅgamā-bhūmi), the Immovable Stage (Acalā-bhūmi), the Stage of Good Wisdom (Sādhumatī-bhūmi), and the Cloud of Dharma Stage (Dharmameghā-bhūmi) should likewise neither increase nor decrease.”
“World-Honored One!

If the meaning that cannot be expressed neither increases nor decreases, then the five eyes should likewise neither increase nor decrease, and the six supernormal powers should likewise neither increase nor decrease.”
“World-Honored One!

If the ineffable meaning neither increases nor decreases, then the gateways of samādhi should likewise neither increase nor decrease, and the gateways of dhāraṇī should likewise neither increase nor decrease.”
“World-Honored One!

If the meaning that cannot be expressed has neither increase nor decrease, then the Buddha’s ten powers should also have neither increase nor decrease; likewise, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha should also have neither increase nor decrease.”
“World-Honored One!

If the ineffable meaning neither increases nor decreases, then the quality of non-forgetfulness should likewise neither increase nor decrease, and the state of constant abiding in equanimity should likewise neither increase nor decrease.”
“World-Honored One!

If the ineffable meaning neither increases nor decreases, then omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) should likewise neither increase nor decrease; the knowledge of the paths (*mārgākārajñatā*) and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) should also neither increase nor decrease.”

“Bhagavān, if the perfection of generosity neither increases nor decreases, and if the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom likewise neither increase nor decrease, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice the perfection of generosity, and practice the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, in order to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening?”
“World-Honored One!

If the four foundations of mindfulness neither increase nor decrease, and if the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path likewise neither increase nor decrease, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice the four foundations of mindfulness, and practice the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path, in order to realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment?”
“World-Honored One!

If the four dhyānas neither increase nor decrease, and the four immeasurables and the four formless absorptions likewise neither increase nor decrease, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice the four dhyānas, practice the four immeasurables and the four formless absorptions, and realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment?”
“World-Honored One!

If the eight liberations neither increase nor decrease, and the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities likewise neither increase nor decrease, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice the eight liberations, practice the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities, and thereby realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment?”
“World-Honored One!

If the gate of liberation of emptiness neither increases nor decreases, and the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness likewise neither increase nor decrease, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice the gate of liberation of emptiness, practice the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness, and realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment?”
“World-Honored One!

If the Ground of Extreme Joy is neither increasing nor decreasing, and if the Ground of Freedom from Defilement, the Ground of Radiant Light, the Ground of Blazing Wisdom, the Ground of Utmost Difficulty to Conquer, the Ground of Manifestation, the Ground of Far-Going, the Ground of Immovability, the Ground of Excellent Intelligence, and the Ground of Dharma Clouds are likewise neither increasing nor decreasing, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice the Ground of Extreme Joy, practice the Ground of Freedom from Defilement up to the Ground of Dharma Clouds, and realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment?”
“World-Honored One!

If the five eyes neither increase nor decrease, and the six supernormal powers likewise neither increase nor decrease, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva cultivate the five eyes and cultivate the six supernormal powers to realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment?”
“World-Honored One!

If the gateways of samādhi neither increase nor decrease, and the gateways of dhāraṇī likewise neither increase nor decrease, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice the gateways of samādhi, practice the gateways of dhāraṇī, and realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment?”
“World-Honored One!

If the ten powers of a Buddha neither increase nor decrease, and if the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha likewise neither increase nor decrease, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice the ten powers of a Buddha, practice the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and thereby realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment?”
“World-Honored One!

If the quality of non-forgetfulness neither increases nor decreases, and the state of constant abiding in equanimity likewise neither increases nor decreases, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice the quality of non-forgetfulness, practice the state of constant abiding in equanimity, and realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment?”
“World-Honored One!

If all-knowledge (sarvajñatā) neither increases nor decreases, and if the knowledge of the paths (mārgajñatā) and the knowledge of all aspects (sarvākārajñatā) likewise neither increase nor decrease, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice all-knowledge, practice the knowledge of the paths, and practice the knowledge of all aspects to realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment?”

The Buddha said: "Suvīta!..."

"So it is! So it is! The ineffable meaning neither increases nor decreases; the perfection of generosity likewise neither increases nor decreases, and the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom likewise neither increase nor decrease."

The four foundations of mindfulness are neither increasing nor decreasing; the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path are also neither increasing nor decreasing.
The four dhyānas are neither increasing nor decreasing; the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments are also neither increasing nor decreasing.
The eight liberations are neither increasing nor decreasing; the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities are also neither increasing nor decreasing.
The liberation door of emptiness is neither increasing nor decreasing; the liberation doors of signlessness and wishlessness are likewise neither increasing nor decreasing.

The Stage of Extreme Joy is neither increasing nor decreasing, and the Stages of Purity, Radiance, Blazing Wisdom, Difficult to Conquer, Presence, Far-Going, Immovability, Good Intelligence, and Dharma Cloud are also neither increasing nor decreasing.
The five eyes are neither increasing nor decreasing, and the six supernormal powers are also neither increasing nor decreasing.
The gates of samādhi neither increase nor decrease; the gates of dhāraṇī also neither increase nor decrease.

The ten powers of a Buddha neither increase nor decrease; the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha also neither increase nor decrease.
The quality of non-forgetfulness neither increases nor decreases; the nature of constant abiding in equanimity also neither increases nor decreases.

All-knowledge (sarvajñatā) is likewise without increase or decrease; the knowledge of the paths (mārgajñatā) and the knowledge of all aspects (sarvākārajñatā) are also without increase or decrease. "Subhūti!
When bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom and abide in the skillful means of the perfection of wisdom, they do not form such a thought:"
They do not form the thought: "I am increasing or decreasing in the perfection of wisdom," nor do they form the thought:
"I am increasing or decreasing in the perfections of meditative concentration, diligence, patience, ethical discipline, or generosity."
One should simply form this thought:
"There is only a name and a concept, which is called 'Prajñāpāramitā.
One should simply form this thought:
"Subhūti, there are only names and concepts, which are called the perfections of meditative concentration, diligence, patience, ethical discipline, and generosity.
"Subhūti! [he said.]

When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of generosity, they take these mental engagements concurrent with generosity, as well as the states of mind and roots of virtue arising therefrom, and share them equally with all sentient beings, dedicating them toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, dedicating them in a manner as subtle, profound, and sublime as the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of a Buddha.

“Subhūti! When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*), he takes up this mental attention (*manasikāra*) that accompanies pure ethical discipline, and based upon the mind and roots of goodness thus arisen, he shares them equally with all sentient beings and dedicates them toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*). He performs this dedication in a manner as subtle, profound, and wondrous as the Buddha’s own unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.”

“Subhūti! When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of patience, he takes this mental attention associated with patience, as well as the mind and roots of goodness arising from it, and shares them equally with all sentient beings, dedicating them toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment. He performs this dedication in a manner that accords with the subtle, profound, and unsurpassed nature of the Buddha’s unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.”

“Subhūti! When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of diligence, he takes this mental attention associated with diligence, as well as the mind and roots of goodness arising from it, and shares them equally with all sentient beings, dedicating them toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. He performs this dedication in a manner that accords with the subtle, profound, and unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas.”

“Subhūti! When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of meditative concentration, he takes this mental attention associated with that concentration, as well as the mind and roots of goodness arising from it, and shares them equally with all sentient beings, dedicating them toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment. He performs this dedication in a manner as subtle, profound, and wondrous as the unexcelled, perfect enlightenment of the Buddhas.”

“Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they take this mental engagement that accompanies the perfection of wisdom, as well as the mind and roots of virtue arising from it, and share them equally with all sentient beings. They dedicate these toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, dedicating them in a manner as subtle, profound, and sublime as the unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment of a Buddha. By the power of such skillful means of dedication, they realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.”
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha,
saying: “World-Honored One,
what is meant by unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?”
The Buddha said,
“Suvikrāntavikrāmin!
The suchness of all phenomena is what is called unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.”
The Venerable Subhūti spoke again:
“World-Honored One,
what is the suchness of all phenomena (dharmatathatā), such that you say the suchness of all phenomena is called unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?”
The Buddha said, “Subhūti!

The suchness of all form is called unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; the suchness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is called unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.”

“Subhūti! The suchness of the eye-base is called unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; the suchness of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-bases is called unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.”

“Subhūti! The suchness of the sense-base of form is called unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; the suchness of the sense-bases of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena is called unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.”

"Subhūti! The suchness of the eye-element is called unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; the suchness of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-elements is called unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

"Subhūti! The suchness of the form realm (rūpadhātu) is called unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; the suchness of the realms of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena (dharmadhātu) is called unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

"Subhūti! The suchness of the eye-consciousness element is called unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; the suchness of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-consciousness elements is called unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

“Subhūti! The suchness of eye-contact is called unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; the suchness of ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact is called unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.”

"Subhūti! The suchness of all feelings produced with eye-contact as condition is called unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; the suchness of all feelings produced with ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact as conditions is called unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

“Subhūti! The suchness of the earth element is called unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; the suchness of the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements is called unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.”

"Subhūti! The suchness of the nature of causal conditions is called unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; the suchness of the nature of the immediately preceding condition, the object-condition, and the dominant condition is called unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

“Subhūti! The suchness of ignorance is called unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; the suchness of volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, and old age and death is called unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.”

“Subhūti! The suchness of the perfection of giving is called unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; the suchness of the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom is called unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.”

“Subhūti! The suchness of internal emptiness is called unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; the suchness of external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, the emptiness of the ultimate truth, the emptiness of conditioned phenomena, the emptiness of unconditioned phenomena, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, the emptiness of non-alteration, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, the emptiness of self-characteristics, the emptiness of common characteristics, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of non-apprehensibility, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence is called unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.”

"Subhūti! Suchness is what is called unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu), the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), non-falsity, immutability, equality, the state beyond birth, the fixed nature of phenomena (dharmatā-sthititā), the stability of phenomena (dharma-vyavasthāna), the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi), the realm of space (ākāśadhātu), and the inconceivable realm—suchness is what is called unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

"Subhūti! The suchness of the four foundations of mindfulness is called unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; the suchness of the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of awakening, and the eightfold noble path is called unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

"Subhūti! The suchness of the noble truth of suffering is called unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; the suchness of the noble truths of origin, cessation, and the path is called unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

“Subhūti! The suchness of the four dhyānas is called unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; the suchness of the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments is called unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.”

"Subhūti! The suchness of the eight liberations is called unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; the suchness of the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative attainments, and the ten totalities is called unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

“Subhūti! The suchness of the gate of liberation of emptiness is called unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; the suchness of the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness is called unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.”

“Subhūti! The suchness of the Stage of Extreme Joy is what is called unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; the suchness of the Stage of Purity, the Stage of Radiance, the Stage of Blazing Wisdom, the Stage of Utmost Difficulty to Conquer, the Stage of Manifestation, the Stage of Far-Going, the Immovable Stage, the Stage of Excellent Intelligence, and the Stage of the Cloud of Dharma—these are what is called unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.”

“Subhūti! The suchness of the five eyes is called unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; the suchness of the six supernormal powers is called unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.”

“Subhūti! The suchness of the gateways of samādhi is called unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; the suchness of the gateways of dhāraṇī is called unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.”

“Subhūti! The suchness of the ten powers of a Buddha is called unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; the suchness of the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha is called unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.”

“Subhūti! The suchness of the quality of non-forgetfulness is called unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; the suchness of the state of constant equanimity is called unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.”

“Subhūti! The fruit of stream-entry is indeed thus called unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; the fruits of once-returning, non-returning, and arhatship are indeed thus called unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.”
“Subhūti! The suchness of the awakening of a pratyekabuddha is what is called unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening. Subhūti!”

The suchness of all-knowledge (sarvajñatā) is called unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; the suchness of the knowledge of the paths (mārgajñatā) and the knowledge of all aspects (sarvākārajñatā) is called unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
"Subhūti! The suchness of saṃsāra is called unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; the suchness of nirvāṇa is called unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

“Subhūti! Because the suchness of all phenomena neither increases nor decreases, the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas likewise neither increases nor decreases. Subhūti!”

All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas do not depart from the perfection of wisdom; they always delight in dwelling securely within the suchness of all phenomena, never perceiving any phenomenon as increasing or decreasing.

For this reason, the ineffable meaning neither increases nor decreases; the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*) also neither increases nor decreases, and the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom likewise neither increase nor decrease.

The four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) neither increase nor decrease, and the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path likewise neither increase nor decrease.
The four dhyānas neither increase nor decrease, and the four immeasurables and the four formless absorptions likewise neither increase nor decrease.
The eight liberations are neither increasing nor decreasing; the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive concentrations, and the ten totalities are also neither increasing nor decreasing.
The gate of liberation of emptiness is neither increasing nor decreasing, and the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness are also neither increasing nor decreasing.

The stage of extreme joy is neither increasing nor decreasing, and the stages of freedom from defilement, radiant emission, blazing wisdom, extremely difficult to conquer, presence, far-reaching, immovability, excellent intelligence, and the cloud of dharma are also neither increasing nor decreasing.
The five eyes are neither increasing nor decreasing; the six supernormal powers are neither increasing nor decreasing;
the gateways of samādhi are neither increasing nor decreasing; the gateways of dhāraṇī are neither increasing nor decreasing;

the ten powers of a Buddha are neither increasing nor decreasing; and the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are also neither increasing nor decreasing.
The quality of non-forgetfulness neither increases nor decreases, and the state of constant equanimity also neither increases nor decreases;
omniscience likewise neither increases nor decreases, and the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects also neither increase nor decrease.

"Subhūti! All bodhisattva mahāsattvas rely upon the skillful means of neither increasing nor decreasing as they practice the perfection of wisdom; by taking this as their gateway, they gather all merits and thereby realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One,

if a bodhisattva mahāsattva relies upon the skillful means of neither increasing nor decreasing while practicing the perfection of wisdom, and by means of this gateway gathers all merits and thereby realizes unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment— does that bodhisattva mahāsattva realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the initial mind?"
"Is it by means of the subsequent mind that one realizes unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?

"World-Honored One, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva were to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the initial mind, then at the moment the initial mind arises, the subsequent mind has not yet arisen; thus, there would be no sense of their conjunction."
If one realizes unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the final moment of mind, then at the time the final moment of mind arises, the preceding moments have already ceased;

thus, there is no sense of conjunction. When one thus examines the preceding and succeeding moments of mind and mental factors from every perspective, there is no sense of conjunction. How, then, can roots of virtue be accumulated?
"If all roots of goodness cannot be accumulated, how can a bodhisattva realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?
The Buddha said,
"Suvikrāntavikrāmin!..."
I shall now briefly provide you with an analogy so that those of wisdom may easily understand the meaning of what has been said.
Subhūti, what do you think?
"When a lamp is lit, is it the initial flame that can burn the wick, or is it the final flame that can burn the wick?
"World-Honored One! [The interlocutor replied.]
As I understand it, it is not the first flame that can burn the wick, nor is it apart from the first flame that it can burn the wick;
it is not the last flame that can burn the wick, nor is it apart from the last flame that it can burn the wick.
“Suvikrāntavikrāmin! What do you think?
Is the wick burned?”
“World-Honored One!
We see with our own eyes in the world that the wick is indeed scorched.
The Buddha said:

"Subhūti! It is the same for all bodhisattva mahāsattvas: they do not realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the initial mind, nor do they realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment apart from the initial mind;

they do not realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the final mind, nor do they realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment apart from the final mind—and yet, bodhisattva mahāsattvas do realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

All bodhisattva mahāsattvas, from the moment they first resolve their minds upon awakening, practice the perfection of wisdom until they fulfill the ten stages and realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
What ten stages do the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cultivate and study to fully realize and attain unexcelled, perfect enlightenment?"
The Buddha said, “Suvikrāntavikrāmin!

Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the stages from the Stage of Extreme Joy up to the Cloud of Dharma, bringing them to fulfillment so as to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. They also study the Stage of Pure Observation, the Stage of the Spiritual Lineage, the Eighth Stage, the Stage of Vision, the Stage of Refinement, the Stage of Freedom from Desire, the Stage of Completion, the Stage of the Pratyekabuddha, the Stage of the Bodhisattva, and the Stage of the Tathāgata, bringing them to fulfillment so as to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.”

"Subhūti! When bodhisattva mahāsattvas have attained perfection through diligent cultivation and study of these ten stages, they do not realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the initial mind, nor do they realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment apart from the initial mind;

they do not realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the final mind, nor do they realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment apart from the final mind—and yet, bodhisattva mahāsattvas do realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

This dependent origination is so profound and so subtle that it means Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas do not realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the initial mind, nor do they realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment apart from the initial mind.”

It is not by means of the final mind that bodhisattva mahāsattvas realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, nor is it apart from the final mind that they realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; yet, bodhisattva mahāsattvas do realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
The Buddha said to Subhūti: "What do you think?
If a mind has already ceased, can it arise again?"
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One!”
"No, Sugata! The Buddha said to Subhūti:
“What do you think? If a mind has already arisen, does it have the nature of cessation? Subhūti replied:
"So it is, World-Honored One! So it is!"
“Excellent, Sugata!
The Buddha said to Subhūti, “What do you think?”
“Is it not the case that the mind, being subject to the nature of cessation,
will necessarily cease? Subhūti replied, “No!”
"No, World-Honored One! No, Sugata!"
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"What do you think? Does the mind abide in the same manner as the suchness of the mind?"
Subhūti replied, “So it is, World-Honored One!”
"So it is! Well-gone One!
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"What do you think? Does the mind abide as true suchness (tathatā), just as the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) does? Subhūti replied:
"No, World-Honored One! No!"
“Excellent, Sugata!
The Buddha said to Subhūti, “What do you think?”
“Are suchness and the limit of reality profound?
Subhūti replied, “Indeed they are.”
"So it is, World-Honored One!
So it is, Sugata!"
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"What do you think? Is that very suchness the mind?"
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One!”
"No, Sugata! The Buddha said to Subhūti:
“What do you think? Is there a mind apart from suchness? Subhūti replied:
"No, World-Honored One! No!"
“Excellent, Sugata!
The Buddha said to Subhūti: “What do you think?”
"Is this very mind suchness? Subhūti replied, "No!"
"No, World-Honored One! No, Sugata!"
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"What do you think? Is there a true suchness apart from the mind?"
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One!”
"No, Sugata! The Buddha said to Subhūti:
“What do you think? Does suchness perceive suchness? Subhūti replied:
"No, World-Honored One! No!"
“Excellent, Sugata!
The Buddha said to Subhūti, “What do you think?”
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can practice in this way, is he practicing the profound perfection of wisdom? Subhūti replied,
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can practice in this way, he is practicing the profound perfection of wisdom."
The Buddha said to Subhūti: "What do you think?
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can practice in this manner, where does he practice?"
Subhūti replied: "If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can practice in this way, there is no place of practice at all. Why is that? Because..."
World-Honored One!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), there is no mind that manifests, nor any locus for manifestation. Why is this?
“World-Honored One!
Within true suchness (tathatā), there is absolutely no manifestation, because there is no locus for manifestation.
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"What do you think?
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), where does he practice? Subhūti replied:

"When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, they practice within the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*); herein, both the active manifestation and the locus of manifestation are non-existent, for neither the grasper nor the grasped can be apprehended."
The Buddha said to Subhūti: "What do you think?
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, although they do not grasp at signs while practicing within the ultimate truth, do they nonetheless practice signs?"
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One!”
"No, Sugata! The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"What do you think?
When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, does he, while practicing within the ultimate truth, destroy signs?"
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One!”
"No, Sugata! The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"What do you think?
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, does he, while practicing within the ultimate truth, conceive of the notion of disintegration?"
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One!”
"No, Sugata! The Buddha said:
“Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, how is it that they neither destroy signs nor destroy the perception of signs?”
Subhūti replied: "When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, he does not form the thought:
'I shall destroy signs and the perception of signs.'"
Nor does he form the thought:
"I shall destroy signlessness and destroy the perception of signlessness," because he is without discrimination in every respect.
“World-Honored One!

Although this bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, is thus able to remain free from all conceptual discrimination, because his immeasurable and supreme merits—such as the ten powers of a Buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the four unhindered understandings, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha—are not yet perfected, he has not yet realized unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.”
"Bhagavān! This bodhisattva-mahāsattva accomplishes subtle and wondrous skillful means; by the power of these skillful means, they neither grasp at nor destroy any phenomena."
Why is this? World-Honored One!
It is because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas know that all dharmas are empty of their own characteristics.

"Bhagavān! This bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in the emptiness of the intrinsic characteristics of all phenomena, yet for the sake of liberating all sentient beings, he enters the three samādhis; being drawn and impelled by the power of his great compassion and vows, he employs these three concentrations to bring sentient beings to maturity."
The Buddha said,
“So it is, Subhūti! So it is!”
"So it is! It is just as you have said.
Then, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How does this bodhisattva-mahāsattva enter these three samādhis to bring sentient beings to maturity?
The Buddha said:

“Subhūti! This bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling securely in the *śūnyatā-samādhi*, perceives that many sentient beings are attached to a self; through the power of skillful means, he instructs and leads them to dwell securely in the *śūnyatā-samādhi*.

“Subhūti! This bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling in the signless samādhi, perceives that many sentient beings practice with signs; through the power of skillful means, he instructs and leads them to dwell in the signless samādhi.”

“Subhūti! This bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling in the samādhi of wishlessness, perceives sentient beings who have many desires and inclinations, and through the power of skillful means, instructs them to dwell in the samādhi of wishlessness.”
“Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, they enter these three samādhis in this manner to bring sentient beings to maturity.”
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra asked the Venerable Subhūti: “Subhūti!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva enters these three samādhis even in a dream, does this bring about any increase in their profound perfection of wisdom?”
Subhūti replied, “Śāriputra!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva enters these three samādhis during the day and thereby gains increase in the profound perfection of wisdom, they will likewise gain increase by entering them even in a dream.”
Why is this? Śāriputra,
because there is no difference between the daytime and the dream state.

Śāriputra! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom during the day, it is called the cultivation of the profound perfection of wisdom; likewise, when that bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom in a dream, it is also called the cultivation of the three samādhis of the profound perfection of wisdom, and one should understand that it likewise serves to increase their proficiency in the profound perfection of wisdom.
At that time, Śāriputra asked Subhūti:
"Does the karma performed by bodhisattva-mahāsattvas in a dream result in either increase or decrease?"
The Buddha has taught that conditioned phenomena are illusory and unreal, like actions performed in a dream; how, then, could those karmas undergo increase or decrease? Why is this so?

It is because the various karmas performed within a dream cannot be increased or diminished; it is only upon waking, when one recollects and discriminates the actions performed in the dream, that there can be increase or decrease.
Subhūti replied, “There are those who,
having taken the life of another during the day, recall and conceptualize it in their dreams, feeling deep self-congratulation; or again, there are those who,
having taken the life of another in a dream, claim to be in the waking state and experience great joy.”
"What do you think of these two types of karma?

Śāriputra replied, "If there is no objective referent, neither volition nor karma can arise; it is only when there is an objective referent that volition and karma originate. With respect to what, then, do the volitions and karma in a dream arise?"
Subhūti replied, “So it is! So it is!”
Whether in a dream or while awake, volitional action does not arise without an object; it is only when there is an object that volitional action arises.
Why is this? Śāriputra!

Whether in a dream or while awake, it is only when there is the engagement of discerning wisdom (*buddhi*) with respect to phenomena that are seen, heard, sensed, or known that defilement or purification arises.
If there were no seeing, hearing, sensing, or knowing, and thus no engagement of discerning wisdom with phenomena, there would likewise be neither defilement nor purification.

"Therefore, it is known that whether in a dream or while awake, volitional action (*cetanā-karma*) arises only when there is an object of perception; volitional action does not arise in the absence of an object of perception.
At that time, Śāriputra asked Subhūti:
"The Buddha has taught that all volitional action is devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). How can you say that it arises with an object?"

Subhūti replied: "Although the intrinsic nature of all volitional actions and their objects is empty, because one's own mind grasps signs and engages in conceptualization, it is said that volitional action arises with an object; if there were no object, volitional action would not arise."
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra again asked the Venerable Subhūti:

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom while dreaming, and dedicates these roots of virtue to unexcelled, perfect enlightenment in common with all sentient beings, does that bodhisattva mahāsattva truly dedicate them toward great enlightenment?"
Then, the Venerable Subhūti said to Śāriputra:

“The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya has long ago received the prediction of non-retrogression; he is separated from buddhahood by only one more birth and is certain to become a Buddha. He is fully capable of answering all difficult questions; it is fitting that you ask him here in this assembly, for the Compassionate Honored One, who stands as the successor, will surely provide the answer.”
Then, Śāriputra, as Subhūti had said,
respectfully questioned the Bodhisattva Maitreya.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Maitreya spoke to Śāriputra, saying:
"What do you mean by 'Maitreya is able to answer'?
Is it form? Or is it feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness?"
Is it form that is empty?
Or is it feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness that is empty?
Furthermore, form cannot answer; nor can feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness answer.
The emptiness of form cannot answer; the emptiness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness likewise cannot answer.
Why is this? Śāriputra!
I do not perceive any dharma that can answer, nor any dharma that is answered; I do not perceive the place of answering, the time of answering, or that by which one answers.
I do not perceive any dharma that can predict, nor any dharma that is predicted; I do not perceive the place of prediction, the time of prediction, or that by which one predicts.
"Because the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is empty, being entirely non-existent, non-dual, and without distinction, such that they can ultimately not be apprehended through investigation.
At that time, Śāriputra again asked the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya:
"Virtuous One, is the Dharma you have taught as it was realized?"
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya said:
"The Dharma I teach is not as it was realized. Why is this?"
"Śāriputra! This Dharma realized by me is ineffable.
At that time, Śāriputra thought to himself:

“Maitreya Bodhisattva’s wisdom is profound and vast; having long since perfected all forms of the perfections of giving, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, he is able to answer the questions asked in such a manner by employing the skillful means of non-apprehension.”
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra, saying: “Śāriputra,
what do you think?”
"By means of this dharma, you have attained the fruit of arhatship; do you perceive this dharma as something that can be expressed?
Śāriputra replied, "No!"
"No, World-Honored One! No, Sugata!"
The Buddha said,
“Śāriputra, it is likewise with all dharmas realized by bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who practice the profound perfection of wisdom.”
Śāriputra! This bodhisattva mahāsattva does not form such thoughts as:
"By means of this dharma I shall receive the prediction," "By means of this dharma I am currently receiving the prediction," or "By means of this dharma I have already received the prediction."
He does not form this thought:
"By means of this dharma, I shall realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Śāriputra!
This bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the profound perfection of wisdom, does not give rise to doubt, thinking:
"Shall I attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, or shall I not?"
They simply maintain this thought:
"I shall certainly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Śāriputra!

When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom and hears the most profound Dharma, their mind is not startled, not terrified, and not afraid; nor do they fear the attainment of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, for they know with certainty:
"I shall realize the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment that I seek."
Chapter 51: The Chapter on Vows and Practices, Part One. At that time, the Buddha addressed the venerable Subhūti, saying: “Subhūti!

There are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, while practicing the perfection of generosity, see sentient beings oppressed by hunger and thirst, their clothing tattered and worn, and lacking sufficient bedding and seats.
"Subhūti! Having seen this, the bodhisattva mahāsattva reflects:
'How shall I rescue and deliver these classes of sentient beings, causing them to be free from stinginess and greed, so that they lack nothing?'"
Having reflected thus, he made this vow:

"I shall diligently apply myself, regardless of body or life, to practice the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*), maturing sentient beings and purifying Buddha-fields, so that I may swiftly fulfill [the perfections] and quickly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. In my Buddha-field, there shall be no sentient beings who lack such requisites; just as the gods of the Four Great Kings, the Thirty-three Gods, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, and the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven enjoy various kinds of sublime articles of pleasure, so too shall the sentient beings in my Buddha-field enjoy various kinds of sublime articles of pleasure."
"Subhūti! By means of this perfection of giving, these bodhisattva mahāsattvas will swiftly bring it to fulfillment and draw near to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
"Furthermore, Subhūti,
there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practicing the perfection of ethical discipline who see sentient beings whose afflictions are raging,
who kill one another, commit theft, engage in sexual misconduct, and perform [other non-virtuous acts]..."
By uttering false and deceptive words, speaking with harshness, engaging in divisive speech, and employing foul language; and by giving rise to various forms of greed,
malice, and wrong views— for these causes and conditions, one will have a short life, be plagued by many illnesses,
have a haggard appearance, lack majesty and virtue, suffer from meager resources, and be born into a lowly family.
Their physical bodies were coarse and deformed, and their personae were foul and filthy; whatever they spoke was not believed or accepted by others.
Their speech was harsh and crude, causing estrangement from friends and kin. All that they uttered was vulgar and base;
they were stingy, greedy, and envious, burning with evil views, slandering the True Dharma, and insulting the worthy and holy ones.
"Subhūti! Having seen this, that bodhisattva mahāsattva reflects:
'How shall I rescue and deliver these classes of sentient beings, causing them to remain far removed from the fruits of their various evil karmas?'"
Having reflected thus, he made this vow:

"I shall diligently apply myself, regardless of body or life, to practice the perfection of pure ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*), maturing sentient beings and purifying the Buddha-field, so that I may swiftly fulfill [the requirements] and rapidly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. In my Buddha-field, may there be no sentient beings who experience such fruits of various evil karmas; may all sentient beings practice the ten wholesome paths of action and receive superior and wondrous retributions such as long life."
"Subhūti! By means of this perfection of ethical discipline, these bodhisattva mahāsattvas will swiftly bring it to full completion and draw near to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

There are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practicing the perfection of patience who see sentient beings mutually enraged, reviling, and insulting one another; they see them harming each other with swords, staves, tiles, stones, fists, mallets, clods of earth, and so forth, even to the point of taking one another's lives, yet not relinquishing their evil intentions."
"Subhūti! Having seen this, that bodhisattva mahāsattva reflects:
'How shall I rescue and deliver these classes of sentient beings, causing them to remain far removed from such evils?'"
Having reflected thus, he made this vow:

"I shall diligently apply myself, disregarding even body and life, to practice the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*), maturing sentient beings and purifying the Buddha-field, so that I may swiftly fulfill [the requirements] and quickly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. In my Buddha-field, there shall be no such sentient beings characterized by afflictions or evil karma; all sentient beings shall look upon one another as they would a father or a mother, an elder brother or a younger brother, an elder sister or a younger sister, a son or a daughter, or a friend or a relative, turning toward one another with hearts of loving-kindness and mutually benefiting each other."
“Suvikrāntavikrāmin!
By means of this perfection of patience, these bodhisattva mahāsattvas will swiftly bring it to fulfillment and draw near to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.”
"Furthermore, Subhūti,

there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practicing the perfection of diligence who see sentient beings who are indolent and lazy, who do not apply themselves with diligence, who abandon the three vehicles, and who are unable to cultivate the wholesome karma of humans and devas.
"Subhūti! Having seen this, that bodhisattva mahāsattva reflects:
'How shall I rescue and deliver these classes of sentient beings, causing them to remain far removed from indolence and laziness?'"
Having reflected thus, he made this aspiration:

"I shall diligently apply myself, regardless of body or life, to practice the perfection of vigor (*vīrya-pāramitā*), maturing sentient beings and purifying the Buddha-field, so that I may swiftly fulfill [the requirements] and rapidly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. In my Buddha-field, there shall be no such sentient beings who are indolent or lazy; all sentient beings shall be vigorous and courageous, diligently cultivating the causes for the happy realms and the three vehicles, and quickly attaining liberation among gods and humans."
"Subhūti! By means of this perfection of diligence, these bodhisattva mahāsattvas will swiftly bring it to fulfillment and draw near to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

There are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practicing the perfection of meditative concentration who see sentient beings shrouded by the hindrances of sensual desire, ill will, sloth and torpor, restlessness and remorse, and doubt; they have lost mindfulness and are negligent, such that they cannot even cultivate the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, or the four formless attainments, let alone cultivate supramundane concentrations!"
"Subhūti! Having seen this, that bodhisattva mahāsattva reflects thus:
'How shall I rescue and deliver these classes of sentient beings, causing them to remain far removed from all hindrances and mental distractions?'"
Having reflected thus, he made this aspiration:

"I shall apply myself with diligence, regardless of body or life, to practice the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-pāramitā*), maturing sentient beings and purifying the Buddha-field, so that I may swiftly fulfill [the requirements] and quickly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. In my Buddha-field, there shall be no such sentient beings who possess the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) or mental agitation; all sentient beings therein shall freely sport in the meditative concentrations, the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), and the formless absorptions (*ārūpya-samāpatti*)."

"Subhūti! By means of this perfection of meditative concentration, these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas will swiftly bring it to fulfillment and draw near to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

There are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practicing the perfection of wisdom who see that sentient beings are foolish and possess corrupt intelligence; they have lost both mundane and supramundane right view, and they deny the existence of good and evil karma as well as their fruits. They cling to various false doctrines, such as the views of annihilationism, eternalism, identity, difference, or both and neither."
"Subhūti! Having seen this, that bodhisattva mahāsattva reflects:
'How shall I rescue and deliver these classes of sentient beings, causing them to remain far removed from evil views and perverse attachments?'"
Having reflected thus, he made this vow:

"I shall apply myself with diligence, regardless of body or life, to practice the *prajñāpāramitā*, maturing sentient beings and purifying Buddha-fields, so that I may swiftly fulfill all requirements and quickly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. In my Buddha-field, there shall be no such sentient beings characterized by evil wisdom or false attachments; all sentient beings shall achieve right view and be endowed with various sublime wisdoms and the three types of supernormal knowledge (*traividya*)."
"Subhūti! By means of this perfection of wisdom, these bodhisattva mahāsattvas will swiftly bring it to fulfillment and draw near to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

"Furthermore, Subhūti, there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, while fully practicing the six perfections, perceive the three categories of sentient beings: first, the category of those fixed in error;
second, the category of those fixed in correctness; and third, the category of those who are not yet fixed."
"Subhūti! Having seen this, that bodhisattva mahāsattva reflects:
'By what skillful means shall I rescue these classes of sentient beings and cause them to leave behind the group of those fixed in error and the group of those who are undetermined?'"
Having reflected thus, he made this aspiration:

"I shall apply myself with diligence, disregarding even body and life, to practice the six perfections, to bring sentient beings to maturity, and to purify the Buddha-field, so that I may swiftly fulfill [these requirements] and rapidly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. In my Buddha-field, there shall be no sentient beings belonging to the categories of the 'wrongly fixed' or the 'undetermined'; even the very names of these two groups shall not exist, and all sentient beings shall belong exclusively to the category of the 'rightly fixed.'"
"Subhūti! By means of these six perfections, this bodhisattva mahāsattva will swiftly bring them to fulfillment and draw near to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
"Furthermore, Subhūti, there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who fully cultivate the six perfections and see sentient beings fallen into the three evil destinies:
first, the hells; second, the animal realm; and third, the realm of hungry ghosts."
"Subhūti! Having seen this, that bodhisattva mahāsattva reflects thus:
'How shall I rescue these classes of sentient beings and cause them to be forever free from the sufferings of the three evil destinies?'"
Having reflected thus, he made this aspiration:

"I shall apply myself with diligence, regardless of body or life, to practice the six perfections, maturing sentient beings and purifying Buddha-fields, so that I may swiftly fulfill them and quickly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. In my Buddha-field, there shall be no hells, no animal realm, and no realm of hungry ghosts; even the names of these three evil destinies shall not exist, and all sentient beings shall be comprised within the happy realms."
"Subhūti! By means of these six perfections, this bodhisattva mahāsattva will swiftly bring them to fulfillment and draw near to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
"Furthermore, Subhūti,

there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who fully cultivate the six perfections and see that sentient beings, due to the obstructions of their evil karma, dwell upon a great earth that is uneven with highs and lows, filled with mounds, ravines, pits, foul grass, stumps, poisonous thorns, brambles, and impurities."
"Subhūti! Having seen this, the bodhisattva mahāsattva reflects:

'How shall I rescue these classes of sentient beings so that their various karmic obstacles of evil are forever extinguished, and the ground where they dwell is as level as the palm of a hand, free from all foul weeds, stumps, and the like?'"
Having reflected thus, he made this vow:

"I shall apply myself with diligence, disregarding body and life, to practice the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*), to bring sentient beings to maturity, and to purify the Buddha-fields, so that these may be swiftly perfected and I may quickly realize unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. In my Buddha-field, there shall be no such various defiled karmas; the great earth where sentient beings dwell shall be level, adorned with groves, ponds, and various exquisite fragrant flowers interspersed together, being most delightful."
"Subhūti! By means of these six perfections, this bodhisattva mahāsattva will swiftly bring them to full completion and draw near to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
"Furthermore, Subhūti,

there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who fully cultivate the six perfections and see that because sentient beings have meager merit, the great earth they inhabit lacks all precious treasures and consists only of various kinds of soil, stones, tiles, and rubble."
"Subhūti! Having seen this, that bodhisattva mahāsattva reflects:
'How shall I rescue these classes of sentient beings who have committed many sins and possess little merit, so that the places where they dwell may abound in precious treasures?'"
Having reflected thus, he made this aspiration:

"I shall apply myself with diligence, regardless of body or life, to practice the six perfections, maturing sentient beings and purifying Buddha-fields, so that I may swiftly fulfill [the requirements] and rapidly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. In my Buddha-field, there shall be no such sentient beings who possess little merit and much sin; the ground shall be strewn everywhere with golden sand and various wondrous, exquisite jewels such as lapis lazuli, and sentient beings shall enjoy them without attachment."
"Subhūti! By means of these six perfections, this bodhisattva mahāsattva will swiftly bring them to fulfillment and draw near to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
"Furthermore, Subhūti,

there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who fully cultivate the six perfections and see that sentient beings, regarding all that they have grasped and appropriated, give rise to much attachment and commit various evil deeds."
"Subhūti! Having seen this, that bodhisattva mahāsattva reflects:
'How shall I rescue these classes of sentient beings who are possessed by such evil, so that they may forever be free from their attachment to unwholesome karma?'"
Having reflected thus, he made this vow:

"I shall apply myself with diligence, regardless of body or life, to practice the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā), to bring sentient beings to maturity, and to purify the Buddha-fields, so that I may swiftly fulfill [the requirements] and quickly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. In my Buddha-field, there shall be no such sentient beings who are possessed by evil; all sentient beings shall have no grasping whatsoever toward objects such as form, and shall give rise to no attachment."
"Subhūti! By means of these six perfections, this bodhisattva mahāsattva will swiftly bring them to fulfillment and draw near to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
"Furthermore, Subhūti, there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who fully cultivate the six perfections and perceive that sentient beings are divided into four classes of high and low status:
first, kṣatriyas; second, brāhmaṇas; third, vaiśyas; and fourth, śūdras."
"Subhūti! Having seen this, that bodhisattva mahāsattva reflects thus:
'By what skillful means shall I rescue and deliver all classes of sentient beings, so that there may be no such fourfold distinctions of high and low among them?'"
Having reflected thus, he made this vow:

"I shall apply myself with diligence, disregarding body and life, to practice the six perfections, to bring sentient beings to maturity, and to purify the Buddha-fields, so that I may swiftly fulfill them and quickly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. In my Buddha-field, there shall be no such fourfold distinctions of noble and base; all sentient beings shall be of one kind, all equally noble, and comprised within the human realm."
"Subhūti! By means of these six perfections, this bodhisattva mahāsattva will swiftly bring them to fulfillment and draw near to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
"Furthermore, Subhūti,
there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who fully cultivate the six perfections and perceive that sentient beings have distinctions of inferior, middling, and superior families.
"Subhūti! Having seen this, that bodhisattva mahāsattva reflects:
'By what skillful means should I rescue and deliver all classes of sentient beings, so that there shall be no such distinctions among families—whether inferior, middling, or superior?'"
Having reflected thus, he made this aspiration:

"I shall diligently apply myself, disregarding even body and life, to practice the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā), to bring sentient beings to maturity, and to purify Buddha-fields, so that I may swiftly fulfill [the requirements] and quickly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. In my Buddha-field, there shall be no such distinctions among families—inferior, middling, or superior—and all sentient beings therein shall be of the highest quality."
"Subhūti! By means of these six perfections, this bodhisattva mahāsattva will swiftly bring them to full completion and draw near to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
There are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, while fully practicing the six perfections, see that sentient beings differ in their physical appearance, being either handsome or ugly.
"Subhūti! Having seen this, that bodhisattva mahāsattva reflects:
'By what skillful means shall I rescue these classes of sentient beings so that they no longer have such differences in form and color?'"
Having reflected thus, he made this aspiration:

"I shall apply myself with diligence, disregarding body and life, to practice the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*), to bring sentient beings to maturity, and to purify the Buddha-fields, so that I may swiftly fulfill [these aims] and rapidly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. In my Buddha-field, there shall be no sentient beings of differing forms and colors; all sentient beings shall be of a true golden hue, upright, majestic, and exquisite, a sight for all to delight in, having achieved the foremost, perfect, and pure physical form."
"Subhūti! By means of these six perfections, this bodhisattva mahāsattva will swiftly bring them to fulfillment and draw near to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle 333. Translated by the Dharma Master Xuanzang under Imperial Order. Part One: Chapter Fifty-one, "Vows and Practices," Section Two. "Furthermore, Subhūti!"
There are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who fully cultivate the six perfections and perceive that all sentient beings are bound to a sovereign, such that they lack autonomy in whatever they do.
"Subhūti! Having seen this, the bodhisattva mahāsattva reflects:
'By what skillful means shall I rescue these classes of sentient beings and cause them to attain mastery?'"
Having reflected thus, he made this vow:

"I shall diligently apply myself, disregarding body and life, to practice the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*), to bring sentient beings to maturity, and to adorn and purify a Buddha-field, so that I may swiftly fulfill [these perfections] and rapidly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. In my Buddha-field, all classes of sentient beings shall be without a master; in all their activities they shall attain sovereignty, such that they do not even see the form of a master, nor hear the name of a master, except for the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, who governs by means of the Dharma and is therefore called the Dharma-King."
"Subhūti! By means of these six perfections, this bodhisattva mahāsattva will swiftly attain fulfillment and draw near to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
"Furthermore, Subhūti,
there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who fully cultivate the six perfections and perceive the various distinctions among the realms of rebirth for all sentient beings."
"Subhūti! Having seen this, that bodhisattva mahāsattva reflects:

'By what skillful means shall I rescue and deliver all classes of sentient beings, so that there are no longer distinctions between the various realms of existence, whether wholesome or unwholesome?'"
Having reflected thus, he made this aspiration:

"I shall diligently apply myself, disregarding body and life, to practice the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*), maturing sentient beings and purifying Buddha-fields, so that I may swiftly fulfill [the requirements] and rapidly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. In my Buddha-field, there shall be no distinctions between the various realms of good or evil; even the names of the hells, the animal realm, the realm of hungry ghosts, the asuras, humans, and devas shall not exist. All sentient beings therein shall be of one kind, equally practicing a single activity—namely, all harmoniously practicing the perfection of generosity (*dāna-pāramitā*), and practicing the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom."

They abide in internal emptiness; they abide in external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, non-alteration emptiness, essential nature emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common characteristic emptiness, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence.

They abide in suchness; they abide in the dharma-realm, the dharma-nature, non-falsity, non-alteration, equality, the state beyond birth, the fixed nature of dharmas, the stability of dharmas, the limit of reality, the realm of space, and the inconceivable realm.

They practice the four foundations of mindfulness; they practice the four right endeavors, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path;
they abide in the noble truth of suffering, and they abide in the noble truths of its origin, its cessation, and the path;
they practice the four dhyānas, and they practice the four immeasurables and the four formless absorptions.
They practice the eight liberations; they practice the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative attainments, and the ten totalities;
they practice the gate of liberation of emptiness, and they practice the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness;
they practice the five eyes, and they practice the six supernormal powers.
They cultivate the gateways of samādhi; they cultivate the gateways of dhāraṇī;

they cultivate the ten powers of a Buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
they cultivate the quality of non-forgetfulness, and they cultivate the nature of constant abiding in equanimity.
They practice all-knowledge; they practice the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects;
they practice the conduct of a bodhisattva mahāsattva;
they practice unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
"Subhūti! By means of these six perfections, this bodhisattva mahāsattva will swiftly bring them to full completion and draw near to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
"Furthermore, Subhūti, there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who,
while fully practicing the six perfections, perceive the distinctions among the four modes of birth of sentient beings."
First, birth from an egg;
second, birth from a womb;
third, birth from moisture.
Fourth, they are born by transformation. Subhūti!
Having seen this, the bodhisattva mahāsattva reflects as follows:
"How shall I employ skillful means to rescue and deliver all classes of sentient beings so that there are no such distinctions among the four modes of birth?
Having reflected thus, he made this vow:

"I shall diligently apply myself, disregarding even body and life, to practice the six perfections, maturing sentient beings and purifying Buddha-fields, so that I may swiftly fulfill these requirements and quickly realize unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. In my Buddha-field, may the various classes of sentient beings be free from such distinctions among the four modes of birth; may all sentient beings be born through transformation alone."
"Subhūti! By means of these six perfections, this bodhisattva mahāsattva will swiftly bring them to fulfillment and draw near to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
There are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who fully cultivate the six perfections and see that sentient beings lack the five supernormal powers and thus do not attain mastery over their actions."
"Subhūti! Having seen this, that bodhisattva mahāsattva reflects:
'By what skillful means shall I rescue all classes of sentient beings, so that they may all attain the wisdom of the five supernormal powers?'"
Having reflected thus, he made this vow:

"I shall diligently apply myself, disregarding even my own body and life, to practice the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā), to bring sentient beings to maturity, and to purify the Buddha-fields, so that I may swiftly fulfill all requirements and quickly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; and within my Buddha-field, may all classes of sentient beings attain mastery over the five supernormal powers and wisdom."
"Subhūti! By means of these six perfections, this bodhisattva mahāsattva will swiftly bring them to fulfillment and draw near to unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

There are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who fully cultivate the six perfections and see that sentient beings consume solid food, and that their bodies produce various forms of excrement and urine—pus, blood, and foul impurities so utterly loathsome as to be deeply worthy of renunciation."
"Subhūti! Having seen this, the bodhisattva mahāsattva reflects:
'How shall I rescue these classes of sentient beings who subsist on edible food, so that there may be no excrement or filth within their bodies?'"
Having reflected thus, he made this vow:

"I shall apply myself with diligence, disregarding body and life, to practice the six perfections, maturing sentient beings and purifying the Buddha-field, so that I may swiftly fulfill them and rapidly realize unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. Within my Buddha-field, all classes of sentient beings shall equally enjoy the sublime food of the joy of the Dharma, their bodies fragrant and pure, free from all excrement and urine."
"Subhūti! By means of these six perfections, this bodhisattva mahāsattva will swiftly bring them to fulfillment and draw near to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening."
"Furthermore, Subhūti,

there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who fully cultivate the six perfections and see that sentient beings lack physical radiance, such that they must seek external illumination for all their activities."
"Subhūti! Having seen this, that bodhisattva mahāsattva reflects:
'By what skillful means shall I rescue these classes of sentient beings and cause them to be free from such bodies devoid of light?'"
Having reflected thus, he made this aspiration:

"I shall apply myself with diligence, regardless of body or life, to practice the six perfections, ripening sentient beings and purifying Buddha-fields, so that I may swiftly fulfill [the requirements] and quickly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; and in my Buddha-field, all classes of sentient beings shall possess bodily radiance, rendering external illumination unnecessary."
"Subhūti! By means of these six perfections, this bodhisattva mahāsattva will swiftly bring them to fulfillment and draw near to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

There are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who fully cultivate the six perfections and perceive that the lands where sentient beings dwell have days and nights, months and half-months, and that the changes of seasons and years are not constant."
"Subhūti! Having seen this, that bodhisattva mahāsattva reflects:
'By what skillful means shall I rescue and deliver all classes of sentient beings, so that the land they inhabit shall be free from all transformations such as day and night?'"
Having reflected thus, he made this aspiration:

"I shall apply myself with diligence, regardless of body or life, to practice the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*), maturing sentient beings and purifying Buddha-fields, so that I may swiftly fulfill [the requirements] and quickly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. In my Buddha-field, there shall be no day or night, nor months, half-months, seasons, or years; indeed, even the names 'day' and 'night' shall not exist."
"Subhūti! By means of these six perfections, this bodhisattva mahāsattva will swiftly bring them to fulfillment and draw near to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
There are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who fully cultivate the six perfections and see that the lifespans of sentient beings are short."
"Subhūti! Having seen this, that bodhisattva mahāsattva reflects:
'By what skillful means shall I rescue these classes of sentient beings and cause them to be free from such a short lifespan?'"
Having reflected thus, he made this aspiration:

"I shall diligently apply myself, disregarding body and life, to practice the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā), to bring sentient beings to maturity, and to purify Buddha-fields, so that I may swiftly fulfill [these requirements] and quickly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. In my Buddha-field, the lifespan of all sentient beings shall be so long that its duration in kalpas will be difficult to know."
"Subhūti! By means of these six perfections, this bodhisattva mahāsattva will swiftly bring them to fulfillment and draw near to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
"Furthermore, Subhūti,
there are bodhisattva mahāsattvas who fully cultivate the six perfections and see that sentient beings lack the various marks and signs of excellence."
"Subhūti! Having seen this, the bodhisattva mahāsattva reflects:
'By what skillful means shall I rescue these classes of sentient beings and cause them to attain the primary and secondary marks?'"
Having reflected thus, he made this aspiration:

"I shall apply myself with diligence, regardless of body or life, to practice the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*), to bring sentient beings to maturity, and to purify Buddha-fields, so that I may swiftly fulfill [these requirements] and quickly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*). In my Buddha-field, all classes of sentient beings shall possess the thirty-two marks of a great man (*dvātriṃśan-mahāpuruṣa-lakṣaṇa*) and be fully adorned with the eighty secondary signs (*aśīty-anuvyañjana*), such that sentient beings who see them will give rise to pure and sublime joy."
"Subhūti! By means of these six perfections, this bodhisattva mahāsattva will swiftly bring them to fulfillment and draw near to unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
There are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who fully cultivate the six perfections and see that classes of sentient beings are devoid of all roots of goodness."
"Subhūti! Having seen this, the bodhisattva mahāsattva reflects:
'How shall I deliver these classes of sentient beings so that they may be endowed with roots of goodness?'"
Having reflected thus, he made this aspiration:

"I shall apply myself with diligence, regardless of body or life, to practice the six perfections, maturing sentient beings and purifying Buddha-fields, so that I may swiftly fulfill them and quickly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. In my Buddha-field, all classes of sentient beings shall fully accomplish supreme and wondrous roots of goodness; by virtue of these roots of goodness, they shall be able to provide various kinds of sublime offerings to the Buddhas, and through the power of this merit, wherever they are born, they shall further be able to make offerings to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones."
"Subhūti! By means of these six perfections, this bodhisattva mahāsattva will swiftly bring them to fulfillment and draw near to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
"Furthermore, Subhūti,
there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who fully cultivate the six perfections and see that sentient beings are afflicted by diseases of both body and mind.
There are four types of physical illness:
first, wind-related illnesses;
second, heat-related illnesses.
Third, phlegm diseases;
fourth, various miscellaneous diseases such as wind disorders.
There are likewise four types of mental illnesses:
First is the disease of greed;
second is the disease of hatred;
third is the disease of delusion.
Fourth, the diseases of the afflictions such as pride.
Subhūti! Having seen this, the bodhisattva mahāsattva reflects as follows:
"How shall I rescue these classes of sentient beings who suffer from such physical and mental ailments?
Having thus reflected, he made this vow:

"I shall apply myself with diligence, disregarding body and life, to practice the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā), maturing sentient beings and purifying Buddha-fields, so that I may swiftly fulfill [the requirements] and rapidly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Within my Buddha-field, all classes of sentient beings shall have pure bodies and minds, free from all physical and mental suffering; they shall not even hear the names of wind-diseases, bile-diseases, phlegm-diseases, or diseases resulting from combinations of wind and other humors, nor shall they hear the names of the afflictions (kleśa) of greed, hatred, delusion, pride, and so forth."
"Subhūti! By means of these six perfections, this bodhisattva mahāsattva will swiftly bring them to fulfillment and draw near to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

There are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who fully cultivate the six perfections and perceive the various inclinations of sentient beings: some are inclined toward the vehicle of the śrāvakas, some are inclined toward the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas, and some are inclined toward the unsurpassed vehicle.
"Subhūti! Having seen this, the bodhisattva mahāsattva reflects:
