"I have now attained a vast and sublime benefit; for the sake of benefiting me, those sentient beings have come to cut and sever my body into its various limbs and joints. Yet, I originally received this body for the sake of all sentient beings; they have now come and taken what belongs to them, thereby accomplishing my purpose."

In this way, the bodhisattva reflects with profound discernment upon the true nature of all phenomena and practices patience. Taking these superior roots of goodness of patience, they do not seek the levels of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas; rather, they take these roots of goodness of patience and, sharing them equally with all sentient beings, dedicate them toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Taking non-apprehension as the skillful means, when one thus dedicates toward great enlightenment, one remains free from the three thoughts: namely, who is dedicating? By what means is one dedicating?
To what is one dedicating?
"To where would it be dedicated?
Thus, these three types of thought will never arise again, Subhūti!"
"This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling securely in the perfection of diligence, draws forth and encompasses the perfection of patience.
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha again, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling securely in the perfection of diligence, attract and gather the perfection of meditative concentration?
The Buddha said,
"Suvikrāntavikrāmin!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling securely in the perfection of diligence, cultivates the various meditative concentrations, that bodhisattva mahāsattva—detached from desires and unwholesome states, with directed thought and sustained thought, born of detachment and filled with joy and happiness—enters and dwells fully in the first dhyāna;

with the stilling of directed thought and sustained thought, through internal serenity and mental one-pointedness, without directed thought or sustained thought, born of concentration and filled with joy and happiness, he enters and dwells fully in the second dhyāna;

detached from joy, dwelling in equanimity, mindful and clearly aware, experiencing happiness with the body—that which the noble ones describe as "dwelling in happiness with mindfulness and equanimity"—he enters and dwells fully in the third dhyāna.

With the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, and with the prior disappearance of joy and sorrow, he enters and dwells in the fourth dhyāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant and is characterized by purity of equanimity and mindfulness.

This bodhisattva mahāsattva, generating the mental attention of the thought of bestowing happiness upon all sentient beings, enters and dwells in the perfection of the immeasurable state of loving-kindness;
generating the mental attention of the thought of extracting suffering from all sentient beings, he enters and dwells in the perfection of the immeasurable state of compassion.
One generates the mental attention of the perception of joy toward all sentient beings and enters and dwells in the perfection of the immeasurable state of sympathetic joy (*muditā*);

one generates the mental attention of the perception of equanimity regarding the departure from suffering and pleasure toward all sentient beings and enters and dwells in the perfection of the immeasurable state of equanimity (*upekṣā*).

This bodhisattva mahāsattva gives rise to the mental attention of the perception of loathsomeness regarding all forms and enters the meditative absorption of the sphere of infinite space, dwelling therein in its full perfection;

he gives rise to the mental attention of the perception of tranquility regarding all consciousnesses and enters the meditative absorption of the sphere of infinite consciousness, dwelling therein in its full perfection;

he gives rise to the mental attention of the perception of tranquility regarding nothingness and enters the meditative absorption of the sphere of nothingness, dwelling therein in its full perfection.

He attends with the mental orientation of the perception of tranquility toward the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and enters and dwells in full possession of the meditative absorption of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;

he attends with the mental orientation of the perception of cessation toward the cessation of perception and feeling and enters and dwells in full possession of the meditative absorption of the cessation of perception and feeling.

Although this bodhisattva mahāsattva cultivates such meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*), and the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), they do not grasp at their karmic maturation (*vipāka-phala*); rather, in accordance with the needs of sentient beings who are ready to be transformed, they take birth within those realms as a place to bring about benefit and happiness.

Once they have been born there, he gathers them in through the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) and, by skillful means, establishes them so that they may diligently train in the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom.

Relying on these meditative concentrations, this bodhisattva mahāsattva gives rise to superior supernormal powers, traveling from one buddha-field to another to attend upon and make offerings to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, inquiring about the profound nature and characteristics of all phenomena, and diligently cultivating and bringing forth sublime roots of goodness.

This bodhisattva mahāsattva gathers together these various kinds of roots of goodness and, sharing them equally with all sentient beings, dedicates them toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Taking non-apprehension as the skillful means, when thus dedicating toward great enlightenment, one remains far removed from the three thoughts: namely, who is it that dedicates? By what means does one dedicate?
To what end is it dedicated?
"To what should it be dedicated?
Such threefold thoughts shall never arise again, Subhūti!"
"This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling securely in the perfection of diligence, draws forth and encompasses the perfection of meditative concentration.
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One!"
“How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling securely in the perfection of diligence, attract and gather the perfection of wisdom?
The Buddha said,
“Suvikrāntavikrāmin!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva abides in the perfection of diligence, that bodhisattva mahāsattva is able, regarding the perfection of generosity, not to perceive its name, not to perceive its thing, not to perceive its nature, and not to perceive its characteristic;

and likewise, regarding the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, they do not perceive their names, do not perceive their things, do not perceive their natures, and do not perceive their characteristics.

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva abides in the perfection of diligence, that bodhisattva mahāsattva is able, regarding the four foundations of mindfulness, not to see their names, not to see their entities, not to see their natures, and not to see their characteristics;

and they are likewise able, regarding the four right endeavors, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path, not to see their names, not to see their entities, not to see their natures, and not to see their characteristics."

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva abides in the perfection of diligence, that bodhisattva mahāsattva is able, regarding internal emptiness, not to perceive names, not to perceive things, not to perceive natures, and not to perceive characteristics;

and regarding external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersal emptiness, non-alteration emptiness, essential nature emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common characteristic emptiness, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature, they likewise do not perceive names, do not perceive things, do not perceive natures, and do not perceive characteristics."

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva abides in the perfection of diligence, that bodhisattva mahāsattva is able, with respect to suchness, not to perceive a name, not to perceive a thing, not to perceive a nature, and not to perceive a characteristic;

and they are likewise able, with respect to the dharma-realm, the dharma-nature, the non-erroneous nature, the unchanging nature, the nature of equality, the nature of freedom from arising, the fixedness of dharmas, the stability of dharmas, the limit of reality, the realm of space, and the inconceivable realm, not to perceive a name, not to perceive a thing, not to perceive a nature, and not to perceive a characteristic."

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva abides in the perfection of diligence, that bodhisattva mahāsattva is able, regarding the noble truth of suffering, not to perceive its name, not to perceive its substance, not to perceive its nature, and not to perceive its characteristics;

and regarding the noble truths of origin, cessation, and the path, they likewise do not perceive their names, do not perceive their substances, do not perceive their natures, and do not perceive their characteristics."

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva abides in the perfection of diligence, that bodhisattva mahāsattva is able, regarding the four dhyānas, not to perceive their names, not to perceive their entities, not to perceive their natures, and not to perceive their marks;

they are likewise able, regarding the four immeasurables and the four formless absorptions, not to perceive their names, not to perceive their entities, not to perceive their natures, and not to perceive their marks."

“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva abides in the perfection of diligence, that bodhisattva mahāsattva is able, regarding the eight liberations, not to perceive their names, not to perceive their entities, not to perceive their natures, and not to perceive their characteristics;

and regarding the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities, they likewise do not perceive their names, do not perceive their entities, do not perceive their natures, and do not perceive their characteristics.”

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells securely in the perfection of diligence, that bodhisattva mahāsattva is able, regarding the gate of liberation of emptiness, not to perceive names, not to perceive things, not to perceive natures, and not to perceive marks;
and regarding the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness, likewise not to perceive names, not to perceive things, not to perceive natures, and not to perceive marks."

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva abides in the perfection of diligence, that bodhisattva mahāsattva is able, regarding the five eyes, not to perceive names, not to perceive things, not to perceive natures, and not to perceive marks;
and regarding the six supernormal powers, likewise not to perceive names, not to perceive things, not to perceive natures, and not to perceive marks."

“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva abides in the perfection of diligence, that bodhisattva mahāsattva is able, regarding the ten powers of a buddha, not to perceive their names, not to perceive their entities, not to perceive their natures, and not to perceive their characteristics;

and regarding the four fearlessnesses, the four unhindered understandings, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha, they likewise do not perceive their names, do not perceive their entities, do not perceive their natures, and do not perceive their characteristics.”

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva abides in the perfection of diligence, that bodhisattva mahāsattva is able, regarding the quality of non-forgetfulness, not to perceive its name, not to perceive its object, not to perceive its nature, and not to perceive its characteristics;
and regarding the quality of constant equanimity, they likewise do not perceive its name, do not perceive its object, do not perceive its nature, and do not perceive its characteristics."

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva abides in the perfection of diligence, that bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to neither perceive names, nor perceive things, nor perceive natures, nor perceive characteristics regarding all-knowledge;
they are likewise able to neither perceive names, nor perceive things, nor perceive natures, nor perceive characteristics regarding the knowledge of the paths and the knowledge of all aspects."

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva abides in the perfection of diligence, that bodhisattva mahāsattva is able, regarding all dhāraṇī-doors, not to perceive names, not to perceive things, not to perceive natures, and not to perceive marks;
and regarding all samādhi-doors, likewise not to perceive names, not to perceive things, not to perceive natures, and not to perceive marks."

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva abides in the perfection of diligence, this bodhisattva mahāsattva is able, regarding all the practices of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, not to perceive their names, not to perceive their entities, not to perceive their natures, and not to perceive their marks;

and regarding the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas, they likewise do not perceive their names, do not perceive their entities, do not perceive their natures, and do not perceive their marks."

“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells securely in the perfection of diligence, that bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to not perceive the name, not perceive the thing, not perceive the nature, and not perceive the characteristic of the fruit of a stream-enterer;

they are likewise able to not perceive the name, not perceive the thing, not perceive the nature, and not perceive the characteristic of the fruit of a once-returner, a non-returner, an arhat, or the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha.”

“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells securely in the perfection of diligence, that bodhisattva mahāsattva is able, with respect to form, not to perceive its name, not to perceive its substance, not to perceive its nature, and not to perceive its characteristics;

and with respect to feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, they likewise do not perceive their names, do not perceive their substances, do not perceive their natures, and do not perceive their characteristics.”

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva abides in the perfection of diligence, that bodhisattva mahāsattva is able, regarding the sense base of the eye, not to perceive a name, not to perceive an object, not to perceive an essence, and not to perceive a characteristic;

and regarding the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, they likewise do not perceive a name, do not perceive an object, do not perceive an essence, and do not perceive a characteristic."

“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva abides in the perfection of diligence, that bodhisattva mahāsattva is able, regarding the sphere of form, not to perceive a name, not to perceive an entity, not to perceive a nature, and not to perceive a characteristic;

and regarding the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena, they likewise do not perceive a name, do not perceive an entity, do not perceive a nature, and do not perceive a characteristic.”

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva abides in the perfection of diligence, that bodhisattva mahāsattva is able, regarding the eye-element, not to perceive a name, not to perceive a thing, not to perceive an essence, and not to perceive a characteristic;
they are likewise able, regarding the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-elements, not to perceive a name, not to perceive a thing, not to perceive an essence, and not to perceive a characteristic."

“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva abides in the perfection of diligence, this bodhisattva mahāsattva is able, regarding the realm of form, not to perceive names, not to perceive things, not to perceive natures, and not to perceive characteristics;

and regarding the realms of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena, they likewise do not perceive names, do not perceive things, do not perceive natures, and do not perceive characteristics.”

“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva abides in the perfection of diligence, that bodhisattva mahāsattva is able, regarding the sphere of visual consciousness, not to see a name, not to see an object, not to see an essence, and not to see a characteristic;

and regarding the spheres of auditory, olfactory, gustatory, tactile, and mental consciousness, they likewise do not see a name, do not see an object, do not see an essence, and do not see a characteristic.”

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva abides in the perfection of diligence, that bodhisattva mahāsattva is able, regarding visual contact, not to perceive a name, not to perceive an object, not to perceive a nature, and not to perceive a characteristic;

and regarding auditory, olfactory, gustatory, tactile, and mental contact, they likewise do not perceive a name, do not perceive an object, do not perceive a nature, and do not perceive a characteristic."

“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva abides in the perfection of diligence, that bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to neither perceive a name, nor perceive an entity, nor perceive a nature, nor perceive a characteristic in the feelings produced with eye-contact as condition;

they are likewise able to neither perceive a name, nor perceive an entity, nor perceive a nature, nor perceive a characteristic in the feelings produced with ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-contact as condition.”

“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva abides in the perfection of diligence, this bodhisattva mahāsattva is able, regarding the earth element, not to perceive its name, not to perceive its substance, not to perceive its nature, and not to perceive its characteristics;

and likewise, regarding the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements, they do not perceive their names, do not perceive their substances, do not perceive their natures, and do not perceive their characteristics.”

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells securely in the perfection of diligence, that bodhisattva mahāsattva is able, regarding ignorance, not to perceive its name, not to perceive its substance, not to perceive its nature, and not to perceive its characteristics;

and regarding volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, and old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair, they likewise do not perceive their names, do not perceive their substances, do not perceive their natures, and do not perceive their characteristics."

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells securely in the perfection of diligence, that bodhisattva mahāsattva is able, regarding phenomena that are with form and without form, not to perceive their names, not to perceive their entities, not to perceive their natures, and not to perceive their characteristics;

and regarding phenomena that are visible or invisible, resistant or non-resistant, outflowing or non-outflowing, conditioned or unconditioned, they likewise do not perceive their names, do not perceive their entities, do not perceive their natures, and do not perceive their characteristics."

"In this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not perceive any names, entities, natures, or characteristics within all phenomena; they do not give rise to conceptualizations regarding these phenomena and remain without attachment, acting exactly as described.
Furthermore, with such roots of goodness from sublime wisdom, they share them equally with all sentient beings and dedicate them toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete awakening."

Taking non-apprehension as the skillful means, when thus dedicating toward great enlightenment, one remains far removed from the three thoughts: namely, who is it that dedicates? By what means does one dedicate?
What is it that is dedicated?
"To what should it be dedicated?
Such threefold thoughts shall never arise again, Subhūti!"
"This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling securely in the perfection of diligence, draws forth and gathers the perfection of wisdom.
At that time, the venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha,
saying, "World-Honored One!"
“How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling securely in the perfection of meditative concentration, attract and gather the perfection of generosity?
The Buddha said,
“Suvikrāntavikrāmin!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling securely in the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*), practices the giving of material wealth and the Dharma toward all sentient beings, that bodhisattva mahāsattva—free from desires and unwholesome states, with directed thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*), and possessing the joy and bliss born of seclusion—enters and dwells in the full possession of the first dhyāna;

with the subsiding of directed and sustained thought, through internal tranquility and mental unification, free from directed and sustained thought, and possessing the joy and bliss born of concentration, he enters and dwells in the full possession of the second dhyāna;

free from joy, he dwells in equanimity, mindful and clearly aware, experiencing bliss with the body, which the noble ones describe as "dwelling in bliss with mindfulness and equanimity," and he enters and dwells in the full possession of the third dhyāna.

With the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, and with the prior disappearance of joy and sorrow, he enters and dwells in the fourth dhyāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant and is characterized by the purity of equanimity and mindfulness.
He enters and dwells in the immeasurable state of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), having directed his attention toward all sentient beings with the thought of bestowing happiness upon them;
he enters and dwells in the immeasurable state of compassion (*karuṇā*), having directed his attention toward all sentient beings with the thought of uprooting their suffering.
One enters and dwells in full possession of the immeasurable joy by attending to the perception of gladness toward all sentient beings;
one enters and dwells in full possession of the immeasurable equanimity by attending to the perception of impartiality regarding the departure from suffering and pleasure toward all sentient beings;
and one enters and dwells in full possession of the meditative absorption of the sphere of infinite space by attending to the perception of revulsion toward coarse forms.
By attending to the perception of tranquility regarding all consciousnesses, he enters and dwells in the attainment of the sphere of infinite consciousness;
by attending to the perception of tranquility regarding nothingness, he enters and dwells in the attainment of the sphere of nothingness;

and by attending to the perception of tranquility regarding that which is neither-perception-nor-non-perception, he enters and dwells in the attainment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

Regarding the cessation of the perception of ideation and sensation (*saṃjñā-vedita-nirodha-samāpatti*), he attends to the thought of stillness and enters the cessation of ideation and sensation, dwelling therein in its full perfection.

This bodhisattva mahāsattva, abiding thus in the aforementioned perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-pāramitā*), with an undistracted mind practices the giving of material goods and the Dharma to all sentient beings; he himself constantly practices the giving of material goods and the Dharma, and also constantly encourages others to practice the giving of material goods and the Dharma; he constantly and unerringly extols the method of practicing the giving of material goods and the Dharma, and always joyfully praises those who practice the giving of material goods and the Dharma.

This bodhisattva mahāsattva, upholding these roots of goodness, does not seek the levels of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas; rather, taking these roots of goodness from such giving, they share them equally with all sentient beings and dedicate them toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Taking non-apprehension as the skillful means, when thus dedicating toward great enlightenment, one remains far removed from three thoughts: namely, who is dedicating? By what means is one dedicating?
What is being dedicated?
"To what should they be dedicated?
Such threefold thoughts shall never arise again, Subhūti!"
"This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling securely in the perfection of meditative concentration, draws forth and gathers the perfection of generosity.
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha again, saying,
"World-Honored One!"
“How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling securely in the perfection of meditative concentration, attract and gather the perfection of ethical discipline?
The Buddha said,
“Suvikrāntavikrāmin!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva abides in the perfection of meditative concentration, they maintain pure ethical discipline and never give rise to a mind associated with greed, a mind associated with hatred, or a mind associated with delusion; they never give rise to a mind associated with malice, a mind associated with stinginess, or a mind associated with envy; they never give rise to a mind that delights in violating pure ethical discipline, but always give rise to mental engagement associated with the knowledge of all modes.

Furthermore, taking these roots of virtue and merit, they do not seek the levels of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, but instead dedicate them equally and in common with all sentient beings toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Using non-apprehension as the skillful means, when dedicating in this way toward great enlightenment, one remains far removed from three thoughts: namely, who is dedicating? By what means is one dedicating?
What is being dedicated?
"To where would it be dedicated?
Such threefold thoughts as these shall never arise again, Subhūti!"
"This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling in the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*), draws forth and encompasses the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*).

The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle Three Hundred Forty-nine, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Part Sixty-two of the First Division, Chapter on Mutual Induction and Encompassment. The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
“How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling securely in the perfection of meditative concentration, attract and gather the perfection of patience?
The Buddha said,
“Suvikrāntavikrāmin!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling securely in the perfection of meditative concentration, practices the training in patience, they contemplate form as being like a mass of foam, feeling as being like a bubble on the water, perception as being like a mirage, mental formations as being like a plantain tree, and consciousness as being like a magical illusion. When making such observations, the perception that the five aggregates of clinging are not solid constantly manifests before them.
Again, he reflects thus:
"All phenomena are empty, devoid of self and what belongs to a self; whose form is this?
Whose sensation is this?"
Whose perception is this perception?
Whose volitional formations are these volitional formations?
Whose consciousness is this consciousness?
When observing in this way, he further reflects:
"All phenomena are empty and devoid of self and what belongs to self; who is it that cuts?
Who is it that receives the cutting?"
Who is able to revile and abuse?
Who receives the reviling and abuse?
And who, moreover, gives rise to anger and resentment therein?

Thus, relying upon meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), the bodhisattva carefully and discerningly observes so as to be fully endowed with patience (*kṣānti*); furthermore, he takes these roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) of patience and, sharing them equally with all sentient beings, dedicates them toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).

Taking non-apprehension as the skillful means, when one thus dedicates toward great enlightenment, one remains far removed from three thoughts: namely, who is dedicating? By what means is one dedicating?
What is being dedicated?
"To where would they dedicate them?
Such threefold thoughts will never arise again, Subhūti!"
"This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling securely in the perfection of meditative concentration, draws forth and encompasses the perfection of patience.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One!"
“How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling in the perfection of meditative concentration, attract and gather the perfection of diligence?
The Buddha said,
“Suvikrāntavikrāmin!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells securely in the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*), they exert various forms of courageous diligence; that is to say, the bodhisattva mahāsattva, detached from desires and unwholesome states, possessing applied and sustained thought, and with the joy and happiness born of seclusion, enters and dwells in the full possession of the first dhyāna;

with the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, with internal serenity and mental unification, without applied or sustained thought, and with the joy and happiness born of concentration, they enter and dwell in the full possession of the second dhyāna;

being detached from joy, they dwell in equanimity, mindful and clearly aware, experiencing happiness with the body—of which the noble ones say, "One who has equanimity and mindfulness dwells happily"—and thus they enter and dwell in the full possession of the third dhyāna.

"Having abandoned pleasure and abandoned pain, and with the prior disappearance of joy and sorrow, he enters and dwells in the fourth dhyāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant and is characterized by purity of equanimity and mindfulness.
When a bodhisattva thus cultivates dhyāna, he does not grasp at the signs of the various dhyānas or their factors;
rather, he gives rise to the extraordinary supernormal power of the knowledge of psychic transformations (*ṛddhividhi-jñānābhijñā*), whereby he is able to perform boundless great miraculous feats."
That which is called shaking the worlds of the ten directions; transforming one into many and many into one;
appearing or disappearing with rapid and unimpeded ease; passing straight through mountain cliffs and walls as if through space;
traveling back and forth through the air like a flying bird; emerging from and submerging in the earth as if in water; and walking upon the surface of the water.
As when walking upon the earth, his body emits smoke and flames like a wildfire on a high plateau; as when his person pours forth streams of water like the melting of the Snowy Mountains;

and as the divine majesty of the sun and moon is difficult to withstand, yet he can touch them with his hand until their radiance is eclipsed—even unto the Pure Abodes where he transforms at will—such miraculous transformations are beyond measure.
He exercises the supernormal power of the divine ear, which is preeminent, clear, and pure, surpassing that of humans and gods;
he is able to hear, exactly as they are, the various sounds of sentient and insentient beings throughout the worlds of the ten directions—
namely, hearing everywhere the sounds of the various hells, the sounds of animals, the sounds of the realm of hungry ghosts, the sounds of humans, and the sounds of devas.
The sound of śrāvakas, the sound of pratyekabuddhas, the sound of bodhisattvas, the sound of all buddhas; the sound of censuring and reviling birth-and-death (saṃsāra), the sound of praising nirvāṇa,
the sound of turning one’s back on the conditioned (saṃskṛta), the sound of proceeding toward awakening (bodhi), the sound of loathing that which is with outflows (sāsrava),
the sound of delighting in that which is without outflows (anāsrava), the sound of extolling the Triple Gem (triratna), and the sound of subduing...
The sound of heterodox paths, the sound of debating and discerning, the sound of chanting the sūtras, the sound of exhorting the severance of unwholesome dharmas,
the sound of inducing the cultivation of wholesome dharmas, and the sound of rescuing from suffering and distress—
whether these sounds were great or small, he heard them all without obstruction.
“Having induced the supernormal knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna-abhijñā) that is preeminent, one is able to know, as they truly are,
the minds and mental factors of other sentient beings throughout the worlds of the ten directions; that is to say,
one thoroughly knows whether other sentient beings possess a mind of attachment or a mind free from attachment, a mind of aversion or a mind free from aversion, or a mind of delusion...”
The mind free from delusion; whether the mind has attachment or is free from attachment, whether it has grasping or is free from grasping,
whether it is concentrated or scattered, whether it is small or great, whether it is uplifted or depressed,
whether it is tranquil or not tranquil, whether it is restless or not restless.
Whether the mind is concentrated or unconcentrated, liberated or unliberated,
with outflows or without outflows, cultivated or uncultivated, surpassable or unsurpassable— he knows all such minds as they truly are.

“Having aroused the supernormal knowledge of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñānasākṣātkriyābhijñā*), he truly recollects and knows the various matters of the past lives of immeasurable sentient beings in the worlds of the ten directions;
that is to say, he recollects, whether for himself or others, the events of past lives during the duration of one thought-moment,
ten thought-moments, a hundred thought-moments, a thousand thought-moments, or many hundreds of thousands of thought-moments, or furthermore, he follows...”
He recollects various past lives for one day, ten days, a hundred days, a thousand days, or many hundreds of thousands of days;
or again, he recollects various past lives for one month, ten months, a hundred months, a thousand months, or many hundreds of thousands of months;
or again, he recollects [past lives] for one year, ten years, a hundred years, or many hundreds of thousands of years.
He recollects events from past lives spanning a thousand years, many hundreds of thousands of years; or, according to his recollection,
one eon, ten eons, a hundred eons, a thousand eons, many hundreds of thousands of eons, even up to immeasurable, incalculable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of eons—
all such events of past lives, or whatever belongs to the prior limit of existence, he recollects according to his recollection.

Regarding all matters of past lives: in such a place and at such a time, there was one with such a name, such a clan, such a caste, such food, such a duration of stay, such a limit of lifespan, such longevity, such experience of pleasure, and such experience of suffering; passing away from that place, they were reborn here.

In the meantime, he recollects all matters of former existences—whether briefly or in detail, whether his own or those of others—including passing away from this place and being reborn in that place, their physical appearances, and their speech. He knows them all through recollection.

He has brought forth the supernormal power of the sublime divine eye-knowledge, possessing a clear and pure vision that transcends that of human or celestial eyes; he is able to see, as they truly are, the various forms of sentient and insentient beings throughout the worlds of the ten directions—namely, seeing universally the subtle and coarse forms of all classes of sentient beings at the time of death and the time of birth, their rebirths in happy or miserable realms, whether superior or inferior, and all such various forms.

Therefore, one further understands that among the various classes of sentient beings, there are differences in rebirth according to the power of their karma. Thus, there are sentient beings who have accomplished misconduct of body, accomplished misconduct of speech, and accomplished misconduct of mind; who, through the causes and conditions of slandering the noble ones and holding wrong views, at the dissolution of the body after death, shall fall into the evil destinies—either being born in hell, or born as an animal, or born in the realm of hungry ghosts, or born among the base and wicked sentient beings of the borderlands, where they undergo various sufferings and afflictions.

In this way, he knows as it truly is how sentient beings who have accomplished virtuous conduct of body, accomplished virtuous conduct of speech, and accomplished virtuous conduct of mind—due to the causes and conditions of praising the noble ones and right view—upon the dissolution of the body after death, shall ascend to a happy destination, whether being born among the devas or among human beings, and experience various forms of happiness; thus he knows the distinctions in the fruits experienced by sentient beings according to their various types of karma.

“Abiding in these five sublime supernormal powers, the bodhisattva travels from one buddha-field to another, approaching and making offerings to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones; he inquires about the profound meaning of the Dharma from the Buddhas, plants immeasurable and subtle roots of goodness, brings sentient beings to maturity, purifies buddha-fields, and diligently cultivates the various practices of a bodhisattva.”

Taking these roots of goodness, they do not seek the levels of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, but instead dedicate them equally and in common with all sentient beings toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Taking non-apprehension as the skillful means, when one thus dedicates toward great enlightenment, one remains far removed from the three thoughts: namely, who is dedicating? By what means is one dedicating?
What is being dedicated?
"To what would they dedicate them?
Such threefold thoughts will never arise again, Subhūti!"
"This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling securely in the perfection of meditative concentration, draws forth and encompasses the perfection of diligence.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One!"
“How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling securely in the perfection of meditative concentration, draw forth and encompass the perfection of wisdom?
The Buddha said,
“Suvikrāntavikrāmin!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells securely in the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*), they observe that form (*rūpa*) is unapprehendable; they observe that feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) are unapprehendable.
They observe that the eye-base (*cakṣur-āyatana*) is unapprehendable; they observe that the ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-bases (*śrotra-ghrāṇa-jihvā-kāya-manas-āyatana*) are unapprehendable.

They observe that the form-base (*rūpāyatana*) is unapprehendable; they observe that the sound-, odor-, taste-, tangible-, and mental-object-bases (*śabda-gandha-rasa-spraṣṭavya-dharmāyatana*) are unapprehendable.
One contemplates that the eye-element is unapprehendable; one contemplates that the ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-elements are unapprehendable.
One contemplates that the form-element is unapprehendable; one contemplates that the sound-, odor-, taste-, tangible-, and mental-object-elements are unapprehendable.
One contemplates that the eye-consciousness-element is unapprehendable; one contemplates that the ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-consciousness-elements are unapprehendable.
One contemplates that eye-contact is unapprehendable; one contemplates that ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact are unapprehendable.

One contemplates that the various feelings produced with eye-contact as condition are unapprehendable; one contemplates that the various feelings produced with ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact as conditions are unapprehendable.
One contemplates that the earth element is unapprehendable; one contemplates that the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements are unapprehendable.

One contemplates that ignorance is unapprehendable; one contemplates that volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, existence, birth, and old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are unapprehendable;

one contemplates that the perfection of generosity is unapprehendable; and one contemplates that the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom are unapprehendable.

One contemplates that internal emptiness is unapprehendable; one contemplates that external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, non-altering emptiness, essential emptiness, emptiness of self-characteristic, emptiness of common characteristic, emptiness of all phenomena, emptiness of the unapprehendable, emptiness of non-existence, emptiness of intrinsic nature, and emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence are unapprehendable.

One contemplates that suchness is unapprehendable; one contemplates that the dharma-realm, dharma-nature, non-falsity, non-alteration, equality, the nature of being free from birth, the fixedness of dharmas, the stability of dharmas, the limit of reality, the realm of space, and the inconceivable realm are unapprehendable.
One contemplates that the Noble Truth of Suffering is unattainable; one contemplates that the Noble Truths of Origination, Cessation, and the Path are unattainable.
One contemplates that the four dhyānas are unattainable; one contemplates that the four immeasurables and the four formless absorptions are unattainable.
One contemplates that the eight liberations are unattainable; one contemplates that the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive absorptions, and the ten totalities are unattainable.

One contemplates that the four foundations of mindfulness are unapprehendable; one contemplates that the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path are unapprehendable;
one contemplates that the gate of liberation of emptiness is unapprehendable; one contemplates that the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness are unapprehendable;
one contemplates that the five eyes are unapprehendable; and one contemplates that the six supernormal powers are unapprehendable.

One contemplates that the ten powers of a Buddha are unattainable; one contemplates that the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are unattainable;
one contemplates that the quality of non-forgetfulness is unattainable; one contemplates that the nature of constant abiding in equanimity is unattainable;
one contemplates that all-knowledge is unattainable; and one contemplates that the knowledge of the paths and the knowledge of all aspects are unattainable.
One contemplates that all dharani-doors are unapprehendable; one contemplates that all samadhi-doors are unapprehendable;
one contemplates that the fruit of stream-entry is unapprehendable; one contemplates that the fruits of once-returning, non-returning, and arhatship are unapprehendable;
one contemplates that pratyekabuddha-enlightenment is unapprehendable; and one contemplates that all bodhisattva-mahasattva practices are unapprehendable.
One contemplates that the unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment of all Buddhas is unattainable;
one contemplates that the realm of the conditioned is unattainable, and one contemplates that the realm of the unconditioned is unattainable.

Because the Bodhisattva thus contemplates that all phenomena are unattainable, they are without activity; because they are without activity, they are without arising; because they are without arising, they are without cessation; and because they are without cessation, they are ultimately pure, eternally abiding, and immutable.

Why is this? Because all phenomena, whether a Tathāgata appears in the world or does not appear, abide in the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), abide in the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu), abide in the stability of phenomena (dharmaniyāmatā), and abide in the fixedness of phenomena (dharmasthititā); they are without arising or cessation, and are eternally without change.

This bodhisattva mahāsattva’s mind is always undistracted, constantly dwelling in the mental engagement associated with the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*). He observes, in accordance with reality, that the nature of all phenomena is utterly non-existent. Furthermore, he takes these roots of goodness of such sublime wisdom and, sharing them equally with all sentient beings, dedicates them toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Taking non-apprehension as the skillful means, when one thus dedicates toward great enlightenment, one remains far removed from the three thoughts: namely, who is dedicating? By what means is one dedicating?
What is being dedicated?
"To what should it be dedicated?
Such threefold thoughts shall never arise again, Subhūti!"
"This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling securely in the perfection of meditative concentration, draws forth and gathers the perfection of wisdom.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
“How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling securely in the perfection of wisdom, attract and gather the perfection of generosity?
The Buddha said,
“Suvikrāntavikrāmin!
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells securely in the perfection of wisdom, they contemplate all phenomena as empty and non-existent.
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha, saying,
"In what way does a bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplate all phenomena as empty and non-existent?"
The Buddha said, “Suvikrāntavikrāmin!
This bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling securely in the perfection of wisdom, contemplates the emptiness of the internal; yet the emptiness of the internal is unapprehendable.”
Contemplating external emptiness, external emptiness is unapprehendable;
contemplating internal-and-external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness is unapprehendable;
contemplating the emptiness of emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness is unapprehendable;
One contemplates the emptiness of the great, yet the emptiness of the great is unapprehendable;
one contemplates the emptiness of the ultimate, yet the emptiness of the ultimate is unapprehendable;
one contemplates the emptiness of the conditioned, yet the emptiness of the conditioned is unapprehendable.
One contemplates the emptiness of the unconditioned, yet the emptiness of the unconditioned cannot be apprehended;
one contemplates the emptiness of the ultimate, yet the emptiness of the ultimate cannot be apprehended;
one contemplates the emptiness of the boundless, yet the emptiness of the boundless cannot be apprehended.
One contemplates the emptiness of dispersion, yet the emptiness of dispersion cannot be apprehended;
one contemplates the emptiness of non-alteration, yet the emptiness of non-alteration cannot be apprehended;
one contemplates the emptiness of intrinsic nature, yet the emptiness of intrinsic nature cannot be apprehended.
One contemplates the emptiness of specific characteristics, yet the emptiness of specific characteristics cannot be apprehended;
one contemplates the emptiness of common characteristics, yet the emptiness of common characteristics cannot be apprehended;
one contemplates the emptiness of all phenomena, yet the emptiness of all phenomena cannot be apprehended.
Contemplating the emptiness of non-apprehensibility, the emptiness of non-apprehensibility is not apprehended;
contemplating the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of non-existence is not apprehended;
contemplating the emptiness of intrinsic nature, the emptiness of intrinsic nature is not apprehended.
One contemplates the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence, yet this emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence cannot be apprehended.

"When a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells thus in these contemplations of emptiness, they do not apprehend form as either empty or not empty; they do not apprehend feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness as either empty or not empty;
they do not apprehend the sense base of the eye as either empty or not empty, nor do they apprehend the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as either empty or not empty."
One does not apprehend the sphere of form as either empty or non-empty; one does not apprehend the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, or mental phenomena as either empty or non-empty.
One does not apprehend the eye-element as either empty or non-empty; one does not apprehend the elements of ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as either empty or non-empty.
One does not apprehend the element of form as either empty or non-empty; one does not apprehend the elements of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, or mental phenomena as either empty or non-empty.
One does not apprehend the eye-consciousness element as either empty or not empty; one does not apprehend the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind-consciousness elements as either empty or not empty.
One does not apprehend eye-contact as either empty or not empty; one does not apprehend ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind-contact as either empty or not empty.

One does not apprehend the various feelings produced with eye-contact as their condition as either empty or not empty; one does not apprehend the various feelings produced with ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind-contact as their conditions as either empty or not empty.
One does not apprehend the earth element as either empty or non-empty; one does not apprehend the water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness elements as either empty or non-empty.

One does not apprehend ignorance as either empty or non-empty; one does not apprehend volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, or old age and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair as either empty or non-empty.

One does not apprehend the perfection of generosity as either empty or non-empty; one does not apprehend the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, or wisdom as either empty or non-empty.

One cannot apprehend internal emptiness as either empty or not empty; nor can one apprehend external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, non-alteration emptiness, essential nature emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common characteristic emptiness, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, or the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature as either empty or not empty.

They do not apprehend whether suchness is empty or not empty; they do not apprehend whether the dharma-realm, the nature of phenomena, the non-illusory nature, the unchanging nature, equality, the nature of freedom from birth, the fixed nature of phenomena, the stability of phenomena, the limit of reality, the realm of space, or the inconceivable realm is empty or not empty;
they do not apprehend whether the noble truth of suffering is empty or not empty; they do not apprehend whether the noble truths of origin, cessation, or the path are empty or not empty;
they do not apprehend whether the four dhyānas are empty or not empty; they do not apprehend whether the four immeasurables or the four formless attainments are empty or not empty.

One does not apprehend the eight liberations as either empty or not empty; one does not apprehend the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative attainments, or the ten totalities as either empty or not empty.

One does not apprehend the four foundations of mindfulness as either empty or not empty; one does not apprehend the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, or the eightfold noble path as either empty or not empty.
One does not apprehend the gate of liberation of emptiness as either empty or not empty; one does not apprehend the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness as either empty or not empty.
One does not apprehend the five eyes as either empty or non-empty; one does not apprehend the six supernormal powers as either empty or non-empty;

one does not apprehend the ten powers of a Buddha as either empty or non-empty; one does not apprehend the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, or the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha as either empty or non-empty;
one does not apprehend the quality of non-forgetfulness as either empty or non-empty; one does not apprehend the nature of constant abiding in equanimity as either empty or non-empty.
One does not apprehend all-knowledge as either empty or non-empty; one does not apprehend the knowledge of the aspects of the path or the knowledge of all aspects as either empty or non-empty;
one does not apprehend any of the doors of dhāraṇī as either empty or non-empty; one does not apprehend any of the doors of samādhi as either empty or non-empty;
one does not apprehend the fruit of a stream-enterer as either empty or non-empty; and one does not apprehend the fruits of a once-returner, a non-returner, or an arhat as either empty or non-empty.
One does not apprehend the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha as either empty or non-empty;
one does not apprehend the practices of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as either empty or non-empty;
one does not apprehend the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas as either empty or non-empty.
One cannot apprehend the conditioned realm as either empty or not empty, nor can one apprehend the unconditioned realm as either empty or not empty.

"When a bodhisattva mahāsattva thus abides in this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they regard all the gifts given by sentient beings—whether food, drink, vehicles, clothing, incense, flowers, bedding, dwellings, lamps, seats, or various precious treasures such as gold, silver, *maṇi* jewels, pearls, *mala-keta*, conch shells, jade, coral, stone treasuries, sapphire, diamond, and lapis lazuli—as well as medicines, ointments, powdered incense, wealth, grain, and requisites—all such things as these, they contemplate as empty."
Whether it be the act of giving, the object given, or the merit of giving—all such things are likewise contemplated as empty.
At that time, the bodhisattva’s mind of stinginess and mind of attachment ultimately do not arise.

Why is this? Because when these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, from their first generation of the mind of awakening until they sit upon the sublime seat of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), no such conceptual discriminations arise at all.

Just as all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas have never at any time given rise to a mind of stinginess or attachment, so too it is with this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva: practicing the profound Prajñāpāramitā, minds of stinginess and attachment never arise at all.

“Subhūti, you should know that this profound *prajñāpāramitā* is the teacher of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; it enables the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas to give rise to no conceptualizations or discriminations whatsoever. When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas abide in such profound *prajñāpāramitā*, all their acts of giving are free from attachment. Furthermore, they take these roots of goodness from such giving and, sharing them equally with all sentient beings, dedicate them toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.”

Using non-apprehension as the skillful means, when one thus dedicates toward great enlightenment, one remains far removed from three thoughts: namely, who is dedicating? By what means is one dedicating?
What is being dedicated?
"To what should it be dedicated?
Such threefold thoughts shall never arise again, Subhūti!"
"This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling securely in the perfection of wisdom, draws forth and gathers the perfection of generosity.
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One!"
“How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling in the perfection of wisdom, attract and gather the perfection of ethical discipline?
The Buddha said,
“Suvikrāntavikrāmin!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva abides in the perfection of wisdom, they do not give rise to the mind of a śrāvaka, a pratyekabuddha, or the like.

Why is this? Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva perceives that the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are all unapprehendable; likewise, the mind directed toward the state of a śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha, as well as their body and speech, are also unapprehendable.

This bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling securely in the perfection of wisdom, from the first generation of the mind of awakening until sitting upon the seat of sublime enlightenment, throughout that interval personally abstains from taking life and also encourages others to abstain from taking life; he correctly extols the dharma of abstaining from taking life and joyfully praises those who abstain from taking life.

He personally abstains from taking what is not given and also encourages others to abstain from taking what is not given; he correctly extols the dharma of abstaining from taking what is not given and joyfully praises those who abstain from taking what is not given.

He personally abstains from sexual misconduct and also encourages others to abstain from sexual misconduct; he correctly extols the dharma of abstaining from sexual misconduct and joyfully praises those who abstain from sexual misconduct.

They themselves abstain from false speech and also encourage others to abstain from false speech; they unerringly praise the practice of abstaining from false speech and rejoice in those who abstain from it.

They themselves abstain from harsh speech and also encourage others to abstain from harsh speech; they unerringly praise the practice of abstaining from harsh speech and rejoice in those who abstain from it.

They themselves abstain from divisive speech and also encourage others to abstain from divisive speech; they unerringly praise the practice of abstaining from divisive speech and rejoice in those who abstain from it.

They themselves abstain from frivolous speech and also encourage others to abstain from frivolous speech; they correctly praise the dharma of abstaining from frivolous speech and joyfully extol those who do so.
They themselves abstain from covetousness and also encourage others to abstain from covetousness; they correctly praise the dharma of abstaining from covetousness and joyfully extol those who do so.
They themselves abstain from malice and also encourage others to abstain from malice; they correctly praise the dharma of abstaining from malice and joyfully extol those who do so.
Having personally abandoned wrong views, they also encourage others to abandon them; they unerringly praise the dharma of abandoning wrong views and joyfully extol those who have done so.

The roots of goodness produced by this bodhisattva mahāsattva’s observance of pure ethical discipline are not sought for the sake of the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm; nor are they sought for the level of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha. Rather, he takes these roots of goodness from such pure ethical discipline and, sharing them equally with all sentient beings, dedicates them toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete awakening.

Taking non-apprehension as the skillful means, when one thus dedicates toward great enlightenment, one remains far removed from the three thoughts: namely, who is dedicating? By what means is one dedicating?
To what is one dedicating?
"To what should it be dedicated?
Such threefold thoughts shall never arise again, Subhūti!"
"This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling securely in the perfection of wisdom, draws forth and encompasses the perfection of ethical discipline.
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha again, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
“How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling in the perfection of wisdom, attract and gather the perfection of patience?
The Buddha said,
“Suvikrāntavikrāmin!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells securely in the perfection of wisdom and gives rise to the patient acceptance that accords with it, having attained this patience, they constantly form this thought:

"Among all phenomena (*dharmas*), there is not a single phenomenon that arises or ceases, is born or perishes, ages or falls ill; nor is there one who can revile or who is reviled, one who can slander or who is slandered, one who can cut or who is cut, one who can sever or who is severed, one who can pierce or who is pierced, one who can shatter or who is shattered, one who can bind or who is bound, one who can strike or who is struck, one who can afflict or who is afflicted, or one who can kill or who is killed. All such natures and characteristics are empty; one should not engage in false conceptualization or discrimination regarding them."

"From the first generation of the mind of awakening until sitting upon the seat of sublime enlightenment, even if all classes of sentient beings were to come during that interval to slander, revile, and insult them, or to inflict harm with various swords, staves, tiles, stones, and clods of earth—beating, striking, cutting, hacking, and piercing them, even to the point of dismembering their limbs and joints."
At that time, the Bodhisattva’s mind remained unchanging, and he thought only this: "How truly strange!

Within the very nature of all phenomena (*dharmatā*), there is absolutely no such thing as calumny, reproach, insult, or harm; yet sentient beings, through their deluded conceptualization, regard these as real and give rise to various afflictions and evil karmas, thereby undergoing all manner of suffering and distress in the present and the future."

This bodhisattva mahāsattva further takes these roots of goodness from such patience and, sharing them equally with all sentient beings, dedicates them toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Taking non-apprehension as the skillful means, when dedicating in this manner toward great enlightenment, one remains free from three thoughts: namely, who is dedicating? By what means is one dedicating?
What is being dedicated?
"To where would it be dedicated?
Such threefold thoughts as these will never arise again, Subhūti!"
"This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling securely in the perfection of wisdom, draws forth and encompasses the perfection of patience.
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha again, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
“How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling in the perfection of wisdom, attract and gather the perfection of diligence?
The Buddha said,
“Suvikrāntavikrāmin!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells securely in the perfection of wisdom, they teach the sublime Dharma to all sentient beings with courageous diligence, their body and mind never wearying. This bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling in the skillful means of the four bases of power (*ṛddhipāda*), maintains physical and mental diligence that is forever free from slackness or rest. They are able to go to the abodes of sentient beings in one world-system, or ten world-systems, or a hundred, a thousand, a hundred thousand, or even hundreds of thousands of *koṭi-nayuta* world-systems, teaching and instructing them through skillful means so that they may dwell in the perfection of generosity (*dāna-pāramitā*), and instructing and guiding them so that they may dwell in the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom.

By skillful means he instructs and guides them to abide in internal emptiness; by skillful means he instructs and guides them to abide in external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, non-altering emptiness, essential nature emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common characteristic emptiness, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature;

by skillful means he instructs and guides them to abide in suchness; by skillful means he instructs and guides them to abide in the dharma-realm, the dharma-nature, non-falsity, non-alteration, equality, the state beyond birth, the fixed nature of dharmas, the stability of dharmas, the limit of reality, the realm of space, and the inconceivable realm.
They skillfully instruct and guide them to abide in the noble truth of suffering; they skillfully instruct and guide them to abide in the noble truths of origination, cessation, and the path;
they skillfully instruct and guide them to abide in the four dhyānas; they skillfully instruct and guide them to abide in the four immeasurables and the four formless absorptions;
they skillfully instruct and guide them to abide in the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities.

They skillfully instruct and guide them to abide in the four foundations of mindfulness; they skillfully instruct and guide them to abide in the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path;
they skillfully instruct and guide them to abide in the liberation door of emptiness, and they skillfully instruct and guide them to abide in the liberation doors of signlessness and wishlessness;
they skillfully instruct and guide them to abide in the five eyes, and they skillfully instruct and guide them to abide in the six supernormal knowledges.

They provide skillful instruction to cause them to abide in the ten powers of a Buddha; they provide skillful instruction to cause them to abide in the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
they provide skillful instruction to cause them to abide in the quality of non-forgetfulness, and they provide skillful instruction to cause them to abide in the nature of constant equanimity;
they provide skillful instruction to cause them to abide in all-knowledge, and they provide skillful instruction to cause them to abide in the knowledge of the paths and the knowledge of all aspects.
They skillfully instruct and guide them to abide in all dharanī-doors; they skillfully instruct and guide them to abide in all samādhi-doors;
they skillfully instruct and guide them to abide in the fruit of stream-entry; they skillfully instruct and guide them to abide in the fruits of once-returning, non-returning, and arhatship;
and they skillfully instruct and guide them to abide in the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha.
They employ skillful means to instruct and guide them so that they may abide in all the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas;
they employ skillful means to instruct and guide them so that they may abide in the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas.
"Although they cause them to dwell securely in the various merits described above, they do not cause them to abide in the realm of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) or the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

Furthermore, these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas take these roots of virtue born of diligence and, sharing them equally with all sentient beings, dedicate them toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

Taking non-apprehension as the skillful means, when one thus dedicates toward great enlightenment, one remains far removed from the three thoughts: namely, who is dedicating? By what means is it dedicated?
To what is it dedicated?
"To where would it be dedicated?
Such threefold thoughts as these shall never arise again, Subhūti!"
"This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling securely in the perfection of wisdom, draws forth and gathers the perfection of diligence.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One!"
“How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling in the perfection of wisdom, attract and gather the perfection of meditative concentration?
The Buddha said,
“Suvikrāntavikrāmin!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells securely in the perfection of wisdom, with the exception of the Buddha’s samādhi, they are able to enter and emerge at will and with mastery in all other samādhis—whether those of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or bodhisattvas.
This bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling in the samādhi of sovereign mastery, is able to enter and emerge from the eight liberations with mastery in both forward and reverse order.
What are these eight?
That is to say: perceiving forms while having the perception of form is the first liberation;
not having the internal perception of form while perceiving external forms is the second liberation;
realizing the liberation of purity through bodily witness is the third liberation.

Transcending all perceptions of form, with the cessation of perceptions of sensory impact, and not attending to perceptions of diversity, one enters and dwells in the sphere of infinite space, fully possessing the meditative absorption of the sphere of infinite space; this is the fourth liberation.

Transcending the entire meditative absorption of the sphere of infinite space, one enters the sphere of infinite consciousness and dwells, fully possessing the meditative absorption of the sphere of infinite consciousness; this is the fifth liberation.

Transcending the entire meditative absorption of the sphere of infinite consciousness, one enters the sphere of nothingness where there is neither anything nor nothing, and dwells, fully possessing the meditative absorption of the sphere of nothingness; this is the sixth liberation.

Transcending the meditative attainment of the sphere of nothingness, one enters and dwells in the full possession of the meditative attainment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; this is the seventh liberation.

Transcending the meditative attainment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one enters and dwells in the full possession of the meditative attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling; this is the eighth liberation.

This bodhisattva-mahāsattva is able to enter and emerge from these eight liberations in either direct or reverse order with mastery; furthermore, they are able to enter and emerge from those nine successive concentrations at will, in either direct or reverse order, with complete mastery.
What are the nine? They are as follows:

being detached from sensual desires and unwholesome states, possessing applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*), and experiencing the joy and happiness born of seclusion, one enters and dwells in the first *dhyāna*; this is the first successive concentration.

With the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, with internal clarity and mental unification, free from applied and sustained thought, and experiencing the joy and happiness born of concentration, one enters and dwells in the second *dhyāna*; this is the second successive concentration.

Detached from joy, he dwells in equanimity, possessing mindfulness and clear comprehension; he experiences happiness with the body, of which the Noble Ones say, "He who has equanimity and mindfulness dwells happily," and thus enters and abides in the third dhyāna; this is the third successive concentration.

With the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and with the prior disappearance of joy and sorrow, he enters a state that is neither painful nor pleasant, characterized by purity of equanimity and mindfulness, and thus enters and abides in the fourth dhyāna; this is the fourth successive concentration.

Transcending all perceptions of form, with the cessation of perceptions of sensory impact, and not attending to perceptions of diversity, he enters the sphere of infinite space and enters and abides in the meditative absorption of the sphere of infinite space; this is the fifth successive concentration.

Transcending the meditative absorption of the base of infinite space, one enters the base of infinite consciousness and dwells fully accomplished therein; this is the sixth successive absorption. Transcending the meditative absorption of the base of infinite consciousness, one enters the base of nothingness and dwells fully accomplished therein; this is the seventh successive absorption.

Transcending the meditative absorption of the base of nothingness, one enters the meditative absorption of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and dwells fully accomplished therein; this is the eighth successive absorption.

Transcending the meditative absorption of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one enters the meditative absorption of the cessation of perception and feeling and dwells fully accomplished therein; this is the ninth successive absorption.
This bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to enter and emerge from these nine successive meditative absorptions (navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti) with mastery, whether in direct or reverse order.
"Subhūti, you should know this!"
When this bodhisattva mahāsattva has fully matured in the eight liberations and the nine successive attainments, he is further able to enter the bodhisattva mahāsattva samādhi called the Lion’s Yawn.
What is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s lion-stretching samādhi? Subhūti!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, detached from desires and unwholesome states, with directed thought and sustained thought, and with the joy and happiness born of seclusion, enters and dwells fully in the first dhyāna;

With the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, he enters and dwells in the second dhyāna, which is characterized by internal serenity and mental unification, free from applied and sustained thought, and filled with the joy and bliss born of concentration;

with the fading away of joy, he dwells in equanimity, mindful and clearly comprehending, experiencing bliss with the body—of which the noble ones say, "He dwells in bliss who possesses mindfulness and equanimity"—and thus enters and dwells in the third dhyāna;

with the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, he enters and dwells in the fourth dhyāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant and is purified by equanimity and mindfulness.

Transcending all perceptions of form, with the cessation of perceptions of sensory resistance, and not attending to perceptions of diversity, he enters and dwells, having fully attained the sphere of infinite space;
transcending the entire sphere of infinite space, he enters the sphere of infinite consciousness and dwells, having fully attained the sphere of infinite consciousness;
transcending the entire sphere of infinite consciousness, he enters the sphere of nothingness where there is neither anything nor nothing, and dwells, having fully attained the sphere of nothingness.
Transcending the meditative absorption of the sphere of nothingness, he enters and dwells in the perfection of the meditative absorption of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;

transcending the meditative absorption of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, he enters and dwells in the perfection of the meditative absorption of the cessation of perception and feeling.
Again, arising from the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling, he enters the attainment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
arising from the attainment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, he enters the attainment of the sphere of nothingness;
arising from the attainment of the sphere of nothingness, he enters the attainment of the sphere of infinite consciousness.
Emerging from the meditative absorption of the sphere of infinite consciousness, he enters the meditative absorption of the sphere of infinite space;
emerging from the meditative absorption of the sphere of infinite space, he enters the fourth dhyāna;
emerging from the fourth dhyāna, he enters the third dhyāna.
Emerging from the third dhyāna, he enters the second dhyāna;
emerging from the second dhyāna, he enters the first dhyāna. Subhūti!
This is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s Lion-Yawn Samādhi. “Subhūti,
you should know that once this bodhisattva mahāsattva has fully matured in the Lion-Yawn Samādhi, they are further able to enter the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s Samādhi of the Gathering and Dispersion.”
What is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s samādhi of the collection and dispersal? Subhūti!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, detached from desires and unwholesome states, with directed thought and sustained thought, and with the joy and happiness born of detachment, enters and dwells in the first dhyāna;
Arising from the first dhyāna, he enters and dwells in the second dhyāna;
arising from the second dhyāna, he enters and dwells in the third dhyāna;
arising from the third dhyāna, he enters and dwells in the fourth dhyāna.
Emerging from the fourth dhyāna, he enters and dwells in the attainment of the sphere of infinite space;
emerging from the attainment of the sphere of infinite space, he enters and dwells in the attainment of the sphere of infinite consciousness;
emerging from the attainment of the sphere of infinite consciousness, he enters and dwells in the attainment of the sphere of nothingness.
Emerging from the meditative absorption of the sphere of nothingness, he enters and dwells in the meditative absorption of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
