emerging from the meditative absorption of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, he enters and dwells in the meditative absorption of the cessation of perception and feeling;
emerging from the meditative absorption of the cessation of perception and feeling, he enters the first dhyāna.
Emerging from the first dhyāna, he enters the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling;
emerging from the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling, he enters the second dhyāna;
emerging from the second dhyāna, he enters the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling.
Emerging from the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling, he enters the third dhyāna;

emerging from the third dhyāna, he enters the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling; emerging from the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling, he enters the fourth dhyāna;
emerging from the fourth dhyāna, he enters the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling.
Emerging from the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling, one enters the attainment of the sphere of infinite space;
emerging from the attainment of the sphere of infinite space, one enters the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling;
emerging from the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling, one enters the attainment of the sphere of infinite consciousness.
Emerging from the meditative attainment of the base of infinite consciousness, one enters the meditative attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling;
emerging from the meditative attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling, one enters the meditative attainment of the base of nothingness;
emerging from the meditative attainment of the base of nothingness, one enters the meditative attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling.
Emerging from the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling, he enters the attainment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
emerging from the attainment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, he enters the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling;
emerging from the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling, he abides in an unconcentrated state of mind.
From the state of an indeterminate mind, one enters the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling;
arising from the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling, one abides in an indeterminate mind;
from that indeterminate mind, one enters the attainment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Emerging from the meditative absorption of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, he dwells in a non-concentrated state of mind;
from that non-concentrated state of mind, he enters the meditative absorption of the sphere of nothingness;
emerging from the meditative absorption of the sphere of nothingness, he dwells in a non-concentrated state of mind.
From the unconcentrated mind, one enters the meditative absorption of the base of infinite consciousness;
arising from the meditative absorption of the base of infinite consciousness, one abides in the unconcentrated mind;
from the unconcentrated mind, one enters the meditative absorption of the base of infinite space.
Emerging from the concentration of the sphere of infinite space, he dwells in a non-concentrated mind;
from that non-concentrated mind, he enters the fourth dhyāna;
emerging from the fourth dhyāna, he dwells in a non-concentrated mind.
From the state of non-concentrated mind, he enters the third dhyāna;
arising from the third dhyāna, he abides in the state of non-concentrated mind;
from the state of non-concentrated mind, he enters the second dhyāna.
Emerging from the second dhyāna, he dwells in a state of non-concentrated mind;
from that non-concentrated mind, he enters the first dhyāna;
emerging from the first dhyāna, he dwells in a state of non-concentrated mind.
"Subhūti! This is the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva’s samādhi of the collection and dispersal of dharmas.
If a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva abides in this samādhi of the collection and dispersal of dharmas, he attains the equal true nature of all dharmas."

Furthermore, this bodhisattva mahāsattva takes these roots of goodness from meditative concentration and, sharing them equally with all sentient beings, dedicates them toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Using non-apprehension as the skillful means, when dedicating in this manner toward great enlightenment, one remains far removed from the three thoughts: namely, who is dedicating? By what means is it dedicated?
To what is it dedicated?
"To where would they be dedicated?
Such three types of thoughts will never arise again, Subhūti!"
"This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling securely in the perfection of wisdom, draws forth and encompasses the perfection of meditative concentration.

The Great Perfection of Wisdom Sutra, Fascicle Three Hundred and Fifty-Three, translated by the Dharma Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Chapter Sixty-One: The Section on Many Questions and Non-Duality, Part One. Chapter Sixty-One, Part One: The Section on Many Questions and Non-Duality. At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes such skillful means, how much time has elapsed since they first resolved their mind [on awakening]?
The Buddha said,
“Suvikrāntavikrāmin!
"Since this bodhisattva mahāsattva first resolved his mind [on enlightenment], countless hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of kalpas have passed.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One!"
“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes such skillful means, how many buddhas has he already approached, served, and made offerings to?
The Buddha said, “Suvīra! [He has approached, served, and made offerings to many buddhas.]”
"This bodhisattva mahāsattva has already drawn near to, served, and made offerings to Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes such skillful means, how many roots of goodness has he previously planted?
The Buddha said, “Suvikrāntavikrāmin!
[He has planted] many.”

Since this bodhisattva mahāsattva first resolved upon the path, there has been no perfection of generosity that they have not diligently cultivated to fulfillment; there has been no perfection of ethical discipline that they have not diligently cultivated to fulfillment; there has been no perfection of patience that they have not diligently cultivated to fulfillment; there has been no perfection of diligence that they have not diligently cultivated to fulfillment; there has been no perfection of meditative concentration that they have not diligently cultivated to fulfillment; and there has been no perfection of wisdom that they have not diligently cultivated to fulfillment.

Since first generating the mind of awakening, this bodhisattva mahāsattva has never failed to apply themselves with diligent effort and abide therein in the perfection of internal emptiness; nor have they failed to do so regarding external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, endless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, non-altering emptiness, essential emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common-characteristic emptiness, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature.

Since this bodhisattva mahāsattva first resolved upon the mind of awakening, there is no suchness in which they have not diligently and perfectly abided; there is no dharma-realm, dharma-nature, non-falsity, immutability, equality, the state beyond birth, the fixed nature of dharmas, the stability of dharmas, the limit of reality, the realm of space, or the inconceivable realm in which they have not diligently and perfectly abided.

Since this bodhisattva mahāsattva first resolved upon the mind of awakening, there has been no Noble Truth of Suffering in which they have not diligently and fully established themselves; there has been no Noble Truth of Origination, Cessation, or the Path in which they have not diligently and fully established themselves.

Since this bodhisattva mahāsattva first resolved upon the mind of awakening, there has been no among the four dhyānas that they have not diligently cultivated to fulfillment, and no among the four immeasurables or the four formless absorptions that they have not diligently cultivated to fulfillment.

Since this bodhisattva-mahāsattva first resolved their mind [on enlightenment], there has been no among the eight liberations that they have not diligently cultivated to perfection; there has been no among the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, or the ten totalities that they have not diligently cultivated to perfection.

Since this bodhisattva mahāsattva first resolved upon the mind of enlightenment, there has been no application of the four foundations of mindfulness that they have not diligently cultivated to perfection; likewise, there has been no application of the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of awakening, or the eightfold noble path that they have not diligently cultivated to perfection.

Since this bodhisattva-mahāsattva first resolved upon the mind of awakening, there has been no gate of liberation—whether emptiness, signlessness, or wishlessness—that they have not diligently cultivated to perfection.

Since this bodhisattva mahāsattva first resolved upon the mind of awakening, there has been no five eyes that they have not fully perfected through diligent cultivation, and no six supernormal powers that they have not fully perfected through diligent cultivation.

Since this bodhisattva mahāsattva first resolved upon the mind of enlightenment, there has been no among the ten powers of a Buddha that they have not diligently cultivated to perfection; nor has there been any among the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, or the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha that they have not diligently cultivated to perfection.

Since this bodhisattva mahāsattva first resolved upon the mind of awakening, there has been no dharma of non-forgetfulness that they have not diligently cultivated to perfection, and there has been no state of constant abiding in equanimity that they have not diligently cultivated to perfection.

Since this bodhisattva mahāsattva first resolved upon the mind [of awakening], there is no knowledge of all modes that they have not diligently cultivated to perfection, and no knowledge of the paths or knowledge of all aspects that they have not diligently cultivated to perfection.

Since this bodhisattva mahāsattva first resolved upon the path, there has been no dharanī-door that they have not diligently cultivated to perfection, and no samādhi-door that they have not diligently cultivated to perfection.

Since this bodhisattva mahāsattva first resolved upon the mind of awakening, there has been no bodhisattva practice that they have not diligently cultivated to perfection, and there is no unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment that they have not diligently cultivated to perfection.

“Subhūti! Since this bodhisattva mahāsattva first resolved upon the path, he has planted the aforementioned perfect roots of goodness; by virtue of these causes and conditions, he has accomplished such skillful means.”
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes such skillful means, it is truly rare.”
The Buddha said,
“So it is, Subhūti! It is just so.”
"So it is! It is just as you have said; that a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes such skillful means is truly rare.
Subhūti, you should know this!"

Just as the orbs of the sun and moon revolve around and illuminate the four great continents, performing great deeds, all things therein—whether sentient or insentient—turn according to the power of that light and each accomplishes its own task.

In this way, the perfection of wisdom illuminates the other five perfections and accomplishes the great task; the five perfections, such as generosity, proceed in accordance with the power of the perfection of wisdom, each fulfilling its own function.

“Subhūti, you should know that the five perfections, beginning with generosity, are designated as ‘perfections’ only because they are embraced by the perfection of wisdom. If they were separated from the perfection of wisdom, these five, beginning with generosity, would not be called ‘perfections.’”

"Subhūti, you should know that just as a wheel-turning monarch cannot be called a 'Holy Wheel-Turning King' if he lacks the seven treasures, but only when he possesses all seven treasures can he be so named."

The same applies to the five perfections, such as generosity and the rest: if they are not embraced by the perfection of wisdom, they cannot be called "perfections"; only when they are embraced by the perfection of wisdom do they receive the name "perfection."
“Subhūti, you should know that it is like a woman who is beautiful and very wealthy; if she is not protected by a powerful husband, she is easily assaulted by wicked men.”

The same applies to the five perfections, such as generosity and the rest: if they are not sustained by the power of the perfection of wisdom, they are easily thwarted and destroyed by Māra and his retinue.
“Subhūti, you should know this:
it is like a woman who is beautiful and very wealthy; if she is protected by a powerful husband, she will not be assaulted by wicked men.”

The same applies to the five perfections, such as generosity; if they are embraced and protected by the power of the perfection of wisdom, all Māras, celestial kings, and their retinues cannot obstruct or destroy them.

“Subhūti, you should know that it is like a military general who, when facing the lines of battle, is well-equipped with various kinds of armor, shields, swords, and weapons, such that he cannot be harmed by the enemy forces of neighboring kingdoms.”

The same applies to the five perfections, such as generosity: if they do not depart from the profound perfection of wisdom, neither the retinues of Māra, nor those with overweening pride, nor even the *caṇḍāla*-like bodhisattvas can destroy them.

“Subhūti, you should know that just as the various minor kings of Jambudvīpa attend upon a universal monarch (cakravartin) at all times, and by reason of that universal monarch they are able to travel to superior places.”

The five pāramitās, beginning with generosity, are likewise; by conforming to the prajñāpāramitā and being guided by its power, they swiftly proceed toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
“Subhūti, you should know that just as all the waters in the eastern regions of Jambudvīpa flow toward the great river Gaṅgā and enter the great ocean together with it, so it is here.”

The same applies to the five perfections, such as generosity and the rest; because they are all invariably encompassed and drawn forth by the profound perfection of wisdom, they are able to reach unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

“Subhūti, you should know that just as a person’s right hand is able to perform all manner of tasks, so too is the profound perfection of wisdom; it is able to bring forth all supreme and virtuous dharmas.”

"Subhūti, you should know that just as a person's left hand is clumsy in its function, so too are the five perfections, such as generosity; they cannot induce the arising of sublime wholesome dharmas."
“Subhūti, you should know this!
Just as all streams, whether great or small, enter the great ocean and become of one salty taste, so it is with the five perfections beginning with generosity;

because they are all gathered and drawn forth by the perfection of wisdom, they together reach unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. For this reason, they are all called ‘those that lead to the further shore.’”
“Subhūti, you should know this:

when a wheel-turning monarch wishes to go somewhere, his fourfold army follows him with the wheel-treasure leading the way. When the king and the fourfold army intend to eat or drink, the wheel comes to a halt; once they have eaten and drunk, if the king intends to travel, the wheel moves on ahead. Thus, whether the wheel halts or proceeds, it follows the monarch’s will, and only upon reaching its destination does it no longer move forward.”

The same applies to the five perfections, such as generosity and the rest: when they aspire toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment along with all other wholesome dharmas, they must have the perfection of wisdom as their guide; they follow it in both advancing and halting without ever being separated from it, and once the fruit of Buddhahood is reached, they no longer proceed further.
"Subhūti, you should know this!

It is like a wheel-turning monarch who possesses the seven treasures—namely, the wheel treasure, the elephant treasure, the horse treasure, the minister-treasure of the treasury, the woman treasure, the general treasure, and the wish-fulfilling jewel treasure. When that wheel-turning monarch wishes to go somewhere, his fourfold army and the seven treasures precede and follow him in attendance; at that time, although the wheel treasure is foremost, it does not discriminate between the characteristics of front and back."

The five perfections, beginning with generosity, are likewise thus: when they seek to proceed toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment along with all wholesome dharmas, they must necessarily have the perfection of wisdom as their precursor. Yet, this perfection of wisdom does not form the thought:
"I am the foremost precursor among the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, and meditative concentration; they follow after me."
The five perfections, such as generosity and the rest, do not form this thought:
"The profound perfection of wisdom stands before us; we shall follow her."
Why is this? Subhūti!

The self-nature of the pāramitās and all dharmas is insentient; it is incapable of agency, false and unreal, empty and non-existent, and characterized by a lack of autonomy. It is like a mirage, a reflection of light, the moon in water, or an image in a mirror; within these, there is no real essence of conceptualization or activity.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If the intrinsic nature of all dharmas is empty, how can a bodhisattva mahāsattva diligently practice and train in the perfections of giving, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, so as to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?”
The Buddha said,
“Subhūti! When bodhisattva mahāsattvas diligently train in these six perfections, they constantly maintain this thought:”

“Sentient beings in the world all possess perverted minds; they are submerged in the suffering of birth and death and cannot liberate themselves. If I do not cultivate skillful means, I will be unable to release them from the suffering of birth and death.

Therefore, for the sake of these classes of sentient beings, I shall diligently train in the skillful means of the perfections of giving, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom.”
"Subhūti! Having formed this thought, that bodhisattva mahāsattva relinquishes internal and external things for the sake of all sentient beings.
Having relinquished them, he further reflects in this way:"
"I have not relinquished anything at all regarding these things.
Why is this? Because the intrinsic nature of these internal and external things is entirely empty; they do not pertain to me, and thus cannot be relinquished."

"Subhūti! By means of this contemplation, these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of generosity until it is swiftly fulfilled, and they quickly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
“Subhūti! This bodhisattva mahāsattva never violates the precepts for the sake of sentient beings. Why is that?
This bodhisattva mahāsattva constantly reflects:

"I seek to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment for the sake of sentient beings; therefore, it is improper for me to take life, take what is not given, or engage in sexual misconduct."
For me, seeking unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment for the sake of sentient beings, to engage in false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, or frivolous chatter would be improper.
For the sake of sentient beings, as I seek to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, it is improper for me to give rise to desire, hatred, or wrong views.

For the sake of sentient beings, as I seek to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, it is improper for me to seek the objects of exquisite sensual pleasure, to seek the wealth and enjoyments of the heavens, or to seek to become Śakra, Māra, Brahmā, or any other such king.
"I seek unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment for the sake of sentient beings; it would be improper for me to seek to abide in the level of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha.
Thus, Subhūti!

By means of this contemplation, these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas swiftly bring the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā) to fulfillment and rapidly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

“Subhūti! This bodhisattva mahāsattva does not give rise to anger or resentment toward sentient beings; even if they are constantly slandered and insulted, and their heart and marrow are pierced by harsh and painful words, they never give rise to a single thought of anger or resentment.”

Even if they were constantly subjected to blows from weapons, blades, tiles, stones, clubs, or clods of earth, or were cut, sliced, pierced, and dismembered limb by limb, they would not give rise to even a single thought of malice.
Why is this? Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva observes all sounds as being like echoes and all forms as being like masses of foam, thinking:
"For the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, I must not give rise to false anger or resentment toward them."

"Subhūti! By means of this contemplation, these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of patience until it is swiftly brought to fulfillment, and they quickly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

“Subhūti! This bodhisattva mahāsattva diligently seeks wholesome dharmas for the sake of all sentient beings, remaining ever free from indolence throughout this interval until the attainment of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.”
Why is this? It is because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas constantly reflect:

"If I am indolent, I will be unable to rescue and deliver all classes of sentient beings from birth, old age, sickness, and death, nor will I be able to attain the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment that I seek."

"Subhūti! By means of this observation, these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cultivate the perfection of diligence until it is swiftly fulfilled, and they quickly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

“Subhūti! For the sake of all sentient beings, these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cultivate various sublime concentrations; until they attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they never give rise to distracted states of mind such as greed, hatred, or delusion.”
Why is this? It is because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas constantly reflect:

"If I give rise to a mind associated with greed, a mind associated with hatred, a mind associated with delusion, or a mind distracted by other matters, I will be unable to accomplish the welfare of others, nor will I be able to attain the sought-after unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

"Subhūti! By means of this contemplation, these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyānapāramitā) until it is swiftly brought to fulfillment, and they quickly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

"Subhūti! For the sake of all sentient beings, this bodhisattva mahāsattva never remains apart from the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, and until reaching unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*), he constantly and diligently cultivates the subtle and supreme wisdom of both the mundane and the supramundane."
Why is this? It is because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas constantly maintain this thought:

"Apart from the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), one can never accomplish the task of benefiting and bringing happiness to others, nor can one attain the sought-after unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi)."

"Subhūti! By means of this contemplation, these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas will swiftly bring the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) to fulfillment and rapidly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If the six pāramitās have no distinct characteristics, because they are all embraced by the prajñāpāramitā and are all brought to fulfillment through the cultivation of the prajñāpāramitā, they should be combined into a single pāramitā, namely, the prajñāpāramitā.”

How can it be said that the profound perfection of wisdom is the foremost, the most excellent, the longest, the most venerable, the most sublime, the most exquisite, the highest, and the unsurpassed among the perfections such as generosity?
The Buddha said,
"Excellent, Subhūti! It is so!"
It is so! It is as you have said.

The six perfections, beginning with generosity, possess no distinct characteristics; if there were no perfection of wisdom, the other five perfections, such as generosity, could not be called "perfections. It is only by depending upon the perfection of wisdom that the other five perfections, such as generosity, are then able to be designated as "perfections."

Because these first five perfections are subsumed within the perfection of wisdom, there is but one single perfection, namely the perfection of wisdom; therefore, all perfections are without distinction in their characteristics.

"Subhūti, you should know that although sentient beings have various differences in their physical forms, if they are all in proximity to Sumeru, the King of Mountains, they will all be of one and the same color."

The five perfections, such as generosity and the others, are likewise so. Although they possess various distinctions of category, because they are embraced by the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), because they are all brought to fulfillment through the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom, and because one can only enter into the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñājñāna*) by relying upon the perfection of wisdom, they are called "arrivals at the other shore" (*pāramitā*). Thus, they are of a single flavor and without distinction; it is impossible to designate that "this is the perfection of generosity," or "this is the perfection of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, or wisdom."
Why is this? Subhūti!
These six perfections are all equally able to lead one into the knowledge of all modes and to reach the further shore; they are indistinguishable in their characteristics.
"For this reason, there is no distinction between the six perfections, such as generosity and the others.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"If, according to their true meaning, the perfections and all phenomena are devoid of any distinctions of 'this' or 'that,' superiority or inferiority, for what reason is it said that the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is the foremost, the most excellent, the longest, the most venerable, the most sublime, the most subtle, the highest, and the unsurpassed among the perfections such as generosity?"
The Buddha said:
"Excellent, Subhūti! It is so!"
It is so! It is as you have said.

If one follows the ultimate meaning, the pāramitās and all phenomena are entirely devoid of such distinctions as "this" and "that," or superiority and inferiority; it is only by relying upon conventional linguistic usage and functional activity that one speaks of such distinctions as "this" and "that," or superiority and inferiority.

The perfection of generosity is established, and the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom are established, for the purpose of liberating all sentient beings from the worldly processes of birth, aging, sickness, and death; yet these births, aging, sickness, and deaths of sentient beings are not truly existent, but are merely conventional designations.

Why is this? Because sentient beings do not exist, one should know that all phenomena likewise have no existence. The profound *prajñāpāramitā* thoroughly penetrates the fact that everything is non-existent, and is thus able to uproot the worldly functions of sentient beings—birth, old age, sickness, and death.

For this reason, it is said that the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is the foremost, the most excellent, the longest, the most venerable, the most wonderful, the most subtle, the highest, and the unsurpassed among the *pāramitās* such as generosity (*dāna*).
“Subhūti, you should know this!

Just as the woman-jewel possessed by a wheel-turning monarch is the most supreme, the most excellent, the longest-lasting, the most venerable, the most wonderful, the most exquisite, the highest, and the unsurpassed among all women of the human realm, so too is the perfection of wisdom the most supreme, the most excellent, the longest-lasting, the most venerable, the most wonderful, the most exquisite, the highest, and the unsurpassed among the perfections such as generosity.”
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"With what intention does the Buddha declare that among the perfections such as giving, it is only the perfection of wisdom that is the most supreme, the most excellent, the longest, the most honored, the most sublime, the most exquisite, the highest, and the unsurpassed?"
The Buddha said,
“Suvikrāntavikrāmin!

It is because this prajñāpāramitā can skillfully encompass all wholesome dharmas, harmonizing them to enter into the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñājñāna), remaining steadfastly unmoving by employing non-abiding as its expedient means.”
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Does this perfection of wisdom involve the grasping or abandoning of any wholesome dharmas?
The Buddha said:
"No, indeed! The profound perfection of wisdom neither grasps nor abandons any phenomena. Why is this?
"Subhūti! This is because all dharmas are neither to be grasped nor to be relinquished.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

in regard to what dharmas does the profound *prajñāpāramitā* neither grasp nor abandon?
The Buddha said:

"The profound perfection of wisdom neither grasps nor abandons the sense base of the eye; it neither grasps nor abandons the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind."
"The profound perfection of wisdom neither grasps nor abandons the sphere of form; it neither grasps nor abandons the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, or mental phenomena."
“The profound perfection of wisdom neither grasps nor rejects the eye-element; it neither grasps nor rejects the ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-element.”
“The profound perfection of wisdom neither grasps nor abandons the realm of form; it neither grasps nor abandons the realms of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, or mental phenomena.”

"The profound perfection of wisdom neither grasps nor abandons the element of visual consciousness; it neither grasps nor abandons the elements of auditory, olfactory, gustatory, tactile, or mental consciousness."
“The profound perfection of wisdom neither grasps nor rejects visual contact; it neither grasps nor rejects auditory, olfactory, gustatory, tactile, or mental contact.”

"The profound perfection of wisdom neither grasps nor rejects the various feelings produced with eye-contact as condition; it neither grasps nor rejects the various feelings produced with ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-contact as condition."
"The profound perfection of wisdom neither grasps nor abandons the earth element; it neither grasps nor abandons the water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness elements."

“The profound perfection of wisdom neither grasps nor rejects ignorance; it neither grasps nor rejects volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, existence, birth, or old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair.”

“The profound perfection of wisdom neither grasps nor abandons the perfection of generosity; it neither grasps nor abandons the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom.”

"In the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, there is neither grasping nor relinquishing regarding internal emptiness; likewise, there is neither grasping nor relinquishing regarding external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, non-alteration emptiness, essential emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common-characteristic emptiness, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature."

"The profound perfection of wisdom neither grasps nor rejects suchness; it neither grasps nor rejects the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), the non-erroneous nature, the unchanging nature, equality, the nature free from birth, the fixed nature of phenomena, the stability of phenomena, the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), the element of space, and the inconceivable realm."
"The profound perfection of wisdom neither grasps nor abandons the noble truth of suffering; it neither grasps nor abandons the noble truths of origination, cessation, and the path."
"The profound perfection of wisdom neither grasps nor relinquishes the four dhyānas; it neither grasps nor relinquishes the four immeasurables or the four formless absorptions."

"The profound Prajñāpāramitā neither grasps nor abandons the eight liberations; it neither grasps nor abandons the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative attainments, or the ten totalities."

“The profound perfection of wisdom neither grasps nor abandons the four foundations of mindfulness; it neither grasps nor abandons the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, or the eightfold noble path.”
"The profound perfection of wisdom neither grasps nor abandons the gate of liberation of emptiness; it neither grasps nor abandons the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness."
“The profound perfection of wisdom neither grasps nor relinquishes the five eyes; it neither grasps nor relinquishes the six supernormal powers.

The profound perfection of wisdom neither grasps nor relinquishes the ten powers of a Buddha; it neither grasps nor relinquishes the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.”

"In the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, there is neither grasping nor relinquishing regarding the quality of non-forgetfulness, and there is neither grasping nor relinquishing regarding the nature of constant equanimity."
"The profound perfection of wisdom neither grasps nor abandons all-knowledge; it neither grasps nor abandons the knowledge of the paths or the knowledge of all aspects."
"The profound perfection of wisdom neither grasps nor relinquishes any of the gateways to dhāraṇī; it neither grasps nor relinquishes any of the gateways to samādhi."
"The profound perfection of wisdom neither grasps nor abandons the fruit of stream-entry; it neither grasps nor abandons the fruits of once-returning, non-returning, or arhatship."
“The profound perfection of wisdom neither grasps nor abandons the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha.
The profound perfection of wisdom neither grasps nor abandons any of the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.”
“The profound perfection of wisdom neither grasps nor abandons the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
Regarding the profound perfection of wisdom: how is there neither grasping nor relinquishing with respect to form?
How is there neither grasping nor relinquishing with respect to feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness?
“How is it that the profound perfection of wisdom neither grasps nor rejects the sphere of the eye?

"How does the profound *prajñāpāramitā* neither grasp nor abandon eye-contact?

"How is it that the profound perfection of wisdom neither grasps nor abandons the noble truth of suffering?

One does not conceptualize the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*) or the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*); thus, regarding the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects, there is neither grasping nor relinquishing."
"In the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, one does not contemplate any of the *dhāraṇī* gates; thus, regarding all *dhāraṇī* gates, there is neither grasping nor relinquishing.
One does not contemplate any of the *samādhi* gates; thus, regarding all *samādhi* gates, there is neither grasping nor relinquishing."
"In the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, one does not contemplate the fruit of stream-entry; thus, regarding the fruit of stream-entry, there is neither grasping nor abandoning.

One does not contemplate the fruits of once-returning, non-returning, or arhatship; thus, regarding the fruits of once-returning, non-returning, or arhatship, there is neither grasping nor abandoning."
"The profound Prajñāpāramitā does not contemplate the enlightenment of a Pratyekabuddha; thus, regarding the enlightenment of a Pratyekabuddha, there is neither grasping nor abandoning."

"The profound perfection of wisdom does not conceptualize any of the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; thus, regarding all the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, it neither grasps nor abandons."

"In the profound perfection of wisdom, one does not conceptualize the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas; thus, regarding the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas, there is neither grasping nor relinquishing."
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

how does the profound perfection of wisdom not contemplate form?”
How does one not contemplate feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness?
"In what way does one not contemplate the sense base of the eye within the profound *prajñāpāramitā*?"
How does one not contemplate the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind?
"In the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, how does one not contemplate the sense base of form?"
How does one not contemplate the spheres of sound, odor, taste, touch, and mental phenomena?
"How, in the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, does one not contemplate the eye-sphere?"
How does one not contemplate the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind elements?
"How does one not contemplate the form element within the profound *prajñāpāramitā*?"
How does one not contemplate the realms of sound, odor, taste, touch, and mental phenomena?
"How does one not contemplate the realm of eye-consciousness within the profound *prajñāpāramitā*?"
How does one not contemplate the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-consciousness elements?
"In the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, how does one not contemplate eye-contact?"
How does one not contemplate the contact of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind?
"In the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, how does one not contemplate the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition?"
How does one not contemplate the various feelings produced with the contact of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind as conditions?

How is it that one does not contemplate the elements of water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness?
"In the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, how is it that one does not contemplate ignorance?"

What is the practice of not reflecting upon volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, existence, birth, and aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair?
"In the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, why does one not contemplate the *dānapāramitā*?
Why does one not contemplate the *śīla*, *kṣānti*, *vīrya*, *dhyāna*, and *prajñāpāramitās*?"
"In the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, how does one not contemplate internal emptiness?

How does one not contemplate external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, endless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, non-alteration emptiness, essential nature emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common characteristic emptiness, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature?"
"How is it that in the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, one does not contemplate *tathatā*?

How is it that one does not contemplate the *dharmadhātu*, the *dharmatā*, the nature of non-falsity, the nature of non-alteration, equality, the nature of being free from birth, the fixedness of phenomena, the stability of phenomena, the limit of reality, the realm of space, and the inconceivable realm?"
"In the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, how is it that one does not contemplate the noble truth of suffering?
How is it that one does not contemplate the noble truths of origination, cessation, and the path?"
"In the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, how is it that one does not contemplate the four dhyānas?
How is it that one does not contemplate the four immeasurables or the four formless attainments?"
"In the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, how is it that one does not contemplate the eight liberations?
How is it that one does not contemplate the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative attainments, or the ten totalities?"
"In the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, how is it that one does not contemplate the four foundations of mindfulness?

"In the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, how is it that one does not contemplate the gate of liberation of emptiness?
How is it that one does not contemplate the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness?"
"In the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, how is it that one does not contemplate the five eyes?
How is it that one does not contemplate the six supernormal powers?
In the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, how is it that one does not contemplate the ten powers of a Buddha?"

How is it that one does not contemplate the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha?
"In the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, how is it that one does not contemplate the quality of non-forgetfulness?
How is it that one does not contemplate the nature of constant equanimity?"
"In the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, how is it that one does not contemplate all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*)?
How is it that one does not contemplate the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*) or the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*)?"

How does one not contemplate any of the gateways of samādhi?"

How is it that one does not contemplate the fruits of a once-returner, a non-returner, or an arhat?"

“How is it that the profound *prajñāpāramitā* does not contemplate the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas?

The Buddha said, “Suvikrāntavikrāmin! [This is from] the Great *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Fascicle 351, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree, Part One, Chapter Sixty-one (Two), ‘The Many Questions on Non-duality,’ Section Two.
The Buddha said, “Suvikrāntavikrāmin!”
In the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, one does not contemplate any marks regarding form, nor does one contemplate any objects of focus; in this way, one does not contemplate form.

One does not contemplate any marks regarding feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, nor does one contemplate any objects of focus; in this way, one does not contemplate feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.

"In the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, one does not contemplate any marks regarding the sense base of the eye, nor does one contemplate any objects of perception; thus one does not contemplate the sense base of the eye.

One does not contemplate any marks regarding the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, nor does one contemplate any objects of perception; thus one does not contemplate the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind."

"In the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, one does not contemplate any marks regarding the sphere of form (*rūpa-āyatana*), nor does one contemplate any objects of focus; thus one does not contemplate the sphere of form.

Likewise, regarding the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena (*dharma-āyatana*), one does not contemplate any marks, nor does one contemplate any objects of focus; thus one does not contemplate the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena."
"In the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, one does not contemplate any marks regarding the eye-element, nor does one contemplate any objects of perception; thus one does not contemplate the eye-element.

One does not contemplate any marks regarding the ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-element, nor does one contemplate any objects of perception; thus one does not contemplate the ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-element."

"In the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, one does not contemplate any marks regarding the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), nor does one contemplate any objects of perception; in this way, one does not contemplate the realm of form.

One does not contemplate any marks regarding the realms of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), nor does one contemplate any objects of perception; in this way, one does not contemplate the realms of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena."

"In the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, one does not contemplate any marks regarding the element of eye-consciousness, nor does one contemplate any objects of perception; thus one does not contemplate the element of eye-consciousness.

One does not contemplate any marks regarding the elements of ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-consciousness, nor does one contemplate any objects of perception; thus one does not contemplate the elements of ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-consciousness."
"In the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, one does not conceptualize any marks regarding eye-contact, nor does one conceptualize any objects of focus; thus one does not conceptualize eye-contact.

One does not conceptualize any marks regarding ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-contact, nor does one conceptualize any objects of focus; thus one does not conceptualize ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-contact."

"In the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, one does not contemplate any signs regarding the feelings produced with eye-contact as condition, nor does one contemplate any objects of focus; thus one does not contemplate the feelings produced with eye-contact as condition.

One does not contemplate any signs regarding the feelings produced with ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-contact as condition, nor does one contemplate any objects of focus; thus one does not contemplate the feelings produced with ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-contact as condition."
"In the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, one does not contemplate any marks regarding the earth element, nor does one contemplate any objects of focus; thus one does not contemplate the earth element.

One does not contemplate any marks regarding the water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness elements, nor does one contemplate any objects of focus; thus one does not contemplate the water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness elements."
"In the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, one does not contemplate any characteristics regarding ignorance, nor does one contemplate any objects of focus; thus one does not contemplate ignorance.

Regarding volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, existence, birth, and old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair, one does not contemplate any characteristics, nor does one contemplate any objects of focus; thus one does not contemplate anything from volitional formations up to old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair."
"In the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, one does not contemplate any marks regarding the *dānapāramitā*, nor does one contemplate any objects of focus; thus one does not contemplate the *dānapāramitā*.

One does not contemplate any marks regarding the *śīla*, *kṣānti*, *vīrya*, *dhyāna*, and *prajñāpāramitās*, nor does one contemplate any objects of focus; thus one does not contemplate anything from *śīla* up to *prajñāpāramitā*."
"In the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, one does not contemplate any marks regarding internal emptiness, nor does one contemplate any objects of focus; thus one does not contemplate internal emptiness.

Regarding external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, non-altering emptiness, essential emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common-characteristic emptiness, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence—one does not contemplate any marks, nor does one contemplate any objects of focus; thus one does not contemplate [these] from external emptiness up to the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence."
"In the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, one does not contemplate any marks regarding *tathatā* (suchness), nor does one contemplate any objects of focus; in this way, one does not contemplate *tathatā*.

Regarding the *dharmadhātu* (dharma-realm), *dharmatā* (dharma-nature), non-falsity, non-alteration, equality, the nature of being free from birth, the fixed nature of dharmas, the stability of dharmas, the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), the realm of space, and the inconceivable realm, one does not contemplate any marks, nor does one contemplate any objects of focus; in this way, one does not contemplate anything from the *dharmadhātu* up to the inconceivable realm."

"In the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, one does not contemplate any marks regarding the noble truth of suffering, nor does one contemplate any objects of focus; thus one does not contemplate the noble truth of suffering.

One does not contemplate any marks regarding the noble truths of origin, cessation, and the path, nor does one contemplate any objects of focus; thus one does not contemplate the noble truths of origin, cessation, and the path."
"In the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, one does not contemplate any signs regarding the four dhyānas, nor does one contemplate any objects of focus; thus one does not contemplate the four dhyānas.

Regarding the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments, one does not contemplate any signs, nor does one contemplate any objects of focus; thus one does not contemplate the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments."

"In the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, one does not contemplate any marks regarding the eight liberations (*aṣṭavimokṣa*), nor does one contemplate any objects of focus; thus one does not contemplate the eight liberations.

Regarding the eight bases of mastery (*aṣṭābhibhvāyatana*), the nine successive meditative attainments (*navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti*), and the ten totalities (*daśakṛtsnāyatana*), one does not contemplate any marks, nor does one contemplate any objects of focus; thus one does not contemplate the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative attainments, or the ten totalities."

"In the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, one does not contemplate any marks regarding the four foundations of mindfulness, nor does one contemplate any objects of focus; thus one does not contemplate the four foundations of mindfulness.

One does not contemplate any marks regarding the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, or the eightfold noble path, nor does one contemplate any objects of focus; thus one does not contemplate the four right efforts up to the eightfold noble path."

"In the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, one does not contemplate any signs within the gate of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vimokṣamukha*), nor does one contemplate any objects of focus; thus one does not contemplate the gate of emptiness.

Within the gates of signlessness (*animitta*) and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*), one does not contemplate any signs, nor does one contemplate any objects of focus; thus one does not contemplate the gates of signlessness and wishlessness."
"In the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, one does not contemplate any marks regarding the five eyes, nor does one contemplate any objects of focus; thus one does not contemplate the five eyes.
Regarding the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*), one does not contemplate any marks, nor does one contemplate any objects of focus; thus one does not contemplate the six supernormal powers."

"In the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, one does not contemplate any marks regarding the ten powers (*daśabala*) of a Buddha, nor does one contemplate any objects of focus; thus one does not contemplate the ten powers of a Buddha.

Regarding the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), great loving-kindness (*maitrī*), great compassion (*karuṇā*), great sympathetic joy (*muditā*), great equanimity (*upekṣā*), and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇikabuddhadharma*), one does not contemplate any marks, nor does one contemplate any objects of focus; thus one does not contemplate the four fearlessnesses up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha."

"In the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, one does not contemplate any marks regarding the quality of non-forgetfulness (*asaṃpramoṣadharma*), nor does one contemplate any objects of focus; thus one does not contemplate the quality of non-forgetfulness.

One does not contemplate any marks regarding the nature of constant equanimity (*upekṣā*), nor does one contemplate any objects of focus; thus one does not contemplate the nature of constant equanimity."
“The profound *prajñāpāramitā* does not contemplate any signs regarding all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), nor does it contemplate any objects of focus; thus it does not contemplate all-knowledge.

Regarding the knowledge of the paths (*mārgākārajñatā*) and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), it does not contemplate any signs, nor does it contemplate any objects of focus; thus it does not contemplate the knowledge of the paths or the knowledge of all aspects.”
"The profound *prajñāpāramitā* does not contemplate any signs regarding all *dhāraṇī* gates, nor does it contemplate any objects of focus; thus it does not contemplate any *dhāraṇī* gates.
It does not contemplate any signs regarding all *samādhi* gates, nor does it contemplate any objects of focus; thus it does not contemplate any *samādhi* gates."

"In the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, one does not conceptualize any marks regarding the fruit of a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*), nor does one conceptualize any objects of focus; thus one does not conceptualize the fruit of a stream-enterer.

One does not conceptualize any marks regarding the fruits of a once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*), a non-returner (*anāgāmin*), or an arhat, nor does one conceptualize any objects of focus; thus one does not conceptualize the fruits of a once-returner, a non-returner, or an arhat."

"In the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, one does not contemplate any signs regarding the enlightenment of a *pratyekabuddha*, nor does one contemplate any objects of focus; in this way, one does not contemplate the enlightenment of a *pratyekabuddha*."

"The profound perfection of wisdom does not conceptualize any signs regarding all the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, nor does it conceptualize any objects of focus; in this way, it does not conceptualize any of the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas."

“The profound perfection of wisdom does not conceptualize any signs regarding the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas, nor does it conceptualize any objects of focus; in this way, it does not conceptualize the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas.”
