"World-Honored One!"
“Is it by abiding in the ultimate truth that one realizes unsurpassed, perfect,
and complete enlightenment?
“No, Subhūti!”
“World-Honored One!
Is one who dwells in perversion able to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment? “No!”
"Subhūti! "World-Honored One!

If one does not dwell in the ultimate truth to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, nor does one dwell in perversion to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, would it not be the case, World-Honored One, that you have not realized unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?"
"No, Subhūti! Although I have realized unsurpassed,
perfect, and complete awakening, I do not abide in the realm of the conditioned, nor do I abide in the realm of the unconditioned."

"Subhūti! Just as those who are emanated by the Tathāgatas do not abide in the realm of the conditioned, nor do they abide in the realm of the unconditioned, yet they still perform such acts as going, coming, sitting, and standing."
“Subhūti! If this emanated being practices the perfection of generosity, they also practice the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom.”

Those who are to be converted, if they abide in internal emptiness, also abide in external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, the emptiness of the ultimate truth, the emptiness of conditioned phenomena, the emptiness of unconditioned phenomena, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, the emptiness of dispersion, the emptiness of non-alteration, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, the emptiness of specific characteristics, the emptiness of common characteristics, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of non-apprehensibility, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of self-nature, and the emptiness of the self-nature of non-existence.

Those who are to be transformed, if they abide in suchness, also abide in the dharma-realm, the dharma-nature, non-illusory nature, non-alteration, equality, the nature of being free from birth, the fixedness of dharmas, the stability of dharmas, the limit of reality, the realm of space, and the inconceivable realm.

Those who are to be transformed, if they cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness, also cultivate the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path.
Those who are to be transformed, if they abide in the noble truth of suffering, also abide in the noble truths of origination, cessation, and the path.
Those who are to be transformed, if they cultivate the four dhyānas, also cultivate the four immeasurables and the four formless absorptions.
Those who are to be transformed, if they cultivate the eight liberations, also cultivate the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive concentrations, and the ten totalities.
Those who are to be transformed, if they cultivate all gateways of samādhi, also cultivate all gateways of dhāraṇī.
Those who are to be transformed, if they cultivate the gate of liberation of emptiness, also cultivate the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness.
Those who are to be transformed, if they cultivate the five eyes, also cultivate the six supernormal powers.

Those who are to be transformed, if they cultivate the ten powers of a Buddha, also cultivate the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
Those who are to be converted, if they cultivate the quality of non-forgetfulness, also cultivate the nature of constant equanimity.
Those who are to be converted, if they cultivate all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), also cultivate the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*) and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Those who are to be transformed, if they realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, will turn the sublime wheel of Dharma and perform the deeds of a Buddha.

Those who are to be transformed, in turn, manifest through transformation an immeasurable number of sentient beings, within whom they establish the distinctions of the three groups, such as those fixed in the right nature and so forth.
“Subhūti, what do you think?

Do those emanations created by the Tathāgatas truly have coming and going, or even walking, standing, practicing, and realizing unexcelled, perfect enlightenment; or do they turn the sublime wheel of Dharma, perform the various deeds of a Buddha, and establish the distinctions of the three categories of beings?”
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One!”
"No, Sugata! The Buddha said:
“Subhūti! The Tathāgata is likewise:

he knows that all phenomena are like magical transformations and teaches that all phenomena are like magical transformations. Although he performs deeds, they lack true reality; although he delivers sentient beings, there are no beings delivered—just as a magically created being delivers other sentient beings.”
Thus it is, Subhūti!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom should be like one emanated by the Buddhas; though they perform various deeds, they remain without attachment.
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If all dharmas are like magical transformations, and the Tathāgata is likewise so, what difference is there between a Buddha and a magically created person?”
The Buddha said:
“Suvikrāntavikrāmin!
A Buddha, an emanated person, and all phenomena are equal and without distinction.”
Why is this? Subhūti!
Because that which is the work performed by a Buddha can also be performed by a person emanated by a Buddha.
Subhūti said: "Even if there were no Buddha, could the emanation of a Buddha perform an action?
The Buddha said:
“It can do so. Subhūti asked, “In what way?”
The Buddha said, “Subhūti!

For example, in the past there was a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Śāntamati. Having already delivered all those who were to be delivered by him, and finding no bodhisattva at that time capable of receiving the Buddha’s prediction, he then manifested a transformed Buddha to remain in the world, while he himself entered the realm of great nirvāṇa without remainder.”

At that time, those emanated Buddhas performed the works of a Buddha for half an eon; once the half-eon had passed, they bestowed predictions of enlightenment upon a bodhisattva mahāsattva and manifested entry into parinirvāṇa.
At that time, the devas, humans, asuras, and others all thought that the Buddha had now entered parinirvāṇa; yet the body of the transformation Buddha truly has neither arising nor ceasing.
"In this way, Subhūti,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom should have faith that all phenomena are like magical transformations.
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If the body of the Tathāgata is no different from that of an emanation, how can it constitute a truly pure field of merit?

If sentient beings, for the sake of liberation, offer respectful worship to the Tathāgata, their merit is inexhaustible until they finally enter the realm of nirvāṇa without remainder; likewise, if those who, for the sake of liberation, make offerings to an emanation Buddha, should not the mass of merit they obtain also be inexhaustible until they finally enter the realm of nirvāṇa without remainder?”
The Buddha said, “Subhūti!

Just as the body of a Tathāgata, by virtue of its dharmatā, is able to serve as a pure field of merit for devas, humans, asuras, and others, so too is a transformation Buddha; by virtue of its dharmatā, it is able to serve as a pure field of merit for devas, humans, asuras, and others.”

Just as when the Tathāgata receives offerings from others, it causes the merit of those donors to be inexhaustible until the end of the cycle of birth and death, so too when an emanation Buddha receives offerings from others, it likewise causes the merit of those donors to be inexhaustible until the end of the cycle of birth and death.

“Subhūti! Let alone the mass of merit obtained by making offerings to a Tathāgata or to a manifested Buddha; if a son of good family or a daughter of good family conceives thoughts of loving-kindness and reverence toward a Tathāgata and recollects him with mindfulness, the roots of goodness of those sons and daughters of good family will be inexhaustible, until they finally reach the end of suffering.”

"Subhūti! Setting aside for a moment the mass of merit obtained by recollecting the Tathāgata with a mind of loving-kindness and reverence, if a son of good family or a daughter of good family, for the sake of making an offering to the Buddha, were to take even a single flower and scatter it into space, the roots of virtue of that son or daughter of good family would be inexhaustible, until they finally reach the end of suffering."

"Subhūti! Let alone the mass of merit obtained by scattering even a single flower into space as an offering to the Buddha; if a son of good family or a daughter of good family, at the very least, utters 'Namo Buddhāya' once, the roots of virtue of such sons and daughters of good family will be inexhaustible, until they finally reach the end of suffering."
Thus it is, Subhūti! By reverently making offerings to the Tathāgata, one obtains such great merit and benefit that its measure is difficult to fathom.
Therefore, Subhūti, you should know this!
The Tathāgata and the body of an emanation Buddha are equal and without distinction, because the *dharmatā* (the true nature) of all phenomena is the definitive standard.

"In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should take the *dharmatā* of all phenomena as the definitive standard while practicing the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*). Having skillfully entered the *dharmatā* of all phenomena through expedient means (*upāya-kauśalya*), they do not destroy the *dharmatā* of those phenomena; that is to say, they do not engage in conceptual discrimination: [as follows...]"
"This is the perfection of wisdom; this is the dharmatā of the perfection of wisdom.
This is the perfection of meditative concentration, diligence, patience, ethical discipline, and generosity; this is the dharmatā of the perfections from meditative concentration down to generosity."
"This is internal emptiness; this is the dharma-nature of internal emptiness.

This is external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, non-alteration emptiness, essential nature emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common characteristic emptiness, the emptiness of all dharmas, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence. This is the dharma-nature of external emptiness, up to and including the dharma-nature of the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence."
This is suchness; this is the dharma-nature of suchness.

This is the dharma-realm, the dharma-nature, the non-illusory nature, the unchanging nature, the nature of equality, the nature of being free from birth, the fixedness of dharma, the stability of dharma, the limit of reality, the realm of space, and the inconceivable realm; this is the dharma-nature of the dharma-realm up to the inconceivable realm.
"These are the four foundations of mindfulness; this is the dharma-nature of the four foundations of mindfulness.

These are the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path; this is the dharma-nature of the four right efforts up to the eightfold noble path."
"This is the noble truth of suffering; this is the dharma-nature of the noble truth of suffering.
This is the noble truth of origination, cessation, and the path; this is the dharma-nature of the noble truths of origination, cessation, and the path."
"These are the four dhyānas; this is the dharmatā of the four dhyānas.
These are the four immeasurables and the four formless absorptions; this is the dharmatā of the four immeasurables and the four formless absorptions."
These are the eight liberations; this is the dharma-nature of the eight liberations.

These are the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities; this is the dharma-nature of the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities.
This is all the gateways of samādhi; this is the dharmatā of all the gateways of samādhi.
This is all the gateways of dhāraṇī; this is the dharmatā of all the gateways of dhāraṇī.
"This is the gate of liberation of emptiness; this is the dharma-nature of the gate of liberation of emptiness.
This is the gate of liberation of signlessness and the gate of liberation of wishlessness; this is the dharma-nature of the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness."
These are the five eyes; this is the dharma-nature of the five eyes.
These are the six supernormal powers; this is the dharma-nature of the six supernormal powers.
These are the ten powers of a Buddha; this is the dharma-nature of the ten powers of a Buddha.

These are the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; these are the dharmic nature of the four fearlessnesses up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
This is the quality of non-forgetfulness; this is the dharmic nature of the quality of non-forgetfulness.
This is the state of constant abiding in equanimity; this is the dharmic nature of the state of constant abiding in equanimity.
This is omniscience; this is the dharmatā of omniscience.
This is the knowledge of the paths and the knowledge of all aspects; this is the dharmatā of the knowledge of the paths and the knowledge of all aspects.
"This is the fruit of stream-entry; this is the dharma-nature of the fruit of stream-entry.
This is the fruit of once-returning, non-returning, and arhatship; this is the dharma-nature of the fruits of once-returning, non-returning, and arhatship."
This is the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha; this is the dharma-nature of the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha.
This is the practice of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; this is the dharma-nature of the practice of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
"This is the unexcelled, perfect enlightenment of all Buddhas; this is the dharma-nature of the unexcelled, perfect enlightenment of all Buddhas. "Subhūti!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they should not thus differentiate the dharma-natures of various phenomena and thereby destroy that dharma-nature."
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
if a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not destroy the dharma-nature of all phenomena, how is it that the Tathāgata himself destroys the dharma-nature of all phenomena?”
That is to say, the Buddha constantly teaches:
"This is form; this is feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness;
this is the sense-base of the eye; these are the sense-bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind."
"This is the sense-base of form; these are the sense-bases of sound, odor, taste, tangibles, and mental phenomena.
This is the eye-element; these are the elements of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
This is the element of form; these are the elements of sound, odor, taste, tangibles, and mental phenomena."
This is the eye-consciousness element; these are the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-consciousness elements.
This is eye-contact; these are ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-contact.
These are the various feelings produced with eye-contact as condition; these are the various feelings produced with ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-contact as condition.
"This is the earth element; this is the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements.

This is ignorance; these are volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, existence, birth, and old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair.
These are internal phenomena; these are external phenomena."
"This is a wholesome dharma; this is an unwholesome dharma.
This is a dharma with outflows; this is a dharma without outflows.
This is a mundane dharma; this is a supramundane dharma."
"These are shared dharmas; these are unshared dharmas;
these are dharmas associated with contention; these are dharmas free from contention;
these are conditioned dharmas; these are unconditioned dharmas."
“Since the Buddha has already taught such dharmas as these, will he not be destroying the dharma-nature (dharmatā) of all phenomena?
The Buddha said,
“Suvikrāntavikrāmin!...”

I do not destroy the dharmatā of all phenomena; rather, by means of names and signs as a skillful expedient, I provisionally designate the dharmatā of all phenomena, so that all sentient beings may attain realization and entry into the principle of the non-differentiation of the dharmatā of all phenomena.
"Therefore, Subhūti, I have never destroyed the dharma-nature of phenomena.
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If the Buddha merely uses names and signs to proclaim the dharma-nature of all phenomena so that sentient beings may attain awakening and entry, how is it that the Buddha, regarding phenomena that are nameless and signless, uses names and signs to speak of them and cause others to awaken and enter?”
The Buddha said, “Subhūti!
Following worldly convention, I employ the skillful means of provisional designations for names and signs to proclaim the dharma-nature of all phenomena, yet without attachment.”

"Subhūti! Just as ordinary foolish people, upon hearing the teaching of suffering and so forth, cling to names and signs and do not understand them as mere designations, so it is not with the Tathāgatas and the disciples of the Buddha when they hear the teaching of suffering and so forth; rather, they know them as they truly are, understanding that these names and signs of dharmas exist only as conventional expressions and possess no ultimate reality."

"Subhūti! If noble ones were to be attached to names as names, and to signs as signs, then they would likewise be attached to emptiness as emptiness, to signlessness as signlessness, to wishlessness as wishlessness, to suchness as suchness, to the reality limit as the reality limit, to the dharma-realm as the dharma-realm, and to the unconditioned as the unconditioned."

"Subhūti! All these dharmas possess only provisional names and only provisional marks, lacking any reality; even the noble ones do not dwell in attachment to them, for they are merely provisional names and marks."
Thus it is, Subhūti!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva dwelling in all phenomena—which are merely conventional designations and signs—should practice the perfection of wisdom, yet should not dwell in attachment to them.
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
If all dharmas are merely names and signs, for what purpose does a bodhisattva mahāsattva generate the mind of enlightenment?"

Having already generated the mind of enlightenment, they undergo various diligent and ascetic practices as they carry out the bodhisattva conduct; they practice the perfection of generosity, and they practice the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom.

They abide in internal emptiness, and they abide in external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, non-alteration emptiness, essential nature emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common characteristic emptiness, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature.

They abide in suchness; they abide in the dharma-realm, the nature of phenomena, non-falsity, immutability, equality, the state beyond birth, the fixed nature of phenomena, the stability of phenomena, the limit of reality, the realm of space, and the inconceivable realm.

They practice the four foundations of mindfulness; they practice the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path.
They abide in the noble truth of suffering; they abide in the noble truths of the origin, cessation, and the path.
They practice the four dhyānas; they practice the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments;
they practice the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities;
they practice all doors of samādhi and all doors of dhāraṇī.
They practice the gate of liberation of emptiness; they practice the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness;
they practice the five eyes; they practice the six supernormal powers;

they practice the ten powers of a Buddha; they practice the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
How does one practice the quality of non-forgetfulness, practice the state of constant equanimity,
and practice all-knowledge, the knowledge of the aspects of the path, and the knowledge of all aspects, so as to bring them all to full perfection?
The Buddha said, "Subhūti!
As you have said, if all phenomena are merely names and signs, for what purpose does a bodhisattva mahāsattva generate the mind of awakening and practice the conduct of a bodhisattva? Subhūti!"

Because all phenomena possess only names and signs, and such names and signs are merely conventional designations, their nature is empty. Yet sentient beings, through inverted attachments, transmigrate through birth and death and fail to attain liberation. Therefore, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva resolves upon the bodhicitta and practices the bodhisattva path, gradually realizing the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*). He turns the wheel of the true Dharma and delivers sentient beings by means of the three vehicles, causing them to emerge from birth and death and enter the realm of *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*. Nevertheless, these names and signs are neither born nor extinguished, nor can any designation of abiding or change be found.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
does the Buddha speak of ‘all-aspect omniscience’ as being ‘all-aspect omniscience’?”
The Buddha said,
“Suvikrāntavikrāmin!
I speak of all-aspect omniscience as all-aspect omniscience.”
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

The Tathāgata has often spoken of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*). What are the characteristics of these three knowledges, and what is their distinction?”
The Buddha said,
“Suvikrāntavikrāmin!
‘All-knowledge’ (sarvajñatā) is the knowledge shared by śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.”
The knowledge of the characteristics of the path is the wisdom shared with bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
The knowledge of all characteristics is the sublime, unshared wisdom of all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,
for what reason is all-knowledge (sarvajñatā) the wisdom common to śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas?"
The Buddha said, “Suvikrāntavikrāmin!

‘All-knowledge’ refers to the five aggregates, the twelve bases, the eighteen elements, and so forth; these can also be thoroughly understood by śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, yet they cannot know all aspects of the paths, all phenomena, and all modes of appearance.”
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
for what reason is the knowledge of the aspects of the path the wisdom common to bodhisattva-mahāsattvas?”
The Buddha said, “Suvikrāntavikrāmin!

All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should train in the thorough knowledge of all the characteristics of the paths—namely, the characteristics of the path of the śrāvaka, the characteristics of the path of the pratyekabuddha, the characteristics of the path of the bodhisattva, and the characteristics of the path of the Tathāgata. Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should constantly train in these various paths so that they may quickly reach fulfillment; although they cause these paths to perform their respective functions, they do not cause them to realize the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi).”
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
once a bodhisattva mahāsattva has cultivated the path of the Tathāgata to full completion, would he not then realize the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi)?”
The Buddha said,
“Suvikrāntavikrāmin!
If bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have not yet perfected the purification of buddha-fields, matured sentient beings, and cultivated their great vows, they should not yet realize the limit of reality.”
"If one has already perfected the adornment and purification of Buddha-fields, matured sentient beings, and cultivated the great vows, then one should realize the ultimate reality.
"World-Honored One!"
“Does a bodhisattva mahāsattva abide in the path in order to realize the limit of reality? “No, Subhūti!”
“World-Honored One!
Does a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwell in what is not the path in order to realize the limit of reality? “No!”
“Excellent, Subhūti!
“World-Honored One,
does a bodhisattva mahāsattva abide in what is both the path and not the path to realize the limit of reality?”
“No, World-Honored One!
[It is not so], Subhūti.
“World-Honored One! [Subhūti replied.]
“Does a bodhisattva mahāsattva abide in that which is neither a path nor a non-path in order to realize the limit of reality?
“No, Subhūti!”
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One, if that is so,
in what does a bodhisattva mahāsattva abide when realizing the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi)?”
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"What do you think? Do you abide in the path and thereby attain the liberation of mind through the exhaustion of all outflows?"
"No, World-Honored One! " "Excellent, Subhūti!"
“Do you attain the liberation of mind through the exhaustion of all taints by abiding in what is not the path? “No,
World-Honored One!”
“Subhūti! Do you attain liberation of mind through the exhaustion of all outflows by abiding in either the path or non-path?
“No, [World-Honored One].”
“World-Honored One!
“Subhūti! Do you attain the liberation of the mind through the exhaustion of all outflows by abiding in that which is neither the path nor the non-path?”
"No, World-Honored One!

It is not that I attained the exhaustion of all outflows and the permanent liberation of mind by abiding in something; rather, I attained the exhaustion of outflows and the liberation of mind while abiding in nothing at all."
The Buddha said, “Subhūti,
it is the same for a bodhisattva mahāsattva: practicing the perfection of wisdom, they realize the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) while abiding nowhere at all.”
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,
for what reason is 'all-aspect omniscience' called 'all-aspect omniscience'?"
The Buddha said,
“Suvikrāntavikrāmin!
To know that all phenomena are of one single characteristic— that is, the characteristic of quiescence— is therefore called ‘knowledge of all aspects.’”
Furthermore, Subhūti!

The Tathāgata has realized, in accordance with reality, all the formations, characteristics, and signs that can represent all phenomena; therefore, it is called the Knowledge of All Aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

Regarding all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*)—is there any distinction among these three knowledges in terms of the abandonment of the afflictions?”
“Is there abandonment with remainder and abandonment without remainder?
The Buddha said,
“Suvikrāntavikrāmin!

It is not that there is any difference in the abandonment of the afflictions themselves; rather, all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas have forever severed the continuity of the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of all afflictions, whereas the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas have not yet forever severed the continuity of their habitual tendencies.
“World-Honored One!
Are the various afflictions severed and does one attain the unconditioned? “It is so!”
“Excellent, Subhūti!
“World-Honored One!
Do Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas not attain the unconditioned, yet sever their afflictions?”
"No, World-Honored One!
Subhūti, [it is not so].
"World-Honored One!"
“Are there any distinctions among unconditioned phenomena? “No, Subhūti!”
“World-Honored One!

If unconditioned phenomena have no distinctions, for what reason does the Buddha say that all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas have forever severed the continuity of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā-saṃtati*), whereas Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas have not yet forever severed the continuity of habitual tendencies?”

“Subhūti! The continuity of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā-saṃtati*) is not actually an affliction (*kleśa*). Nevertheless, although the afflictions of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas have been severed, there still remains a slight semblance of greed, hatred, and delusion manifesting in their physical, verbal, and mental activities; this is what is called the continuity of habitual tendencies.”

This exists within the mental continuums of foolish ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and is capable of inducing what is meaningless; it does not exist within the mental continuums of Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas as something that induces what is meaningless. All such continuums of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) are forever absent in the Buddhas.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

Since both the Path and Nirvāṇa are devoid of intrinsic nature, for what reason does the Buddha say, ‘This is a stream-enterer,’ ‘This is a once-returner,’ ‘This is a non-returner,’ ‘This is an arhat,’ ‘This is a pratyekabuddha,’ ‘This is a bodhisattva mahāsattva,’ and ‘This is a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha’?”
The Buddha said, “Suvikrāntavikrāmin!

Whether it be a stream-enterer, a once-returner, a non-returner, an arhat, a pratyekabuddha, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, or a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha— all such as these are manifested by the unconditioned.”
“World-Honored One!
Within unconditioned phenomena, is there truly a distinction in meaning between those ranging from stream-enterers up to Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas? “No!”
"Subhūti! [Subhūti replied: "World-Honored One!
If that is so, for what reason has the Buddha taught that everything from the stream-enterer up to the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is all manifested by the unconditioned?"
"Subhūti! I have displayed this by relying on conventional discourse, not by relying on the ultimate truth; for within the ultimate truth, there can be no display. Why is that?
"Subhūti! In the ultimate sense, there is no path of language, nor analytical wisdom, nor even both; yet, by severing various extremes, one establishes various subsequent limits."
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!

Since all dharmas are empty of their own characteristics and even a prior limit does not exist, how much less could there be a subsequent limit? How, then, can one establish that there is a subsequent limit?"
The Buddha said, “So it is, Subhūti!”
So it is! As you have said, all phenomena are empty of their own intrinsic characteristics; since even a prior limit does not exist, how much less could there be a subsequent limit!
To establish that a subsequent limit exists is certainly impossible.
However, because sentient beings are unable to understand that the self-characteristics of all phenomena are empty, for their benefit he skillfully teaches them:
"This is the prior limit; this is the subsequent limit."
"However, within the emptiness of intrinsic characteristics of all phenomena, neither the prior limit nor the subsequent limit can be apprehended. Thus, Subhūti,
having realized that all phenomena are empty of intrinsic characteristics, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should practice the perfection of wisdom."

"Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva realizes that the self-characteristics of all phenomena are empty and practices the perfection of wisdom, they will have no attachments toward any phenomena—namely, they do not attach to internal phenomena or external phenomena; wholesome phenomena or unwholesome phenomena; mundane phenomena or supramundane phenomena; contaminated phenomena or uncontaminated phenomena; conditioned phenomena or unconditioned phenomena; whether they be the phenomena of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, or tathāgatas—they do not attach to any of these."
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One, the Tathāgata has often spoken of the *prajñāpāramitā*. For what reason is it called *prajñāpāramitā*?”
The Buddha said,
“Subhūti! Because this perfection of wisdom reaches the ultimate further shore of all phenomena, it is called the perfection of wisdom.”
Furthermore, Subhūti!

Because all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, reach the further shore by means of this perfection of wisdom, it is called the perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, Subhūti!

All Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, and the assembly of Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, by means of this Prajñāpāramitā, analyze all phenomena according to the principle of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). Just as when matter (*rūpa*) is analyzed down to its most subtle atoms (*paramāṇu*), not even the slightest substantiality can be found; therefore, it is called Prajñāpāramitā.
Furthermore, Subhūti,
because this perfection of wisdom encompasses suchness, the limit of reality, and the dharma-realm, it is called the perfection of wisdom.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

This perfection of wisdom does not possess even the slightest dharma that is either joined or dispersed, whether it be with form or formless, visible or invisible, resistant or non-resistant, with outflows or without outflows, conditioned or unconditioned."
Why is this so? Subhūti!

This perfection of wisdom is formless, invisible, non-obstructive, and of a single characteristic—namely, the characteristic of being signless—and for this reason it is called the perfection of wisdom.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

Because this perfection of wisdom can give birth to all sublime and wholesome dharmas, can bring forth all wisdom and eloquence, and can lead to all mundane and supramundane happiness, it is called the 'perfection of wisdom.'"
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

This profound and solid perfection of wisdom is immovable and indestructible. If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices this perfection of wisdom, no evil Māras, nor their retinues, nor śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, non-Buddhists, brahmins, evil friends, or enemies can destroy them."
Why is this so? Subhūti!

Because by means of this perfection of wisdom, one discerns that the specific characteristics of all phenomena are empty and that no evil Māras can be apprehended, it is called the perfection of wisdom.
"Subhūti! All bodhisattva mahāsattvas should practice according to reality the profound meaning and intent of this perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, Subhūti!"

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to practice the profound meaning and intent of the *prajñāpāramitā*, they should practice the meaning of impermanence, the meaning of suffering, the meaning of emptiness, and the meaning of non-self; they should practice the meaning of the knowledge of suffering, the meaning of the knowledge of the origin, the meaning of the knowledge of cessation, and the meaning of the knowledge of the path; they should practice the meaning of the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), the meaning of subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), the meaning of conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), and the meaning of the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*); they should practice the meaning of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), the meaning of the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), and the meaning of the knowledge as it is (*yathābhūtajñāna*).
"Subhūti! In order to practice the profound meaning and intent of the perfection of wisdom, bodhisattva mahāsattvas should practice the perfection of wisdom."
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:

“World-Honored One, within this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, neither meaning nor non-meaning can be apprehended. How, then, should a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice the *prajñāpāramitā* by way of practicing the profound significance of the *prajñāpāramitā*?”
The Buddha said, “Subhūti!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the profound meaning and intent of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), should form this thought:”

"I should not engage in the pursuit of what is beneficial or harmful through sensual desire; I should not engage in the pursuit of what is beneficial or harmful through ill will; I should not engage in the pursuit of what is beneficial or harmful through delusion; I should not engage in the pursuit of what is beneficial or harmful through wrong view; I should not engage in the pursuit of what is beneficial or harmful through wrong concentration; I should not engage in the pursuit of what is beneficial or harmful through any of the various evil views."
Why is this so? Subhūti!
Greed, hatred, delusion, wrong views, wrong concentration, dogmatic views, suchness, and the limit of reality do not constitute benefit or non-benefit for any phenomena.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the profound meaning and purpose of the perfection of wisdom should form this thought:

'I should not practice with regard to the meaning or non-meaning of form; I should not practice with regard to the meaning or non-meaning of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.'"

I should not engage with the sense-base of the eye as being meaningful or meaningless; I should not engage with the sense-bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as being meaningful or meaningless.

I should not engage with the sense-base of forms as being meaningful or meaningless; I should not engage with the sense-bases of sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena as being meaningful or meaningless.
I should not engage with the eye-element as being meaningful or meaningless; I should not engage with the elements of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as being meaningful or meaningless.

I should not engage with the notions of benefit or harm regarding the realm of form; I should not engage with the notions of benefit or harm regarding the realms of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena.

I should not engage with the notions of benefit or harm regarding the realm of eye-consciousness; I should not engage with the notions of benefit or harm regarding the realms of ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-consciousness.
I should not engage with the notions of benefit or harm regarding eye-contact; I should not engage with the notions of benefit or harm regarding ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact.

I should not engage with the sense of benefit or non-benefit regarding the feelings produced with eye-contact as condition; I should not engage with the sense of benefit or non-benefit regarding the feelings produced with ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-contact as condition.

I should not engage with the sense of benefit or non-benefit regarding the earth element; I should not engage with the sense of benefit or non-benefit regarding the water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness elements.

I should not engage with the sense of benefit or non-benefit regarding ignorance; I should not engage with the sense of benefit or non-benefit regarding volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, existence, birth, or aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair.

I should not practice for the sake of either benefit or non-benefit regarding the perfection of generosity; I should not practice for the sake of either benefit or non-benefit regarding the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom; I should not practice for the sake of either benefit or non-benefit regarding inner emptiness;

I should not practice for the sake of either benefit or non-benefit regarding outer emptiness, inner-and-outer emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, the emptiness of the ultimate, the emptiness of conditioned phenomena, the emptiness of unconditioned phenomena, absolute emptiness, the emptiness of the limitless, the emptiness of dispersion, the emptiness of non-alteration, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, the emptiness of specific characteristics, the emptiness of common characteristics, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature.

I should not practice with regard to the meaning or non-meaning of *tathatā* (suchness); I should not practice with regard to the meaning or non-meaning of the *dharmadhātu* (dharma-realm), *dharmatā* (dharma-nature), *avitathatā* (non-falsity), *ananyathābhāvatā* (unchanging nature), *samatā* (equality), *niyāmatā* (the state of being fixed), *dharmasthititā* (stability of phenomena), *dharmadhātusthititā* (stability of the dharma-realm), *bhūtakoṭi* (the limit of reality), *ākāśadhātu* (space-element), or the *acintyadhātu* (inconceivable realm).
I should not practice with regard to the meaning or non-meaning of the four foundations of mindfulness;

I should not practice with regard to the meaning or non-meaning of the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, or the eightfold noble path.

I should not practice for the sake of the meaning or the non-meaning of the noble truth of suffering; I should not practice for the sake of the meaning or the non-meaning of the noble truths of origin, cessation, and the path;

I should not practice for the sake of the meaning or the non-meaning of the four dhyānas; I should not practice for the sake of the meaning or the non-meaning of the four immeasurables or the four formless attainments;
I should not practice for the sake of the meaning or the non-meaning of the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, or the ten totalities.
I should not practice with regard to the meaning or non-meaning of all doors of samādhi; I should not practice with regard to the meaning or non-meaning of all dhāraṇī-doors;
I should not practice with regard to the meaning or non-meaning of the door of emptiness liberation, nor the doors of signlessness and wishlessness liberations;
I should not practice with regard to the meaning or non-meaning of the five eyes, nor the meaning or non-meaning of the six supernormal powers.

I should not engage with the meaning or non-meaning of the ten powers of a Buddha; I should not engage with the meaning or non-meaning of the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
I should not engage with the meaning or non-meaning of the quality of non-forgetfulness; I should not engage with the meaning or non-meaning of the nature of constant equanimity;
I should not engage with the meaning or non-meaning of all-knowledge; and I should not engage with the meaning or non-meaning of the knowledge of the paths or the knowledge of all aspects.

I should not engage with the notion of what is meaningful or meaningless regarding the fruit of stream-entry; I should not engage with the notion of what is meaningful or meaningless regarding the fruits of once-returning, non-returning, or arhatship;
I should not engage with the notion of what is meaningful or meaningless regarding pratyekabuddha-enlightenment;
and I should not engage with the notion of what is meaningful or meaningless regarding any of the practices of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
"I should not engage in the notion of what is meaningful or meaningless regarding the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas.
Why is that? Subhūti!
When the Tathāgata attained unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, he did not perceive any dharma that could serve as a benefit or a non-benefit to even the slightest dharma. Subhūti!

Whether the Tathāgata appears in the world or does not appear in the world, the dharma-nature of all dharmas, the stability of dharmas, the fixedness of dharmas, and the suchness of dharmas remain eternally abiding; no dharma serves as a benefit or a non-benefit to any other dharma.
Thus it is, Subhūti!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva should remain free from both the meaningful and the meaningless, and should always practice the profound significance of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,
for what reason does the perfection of wisdom not constitute either benefit or harm toward all phenomena?"
The Buddha said, “Suvikrāntavikrāmin!

The profound perfection of wisdom performs no action toward either conditioned or unconditioned phenomena; it is neither a benefactor nor an adversary, neither beneficial nor harmful. Therefore, the perfection of wisdom does not function as the meaning or the non-meaning of any phenomena.”
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
Is it not the case that all Buddhas, as well as the disciples of the Buddhas and all noble sages, take the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) as the ultimate truth?"
The Buddha said, “So it is, Subhūti!”

"So it is! It is as you have said: the Buddha and his disciples, all the worthy and holy ones, take the unconditioned (*asamskṛta*) as the primary meaning; yet the unconditioned dharma neither benefits nor harms any phenomena."
"Subhūti! Just as the suchness of space neither benefits nor harms any phenomena, so too is the profound prajñāpāramitā of the bodhisattva mahāsattva; it neither benefits nor harms any phenomena."
"Therefore, the Prajñāpāramitā does not function as either a benefit or a detriment toward any phenomena.
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
“Does a bodhisattva mahāsattva not need to train in the profound, unconditioned perfection of wisdom in order to realize the knowledge of all modes?
The Buddha said,
“Suvikrāntavikrāmin!

"So it is! So it is! Just as you have said, a bodhisattva mahāsattva must study the profound, unconditioned *prajñāpāramitā* in order to realize the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*), not by means of dualistic dharmas."
“World-Honored One!
Is it by means of the non-dual dharma that one attains the non-dual dharma? “No!”
"Subhūti! "World-Honored One!
Is it by means of two dharmas that one attains the dharma of non-duality?"
"No, World-Honored One!
[It is not so], Subhūti.
"World-Honored One!"
"If neither duality nor non-duality can be attained by means of either dual or non-dual dharmas, how then shall a bodhisattva mahāsattva attain the knowledge of all modes? "Subhūti!..."

Second, since both duality and non-duality are equally unattainable, the wisdom of all-knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*) that is attained is not attained because there is something to be attained, nor is it attained because there is nothing to be attained; for neither attainable phenomena nor unattainable phenomena can be apprehended. If one knows in this way, one is able to realize the wisdom of all-knowledge.
62. Chapter on Speaking Truthfully, Part One: Chapter Sixty-Two, Part One, "Speaking Truthfully. At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
“Thus, Blessed One, this perfection of wisdom is exceedingly profound.

Since bodhisattva mahāsattvas do not apprehend sentient beings, nor do they apprehend the designation ‘sentient being,’ yet they seek to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment for the sake of sentient beings— this is indeed a most difficult matter.”

"Bhagavān! It is just as if there were a person who wished to plant a tree in space—which is formless, invisible, non-obstructive, and without support—that would be extremely difficult. So it is with the bodhisattva mahāsattvas: since they neither apprehend a sentient being nor apprehend the designation 'sentient being,' yet they seek to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment for the sake of sentient beings, this is an exceedingly difficult matter."
The Buddha said,
“So it is, Subhūti! It is just so.”

"So it is! It is just as you have said. This *prajñāpāramitā* is exceedingly profound; that bodhisattva-mahāsattvas do not apprehend a sentient being, nor do they apprehend the designation of a sentient being, yet they seek to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening for the sake of sentient beings—this is indeed a most difficult matter."

“Subhūti! Although bodhisattva-mahāsattvas do not perceive any truly existent sentient beings nor the designations for them, sentient beings—due to ignorance and perversion—cling to them as being real. Consequently, they transmigrate through birth and death, undergoing endless suffering. To deliver them, bodhisattvas seek to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; having attained enlightenment, they sever the grasping at self and others, and cause those beings to be liberated from the manifold sufferings of birth and death.”

"Subhūti! It is as if there were a person who plants a tree in a fertile field. Although that person does not see the roots, trunk, branches, leaves, flowers, or fruits of this tree while it is being planted, once the tree has been planted, they irrigate it at the proper times and diligently protect it. Later, this tree gradually grows, and its branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits all become lush and abundant; many people enjoy them, and their illnesses are cured and they obtain peace."

Subhūti! It is just so for the bodhisattva mahāsattvas: although they do not perceive any sentient beings as having attained the fruit of buddhahood, they seek unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment for the sake of sentient beings. Having gradually practiced the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, and having brought them to fulfillment, they realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, enabling all sentient beings to partake of the branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits of the Buddha-tree, each obtaining their respective benefit.
“Subhūti, you should know that ‘abounding in leaves’ refers to how all sentient beings, by means of this Buddha-tree, are liberated from the suffering of the evil realms.
‘Abounding in flowers’ refers to how all sentient beings, by means of this Buddha-tree, are born into great kṣatriya clans.”
Some are born into great clans of brahmins, some are born into great clans of householders, some are born into great clans of lay devotees;
some are born among the gods of the Four Great Kings, some among the Trāyastriṃśa gods,
some among the Yāma gods, some among the Tuṣita gods, some among the Nirmāṇarati gods, or some are born among...
They may be reborn in the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Emanations, or in the Heaven of the Brahma-multitude,
or in the Heaven of the Brahma-assistants, or in the Heaven of the Great Brahma, or in the Heavens of Light, or in the Heaven of Limited Light,
or in the Heaven of Immeasurable Light, or in the Heaven of Utmost Purity of Light, or in the Heaven of Purity.
Some are born in the Heaven of Limited Purity, some in the Heaven of Immeasurable Purity, some in the Heaven of Universal Purity, some in the Vast Heaven,
some in the Heaven of Limited Vastness, some in the Heaven of Immeasurable Vastness, some in the Heaven of Vast Results,
some in the Heaven Free from Affliction, some in the Heaven Free from Heat, and some in the Heaven of Excellent Manifestation.
Some are reborn in the Heaven of Good Vision; some are reborn in the Heaven of Ultimate Form; some are reborn in the Heaven of Infinite Space;
some are reborn in the Heaven of Infinite Consciousness; some are reborn in the Heaven of Nothingness;
and some are reborn in the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-Perception.

Regarding the benefit of the fruit: it means that because of this Buddha-tree, sentient beings may abide in the fruit of stream-entry, or abide in the fruit of once-returning, or abide in the fruit of non-returning, or abide in the fruit of arhatship, or abide in the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, or abide in unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Once these sentient beings have attained buddhahood, they further benefit sentient beings by means of the branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits of the Buddha-trees, causing them to escape the sufferings of the evil realms and obtain the happiness of humans and devas. They gradually establish them so that they enter the realm of parinirvāṇa through the three vehicles—namely, the realm of parinirvāṇa of the Śrāvaka vehicle, the realm of parinirvāṇa of the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, or the realm of parinirvāṇa of the Unsurpassed Vehicle (Mahāyāna).

"Subhūti! Although these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas perform such great deeds of benefit, they do not perceive any truly existent sentient beings who attain nirvāṇa; they perceive only the cessation of the manifold sufferings of conceptual construction."

"So it is, Subhūti! When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom, they do not apprehend sentient beings nor their designations; yet, in order to eliminate the inversion of self-grasping and to seek the attainment of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, they engage in this for such reasons—it is indeed a most difficult task."
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha,
saying: “World-Honored One,
you should know that a bodhisattva mahāsattva is himself the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.”
Why is this so? World-Honored One!

It is because of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas that one is able to forever sever all hells, forever sever all animal realms, forever sever all ghost realms, forever sever all states of no leisure, forever sever all poverty, forever sever all inferior destinies, and forever sever all the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm.
The Buddha said,
“So it is, Subhūti! It is just so.”
So it is! It is as you have said.
You should know that a bodhisattva mahāsattva is himself a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a Samyaksaṃbuddha.
“Subhūti! If there were no bodhisattva mahāsattvas who set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment,
then there would be no Buddhas of the past, future, or present in the world who have realized unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, nor...
No Pratyekabuddhas appear in the world; nor do Arhats appear in the world; nor do Anāgāmins appear in the world;
nor do Sakṛdāgāmins appear in the world; nor do Srotāpannas appear in the world.
Nor is there anyone capable of eternally severing [the roots of] hell, nor is there anyone capable of eternally severing [the other realms].
Among animals, there is likewise none who can forever sever the realm of hungry ghosts; none who can forever sever the states of no-leisure;
none who can forever sever poverty; none who can forever sever the inferior destinies;
and none who can forever sever the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm.
"Therefore, Subhūti, it is as you have said.

You should know that a bodhisattva mahāsattva is indeed a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha; in this very way, you should know that a bodhisattva mahāsattva is indeed a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha."
Why is this? Subhūti!
If by means of this very suchness a Tathāgata is designated, it is by means of this very same suchness that a Pratyekabuddha is designated.
If by means of this suchness a pratyekabuddha is designated, then by that same suchness a śrāvaka is designated;
if by means of this suchness a śrāvaka is designated, then by that same suchness all noble ones (ārya) are designated;
if by means of this suchness all noble ones are designated, then by that same suchness form (rūpa) is designated.
If by means of this suchness one designates form, then by means of that same suchness one designates feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness;
if by means of this suchness one designates feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness, then by means of that same suchness one designates the eye-base;
if by means of this suchness one designates the eye-base, then by means of that same suchness one designates the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-bases.
If by means of this suchness the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are designated, then by that same suchness the sense base of form is designated;
if by means of this suchness the sense base of form is designated, then by that same suchness the sense bases of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena are designated;
if by means of this suchness the sense bases of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena are designated, then by that same suchness the eye element is designated.
If by means of this suchness the eye-element is designated, then by that same suchness the ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-elements are designated;
if by means of this suchness the ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-elements are designated, then by that same suchness the form-element is designated;
if by means of this suchness the form-element is designated, then by that same suchness the sound-, odor-, taste-, tangible-, and phenomena-elements are designated.
If, by means of this suchness, the element of sound, smell, taste, touch, and mental phenomena is designated, then by that same suchness the element of eye-consciousness is designated;
if, by means of this suchness, the element of eye-consciousness is designated, then by that same suchness the elements of ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-consciousness are designated;
if, by means of this suchness, the elements of ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-consciousness are designated, then by that same suchness eye-contact is designated.
If by means of this suchness eye-contact is designated, then by that same suchness ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact are designated;
if by means of this suchness ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact are designated, then by that same suchness the various feelings produced with eye-contact as condition are designated;

if by means of this suchness the various feelings produced with eye-contact as condition are designated, then by that same suchness the various feelings produced with ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact as condition are designated.

If, by means of this suchness, one designates the various feelings produced with the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mental contact as conditions, it is by means of this very same suchness that one designates the earth element.

The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle 363. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Part One: Chapter Sixty-Two on the True Exposition, Part Two. “If by means of this suchness (*tathatā*) the earth element is designated, then by that same suchness the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements are designated;
if by means of this suchness the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements are designated, then by that same suchness ignorance (*avidyā*) is designated;

if by means of this suchness ignorance is designated, then by that same suchness formations (*saṃskāra*), consciousness (*vijñāna*), name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), contact (*sparśa*), feeling (*vedanā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), becoming (*bhava*), birth (*jāti*), and old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair are designated.”

If by means of this suchness one designates the formations up to old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair, then by that same suchness one designates the perfection of generosity;

if by means of this suchness one designates the perfection of generosity, then by that same suchness one designates the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom;
if by means of this suchness one designates the perfections from ethical discipline up to wisdom, then by that same suchness one designates internal emptiness.

If by means of this suchness one designates internal emptiness, then by means of that same suchness one designates external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, non-altering emptiness, essential emptiness, emptiness of specific characteristics, emptiness of common characteristics, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature;

if by means of this suchness one designates external emptiness up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature, then by means of that same suchness one designates the four applications of mindfulness.

If, by means of this suchness, the four applications of mindfulness are designated, then by means of this very same suchness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path are designated;
if, by means of this suchness, the four right efforts up to the eightfold noble path are designated, then by means of this very same suchness, the noble truth of suffering is designated;
if, by means of this suchness, the noble truth of suffering is designated, then by means of this very same suchness, the noble truths of origin, cessation, and the path are designated.
If, by means of this suchness, the noble truths of origin, cessation, and the path are designated, then by means of that same suchness, the four dhyānas are designated;
if, by means of this suchness, the four dhyānas are designated, then by means of that same suchness, the four immeasurables and the four formless absorptions are designated;
if, by means of this suchness, the four immeasurables and the four formless absorptions are designated, then by means of that same suchness, the eight liberations are designated.

If by means of this suchness the eight liberations are designated, then by means of this very same suchness the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities are designated;

if by means of this suchness the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities are designated, then by means of this very same suchness all doors of samādhi are designated;
if by means of this suchness all doors of samādhi are designated, then by means of this very same suchness all doors of dhāraṇī are designated.
If by means of this suchness all doors of dhāraṇī are designated, then by means of this very same suchness the door of liberation that is emptiness is designated;

if by means of this suchness the door of liberation that is emptiness is designated, then by means of this very same suchness the doors of liberation that are signlessness and wishlessness are designated;
if by means of this suchness the doors of liberation that are signlessness and wishlessness are designated, then by means of this very same suchness the five eyes are designated.
If by means of this suchness the five eyes are designated, then by means of this very same suchness the six supernormal powers are designated;
if by means of this suchness the six supernormal powers are designated, then by means of this very same suchness the ten powers of a Buddha are designated;

if by means of this suchness the ten powers of a Buddha are designated, then by means of this very same suchness the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are designated.

If, by means of this suchness, the four fearlessnesses up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are designated, then by means of this very same suchness, the quality of non-forgetfulness is designated;
if, by means of this suchness, the quality of non-forgetfulness is designated, then by means of this very same suchness, the state of constant abiding in equanimity is designated;
if, by means of this suchness, the state of constant abiding in equanimity is designated, then by means of this very same suchness, all-knowledge is designated.

If it is by means of this suchness that all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) is designated, then it is by means of this very same suchness that the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*) and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) are designated;

if it is by means of this suchness that the knowledge of the paths and the knowledge of all aspects are designated, then it is by means of this very same suchness that all the practices of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are designated;

and if it is by means of this suchness that all the practices of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are designated, then it is by means of this very same suchness that the unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*) is designated.

If it is by means of this suchness that the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas is designated, then it is by means of this same suchness that the realm of the conditioned is designated;
if it is by means of this suchness that the realm of the conditioned is designated, then it is by means of this same suchness that the realm of the unconditioned is designated;
and if it is by means of this suchness that the realm of the unconditioned is designated, then it is by means of this same suchness that all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas are designated.
If it is by means of this suchness that all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas are designated, then it is by means of this very same suchness that all Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas are designated;
if it is by means of this suchness that all Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas are designated, then it is by means of this very same suchness that all sentient beings are designated;
and if it is by means of this suchness that all sentient beings are designated, then it is by means of this very same suchness that all phenomena are designated.
"So it is, Subhūti!

The suchness of all phenomena, the suchness of all sentient beings, and the suchness of all Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas—all these suchnesses of Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas are in reality without distinction. Because they are without distinction, they are called 'suchness.'"
Because the bodhisattva mahāsattvas, having fully trained in this suchness, realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they are called Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas.

Therefore, Subhūti, you should know that a bodhisattva mahāsattva is indeed a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a Samyaksaṃbuddha, because all phenomena and all sentient beings take true thusness (tathatā) as their definitive standard.
"So it is, Subhūti! A bodhisattva mahāsattva should train in the profound perfection of wisdom, which is suchness."
Subhūti! If bodhisattva mahāsattvas train in the profound perfection of wisdom that is suchness, they are able to train in the suchness of all phenomena.
If one can study the suchness of all phenomena, then one can fulfill the suchness of all phenomena.
If one can fulfill the suchness of all phenomena, then one attains sovereign dwelling within the suchness of all phenomena.
If one attains abiding mastery over the suchness of all phenomena, then one can skillfully know the superior or inferior faculties of all sentient beings.
If one can skillfully know the superior or inferior faculties of all sentient beings, then one can fully know the differences in the inclinations of all sentient beings.
If one can fully know the differences in the inclinations (*adhimukti*) of all sentient beings, then one knows that sentient beings experience the fruits of their own karma.
If one knows that sentient beings experience the fruits of their own karma, then one will be able to fulfill the knowledge of aspiration (*praṇidhijñāna*).
If one can fully possess the wisdom of aspiration, then one can purify and cultivate the sublime wisdom of the three periods of time.
If one can purify and cultivate the sublime wisdom of the three periods of time, then one can practice the bodhisattva conduct without error.
If one can practice the bodhisattva conduct without error, then one can mature sentient beings according to reality.
If one can mature sentient beings according to reality, then one can purify buddha-fields according to reality.
If one can, in accordance with reality, adorn and purify the Buddha-fields, then one can realize the knowledge of all modes.
If one can realize the knowledge of all modes, then one can turn the sublime wheel of Dharma.
If one is able to turn the sublime wheel of Dharma, then one can establish sentient beings upon the paths of the three vehicles.
If one is able to establish sentient beings upon the paths of the three vehicles, then one causes sentient beings to enter the realm of nirvana without remainder.

“Subhūti! When bodhisattva mahāsattvas perceive such merits of both self-benefit and benefiting others, they should resolve upon the mind of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and with courageous diligence, practice the perfection of wisdom with firmness and without retreat.”
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to give rise to the mind of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment and practices the profound perfection of wisdom as it has been taught, then all those in the world—gods, humans, and asuras—should prostrate themselves before them, honoring and making offerings to them.”

The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"For what reason is the intrinsic nature of the knowledge of all aspects non-existent? The Buddha said, "Subhūti!"
“Because all-aspect omniscience has no nature of synthesis, if a dharma has no nature of synthesis, that dharma takes non-existence as its nature.
“World-Honored One!”
"For what reason are form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness devoid of intrinsic nature?

"Subhūti, it is because form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness lack an intrinsic nature of synthesis. If a phenomenon lacks an intrinsic nature of synthesis, then that phenomenon has non-existence as its intrinsic nature."
“World-Honored One!
For what reason are the bases of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind devoid of intrinsic nature? “Subhūti!

The sense bases of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind lack an inherent nature of combination; since a phenomenon lacks an inherent nature of combination, that phenomenon takes non-existence as its nature.
“World-Honored One!
For what reason are the self-natures of the sense bases of form, sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena non-existent? “Subhūti!

Because the sense bases of form, sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena lack an inherent nature of combination, if a phenomenon lacks an inherent nature of combination, that phenomenon has non-existence as its nature.
“World-Honored One!
For what reason do the eye-element, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-elements lack intrinsic nature? “Subhūti!
Because the eye-element, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-elements lack a nature of synthesis, if a dharma lacks a nature of synthesis, that dharma takes non-existence as its nature.
“World-Honored One!
For what reason are the intrinsic natures of the realms of form, sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena non-existent? “Subhūti!”

Because the realms of form, sound, odor, taste, touch, and mental phenomena lack an intrinsic nature of combination, if a phenomenon lacks an intrinsic nature of combination, that phenomenon has non-existence as its very nature.
“World-Honored One!
For what reason are the nature of the eye-consciousness element, and those of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-consciousness elements, non-existent? “Subhūti!

Because the eye-consciousness element, as well as the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-consciousness elements, lack an inherent nature of combination; and if a dharma lacks an inherent nature of combination, that dharma has non-existence as its nature.
“World-Honored One!
For what reason are the natures of eye-contact, ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, and mind-contact non-existent? “Subhūti!

Because eye-contact, ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, and mind-contact lack an inherent nature of combination, whatever dharma lacks an inherent nature of combination has non-existence as its very nature.
“World-Honored One!
For what reason do all feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition, and all feelings produced with ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-contact as conditions, lack intrinsic nature?”

“Subhūti! Because the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition, and those produced with ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact as conditions, lack an inherent nature of combination; and because any dharma that lacks an inherent nature of combination has non-existence as its very nature.”
“World-Honored One!
For what reason are the intrinsic natures of the earth element, water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements non-existent?
“Suvikrāntavikrāmin! [They are so because]...”

Because the elements of earth, water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness lack an inherent nature of combination, if a phenomenon lacks an inherent nature of combination, that phenomenon has non-existence as its nature.
“World-Honored One!

For what reason are ignorance, volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, existence, birth, and old age, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair devoid of intrinsic nature?”

“Subhūti! Because ignorance up to old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair have no inherent nature of aggregation, whatever dharma lacks an inherent nature of aggregation, that dharma has non-existence as its nature.”
“World-Honored One!
For what reason do internal phenomena and external phenomena lack intrinsic nature? “Suvikrāntavikrāmin!
“Because internal and external phenomena lack an inherent nature of combination, if a phenomenon lacks an inherent nature of combination, that phenomenon takes non-existence as its nature.
“World-Honored One!”
"For what reason do the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments lack intrinsic nature?

"Subhūti, it is because the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments lack an intrinsic nature of synthesis. If a phenomenon lacks an intrinsic nature of synthesis, then that phenomenon has non-existence as its nature."
“World-Honored One!

For what reason do the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right endeavors, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path lack intrinsic nature?”

“Subhūti! Because the four applications of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path lack an inherent nature of combination, any dharma that lacks an inherent nature of combination has non-existence as its very nature.”
“World-Honored One!
For what reason are the emptiness gate of liberation, the signless gate of liberation, and the wishless gate of liberation devoid of intrinsic nature?
“Suvikrāntavikrāmin! [Because]...”

Because the gate of liberation of emptiness, the gate of liberation of signlessness, and the gate of liberation of wishlessness lack an inherent nature of combination, if a phenomenon lacks an inherent nature of combination, that phenomenon has non-existence as its nature.
“World-Honored One!
For what reason do the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities lack intrinsic nature? “Subhūti!
Because the eight liberations up to the ten spheres of totality lack an inherent nature of synthesis, any dharma that lacks an inherent nature of synthesis has non-existence as its very nature.
“World-Honored One!
For what reason do the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom lack intrinsic nature?”

“Subhūti! Because the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom have no inherent nature of combination, any dharma that lacks an inherent nature of combination has non-existence as its very nature.”
“World-Honored One!

For what reason do internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, unchanging emptiness, essential emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common-characteristic emptiness, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of non-apprehensibility, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence lack any intrinsic nature?”

“Subhūti! Because inner emptiness, up to the emptiness of non-existence of intrinsic nature, lacks an inherent nature of synthesis; and if a dharma lacks an inherent nature of synthesis, that dharma has non-existence as its very nature.”
“World-Honored One!
For what reason do the noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of origination, the noble truth of cessation, and the noble truth of the path lack intrinsic nature? “Subhūti!
