Having realized the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna), wherever they are born, they shall never forget the meanings and doctrines of the sublime Dharma that they have heard and retained;
having planted immeasurable and vast roots of goodness (kuśalamūla) in the presence of the Buddhas, and being sustained by those roots of goodness,
they shall never be reborn pointlessly in the evil destinies or unfavorable states.

Furthermore, because they are sustained by these roots of virtue, their mental dispositions remain pure at all times; and because their mental dispositions are pure, they are constantly able to adorn and purify the Buddha-fields they seek, while also constantly bringing the sentient beings to be converted to spiritual maturity.

Furthermore, because they are sustained by these roots of goodness, they are never separated from true spiritual friends—namely, the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, as well as the assembly of Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, Śrāvakas, and others who can praise the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha—and they constantly draw near to, revere, and make offerings to them.
"In this way, Subhūti,

a bodhisattva mahāsattva who reverently makes offerings to the Buddhas, fulfills sublime roots of virtue, and is extensively sustained by true spiritual friends, will swiftly realize the knowledge of all modes."

Therefore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the profound perfection of wisdom who wishes to swiftly realize all-knowledge (sarvajñajñāna) should diligently honor and make offerings to the Buddhas, gather and perfect sublime roots of goodness, and constantly seek proximity to true spiritual friends without ever becoming weary.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not reverently make offerings to the Buddhas, does not fulfill sublime roots of goodness, and is not sustained by many spiritual friends, could such a bodhisattva mahāsattva possibly attain the knowledge of all modes?"
The Buddha said, “Subhūti!

If one does not reverently honor and make offerings to the Buddhas, cannot fulfill sublime roots of goodness, and is not sustained by many spiritual friends, one would not even deserve the name ‘bodhisattva mahāsattva,’ let alone be able to realize the knowledge of all modes.”
Why is this? Subhūti!

There are those who have reverently made offerings to the Buddhas, planted perfect and supreme roots of goodness, and been extensively sustained by true spiritual friends; yet even they cannot attain the knowledge of all modes. How much less could one who does not reverently make offerings to the Buddhas, who fails to perfect supreme roots of goodness, and who is not sustained by true spiritual friends, ever realize the knowledge of all modes!
It is impossible that he could attain the knowledge of all modes; such a thing cannot occur.

Therefore, Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to abide in the name ‘bodhisattva mahāsattva’ and wishes to swiftly realize the knowledge of all modes, they should diligently honor, respect, and make offerings to the Buddhas, plant and perfect supreme roots of goodness, and attend upon and serve true spiritual friends without ever becoming weary.
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One,

for what reason is it that some bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, though they have already reverently made offerings to the Buddhas, planted perfect and supreme roots of goodness, and been extensively sustained by true spiritual friends, are nevertheless unable to attain the knowledge of all modes?”
The Buddha said, “Sudhana!

Because those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are far removed from the power of skillful means, they are unable to realize the knowledge of all modes. That is to say, because those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have not heard such teachings on skillful means from the Buddhas; nor have they reverently made offerings to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, planted perfect and supreme roots of goodness, and drawn near to and made offerings to true spiritual friends, they are unable to attain the knowledge of all modes.”
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:

“World-Honored One, what is called ‘skillful means’? By accomplishing such skillful means, how is it that a bodhisattva mahāsattva is certain to realize all-knowledge (sarvajñajñāna) in whatever they undertake?”
The Buddha said,
“Suvikrāntavikrāmin!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of generosity from the first production of the thought of enlightenment, they do so with a mental orientation associated with the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*). Whether they give to a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha; or to a pratyekabuddha; or to a śrāvaka; or to a bodhisattva mahāsattva; or to other śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas; or to non-Buddhist practitioners of the holy life; or to the poor, those on the road, those practicing austerities, and those who come as supplicants; or to all humans and non-humans—this bodhisattva mahāsattva, having accomplished such a mental orientation associated with the knowledge of all modes, practices generosity without the notion of a gift, without the notion of a recipient, without the notion of a giver, and without any notion of "I" or "mine."

Why is this? It is because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas contemplate that the self-characteristics of all phenomena are empty—without arising, without formation, without transformation, and without cessation—and thus they enter into the characteristics of all phenomena; knowing that all phenomena are without action and without agency, they enter into the characteristics of all conditioned formations.

This bodhisattva mahāsattva, having accomplished such skillful means, constantly increases their sublime roots of goodness; because these sublime roots of goodness are constantly increasing, they are able to practice the perfection of generosity, maturing sentient beings and purifying buddha-fields.

Although they practice generosity, they do not seek the fruits obtained from giving; that is, they do not crave the various desirable objects obtained through giving, nor do they long for the superior rewards within saṃsāra obtained through giving. Rather, they practice the perfection of generosity solely for the sake of protecting those who lack protection and desiring to liberate those who are not yet liberated.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of ethical discipline from the first moment of generating the mind of awakening, they uphold that discipline with a mental orientation associated with the knowledge of all modes. Their mind is not obscured by desire, nor is it obscured by hatred, nor is it obscured by delusion. Furthermore, it is not shrouded by latent tendencies or active fetters, nor by any other various evil and unwholesome factors that obstruct awakening—namely, stinginess, immoral conduct, anger, laziness, inferiority of mind, distraction, faulty wisdom, pride, excessive pride, pride beyond pride, the pride of "I am," overweening pride, the pride of inferiority, and false pride—and they never give rise to mental orientations associated with the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.

Why is this? Because this bodhisattva-mahāsattva contemplates that the self-characteristics of all phenomena are empty—without arising, without formation, without transformation, and without cessation—and thus enters into the characteristics of all phenomena. Knowing that all phenomena are without agency and without capacity, he enters into the characteristics of all conditioned formations.

This bodhisattva mahāsattva, having accomplished such skillful means, constantly increases superior roots of goodness; because these superior roots of goodness increase perpetually, they are able to practice the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*), maturing sentient beings and purifying buddha-fields.

Although they practice pure ethical discipline, they do not seek the fruits obtained from that discipline; that is, they do not crave the various desirable objects obtained through discipline, nor do they indulge in seeking the superior rewards within saṃsāra obtained through discipline. Rather, they cultivate the perfection of pure ethical discipline solely for the sake of protecting those who are unprotected and desiring to liberate those who are not yet liberated.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of patience from the first production of the thought of enlightenment, training in patience with a mental orientation associated with the knowledge of all modes, that bodhisattva mahāsattva will not, even for the sake of protecting his own life, give rise to a single thought of anger, harsh speech, or a mind of resentment seeking retribution.

Suppose someone should come wishing to take this bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s life, to plunder his wealth and property, to violate his wife, to deceive and mislead him, to cause estrangement between his relatives and friends, to insult him with coarse speech, or to mock him with foul and impure words; or suppose they should beat, strike, cut, or mutilate him, or inflict various other harmful acts upon him—toward such sentient beings, he harbors no anger or resentment whatsoever, but desires only their benefit and happiness.
Why is this? Subhūti!

This bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates that the self-characteristics of all phenomena are empty—without arising, without formation, without transformation, and without cessation—and enters into the characteristics of all phenomena; he knows that all phenomena are without agency and without capacity, and enters into the characteristics of all conditioned formations.

This bodhisattva mahāsattva, having accomplished such skillful means, constantly increases superior roots of goodness; because these superior roots of goodness increase perpetually, they are able to practice the perfection of patience, maturing sentient beings and purifying buddha-fields.

Although they practice patience, they do not seek the fruits obtained through patience; that is, they do not crave the various desirable objects obtained through patience, nor do they hanker after the superior rewards within saṃsāra obtained through patience. Rather, they cultivate the perfection of patience solely for the sake of protecting those who lack protection and desiring to liberate those who are not yet liberated.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of diligence from the first production of the thought of enlightenment, they apply mental attention associated with the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), arouse right effort, don the firm armor, and act with courage and fearlessness, remaining far removed from the mind of indolence and laziness.

For the sake of seeking unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, this bodhisattva mahāsattva applies courageous and right effort without fearing any suffering; they are also able to skillfully prevent and subdue it—namely, the sufferings of humans, asuras, the realm of hungry ghosts, animals, and hell-beings, as well as other various sufferings—remaining neither afraid nor timid, and being able to skillfully prevent and subdue them while diligently cultivating wholesome dharmas without ever becoming weary or negligent."
Why is this? Subhūti!

This bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates that the self-characteristics of all phenomena are empty—without arising, without formation, without transformation, and without cessation—and enters into the characteristics of all phenomena; he knows that all phenomena are without action and without agency, and enters into the characteristics of all conditioned formations.

This bodhisattva mahāsattva, having accomplished such skillful means, constantly increases superior roots of goodness; because these superior roots of goodness are constantly increasing, they are able to practice the perfection of diligence, maturing sentient beings and purifying buddha-fields.

Although they practice diligence, they do not seek with longing the fruits obtained through such effort; that is, they do not crave the various desirable objects obtained through diligence, nor do they hanker after the superior rewards within saṃsāra obtained through diligence. Rather, they practice the perfection of diligence solely for the sake of protecting those who lack protection and desiring to liberate those who are not yet liberated.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva, from the first production of the thought of awakening, practices the perfection of meditative concentration, they train in various concentrations by means of mental attention associated with the knowledge of all modes."

When this bodhisattva-mahāsattva has seen forms with the eye, he does not grasp at their signs nor grasp at their secondary characteristics. He immediately guards the faculty of the eye at that point and dwells without negligence, so that the mind may not give rise to worldly greed and sorrow, evil and unwholesome states, or the outflows of various afflictions; he single-mindedly cultivates mindfulness and concentration to protect the faculty of the eye.

When this bodhisattva-mahāsattva hears sounds with the ear, they do not grasp at their signs nor grasp at their secondary characteristics. Immediately in that regard, they guard the faculty of the ear and abide without negligence, ensuring that the mind does not give rise to worldly greed, sorrow, evil and unwholesome dharmas, or the outflows of various afflictions; they single-mindedly cultivate mindfulness and concentration to protect the faculty of the ear.

When this bodhisattva-mahāsattva has smelled an odor, he does not grasp at its signs nor its secondary characteristics; rather, in that regard, he guards the faculty of the nose and dwells without negligence, so that the mind may not give rise to worldly greed and sorrow, evil and unwholesome states, or the outflows of various afflictions, but instead exclusively cultivates mindfulness and concentration to protect the faculty of the nose.

When this bodhisattva-mahāsattva has tasted flavors with the tongue, he does not grasp at their signs nor grasp at their secondary characteristics. He immediately guards the faculty of the tongue in that regard and dwells without negligence, so that the mind does not give rise to worldly greed and sorrow, evil and unwholesome states, or the outflows of various afflictions; he single-mindedly cultivates mindfulness and concentration to protect the faculty of the tongue.

When this bodhisattva-mahāsattva experiences tactile sensations with the body, he does not grasp at their signs nor grasp at their secondary characteristics. He immediately guards the faculty of the body in that regard and dwells without negligence, so that the mind does not give rise to worldly greed, sorrow, evil and unwholesome states, or the outflows of various afflictions; he single-mindedly cultivates mindfulness and concentration to protect the faculty of the body.

When this bodhisattva-mahāsattva has fully understood phenomena with the mind, he does not grasp at their signs nor grasp at their secondary characteristics; rather, in that very state, he guards the faculty of the mind and dwells without negligence, so that the mind does not give rise to worldly greed or sorrow, evil and unwholesome states, or the outflows of various afflictions, but instead single-mindedly cultivates mindfulness and concentration to protect the faculty of the mind.
Whether walking, standing, sitting, lying down, speaking, or remaining silent, this bodhisattva mahāsattva never abandons the state of samāhita śamatha.
This bodhisattva mahāsattva neither greedily gobbles with hand nor foot; his speech is not harsh, and his words are not noisy or confused;
his eyes and all his sense faculties are not distracted; he is neither fickle, nor restless, nor arrogant;
his body is undistracted, his speech is undistracted, and his mind is undistracted.
With tranquility of body, tranquility of speech, and tranquility of mind, whether in private or in public, his deportment remains unchanged;
he is content with all food, clothing, bedding, medicinal requisites for illness, and other material assets;
he is easy to satisfy, easy to support, and easy to serve; and his conduct conforms to the rules of discipline.
There is nothing he does not master; though dwelling amidst clamor and confusion, he practices seclusion.
Toward gain and loss, pleasure and pain, praise and blame, fame and insignificance, life and death, he remains equal and unchanging—neither elated nor dejected.
Toward enemies and toward kin, toward the virtuous and toward the wicked, his mind is free from hatred and love, and free from joy and sorrow.
Toward the words of the noble ones and the words of the ignoble, toward solitude and toward the clamor of the crowd, his mind remains equanimous and unchanging.

Regarding pleasant forms and unpleasant forms, and regarding all things that are either favorable or adverse, he does not engage in discrimination at all, but his mind remains constantly settled. "Why is this?

"Subhūti! This bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates that the self-characteristics of all phenomena are empty, without arising, without formation, without transformation, and without cessation; he enters into the characteristics of all phenomena and knows that all phenomena are without action and without agency, thereby entering into the characteristics of all conditioned formations."

This bodhisattva mahāsattva, having accomplished such skillful means, constantly increases superior roots of goodness; because these superior roots of goodness increase perpetually, they are able to practice the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*), maturing sentient beings and purifying buddha-fields.

Although they practice meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), they do not seek the fruits obtained through that concentration; that is, they do not crave the various desirable objects obtained through concentration, nor do they hanker after the superior rewards within cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) obtained through concentration. Rather, they practice the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*) solely for the sake of protecting those who lack protection and desiring to liberate those who are not yet liberated.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva, from the first production of the thought of awakening, practices the perfection of wisdom by training in wisdom with a mental orientation associated with the knowledge of all modes, that bodhisattva mahāsattva possesses no faulty wisdom and cannot be led astray by others. They remain far removed from all grasping at "I" and "mine," and they remain far removed from all views of a self, a sentient being, a life-force, a nourisher, a spirit, a person, a soul, a human, a youth, an agent, an experiencer, a knower, and a seer. They remain far removed from all views of existence and non-existence, from all evil paths of view, and from arrogance; they cultivate sublime wisdom without conceptualization and without transformation.
Why is this? Subhūti!

This bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates that the self-characteristics of all phenomena are empty—without arising, without accomplishment, without transformation, and without cessation—and enters into the characteristics of all phenomena; he knows that all phenomena are without agency and without capacity, and enters into the characteristics of all conditioned formations.

This bodhisattva mahāsattva, having accomplished such skillful means, constantly increases superior roots of goodness; because these superior roots of goodness are perpetually increasing, they are able to practice the perfection of wisdom, bringing sentient beings to maturity and purifying buddha-fields.

Although they practice *prajñā*, they do not seek with longing the fruits obtained through wisdom; that is, they do not crave the various desirable objects obtained through wisdom, nor do they indulge in seeking the superior rewards within *saṃsāra* obtained through wisdom. Rather, they practice the *prajñāpāramitā* solely for the sake of protecting those who lack protection and desiring to liberate those who are not yet liberated.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva, from the first production of the thought of awakening, practices the perfection of wisdom, they enter the first dhyāna with a mental orientation associated with the knowledge of all modes; they enter the second, third, and fourth dhyānas; they enter the immeasurable state of loving-kindness, and enter the immeasurable states of compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity; they enter the meditative absorption of the sphere of infinite space, and enter the meditative absorptions of the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Although this bodhisattva mahāsattva possesses mastery in entering and emerging from these dhyānas, immeasurables, and formless attainments, they do not crave or cling to their karmic maturation."
Why is this? Subhūti!

This bodhisattva mahāsattva has accomplished the most supreme skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*). By the power of these skillful means, he contemplates that the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of all the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), and the formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*) are all empty; they are without arising, without accomplishment, without transformation, and without cessation. He enters into the characteristics of all phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), knowing that all phenomena are without action and without agency, and he enters into the characteristics of all conditioned formations (*saṃskāralakṣaṇa*).

This bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes such skillful means that they constantly increase their sublime roots of goodness; because these sublime roots of goodness are ever-increasing, they are able to practice the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), and the formless attainments (*ārūpya*). By practicing the meditative concentrations, the immeasurables, and the formless attainments, they are able to act with mastery to bring sentient beings to maturity and to adorn and purify buddha-fields.

Although they practice the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), and the formless attainments (*ārūpya*), they do not seek the fruits thereof; that is to say, they do not crave or cling to the various maturations (*vipāka*) within birth and death obtained through the concentrations, immeasurables, and formless attainments. Rather, for the sake of protecting those who lack protection and liberating those who are not yet liberated, they cultivate the concentrations, immeasurables, and formless attainments without any grasping or attachment.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom from the first production of the thought of enlightenment, they train in all the factors conducive to awakening with a mental orientation associated with the knowledge of all modes. Having accomplished such skillful means, although they practice the path that abandons through vision and cultivation, they do not take up the fruit of stream-entry, nor do they take up the fruits of once-returner, non-returner, arhatship, or the awakening of a pratyekabuddha."
Why is this? Subhūti!

This bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates that the self-characteristics of all phenomena are empty, without arising, without formation, without transformation, and without cessation; he enters into the characteristics of all phenomena, knowing that all phenomena are without action and without agency, and he enters into the characteristics of all conditioned formations.

This bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes such skillful means and constantly increases superior roots of goodness; because these superior roots of goodness are always increasing, they practice the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment.
Although they practice these factors of enlightenment, they transcend the levels of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and enter the bodhisattva’s state of rightness and departure from birth. Subhūti!
This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). "Furthermore, Subhūti!..."

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the *prajñāpāramitā*, through mental engagement associated with the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), although they attain mastery in entering and emerging from the eight liberations (*aṣṭavimokṣa*) in both forward and reverse order, and likewise attain mastery in entering and emerging from the eight bases of mastery (*aṣṭābhibhvāyatana*), and likewise attain mastery in entering and emerging from the nine successive meditative attainments (*navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti*), and likewise attain mastery in entering and emerging from the ten totalities (*daśakṛtsnāyatana*), and are able to cultivate the contemplation of the four noble truths (*caturāryasatya*), and freely enter and emerge from the gates of samādhi, the gates of dhāraṇī, and the three doors of liberation (*trivimokṣamukha*), they are nonetheless able to accomplish skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*) and do not take up the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpattiphala*), nor do they take up the fruits of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmiphala*), non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*), arhatship (*arhattvaphala*), or the enlightenment of a solitary buddha (*pratyekabodhi*).
Why is this? Subhūti!

This bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates that the self-characteristics of all phenomena are empty—without arising, without accomplishment, without transformation, and without cessation—and thus enters into the characteristics of all phenomena. Knowing that all phenomena are without agency and without capacity, he enters into the characteristics of all conditioned formations.

This bodhisattva mahāsattva, having accomplished such skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), constantly increases superior roots of goodness (*kuśala-mūla*). Because these superior roots of goodness are perpetually increasing, they are able to practice the eight liberations (*aṣṭa-vimokṣa*), the eight bases of mastery (*aṣṭābhibhv-āyatana*), the nine successive attainments (*navānupūrva-samāpatti*), the ten universal bases (*daśa-kṛtsnāyatana*), the contemplation of the four noble truths (*catuḥ-āryasatya*), the doors of samādhi, the doors of dhāraṇī, and the three doors of liberation (*tri-vimokṣa-mukha*).

Although they are able to practice the eight liberations and even the three gates of liberation, they transcend the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, attaining entry into the stage of non-retrogression of a bodhisattva.
"Subhūti! This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s patient acceptance of the prediction regarding the non-arising of dharmas.
Furthermore, Subhūti!"

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they do so with a mental orientation associated with the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), training in the ten powers of a buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity; the quality of non-forgetfulness, the nature of constant equanimity, the knowledge of all things, the knowledge of the paths, the knowledge of all aspects, the five eyes, and the six supernormal powers—until such time as they have fully matured sentient beings, purified the buddha-fields, and realized the knowledge of all modes.
Why is this? Subhūti!

This bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates that the self-characteristics of all phenomena are empty—without arising, without formation, without transformation, and without cessation—and thus enters into the characteristics of all phenomena. He knows that all phenomena are without agency and without capacity, and thus enters into the characteristics of all conditioned formations.

This bodhisattva mahāsattva, having accomplished such skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), constantly increases superior roots of goodness (*kuśala-mūla*). Because these superior roots of goodness increase perpetually, they are able to practice the ten powers (*bala*) of a Buddha, the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), the four analytical knowledges (*pratisamvid*), the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*), great loving-kindness (*maitrī*), great compassion (*karuṇā*), great sympathetic joy (*muditā*), great equanimity (*upekṣā*), the quality of non-forgetfulness (*asaṃpramoṣadharman*), the nature of constant dwelling in equanimity (*upekṣāvihāritā*), all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), the five eyes (*pañca-cakṣus*), and the six supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). By being able to practice the ten powers of a Buddha up to the six supernormal powers, they are then able to bring sentient beings to fulfillment and maturity, purify buddha-fields, and gradually realize the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā-jñāna*).

“Subhūti! This is called skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*). If a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes such skillful means, whatever they undertake will certainly enable them to realize the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*).”
"Subhūti! Such skillful means are all accomplished by means of the perfection of wisdom. Therefore, Subhūti!"
“Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), seeking no karmic reward for whatever they do.
Chapter Sixty-Four: The Universal Training in the Path, Part One. At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
“Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas possess the most supreme awakening; although they are able to receive and practice such profound dharmas, they do not seek karmic retribution therein.
The Buddha said, “Suvikrāntavikrāmin!

"So it is! So it is! Just as you have said, the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas possess the most supreme awakening; although they are able to receive and practice such profound dharmas, they do not seek any karmic retribution therein."
Why is this? Subhūti!
It is because all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are immovable within their own nature.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
in what intrinsic nature do the bodhisattva mahāsattvas remain unmoved?”
The Buddha said,
“Subhūti! All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are able to remain unmoved within the self-nature of non-existence.”
“World-Honored One!
In what dharmas can the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas find no movement regarding the non-existent intrinsic nature? “Suvikrāntavikrāmin!

All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are able to remain unmoved within the absence of intrinsic nature and the immutability of the intrinsic nature of form; they are able to remain unmoved within the absence of intrinsic nature and the immutability of the intrinsic nature of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness;

they are able to remain unmoved within the absence of intrinsic nature and the immutability of the intrinsic nature of the sense base of the eye; they are able to remain unmoved within the absence of intrinsic nature and the immutability of the intrinsic nature of the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind;

they are able to remain unmoved within the absence of intrinsic nature and the immutability of the intrinsic nature of the sense base of forms; and they are able to remain unmoved within the absence of intrinsic nature and the immutability of the intrinsic nature of the sense bases of sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and phenomena.

They are able to remain unmoved within the naturelessness and self-nature of the eye-element; they are able to remain unmoved within the naturelessness and self-nature of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-elements.

They are able to remain unmoved within the naturelessness and self-nature of the form-element; they are able to remain unmoved within the naturelessness and self-nature of the sound, odor, taste, tangible, and mental-object elements.

They are able to remain unmoved within the naturelessness and self-nature of the eye-consciousness-element; they are able to remain unmoved within the naturelessness and self-nature of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-consciousness elements. They are able to remain unmoved within the naturelessness and self-nature of eye-contact; they are able to remain unmoved within the naturelessness and self-nature of ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-contact.

They are able to remain unmoved in the absence of intrinsic nature regarding all feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition; they are able to remain unmoved in the absence of intrinsic nature regarding all feelings produced with ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-contact as conditions;

they are able to remain unmoved in the absence of intrinsic nature regarding the earth element; they are able to remain unmoved in the absence of intrinsic nature regarding the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements;

they are able to remain unmoved in the absence of intrinsic nature regarding ignorance; and they are able to remain unmoved in the absence of intrinsic nature regarding volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, and old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair.

They are immovable within the absence of intrinsic nature in the perfection of generosity; they are immovable within the absence of intrinsic nature in the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom;

they are immovable within the absence of intrinsic nature in internal emptiness; and they are immovable within the absence of intrinsic nature in external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, endless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, non-alteration emptiness, essential emptiness, emptiness of self-characteristic, emptiness of common characteristic, emptiness of all phenomena, unapprehendable emptiness, emptiness of non-existence, emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence.

They are able to remain unmoved within the four dhyānas by virtue of the non-substantiality of their own-being; they are able to remain unmoved within the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments by virtue of the non-substantiality of their own-being;

they are able to remain unmoved within the four foundations of mindfulness by virtue of the non-substantiality of their own-being; they are able to remain unmoved within the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path by virtue of the non-substantiality of their own-being;

they are able to remain unmoved within the gate of liberation of emptiness by virtue of the non-substantiality of its own-being; and they are able to remain unmoved within the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness by virtue of the non-substantiality of their own-being.

They are able to remain unmoved within the noble truth of suffering regarding its lack of intrinsic nature and its immutability; they are able to remain unmoved within the noble truths of origin, cessation, and the path regarding their lack of intrinsic nature and their immutability;

they are able to remain unmoved within the eight liberations regarding their lack of intrinsic nature and their immutability; they are able to remain unmoved within the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative attainments, and the ten totalities regarding their lack of intrinsic nature and their immutability;

they are able to remain unmoved within all doors of samādhi regarding their lack of intrinsic nature and their immutability; and they are able to remain unmoved within all doors of dhāraṇī regarding their lack of intrinsic nature and their immutability.
They are able to remain unmoved by the non-substantiality of the intrinsic nature of the ten bodhisattva stages;

they are able to remain unmoved by the non-substantiality of the intrinsic nature of the five eyes; they are able to remain unmoved by the non-substantiality of the intrinsic nature of the six supernormal powers;

they are able to remain unmoved by the non-substantiality of the intrinsic nature of the ten powers of a buddha; and they are able to remain unmoved by the non-substantiality of the intrinsic nature of the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha.

They are able to remain unmoved within the absence of intrinsic nature and the non-arising of intrinsic nature regarding great loving-kindness; they are able to remain unmoved within the absence of intrinsic nature and the non-arising of intrinsic nature regarding great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity;

they are able to remain unmoved within the absence of intrinsic nature and the non-arising of intrinsic nature regarding the quality of non-forgetfulness; they are able to remain unmoved within the absence of intrinsic nature and the non-arising of intrinsic nature regarding the constant abiding in equanimity;

they are able to remain unmoved within the absence of intrinsic nature and the non-arising of intrinsic nature regarding all-knowledge; and they are able to remain unmoved within the absence of intrinsic nature and the non-arising of intrinsic nature regarding the knowledge of the paths and the knowledge of all aspects.

They are able to remain unmoved by the absence of intrinsic nature in the fruit of stream-entry; they are able to remain unmoved by the absence of intrinsic nature in the fruits of once-returner, non-returner, and arhatship;
they are able to remain unmoved by the absence of intrinsic nature in the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha;
and they are able to remain unmoved by the absence of intrinsic nature in all the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
They are able to remain unshakable regarding the non-existent intrinsic nature of the unsurpassed, perfect,
and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas.
Why is this, Subhūti?
"The intrinsic nature of all phenomena is itself the absence of nature; that which is the absence of nature cannot realize the absence of nature.

*The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Fascicle 366, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree, Part One, Chapter Sixty-four on the Path of Universal Training, Section Two. At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
“Can a phenomenon that possesses intrinsic nature directly realize the absence of intrinsic nature?
“No, Subhūti!”
“World-Honored One!
Can a dharma that lacks intrinsic nature realize the presence of intrinsic nature? “No!”
"Subhūti! "World-Honored One!
Can a dharma that has intrinsic nature realize an intrinsic nature?"
"No, World-Honored One!
[It would not be so], Subhūti. "World-Honored One!"
“Can a dharma that lacks intrinsic nature directly realize a dharma that lacks intrinsic nature?
“No, Subhūti!”
“World-Honored One!

If that is so, then there must also be a nature that cannot realize the absence of nature, an absence of nature that cannot realize the presence of nature, a presence of nature that cannot realize the presence of nature, and an absence of nature that cannot realize the absence of nature. Would it not then be the case, World-Honored One, that you have not attained realization?”
The Buddha said, “Suvikrāntavikrāmin!
There is the attainment of clear realization that is nonetheless free from the four extremes.”
“World-Honored One!
How can there be the attainment of clear realization while remaining free from the four propositions?
“Suvikrāntavikrāmin! [The Tathāgata] says:”

That which is neither existent nor non-existent, transcending all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), is what is called "clear realization" (*abhisamaya*); its attainment is likewise so. Therefore, I say that there is an attainment of clear realization, yet it is free from the four extremes (*catuṣkoṭi*).
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
what constitutes conceptual proliferation for a bodhisattva mahāsattva?”
The Buddha said, “Suvikrāntavikrāmin!

For a bodhisattva mahāsattva, to contemplate form as either permanent or impermanent is conceptual proliferation; to contemplate feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as either permanent or impermanent is conceptual proliferation.”

To contemplate form as either pleasant or painful is conceptual proliferation; to contemplate feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as either pleasant or painful is conceptual proliferation.

To contemplate form as either self or non-self is conceptual proliferation; to contemplate feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as either self or non-self is conceptual proliferation.
To contemplate form as either pure or impure is conceptual proliferation; to contemplate feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as either pure or impure is conceptual proliferation.

To contemplate form as either tranquil or untranquil is conceptual proliferation; to contemplate feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as either tranquil or untranquil is conceptual proliferation.

To contemplate form as either detached or undetached is conceptual proliferation; to contemplate feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as either detached or undetached is conceptual proliferation.

To contemplate form as either that which is to be fully known or that which is not to be fully known is conceptual proliferation; to contemplate feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as either that which is to be fully known or that which is not to be fully known is conceptual proliferation.

“Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva should think:

"Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva should form such a thought as:

“Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva should think: ‘One should give rise to the ten powers of a Buddha—this is conceptual proliferation;

"Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva should think: 'One should give rise to great loving-kindness—this is conceptual proliferation;

"Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva should think:

"Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva should think: 'One should give rise to all-knowledge (sarvajñatā)—this is conceptual proliferation (prapañca);

"Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva should think:
'To give rise to all doors of samādhi is conceptual proliferation; to give rise to all doors of dhāraṇī is conceptual proliferation.'"
“Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva should think:

‘The severance of the continuity of all afflictive habitual tendencies is conceptual proliferation; the realization of the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas is conceptual proliferation.’”

“Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, they should contemplate all such phenomena and all sentient beings as being beyond conceptual proliferation; therefore, they should not engage in conceptual proliferation regarding them.”
"Why is this so, Subhūti?

Because one cannot engage in conceptual proliferation regarding the existence-nature of all phenomena; one cannot engage in conceptual proliferation regarding existence-nature and non-existence-nature; one cannot engage in conceptual proliferation regarding non-existence-nature and existence-nature; and one cannot engage in conceptual proliferation regarding non-existence-nature and non-existence-nature."

Since neither an existent nature nor a non-existent nature apart from existence can be apprehended, that which constitutes conceptual proliferation, that which is the object of conceptual proliferation, and the locus of conceptual proliferation are all entirely non-existent.
"Therefore, Subhūti, form is without conceptual proliferation;
feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are without conceptual proliferation.
The eye-base is without conceptual proliferation; the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-bases are without conceptual proliferation."
The sphere of form is without conceptual proliferation; the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena are without conceptual proliferation.
The eye-element is without conceptual proliferation; the elements of ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are without conceptual proliferation.
The form-element is without conceptual proliferation; the elements of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena are without conceptual proliferation.
The eye-consciousness element is without conceptual proliferation; the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-consciousness elements are without conceptual proliferation.
Eye-contact is without conceptual proliferation; ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-contact are without conceptual proliferation.

All feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition are without conceptual proliferation; all feelings produced with ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-contact as conditions are without conceptual proliferation.
The earth element is without conceptual proliferation; the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements are without conceptual proliferation.

Ignorance is without conceptual proliferation; volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, and old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are without conceptual proliferation.

The perfection of generosity is without conceptual proliferation; the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom are without conceptual proliferation.

Internal emptiness is without conceptual proliferation; external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersion emptiness, non-alteration emptiness, essential nature emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common characteristic emptiness, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence are without conceptual proliferation.

Suchness is without conceptual proliferation; the dharma-realm, the dharma-nature, non-falsity, non-alteration, equality, the state beyond birth, the fixed nature of dharmas, the stability of dharmas, the limit of reality, the realm of space, and the inconceivable realm are without conceptual proliferation.

The four foundations of mindfulness are without conceptual proliferation; the four right endeavors, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path are without conceptual proliferation;
the noble truth of suffering is without conceptual proliferation, and the noble truths of origin, cessation, and the path are without conceptual proliferation;
the four dhyānas are without conceptual proliferation, and the four immeasurables and the four formless absorptions are without conceptual proliferation.
The eight liberations are without conceptual proliferation; the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities are without conceptual proliferation;
all doors of samādhi are without conceptual proliferation; all doors of dhāraṇī are without conceptual proliferation;
the door of liberation of emptiness is without conceptual proliferation; and the doors of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness are without conceptual proliferation.

The Ground of Utmost Joy is without conceptual proliferation; the Ground of Purity, the Ground of Radiance, the Ground of Blazing Wisdom, the Ground of Difficult Victory, the Ground of Presence, the Ground of Far-Going, the Ground of Immovability, the Ground of Good Intelligence, and the Ground of the Dharma Cloud are without conceptual proliferation.
The five eyes are without conceptual proliferation; the six supernormal powers are without conceptual proliferation.

The ten powers of a Buddha are without conceptual proliferation; the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are without conceptual proliferation.
Great loving-kindness is without conceptual proliferation; great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity are without conceptual proliferation;
the quality of non-forgetfulness is without conceptual proliferation; the state of constant abiding in equanimity is without conceptual proliferation;
all-knowledge is without conceptual proliferation; the knowledge of the paths and the knowledge of all aspects are without conceptual proliferation.

The fruit of stream-entry is free from conceptual proliferation; the fruits of once-returning, non-returning, and arhatship, as well as the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, are free from conceptual proliferation;

all the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are free from conceptual proliferation; the permanent severance of the continuity of all afflictions and habitual tendencies is free from conceptual proliferation; and the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas is free from conceptual proliferation.
“In this way, Subhūti, bodhisattva mahāsattvas should practice the profound perfection of wisdom that is free from conceptual proliferation.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, how does he contemplate all phenomena as being without conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*)?”
The Buddha said, “Suvikrāntavikrāmin!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, they contemplate that form has no intrinsic nature, and they contemplate that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness have no intrinsic nature.”

If a phenomenon lacks intrinsic nature, it should not be the object of conceptual proliferation; therefore, form is free from conceptual proliferation, and feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise free from conceptual proliferation.

"Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, they contemplate that the sense base of the eye lacks intrinsic nature, and they contemplate that the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind lack intrinsic nature."

If phenomena lack intrinsic nature, they should not be the object of conceptual proliferation; therefore, the sense base of the eye is free from conceptual proliferation, and the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are likewise free from conceptual proliferation.

“Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, they contemplate that the sphere of form lacks intrinsic nature; they contemplate that the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena lack intrinsic nature.”

If phenomena lack intrinsic nature, they should not be the object of conceptual proliferation; therefore, the sense-base of form is free from conceptual proliferation, and the sense-bases of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental objects are likewise free from conceptual proliferation.

“Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, they contemplate that the eye-element has no intrinsic nature, and they contemplate that the ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-elements have no intrinsic nature.”

If a phenomenon lacks intrinsic nature, it should not be the object of conceptual proliferation; therefore, there is no conceptual proliferation regarding the eye-element, and likewise no conceptual proliferation regarding the ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-element.

“Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, they contemplate that the realm of form has no intrinsic nature; they contemplate that the realms of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena have no intrinsic nature.”

If a phenomenon lacks intrinsic nature, it should not be the object of conceptual proliferation; therefore, the realm of form is free from conceptual proliferation, and the realms of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena are likewise free from conceptual proliferation.

"Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, they contemplate that the eye-consciousness element lacks intrinsic nature; they contemplate that the ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-consciousness elements lack intrinsic nature."

If phenomena lack intrinsic nature, they should not be the object of conceptual proliferation; therefore, the eye-consciousness element is free from conceptual proliferation, and the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-consciousness elements are likewise free from conceptual proliferation.

"Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, they contemplate that eye-contact has no intrinsic nature, and they contemplate that ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact have no intrinsic nature."

If phenomena lack intrinsic nature, they should not be the object of conceptual proliferation; therefore, eye-contact is without conceptual proliferation, and ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact are likewise without conceptual proliferation.

“Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, they contemplate that all feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition are without intrinsic nature; they contemplate that all feelings produced with ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-contact as conditions are without intrinsic nature.”

If phenomena lack intrinsic nature, they should not be the object of conceptual proliferation; therefore, the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition are without conceptual proliferation, and the various feelings produced with ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact as conditions are likewise without conceptual proliferation.

“Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, he contemplates that the earth element has no intrinsic nature, and he contemplates that the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements have no intrinsic nature.”

If a phenomenon lacks intrinsic nature, it should not be the object of conceptual proliferation; therefore, the earth element is free from conceptual proliferation, and the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements are likewise free from conceptual proliferation.

"Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, they contemplate that ignorance has no intrinsic nature; they contemplate that volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, and old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair have no intrinsic nature."

If phenomena lack intrinsic nature, they should not be the object of conceptual proliferation; therefore, ignorance is without conceptual proliferation, and so too are the formative forces up to old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair, which are likewise without conceptual proliferation.

“Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, they contemplate that the perfection of generosity has no intrinsic nature; they contemplate that the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom have no intrinsic nature.”

If phenomena lack intrinsic nature, they should not be the object of conceptual proliferation; therefore, the perfection of generosity is free from conceptual proliferation, and the perfections from ethical discipline up to wisdom are likewise free from conceptual proliferation.

“Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, they contemplate that internal emptiness is without intrinsic nature; they contemplate that external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, limitless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, non-alteration emptiness, essential emptiness, emptiness of specific characteristics, emptiness of common characteristics, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence are without intrinsic nature.”

If phenomena lack intrinsic nature, they should not be the object of conceptual proliferation; therefore, internal emptiness is without conceptual proliferation, and external emptiness, up to the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence, is likewise without conceptual proliferation.

“Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, they contemplate that suchness has no intrinsic nature; they contemplate that the dharma-realm, the dharma-nature, the non-erroneous nature, the unchanging nature, the nature of equality, the nature free from birth, the fixedness of dharma, the stability of dharma, the limit of reality, the realm of empty space, and the inconceivable realm have no intrinsic nature.”

If phenomena lack intrinsic nature, they should not be the subject of conceptual proliferation; therefore, suchness is free from conceptual proliferation, and so too are the dharma-realm and even the inconceivable realm.

"Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, they contemplate the four applications of mindfulness as being without intrinsic nature; they contemplate the four right endeavors, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path as being without intrinsic nature."

If phenomena lack intrinsic nature, they should not be the object of conceptual proliferation; therefore, the four foundations of mindfulness are free from conceptual proliferation, and the four right endeavors up to the eight branches of the noble path are likewise free from conceptual proliferation.

“Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, they contemplate the noble truth of suffering as being without intrinsic nature, and they contemplate the noble truths of origination, cessation, and the path as being without intrinsic nature.”

If a phenomenon lacks intrinsic nature, it should not be the object of conceptual proliferation; therefore, the Noble Truth of Suffering is free from conceptual proliferation, and the Noble Truths of Origination, Cessation, and the Path are likewise free from conceptual proliferation.

"Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, they contemplate the four dhyānas as being without intrinsic nature, and they contemplate the four immeasurables and the four formless absorptions as being without intrinsic nature."

If phenomena lack intrinsic nature, they should not be the object of conceptual proliferation; therefore, the four dhyānas are free from conceptual proliferation, and the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments are likewise free from conceptual proliferation.

“Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, they contemplate the eight liberations as being without intrinsic nature; they contemplate the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative attainments, and the ten totalities as being without intrinsic nature.”

If phenomena lack intrinsic nature, they should not be the object of conceptual proliferation; therefore, the eight liberations are free from conceptual proliferation, and the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities are likewise free from conceptual proliferation.

“Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, they contemplate all samādhi-gates as being without intrinsic nature, and they contemplate all dhāraṇī-gates as being without intrinsic nature.”

If phenomena lack intrinsic nature, they should not be the object of conceptual proliferation; therefore, all gateways of samādhi are free from conceptual proliferation, and all gateways of dhāraṇī are likewise free from conceptual proliferation.

“Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, they contemplate that the gate of liberation of emptiness lacks intrinsic nature, and they contemplate that the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness lack intrinsic nature.”

If phenomena lack intrinsic nature, they should not be the object of conceptual proliferation; therefore, the liberation door of emptiness is free from conceptual proliferation, and the liberation doors of signlessness and wishlessness are likewise free from conceptual proliferation.

“Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, they contemplate that the Ground of Extreme Joy has no intrinsic nature; they contemplate that the Ground of Purity, the Ground of Radiance, the Ground of Blazing Wisdom, the Ground of Utmost Difficulty to Conquer, the Ground of Presence, the Ground of Far-reaching Progress, the Ground of Immovability, the Ground of Excellent Intelligence, and the Ground of the Cloud of Dharma have no intrinsic nature.”

If phenomena lack intrinsic nature, they should not be the object of conceptual proliferation; therefore, the Ground of Utmost Joy is free from conceptual proliferation, and the Grounds from the Stainless up to the Cloud of Dharma are likewise free from conceptual proliferation.

“Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, they contemplate that the five eyes lack intrinsic nature, and they contemplate that the six supernormal powers lack intrinsic nature.”

If dharmas lack intrinsic nature, they should not be the object of conceptual proliferation; therefore, the five eyes are without conceptual proliferation, and the six supernormal powers are likewise without conceptual proliferation. "Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, they contemplate that the ten powers of a buddha lack intrinsic nature, and they contemplate that the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha lack intrinsic nature.

If phenomena lack intrinsic nature, they should not be the object of conceptual proliferation; therefore, the Buddha’s ten powers are free from conceptual proliferation, and his four fearlessnesses, four analytical knowledges, and eighteen unique qualities of a buddha are likewise free from conceptual proliferation.

“Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, they contemplate that great loving-kindness lacks intrinsic nature; they contemplate that great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity lack intrinsic nature.”

If phenomena lack intrinsic nature, they should not be the object of conceptual proliferation; therefore, great loving-kindness is free from conceptual proliferation, and great compassion, great joy, and great equanimity are likewise free from conceptual proliferation.

“Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, they contemplate that the quality of non-forgetfulness lacks intrinsic nature, and they contemplate that the state of constant equanimity lacks intrinsic nature.”

If phenomena lack intrinsic nature, they should not be the object of conceptual proliferation; therefore, the quality of non-forgetfulness is without conceptual proliferation, and the state of constant abiding in equanimity is likewise without conceptual proliferation.

“Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, they contemplate that all-knowledge (sarvajñatā) lacks intrinsic nature, and they contemplate that the knowledge of the paths (mārgākārajñatā) and the knowledge of all aspects (sarvākārajñatā) lack intrinsic nature.”

If phenomena lack intrinsic nature, they should not be the object of conceptual proliferation; therefore, omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) is without conceptual proliferation, and the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*) and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) are likewise without conceptual proliferation.

“Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, they contemplate that the fruit of stream-entry lacks intrinsic nature; they contemplate that the fruits of once-returning, non-returning, arhatship, and the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha lack intrinsic nature.”

If phenomena lack intrinsic nature, they should not be the object of conceptual proliferation; therefore, the fruit of stream-entry is without conceptual proliferation, and likewise the fruits of once-returning, non-returning, arhatship, and the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha are also without conceptual proliferation.

“Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, they contemplate that all the practices of bodhisattva mahāsattvas lack intrinsic nature; they contemplate that the perpetual severance of the continuity of all afflictions and habitual tendencies, as well as the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas, lack intrinsic nature.”

If phenomena lack intrinsic nature, they should not be the object of conceptual proliferation; therefore, all practices of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are free from conceptual proliferation, as they have forever severed the continuity of all afflictions and habitual tendencies, and even the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas is likewise free from conceptual proliferation.

“Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can practice this profound *prajñāpāramitā* free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*) in such a manner—realizing that all phenomena are without intrinsic nature and thus entirely free from conceptual proliferation—they shall enter the bodhisattva’s state of rightness and departure from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*).”
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If all dharmas are without intrinsic nature and are unattainable because they are free from conceptual proliferation, by means of what path does a bodhisattva mahāsattva enter the bodhisattva’s state of certainty beyond regression?”
Is it by means of the path of the śrāvaka?
Is it by means of the path of the pratyekabuddha?
Or is it by means of the path of the Buddha?
The Buddha said, “Subhūti!

A bodhisattva mahāsattva does not enter the bodhisattva’s state of certainty (samyaktva-niyāma) by means of the path of the śrāvaka, nor by means of the path of the pratyekabuddha, nor by means of the path of the buddha; rather, after first training extensively in all paths, the bodhisattva mahāsattva enters the bodhisattva’s state of certainty by means of the bodhisattva path.”

"Subhūti! Just as one who is an eighth-rank person first trains in all paths and subsequently employs their own path to enter the state of rightness and departure from birth, yet until they have given rise to the path of the fruit of no-more-learning, they have not yet realized the fruit of arhatship."

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this: having first studied all paths extensively, they enter the Bodhisattva’s state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*) by means of the Bodhisattva path; yet, until they have given rise to the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*), they are still unable to attain the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*).
"If one enters this meditative absorption, one can realize the knowledge of all modes through a single moment of associated sublime wisdom.
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

Blessed One, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva, desiring to fulfill all-aspect omniscience, first trains extensively in all paths and then enters the bodhisattva’s state of right determination through the bodhisattva path—Blessed One!

Is it not the case that the path of the eighth [stage] is distinct, the path of the fruit of stream-entry is distinct, the path of the candidate for the fruit of once-returning is distinct, the path of the fruit of once-returning is distinct, the path of the candidate for the fruit of non-returning is distinct, the path of the fruit of non-returning is distinct, the path of the candidate for arhatship is distinct, the path of the fruit of arhatship is distinct, the path of the pratyekabuddha is distinct, and the path of the Tathāgata is distinct?
“World-Honored One!

Since these various paths are each distinct, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who wish to fulfill all-aspect knowledge must first study all paths exhaustively before entering the bodhisattva’s state of right nature and transcendence of birth.”

When this bodhisattva-mahāsattva gives rise to the eighth path, he should become an eighth-rank practitioner; when he gives rise to the path of vision (*darśanamārga*), he should become a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*); when he gives rise to the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), he should become one heading toward the fruit of once-returning, or attain the fruit of once-returning, or become one heading toward the fruit of non-returning, or attain the fruit of non-returning, or become one heading toward arhatship; when he gives rise to the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*), he should attain the fruit of arhatship; and when he gives rise to the path of the solitary realizer (*pratyekabuddha*), he should attain the enlightenment of a solitary realizer.
“World-Honored One!

It is impossible for a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has become an eighth-rank [śrāvaka] to enter the bodhisattva’s state of certainty (samyaktva-niyāma); it is likewise impossible for one who does not enter the bodhisattva’s state of certainty to realize the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna).”
“World-Honored One!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva has already attained the fruit of a stream-enterer, or is a candidate for the fruit of a once-returner, or has attained the fruit of a once-returner, or is a candidate for the fruit of a non-returner, or has attained the fruit of a non-returner, or is a candidate for arhatship, or has attained the fruit of arhatship, or has attained the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, it is impossible that they could enter the bodhisattva’s state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*). It is likewise impossible that one who has not entered the bodhisattva’s state of right determination could realize the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*).”
“World-Honored One!

How may I truly understand how it is not contrary to principle that bodhisattva-mahāsattvas must first train thoroughly in all paths before entering the bodhisattva’s state of rightness and departure from birth?”
The Buddha said,
“So it is, Subhūti! It is just so.”
"So it is! It is just as you have said.

That a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having already become an eighth-rank practitioner, could enter the bodhisattva’s state of certainty (samyaktva-niyāma) is impossible. That one who has not entered the bodhisattva’s state of certainty could realize the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna) is likewise impossible."

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva has already attained the fruit of stream-entry, or the stage of a once-returner, or the fruit of a once-returner, or the stage of a non-returner, or the fruit of a non-returner, or the stage of an arhat, or the fruit of an arhat, or has already attained the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, yet is able to enter the bodhisattva’s state of rightness and departure from birth—this is impossible. Likewise, it is also impossible to realize the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna) without having entered the bodhisattva’s state of rightness and departure from birth.

Nevertheless, it is also not contrary to reason that all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas must first train exhaustively in all paths before entering the bodhisattva’s state of right determination and departure from birth.

This refers to how Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, from their first generation of the mind of awakening, practice with courageous and correct diligence the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, thereby surpassing the eight stages through their superior insight and vision.
What are the eight? They are:

the stage of pure observation, the stage of the spiritual lineage, the eighth stage, the stage of seeing, the stage of attenuation, the stage of freedom from desire, the stage of having completed what was to be done, and the stage of the solitary realizer.

Although this bodhisattva mahāsattva thoroughly trains in all eight stages thus described, they are able to transcend them by means of superior wisdom and vision, and enter the bodhisattva's state of rightness and departure from birth by means of the knowledge of the aspects of the path.

Having already entered the bodhisattva stage of the certainty of rightness (*samyaktvaniyāma*), one further employs the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) to eternally sever all continuities of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) and enter the stage of a Tathāgata; only then does one accomplish the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*).
“Subhūti! Whatever wisdom or abandonment a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices in the eighth stage is all the patience of that bodhisattva mahāsattva;

whatever wisdom or abandonment a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices in the stage of stream-enterer, as well as in the stages of once-returner, non-returner, arhat, and pratyekabuddha, is likewise the patience of that bodhisattva mahāsattva.”

“Subhūti! This bodhisattva mahāsattva, having fully studied all the paths of the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and others, and having attained perfection therein, enters the bodhisattva’s state of right determination through the knowledge of the aspects of the path.”

Once they have entered the bodhisattva stage of the certainty of correctness (*samyaktvaniyāma*), they further employ the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) to forever sever the continuity of all habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) and enter the stage of a Tathāgata; only then do they achieve the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*).
"So it is, Subhūti! Only after a bodhisattva mahāsattva has thoroughly trained in and perfected all paths will they realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
"Having realized unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, one benefits all classes of sentient beings through its fruit.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

Regarding all the characteristics of the paths as taught by the Buddha—whether the path of the śrāvakas, the path of the pratyekabuddhas, or the path of the Buddhas—how should bodhisattva-mahāsattvas give rise to the path-knowledge of the path within the Buddha-path?
The Buddha said,
“Subhūti! All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should give rise to the knowledge of all aspects of the pure path.”
“World-Honored One!
How should a bodhisattva mahāsattva give rise to the knowledge of all aspects of the pure path? “Subhūti!

If there are any modes of conduct, characteristics, or signs that can manifest and give rise to the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) of the pure path, then this bodhisattva mahāsattva fully awakens to all such modes of conduct, characteristics, and signs. Having fully awakened, he correctly expounds, reveals, designates, and establishes them for others, enabling sentient beings to attain non-erroneous understanding and to proceed accordingly toward their benefit and happiness.

“Subhūti! This bodhisattva mahāsattva should attain skillfulness in all sounds and languages. Using this skillful mastery of sound and language, they should proclaim the true Dharma for all sentient beings throughout the trichiliocosm, causing them to understand that what is heard is like an echo—though there is comprehension, there is no attachment.”
“Subhūti! By means of these causes and conditions, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should train to bring the knowledge of the aspects of all paths to perfection.

Having trained to bring the knowledge of the aspects of all paths to perfection, they should, in accordance with reality, know the various differences in the latent tendencies and inclinations of all sentient beings.”

One should know, as it truly is, that sentient beings in the hells have the hellish path and the causes and conditions for the hells; having known this, one should employ skillful means to obstruct that path and those causes and conditions.

One should know, as it truly is, that sentient beings among the animals have the animal path and the causes and conditions for the animal realm; having known this, one should employ skillful means to obstruct that path and those causes and conditions.

One should know, as it truly is, that sentient beings in the realm of hungry ghosts have the path of hungry ghosts and the causes and conditions for the realm of hungry ghosts; having known this, one should employ skillful means to obstruct that path and those causes and conditions.

One should know, as it truly is, that for the nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, kiṃnaras, gandharvas, garuḍas, kumbhāṇḍas, mahoragas, vidyādharas, and so forth, each has its own path and its own causes and effects; having known this, one should employ skillful means to obstruct those paths and those causes and effects.

One should know, as it truly is, the causes and effects of the human realm; and one should know, as it truly is, [the realms of] the Cāturmahārājika devas, the Trāyastriṃśa devas, the Yāma devas, the Tuṣita devas, the Nirmāṇarati devas, and the Paranirmitavaśavartin devas.
One should know, as they truly are, the causes and effects of the various paths of the Īśvara devas;
one should know, as they truly are, the causes and effects of the various paths of the Brahmakāyika, Brahmapurohita, Brahmakāyika-parṣadya, and Mahābrahmā devas;
one should know, as they truly are, the causes and effects of the various paths of the Ābhāsvara, Parīttābhā, Apramāṇābhā, and Ābhāsvarābha devas. One should know, as they truly are...
One should know, as they truly are, the causes and effects of the paths of the Śubhakṛtsna, Parīttaśubha, Apramāṇaśubha, and Śubhakṛtsna heavens;
one should know, as they truly are, the causes and effects of the paths of the Vṛhatphala, Parīttabṛhatphala, Apramāṇabṛhatphala, and Bṛhatphala heavens;
