When I was originally practicing the conduct of a bodhisattva, having realized that all supernormal powers have non-existence as their intrinsic nature, I was able to cause the mind to give rise to the supernormal power of the realization of knowledge regarding the bases of psychic power, and likewise caused the mind to give rise to the supernormal powers of the realization of knowledge regarding the divine ear, the minds of others, the recollection of past lives, and the divine eye; thus I attained mastery and unimpededness regarding all objective spheres.

“Subhūti! If the unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment of a Buddha possessed even the slightest intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) or extrinsic nature (*parabhāva*) as its essence, then when I was formerly practicing the bodhisattva path, I would not have attained the realization that the unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment of all Buddhas has non-existence as its essence, and thus realized unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. This is because the unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment of a Buddha possesses neither intrinsic nor extrinsic nature, but has only non-existence as its essence.”

When I originally practiced the conduct of a bodhisattva and attained mastery over unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, I did so by realizing that all things have non-existence as their intrinsic nature. Having thus realized unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment through the sublime wisdom corresponding to a single thought-moment, I perceived, in accordance with reality, that the noble truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path are entirely non-existent. I thereby accomplished the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great joy, great equanimity, the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha, and other boundless merits.

"Subhūti! If sentient beings possessed even a slight intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) or a nature derived from another (*parabhāva*), then after I had attained Buddhahood, I would not have realized that all sentient beings have the absence of nature as their intrinsic nature, nor would I have established the distinctions between the three categories of sentient beings. This is because sentient beings possess neither an intrinsic nature nor a nature derived from another; they have only the absence of nature as their intrinsic nature."

Once I have attained Buddhahood and realized that all sentient beings have the absence of intrinsic nature as their very essence, I shall be able to establish the distinctions among the three categories of sentient beings and provide them with appropriate skillful means and instruction, enabling them to attain supreme benefit and peace.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, relying on dharmas whose intrinsic nature is non-existence (*abhāvasvabhāva*), gives rise to the four dhyānas, manifests the five supernormal powers, realizes unexcelled perfect enlightenment, and establishes the distinctions among the three groups of sentient beings—teaching and instructing them through appropriate skillful means so that they may attain extraordinary benefit and happiness—how can it be that within these dharmas whose intrinsic nature is non-existence, there is gradual karma, gradual training, and gradual practice; and by virtue of this gradual karma, gradual training, and gradual practice, how does one realize unexcelled perfect enlightenment?”
The Buddha said, “Suvikrāntavikrāmin!

Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas first hear this from the Buddha, the World-Honored One; or they hear it from bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have already made extensive offerings to many Buddhas; or they hear it from pratyekabuddhas; or they hear it from arhats; or they hear it from non-returners, once-returners, and stream-enterers.”

"The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, take non-existence as their intrinsic nature; because they have ultimately realized the dharma that takes non-existence as its intrinsic nature, they are called Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones.

The Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas likewise take non-existence as their intrinsic nature; because they have gradually realized the dharma that takes non-existence as its intrinsic nature, they are called Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas."

All Pratyekabuddhas likewise take non-existence as their intrinsic nature; because they gradually realize the dharmas that take non-existence as their intrinsic nature, they are called Pratyekabuddhas.
All Arhats likewise take non-existence as their intrinsic nature; because they gradually realize the dharmas that take non-existence as their intrinsic nature, they are called Arhats.

All non-returners, once-returners, and stream-enterers likewise have non-existence as their intrinsic nature; because they realize the dharmas that have non-existence as their intrinsic nature through gradual stages, they are called non-returners, once-returners, and stream-enterers.

Worthy and virtuous persons likewise take the absence of intrinsic nature as their own nature; because they possess resolute faith and understanding that all phenomena have the absence of intrinsic nature as their nature, they are called "worthy and virtuous persons.

All other sentient beings, all conditioned formations, and all phenomena likewise have the absence of intrinsic nature as their nature; there is not even anything the size of a hair-tip—whether a formation or a phenomenon—that can be found to possess a truly existent intrinsic nature.
When this bodhisattva mahāsattva has heard this matter, he reflects thus:

"If all sentient beings, all conditioned phenomena, and all dharmas have 'absence of intrinsic nature' as their intrinsic nature, and it is because they have realized and attained the understanding that dharmas have 'absence of intrinsic nature' as their intrinsic nature that they are called Buddhas, bodhisattvas, pratyekabuddhas, śrāvakas, and noble persons; then whether I shall realize or not realize unsurpassed perfect enlightenment, since all sentient beings, all conditioned phenomena, and all dharmas always have 'absence of intrinsic nature' as their intrinsic nature, I must certainly set out for unsurpassed perfect enlightenment. Once I have attained enlightenment, if there are sentient beings whose conduct is characterized by conceptualization, I shall use skillful means to establish them so that they abide in non-conceptualization."

"Subhūti! Having reflected thus, that bodhisattva mahāsattva sets out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; for the sake of universally rescuing and delivering all sentient beings, they perform gradual deeds, cultivate gradual training, and practice gradual conduct."

Just as the bodhisattva mahāsattvas of the past set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by first practicing the gradual sequence of karma, training, and conduct, thereby realizing unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, so too this bodhisattva mahāsattva should likewise first practice the perfection of generosity, next practice the perfection of ethical discipline, next practice the perfection of patience, next practice the perfection of diligence, next practice the perfection of meditative concentration, and finally practice the perfection of wisdom.

“Subhūti! When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of generosity from the first generation of the mind of awakening, they should personally practice the perfection of generosity, encourage others to practice the perfection of generosity, proclaim and reveal the merits of the perfection of generosity, and joyfully praise those who practice the perfection of generosity.”

By these causes and conditions, their generosity becomes perfected; they are born among gods and humans and attain great wealth and status. Constantly practicing giving, they remain free from the mind of stinginess. Following the needs of sentient beings, they give food to those who need food, drink to those who need drink, clothing to those who need clothing, vehicles to those who need vehicles, incense and flowers to those who need incense and flowers, necklaces to those who need necklaces, houses to those who need houses, bedding to those who need bedding, lamps to those who need lamps, wealth and treasures to those who need wealth and treasures, and servants to those who need servants. Whatever various requisites others may require, they give them all.

By means of giving, this bodhisattva-mahāsattva upholds the aggregate of ethical discipline (*śīlaskandha*) and attains great nobility among gods and humans; by means of giving and ethical discipline, they further attain the aggregate of meditative concentration (*samādhiskandha*); by means of giving, ethical discipline, and meditative concentration, they further attain the aggregate of wisdom (*prajñāskandha*); by means of giving, ethical discipline, meditative concentration, and wisdom, they further attain the aggregate of liberation (*vimuktiskandha*); and by means of giving, ethical discipline, meditative concentration, wisdom, and liberation, they further attain the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation (*vimuktijñānadarśanaskandha*). Through the perfection of these aggregates of giving, ethical discipline, meditative concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation, they transcend the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas and enter the bodhisattva’s state of rightness and departure from birth (*samyaktvaniyāmāvakrānti*).
Having entered the stage of the bodhisattva’s state of rightness and departure from birth, they are then able to purify buddha-fields and bring sentient beings to maturity.
Having perfected the purification of buddha-fields and the maturation of sentient beings, one is able to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment;

having realized unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, one is able to turn the wheel of the true Dharma; by turning the wheel of the true Dharma, one establishes sentient beings in the three vehicles of the Dharma;
once sentient beings are established in the three vehicles of the Dharma, they are liberated from birth and death and realize nirvana.

"Subhūti! Because of their practice of giving, although these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are thus able to perform gradual deeds, cultivate gradual training, and carry out gradual practices, they observe that all things are ultimately unapprehendable."
Why is this? Because all phenomena lack intrinsic nature. Furthermore, Subhūti!

When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of ethical discipline from the first moment of generating the mind of awakening, they should personally practice the perfection of ethical discipline, encourage others to practice the perfection of ethical discipline, proclaim and demonstrate the merits of the perfection of ethical discipline, and joyfully praise those who practice the perfection of ethical discipline.

By virtue of these causes and conditions, this bodhisattva mahāsattva’s aggregate of ethical discipline (*śīlaskandha*) becomes pure; being born among gods and humans, they attain great nobility. Having bestowed various kinds of wealth and goods upon the poor, they abide in the aggregate of ethical discipline, the aggregate of concentration (*samādhiskandha*), the aggregate of wisdom (*prajñāskandha*), the aggregate of liberation (*vimuktiskandha*), and the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation (*vimuktijñānadarśanaskandha*).

By virtue of the purification of the aggregates of ethical discipline, meditative concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation, one transcends the levels of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas and enters the bodhisattva’s state of rightness and departure from birth;
having entered the stage of the bodhisattva’s state of rightness and departure from birth, one is then able to purify buddha-fields and mature sentient beings;
once the purification of buddha-fields and the maturation of sentient beings are perfected, one is then able to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Having realized unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, one is then able to turn the wheel of the true Dharma;
by turning the wheel of the true Dharma, one establishes sentient beings in the three vehicles of the Dharma;
once sentient beings are established in the three vehicles of the Dharma, they are liberated from birth and death and realize nirvāṇa.

"Subhūti! Because of their pure ethical discipline, although these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are able to perform gradual deeds, cultivate gradual training, and practice gradual conduct in this way, they observe that all things are ultimately unapprehendable."
Why is this? Because all phenomena lack intrinsic nature. Furthermore, Subhūti!

When these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of patience from the time they first resolve their minds toward awakening, they should personally practice the perfection of patience, encourage others to practice the perfection of patience, proclaim and display the merits of the perfection of patience, and joyfully praise those who practice the perfection of patience.
When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices patience, he is able to satisfy all sentient beings by giving them material wealth;

having practiced generosity, he dwells in the aggregate of ethical discipline, dwells in patience, and dwells in the aggregates of concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation.

By virtue of the purification of the aggregates of ethical discipline, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation, one transcends the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas and enters the bodhisattva’s state of rightness and departure from corruption;
having entered the stage of the bodhisattva’s state of rightness and departure from corruption, one is then able to purify buddha-fields and mature sentient beings;
once the purification of buddha-fields and the maturation of sentient beings are perfected, one is then able to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Having realized unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, one is then able to turn the wheel of the true Dharma;
by turning the wheel of the true Dharma, one establishes sentient beings in the three vehicles of the Dharma;
once sentient beings are established in the three vehicles of the Dharma, they are liberated from birth and death and realize nirvāṇa.

"Subhūti! Because of their patience, although these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are able to perform gradual deeds, cultivate gradual training, and practice gradual conduct in this manner, they observe that all things are ultimately unapprehendable."
Why is this? Because all phenomena lack intrinsic nature. Furthermore, Subhūti!

When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of diligence from the first moment of generating the mind of awakening, they should personally exert diligent effort toward all wholesome dharmas; they should also encourage others to exert diligent effort toward all wholesome dharmas; they should praise and proclaim the merits of exerting diligent effort toward all wholesome dharmas; and they should rejoice in and laud those who exert diligent effort toward all wholesome dharmas.
When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices diligence, he is able to satisfy all sentient beings by bestowing material wealth upon them;

having practiced giving, he dwells securely in the aggregate of ethical discipline, dwells securely in patience, dwells securely in diligence, and dwells securely in the aggregates of concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation.

By virtue of the purification of the aggregates of ethical discipline, meditative concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation, one transcends the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas and enters the bodhisattva’s state of correct determination free from outflows (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
Having entered this stage of the bodhisattva’s correct determination free from outflows, one is then able to purify buddha-fields and bring sentient beings to maturity.
Once the purification of buddha-fields and the maturation of sentient beings are perfected, one is then able to realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
Having realized unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, one is then able to turn the wheel of the true Dharma;
by turning the wheel of the true Dharma, one establishes sentient beings in the three vehicles of the Dharma;
once sentient beings are established in the three vehicles of the Dharma, they are liberated from birth and death and realize nirvana.

"Subhūti! By virtue of this diligence, although these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are able to perform gradual deeds, cultivate gradual training, and practice gradual conduct in this manner, they observe that all things are ultimately unapprehendable."
Why is this? Because all phenomena lack intrinsic nature. Furthermore, Subhūti!

When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of dhyāna from the first production of the thought of enlightenment, they should personally enter the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments; they should also encourage others to enter the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments; they should proclaim and demonstrate the merits of entering the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments; and they should rejoice in and praise those who enter the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments.

This bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling securely in the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments, is able to bestow material wealth upon all sentient beings so that they are fully satisfied;

having practiced giving, they dwell securely in the aggregate of ethical discipline, dwell securely in patience, dwell securely in diligence, and dwell securely in the aggregates of concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation.

Because of the purification of the aggregates of ethical discipline, meditative concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation, one transcends the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas and enters the bodhisattva’s state of rightness and departure from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
Having entered the stage of the bodhisattva’s state of rightness and departure from birth, one is then able to purify buddha-fields and bring sentient beings to maturity.
Once the purification of buddha-fields and the maturation of sentient beings are perfected, one is then able to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
Having realized unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, one is then able to turn the wheel of the true Dharma;
by turning the wheel of the true Dharma, one establishes sentient beings in the three vehicles of the Dharma;
once sentient beings are established in the three vehicles of the Dharma, they are liberated from birth and death and realize nirvāṇa.

“Subhūti! Because of their meditative concentration, although these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are able to perform gradual deeds, cultivate gradual training, and practice gradual conduct in this way, they observe that all things are ultimately unapprehendable.”
Why is this? Because all phenomena lack intrinsic nature. Furthermore, Subhūti!
When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom from the first moment of generating the mind of awakening,
they bestow various material goods upon all sentient beings; they abide in the aggregate of ethical discipline,
abide in patience, abide in diligence, and abide in the aggregates of concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation.
The aggregates: one personally practices the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom,
and also encourages others to practice generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence,
meditative concentration, and wisdom, praising and elucidating generosity, ethical discipline, and so forth.
They praise with joy the merits of the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom,
as well as those who practice generosity, pure ethical discipline, patience, diligence,
meditative concentration, and wisdom.

By the power of skillful means in the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, this bodhisattva mahāsattva transcends the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas and enters the bodhisattva’s state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
Having entered the stage of the bodhisattva’s state of right determination, they are then able to purify buddha-fields and bring sentient beings to maturity.
Once the purification of buddha-fields and the maturation of sentient beings are perfected, they are then able to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Having realized unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, one is then able to turn the wheel of the true Dharma;
by turning the wheel of the true Dharma, one establishes sentient beings in the three vehicles of the Dharma;
once sentient beings are established in the three vehicles of the Dharma, they are liberated from birth and death and realize nirvana.

"Subhūti! Because of this prajñā, although these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are thus able to perform gradual deeds, cultivate gradual training, and practice gradual conduct, they observe that all things are utterly unapprehendable."
Why is this? Because all phenomena lack intrinsic nature, Subhūti!
This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, relying on the practice of the six perfections, performs gradual karma, cultivates gradual training, and carries out gradual conduct.

"Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva performs gradual deeds, cultivates gradual training, and practices gradual conduct, they should— starting from the first production of the thought of enlightenment and with a mental orientation associated with the knowledge of all modes— first cultivate the recollection of the Buddha, next the recollection of the Dharma, next the recollection of the Saṅgha, next the recollection of ethical discipline, next the recollection of relinquishment, and finally the recollection of the devas, while resolving that all phenomena have non-existence as their intrinsic nature."
“Subhūti! How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice the recollection of the Buddha? Subhūti!”

When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they should not contemplate the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha by means of form; they should not contemplate the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha by means of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
Why is this? Subhūti!
Form has no intrinsic nature; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness have no intrinsic nature.
If a phenomenon lacks intrinsic nature, it does not exist; if it does not exist, it cannot be recollected.
Why is that? Subhūti!
If there is no mindfulness and no mental engagement, this is the recollection of the Buddha.

"Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not engage in mental engagement with the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, by way of the thirty-two marks of a great man; nor should they engage in mental engagement with the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, by way of a body of golden color; nor should they engage in mental engagement with the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, by way of a body that has a constant radiance extending one fathom in every direction; nor should they engage in mental engagement with the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, by way of the eighty minor marks."
Why is this? Subhūti!

Such a body of marks and signs, with its golden hue, is entirely devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). If a phenomenon lacks intrinsic nature, it is non-existent; if it is non-existent, it cannot be recollected.
Why is that? Subhūti! If there is no recollection and no mental engagement, this is the recollection of the Buddha.

"Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not contemplate the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha by means of the aggregate of ethical discipline; nor should they contemplate the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha by means of the aggregate of meditative concentration, the aggregate of wisdom, the aggregate of liberation, or the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation."
Why is this? Subhūti!
These aggregates are all devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). If a phenomenon lacks intrinsic nature, it does not exist; if it does not exist, it cannot be brought to mind.
Why is this so? Subhūti!
If there is no recollection and no mental engagement, this is the recollection of the Buddha.

"Furthermore, Subhūti! A bodhisattva mahāsattva should not contemplate the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha by means of the five eyes or the six supernormal powers; they should not contemplate the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha by means of the ten powers of a Buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, or the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; they should not contemplate the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha by means of great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, or great equanimity; they should not contemplate the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha by means of the quality of non-forgetfulness or the nature of constant dwelling in equanimity; and they should not contemplate the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha by means of all-knowledge, the knowledge of the paths, or the knowledge of all aspects."
Why is this? Subhūti!
All these phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature; if a phenomenon lacks intrinsic nature, it is non-existent, and if it is non-existent, it cannot be recollected.
Why is this so? Subhūti!
If there is no recollection and no mental engagement, this is the recollection of the Buddha.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva should not contemplate the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha by means of the phenomena of dependent origination."
Why is this? Subhūti!
The phenomena of dependent origination have no intrinsic nature at all. If a phenomenon has no intrinsic nature, it does not exist; if it does not exist, it cannot be recollected.
Why is this so? Subhūti!
If there is no mindfulness and no mental engagement, this is the recollection of the Buddha.

"Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they should cultivate the recollection of the Buddha in this manner. If they cultivate the recollection of the Buddha in this manner, this constitutes the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s gradual karma, the cultivation of gradual training, and the practice of gradual conduct."

“Subhūti! When this bodhisattva mahāsattva thus performs gradual deeds, cultivates gradual training, and practices gradual conduct, he is then able to fulfill the four foundations of mindfulness; he is also able to fulfill the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path;
he is then able to fulfill the gate of liberation of emptiness, and is also able to fulfill the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness.”
Then one is able to fulfill the first dhyāna, and is also able to fulfill the second, third, and fourth dhyānas;

one is able to fulfill the immeasurable state of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), and is also able to fulfill the immeasurable states of compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*);

one is able to fulfill the concentration of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana-samādhi*), and is also able to fulfill the concentrations of the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*), the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
Then one will be able to fulfill the eight liberations, as well as the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative attainments, and the ten universal bases;
one will be able to fulfill all doors of samādhi, as well as all doors of dhāraṇī;
and one will be able to fulfill the perfection of generosity, as well as the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom.

Then one will be able to fulfill internal emptiness, and also fulfill external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, non-alteration emptiness, essential nature emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common characteristic emptiness, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of non-apprehensibility, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature;

then one will be able to fulfill true thusness, and also fulfill the dharma-realm, the dharma-nature, non-falsity, non-alteration, equality, the state beyond birth, the fixed nature of dharmas, the stability of dharmas, the limit of reality, the realm of space, and the inconceivable realm.
Then one will be able to fulfill the five eyes and also fulfill the six supernormal powers;
then one will be able to fulfill the ten powers of a Buddha, as well as the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
then one will be able to fulfill great loving-kindness, as well as fulfill great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity.
Thus, one can fulfill the quality of non-forgetfulness and also fulfill the state of constant equanimity;

one can fulfill all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), as well as fulfill the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*) and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), thereby realizing the knowledge of all modes of knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*).

"Subhūti! By means of the power of skillful means that takes non-existence as its own nature, this bodhisattva mahāsattva awakens to the fact that all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature; therein, there is neither perception nor even non-perception."
"Subhūti! A bodhisattva mahāsattva should cultivate the recollection of the Buddha in this way: therein, there is not even the slightest thought, let alone the recollection of the Buddha!"

The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle Three Hundred and Seventy-Two. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. First Division: Chapter Sixty-Five, Part Two, "The Three Gradual Stages. "Subhūti!
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice the recollection of the dharma? Subhūti!

When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they should not contemplate wholesome dharmas, they should not contemplate unwholesome dharmas, and they should not contemplate indeterminate dharmas.
One should not contemplate worldly dharmas, nor should one contemplate supramundane dharmas;
one should not contemplate dharmas associated with craving and attachment, nor should one contemplate dharmas free from craving and attachment;
one should not contemplate dharmas involving contention, nor should one contemplate dharmas free from contention.
One should not contemplate noble dharmas, nor should one contemplate non-noble dharmas;
one should not contemplate tainted dharmas, nor should one contemplate untainted dharmas;
one should not contemplate dharmas bound to the desire realm, nor should one contemplate dharmas bound to the form realm, nor should one contemplate dharmas bound to the formless realm.
One should not contemplate dharmas that fall away, nor should one contemplate dharmas that do not fall away;
one should not contemplate conditioned dharmas, nor should one contemplate unconditioned dharmas.
Why is this? Subhūti!
All these dharmas are devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). If a dharma lacks intrinsic nature, it is non-existent; if it is non-existent, it cannot be recollected.
Why is this so? Subhūti!
If there is no recollection and no mental engagement, this is the mindfulness of phenomena (dharmānusmṛti).

"Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they should practice the recollection of the Dharma in this way. If they practice the recollection of the Dharma in this way, this constitutes the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s gradual karma, the cultivation of gradual training, and the performance of gradual conduct."

"Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva thus performs gradual deeds, cultivates gradual training, and practices gradual conduct, they are then able to fulfill the four foundations of mindfulness; they are also able to fulfill the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path;
they are then able to fulfill the liberation door of emptiness, and they are also able to fulfill the liberation doors of signlessness and wishlessness."
Then one can fulfill the four dhyānas, and also fulfill the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments;
then one can fulfill the eight liberations, and also fulfill the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities;
then one can fulfill all doors of samādhi, and also fulfill all doors of dhāraṇī.
Then one will be able to fulfill the perfection of generosity, and also fulfill the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom;

then one will be able to fulfill internal emptiness, and also fulfill external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersion emptiness, non-alteration emptiness, essential nature emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common characteristic emptiness, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence.

Then one can fulfill true suchness (*tathatā*), and also fulfill the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), non-falsity, immutability, equality, the state beyond birth, the fixed nature of phenomena (*dharmaniyāmatā*), the stability of phenomena (*dharmaniyāmatā*), the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), the realm of space (*ākāśadhātu*), and the inconceivable realm;
then one can fulfill the five eyes, and also fulfill the six supernormal powers (*abhijñā*);

then one can fulfill the ten powers of a Buddha (*buddhabala*), and also fulfill the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇikabuddhadharma*).
Thus, one can fulfill great loving-kindness, and likewise fulfill great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity;
one can fulfill the quality of non-forgetfulness, and likewise fulfill the state of constant abiding in equanimity;
one can fulfill all-knowledge, and likewise fulfill the knowledge of the paths and the knowledge of all aspects, thereby realizing the knowledge of all modes of knowledge.

“Subhūti! By means of the skillful power of taking non-existence as their intrinsic nature, these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas realize that all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature; therein, there is neither perception nor even the absence of perception.”

"Subhūti! A bodhisattva mahāsattva should practice the recollection of the Dharma in this way: that within it there is not even the slightest recollection, much less the recollection of dharmas! Subhūti!"
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva cultivate the recollection of the Saṃgha? Subhūti!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they should form this thought:

“The assembly of the Buddha’s disciples—possessing the aggregate of pure ethical discipline, the aggregate of concentration, the aggregate of wisdom, the aggregate of liberation, and the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation; the four pairs and eight classes of individuals—all these are manifested through the absence of intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāva), and all take the absence of intrinsic nature as their own essence. For this reason, they should not be conceptualized.”
Why is this? Subhūti!
The assembly of the Buddha’s disciples is entirely without intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). If a phenomenon lacks intrinsic nature, it does not exist; if it does not exist, it cannot be recollected.
Why is that? Subhūti! If there is no recollection and no mental engagement, this is the recollection of the Saṃgha.

"Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they should cultivate the recollection of the Saṃgha in this way. If they cultivate the recollection of the Saṃgha in this manner, this constitutes the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s gradual karma, the cultivation of gradual training, and the practice of gradual conduct."

“Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva thus performs gradual deeds, cultivates gradual training, and practices gradual conduct, they are then able to fulfill the four foundations of mindfulness; they are also able to fulfill the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of awakening, and the eightfold noble path;
they are then able to fulfill the liberation door of emptiness, and they are also able to fulfill the liberation doors of signlessness and wishlessness.”
Then one can fulfill the four dhyānas, as well as fulfill the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments;
then one can fulfill the eight liberations, as well as fulfill the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities;
then one can fulfill all doors of samādhi, as well as fulfill all doors of dhāraṇī.
Then one will be able to fulfill the perfection of generosity, and also fulfill the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom;

one will be able to fulfill internal emptiness, and also fulfill external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, endless emptiness, dispersal emptiness, non-alteration emptiness, essential nature emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common characteristic emptiness, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature.

Then one can fulfill true thusness (*tathatā*), and also fulfill the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), non-illusoriness, immutability, equality, the state beyond birth, the fixed nature of phenomena (*dharmaniyāmatā*), the stability of phenomena (*dharmasthititā*), the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), the realm of empty space (*ākāśadhātu*), and the inconceivable realm;
then one can fulfill the five eyes, and also fulfill the six supernormal powers (*abhijñā*);

then one can fulfill the ten powers of a Buddha (*buddhabala*), and also fulfill the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇikabuddhadharma*).
Then one will be able to fulfill great loving-kindness, and likewise fulfill great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity;
one will be able to fulfill the quality of non-forgetfulness, and likewise fulfill the state of constant abiding in equanimity;

one will be able to fulfill all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), and likewise fulfill the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*) and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), thereby realizing the knowledge of all modes of knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*).

“Subhūti! By means of the skillful power of taking non-existence as their intrinsic nature, these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas realize that all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature; therein, there is neither perception nor even non-perception.”

"Subhūti! A bodhisattva mahāsattva should cultivate the recollection of the Saṅgha in this way: therein, there is not even the slightest recollection, let alone a recollection of the Saṅgha! Subhūti!"
What is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s cultivation of the recollection of ethical discipline (*śīlānusmṛti*)? Subhūti!

When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), from the first generation of the mind of awakening until sitting upon the seat of sublime enlightenment, they constantly abide in pure ethical discipline—without defect, without breach, without flaw, and without impurity; free from attachment, worthy of offerings, praised by the wise, well-undertaken, and perfectly consummated. Contemplating this ethical discipline as having non-existence as its intrinsic nature in accordance with supreme meditative concentration, for this reason, one should not engage in conceptualization.
Why is this? Subhūti!
Such pure ethical discipline has no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). If a phenomenon lacks intrinsic nature, it does not exist; if it does not exist, it cannot be brought to mind.
Why is that? Subhūti! If there is no recollection and no mental engagement, this is the recollection of ethical discipline.

"Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they should cultivate the recollection of ethical discipline in this way. If they cultivate the recollection of ethical discipline in this way, this constitutes the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s gradual activity, the cultivation of gradual training, and the practice of gradual conduct."

“Subhūti! When this bodhisattva mahāsattva thus performs gradual deeds, cultivates gradual training, and practices gradual conduct, he is then able to fulfill the four foundations of mindfulness; he is also able to fulfill the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of awakening, and the eightfold noble path;
he is then able to fulfill the liberation door of emptiness, and is also able to fulfill the liberation doors of signlessness and wishlessness.”
Then one will be able to fulfill the four dhyānas, and also fulfill the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments;
then one will be able to fulfill the eight liberations, and also fulfill the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities;
then one will be able to fulfill all doors of samādhi, and also fulfill all doors of dhāraṇī.
Then one will be able to fulfill the perfection of generosity, and also fulfill the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom;

then one will be able to fulfill internal emptiness, and also fulfill external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, non-alteration emptiness, essential nature emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common characteristic emptiness, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature.

Then one will be able to fulfill true thusness (*tathatā*), and also fulfill the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), non-falsity, immutability, equality, the state beyond birth, the fixed nature of phenomena (*dharmaniyāmatā*), the stability of phenomena (*dharmaniyāmatā*), the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), the realm of empty space (*ākāśadhātu*), and the inconceivable realm;
then one will be able to fulfill the five eyes, and also fulfill the six supernormal powers (*abhijñā*);

then one will be able to fulfill the ten powers of a Buddha, and also fulfill the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇikabuddhadharma*).
Then one will be able to fulfill great loving-kindness, and likewise fulfill great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity;
one will be able to fulfill the quality of non-forgetfulness, and likewise fulfill the state of constant abiding in equanimity;

one will be able to fulfill all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), and likewise fulfill the knowledge of the paths (*mārgākārajñatā*) and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), thereby realizing the knowledge of all modes of knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*).

“Subhūti! By means of the power of skillful means that takes non-existence as its intrinsic nature, this bodhisattva mahāsattva realizes that all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature; therein, there is neither perception nor even the absence of perception.”

"Subhūti! A bodhisattva mahāsattva should cultivate the recollection of ethical discipline (*śīlānusmṛti*) in this way: that within it there is not even the slightest recollection, let alone the recollection of ethical discipline! Subhūti!"
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva cultivate the recollection of equanimity? Subhūti!

When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, by means of the skillful power of taking non-existence as their intrinsic nature, they cultivate the recollection of equanimity; whether giving material wealth or giving the Dharma, they give rise to no thought whatsoever.

"I give; I do not give. I relinquish; I do not relinquish. Even if one were to relinquish all the limbs and members of one's body, one would still not give rise to the thought: "I give; I do not give. I relinquish; I do not relinquish."
"Nor does he contemplate that which is relinquished, that which is given, or the merit of the act of giving.
Why is this? Subhūti!"
Thus, all these phenomena lack intrinsic nature; if a phenomenon lacks intrinsic nature, it is non-existent, and if it is non-existent, it cannot be recollected. Why is this so?
"Subhūti! If there is no recollection and no mental engagement, this is the recollection of relinquishment. Subhūti!"

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they should practice the recollection of equanimity in this way; if they practice the recollection of equanimity in this way, this constitutes the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s gradual activity, the cultivation of gradual training, and the performance of gradual conduct.

“Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva thus performs gradual deeds, cultivates gradual training, and practices gradual conduct, they are then able to fulfill the four foundations of mindfulness; they are also able to fulfill the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of awakening, and the eightfold noble path;
they are then able to fulfill the gate of liberation of emptiness, and are also able to fulfill the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness.”
Then one can fulfill the four dhyānas, and also fulfill the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments;
then one can fulfill the eight liberations, and also fulfill the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities;
then one can fulfill all doors of samādhi, and also fulfill all doors of dhāraṇī.
Then one will be able to fulfill the perfection of generosity, and likewise fulfill the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom;

one will be able to fulfill internal emptiness, and likewise fulfill external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, the emptiness of the ultimate, the emptiness of conditioned phenomena, the emptiness of unconditioned phenomena, absolute emptiness, the emptiness of the limitless, the emptiness of dispersion, the emptiness of non-alteration, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, the emptiness of self-characteristic, the emptiness of common characteristic, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature.

Then one will be able to fulfill true thusness (*tathatā*), and also fulfill the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), non-falsity, immutability, equality, the state beyond birth, the fixed nature of phenomena (*dharmaniyāmatā*), the stability of phenomena (*dharmasthititā*), the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), the realm of empty space (*ākāśadhātu*), and the inconceivable realm;
then one will be able to fulfill the five eyes, and also fulfill the six supernormal powers (*abhijñā*);

then one will be able to fulfill the ten powers of a Buddha, and also fulfill the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇikabuddhadharma*).
Then one can fulfill great loving-kindness, and likewise fulfill great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity;
one can fulfill the quality of non-forgetfulness, and likewise fulfill the nature of constant abiding in equanimity;

one can fulfill all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), and likewise fulfill the knowledge of the paths (*mārgākārajñatā*) and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), thereby realizing the knowledge of all modes of knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*).

“Subhūti! By means of the skillful power of taking non-existence as their intrinsic nature, these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas realize that all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature; therein, there is neither perception nor even the absence of perception.”
"Subhūti! A bodhisattva mahāsattva should cultivate the recollection of equanimity in this way: therein there is not even the slightest thought, much less the thought of 'equanimity'! Subhūti!"
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva cultivate the recollection of the devas? Subhūti!
When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they cultivate the recollection of the devas through the skillful means of taking non-existence as their intrinsic nature.

When observing those who have attained the stage of stream-entry and so forth, although they may be born among the Gods of the Four Great Kings, or the Heaven of the Thirty-three, or the Yāma Heaven, or the Tuṣita Heaven, or the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations, or the Heaven of Mastery over Others' Emanations, these are unapprehendable and should not be conceptualized.
When observing non-returners and others, although they may be born among the gods of the form realm or the formless realm, they cannot be apprehended and should not be conceptualized. Why is this?
"Subhūti! Thus all these devas are devoid of intrinsic nature. If a dharma lacks intrinsic nature, it does not exist; if it does not exist, it cannot be recollected."
Why is that? Subhūti!
That which is without recollection and without mental engagement is the recollection of the devas.

"Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they should practice the recollection of the devas in this way. If they practice the recollection of the devas in this way, this constitutes the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s gradual karma, the cultivation of gradual training, and the performance of gradual conduct."

“Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva thus performs gradual deeds, cultivates gradual training, and practices gradual conduct, they are then able to fulfill the four foundations of mindfulness; they are also able to fulfill the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path;
they are then able to fulfill the gate of liberation of emptiness, and they are also able to fulfill the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness.”
Then one can fulfill the four dhyānas, and also fulfill the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments;
then one can fulfill the eight liberations, and also fulfill the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities;
then one can fulfill all doors of samādhi, and also fulfill all doors of dhāraṇī.
Then one will be able to fulfill the perfection of generosity, and also fulfill the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom;

one will be able to fulfill inner emptiness, and also fulfill outer emptiness, inner-and-outer emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, non-alteration emptiness, essential nature emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common characteristic emptiness, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature.

Then one will be able to fulfill true thusness (*tathatā*), and also fulfill the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), non-falsity, immutability, equality, the state beyond birth, the fixed nature of phenomena (*dharmaniyāmatā*), the stability of phenomena (*dharmasthititā*), the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), the realm of space (*ākāśadhātu*), and the inconceivable realm;
then one will be able to fulfill the five eyes, and also fulfill the six supernormal powers (*abhijñā*);

then one will be able to fulfill the ten powers of a Buddha, and also fulfill the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*).
Then one can fulfill great loving-kindness, and likewise fulfill great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity;
then one can fulfill the quality of non-forgetfulness, and likewise fulfill the state of constant abiding in equanimity;

then one can fulfill all-knowledge (*sarvajñā*), and likewise fulfill the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*) and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), thereby realizing the knowledge of all modes of knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*).

“Subhūti! By means of the power of skillful means that takes non-existence as its intrinsic nature, this bodhisattva mahāsattva realizes that all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature; therein, there is neither perception nor even non-perception.”
"Subhūti! A bodhisattva mahāsattva should cultivate the recollection of the devas in this way: therein, there is not even the slightest recollection, let alone the recollection of devas! Subhūti!"
This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, relying on the cultivation of the six recollections, performs gradual karma, cultivates gradual training, and practices gradual conduct.
Furthermore, Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, desiring to fulfill the gradual activity, cultivate the gradual training, and perform the gradual practice, they should, by means of the skillful power of taking non-existence as their own nature, train in internal emptiness; they should train in external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, non-altering emptiness, essential emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common-characteristic emptiness, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of own-nature, and the emptiness of the own-nature of non-existence.

By means of the skillful means of taking non-existence as the intrinsic nature, one should study true suchness (*tathatā*); one should study the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*), the non-erroneous nature, the unchanging nature, equality, the nature free from birth, the fixed nature of dharmas, the stability of dharmas, the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), the realm of space, and the inconceivable realm.

By means of the skillful means of taking non-existence as the intrinsic nature, one should study the four foundations of mindfulness; one should study the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path.
By means of the skillful means of taking non-existence as the intrinsic nature, one should study the noble truth of suffering; one should study the noble truths of origin, cessation, and the path.

By means of the skillful power of taking non-existence as the intrinsic nature, one should study the four dhyānas; by means of the skillful power of taking non-existence as the intrinsic nature, one should study the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments;

by means of the skillful power of taking non-existence as the intrinsic nature, one should study the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities;

by means of the skillful power of taking non-existence as the intrinsic nature, one should study the gate of liberation of emptiness, and study the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness.

By means of the skillful means of taking non-existence as intrinsic nature, one should train in the perfection of generosity; one should train in the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, wisdom, skillful means, aspiration, power, and knowledge.

By means of the skillful means of taking non-existence as intrinsic nature, one should train in the Ground of Utmost Joy; one should train in the Ground of Purity, the Ground of Radiance, the Ground of Blazing Wisdom, the Ground of Difficult Victory, the Ground of Manifestation, the Ground of Far-Going, the Ground of Immovability, the Ground of Excellent Intelligence, and the Ground of the Dharma Cloud.
By means of the skillful means of taking non-existence as intrinsic nature, one should train in the five eyes and one should train in the six supernormal powers.

By means of the skillful power of taking non-existence as intrinsic nature, one should train in the ten powers of a Buddha; one should train in the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.

By means of the skillful power of taking non-existence as intrinsic nature, one should train in great loving-kindness; one should train in great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity.
By means of the skillful power of taking non-existence as intrinsic nature, one should train in the quality of non-forgetfulness and train in the nature of constant abiding in equanimity.

By means of the skillful power of taking non-existence as intrinsic nature, one should study all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), one should study the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and one should study the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*);
by means of the skillful power of taking non-existence as intrinsic nature, one should study all doors of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and all doors of dhāraṇī (*dhāraṇīmukha*).

“Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this way on the path to enlightenment, they realize that all phenomena have non-existence as their intrinsic nature; therein, not even the slightest thought can be apprehended, much less a thought of form, or a thought of feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness!”
How much more so for one who maintains mindfulness of the sense base of the eye, and maintains mindfulness of the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind!
How much more so for one who maintains mindfulness of the sense base of forms, and maintains mindfulness of the sense bases of sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena!
How much less could there be mindfulness of the eye-element, or mindfulness of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-elements!
How much less could there be mindfulness of the form-element, or mindfulness of the sound, odor, taste, tangible, and mental-object elements!
How much more so for one who attends to the element of eye-consciousness, or attends to the elements of ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-consciousness!
How much more so for one who attends to eye-contact, or attends to ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact!

How much more so for one who maintains mindfulness of the various feelings arising with eye-contact as condition, and maintains mindfulness of the various feelings arising with ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-contact as conditions!
How much more so for one who attends to the earth element, or attends to the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements!
How much more so for one who attends to conditions, or attends to the immediately preceding condition, the object-condition, and the dominant condition!

How much more so for mindfulness and ignorance, and for the formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, becoming, birth, and old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair!

How much more so for one who maintains mindfulness of the perfection of generosity, and maintains mindfulness of the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom!

How much more so for one who contemplates internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, the emptiness of the ultimate truth, the emptiness of conditioned phenomena, the emptiness of unconditioned phenomena, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, the emptiness of dispersion, the emptiness of non-alteration, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, the emptiness of specific characteristics, the emptiness of common characteristics, the emptiness of all dharmas, the emptiness of non-apprehensibility, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of self-nature, and the emptiness of the self-nature of non-existence!

How much more so for one who maintains mindfulness of the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path!
How much more so for one who recollects the Noble Truth of Suffering, and recollects the Noble Truths of Origination, Cessation, and the Path!
How much more so for one who recollects the four dhyānas, and recollects the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments!
How much more so for those who maintain mindfulness of the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities!
How much more so for those who maintain mindfulness of all doors of samādhi and all doors of dhāraṇī!
How much more so for those who mindfully contemplate the gate of liberation of emptiness, and mindfully contemplate the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness!

How much more so for those who mindfully contemplate the Ground of Utmost Joy, and mindfully contemplate the Ground of Purity, the Ground of Radiant Light, the Ground of Blazing Wisdom, the Ground of Extreme Difficulty to Conquer, the Ground of Presence, the Ground of Far-Going, the Ground of Immovability, the Ground of Excellent Intelligence, and the Ground of the Dharma Cloud!
How much more so for those who bring to mind the five eyes, or the six supernormal powers!
How much more so for those who bring to mind the Buddha’s ten powers, his four fearlessnesses, his four kinds of analytical knowledge, and his eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha!
How much more so for those who maintain mindfulness of great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity!
How much more so for those who maintain mindfulness of the quality of non-forgetfulness and mindfulness of the nature of constant equanimity!
How much more so for one who recollects omniscience, or recollects the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects!
How much more so for one who recollects the fruit of stream-entry, or recollects the fruits of once-returning, non-returning, arhatship, and pratyekabuddha enlightenment!
How much more so for one who recollects the practices of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and recollects the unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas!
It is impossible that there should be even the slightest reality in these various recollections or in the phenomena recollected.

“Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom in this way, although they perform gradual deeds, cultivate gradual training, and carry out gradual practices, none of the mental activities, trainings, or practices involved therein proceed, because all phenomena have non-existence as their intrinsic nature.”
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
If all dharmas have non-existence as their intrinsic nature, then there should be no form, nor sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness."
There should be no eye-base, nor ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind-base;
there should be no form-base, nor sound, odor, taste, tangible object, or mental-object base;
there should be no eye-element, nor ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind-element.
There should be no formless realm, nor the realms of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, or mental objects;
there should be no visual consciousness realm, nor the realms of auditory, olfactory, gustatory, tactile, or mental consciousness;
there should be no visual contact, nor auditory, olfactory, gustatory, tactile, or mental contact.
There should be no feelings produced with eye-contact as condition, nor any feelings produced with ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind-contact as condition;
there should be no earth element, nor water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness elements;
there should be no causal condition (hetu-pratyaya), nor immediate condition (samanantara-pratyaya), object condition (ālambana-pratyaya), or predominant condition (adhipati-pratyaya).

There would be no ignorance, nor would there be volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, or old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair;
there would be no perfection of generosity, nor would there be the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, or wisdom.

There should be no internal emptiness, nor external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, endless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, non-alteration emptiness, essential nature emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common characteristic emptiness, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, or the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature;

there should be no four applications of mindfulness, nor the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, or the eightfold noble path;
there should be no noble truth of suffering, nor the noble truths of origin, cessation, or the path.
There should be no four dhyānas, nor the four immeasurables, nor the four formless attainments;
there should be no eight liberations, nor the eight bases of mastery, nor the nine successive attainments, nor the ten totalities;
there should be no gates of all samādhis, nor gates of all dhāraṇīs.
There should be no gate of liberation of emptiness, nor the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness;

there should be no Ground of Extreme Joy, nor the Ground of Purity, the Ground of Radiance, the Ground of Blazing Wisdom, the Ground of Difficult Victory, the Ground of Presence, the Ground of Far-reaching Practice, the Ground of Immovability, the Ground of Good Wisdom, or the Ground of the Dharma Cloud;
there should be no five eyes, nor the six supernormal powers.
There should be no ten powers of a Buddha, nor the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, or the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
there should be no great loving-kindness, nor great compassion, great joy, or great equanimity;
there should be no quality of non-forgetfulness, nor the nature of constant abiding in equanimity.
There would be no omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), nor the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), nor the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*);

there would be no fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpattiphala*), nor the fruits of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmiphala*), non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*), arhatship (*arhattvaphala*), or the enlightenment of a solitary buddha (*pratyekabuddhabodhi*);
there would be no conduct of any bodhisattva mahāsattva, nor the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment of all buddhas (*anuttarasamyaksaṃbodhi*).
There should be no Buddha, nor Dharma, nor Sangha;
there should be no Path, nor Fruit;
there should be no defilement, nor purity.
"There should be no practice, nor any attainment, nor any clear realization; indeed, all dharmas should be non-existent.
The Buddha said, "Subhūti!"
"What do you think?
Within the state where all phenomena have non-existence as their intrinsic nature, can existence or non-existence be apprehended? Subhūti replied:
"No, World-Honored One! No!"
“Sugata! Within all phenomena, which have non-existence as their very nature, neither existence nor non-existence can be apprehended.
The Buddha said:
"Subhūti! If, within the state where all phenomena have non-existence as their intrinsic nature, both existence and non-existence are unapprehendable, how can you now ask this question:
'If all phenomena have non-existence as their intrinsic nature, then there should be no form, nor feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness'?"
There should be no sense-base of the eye, nor of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind;
there should be no sense-base of forms, nor of sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena;
there should be no element of the eye, nor of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind.
There should be no form realm, nor the realms of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, or mental objects;
there should be no eye-consciousness realm, nor the realms of ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind-consciousness;
there should be no eye-contact, nor ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind-contact.
There should be no feelings produced with eye-contact as condition, nor any feelings produced with ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind-contact as condition;
there should be no earth element, nor water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness elements;
there should be no causal condition, nor immediate condition, object-condition, or dominant condition.

There should be no ignorance, nor should there be volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, or old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair;
there should be no perfection of generosity, nor should there be the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, or wisdom.

There should be no internal emptiness, nor external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, emptiness of the ultimate truth, emptiness of conditioned phenomena, emptiness of unconditioned phenomena, absolute emptiness, emptiness of the limitless, emptiness of dispersion, emptiness of non-alteration, emptiness of intrinsic nature, emptiness of specific characteristics, emptiness of common characteristics, emptiness of all phenomena, emptiness of the unapprehendable, emptiness of non-existence, emptiness of self-nature, or emptiness of the self-nature of non-existence;

there should be no four foundations of mindfulness, nor the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, or the eightfold noble path;
there should be no noble truth of suffering, nor the noble truths of origination, cessation, or the path.
There should be no four dhyānas, nor the four immeasurables, nor the four formless attainments;
there should be no eight liberations, nor the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, or the ten totalities;
there should be no gateways to all samādhis, nor gateways to all dhāraṇīs.
There should be no gate of liberation of emptiness, nor the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness;

there should be no Stage of Extreme Joy, nor the Stages of Freedom from Defilement, Radiant Light, Blazing Wisdom, Difficult to Conquer, Presence, Far-Going, Immovable, Good Intelligence, and Cloud of Dharma;
there should be no five eyes, nor the six supernormal powers.
There should be no ten powers of a Buddha, nor the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, or the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
there should be no great loving-kindness, nor great compassion, great joy, or great equanimity;
there should be no quality of non-forgetfulness, nor the nature of constant abiding in equanimity.
There would be no omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), nor the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), nor the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*);
there would be no fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpattiphala*), nor the fruits of once-returning, non-returning, or arhatship, nor the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha;
there would be no conduct of any bodhisattva mahāsattva, nor the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas.
There should be no Buddha, nor Dharma, nor Sangha;
there should be no Path, nor Fruit;
there should be no defilement, nor purity.
“Then there should be no practice, nor attainment, nor clear realization; indeed, all phenomena should be non-existent?
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”

I have no doubt and no uncertainty regarding this Dharma; however, in future ages there will be bhikṣus who seek the Śrāvaka-yāna, or seek the Pratyekabuddha-yāna, or seek the Bodhisattva-mahāsattva-yāna, and they will say:

"The Buddha has taught that all dharmas take non-existence as their intrinsic nature. If all dharmas take non-existence as their intrinsic nature, who is it that is defiled? Who is it that is purified?"
Who is purified?
Who is bound?
Who is liberated?

Because they do not understand defilement and purification, nor bondage and liberation, they violate their precepts, their views, their conduct, and their pure livelihood. Due to these violations of precepts, views, conduct, and pure livelihood, they shall fall into the realms of hell, animals, or hungry ghosts to undergo various intense sufferings; thus they will cycle through birth and death, finding it difficult to attain liberation.

I observe that such terrifying events will occur in the future; therefore, I have asked the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha about this profound meaning. Nevertheless, regarding this matter, I have no confusion and no doubt.
The Buddha said:
“Excellent, Subhūti! Excellent!”
Excellent! So it is! So it is!
It is as you have said.

Within all phenomena, which have non-existence as their very nature, both existence and non-existence are unapprehendable; one should not, therefore, cling to the notion that there is either existence or non-existence therein.
Chapter Sixty-Six: On Signlessness and Non-Attainment, Part One. At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”

If all phenomena have non-existence as their intrinsic nature, for what purpose does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, desiring to bring benefit and happiness to all sentient beings, seek to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?
The Buddha said, “Subhūti!

Because all phenomena have non-existence as their intrinsic nature, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas seek to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment for the sake of benefiting and bringing happiness to all sentient beings.”
Why is this? Subhūti!

Sentient beings are possessed of the views of annihilationism and eternalism; dwelling in the apprehension of objects, they are difficult to discipline, and being deluded and inverted, they are difficult to liberate.
"Subhūti! Those who dwell in apprehension, by virtue of their perception of apprehension, have neither attainment nor clear realization, nor even unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha,
saying: “World-Honored One,
for one who has nothing to attain, is there attainment, is there clear realization, or is there unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?”
The Buddha said, “Suvikrāntavikrāmin!
That which is non-apprehension is itself attainment, itself clear realization, and itself unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, because it does not destroy the dharma-realm.”

"Subhūti! If there are those who, within this state of non-apprehension, desire to have something apprehended, desire to attain clear realization, or desire to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, you should know that they wish to destroy the dharma-realm."
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If non-apprehension is itself attainment, itself clear realization, and itself unsurpassed perfect enlightenment—and if within non-apprehension there is no attainment, no clear realization, and no unsurpassed perfect enlightenment—how can there be for a bodhisattva mahāsattva the Ground of Extreme Joy, the Ground of Purity, the Ground of Radiant Light, the Ground of Blazing Wisdom, the Ground of Difficult Victory, the Ground of Presence, the Ground of Far-Going, the Ground of Immovability, the Ground of Excellent Intelligence, and the Ground of the Dharma Cloud?”
How can a bodhisattva mahāsattva attain the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*)?
How can they attain supernormal powers born of maturation (*vipākaja-abhijñā*)?
And how can they attain the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom born of maturation?
