*The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Scroll 375, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. First Division, Chapter Sixty-Six, Part Four: "The Non-Characteristic and Non-Attainment. "Subhūti!
Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, when dwelling in internal emptiness, they dwell in internal emptiness with an uncontaminated mind;

and when dwelling in external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, non-altering emptiness, essential emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common-characteristic emptiness, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence, they dwell in external emptiness up to the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence with an uncontaminated mind.
Therefore, although they abide in inner emptiness up to the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence, they have no dualistic perception. "Subhūti!
Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, when they abide in suchness, they abide in suchness while abiding in an untainted mind."

When one dwells in the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), non-falsity (*avitathatā*), non-alteration (*ananyathātā*), equality (*samatā*), the state beyond birth (*anirodhatā*), the fixedness of phenomena (*dharmaniyāmatā*), the stability of phenomena (*dharmasthititā*), the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), the realm of space (*ākāśadhātu*), and the inconceivable realm (*acintyadhātu*), one dwells in an untainted mind (*anāsravacitta*) while abiding in the dharma-realm up to the inconceivable realm.
Therefore, although they abide in true thusness (tathatā) up to the inconceivable realm, they have no dualistic perception. "Subhūti!

Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), when cultivating the five eyes, they cultivate the five eyes while abiding in an outflow-free mind (anāsrava-citta)."
When cultivating the six supernormal powers, one dwells in an untainted mind while cultivating them.
Therefore, although one cultivates the five eyes and the six supernormal powers, there is no dualistic conception.

“Subhūti! Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, when practicing the ten powers of a buddha, he dwells in an untainted mind while practicing the ten powers of a buddha;

when practicing the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha, he dwells in an untainted mind while practicing the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha.”

Therefore, although they cultivate the ten powers of a Buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, they maintain no notion of duality.
“Subhūti! Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, when practicing great loving-kindness, they dwell in an untainted mind while practicing great loving-kindness;
when practicing great compassion, great joy, and great equanimity, they dwell in an untainted mind while practicing great compassion, great joy, and great equanimity.”
Therefore, although they cultivate great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity, they remain free from dualistic conceptualization. "Subhūti!

Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, when they cultivate the quality of non-forgetfulness, they dwell in an untainted mind while cultivating that quality of non-forgetfulness."
When cultivating the state of constant abiding in equanimity, one dwells in an untainted mind while cultivating that state of constant abiding in equanimity.
Therefore, although one cultivates both the quality of non-forgetfulness and the state of constant abiding in equanimity, there is no dualistic conception between them.

“Subhūti! Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, when cultivating all-knowledge (sarvajñatā), he dwells in an untainted mind (anāsrava-citta) while cultivating all-knowledge;

when cultivating the knowledge of the aspects of the path (mārgākārajñatā) and the knowledge of all aspects (sarvākārajñatā), he dwells in an untainted mind while cultivating the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects.”

Therefore, although they cultivate all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), they have no dualistic conception. "Subhūti!

Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), when they bring forth the thirty-two marks of a great man (*dvātriṃśanmahāpuruṣalakṣaṇa*), they do so while abiding in an outflow-free mind (*anāsravacitta*)."
When manifesting the eighty minor marks, one abides in an untainted mind while manifesting them.
Therefore, although one manifests the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty minor marks, there is no dualistic conception.
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,

how is it that when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of giving by virtue of practicing the perfection of wisdom, they abide in an untainted mind while practicing the perfection of giving?"

When practicing the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, does one abide in an uncontaminated mind while practicing ethical discipline up to the perfection of wisdom?
“World-Honored One!
How is it that when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they cultivate the four dhyānas while abiding in an untainted mind;
and how do they cultivate the four immeasurables and the four formless absorptions while abiding in an untainted mind?”
“World-Honored One!
How is it that when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they dwell in an untainted mind while practicing the four foundations of mindfulness;

and how is it that when they practice the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path, they dwell in an untainted mind while practicing the four right efforts up to the eightfold noble path?”
“World-Honored One!

How is it that when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, while practicing the liberation door of emptiness, they abide in an untainted mind to practice the liberation door of emptiness;
and while practicing the liberation doors of signlessness and wishlessness, they abide in an untainted mind to practice the liberation doors of signlessness and wishlessness?”
“World-Honored One!
How is it that when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they abide in the noble truth of suffering while abiding in an untainted mind;
and when they abide in the noble truths of origin, cessation, and the path, they abide in those noble truths of origin, cessation, and the path while abiding in an untainted mind?”
“World-Honored One!
How is it that when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they dwell in an untainted mind while practicing the eight liberations;

and how is it that when they practice the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities, they dwell in an untainted mind while practicing the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities?”
“World-Honored One!

How is it that when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, while practicing all the gates of samādhi, they dwell in an untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*) while practicing all the gates of samādhi;
and while practicing all the gates of dhāraṇī, they dwell in an untainted mind while practicing all the gates of dhāraṇī?”
“Bhagavān, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, by practicing the perfection of wisdom, abide in inner emptiness while abiding with an uncontaminated mind;

and how does he abide in outer emptiness, inner-and-outer emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, non-alteration emptiness, essential nature emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common characteristic emptiness, the emptiness of all dharmas, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature, while abiding with an uncontaminated mind?”
“World-Honored One!
How is it that when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they abide in true thusness while abiding in an untainted mind;

and when they abide in the dharma-realm, the dharma-nature, non-illusory nature, unchanging nature, equality, the nature of being free from birth, the fixed nature of dharmas, the stability of dharmas, the limit of reality, the realm of empty space, and the inconceivable realm, they abide in an untainted mind while abiding in the dharma-realm up to the inconceivable realm?”
“World-Honored One!
How is it that when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they cultivate the five eyes while abiding in an untainted mind;
and when they cultivate the six supernormal powers, they do so while abiding in an untainted mind?”
“World-Honored One!
How is it that when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they dwell in an untainted mind while cultivating the ten powers of a buddha;

and how is it that when they cultivate the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha, they dwell in an untainted mind while cultivating the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha?”
“World-Honored One!
How is it that when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they cultivate great loving-kindness while abiding in an untainted mind;
and how is it that when they cultivate great compassion, great joy, and great equanimity, they abide in an untainted mind while cultivating great compassion, great joy, and great equanimity?”
“World-Honored One!

How is it that when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, while cultivating the quality of non-forgetfulness, they abide in an untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*) to cultivate non-forgetfulness;
and while cultivating the nature of constant equanimity (*upekṣā*), they abide in an untainted mind to cultivate the nature of constant equanimity?”
“World-Honored One!
How is it that when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they dwell in an untainted mind while cultivating all-knowledge;

and how is it that when they cultivate the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects, they dwell in an untainted mind while cultivating the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects?”
“World-Honored One!
How is it that when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they manifest the thirty-two marks of a great man while abiding in an untainted mind,
and manifest the eighty secondary signs while abiding in an untainted mind?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they practice the perfection of generosity with a mind free from signs—meaning they do not perceive: 'I am able to give,' 'I am able to relinquish this,' 'I am practicing this giving,' 'I give because of this,' 'I give for the sake of that,' or 'I practice giving in such a manner.'"

Abiding in this untainted mind that is free from signs, one practices the perfection of giving while being free from craving and free from stinginess; at that time, one does not perceive the act of giving, nor does one perceive this untainted mind, nor even perceive any of the Buddha-dharmas.
In this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in an untainted mind and practices the perfection of generosity. "Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they practice the perfection of ethical discipline with a mind free from signs—meaning they do not perceive: 'I am able to maintain ethical discipline,' 'I am able to relinquish this,' 'I am maintaining ethical discipline toward this,' 'I am maintaining ethical discipline by means of this,' 'I am maintaining ethical discipline for the sake of this,' or 'I am maintaining ethical discipline in this manner.'"

Abiding in this mind that is free from signs and untainted, one practices the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*) without defilement or attachment; at that time, one does not perceive the ethical discipline being practiced, nor does one perceive this untainted mind, and so on, up to not perceiving any of the Buddha-dharmas.
In this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in the untainted mind and practices the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*). "Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*), they practice the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*) with a mind free from signs (*animitta*), such that they do not perceive: 'I am able to cultivate patience,' 'I am able to relinquish this,' 'I am cultivating patience toward this,' 'I am cultivating patience by means of this,' 'I am cultivating patience for the sake of this,' or 'I am cultivating patience in this manner.'"

Abiding in this mind that is free from signs and untainted, one practices the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā) without defilement or attachment; at that time, one does not perceive the patience being practiced, nor does one perceive this untainted mind, nor even perceive all the Buddha-dharmas.
In this way, the bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in the untainted mind and practices the perfection of patience.

Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they practice the perfection of diligence with a mind free from signs—meaning they do not perceive: "I am able to exert diligence," "I can relinquish this," "in this diligence," "by means of this diligence," "for the sake of this diligence," or "such is diligence."

Abiding in this untainted mind that is free from signs, one practices the perfection of vigor without defilement or attachment; at that time, one does not perceive the vigor being practiced, nor does one perceive this untainted mind, nor even perceive any of the Buddha-dharmas.
In this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in an untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*) while practicing the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*). "Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*), they practice the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-pāramitā*) with a mind free from signs (*animitta*), such that they do not perceive: 'I am able to cultivate concentration,' 'I am able to relinquish this,' 'I am cultivating concentration in this,' 'I am cultivating concentration by means of this,' 'I am cultivating concentration for the sake of this,' or 'I am cultivating concentration in this manner.'"

Abiding in this mind that is free from signs and untainted, one practices the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*) without defilement or attachment; at that time, one does not perceive the meditative concentration being practiced, nor does one perceive this untainted mind, nor even perceive any of the Buddha-dharmas.
In this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in the untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*) and practices the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-pāramitā*). "Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*), they practice the perfection of wisdom with a mind free from signs (*animitta-citta*). That is to say, they do not perceive: 'I am able to cultivate wisdom,' 'I am able to relinquish this,' 'in this [context] I cultivate wisdom,' 'by means of this I cultivate wisdom,' 'for the sake of this I cultivate wisdom,' or 'thus I cultivate wisdom.'"

Abiding in this mind that is free from signs and untainted, one practices the *prajñāpāramitā* without defilement or attachment; at that time, one does not perceive the *prajñāpāramitā* being practiced, nor does one perceive this untainted mind, nor even perceive all the Buddha-dharmas.
In this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in an untainted mind and practices the perfection of wisdom.

Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they practice the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments with a mind free from signs; that is to say, they do not perceive a self who can practice the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments.
"I am able to relinquish this, for this, by means of this, and for the sake of this; thus I cultivate the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments."

Abiding in this mind that is free from signs and untainted, one cultivates the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments without defilement or attachment; at that time, one does not perceive the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, or the four formless attainments being cultivated, nor does one perceive this untainted mind, nor even perceive all the Buddha-dharmas.
In this way, the bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in the untainted mind and cultivates the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments. "Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they practice the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of awakening, and the eightfold noble path with a mind free from signs. That is to say, they do not perceive a self that thinks: "I am practicing the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path";
nor do they think: "I can abandon this, for this, by means of this, or for the sake of this," as they thus practice the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path.

Abiding in this untainted mind that is free from signs, one cultivates the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path without defilement or attachment; at that time, one does not perceive the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path being cultivated, nor does one perceive this untainted mind, nor even perceive all the Buddha-dharmas.
In this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in an untainted mind and cultivates the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path.

Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they practice the gateways to liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—with a mind free from signs; that is to say, they do not perceive a self that can cultivate the gateways to liberation of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.

I am able to relinquish this, for this, by means of this, and for the sake of this; thus I cultivate the gates of liberation of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*).

Abiding in this untainted (*anāsrava*) mind that is free from signs, I cultivate the gates of liberation of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness without defilement or attachment. At that time, I do not perceive the gates of liberation of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness that are being cultivated, nor do I perceive this untainted mind, nor even all the Buddha-dharmas.
In this way, the bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in the untainted mind and cultivates the gates of liberation: emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness. "Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they dwell in the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path with a mind free from signs; that is to say, they do not perceive a self that can dwell in the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path."
I am able to relinquish this, for this, by means of this, and for the sake of this; thus I abide in the Noble Truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.

Abiding in this untainted mind that is free from characteristics, I dwell in the Noble Truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path without defilement or attachment. At that time, I do not perceive the Noble Truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path in which I abide, nor do I perceive this untainted mind, nor even all the Buddha-dharmas.
In this way, the bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in an untainted mind while dwelling in the noble truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path. "Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they cultivate the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative attainments, and the ten totalities with a mind free from signs—meaning they do not perceive a self that can cultivate the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative attainments, or the ten totalities."

I am able to relinquish this, for this, by means of this, and for the sake of this; in this manner, I cultivate the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities.

Abiding in this outflow-free mind that is free from signs, one practices the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities without defilement or attachment; at that time, one does not perceive the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, or the ten totalities that are being practiced, nor does one perceive this outflow-free mind, nor even all the Buddha-dharmas.
In this way, the bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in the untainted mind and cultivates the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive absorptions, and the ten totalities.

“Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they cultivate all the doors of samādhi and dhāraṇī with a mind free from signs. That is to say, they do not perceive a self that can cultivate all the doors of samādhi and dhāraṇī;
nor do they perceive one who can abandon these, or for whom, or by what means, or for what purpose, as they thus cultivate all the doors of samādhi and dhāraṇī.”

Abiding within this untainted mind that is free from marks, one cultivates all gateways of samādhi and dhāraṇī without defilement or attachment; at that time, one does not perceive any of the cultivated gateways of samādhi or dhāraṇī, nor does one perceive this untainted mind, and so on, up to not perceiving any of the Buddha-dharmas.
In this way, the bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in the untainted mind and cultivates all gateways of samādhi and gateways of dhāraṇī. "Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they abide in internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, non-alteration emptiness, essential emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common-characteristic emptiness, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature—by means of a mind free from signs. That is to say, they do not perceive a "self" that can abide in internal emptiness up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature;

nor do they perceive a "self" that can abandon these, or [abide] in these, or by means of these, or for the sake of these, while thus abiding in internal emptiness up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature.

Abiding in this untainted mind that is free from signs, one dwells in internal emptiness up to the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence without defilement or attachment; at that time, one does not perceive the internal emptiness up to the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence in which one abides, nor does one perceive this untainted mind, nor even perceive all the Buddha-dharmas.
In this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in an untainted mind, dwelling in internal emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence and intrinsic nature. "Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they dwell with a mind free from signs in suchness, the dharma-realm, the dharma-nature, non-illusoriness, immutability, equality, the state beyond birth, the fixed nature of dharmas, the stability of dharmas, the limit of reality, the realm of space, and the inconceivable realm—namely, not perceiving a self that can dwell in suchness up to the inconceivable realm."
I am able to relinquish this, from this, by means of this, and for the sake of this; thus I abide in true suchness (*tathatā*) up to the inconceivable realm.

Abiding within this untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*) free from marks, I dwell without defilement or attachment in true suchness up to the inconceivable realm. At that time, I do not perceive the true suchness up to the inconceivable realm in which I abide, nor do I perceive this untainted mind, nor even all the Buddha-dharmas.
In this way, the bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in the untainted mind, dwelling in suchness and so forth up to the inconceivable realm. "Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they cultivate the five eyes and the six supernormal powers with a mind free from signs, such that they do not perceive a self that can cultivate the five eyes and the six supernormal powers."
I am able to relinquish this, for this, by means of this, and for the sake of this; thus I cultivate the five eyes and the six supernormal powers.

Abiding in this untainted mind free from signs, I cultivate the five eyes and the six supernormal powers without defilement or attachment. At that time, I do not perceive the five eyes and six supernormal powers being cultivated, nor do I perceive this untainted mind, nor even all the Buddha-dharmas.
In this way, the bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in an untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*) while cultivating the five eyes and the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍ-abhijñā*). "Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), they cultivate the ten powers of a buddha (*daśa-tathāgatabala*), the four fearlessnesses (*catvāri vaiśāradyāni*), the four analytical knowledges (*catasraḥ pratisamvidah*), and the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharmāḥ*) with a mind free from signs (*animitta-citta*). That is to say, they do not perceive a self that can cultivate the ten powers of a buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, or the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha."

I am able to relinquish this, for this, by means of this, and for the sake of this; thus do I cultivate the ten powers of a Buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.

Abiding in this mind that is free from signs and untainted, one cultivates the ten powers of a Buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, yet at that time one does not perceive the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, or the eighteen unique qualities being cultivated; nor does one perceive this untainted mind, nor even all the Buddha-dharmas.

In this way, the bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling in the untainted mind, cultivates the ten powers of a buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha.

“Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they cultivate great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity with a mind free from signs. That is to say, they do not perceive: ‘I am able to cultivate great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity;
I am able to relinquish this, for this, by means of this, or for the sake of this’—thus they cultivate great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity.”

Abiding in this mind that is free from marks and untainted, one cultivates great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity without defilement or attachment; at that time, one does not perceive the great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, or great equanimity being cultivated, nor does one perceive this untainted mind, nor even perceive any of the Buddha-dharmas.
In this way, the bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in the untainted mind and cultivates great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity.
"Suvikrāntavikrāmin!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they cultivate the quality of non-forgetfulness and the state of constant equanimity with a mind free from signs. That is to say, they do not perceive: "I am able to cultivate non-forgetfulness and the state of constant equanimity";
nor do they perceive: "I am able to abandon this, for this, by this, or on account of this," as they thus cultivate non-forgetfulness and the state of constant equanimity.

Abiding in this untainted mind that is free from signs, one practices the quality of non-forgetfulness and the state of constant equanimity without defilement or attachment; at that time, one does not perceive the practiced qualities of non-forgetfulness and constant equanimity, nor does one perceive this untainted mind, nor even perceive any of the Buddha-dharmas.
In this way, the bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in an untainted mind and cultivates the quality of non-forgetfulness and the nature of constant equanimity. "Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they cultivate all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) with a mind free from signs; that is to say, they do not perceive a self that can cultivate all-knowledge, the knowledge of the paths, or the knowledge of all aspects."

I am able to relinquish this, for this, by means of this, and for the sake of this; in this manner, I cultivate all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).

Abiding in this mind that is free from signs and untainted, one cultivates all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) without defilement or attachment; at that time, one does not perceive the all-knowledge, the knowledge of the aspects of the path, or the knowledge of all aspects being cultivated, nor does one perceive this untainted mind, nor even perceive any of the Buddha-dharmas.
In this way, the bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in the untainted mind and cultivates all-knowledge, the knowledge of the aspects of the path, and the knowledge of all aspects. "Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they draw forth the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty secondary signs with a mind free from signs. That is to say, they do not perceive a self that can draw forth the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty secondary signs;

nor do they perceive one who can abandon them, or that which is abandoned, or that by which they are drawn forth, or that for whose sake they are drawn forth—thus drawing forth the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty secondary signs.

Abiding in this untainted mind that is free from signs, one is without defilement or attachment while manifesting the thirty-two marks of a Great Man and the eighty minor characteristics; yet at that time, one does not perceive the thirty-two marks of a Great Man and the eighty minor characteristics being manifested, nor does one perceive this untainted mind, nor even perceive any of the Buddha-dharmas.
"In this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling in the untainted mind, brings forth the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty secondary signs.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, how can they fulfill the *pāramitās* of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom within all things that are signless, without conceptualization, unattainable, shadowless, and non-conditioned?

How can one bring to perfection the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right endeavors, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path?
How can one fulfill the gates of liberation of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*)?

How can one fulfill internal emptiness (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*), external emptiness (*bahirdhā-śūnyatā*), internal-and-external emptiness (*adhyātma-bahirdhā-śūnyatā*), the emptiness of emptiness (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*), great emptiness (*mahā-śūnyatā*), ultimate emptiness (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*), conditioned emptiness (*saṃskṛta-śūnyatā*), unconditioned emptiness (*asaṃskṛta-śūnyatā*), absolute emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*), boundless emptiness (*anavara-agra-śūnyatā*), dispersal emptiness (*anavakāra-śūnyatā*), non-alteration emptiness (*anavakāra-śūnyatā*), essential nature emptiness (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*), self-characteristic emptiness (*svalakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*), common characteristic emptiness (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*), the emptiness of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-śūnyatā*), the emptiness of the unapprehendable (*anupalambha-śūnyatā*), the emptiness of non-existence (*abhāva-śūnyatā*), the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*), and the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence (*abhāva-svabhāva-śūnyatā*)?

How can one bring to perfection suchness, the dharma-realm, the nature of phenomena, non-falsity, immutability, equanimity, the state beyond birth, the fixed nature of phenomena, the stability of phenomena, the limit of reality, the realm of space, and the inconceivable realm?
How can one bring to fulfillment the noble truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path?
How can one bring to fulfillment the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless absorptions?
How can one fulfill the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative attainments, and the ten totalities?
How can one fulfill all the gateways of samādhi and the gateways of dhāraṇī?
How can one bring to perfection the five eyes and the six supernormal powers?
How can one bring to perfection the ten powers of a Buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha?
How can one fulfill great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity?
How can one fulfill the quality of non-forgetfulness and the state of constant abiding in equanimity?
How can one fulfill all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*)?
How can one fulfill the thirty-two marks of a great man (*dvātriṃśanmahāpuruṣalakṣaṇa*) and the eighty secondary signs (*aśītyanuvyañjana*)?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, they are able to practice giving with a mind that is free from signs and untainted.
If there are sentient beings who require food, they give them food; if they require drink, [they give them drink].”

If they require drink, provide them with drink; if they require clothing, provide them with clothing; if they require bedding, provide them with bedding; if they require vehicles, provide them with vehicles;
if they require servants, provide them with servants; if they require precious gems, provide them with precious gems;

if they require wealth and grain, provide them with wealth and grain; if they require incense and flowers, provide them with incense and flowers; if they require dwellings, provide them with dwellings; if they require...
Ornaments and ornaments, and even all necessary requisites as they may require, he gives them all;
if there are those who require his internal head, eyes, marrow, brain, skin, flesh, limbs, joints, tendons, bones, or even his life, he gives these all away;
if there are those who require foreign lands, cities, wives, children, or beloved kinsmen, [he gives these as well].
He gives with various adornments and with joy.
While he is giving in this manner, suppose someone were to come before him and revile him, saying: "Alas!..."
"O Great Being!
Why do you practice this useless giving? For one who gives in such a manner will experience much suffering and affliction in both this life and future lives!
Although the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva hears these words because he practices the profound Prajñāpāramitā, he does not retreat or become disheartened; rather, he thinks to himself:

"Although that person comes to revile and disparage me, I should not give rise to sorrow or regret in my mind; I shall courageously bestow upon all sentient beings whatever wealth and goods they require, without weariness of body or mind."
"This bodhisattva mahāsattva takes this merit from giving and, sharing it equally with all sentient beings, dedicates it toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

When practicing such giving and dedicating [the merit], one does not perceive their characteristics; that is to say, one does not perceive who gives, who receives, what is given, where it is given, by means of what it is given, for what purpose it is given, or how the giving is performed. Furthermore, one does not perceive who can dedicate, what is dedicated, where it is dedicated, by means of what it is dedicated, for what it is dedicated, or how it is dedicated. In this way, one does not perceive any of these things whatsoever.
Why is this? These phenomena are empty either by virtue of internal emptiness, or by virtue of external emptiness,
or by virtue of internal-and-external emptiness, or by virtue of the emptiness of emptiness, or by virtue of great emptiness.
...or it is empty because of the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*), or empty because of the emptiness of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta-śūnyatā*),

or empty because of the emptiness of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta-śūnyatā*), or empty because of the emptiness of the absolute (*atyanta-śūnyatā*), or empty because of the emptiness of the beginningless and endless (*anavarāgra-śūnyatā*),
or empty because of the emptiness of dispersion (*anavakāra-śūnyatā*), or empty because of the emptiness of non-alteration (*anavakāra-śūnyatā*), or by its original...

It is empty because its nature is empty; or it is empty because it is empty of its own-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*); or it is empty because it is empty of common-characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*); or it is empty because all phenomena (*sarvadharma*) are empty;
or it is empty because of the emptiness of non-apprehensibility (*anupalambha-śūnyatā*); or it is empty because of the emptiness of non-existence (*abhāva-śūnyatā*);
or it is empty because of the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*); or it is empty because of the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature (*abhāvasvabhāva-śūnyatā*).
Because their nature is empty, they are empty.
Having observed that there are no phenomena that are not empty, this bodhisattva mahāsattva further reflects:
"Who is it that can perform the dedication?"
What is it that is dedicated?
To what is it dedicated?
By means of what is it dedicated?
For what purpose is there dedication? How is there dedication?
Such phenomena as these are all unapprehendable.

When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva performs dedication through such contemplation and such mindfulness, it is called a "virtuous dedication" and a "poison-free dedication"; it is also called the "dedication of entering the dharma-realm."
By means of this, one is further able to adorn and purify buddha-fields and bring sentient beings to maturity;
one is also able to fulfill the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom;
and one is also able to fulfill the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of miraculous power, the five faculties, and the five [powers].
The powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eight branches of the noble path; they are also able to fulfill the gates of liberation—
emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness— and are also able to fulfill internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal and external emptiness,
the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, and the emptiness of the limit of reality.
They also fulfill the emptiness of the ultimate limit, the emptiness of the boundless, the emptiness of dispersion, the emptiness of non-alteration, the emptiness of intrinsic nature,
the emptiness of self-characteristics, the emptiness of common characteristics, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unobtainable,
the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence; furthermore, they are able to perfect suchness and the dharma-realm.
...the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), the non-falsity of phenomena, the immutability of phenomena, the equality of phenomena, the state beyond birth,

the fixed nature of phenomena (*dharmaniyāmatā*), the stability of phenomena (*dharmasthititā*), the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), the realm of space (*ākāśadhātu*), and the inconceivable realm (*acintyadhātu*);
they are also able to fulfill the noble truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path, and they are also able to fulfill the four meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*).
They can also fulfill the four immeasurables and the four formless absorptions;
they can also fulfill the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive absorptions, and the ten totalities;
they can also fulfill all doors of samādhi and dhāraṇī, as well as the five eyes and the six supernormal powers.
They are able to fulfill the ten powers of a Buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
they are also able to fulfill great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity;
they are also able to fulfill the quality of non-forgetfulness and the nature of constant dwelling in equanimity; and they are also able to fulfill all [other qualities].

They also fulfill the knowledge of paths (*mārgajñatā*), the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), as well as the thirty-two marks of a great man (*dvātriṃśanmahāpuruṣalakṣaṇa*) and the eighty secondary signs (*aśītyanuvyañjana*).

Although this bodhisattva mahāsattva is thus able to fulfill the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*), they do not grasp at the karmic maturation (*vipāka*) of that generosity. While they do not grasp at the maturation of generosity, because the perfection of generosity is thoroughly purified, they are able to procure all material wealth according to their wishes.

Just as for the gods of the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations, everything they require appears according to their wishes, so it is with this bodhisattva mahāsattva: whatever they require can be accomplished according to their wishes.

By the predominant power of this generosity, one is able to provide various kinds of sublime offerings to honor, revere, respect, and praise the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones; one is also able to fully satisfy the needs and desires of gods, humans, asuras, and others in the world with all requisite provisions.

By means of this perfection of giving, these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas gather in all sentient beings; through skillful means, they establish them in the vehicles of the Three Vehicles, causing each to obtain benefit and happiness according to what is appropriate for them.

"In this way, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, by the power of the mind that is free from all signs and untainted, they are able to fulfill the perfection of generosity within all signless, non-conceptual, unattainable, shadowless, and unconditioned phenomena, and likewise fulfill all other meritorious qualities."
"Furthermore, Subhūti, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva,

when practicing the profound perfection of wisdom, fulfill the perfection of ethical discipline within all things that are signless, without conceptualization, without attainment, without shadow, and without conditioned activity?"

“Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, they are able to uphold pure ethical discipline with a mind free from signs and untainted by outflows—namely, the naturally attained, perfectly pure ethical discipline comprised within the noble, untainted factors of the path.”

Such pure ethical discipline is without deficiency or flaw, without blemish or impurity, and free from attachment; it is worthy of offerings, praised by the wise, excellently undertaken, excellently perfected, and, being in accordance with supreme meditative concentration, is invincible.

"By means of this pure ethical discipline, one has no grasping or attachment toward any phenomena; that is to say, one does not grasp at or attach to form, nor does one grasp at or attach to feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness;
one does not grasp at or attach to the eye-base, nor does one grasp at or attach to the bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind;
one does not grasp at or attach to the form-base, nor does one grasp at or attach to the bases of sound, odor, taste, tangibles, or mental objects."
They do not grasp at or adhere to the eye-element, nor do they grasp at or adhere to the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind-elements;
they do not grasp at or adhere to the form-element, nor do they grasp at or adhere to the sound, odor, taste, tangible, or mental-object elements;
they do not grasp at or adhere to the eye-consciousness-element, nor do they grasp at or adhere to the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind-consciousness-elements.
They do not grasp at or cling to the thirty-two marks of a great man, nor do they grasp at or cling to the eighty secondary signs;

they do not grasp at or cling to the great clans of the Kṣatriyas, nor do they grasp at or cling to the great clans of the Brāhmaṇas, the great clans of the Śreṣṭhins, or the great clans of the Gṛhapatis;

they do not grasp at or cling to the Heaven of the Four Great Kings, nor do they grasp at or cling to the Heaven of the Thirty-three, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, or the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven.
They do not cling to the Brahmakāyika devas, nor do they cling to the Brahmapurohita, the Brahmakāyika-pariṣad-devas, or the Mahābrahmā devas;
they do not cling to the Ābhāsvara devas, nor do they cling to the Parīttābha, the Apramāṇābha, or the Ābhāsvara-śuddha devas;
they do not cling to the Śubhakṛtsna devas, nor do they cling to the Parīttaśubha, the Apramāṇaśubha, or the Śubhakṛtsna devas.

They do not grasp at or cling to the Vast Heaven (*Vehapphalā*), nor do they grasp at or cling to the Limited Vast Heaven (*Appamāṇasubhā*), the Immeasurable Vast Heaven (*Subhakinhā*), the Fruit of Vastness Heaven (*Vehapphalā*), or the Heaven of Non-perception (*Asaññasattā*);

they do not grasp at or cling to the Heaven of No Affliction (*Avihā*), nor do they grasp at or cling to the Heaven of No Heat (*Atappā*), the Beautifully Manifest Heaven (*Sudassā*), the Beautifully Seeing Heaven (*Sudassī*), or the Ultimate Form Heaven (*Akaniṭṭhā*);

they do not grasp at or cling to the Heaven of the Sphere of Infinite Space (*Ākāsānañcāyatanā*), nor do they grasp at or cling to the Heaven of the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness (*Viññāṇañcāyatanā*), the Heaven of Nothingness (*Ākiñcaññāyatanā*), or the Heaven of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-perception (*Nevasaññānāsaññāyatanā*).
They do not cling to the fruit of stream-entry, nor do they cling to the fruits of once-returner, non-returner, or arhatship, nor to the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha;
they do not cling to the rank of a universal monarch (cakravartin), nor do they cling to any other royal positions or the wealth, power, and sovereignty of high officials.

"However, by means of this very pure ethical discipline thus protected, one dedicates it in common with all sentient beings toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. One performs this dedication through the skillful means of signlessness, non-attainment, and non-duality, not through the skillful means of signs, attainment, and duality; one performs this dedication by way of conventional truth, not by way of ultimate truth."
By virtue of these causes and conditions, all Buddha-dharmas are fully perfected.

Through this perfection and purity of the *śīlapāramitā* (perfection of ethical discipline) and skillful means, this bodhisattva mahāsattva gives rise to the stages of further progress within the four *dhyānas* (meditative concentrations). By employing non-attachment as his skillful means, he brings forth the various *abhijñās* (supernormal knowledges).

This bodhisattva mahāsattva, by means of the pure divine eye born of karmic maturation, constantly beholds the present Buddhas dwelling in peace and stability throughout the infinite worlds of the ten directions as they proclaim the sublime Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings; having seen them, he shall never forget this until he attains unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

This bodhisattva mahāsattva, by means of the pure divine ear that transcends that of humans, constantly hears the Dharma being preached by the Buddhas of the ten directions; having heard it, they do not forget it until they realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and according to the Dharma they have heard, they are able to perform deeds for the benefit and happiness of both themselves and others without any being in vain.

By means of the knowledge of the distinctions of others' minds, this bodhisattva mahāsattva knows the minds and mental factors of the Buddhas of the ten directions and of all sentient beings; having known them, he is able to initiate all manner of beneficial and blissful activities for the sake of all sentient beings.

By means of the knowledge of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñāna*), this bodhisattva mahāsattva knows the karma previously created by sentient beings; because that created karma is neither lost nor destroyed, they are born in various places to experience various forms of suffering and happiness. Having known this, he explains the causal conditions of their original karma to them, causing them to remember and recognize it so as to perform beneficial deeds for them.

By means of the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows, these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas establish sentient beings, causing them to abide either in the fruit of a stream-enterer, or in the fruit of a once-returner, or in the fruit of a non-returner, or in the fruit of arhatship, or in pratyekabuddha enlightenment, or in the stage of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, or in unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment.
In brief, wherever these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas may be, they employ skillful means according to the varying capacities of sentient beings to establish them in all wholesome dharmas.

"So it is, Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, by means of the power of the mind that is free from all marks and untainted, they are able to fulfill the perfection of ethical discipline within all things that are markless, without conceptualization, without attainment, without shadow, and without conditioned activity; and they are likewise able to fulfill all other meritorious qualities."
"Furthermore, Subhūti, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva,
when practicing the profound perfection of wisdom, fulfill the perfection of patience within all things that are signless, without conceptualization, unattainable, shadowless, and non-active?"
“Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, they cultivate patience with a mind that is free from signs and untainted.”

From the first generation of the mind of awakening until sitting upon the seat of sublime enlightenment, even if all sentient beings were to come together and compete to inflict harm with various tiles, stones, swords, and staves, this bodhisattva mahāsattva would not give rise to even a single thought of anger or resentment.
At that time, a bodhisattva should cultivate two kinds of patience. What are these two?
First, one should endure all verbal abuse, insults, and physical harm from sentient beings without giving rise to anger or resentment, thereby subduing hatred through patience.
Second, they should give rise to the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
If this bodhisattva-mahāsattva is reviled and insulted with various harsh words, or is harmed by various weapons and staves, they should carefully reflect, deliberate, and observe:
"Who is it that can revile and insult?"
Who can inflict harm?
Who receives insult? Who undergoes injury?
"Who gives rise to anger and resentment?
Who should endure it?
Furthermore, one should observe that the nature of all phenomena is ultimately empty; since even phenomena themselves cannot be apprehended, how much less could there be a "nature of phenomena"!
Since even the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) does not exist, how much less could there be sentient beings!

When observing in this way, one perceives neither the one who reviles nor the one being reviled, neither the one who inflicts harm nor the one being harmed. Even when one’s limbs and body are cut into pieces, the mind remains patient and free from any other thought. By thus observing the nature of all phenomena as it truly is, one further attains the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
What is called the "patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena" (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*)?

It refers to causing afflictions to never arise again and observing that all phenomena ultimately do not originate; because subtle wisdom is thus constantly uninterrupted, it is therefore called the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena.
“Abiding in these two kinds of patience, this bodhisattva mahāsattva can swiftly fulfill the perfections of generosity,
ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom,
as well as the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, and the five faculties.”
...the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eight branches of the noble path; they can also fulfill the gates of liberation—
emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness— and they can also fulfill internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness,
the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, and unconditioned emptiness.
...the emptiness of ultimate reality, the emptiness of the limitless, the emptiness of dispersion, the emptiness of non-alteration, the emptiness of intrinsic nature,
the emptiness of specific characteristics, the emptiness of common characteristics, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of non-apprehensibility,
the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence; and they are also able to fulfill suchness.
The dharma-realm, the dharma-nature, the non-illusory nature, the unchanging nature, equality,
the state beyond birth, the fixedness of dharma, the stability of dharma, the limit of reality, the realm of space,
and the inconceivable realm; these can also fulfill the noble truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path, and they can also fulfill—
The four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments can also bring to fulfillment the eight liberations,
the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative concentrations, and the ten totalities;
they can also bring to fulfillment all doors of samādhi and dhāraṇī, as well as the five eyes and the six supernormal powers.
They can also fulfill the ten powers of a Buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
they can also fulfill great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity;
they can also fulfill the quality of non-forgetfulness and the nature of constant dwelling in equanimity; and they can also fulfill...

All-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*), and knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) can also bring to perfection the thirty-two marks of a great being and the eighty minor marks.

"Once this bodhisattva-mahāsattva is established in these qualities of a Buddha, they attain mastery over all the noble, untainted, supramundane, and unique supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas."

Having become established in such supreme supernormal powers, this bodhisattva mahāsattva, with the pure divine eye, constantly beholds the present Buddhas dwelling in peace and stability throughout the boundless worlds of the ten directions as they proclaim the sublime Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings; having seen them, until they attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, they give rise to the recollection of the Buddha (buddhānusmṛti) without interruption.

This bodhisattva mahāsattva, by means of the purified divine ear, constantly hears the Dharma teachings of all Buddhas in the ten directions; having heard them, they receive and uphold them without ever forgetting, and proclaim them to all sentient beings exactly as they are.

By means of this purified knowledge of others' minds, these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are able to correctly measure the minds and mental factors of the Buddhas of the ten directions; they are also able to correctly know the minds and mental factors of all bodhisattvas, pratyekabuddhas, and śrāvakas; and they are also able to correctly know the minds and mental factors of all sentient beings, preaching the true Dharma to them according to what is appropriate for each.

By means of the knowledge of recollecting past lives, this bodhisattva mahāsattva knows the various distinctions among the roots of goodness planted by sentient beings in the past; having known them, he employs skillful means to manifest, exhort, encourage, and gladden them, causing them to obtain supreme benefit and peace.
By means of the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows, this bodhisattva mahāsattva establishes sentient beings in the three vehicles according to what is appropriate for them.

This bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom through skillful means, matures sentient beings and purifies buddha-fields; they are swiftly able to fulfill all-aspect omniscience, realize unsurpassed perfect enlightenment, and turn the sublime wheel of Dharma to deliver immeasurable multitudes.

"In this way, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, by means of the power of the mind free from outflows and devoid of all signs, they are able to fulfill the perfection of patience within all signless, non-conceptual, unobtainable, shadowless, and unconditioned phenomena, and they are also able to fulfill all other meritorious qualities."

The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle 376. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Order. Part One: Chapter Sixty-Six, "Signlessness and Non-Attainment," Section Five. "Furthermore, Subhūti!

How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the profound perfection of wisdom, fulfill the perfection of diligence within all phenomena that are signless, without conceptualization, unattainable, shadowless, and non-active?
“Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, they are able to cultivate diligence with a mind that is free from signs and untainted.”

This bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes courageous physical and mental diligence; by means of this, they are able to enter and dwell fully in the first dhyāna, and are able to enter and dwell fully in the second, third, and fourth dhyānas. Relying on the fourth dhyāna, they manifest immeasurable kinds of supernatural transformations, even to the point of touching and stroking the sun and moon with their hands, turning them about at will without finding it difficult.

Because they have accomplished the physical diligence of valor, by means of their supernormal powers they are able to reach immeasurable hundreds of thousands of Buddha-worlds in other directions within a mere moment. Furthermore, with various kinds of superior and exquisite food and drink, clothing, bedding, medicine, incense and flowers, banners and canopies, lamps, precious wealth, and music, they reverently make offerings to, respect, and praise the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones. Through the inexhaustible fruit and retribution of these roots of goodness, they gradually attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Having attained awakening through these roots of goodness, they shall, in turn, be reverently honored, respected, and praised by immeasurable multitudes of worldly devas, humans, and asuras, who will offer them various kinds of supreme and exquisite food and drink, clothing, bedding, medicine, incense, flowers, banners, canopies, lamps, precious wealth, and music.

By virtue of these roots of goodness, even after his parinirvāṇa, his own śarīra relics and his disciples shall still be venerated, honored, respected, and praised by immeasurable worlds of devas, humans, asuras, and others.

"Furthermore, by means of their supernormal powers, these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are able to travel to immeasurable hundreds of thousands of Buddha-worlds in other directions. In the presence of those Buddhas, they listen to the True Dharma; having heard it, they receive and uphold it, never forgetting it until they reach unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

This bodhisattva mahāsattva further employs supernormal powers to bring sentient beings to maturity and to purify buddha-fields; through diligent cultivation and study of the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), once that knowledge of all aspects is perfected, they realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment and turn the sublime wheel of Dharma to deliver immeasurable multitudes.
Thus it is, Subhūti!
Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom and achieves courageous physical diligence, he is able to swiftly bring the perfection of diligence to full completion.
“Subhūti! How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, by virtue of accomplishing a courageous mind of diligence, cause the perfection of diligence to be swiftly fulfilled?”

“Subhūti! Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom and achieves a courageous mind of diligence, they are able to swiftly fulfill the perfection of diligence included within the noble, untainted path and its branches. By means of this, they ensure that no unwholesome actions of body, speech, or mind have any opportunity to arise.”

"This bodhisattva mahāsattva never grasps at or becomes attached to form as being either permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, pure or impure, tranquil or not tranquil, or secluded or not secluded; nor does he grasp at or become attached to feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as being either permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, pure or impure, tranquil or not tranquil, or secluded or not secluded."

"One never grasps at or adheres to the sense base of the eye as being either permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, pure or impure, tranquil or not tranquil, or secluded or not secluded; nor does one grasp at or adhere to the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as being either permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, pure or impure, tranquil or not tranquil, or secluded or not secluded."

"One never grasps at or clings to the sphere of forms as permanent or impermanent, as pleasant or painful, as self or non-self, as pure or impure, as tranquil or not tranquil, or as secluded or not secluded; nor does one grasp at or cling to the spheres of sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena as permanent or impermanent, as pleasant or painful, as self or non-self, as pure or impure, as tranquil or not tranquil, or as secluded or not secluded."

"One never grasps at or adheres to the eye-element as either permanent or impermanent, as pleasant or painful, as self or non-self, as pure or impure, as tranquil or untranquil, or as secluded or unsecluded; nor does one grasp at or adhere to the ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-element as either permanent or impermanent, as pleasant or painful, as self or non-self, as pure or impure, as tranquil or untranquil, or as secluded or unsecluded."

"One never grasps or clings to the realm of form as being either permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, pure or impure, tranquil or not tranquil, or secluded or not secluded; nor does one grasp or cling to the realms of sound, odor, taste, touch, or mental phenomena as being either permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, pure or impure, tranquil or not tranquil, or secluded or not secluded."
"One never grasps at or clings to the eye-consciousness element as permanent or impermanent, as pleasant or painful,
as self or non-self, as pure or impure, as tranquil or untranquil, or as secluded or not secluded;
nor does one grasp at or cling to the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind."
Whether the element of consciousness is permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful,
self or non-self, pure or impure, tranquil or untranquil, detached or undetached—
one will never grasp at or cling to eye-contact as being permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, or self... [and so forth].
Whether it be self or non-self, pure or impure, tranquil or not tranquil,
detached or not detached; nor does one grasp at the contact of the ear, nose, tongue, body,
or mind as being either permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, or pure.
[He does not grasp at] as impure, or as tranquil or untranquil, or as secluded or unsecluded.

He never grasps at the various feelings produced with eye-contact as condition, whether as permanent or impermanent, as pleasant or painful, as self or non-self, as pure or impure, as tranquil or untranquil, or as secluded or unsecluded. Likewise, he does not grasp at the various feelings produced with ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-contact as condition, whether as permanent or impermanent, as pleasant or painful, as self or non-self, as pure or impure, as tranquil or untranquil, or as secluded or unsecluded.

"One never grasps at or adheres to the earth element as permanent or impermanent, as pleasant or painful, as self or non-self, as pure or impure, as tranquil or non-tranquil, or as secluded or non-secluded; nor does one grasp at or adhere to the water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness elements as permanent or impermanent, as pleasant or painful, as self or non-self, as pure or impure, as tranquil or non-tranquil, or as secluded or non-secluded."

"One never grasps or clings to conditions as being either permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, pure or impure, tranquil or untranquil, or secluded or unsecluded; nor does one grasp or cling to the immediately preceding condition, the object condition, or the dominant condition as being either permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, pure or impure, tranquil or untranquil, or secluded or unsecluded."

"One never grasps at ignorance as being either permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, pure or impure, tranquil or untranquil, or secluded or not secluded; nor does one grasp at volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, existence, birth, or old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair as being either permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, pure or impure, tranquil or untranquil, or secluded or not secluded."

"One never clings to the conditioned realm (*saṃskṛtadhātu*) as permanent or impermanent, as pleasant or painful, as self or non-self, as pure or impure, as tranquil or untranquil, or as secluded or unsecluded; nor does one cling to the unconditioned realm (*asaṃskṛtadhātu*) as permanent or impermanent, as pleasant or painful, as self or non-self, as pure or impure, as tranquil or untranquil, or as secluded or unsecluded."

"One never grasps at or clings to the desire realm as either permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, pure or impure, tranquil or non-tranquil, or secluded or non-secluded; nor does one grasp at or cling to the form and formless realms as either permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, pure or impure, tranquil or non-tranquil, or secluded or non-secluded."

"One never grasps at or clings to the tainted realm (*sāsravadhātu*) as being either permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, pure or impure, tranquil or not tranquil, or secluded or not secluded; nor does one grasp at or cling to the untainted realm (*anāsravadhātu*) as being either permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, pure or impure, tranquil or not tranquil, or secluded or not secluded."

He never grasps at or clings to the first dhyāna as permanent or impermanent, as pleasant or painful, as self or non-self, as pure or impure, as peaceful or not peaceful, or as secluded or not secluded; nor does he grasp at or cling to the second, third, or fourth dhyānas as permanent or impermanent, as pleasant or painful, as self or non-self, as pure or impure, as peaceful or not peaceful, or as secluded or not secluded.

"One never grasps at or adheres to the immeasurable loving-kindness as being either permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, pure or impure, tranquil or untranquil, or secluded or unsecluded; nor does one grasp at or adhere to the immeasurable compassion, sympathetic joy, or equanimity as being either permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, pure or impure, tranquil or untranquil, or secluded or unsecluded."

"One never grasps at or clings to the concentration of the base of infinite space as permanent or impermanent, as pleasant or painful, as self or non-self, as pure or impure, as peaceful or not peaceful, or as secluded or not secluded; nor does one grasp at or cling to the concentrations of the base of infinite consciousness, the base of nothingness, or the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception as permanent or impermanent, as pleasant or painful, as self or non-self, as pure or impure, as peaceful or not peaceful, or as secluded or not secluded."

"One never grasps at or adheres to the four foundations of mindfulness as being either permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, pure or impure, peaceful or not peaceful, or secluded or not secluded; nor does one grasp at or adhere to the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, or the eightfold noble path as being either permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, pure or impure, peaceful or not peaceful, or secluded or not secluded."

"One never grasps at or adheres to the liberation door of emptiness as being either permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, pure or impure, tranquil or not tranquil, or secluded or not secluded; nor does one grasp at or adhere to the liberation doors of signlessness and wishlessness as being either permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, pure or impure, tranquil or not tranquil, or secluded or not secluded."

"One never grasps at or clings to the perfection of generosity as being either permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, pure or impure, tranquil or not tranquil, or secluded or not secluded; nor does one grasp at or cling to the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, or wisdom as being either permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, pure or impure, tranquil or not tranquil, or secluded or not secluded."
"One never grasps at internal emptiness as permanent or impermanent,
as pleasant or painful, as self or non-self, as pure or impure, as tranquil or not tranquil, or as secluded or not secluded;
nor does one grasp at external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, or the emptiness of emptiness."
Great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, emptiness of dispersion, emptiness of non-alteration,
emptiness of intrinsic nature, emptiness of self-characteristics, emptiness of common characteristics,
emptiness of all phenomena, emptiness of non-apprehensibility, emptiness of non-existence, and emptiness of intrinsic nature.
The emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence is neither permanent nor impermanent, neither pleasant nor painful,
neither self nor non-self, neither pure nor impure, neither tranquil nor non-tranquil,
and neither detached nor non-detached.

"One never grasps at or clings to true suchness as being either permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, pure or impure, tranquil or non-tranquil, or secluded or non-secluded. Nor does one grasp at or cling to the dharma-realm, the nature of phenomena, the non-falsity of phenomena, the unchanging nature of phenomena, equality, the state beyond birth, the fixed nature of phenomena, the stability of phenomena, the limit of reality, the realm of space, or the inconceivable realm—whether as permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, pure or impure, tranquil or non-tranquil, or secluded or non-secluded."

"One never grasps or clings to the noble truth of suffering as permanent or impermanent, as pleasant or painful, as self or non-self, as pure or impure, as tranquil or untranquil, or as secluded or non-secluded; nor does one grasp or cling to the noble truths of origin, cessation, and the path as permanent or impermanent, as pleasant or painful, as self or non-self, as pure or impure, as tranquil or untranquil, or as secluded or non-secluded."

"One never grasps at or adheres to the eight liberations as being permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, pure or impure, tranquil or untranquil, or secluded or unsecluded; nor does one grasp at or adhere to the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, or the ten totalities as being permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, pure or impure, tranquil or untranquil, or secluded or unsecluded."

"He never grasps at or clings to any gate of samādhi as being either permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, pure or impure, tranquil or untranquil, or detached or undetached; nor does he grasp at or cling to any gate of dhāraṇī as being either permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, pure or impure, tranquil or untranquil, or detached or undetached."

"One never grasps at or clings to the five eyes as permanent or impermanent, as pleasant or painful, as self or non-self, as pure or impure, as tranquil or not tranquil, or as secluded or not secluded; nor does one grasp at or cling to the six supernormal powers as permanent or impermanent, as pleasant or painful, as self or non-self, as pure or impure, as tranquil or not tranquil, or as secluded or not secluded."

"One never grasps at or adheres to the ten powers of a Buddha as being either permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, pure or impure, tranquil or not tranquil, or secluded or not secluded; nor does one grasp at or adhere to the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, or the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha as being either permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, pure or impure, tranquil or not tranquil, or secluded or not secluded."

"One never grasps at or clings to Great Loving-kindness as being permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, pure or impure, tranquil or not tranquil, or secluded or not secluded; nor does one grasp at or cling to Great Compassion, Great Sympathetic Joy, or Great Equanimity as being permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, pure or impure, tranquil or not tranquil, or secluded or not secluded."

"One never grasps at or becomes attached to the quality of non-forgetfulness as being either permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, pure or impure, tranquil or untranquil, or secluded or unsecluded; nor does one grasp at or become attached to the nature of constant equanimity as being either permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, pure or impure, tranquil or untranquil, or secluded or unsecluded."

"One never grasps at or adheres to all-knowledge as being either permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, pure or impure, tranquil or not tranquil, or secluded or not secluded; nor does one grasp at or adhere to the knowledge of the paths or the knowledge of all aspects as being either permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, pure or impure, tranquil or not tranquil, or secluded or not secluded."
