"One never grasps at or adheres to the fruit of stream-entry as being either permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, pure or impure, tranquil or not tranquil, or secluded or not secluded; nor does one grasp at or adhere to the fruits of once-returning, non-returning, or arhatship, or to the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, as being either permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, pure or impure, tranquil or not tranquil, or secluded or not secluded."

"One never grasps at or clings to any of the practices of a bodhisattva mahāsattva—whether as permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, pure or impure, tranquil or non-tranquil, or secluded or non-secluded; nor does one grasp at or cling to the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas—whether as permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, pure or impure, tranquil or non-tranquil, or secluded or non-secluded."

"This bodhisattva mahāsattva never grasps at or adheres to the notion that 'this is a stream-enterer,' 'this is a once-returner,' 'this is a non-returner,' 'this is an arhat,' 'this is a pratyekabuddha,' 'this is a bodhisattva,' or 'this is a Tathāgata. Nor does he grasp at the view that a sentient being is called a 'stream-enterer' because they are endowed with such a vision; nor that a sentient being is called a 'once-returner' because their lower fetters are attenuated; nor that a sentient being is called a 'non-returner' because their lower fetters are exhausted; nor that a sentient being is called an 'arhat' because their higher fetters are exhausted; nor that a sentient being is called a 'pratyekabuddha' because they have attained the path of a pratyekabuddha; nor that a sentient being is called a 'bodhisattva' because they have attained the knowledge of the aspects of the path; nor that a sentient being is called a 'Tathāgata' because they have attained all-aspect omniscience."
Why is this? Because the dharmas that are grasped and all sentient beings lack any intrinsic nature that can be grasped.

"Because this bodhisattva-mahāsattva has accomplished a courageous mind of diligence, although he performs deeds to benefit all sentient beings without regard for his own body or life, he apprehends no sentient beings at all."
Although they can bring the perfection of diligence to fulfillment, they do not apprehend the perfection of diligence at all;
although they can fulfill all Buddha-dharmas, they do not apprehend any Buddha-dharma at all;
although they can adorn and purify all Buddha-fields, they do not apprehend any Buddha-field at all.

This bodhisattva mahāsattva, having accomplished such physical and mental diligence, is able to remain far removed from all unwholesome dharmas and is also able to embrace all wholesome dharmas without attachment.

Because they are free from grasping and attachment, they travel from one buddha-field to another buddha-field and from one world-system to another world-system; for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, whatever supernormal feats they wish to manifest, they are able to display them with mastery and without obstruction.

That is to say, they may manifest the raining down of various exquisite flowers; or again, they may manifest the scattering of various renowned incenses; or again, they may manifest the performance of various musical instruments; or again, they may manifest the shaking of the great earth; or again, they may manifest worlds adorned with various exquisite seven-jeweled treasures.
Alternatively, he may manifest his body emitting radiance, so that sentient beings in blindness and darkness are all granted illumination and understanding.
Alternatively, he may manifest his body producing wondrous fragrances, causing all who are foul and impure to become fragrant and pure.

Or again, they may manifest the performance of great sacrificial rites, yet within them they do not afflict any sentient beings; through this, they guide and transform boundless sentient beings, causing them to enter the right path and to abstain from taking life, abstain from taking what is not given, abstain from sexual misconduct, abstain from false speech, abstain from divisive speech, abstain from harsh speech, abstain from frivolous speech, abstain from covetousness, abstain from malice, and abstain from wrong views.

Either they gather sentient beings through generosity, or they gather sentient beings through ethical discipline, or they gather sentient beings through patience, or they gather sentient beings through diligence, or they gather sentient beings through meditative concentration, or they gather sentient beings through wisdom.

For the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, they may relinquish wealth and treasures, or relinquish wife and children, or relinquish royal sovereignty, or relinquish their limbs and members, or relinquish their very body and life.
According to whatever means are appropriate to benefit each sentient being, he benefits them by employing those very same means.

"So it is, Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, by means of the power of the mind that is free from all signs and untainted, they are able to fulfill the perfection of diligence within all signless, non-conceptual, unattainable, shadowless, and unconditioned phenomena, and they are likewise able to fulfill all other meritorious qualities."
"Furthermore, Subhūti, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva,

when practicing the profound perfection of wisdom, fulfill the perfection of meditative concentration within all phenomena that are signless, without conceptualization, unattainable, shadowless, and non-active?
“Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, they are able to cultivate meditative concentration with a mind that is free from signs and untainted.”

This bodhisattva mahāsattva, with the exception of the concentration of the Tathāgata, is able to bring all other concentrations to full perfection. This bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to leave behind sensual desires and unwholesome states; possessing applied thought and sustained thought, and experiencing the joy and happiness born of seclusion, he enters and dwells in the first dhyāna, having attained it in its completeness.

With the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, and with internal clarity and mental unification, being without applied or sustained thought, he experiences the joy and happiness born of concentration; he enters and dwells in the second dhyāna, having attained it in its completeness.

Free from joy, he dwells in equanimity, mindful and clearly aware, experiencing happiness with the body—of which the Noble Ones say, "One who is equanimous and mindful dwells happily"—he enters and dwells in the third dhyāna, having attained it in its completeness.

With the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and sorrow, he enters and dwells in the fourth dhyāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant and possesses purity of equanimity and mindfulness.
This bodhisattva-mahāsattva dwells pervasively throughout one direction, and even throughout all worlds in the ten directions, with a mind imbued with loving-kindness;
he dwells pervasively throughout one direction, and even throughout all worlds in the ten directions, with a mind imbued with compassion;
he dwells pervasively throughout one direction, and even throughout all worlds in the ten directions, with a mind imbued with sympathetic joy.
With a mind accompanied by equanimity, he dwells pervading one direction, and so on, up to all ten directions, suffusing the entire world.

This bodhisattva mahāsattva transcends all perceptions of form, extinguishes perceptions of sensory resistance, and does not attend to perceptions of diversity; he enters the sphere of infinite space and dwells, having fully attained the sphere of infinite space.
Transcending every kind of sphere of infinite space, he enters the sphere of infinite consciousness and dwells, having fully attained the sphere of infinite consciousness.
Transcending the sphere of infinite consciousness in every respect, he enters and dwells, having fully attained, the sphere of nothingness;
transcending the sphere of nothingness in every respect, he enters and dwells, having fully attained, the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

This bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling securely in the perfection of meditative concentration, is able to enter the eight liberations in both forward and reverse order, abiding fully therein; he is able to enter the eight bases of mastery in both forward and reverse order, abiding fully therein; he is able to enter the nine successive attainments in both forward and reverse order, abiding fully therein; and he is able to enter the ten totalities in both forward and reverse order, abiding fully therein.

This bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to enter the samādhi of emptiness and dwell therein in its full perfection; enter the samādhi of signlessness and dwell therein in its full perfection; enter the samādhi of wishlessness and dwell therein in its full perfection; enter the uninterrupted samādhi and dwell therein in its full perfection; enter the lightning-like samādhi and dwell therein in its full perfection; enter the noble right samādhi and dwell therein in its full perfection; and enter the vajra-like samādhi and dwell therein in its full perfection.

"This bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling securely in the perfection of meditative concentration, cultivates the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment and the knowledge of the aspects of the path, bringing them all to full completion."

Having embraced all samādhis through the knowledge of the aspects of the path, one gradually cultivates and transcends the stage of pure observation, the stage of the spiritual lineage, the eighth stage, the stage of seeing, the stage of refinement, the stage of freedom from desire, the stage of completion, and the stage of the pratyekabuddha; having entered the bodhisattva’s state of rightness and departure from birth, and once established in that state of rightness and departure from birth, one cultivates the practices of the stages until the Buddha-stage is perfected.

Although this bodhisattva mahāsattva gradually cultivates and transcends the various stages, they do not realize the fruit of fruition in the interim until they have attained all-aspect omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*).

"This bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling securely in the perfection of meditative concentration, travels from one buddha-field to another, making offerings to, honoring, respecting, and praising the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones; in the presence of those Buddhas, he plants many roots of goodness, matures sentient beings, and purifies buddha-fields."
Proceeding from one world-system to another world-system, they benefit sentient beings with bodies and minds free from weariness;
they may gather sentient beings through generosity, or gather them through ethical discipline,
or gather them through patience, or gather them through diligence, or gather them through meditative concentration.
Sentient beings, or those who gather sentient beings through wisdom (*prajñā*), or those who gather sentient beings through liberation (*vimukti*),

or those who gather sentient beings through the knowledge and vision of liberation (*vimukti-jñāna-darśana*); or those who teach sentient beings to abide in the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*),
or those who teach sentient beings to abide in the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmi-phala*), or those who teach sentient beings to abide in the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmi-phala*), or...
They instruct sentient beings to abide in the fruit of arhatship, or instruct them to abide in the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha,
or instruct them to dwell securely in the stage of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, or instruct them to dwell securely in unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment;
according to the power of the roots of goodness of each sentient being, various wholesome dharmas increase.
By means of skillful methods, he causes them to dwell securely.

"This bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling securely in the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyānapāramitā), is able to bring forth all gateways of samādhi, is able to bring forth all gateways of dhāraṇī, is able to attain the four supreme analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid), and is able to attain the supreme supernormal powers (abhijñā) resulting from karmic maturation."

By virtue of having attained these extraordinary supernormal powers as a result of karmic maturation, this bodhisattva mahāsattva will certainly never again enter a mother’s womb, will certainly never again experience the pleasure of sexual desire, will certainly never again take up rebirth in the vehicles, and will likewise never be defiled by the faults of birth.
Why is this? Because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas clearly perceive and thoroughly penetrate that the nature of all phenomena is entirely like an illusion or a magical transformation.
Although they know that all conditioned formations are like illusions and transformations, they benefit sentient beings by means of their compassionate vows.
Although they benefit sentient beings by riding upon compassionate vows, they realize that both sentient beings and their designations are unapprehendable.

Although they realize that both sentient beings and their designations are unapprehendable, they are nevertheless able to establish all sentient beings, causing them to abide in the dharma of non-apprehensibility; this is done by relying on conventional truth, not ultimate truth.

This bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling securely in the perfection of meditative concentration, practices all dhyānas, liberations, samādhis, and attainments; until they fully realize the unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment they seek, they never abandon the perfection of meditative concentration they have cultivated.

This bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the knowledge of the aspects of the path, skillfully brings forth the knowledge of all aspects, and abiding therein, forever severs the continuity of all habitual tendencies.
Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to forever sever the continuity of all habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), they are able to correctly benefit themselves and correctly benefit others.

Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to correctly benefit themselves and correctly benefit others, they become a pure field of merit for all the world—including its devas, humans, and asuras—and are worthy of receiving the offerings and respect of all the world—including its devas, humans, and asuras.

"In this way, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, by means of the power of the mind free from outflows and devoid of all signs, they are able to fulfill the perfection of meditative concentration within all signless, non-conceptual, unattainable, shadowless, and unconditioned phenomena, and they are likewise able to fulfill all other meritorious qualities."
"Furthermore, Subhūti, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva,

when practicing the profound perfection of wisdom, fulfill the perfection of wisdom within all things that are signless, without conceptualization, without attainment, without shadow, and without conditioned activity?"

“Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, they cultivate wisdom with a mind that is free from signs and untainted; this bodhisattva mahāsattva does not perceive even the slightest phenomenon as truly existent or established.”
That is to say: one does not see form as truly existent or established; one does not see feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness as truly existent or established;
one does not see the arising of form, nor the arising of feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness;
one does not see the cessation of form, nor the cessation of feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness.
Not seeing form is a gate of augmentation; not seeing feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness is a gate of augmentation.
Not seeing form is a gate of diminution; not seeing feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness is a gate of diminution.
Not seeing form as having accumulation; not seeing feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness as having accumulation.
He does not see form as having disintegration; he does not see feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as having disintegration.

He contemplates form as it truly is: as false, unsubstantial, and lacking self-mastery; he contemplates feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as they truly are: as false, unsubstantial, and lacking self-mastery.
“He does not perceive the eye-base as truly existent or established; he does not perceive the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind-base as truly existent or established.
He does not perceive the arising of the eye-base; he does not perceive the arising of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind-base.
He does not perceive the cessation of the eye-base; he does not perceive the cessation of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind-base.”
Not seeing the eye-base as a door of augmentation; not seeing the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind-bases as doors of augmentation.
Not seeing the eye-base as a door of diminution; not seeing the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind-bases as doors of diminution.
Not seeing the accumulation of the eye-base; not seeing the accumulation of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind-bases.
One does not see the sense-base of the eye as having disintegration; one does not see the sense-bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as having disintegration.

One contemplates the sense-base of the eye as it truly is: as false, unsubstantial, and lacking autonomy; one contemplates the sense-bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind as they truly are: as false, unsubstantial, and lacking autonomy.
"One does not see the sphere of form as truly existent or established; one does not see the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, or mental objects as truly existent or established.
One does not see the arising of the sphere of form; one does not see the arising of the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, or mental objects.
One does not see the cessation of the sphere of form; one does not see the cessation of the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, or mental objects."
Not seeing the sphere of form is a gate of augmentation; not seeing the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena is a gate of augmentation.
Not seeing the sphere of form is a gate of diminution; not seeing the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena is a gate of diminution.
Not seeing the accumulation of the sphere of form, and not seeing the accumulation of the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena;
One does not perceive the sphere of form as having disintegration; one does not perceive the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, or mental phenomena as having disintegration.

One contemplates the sphere of form as it truly is: as false, unsubstantial, and lacking self-mastery; one contemplates the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena as they truly are: as false, unsubstantial, and lacking self-mastery.
"One does not perceive the eye-element as truly existent or established; one does not perceive the ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-element as truly existent or established.
One does not perceive the arising of the eye-element, nor the arising of the ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-element.
One does not perceive the cessation of the eye-element, nor the cessation of the ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-element."
Not seeing the eye-element as a door of increase; not seeing the ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-element as a door of increase.
Not seeing the eye-element as a door of decrease; not seeing the ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-element as a door of decrease.
Not seeing the accumulation of the eye-element; not seeing the accumulation of the ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-element.
He does not perceive the eye-element as having dispersal; he does not perceive the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind-element as having dispersal.

He contemplates the eye-element as it truly is: as false, unsubstantial, and lacking autonomy; he contemplates the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-elements as they truly are: as false, unsubstantial, and lacking autonomy.
"One does not perceive the color realm as truly existent or established; one does not perceive the realms of sound, odor, taste, touch, or mental phenomena as truly existent or established.
One does not perceive the arising of the color realm; one does not perceive the arising of the realms of sound, odor, taste, touch, or mental phenomena.
One does not perceive the cessation of the color realm; one does not perceive the cessation of the realms of sound, odor, taste, touch, or mental phenomena."
One does not perceive the realm of form as a gate of augmentation, nor does one perceive the realms of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, or mental phenomena as gates of augmentation;
one does not perceive the realm of form as a gate of diminution, nor does one perceive the realms of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, or mental phenomena as gates of diminution;
one does not perceive the realm of form as having accumulation, nor does one perceive the realms of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, or mental phenomena as having accumulation.
One does not perceive the realm of form as having disintegration; one does not perceive the realms of sound, odor, taste, touch, or mental phenomena as having disintegration.

One contemplates the realm of form as it truly is: as false, unsubstantial, and lacking self-mastery; one contemplates the realms of sound, odor, taste, touch, and mental phenomena as they truly are: as false, unsubstantial, and lacking self-mastery.

"One does not perceive the eye-consciousness element as truly existent or established; one does not perceive the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind-consciousness elements as truly existent or established.
One does not perceive the arising of the eye-consciousness element; one does not perceive the arising of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind-consciousness elements.
One does not perceive the cessation of the eye-consciousness element; one does not perceive the cessation of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind-consciousness elements."
Not perceiving the eye-consciousness element as a door of increase; not perceiving the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind-consciousness elements as doors of increase.
Not perceiving the eye-consciousness element as a door of decrease; not perceiving the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind-consciousness elements as doors of decrease.
Not perceiving the accumulation of the eye-consciousness element; not perceiving the accumulation of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind-consciousness elements.
He does not perceive the eye-consciousness element as having any disintegration; he does not perceive the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind-consciousness elements as having any disintegration.

He contemplates the eye-consciousness element as it truly is: as false, unsubstantial, and lacking self-mastery; he contemplates the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-consciousness elements as they truly are: as false, unsubstantial, and lacking self-mastery.
"One does not perceive the eye-contact as truly existent or established; one does not perceive the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind-contact as truly existent or established.
One does not perceive the arising of eye-contact; one does not perceive the arising of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind-contact.
One does not perceive the cessation of eye-contact; one does not perceive the cessation of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind-contact."
One does not perceive eye-contact as a door of augmentation, nor does one perceive ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-contact as a door of augmentation;
one does not perceive eye-contact as a door of diminution, nor does one perceive ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-contact as a door of diminution;
one does not perceive eye-contact as having accumulation, nor does one perceive ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-contact as having accumulation.
One does not perceive the eye-contact as having any separation; one does not perceive the ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-contact as having any separation.

One contemplates eye-contact as it truly is: as false, unsubstantial, and lacking autonomy; one contemplates the ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact as they truly are: as false, unsubstantial, and lacking autonomy.

He does not perceive the sensation produced with eye-contact as its condition as being truly existent or established; he does not perceive the sensations produced with ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-contact as their conditions as being truly existent or established.

He does not perceive the arising of the sensation produced with eye-contact as its condition; he does not perceive the arising of the sensations produced with ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-contact as their conditions.

He does not perceive the cessation of the sensation produced with eye-contact as its condition; he does not perceive the cessation of the sensations produced with ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-contact as their conditions.

Not seeing the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition as a door of superimposition; not seeing the various feelings produced with ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind-contact as conditions as a door of superimposition.

Not seeing the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition as a door of deprecation; not seeing the various feelings produced with ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind-contact as conditions as a door of deprecation.

Not seeing the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition as having accumulation; not seeing the various feelings produced with ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind-contact as conditions as having accumulation.

One does not perceive any sensations produced with eye-contact as a condition as having disintegration; one does not perceive any sensations produced with ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind-contact as conditions as having disintegration.

One contemplates, in accordance with reality, that all feelings arising conditioned by eye-contact are illusory, unsubstantial, and lacking self-mastery; one contemplates, in accordance with reality, that all feelings arising conditioned by ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact are likewise illusory, unsubstantial, and lacking self-mastery.

"One does not perceive the actual existence or establishment of any contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*); one does not perceive the actual existence or establishment of any uncontaminated phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*).
One does not perceive the arising of any contaminated phenomena; one does not perceive the arising of any uncontaminated phenomena.
One does not perceive the cessation of any contaminated phenomena; one does not perceive the cessation of any uncontaminated phenomena."
One does not perceive any contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) as a door of increase, nor does one perceive any uncontaminated phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*) as a door of increase;
one does not perceive any contaminated phenomena as a door of decrease, nor does one perceive any uncontaminated phenomena as a door of decrease;
one does not perceive any contaminated phenomena as having accumulation, nor does one perceive any uncontaminated phenomena as having accumulation.
One does not perceive any outflowing phenomena (*sāsravadharma*) as having disintegration, nor does one perceive any non-outflowing phenomena (*anāsravadharma*) as having disintegration.

One contemplates all outflowing phenomena as they truly are: as false, unsubstantial, and lacking self-mastery; one contemplates all non-outflowing phenomena as they truly are: as false, unsubstantial, and lacking self-mastery.

"When this bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates in this manner, he does not apprehend the intrinsic nature of form; he does not apprehend the intrinsic nature of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
He does not apprehend the intrinsic nature of the sense base of the eye; he does not apprehend the intrinsic nature of the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind.
He does not apprehend the intrinsic nature of the sense base of forms; he does not apprehend the intrinsic nature of the sense bases of sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena."
One does not apprehend the intrinsic nature of the eye-element; one does not apprehend the intrinsic nature of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind-element.
One does not apprehend the intrinsic nature of the form-element; one does not apprehend the intrinsic nature of the sound, odor, taste, tangible, or mental-object-element.
One does not apprehend the intrinsic nature of the eye-consciousness-element; one does not apprehend the intrinsic nature of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind-consciousness-element.
One does not apprehend the intrinsic nature of eye-contact; one does not apprehend the intrinsic nature of ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-contact.

One does not apprehend the intrinsic nature of the various feelings produced with eye-contact as condition; one does not apprehend the intrinsic nature of the various feelings produced with ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-contact as condition.
One does not apprehend the intrinsic nature of any contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomena; one does not apprehend the intrinsic nature of any uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) phenomena.
"This bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, develops deep faith and understanding that all phenomena have non-existence as their intrinsic nature."

Once this bodhisattva mahāsattva has given rise to faith and understanding regarding such matters, they are able to practice internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, non-altering emptiness, essential emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common-characteristic emptiness, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature.

"When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices in this manner, they do not cling to any phenomena whatsoever; that is to say, they do not cling to form, nor do they cling to feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness;
they do not cling to the sense base of the eye, nor do they cling to the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind;
they do not cling to the sense base of forms, nor do they cling to the sense bases of sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental objects."
They do not cling to the eye-element; they do not cling to the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind-element.
They do not cling to the form-element; they do not cling to the sound, odor, taste, tangible, or mental-object-element.
They do not cling to the eye-consciousness-element; they do not cling to the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind-consciousness-element.
They do not cling to eye-contact; they do not cling to ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-contact.
They do not cling to the various feelings produced with eye-contact as condition; they do not cling to the various feelings produced with ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-contact as condition.
They do not cling to the earth element; they do not cling to the water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness elements.

They do not cling to the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*); they do not cling to the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), or the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).

They do not cling to ignorance (*avidyā*); they do not cling to volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), consciousness (*vijñāna*), name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), contact (*sparśa*), feeling (*vedanā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), becoming (*bhava*), birth (*jāti*), or old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair (*jarāmaraṇa-śoka-parideva-duḥkha-daurmanasyopāyāsa*).

They do not cling to the perfection of generosity (*dāna-pāramitā*); they do not cling to the perfections of ethical discipline (*śīla*), patience (*kṣānti*), diligence (*vīrya*), meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), or wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*).

They do not cling to internal emptiness; they do not cling to external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, non-alteration emptiness, essential emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common-characteristic emptiness, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, or the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature.

They do not cling to suchness; they do not cling to the dharma-realm, the dharma-nature, non-falsity, non-alteration, equality, the state beyond birth, the fixed nature of dharmas, the stability of dharmas, the limit of reality, the realm of space, or the inconceivable realm.

They do not cling to the four foundations of mindfulness; they do not cling to the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, or the eightfold noble path;
they do not cling to the noble truth of suffering, nor do they cling to the noble truths of origin, cessation, or the path;
they do not cling to the four dhyānas, nor do they cling to the four immeasurables or the four formless attainments.
They do not cling to the eight liberations; they do not cling to the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative attainments, or the ten universal bases;
they do not cling to any gateways of samādhi, nor do they cling to any gateways of dhāraṇī;
they do not cling to the gateway of emptiness, nor do they cling to the gateways of signlessness and wishlessness.
They do not cling to the five eyes; they do not cling to the six supernormal powers;
they do not cling to the ten powers of a Buddha, nor to the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, or the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
they do not cling to great loving-kindness, nor to great compassion, great sympathetic joy, or great equanimity.

The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle 377. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Part One: Chapter Sixty-Six, Part Six: On Non-Attachment and Non-Forgetfulness. "One does not cling to the quality of non-forgetfulness, nor does one cling to the nature of constant equanimity;
one does not cling to all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), nor does one cling to the knowledge of the paths (*mārgākārajñatā*) or the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*);
one does not cling to the fruit of stream-entry, nor does one cling to the fruits of once-returning, non-returning, arhatship, or the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha."
They do not cling to any of the practices of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, nor do they cling to the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas.
When these bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, which has non-existence as its intrinsic nature, they are able to fulfill the bodhisattva path;
that is, they are able to fulfill generosity, ethical discipline, and so forth.
The perfections of patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom can also bring to fulfillment internal emptiness,
external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness,
conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, and non-existence...
They can also fulfill the emptiness of change, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, the emptiness of self-characteristics,
the emptiness of common characteristics, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature,
and the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence; as well as True Suchness, the Dharma-realm, the Dharma-nature, non-falsity, and immutability.
They can also fulfill the otherness, equality, nature of non-arising, fixedness of phenomena, stability of phenomena,
the limit of reality, the realm of space, and the inconceivable realm; as well as the four foundations of mindfulness,
the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path.
They can also fulfill the noble truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path;
they can also fulfill the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments;
they can also fulfill the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities; and they can also fulfill all three...
They can also fulfill the doors of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and the doors of dhāraṇī;
they can also fulfill the gates of liberation of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; they can also fulfill the five eyes and the six supernormal powers;
and they can also fulfill the ten powers of a Buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
They are also able to fulfill great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity;
they are also able to fulfill the quality of non-forgetfulness and the state of constant dwelling in equanimity;
they are also able to fulfill all-knowledge, the knowledge of the paths, and the knowledge of all aspects; they are also able to fulfill the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty...
Regarding the secondary marks:
"This bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling within the path to enlightenment consisting of the dharma of maturation,
is further able to fulfill the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom."
Furthermore, they are also able to fulfill internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness,
the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness,
absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, non-alteration emptiness, essential nature emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, and common characteristic emptiness.
Emptiness, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature,
and the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence; they are also able to fulfill suchness,
the dharma-realm, the dharma-nature, non-falsity, immutability, equality, the state beyond birth, and the fixed nature of dharmas.
The stability of phenomena, the limit of reality, the realm of space, and the inconceivable realm can likewise bring to fulfillment the four foundations of mindfulness,
the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers,
the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path; they can also bring to fulfillment the noble truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.
Furthermore, they are able to fulfill the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments;
they are also able to fulfill the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities;
they are also able to fulfill all doors of samādhi and dhāraṇī, and they are also able to fulfill emptiness.
...the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness, and is also able to fulfill immeasurable merits such as the five eyes and the six supernormal powers.

Once this bodhisattva mahāsattva has perfected such a path to enlightenment, they dwell within the Buddha-way, free from all obscurations of darkness. By means of the superior power of supernormal faculties born of karmic maturation, they skillfully benefit all classes of sentient beings: those who should be gathered through generosity, they gather through generosity; [and so forth].
Those who should be gathered through pure ethical discipline, they gather through pure ethical discipline;
those who should be gathered through patience, they gather through patience;
those who should be gathered through diligence, they gather through diligence.
Those who should be gathered through meditative concentration, he gathers them through meditative concentration;
those who should be gathered through wisdom, he gathers them through wisdom;
those who should be gathered through liberation, he gathers them through liberation.
Those who should be sustained by the knowledge and vision of liberation, they sustain with the knowledge and vision of liberation;
those who should be established in the fruit of stream-entry, they employ skillful means to establish them in the fruit of stream-entry;
those who should be established in the fruit of once-returning, they employ skillful means to establish them in the fruit of once-returning.
Those who should be established in the fruit of non-returning, he uses skillful means to establish them in the fruit of non-returning;
those who should be established in the fruit of arhatship, he uses skillful means to establish them in the fruit of arhatship;
those who should be established in the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, he uses skillful means to establish them in the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha.
Those who should be established in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, he skillfully causes to dwell in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
This bodhisattva-mahāsattva is able to perform various supernatural transformations; if he wishes to go to worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, he can go there at will;
if he wishes to manifest various kinds of precious jewels within those worlds he visits, he can manifest them at will.

Desiring that sentient beings in all the worlds they visit may enjoy a multitude of wondrous and precious jewels, and that they may have their every wish fulfilled according to their inclinations—this bodhisattva mahāsattva travels from one world to another, benefiting and bringing peace and happiness to immeasurable sentient beings. Seeing the signs of adornment and purity in these worlds, they are able to personally appropriate a pure Buddha-field according to their own wishes.

Just as all the various exquisite articles of pleasure required by the gods of the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Emanations appear according to their minds, so too does a bodhisattva, according to his will, take possession of various kinds of adorned and pure, immeasurable buddha-fields.

"Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva possesses the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom born of maturation, as well as the various sublime supernormal powers born of maturation, and the bodhisattva path born of maturation, they practice the knowledge of the aspects of the paths."

Because they have attained maturation through the knowledge of the paths, they are further able to realize the knowledge of all aspects. By attaining this knowledge, they do not grasp at any phenomena; that is to say, they do not grasp at form, nor do they grasp at feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness;
they do not grasp at the sense base of the eye, nor do they grasp at the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind;
they do not grasp at the sense base of forms, nor do they grasp at the sense bases of sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena.
They do not grasp at the eye-element; they do not grasp at the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind-element.
They do not grasp at the form-element; they do not grasp at the sound, odor, taste, tangible, or mental-object-element.
They do not grasp at the eye-consciousness-element; they do not grasp at the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind-consciousness-element.
One does not grasp at eye-contact; one does not grasp at ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-contact.
One does not grasp at the various feelings produced with eye-contact as condition, nor does one grasp at the various feelings produced with ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-contact as condition.

One does not grasp at any phenomena—whether wholesome or unwholesome, mundane or supramundane, outflowing or non-outflowing, conditioned or unconditioned, faulty or faultless—and likewise does not grasp at the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening that is realized, nor does one grasp at any objects of enjoyment in any buddha-field, nor even at the sentient beings therein.

Why is this? Because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have not previously grasped at any phenomena, because they find nothing to be apprehended among all phenomena, and because they correctly proclaim to all sentient beings that the nature of all phenomena is without grasping.

"In this way, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, by means of the power of the mind that is free from all marks and untainted, they are able to fulfill the perfection of wisdom within all things that are markless, without conceptualization, without attainment, without shadow, and without conditioned activity; they are also able to fulfill all other meritorious qualities."
Chapter Sixty-Seven: On the Meaning of Unmixed Dharmas, Part One. At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”

How can one fully cultivate the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom amidst all phenomena that are unmixed, signless, and empty of intrinsic nature?
How is it that within all untainted (anāsrava) phenomena, which are without differentiation, such distinctions among phenomena are established and can be understood?
How is it that within the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), all the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence,
meditative concentration, and wisdom are subsumed, and how is the one [perfection] subsumed?
All internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness,
great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, non-alteration emptiness,
essential nature emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common characteristic emptiness, and the emptiness of all phenomena.
Emptiness, the emptiness of non-apprehensibility, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature,
and the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence encompass all suchness, the dharma-realm, the dharma-nature, non-falsity,
non-alteration, equality, the state beyond birth, the fixedness of phenomena, the stability of phenomena, and the limit of reality.

...the realm of space, and the inconceivable realm; they encompass all the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path;
they encompass all the gateways to liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; they encompass the one...
They encompass all the noble truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path;
they encompass all the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments;
they encompass all the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities; and they encompass all the gateways of samādhi and dhāraṇīs.
The gateway of the *nirukti* (linguistic analysis) encompasses all five eyes and six supernormal powers;

it encompasses all the ten powers of a Buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; it encompasses all the qualities of non-forgetfulness.
Does the state of constant abiding in equanimity encompass all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*),
and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), and does it encompass all mundane and supramundane phenomena?

How is it that one designates a single characteristic—namely, the characteristic of signlessness—within all phenomena that possess diverse characteristics; and how does one designate various differentiated phenomenal characteristics within phenomena that possess a single characteristic or are signless?

The Buddha said, “Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, they abide within the five aggregates of clinging— which are like a dream, like an echo, like a reflection, like a shadow, like a mirage, like a magical illusion, like a city of gandharvas, and like a transformation— and they practice the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, truly understanding that these five aggregates of clinging, which are like a dream, an echo, a reflection, a shadow, a mirage, a magical illusion, a city of gandharvas, and a transformation, are all devoid of marks.”

Why is this so? All dreams, echoes, reflections, shadows, mirages, illusions, cities of the gandharvas, and magical transformations lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). If a phenomenon lacks intrinsic nature, that phenomenon is without marks (*animitta*); if a phenomenon is without marks, that phenomenon has but a single mark, namely, the markless.

“Subhūti! By this causal principle, you should know that all giving is signless, the giver is signless, the recipient is signless, and the gift is signless. If one practices giving while knowing it thus, then one is able to fulfill the cultivation of the perfection of giving.”

If one is able to practice the perfection of generosity to completion, then one does not remain apart from the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom.
Abiding thus in the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom,
one is able to fulfill the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments;
and one is also able to fulfill the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, and the five...
The faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path can also bring to fulfillment the gateways to liberation of emptiness,
signlessness, and wishlessness; they can also bring to fulfillment internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness,
the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, and unconditioned emptiness.
Emptiness, ultimate emptiness, boundless emptiness, emptiness of dispersion, emptiness of non-alteration, emptiness of intrinsic nature,
emptiness of self-characteristic, emptiness of common characteristic, emptiness of all phenomena, emptiness of the unapprehendable, emptiness of non-existence, emptiness of intrinsic nature,
and emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence can also bring the *tathatā* (suchness) to fulfillment.
...the dharma-realm, the dharma-nature, the non-illusory nature, the unchanging nature, the state of equality, the nature free from birth, the fixedness of dharma,
the stability of dharma, the limit of reality, the realm of empty space, and the inconceivable realm;
they are also able to fulfill the noble truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path, and are also able to perfect them.
They fulfill the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative attainments, and the ten totalities;
they are also able to fulfill five hundred gates of samādhi and five hundred gates of dhāraṇī;
they are also able to fulfill the five eyes and the six supernormal powers; and they are also able to fulfill the ten powers of a Buddha and the four fearlessnesses.
The four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity,
as well as the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, can likewise bring to perfection the quality of non-forgetfulness and the state of constant abiding in equanimity;
they can also bring to perfection all-knowledge, the knowledge of the paths, and the knowledge of all aspects.

“Abiding in these various dharmas born of maturation that are noble and untainted, this bodhisattva mahāsattva travels by means of supernormal powers to Buddha-worlds in the ten directions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. There, he honors, reveres, respects, and praises the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, with various kinds of superior and exquisite clothing, food and drink, bedding, medicinal decoctions, incense, flowers, precious banners, pennants, canopies, lamps, music, and other necessities. He brings about the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings: those who should be benefited through giving, he benefits them with giving;
those who should be benefited through pure ethical discipline, he benefits them with pure ethical discipline.”
Those who should be benefited by means of patience, one benefits them by means of patience;
those who should be benefited by means of diligence, one benefits them by means of diligence;
those who should be benefited by means of meditative concentration, one benefits them by means of meditative concentration.
Those who should be benefited by means of *prajñā* are benefited by means of *prajñā*;
those who should be benefited by means of various other wholesome dharmas are benefited by means of those various other wholesome dharmas;
and those who should be benefited by means of all supreme wholesome dharmas are benefited by means of all supreme wholesome dharmas.
This bodhisattva mahāsattva, having accomplished such immeasurable wholesome dharmas, is not defiled by the faults of birth and death even while undergoing them.

For the sake of benefiting and bringing happiness to all sentient beings, they assume the wealth, nobility, and mastery of humans and devas; through the power of this wealth, nobility, and mastery, they are able to perform various acts of benefit and happiness for sentient beings, gathering them in through the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*).

Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva knows that all phenomena are signless, although they know the fruit of stream-entry, they do not abide in the fruit of stream-entry; although they know the fruit of once-returning, they do not abide in the fruit of once-returning; although they know the fruit of non-returning, they do not abide in the fruit of non-returning; although they know the fruit of arhatship, they do not abide in the fruit of arhatship; and although they know the awakening of a pratyekabuddha, they do not abide in the awakening of a pratyekabuddha.

Why is this? Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva, having understood all phenomena as they truly are, desires to realize the knowledge of all aspects, which is not shared with any śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.

"So it is, Subhūti! Because a bodhisattva mahāsattva knows that all phenomena are signless, they understand, as they truly are, that the perfections of giving, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom are also all signless; and they understand, as they truly are, that all other buddha-dharmas are likewise signless. By means of this cause and condition, they are able to universally fulfill all buddha-dharmas."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, they abide within the five aggregates of clinging—which are like a dream, like an echo, like a reflection, like a shadow, like a mirage, like a magical illusion, like a city of gandharvas, and like a transformation—and thereby fulfill the perfection of ethical discipline."

When this bodhisattva mahāsattva has understood these five aggregates of clinging as they truly are—like a dream, like an echo, like a reflection, like a shadow, like a mirage, like a magical illusion, like a city of gandharvas, and like a transformation—he is then able to fulfill the perfection of pure ethical discipline that is signless.

Such pure ethical discipline is without deficiency, without breach, without flaw, and without impurity; it is free from attachment, worthy of offerings, praised by the wise, excellently undertaken, and excellently brought to completion. It is noble, untainted, and comprised within the factors of the supramundane path.

Abiding securely in this precept, one is able to properly receive and uphold the precepts of designation, the precepts acquired through the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), the precepts of restraint (*saṃvara*), manifest precepts, non-manifest precepts, active precepts, non-active precepts, the precepts of dignified conduct (*airyāpathika*), and the precepts of non-dignified conduct.
"Although this bodhisattva-mahāsattva is fully accomplished in such precepts, he is without attachment to them and does not form the thought:

'By means of these precepts, I shall be born into a wealthy and sovereign great kṣatriya clan, or into a wealthy and sovereign great brāhmaṇa clan, or into a wealthy and sovereign great householder clan, or into a wealthy and sovereign great merchant clan.'"
He does not form this thought:
"By means of these precepts, I shall become a minor king, or a great king, or a wheel-turning monarch, possessing wealth, honor, and sovereignty."
He does not form this thought:

"By means of these precepts, I shall be reborn among the Gods of the Four Great Kings, or among the Thirty-three Gods, or among the Yāma Gods, or among the Tuṣita Gods, or among the Gods who Delight in Emanation, or among the Gods who Wield Power over Others' Emanations, possessing wealth and sovereignty."
One does not form this thought:

"By means of these precepts, I shall be reborn among the Brahmakāyika devas, or among the Brahmapurohita devas, or among the Brahmakāyika devas, or among the Mahābrahmā devas, possessing wealth, nobility, and sovereignty."
One does not form such thoughts as:
"By means of this precept, I shall be reborn in the Ābhāsvara Heaven, or the Parīttābha Heaven, or the Apramāṇābha Heaven, or the Ābhāsvara-svabhāva Heaven, to enjoy wealth, honor, and sovereignty."
He does not form such thoughts as:

"By means of this precept, I shall be reborn among the Śuddhāvāsa deities, or the Parīttaśubha deities, or the Apramāṇaśubha deities, or the Śubhakṛtsna deities, possessing wealth, nobility, and sovereignty."
They do not form such thoughts as:

"By means of this precept, I shall be reborn in the Vast Heaven (Vehapphala), or the Heaven of Limited Vastness (Appamāṇasubha), or the Heaven of Infinite Vastness (Appamāṇa), or among the wealthy and sovereign beings of the Heaven of Great Fruit (Bṛhatphala)."
One does not form such thoughts as:

"By means of this precept, I shall be reborn in the Heaven of No Affliction, or the Heaven of No Heat, or the Heaven of Good Appearance, or the Heaven of Good Vision, or the Heaven of Ultimate Form, where I may enjoy wealth, honor, and sovereignty."
He does not form this thought:

"By means of these precepts, I shall be reborn in the Sphere of Infinite Space, or the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness, or the Sphere of Nothingness, or the Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-Perception, where I may enjoy wealth, honor, and sovereignty."
One does not form such thoughts as:

"By means of this precept, I shall attain the fruit of stream-entry, or the fruit of once-returning, or the fruit of non-returning, or the fruit of arhatship; or I shall attain the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, or enter the bodhisattva’s state of correctness and departure from birth, or attain the bodhisattva’s forbearance toward the non-arising of phenomena, or attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

Why is this so? Because all these dharmas are without marks; they are all of one single mark, namely, the markless. A dharma that is markless cannot obtain marklessness, and a dharma that has marks cannot obtain marks. A dharma that is markless cannot obtain marks, and a dharma that has marks cannot obtain marklessness. For these reasons, none of them can be apprehended at all.

"So it is, Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they are swiftly able to fulfill the signless perfection of pure ethical discipline and enter the bodhisattva’s state of rightness and departure from birth;
having entered the bodhisattva’s state of rightness and departure from birth, they further attain the bodhisattva’s endurance of the non-arising of phenomena."

Having attained the Bodhisattva’s patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti), they practice the knowledge of the aspects of the path (mārgākārajñatā) and proceed toward the knowledge of all aspects (sarvākārajñatā). They attain the five supernormal powers as a result of maturation (vipākaja), and further attain five hundred gates of samādhi as well as five hundred gates of dhāraṇī.

Abiding therein, they further attain the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), traveling from one buddha-field to another to make offerings, pay homage, revere, and praise the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, while bringing sentient beings to maturity and adorning and purifying the buddha-fields.

"This bodhisattva mahāsattva, for the sake of transforming sentient beings, although manifests the cycle of birth and death within the various realms of existence, is not defiled by the obstacles of those afflictions, karmic retributions, or other hindrances."

For example, although a magically conjured person manifests such activities as walking, standing, sitting, and lying down, they lack any real karma of coming and going; likewise, although they manifest various ways of benefiting sentient beings, they find nothing at all—neither the sentient beings nor the designations applied to them.

Suppose there were a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Suśānta, who attained unexcelled perfect enlightenment, turned the sublime wheel of Dharma, and delivered immeasurable multitudes, causing them to escape birth and death and realize nirvāṇa; yet, there was no sentient being worthy of receiving a prediction that they would next attain unexcelled perfect enlightenment.

At that time, that Tathāgata manifested a transformation Buddha (nirmāṇa-buddha) and caused it to remain long in the world; he himself relinquished the formations of life and entered the realm of nirvana without remainder. After that transformation Buddha’s body had remained for one kalpa and had bestowed the prediction of unexcelled, perfect enlightenment upon a bodhisattva, it then entered nirvana.

Although that Buddha’s emanation performs various deeds for the benefit of sentient beings, it has no attainment; that is to say, it does not attain form, nor does it attain feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness;
it does not attain the sense-base of the eye, nor the sense-bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind;
it does not attain the sense-base of form, nor the sense-bases of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, or mental phenomena.
One does not apprehend the eye-element; one does not apprehend the ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-element.
One does not apprehend the form-element; one does not apprehend the sound-, odor-, taste-, tangible-, or mental-object-element.
One does not apprehend the eye-consciousness-element; one does not apprehend the ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-consciousness-element.
One does not apprehend eye-contact, nor ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-contact;
one does not apprehend the various feelings produced with eye-contact as condition, nor the various feelings produced with ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-contact as condition;
one does not apprehend any phenomena, whether tainted or untainted, nor sentient beings.
This bodhisattva mahāsattva is also like this: although there is that which is performed, there is nothing attained. "It is thus, Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they fulfill the perfection of ethical discipline. Because they fulfill this perfection of ethical discipline, they are able to encompass all the buddha-dharmas."

"Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, they abide within the five aggregates of clinging— which are like a dream, like an echo, like a reflection, like a shadow, like a mirage, like a magical illusion, like a city of gandharvas, and like a transformation— and thereby fulfill the perfection of patience."

When these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have realized, as they truly are, that these five aggregates of clinging are like a dream, like an echo, like a reflection, like a shadow, like a mirage, like a magical illusion, like a city of gandharvas, and like a transformation, they are then able to fulfill the perfection of signless patience.

"Subhūti! How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom truly understand these five aggregates of clinging to be like a dream, like an echo, like a reflection, like a shadow, like a mirage, like a magical illusion, like a city of gandharvas, and like a transformation, and thereby fulfill the signless perfection of patience?"

Subhūti! Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva understands, as they truly are, that these five aggregates of clinging lack any real characteristic, he cultivates two kinds of patience and is thus able to bring to perfection the perfection of signless patience.
What are the two? First, the patience of acceptance;
second, the patience of discernment.

"Regarding 'patience through acceptance': this refers to when Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, from their first generation of the mind of awakening until they sit peacefully upon the seat of sublime enlightenment, should encounter all classes of sentient beings who come in competition to revile and disparage them, using coarse and evil words to abuse and insult them, and further inflicting harm with tiles, stones, swords, or staves. For the sake of fulfilling the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*), these Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas do not give rise to even a single thought of resentment, nor do they conceive the intention to retaliate;

they simply think: 'These sentient beings are deeply pitiable; their minds are struck by the force of their overwhelming afflictions (*kleśa*) such that they lack self-mastery and thus initiate such evil karma against me. I should not now feel resentment toward them.'"
Again, he reflects:

"It is because I have grasped these aggregates, which are like enemies, that those sentient beings have initiated such evil karma toward me; I should only reproach myself and not feel anger toward them."

When the Bodhisattva thus examines with careful scrutiny, he gives rise to profound compassion for those sentient beings; such categories as these are called "the patience of acceptance" (*anupālambha-kṣānti*).
Regarding "the patience of observation" (*pratyavekṣaṇā-kṣānti*), it refers to the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas who reflect in this way:

"All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are like illusions, false and unreal, and lack autonomy. They are also like space, being without self (*anātman*). Sentient beings, life-principles, born beings, nourished beings, persons, individuals, mind-born beings, youths, agents, experiencers, knowers, and seers are all unfindable; they arise solely from false conceptualization."
Who reviles me? Who scolds me? Who insults me?
"Who is it that inflicts various harms upon me with tiles, stones, blades, or clubs?
And who is it that undergoes such insults and injuries?

All of this is the false conceptualization of one's own mind. I should not now give rise to groundless attachment; for all such phenomena are entirely non-existent due to their emptiness of intrinsic nature and their emptiness of ultimate reality."

When the bodhisattva thus examines with careful scrutiny, he understands as it truly is that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are empty and quiescent; he does not give rise to divergent conceptions regarding any phenomena. Such categories as these are termed "the patience of examination" (*paryeṣaṇā-kṣānti*).

"Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva cultivates these two kinds of patience, he is able to fulfill the perfection of signless patience; by fulfilling the perfection of signless patience, he immediately attains the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena."
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,
what is meant by 'the patient acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas' (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti)?"
"What is this that is abandoned?
Furthermore, what kind of wisdom is it?
The Buddha said:

“Subhūti! By the power of this, even the slightest portion of evil or unwholesome dharmas cannot arise; therefore, it is called the ‘patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas’ (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).”

This brings about the ultimate pacification of all afflictions, such as the conceit of "I" and "mine. It involves the authentic endurance of all phenomena as being like a dream, an echo, a reflection, a shadow, a mirage, a magical illusion, a city of Gandharvas, and a transformation. This endurance is called "knowledge"; because one attains this knowledge, it is said that one has attained the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What is the difference between the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas and the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas?”
The Buddha said, “Subhūti!

The wisdom and the abandonment of all stream-enterers are also called the patience of a bodhisattva mahāsattva; the wisdom and the abandonment of all once-returners are also called the patience of a bodhisattva mahāsattva; the wisdom and the abandonment of all non-returners are also called the patience of a bodhisattva mahāsattva; the wisdom and the abandonment of all arhats are also called the patience of a bodhisattva mahāsattva; and the wisdom and the abandonment of all pratyekabuddhas are also called the patience of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.”
Furthermore, there is the patience of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, which is the patience regarding the ultimate non-arising of all phenomena; this constitutes the distinction.
Subhūti! Because bodhisattva-mahāsattvas accomplish such supreme patience, they surpass all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.

“Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in this way within the path of a bodhisattva—abiding in this sublime, extraordinary maturation and the patience regarding non-arising—they are able to fulfill the knowledge of the aspects of the path.”

Because they are able to fulfill the knowledge of the paths of all aspects (*mārgākārajñatā*), they are never separated from the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path; nor are they separated from the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—nor are they separated from the supernormal powers born of maturation.

Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva does not abandon the supernormal powers born of karmic maturation, they travel from one buddha-field to another, making offerings and showing reverence to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, bringing sentient beings to maturity and purifying buddha-fields.

Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva has attained fulfillment through maturing sentient beings and purifying buddha-fields, they realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of a single moment of corresponding sublime wisdom.

"So it is, Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they are swiftly able to fulfill the signless perfection of patience. Because they have fulfilled the signless perfection of patience, they are then able to realize the knowledge of all modes, such that no aspect of the Buddha-dharmas remains unfulfilled."

"Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, they dwell within the five aggregates of clinging— which are like a dream, like an echo, like an image, like a reflection, like a mirage, like a magical illusion, like a city of gandharvas, and like a transformation— and, having realized as it truly is that these five aggregates of clinging are without real characteristics, being like a dream, like an echo, like an image, like a reflection, like a mirage, like a magical illusion, like a city of gandharvas, and like a transformation, they arouse courageous physical and mental diligence."

Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva has initiated courageous physical diligence, they bring forth superior and swift supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). By means of these supernormal powers, they travel to the worlds of the ten directions to make offerings, pay homage, show respect, and praise the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones; they plant the roots of all virtues in the presence of those Buddhas, benefit and bring peace and happiness to immeasurable sentient beings, and are also able to adorn and purify various Buddha-fields.

By means of physical diligence, this bodhisattva mahāsattva brings sentient beings to maturity, establishing them through appropriate skillful means in the three vehicles so that each may reach ultimate realization.
In this way, Subhūti,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, through physical diligence they are able to swiftly fulfill the signless perfection of diligence.
“Subhūti! Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva has aroused courageous mental diligence, he brings forth the diligence subsumed under the noble,
untainted factors of the path (*ārya-āsravakṣaya-mārgāṅga*), thereby fulfilling the perfection of diligence (*vīryapāramitā*) and being fully endowed therein.”
They are able to encompass all wholesome dharmas, namely: the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right endeavors, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers,
the seven factors of enlightenment, the eightfold noble path, the gateways to liberation of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness,
the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, and the eight [liberations].
The liberations, the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, the ten totalities, the noble truths of suffering,
origin, cessation, and the path, the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration,
and wisdom, the five eyes, the six superknowledges, and the gateways of samādhi.

The gateways of dhāraṇī; the Ground of Utmost Joy, the Ground of Purity, the Ground of Radiance, the Ground of Blazing Wisdom, the Ground of Difficult Victory, the Ground of Presence, the Ground of Far-Going, the Ground of Immovability, the Ground of Excellent Intelligence, and the Ground of the Dharma Cloud;
internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, and great [emptiness].
Emptiness, the emptiness of the ultimate truth, the emptiness of conditioned phenomena, the emptiness of unconditioned phenomena, the emptiness of the absolute limit,
the emptiness of the beginningless and endless, the emptiness of dispersion, the emptiness of non-alteration, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, the emptiness of specific characteristics,
the emptiness of common characteristics, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of non-apprehensibility, the emptiness of non-existence, and the emptiness of self-nature.

The emptiness of the self-nature of non-existence; suchness, the dharma-realm, the dharma-nature, the nature of non-falsity, the nature of non-alteration, equality, the nature of being free from birth, the fixedness of dharmas, the stability of dharmas, the limit of reality, the realm of space, the inconceivable realm; and the ten powers of a Buddha, the four fearlessnesses.
The four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity;
the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; the quality of non-forgetfulness, the nature of constant dwelling in equanimity;
and all-knowledge, knowledge of the paths, and knowledge of all aspects.
“Abiding within this, the bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to fulfill all-aspect omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Because all-aspect omniscience is thus fulfilled, they forever sever the continuity of all habitual tendencies (*vāsanā-saṃtati*).”
Because he has eternally severed the continuity of all habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), his primary marks and secondary signs (*lakṣaṇānuvyañjana*) are fully perfected.

Through the perfection of these primary marks and secondary signs, he realizes unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*); he emits great radiance that universally illumines the trichiliocosm, causes all worlds to undergo six kinds of movement, and turns the wheel of the true Dharma endowed with twelve aspects.

Consequently, all sentient beings within this trichiliocosm, touched by the light and beholding these transformations while hearing the sound of the True Dharma, shall all attain non-retrogression in the three vehicles.

"So it is, Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they fulfill the perfection of diligence. Abiding in this perfection of diligence, that bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to accomplish many beneficial deeds for both themselves and others, swiftly fulfill all the buddha-dharmas, and realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
"Furthermore, Subhūti,

when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, they fulfill the perfection of meditative concentration while abiding within the five aggregates of clinging that are like a dream, like an echo, like a reflection, like a shadow, like a mirage, like a magical illusion, like a city of gandharvas, and like a transformation."

“Subhūti!
