When the World-Honored One expounds the True Dharma with a single voice, each class of sentient beings understands it according to their own capacity.
The World-Honored One’s teaching of the Dharma always follows a sequential order; every word has its cause and condition, and there is nothing that is not wholesome—this is seventy-four.
The World-Honored One observes all classes of sentient beings with equanimity, praising the good and censuring the evil without any love or hatred—this is seventy-five.
The Blessed One acts after first observing; his conduct is complete and he causes others to recognize what is wholesome and pure—this is the seventy-sixth.
The Blessed One’s marks and signs cannot be fully observed by any sentient being—this is the seventy-seventh.
The cranial bone of the World-Honored One is firm, solid, and perfectly rounded; this is the seventy-eighth.
The countenance of the World-Honored One is eternally youthful and does not age, and he delights in visiting his former haunts; this is the seventy-ninth.

The Blessed One’s hands, feet, and the area before his chest are all marked with the auspicious *śrīvatsa* sign; its patterns are like exquisite paintings and its color resembles vermilion. This is the eightieth [mark].
"Subhūti! These are called the eighty minor marks. Subhūti!"

Because the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha has accomplished such primary and secondary marks, the radiance of his body spontaneously illuminates the trichiliocosm, pervading it entirely without exception; when he directs his attention, he can universally illuminate immeasurable, boundless, and innumerable worlds. Nevertheless, out of compassion for all sentient beings, he withdraws this light and constantly illuminates an area of one fathom around each person. If he were to let forth the full radiance of his body, the light of the sun, moon, and other luminaries would cease to appear, and sentient beings would be unable to distinguish day from night, the half-month, the month, the seasons, or the years, and their various undertakings would fail to be accomplished.

The Buddha’s voice spontaneously pervades the trichiliocosm; when he directs his attention, it can fill immeasurable, boundless, and innumerable worlds. Nevertheless, for the sake of benefiting and bringing happiness to all sentient beings, the sound adjusts to the capacity of the assembly without decreasing or increasing.

"Subhūti! Such meritorious benefits and excellences were already accomplished by me previously while practicing the perfection of wisdom in the stage of a bodhisattva; therefore, I am now adorned with the perfection of the primary and secondary marks, so that all sentient beings who see me rejoice and obtain supreme benefit and peace."
Thus it is, Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, they are able to gather in all sentient beings through the two kinds of giving—material wealth and the Dharma. This is an exceedingly marvelous and rare quality.
“Subhūti! How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva gather sentient beings through affectionate speech? Subhūti!”

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, they use a gentle voice to first teach sentient beings the skillful means for gathering them through the perfection of generosity; next, they teach the skillful means for gathering them through the perfection of ethical discipline; next, they teach the skillful means for gathering them through the perfection of patience; next, they teach the skillful means for gathering them through the perfection of diligence; next, they teach the skillful means for gathering them through the perfection of meditative concentration; and finally, they teach the skillful means for gathering them through the perfection of wisdom.

"Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, they use a gentle voice to extensively teach these six perfections in order to gather in classes of sentient beings."
Why is this? Because these six perfections are universally able to encompass all wholesome dharmas. "Subhūti!..."
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva use beneficial conduct to gather in all sentient beings? Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, through various skillful means over the long night, they exhort all sentient beings to diligently cultivate the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, as well as other various superior wholesome dharmas, never becoming weary or negligent.
"Subhūti! How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva gather sentient beings through samānārthatā? Subhūti!"

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, by means of superior supernormal powers and the force of great vows, they manifest within the realms of hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, humans, and devas; there, through shared activities and skillful means, they gather them in and cause them to obtain supreme benefit and peace.

“Subhūti! That a bodhisattva mahāsattva can gather and sustain all sentient beings through such [means] as giving, kind speech, beneficial conduct, and cooperation is a most marvelous and extraordinary dharma.”
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

With my Buddha-eye, I survey throughout the ten directions worlds as numerous as the sands of immeasurable Gaṅgā rivers. Therein, bodhisattva mahāsattvas practicing the profound perfection of wisdom instruct and admonish other bodhisattvas, saying: 'Good son!'"

You should skillfully train in the dhāraṇī-doors that bring forth all syllables; that is, you should skillfully train in one syllable, two syllables, three syllables, four syllables, five syllables, six syllables, seven syllables, eight syllables, nine syllables, ten syllables, and so on, up to twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, sixty, seventy, eighty, ninety, or a hundred, or a thousand, or even an infinite number, until you attain mastery in bringing them forth.

Furthermore, one should skillfully train so that all languages enter into a single syllable, or enter into two syllables, or three, or four, or five, or six, or seven, or eight, or nine, or ten; and likewise, even up to twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, sixty, seventy, eighty, ninety, a hundred, a thousand, or even an infinite number, thereby inducing mastery.
Furthermore, one should skillfully train in how all syllables are subsumed within a single syllable, and how a single syllable is subsumed within all syllables, thereby inducing mastery.
Moreover, one should skillfully train in how a single syllable can subsume forty-two syllables, and how those forty-two syllables can subsume a single syllable.

"Subhūti! This bodhisattva mahāsattva should thus skillfully train so that the forty-two letters enter into a single letter, and that a single letter also enters into the forty-two letters. Having trained in this way, they will develop skillfulness regarding all letters; having attained skillfulness in the elicitation of letters, they will further develop skillfulness in the elicitation of the letterless."

Just as the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas are skillful in phenomena and skillful in syllables—being skillful in all phenomena and all syllables, they also attain skillfulness in the absence of syllables—and by virtue of this skillfulness, they are able to teach sentient beings the dharma with syllables and the dharma without syllables, and to teach the dharma with syllables for the sake of the dharma without syllables.
Why is this so? Subhūti!
There is no difference between the absence of syllables and the absence of words and the Buddha-dharma; that which transcends all syllables is called the true Buddha-dharma.
Why is this? Subhūti!
Because all phenomena and all sentient beings are ultimately empty and boundlessly empty.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If all phenomena and all sentient beings are ultimately empty and boundlessly empty, and thus transcend all syllables, then the intrinsic nature of all phenomena and all sentient beings is ultimately unobtainable. How, then, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice the perfection of wisdom, and practice the perfections of meditative concentration, diligence, patience, ethical discipline, and generosity?”
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice the four dhyānas, and how does he practice the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments?

How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice the four foundations of mindfulness, and how does he practice the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of awakening, and the eightfold noble path?

How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice the gate of liberation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vimokṣamukha*), and how does he practice the gates of liberation of signlessness (*animitta*) and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*)?

How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva abide in internal emptiness (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*), and abide in external emptiness (*bahirdhā-śūnyatā*), internal-and-external emptiness (*adhyātma-bahirdhā-śūnyatā*), the emptiness of emptiness (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*), great emptiness (*mahā-śūnyatā*), ultimate emptiness (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*), conditioned emptiness (*saṃskṛta-śūnyatā*), unconditioned emptiness (*asaṃskṛta-śūnyatā*), absolute emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*), boundless emptiness (*anavara-agra-śūnyatā*), emptiness of dispersion (*anavakāra-śūnyatā*), emptiness of non-alteration (*anavakāra-śūnyatā*), emptiness of intrinsic nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*), emptiness of self-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*), emptiness of common characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*), emptiness of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-śūnyatā*), emptiness of the unapprehendable (*anupalambha-śūnyatā*), emptiness of non-existence (*abhāva-śūnyatā*), emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*), and emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence (*abhāvasvabhāva-śūnyatā*)?

How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwell in true suchness (tathatā), and dwell in the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), the non-illusory nature, the unchanging nature, equality, the nature of being free from birth, the fixed nature of phenomena (dharmaniyāmatā), the stability of phenomena (dharmaniyāmatā), the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi), the realm of empty space (ākāśadhātu), and the inconceivable realm?
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva abide in the noble truth of suffering, and how do they abide in the noble truths of origination, cessation, and the path?
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative attainments, and the ten totalities?
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice all the gates of dhāraṇī and practice all the gates of samādhi?

How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice the Stage of Extreme Joy, and practice the Stage of Purity, the Stage of Radiance, the Stage of Blazing Wisdom, the Stage of Difficult Victory, the Stage of Presence, the Stage of Far-Going, the Immovable Stage, the Stage of Excellent Intelligence, and the Stage of the Dharma Cloud?
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice the five eyes and practice the six supernormal powers?
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice the ten powers of a buddha, and practice the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha?
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice great loving-kindness, and how do they practice great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity?
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice the quality of non-forgetfulness, and how do they practice the state of constant abiding in equanimity?

How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), practice the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and practice the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*)?
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice the thirty-two marks of a great man (*dvātriṃśanmahāpuruṣalakṣaṇa*) and practice the eighty secondary signs (*aśītyanuvyañjana*)?
"How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having dwelled in the six supernormal powers born of maturation, proclaim the true Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings?
"World-Honored One!
All sentient beings are unapprehendable, and even the designation 'sentient being' is unapprehendable."
Because all sentient beings are unapprehendable, form is unapprehendable; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise unapprehendable.
Because all sentient beings are unapprehendable, the eye-base is unapprehendable; the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-bases are likewise unapprehendable.
Because all sentient beings are unapprehendable, the form-base is unapprehendable; the sound, odor, taste, tangible, and phenomena-bases are likewise unapprehendable.
Because all sentient beings are unapprehendable, the eye-element is unapprehendable; likewise, the ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-elements are also unapprehendable.
Because all sentient beings are unapprehendable, the form-element is unapprehendable; likewise, the sound-, odor-, taste-, tangible-, and mental-object-elements are also unapprehendable.
Because all sentient beings are unapprehendable, the eye-consciousness-element is unapprehendable; likewise, the ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-consciousness-elements are also unapprehendable.
Because all sentient beings are unapprehendable, eye-contact is unapprehendable; ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact are likewise unapprehendable.

Because all sentient beings are unapprehendable, the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition are unapprehendable; the various feelings produced with ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact as conditions are likewise unapprehendable.
Because all sentient beings are unapprehendable, the earth element is unapprehendable; the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements are likewise unapprehendable.

Because all sentient beings are unapprehendable, causes and conditions are unapprehendable; likewise, the immediately preceding condition, the object-condition, and the dominant condition are also unapprehendable.
Because all sentient beings are unapprehendable, all phenomena produced from conditions are unapprehendable.

Because all sentient beings are unapprehendable, ignorance is unapprehendable, and formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, and old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are also unapprehendable.

Because all sentient beings are unapprehendable, the perfection of generosity is unapprehendable; likewise, the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom are also unapprehendable.
Because all sentient beings are unapprehendable, the four dhyānas are unapprehendable; the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments are also unapprehendable.

Because all sentient beings are unapprehendable, the four foundations of mindfulness are unapprehendable; the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path are also unapprehendable.
Because all sentient beings are unapprehendable, the gate of liberation of emptiness is unapprehendable; the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness are likewise unapprehendable.

Because all sentient beings are unapprehendable, internal emptiness is unapprehendable; external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, endless emptiness, dispersion emptiness, non-alteration emptiness, essential nature emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common characteristic emptiness, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature are likewise unapprehendable.

Because all sentient beings are unapprehendable, true thusness is unapprehendable; likewise, the dharma-realm, the nature of phenomena, non-erroneousness, immutability, equality, the state beyond birth, the fixed nature of phenomena, the stability of phenomena, the limit of reality, the realm of space, and the inconceivable realm are also unapprehendable.
Because all sentient beings are unapprehendable, the noble truth of suffering is unapprehendable, and the noble truths of origin, cessation, and the path are also unapprehendable.

Because all sentient beings are unapprehendable, the eight liberations are unapprehendable, and the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative attainments, and the ten universal bases are also unapprehendable.
Because all sentient beings are unapprehendable, all dharani-doors are unapprehendable, and all samadhi-doors are likewise unapprehendable;

because all sentient beings are unapprehendable, the Ground of Extreme Joy is unapprehendable, and the Ground of Freedom from Defilement, the Ground of Radiant Light, the Ground of Blazing Wisdom, the Ground of Utmost Difficulty to Conquer, the Ground of Manifestation, the Ground of Far-Going, the Ground of Immovability, the Ground of Excellent Intelligence, and the Ground of the Dharma Cloud are likewise unapprehendable;
because all sentient beings are unapprehendable, the five eyes are unapprehendable, and the six supernormal powers are likewise unapprehendable.

Because all sentient beings are unapprehendable, the ten powers of a Buddha are unapprehendable; likewise, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are also unapprehendable.
Because all sentient beings are unapprehendable, great loving-kindness is unapprehendable; great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity are also unapprehendable.
Because all sentient beings are unapprehendable, the quality of non-forgetfulness is unapprehendable, and the state of constant abiding in equanimity is also unapprehendable.
Because all sentient beings are unapprehendable, omniscience is unapprehendable; likewise, the knowledge of the paths and the knowledge of all aspects are unapprehendable.

Because all sentient beings are unapprehendable, the fruit of stream-entry is unapprehendable, as are the fruits of once-returning, non-returning, arhatship, and the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha.

Because all sentient beings are unapprehendable, the entire conduct of bodhisattva mahāsattvas is unapprehendable, and the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas is also unapprehendable.
Because all sentient beings are unapprehendable, the thirty-two marks of a great man are unapprehendable, and the eighty secondary signs are likewise unapprehendable.
"World-Honored One!..."
In that which is ungraspable, there are no sentient beings, nor is there the designation "sentient being.
There is no form, nor the designation "form";
there is no feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, nor the designations "feeling," "perception," "mental formations," or "consciousness."
There is no eye-base, nor is there the designation of an eye-base;
there is no ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind-base, nor is there the designation of an ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind-base.
There is no sphere of the formless, nor is there any designation of a sphere of the formless;
there is no sphere of sound, odor, taste, tangible object, or mental phenomena, nor is there any designation of a sphere of sound, odor, taste, tangible object, or mental phenomena.
There is no eye-element, nor the designation of an eye-element;
there is no ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-element, nor the designation of an ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-element.
There is no realm of formlessness, nor is there any designation of a realm of formlessness;
there is no realm of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, or mental phenomena, nor is there any designation of a realm of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, or mental phenomena.
There is no eye-consciousness element, nor is there any designation of an eye-consciousness element;
there is no ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-consciousness element, nor is there any designation of an ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-consciousness element.
There is no eye-contact, nor the designation of eye-contact;
there is no ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-contact, nor the designation of ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-contact.
There are no feelings arisen with eye-contact as condition, nor is there any designation of feelings arisen with eye-contact as condition;
there are no feelings arisen with ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind-contact as condition, nor is there any designation of feelings arisen with ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind-contact as condition.
There is no earth element, nor is there any designation of an earth element;
there is no water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness element, nor is there any designation of water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness elements.
There is no cause-condition (hetu-pratyaya), nor the designation of a cause-condition;

there is no immediately preceding condition (samanantara-pratyaya), object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya), or predominant condition (adhipati-pratyaya), nor the designation of an immediately preceding condition, object-condition, or predominant condition.
There are no phenomena produced from conditions, nor is there the designation of phenomena produced from conditions.
There is no ignorance, nor is there the designation of ignorance;

there is no volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, existence, birth, or aging-and-death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair, nor is there the designation of volitional formations up to aging-and-death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair.
There is no perfection of generosity, nor is there any designation of the perfection of generosity;
there is no perfection of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, or wisdom, nor is there any designation of the perfections from ethical discipline up to wisdom.
There are no four dhyānas, nor is there any designation of the four dhyānas;
there are no four immeasurables or four formless attainments, nor is there any designation of the four immeasurables or the four formless attainments.
There are no four foundations of mindfulness, nor is there the designation of the four foundations of mindfulness;

there are no four right efforts, four bases of power, five faculties, five powers, seven factors of enlightenment, or eight factors of the noble path, nor is there the designation of the four right efforts up to the eight factors of the noble path.
There is no door of liberation of emptiness, nor is there any designation of a door of liberation of emptiness;
there is no door of liberation of signlessness or wishlessness, nor is there any designation of a door of liberation of signlessness or wishlessness.
There is no internal emptiness, nor the designation of internal emptiness;

there is no external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, non-alteration emptiness, essential nature emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common characteristic emptiness, emptiness of all phenomena, emptiness of the unapprehendable, emptiness of non-existence, emptiness of intrinsic nature, and emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence—nor is there the designation of external emptiness up to the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence.
There is no such thing as *tathatā* (suchness), nor is there any designation for *tathatā*;

there is no dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), no dharma-nature (*dharmatā*), no non-falsity (*avitathatā*), no unalterability (*ananyathātva*), no sameness (*samatā*), no nature free from birth (*anirodhatā*), no fixedness of dharma (*dharmaniyāmatā*), no stability of dharma (*dharmasthititā*), no reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*), no space-element (*ākāśadhātu*), and no inconceivable realm (*acintyadhātu*), nor is there any designation for the dharma-realm up to the inconceivable realm.
There is no noble truth of suffering, nor is there the designation of the noble truth of suffering;
there is no noble truth of origin, cessation, or path, nor is there the designation of the noble truths of origin, cessation, or path.
There are no eight liberations, nor is there any designation of the eight liberations;

there are no eight bases of mastery, nine successive meditative attainments, or ten totalities, nor is there any designation of the eight bases of mastery, nine successive meditative attainments, or ten totalities.
There are no dhāraṇī-doors, nor any designation of dhāraṇī-doors;
there are no samādhi-doors, nor any designation of samādhi-doors.
There is no Ground of Utmost Joy, nor any designation of the Ground of Utmost Joy.

There is no such thing as the Vimalā-bhūmi, the Prabhākārī-bhūmi, the Arciṣmatī-bhūmi, the Sudurjayā-bhūmi, the Abhimukhī-bhūmi, the Dūraṃgamā-bhūmi, the Acalā-bhūmi, the Sādhumatī-bhūmi, or the Dharmameghā-bhūmi; there is no designation of the Vimalā-bhūmi up to and including the Dharmameghā-bhūmi.
There are no five eyes, nor the designation of five eyes;
there are no six supernormal powers, nor the designation of six supernormal powers.
There are no ten powers of a Buddha, nor the designation of ten powers of a Buddha.

There are no four fearlessnesses, four analytical knowledges, or eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; there is no designation of the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, or the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
There is no great loving-kindness, nor the designation of great loving-kindness;
there is no great compassion, great joy, or great equanimity, nor the designation of great compassion, great joy, or great equanimity.
There is no quality of non-forgetfulness, nor is there any designation of a quality of non-forgetfulness;
there is no state of constant abiding in equanimity, nor is there any designation of a state of constant abiding in equanimity.
There is no omniscience, nor is there any designation of omniscience.
There is no knowledge of the aspects of the path, no knowledge of all aspects, and no designation of the knowledge of the aspects of the path or the knowledge of all aspects.
There is no fruit of stream-entry, and no designation of the fruit of stream-entry;
there is no fruit of once-returning, non-returning, arhatship, or pratyekabuddha-enlightenment, and no designation of the fruit of once-returning up to pratyekabuddha-enlightenment.
There is no such thing as the practice of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, nor is there any designation for the practice of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas;
there is no such thing as the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas, nor is there any designation for the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas.
There are no thirty-two marks of a great man, nor is there any designation of the thirty-two marks of a great man;
there are no eighty secondary characteristics, nor is there any designation of the eighty secondary characteristics.
“World-Honored One!

Since all dharmas of sentient beings and their designations are unobtainable and utterly non-existent, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the profound perfection of wisdom, proclaim all dharmas for the sake of sentient beings?”

"Bhagavān! May it not be that bodhisattva-mahāsattvas themselves abide in non-Dharma, teach non-Dharma to sentient beings, exhort sentient beings to abide in non-Dharma, and establish sentient beings in inverted dharmas."
Why is this? World-Honored One!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, they do not even apprehend awakening, much less any factors of awakening that could be apprehended!
"Since even a bodhisattva mahāsattva cannot be apprehended, how much less can there be any dharma of a bodhisattva mahāsattva that can be apprehended!
The Buddha told Subhūti: "It is so! It is so!"
So it is! It is as you have said.
All sentient beings are unapprehendable, and even the designation of "all sentient beings" is unapprehendable.
All phenomena (*dharma*) are unapprehendable, and even the designation of all phenomena is unapprehendable.

Because they are unapprehendable and entirely non-existent, and because they are non-existent, one should know that there is internal emptiness; one should know external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*), the emptiness of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta-śūnyatā*), the emptiness of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta-śūnyatā*), absolute emptiness, the emptiness of the limitless, the emptiness of dispersion, the emptiness of non-alteration, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, the emptiness of specific characteristics, the emptiness of common characteristics, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature.

One should know that suchness is empty; one should know that the dharma-realm, the dharma-nature, the non-illusory nature, the unchanging nature, equality, the nature of being free from birth, the fixedness of dharmas, the stability of dharmas, the limit of reality, the realm of space, and the inconceivable realm are empty.
One should know that the noble truth of suffering is empty; one should know that the noble truths of origin, cessation, and the path are empty.
One should know that form is empty; one should know that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty.
One should know that the eye-base is empty; one should know that the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-bases are empty.
One should know that the form-base is empty; one should know that the sound, odor, taste, tangible, and mental-object bases are empty.
One should know that the eye-element is empty; one should know that the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-elements are empty.
One should know that the realm of form is empty; one should know that the realms of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena are empty.
One should know that the realm of eye-consciousness is empty; one should know that the realms of ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-consciousness are empty.
One should know that eye-contact is empty; one should know that ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact are empty.

One should know that all feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition are empty; one should know that all feelings produced with ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact as conditions are empty.
One should know that the earth element is empty; one should know that the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements are empty.
One should know that the causal condition is empty; one should know that the immediately preceding condition, the object-condition, and the dominant condition are empty.
One should know that all phenomena arising from conditions are empty;

one should know that ignorance is empty, and that volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, and old age, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are empty;

one should know that the self is empty, and that sentient beings, living souls, creatures, nourishers, persons, individuals, mind-born ones, human youths, agents, instigators, originators, prompters, experiencers, feelers, knowers, and seers are empty.
One should know that the perfection of generosity is empty; one should know that the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom are empty.
One should know that the four dhyānas are empty; one should know that the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments are empty.

One should know that the four foundations of mindfulness are empty; one should know that the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of awakening, and the eightfold noble path are empty.
One should know that the gate of liberation of emptiness is empty; one should know that the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness are empty.
One should know that the eight liberations are empty; one should know that the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities are empty.
One should know that all doors of dhāraṇī are empty; one should know that all doors of samādhi are empty.

One should know that the Ground of Utmost Joy is empty; one should know that the Ground of Freedom from Defilement, the Ground of Radiant Light, the Ground of Blazing Wisdom, the Ground of Extreme Difficult Victory, the Ground of Manifestation, the Ground of Far-Going, the Ground of Immovability, the Ground of Excellent Intelligence, and the Ground of the Dharma Cloud are all empty.
One should know that the five eyes are empty; one should know that the six supernormal powers are empty.
One should know that the ten powers of a Buddha are empty; one should know that the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are empty.
One should know that great loving-kindness is empty; one should know that great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity are empty.
One should know that the quality of non-forgetfulness is empty; one should know that the nature of constant abiding in equanimity is empty.
One should know that all-knowledge is empty; one should know that the knowledge of the paths and the knowledge of all aspects are empty.
One should know that the fruit of stream-entry is empty; one should know that the fruits of once-returning, non-returning, arhatship, and the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha are empty;
one should know that the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s entry into the state of certainty is empty;
and one should know that all the practices of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are empty.
One should know that the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas is empty;
one should know that all Buddha-fields are empty; one should know that the ripening of sentient beings is empty;
one should know that the thirty-two marks of a great man are empty; and one should know that the eighty minor marks are empty.

“Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, having seen that all phenomena are entirely empty, they proclaim various teachings to sentient beings in order to cause them to leave behind their inversions.”

Although they proclaim all dharmas for the sake of sentient beings, they apprehend no sentient beings whatsoever; nor do they apprehend any dharmas. Regarding the characteristics of emptiness, they neither increase nor decrease them, and they neither grasp nor reject them. For this reason, although they speak of all dharmas, there is nothing that is spoken.

"Subhūti! When this bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates all phenomena in this manner, they attain unobstructed wisdom regarding all phenomena. By means of this wisdom, they do not destroy the non-dual discernment of all phenomena, and they proclaim them as they truly are for the sake of all sentient beings, causing them to abandon the deluded attachments of false conceptualization and leading them, according to their respective capacities, to the fruits of the three vehicles."

The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle 381. Translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Part One: Chapter Sixty-Eight, Part Four, "The Characteristics of All Meritorious Qualities. Furthermore, Subhūti:

Suppose a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha were to manifest a single Buddha, and that Buddha were further able to manifest immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of assemblies; then those manifested Buddhas would cause the manifested assemblies to practice the perfection of generosity, or cause them to practice the perfection of ethical discipline, or cause them to practice the perfection of patience, or cause them to practice the perfection of diligence, or cause them to practice the perfection of meditative concentration, or cause them to practice the perfection of wisdom;
or cause them to practice the four dhyānas, or cause them to practice the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments.

Or they cause them to practice the four foundations of mindfulness; or they cause them to practice the four right endeavors, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path;
or they cause them to practice the gate of liberation of emptiness, or they cause them to practice the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness;

or they cause them to abide in internal emptiness, or they cause them to abide in external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersion emptiness, non-alteration emptiness, essential nature emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common characteristic emptiness, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of non-apprehensibility, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature.

Or they cause them to dwell in True Suchness (*tathatā*); or they cause them to dwell in the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), non-falsity, immutability, equality, the state beyond birth, the fixed nature of phenomena (*dharmaniyāmatā*), the stability of phenomena (*dharmasthititā*), the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), the realm of space (*ākāśadhātu*), and the inconceivable realm;
or they cause them to dwell in the Noble Truth of Suffering; or they cause them to dwell in the Noble Truths of Origination, Cessation, and the Path;

or they cause them to practice the eight liberations (*aṣṭavimokṣa*); or they cause them to practice the eight bases of mastery (*aṣṭābhibhvāyatana*), the nine successive meditative attainments (*navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti*), and the ten spheres of totality (*daśakṛtsnāyatana*).
Some they cause to practice all the gateways of dhāraṇī; some they cause to practice all the gateways of samādhi;

some they cause to practice the Ground of Extreme Joy, or the Ground of Purity, the Ground of Radiance, the Ground of Blazing Wisdom, the Ground of Difficult Victory, the Ground of Presence, the Ground of Far-Going, the Ground of Immovability, the Ground of Excellent Intelligence, and the Ground of the Dharma Cloud;
some they cause to practice the five eyes, or some they cause to practice the six supernormal powers.
Some they cause to practice the ten powers of a Buddha; some they cause to practice the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
some they cause to practice great loving-kindness; some they cause to practice great compassion, great joy, and great equanimity;
some they cause to practice the quality of non-forgetfulness; and some they cause to practice the nature of constant abiding in equanimity.

Or they cause them to practice the knowledge of all things (*sarvajñatā*); or they cause them to practice the knowledge of the paths (*mārgākārajñatā*) and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*);
or they cause them to practice the thirty-two marks of a great man (*dvātriṃśanmahāpuruṣalakṣaṇa*), or they cause them to practice the eighty secondary signs (*aśītyanuvyañjana*);

or they cause them to realize the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpattiphala*), or they cause them to realize the fruits of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmiphala*), non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*), arhatship (*arhatphala*), or the enlightenment of a solitary buddha (*pratyekabodhi*).
"Either cause them to realize the supreme state of a bodhisattva, or cause them to realize the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas.
Subhūti, what do you think?"
"At that time, did the emanated Buddha and the emanated assembly have any conceptual discrimination regarding dharmas,
or any destruction [of them]? Subhūti replied, "No!"
"No, World-Honored One! No, Sugata!"
"Because all manifestations are without conceptual discrimination.
The Buddha said,
"Suvikrāntavikrāmin!"

By this causal connection, one should know that it is likewise for the bodhisattva mahāsattva who practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā*: although they preach the Dharma to all sentient beings as is appropriate and do not conceptually differentiate or destroy the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), they are nevertheless able to establish sentient beings in accordance with reality, causing them to dwell securely in the stage (*bhūmi*) in which they ought to abide.

Although there is absolutely nothing to be apprehended regarding sentient beings or all phenomena, one causes sentient beings to be liberated from their deluded, inverted attachments by means of the skillful method of neither bondage nor liberation.
Why is that? "Subhūti!
The intrinsic nature of form is neither bound nor liberated; the intrinsic nature of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is likewise neither bound nor liberated."

If the intrinsic nature of form is neither bound nor liberated, then it is not form; if the intrinsic nature of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is likewise neither bound nor liberated, then they are not feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
Why is this? Because form, up to and including consciousness, are ultimately pure. "Subhūti!
The intrinsic nature of the eye-base is neither bound nor liberated; the intrinsic nature of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-bases is likewise neither bound nor liberated.

That which is the intrinsic nature of the eye-base as neither bound nor liberated is not the eye-base; that which is the intrinsic nature of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-bases as neither bound nor liberated is not the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind-base.
Why is this? Because the sense base of the eye, up to and including the sense base of the mind, is ultimately pure. "Subhūti!

The intrinsic nature of the sense-base of form is neither bound nor liberated; the intrinsic natures of the sense-bases of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena are likewise neither bound nor liberated.

That which is the intrinsic nature of the sense-base of form, being neither bound nor liberated, is not the sense-base of form; that which is the intrinsic nature of the sense-bases of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena, being likewise neither bound nor liberated, is not the sense-bases of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, or mental phenomena.
Why is this? Because the sphere of form, up to and including the sphere of mental phenomena, is ultimately pure. "Subhūti!..."
The intrinsic nature of the eye-element is neither bound nor liberated; the intrinsic natures of the ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-elements are likewise neither bound nor liberated.

That which is the intrinsic nature of the eye-element as neither bound nor liberated is not the eye-element; that which is the intrinsic nature of the ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-elements as neither bound nor liberated is not the ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-element.
Why is this? Because the eye-element, up to and including the mind-element, is ultimately pure. "Subhūti!

The intrinsic nature of the realm of form is neither bound nor liberated; the intrinsic natures of the realms of sound, odor, taste, touch, and mental phenomena are likewise neither bound nor liberated.

That which is the intrinsic nature of the realm of form as neither bound nor liberated is not the realm of form; that which is the intrinsic nature of the realms of sound, odor, taste, touch, and mental phenomena as neither bound nor liberated is not the realms of sound, odor, taste, touch, or mental phenomena.
Why is this? Because the realm of form, up to and including the realm of phenomena, is ultimately pure. "Subhūti!

The intrinsic nature of the eye-consciousness element is neither bound nor liberated; the intrinsic natures of the ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-consciousness elements are likewise neither bound nor liberated.

That which is the intrinsic nature of the eye-consciousness element, being neither bound nor liberated, is not the eye-consciousness element; that which is the intrinsic nature of the ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-consciousness elements, being neither bound nor liberated, is not the ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-consciousness element.
Why is this? Because the眼界 (eye-consciousness element) up to the意識界 (mind-consciousness element) are ultimately pure. "Subhūti!..."
The intrinsic nature of eye-contact is neither bound nor liberated; the intrinsic nature of ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact is likewise neither bound nor liberated.

That which is the intrinsic nature of eye-contact as neither bound nor liberated is not eye-contact; that which is the intrinsic nature of ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact as neither bound nor liberated is not ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-contact.
Why is this? Because visual contact, up to and including mental contact, are ultimately pure. "Subhūti!

The sensations produced with eye-contact as a condition are by nature neither bound nor liberated; the sensations produced with ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-contact as conditions are likewise by nature neither bound nor liberated.

The nature of all feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition is neither bound nor liberated; therefore, they are not "feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition. The nature of all feelings produced with ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-contact as a condition is likewise neither bound nor liberated; therefore, they are not "feelings produced with ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-contact as a condition."

Why is this? Because the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition, up to and including the various feelings produced with mind-contact as a condition, are ultimately pure. "Subhūti!..."
The intrinsic nature of the earth element is neither bound nor liberated; the intrinsic natures of the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements are likewise neither bound nor liberated.

That which is the intrinsic nature of the earth element—being neither bound nor liberated—is not the earth element; that which is the intrinsic nature of the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements—being neither bound nor liberated—is not the water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness element.
Why is this? Because the elements of earth, water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness are ultimately pure. "Subhūti!..."

The intrinsic nature of the causal condition (hetu-pratyaya) is neither bound nor liberated; the intrinsic nature of the equal-and-immediate condition (samanantara-pratyaya), the objective condition (ālambana-pratyaya), and the dominant condition (adhipati-pratyaya) is likewise neither bound nor liberated.

If the intrinsic nature of the causal condition is neither bound nor liberated, it is not a causal condition; if the intrinsic nature of the equal-and-immediate, objective, and dominant conditions is neither bound nor liberated, they are not the equal-and-immediate, objective, or dominant conditions.
Why is this? Because the causal conditions, up to and including the dominant conditions, are ultimately pure. "Subhūti!..."

The intrinsic nature of phenomena produced from conditions is neither bound nor liberated; that which is neither bound nor liberated by its intrinsic nature is not a phenomenon produced from conditions.
Why is this? Because phenomena produced from various conditions are ultimately pure. "Subhūti!

Ignorance is by its very nature neither bound nor liberated; likewise, the nature of volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, existence, birth, and old age, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair is also neither bound nor liberated.

If the intrinsic nature of ignorance is neither bound nor liberated, then it is not ignorance; likewise, if the intrinsic nature of the formative forces up to old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair is also neither bound nor liberated, then they are not the formative forces up to old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair.
Why is this? Because ignorance through to old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair are ultimately pure. "Subhūti!

The intrinsic nature of the perfection of generosity is neither bound nor liberated; likewise, the intrinsic natures of the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom are also neither bound nor liberated.

The intrinsic nature of the perfection of generosity is neither bound nor liberated; therefore, it is not the perfection of generosity. The intrinsic nature of the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom is likewise neither bound nor liberated; therefore, they are not the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, or wisdom.
Why is this? Because from generosity up to the perfection of wisdom, they are ultimately pure.
"Suvikrāntavikrāmin! [It is so]."
The intrinsic nature of the four dhyānas is neither bound nor liberated; the intrinsic nature of the four immeasurables and the four formless absorptions is likewise neither bound nor liberated.

That which is the intrinsic nature of the four dhyānas—being neither bound nor liberated—is not the four dhyānas; that which is the intrinsic nature of the four immeasurables and the four formless absorptions—being neither bound nor liberated—is not the four immeasurables or the four formless absorptions.
Why is this? Because the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless absorptions are ultimately pure.
"Suvikrāntavikrāmin!..."

The four foundations of mindfulness are by nature neither bound nor liberated; the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of awakening, and the eightfold noble path are likewise by nature neither bound nor liberated.

The intrinsic nature of the four foundations of mindfulness is neither bound nor liberated; therefore, they are not the four foundations of mindfulness. Likewise, the intrinsic nature of the four right efforts up to the eightfold noble path is also neither bound nor liberated; therefore, they are not the four right efforts up to the eightfold noble path.
Why is this? Because the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path are ultimately pure. "Subhūti!

The intrinsic nature of the gate of liberation of emptiness is neither bound nor liberated; the intrinsic nature of the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness is likewise neither bound nor liberated.

That which is the intrinsic nature of the gate of liberation of emptiness, being neither bound nor liberated, is not the gate of liberation of emptiness; that which is the intrinsic nature of the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness, being neither bound nor liberated, is not the gate of liberation of signlessness or wishlessness.
Why is this? Because the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—are ultimately pure. "Subhūti!..."

The intrinsic nature of internal emptiness is neither bound nor liberated; the intrinsic nature of external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, limitless emptiness, dispersion emptiness, non-alteration emptiness, intrinsic-nature emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common-characteristic emptiness, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence is neither bound nor liberated.

If the intrinsic nature of internal emptiness is neither bound nor liberated, it is not internal emptiness; likewise, if the intrinsic nature of external emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature, is also neither bound nor liberated, they are not external emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature.
Why is this? Because inner emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence, is ultimately pure.
"Suvikrāntavikrāmin! [It is thus.]”
The noble truth of suffering is by nature neither bound nor liberated; the noble truths of origination, cessation, and the path are likewise by nature neither bound nor liberated.

If the noble truth of suffering is by nature neither bound nor liberated, it is not the noble truth of suffering; if the noble truths of origination, cessation, and the path are by nature neither bound nor liberated, they are not the noble truths of origination, cessation, and the path.
Why is this? Because the noble truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path are ultimately pure. "Subhūti!..."

The eight liberations are by nature neither bound nor liberated; the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities are likewise by nature neither bound nor liberated.

The eight liberations are by nature neither bound nor liberated; thus they are not the eight liberations. The eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities are also by nature neither bound nor liberated; thus they are not the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, or the ten totalities.
Why is this? Because the eight liberations up to the ten totalities are ultimately pure. "Subhūti!..."
The intrinsic nature of all dharani-doors is neither bound nor liberated; the intrinsic nature of all samadhi-doors is likewise neither bound nor liberated.

That which is the intrinsic nature of all dharani-doors as being neither bound nor liberated is not the dharani-doors themselves; that which is the intrinsic nature of all samadhi-doors as being neither bound nor liberated is not the samadhi-doors themselves.
Why is this? Because all dharani-doors and all samadhi-doors are ultimately pure. "Subhūti!..."

The first ground, the Ground of Utmost Joy, is by its very nature neither bound nor liberated; the Ground Free from Defilement, the Ground of Luminous Radiance, the Ground of Blazing Wisdom, the Ground of Difficult Victory, the Ground of Manifestation, the Ground of Far-Going, the Ground of Immovability, the Ground of Excellent Intelligence, and the Ground of the Dharma Cloud are likewise by their very nature neither bound nor liberated.

The intrinsic nature of the Ground of Utmost Joy is neither bound nor liberated; thus, it is not the Ground of Utmost Joy. The intrinsic nature of the Grounds from the Stainless up to the Cloud of Dharma is likewise neither bound nor liberated; thus, they are not the Grounds from the Stainless up to the Cloud of Dharma.
Why is this? Because from the Stage of Extreme Joy up to the Stage of the Cloud of Dharma, they are ultimately pure. "Subhūti!..."
The intrinsic nature of the five eyes is neither bound nor liberated; the intrinsic nature of the six supernormal powers is likewise neither bound nor liberated.

That which is the intrinsic nature of the five eyes as neither bound nor liberated is not the five eyes; that which is the intrinsic nature of the six supernormal powers as neither bound nor liberated is not the six supernormal powers.
Why is this? Because the five eyes and the six supernormal powers are ultimately pure.
"Suvikrāntavikrāmin! [It is so]."

The ten powers of a Buddha are by nature neither bound nor liberated; the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are likewise by nature neither bound nor liberated.

The ten powers of a Buddha are by nature neither bound nor liberated; therefore, they are not the ten powers of a Buddha. The four fearlessnesses, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, are also by nature neither bound nor liberated; therefore, they are not the four fearlessnesses, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
Why is this? Because the Buddha’s ten powers, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, are ultimately pure. "Subhūti!..."

The intrinsic nature of great loving-kindness is neither bound nor liberated; the intrinsic natures of great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity are likewise neither bound nor liberated.

That which is the intrinsic nature of great loving-kindness, being neither bound nor liberated, is not great loving-kindness; that which is the intrinsic nature of great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity, being neither bound nor liberated, is not great compassion, great sympathetic joy, or great equanimity.
Why is this? Because great loving-kindness, up to and including great equanimity, are ultimately pure.
"Suvikrāntavikrāmin! "
The nature of the quality of non-forgetfulness is neither bound nor liberated; the nature of the state of constant equanimity is likewise neither bound nor liberated.

That which is the nature of the quality of non-forgetfulness, being neither bound nor liberated, is not the quality of non-forgetfulness itself; that which is the nature of the state of constant equanimity, being neither bound nor liberated, is not the state of constant equanimity itself.
Why is this? Because the quality of non-forgetfulness and the nature of constant abiding in equanimity are ultimately pure. "Subhūti!

The intrinsic nature of all-knowledge (sarvajñatā) is neither bound nor liberated; the intrinsic nature of the knowledge of the paths (mārgajñatā) and the knowledge of all aspects (sarvākārajñatā) is likewise neither bound nor liberated.

Since the intrinsic nature of all-knowledge is neither bound nor liberated, it is not "all-knowledge"; since the intrinsic nature of the knowledge of the paths and the knowledge of all aspects is neither bound nor liberated, they are not "knowledge of the paths" or "knowledge of all aspects."
Why is this? Because all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) are ultimately pure. "Subhūti!..."
The thirty-two marks of a great man are by nature neither bound nor liberated; the eighty secondary signs are likewise by nature neither bound nor liberated.

Since the thirty-two marks of a great man are by nature neither bound nor liberated, they are not the thirty-two marks of a great man; since the eighty secondary signs are by nature neither bound nor liberated, they are not the eighty secondary signs.
Why is this? Because the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty secondary signs are ultimately pure. "Subhūti!..."

The nature of the fruit of stream-entry is neither bound nor liberated; likewise, the nature of the fruits of once-returning, non-returning, and arhatship, as well as the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, is also neither bound nor liberated.

The intrinsic nature of the fruit of stream-entry is without bondage and without liberation; therefore, it is not the fruit of stream-entry. The intrinsic nature of the fruits of once-returning, non-returning, arhatship, and pratyekabuddha-enlightenment is likewise without bondage and without liberation; therefore, they are not the fruits of once-returning, non-returning, arhatship, or pratyekabuddha-enlightenment.
Why is this? Because the fruit of stream-entry up to the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha is ultimately pure. "Subhūti!..."

The intrinsic nature of all practices of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas is neither bound nor liberated; the intrinsic nature of the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas is likewise neither bound nor liberated.

The intrinsic nature of all the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas is neither bound nor liberated; thus, it is not the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. The intrinsic nature of the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas is likewise neither bound nor liberated; thus, it is not the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the buddhas.
Why is this? Because all the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas are ultimately pure. "Subhūti!..."
The intrinsic nature of worldly dharmas is neither bound nor liberated; the intrinsic nature of supramundane dharmas is likewise neither bound nor liberated.

If the intrinsic nature of worldly dharmas is neither bound nor liberated, they are not worldly dharmas; if the intrinsic nature of supramundane dharmas is likewise neither bound nor liberated, they are not supramundane dharmas.
Why is this? Because worldly and world-transcending dharmas are ultimately pure. "Subhūti!

The intrinsic nature of contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) is neither bound nor liberated; the intrinsic nature of uncontaminated phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*) is likewise neither bound nor liberated.

If the intrinsic nature of contaminated phenomena is neither bound nor liberated, it is not a contaminated phenomenon; if the intrinsic nature of uncontaminated phenomena is neither bound nor liberated, it is not an uncontaminated phenomenon.
Why is this? Because contaminated and uncontaminated phenomena are ultimately pure. "Subhūti!..."
Conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) are by nature neither bound nor liberated; unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*) are likewise by nature neither bound nor liberated.

That which is by nature neither bound nor liberated in conditioned phenomena is not a conditioned phenomenon; that which is by nature neither bound nor liberated in unconditioned phenomena is not an unconditioned phenomenon.
Why is this? Because conditioned phenomena and unconditioned phenomena are ultimately pure. "Thus it is, Subhūti!"

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, although they proclaim all phenomena for the sake of sentient beings, they do not apprehend either sentient beings or the intrinsic nature of phenomena at all.
Why is this? Because sentient beings and all phenomena are unapprehendable. "Furthermore, Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, by taking non-abiding as the skillful means, they abide in the non-apprehension of all phenomena; that is to say, by taking non-abiding as the skillful means, they abide in the emptiness of form;
by taking non-abiding as the skillful means, they abide in the emptiness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
By taking non-abiding as the skillful means, one dwells in the emptiness of the sense-base of the eye;
by taking non-abiding as the skillful means, one dwells in the emptiness of the sense-bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
By taking non-abiding as the skillful means, one dwells in the emptiness of the sphere of form;
by taking non-abiding as the skillful means, one dwells in the emptiness of the spheres of sound, odor, taste, touch, and mental phenomena.
By taking non-abiding as the skillful means, one dwells in the emptiness of the eye-element;
by taking non-abiding as the skillful means, one dwells in the emptiness of the ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-elements.
By taking non-abiding as the skillful means, one dwells in the emptiness of the realm of form;
by taking non-abiding as the skillful means, one dwells in the emptiness of the realms of sound, odor, taste, touch, and mental phenomena.
By taking non-abiding as the means, one dwells in the emptiness of the eye-consciousness element;
by taking non-abiding as the means, one dwells in the emptiness of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-consciousness elements.
By taking non-abiding as the skillful means, one dwells in the emptiness of eye-contact;
by taking non-abiding as the skillful means, one dwells in the emptiness of ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact.
By taking non-abiding as the skillful means, he dwells in the emptiness of all feelings produced with eye-contact as condition;
by taking non-abiding as the skillful means, he dwells in the emptiness of all feelings produced with ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact as conditions.
By taking non-abiding as the skillful means, one dwells in the emptiness of the earth element;
by taking non-abiding as the skillful means, one dwells in the emptiness of the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements.
By taking non-abiding as the skillful means, one dwells in the emptiness of the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*);

by taking non-abiding as the skillful means, one dwells in the emptiness of the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
By taking non-abiding as the means, one abides in the emptiness of phenomena produced from conditions.
By taking non-abiding as the means, one abides in the emptiness of ignorance;

by taking non-abiding as the means, one abides in the emptiness of volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, and old age, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair.
By taking non-abiding as the skillful means, one dwells in the emptiness of the perfection of giving;
by taking non-abiding as the skillful means, one dwells in the emptiness of the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom.
By taking non-abiding as the skillful means, they abide in the emptiness of the four dhyānas;
by taking non-abiding as the skillful means, they abide in the emptiness of the four immeasurables and the four formless absorptions.
Because they take non-abiding as their skillful means, they abide in the emptiness of the four foundations of mindfulness;

because they take non-abiding as their skillful means, they abide in the emptiness of the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path.
By taking non-abiding as the skillful means, one dwells in the emptiness of the gate of liberation of emptiness;
by taking non-abiding as the skillful means, one dwells in the emptiness of the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness.
By taking non-abiding as the skillful means, one dwells in internal emptiness;

by taking non-abiding as the skillful means, one dwells in external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, unchanging emptiness, essential nature emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common characteristic emptiness, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature.
By taking non-abiding as the skillful means, one dwells in the emptiness of the noble truth of suffering;
by taking non-abiding as the skillful means, one dwells in the emptiness of the noble truths of origin, cessation, and the path.
By taking non-abiding as the skillful means, one dwells in the emptiness of the eight liberations;
by taking non-abiding as the skillful means, one dwells in the emptiness of the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities.
By taking non-abiding as the skillful means, they abide in the emptiness of all dhāraṇī-doors;
by taking non-abiding as the skillful means, they abide in the emptiness of all samādhi-doors.
By taking non-abiding as the skillful means, one dwells in the emptiness of the Ground of Supreme Joy;

by taking non-abiding as the skillful means, one dwells in the emptiness of the Ground of Purity, the Ground of Radiance, the Ground of Blazing Wisdom, the Ground of Utmost Difficulty to Conquer, the Ground of Manifestation, the Ground of Far-reaching Practice, the Ground of Immovability, the Ground of Excellent Intelligence, and the Ground of the Dharma Cloud.
By taking non-abiding as the skillful means, one dwells in the emptiness of the five eyes;
by taking non-abiding as the skillful means, one dwells in the emptiness of the six supernormal powers;
by taking non-abiding as the skillful means, one dwells in the emptiness of the ten powers of a Buddha.
By means of non-abiding as a skillful method, they abide in the emptiness of the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
By means of non-abiding as a skillful method, they abide in the emptiness of great loving-kindness;
by means of non-abiding as a skillful method, they abide in the emptiness of great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity.
By taking non-abiding as the skillful means, one dwells in the emptiness of the quality of non-forgetfulness;
by taking non-abiding as the skillful means, one dwells in the emptiness of the nature of constant equanimity.
By taking non-abiding as the skillful means, they abide in the emptiness of all-knowledge;
by taking non-abiding as the skillful means, they abide in the emptiness of the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects.
By taking non-abiding as the skillful means, one dwells in the emptiness of the thirty-two marks of a great man;
by taking non-abiding as the skillful means, one dwells in the emptiness of the eighty minor marks.
By taking non-abiding as the skillful means, one abides in the emptiness of the fruit of stream-entry;
by taking non-abiding as the skillful means, one abides in the emptiness of the fruits of once-returner, non-returner, arhatship, and the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha.
By taking non-abiding as the skillful means, they abide in the emptiness of all bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices;
by taking non-abiding as the skillful means, they abide in the emptiness of the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas.
By taking non-abiding as the means, one abides in the emptiness of worldly phenomena;
by taking non-abiding as the means, one abides in the emptiness of supramundane phenomena.
By taking non-abiding as the skillful means, one dwells in the emptiness of contaminated phenomena;
by taking non-abiding as the skillful means, one dwells in the emptiness of uncontaminated phenomena.
By taking non-abiding as the skillful means, one dwells in the emptiness of conditioned phenomena;
by taking non-abiding as the skillful means, one dwells in the emptiness of unconditioned phenomena.
“Subhūti! Form has no place of abiding; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness likewise have no place of abiding.
The emptiness of form has no place of abiding; the emptiness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness likewise has no place of abiding.”
Why is this? Subhūti!

Form has no intrinsic nature and is unapprehendable; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness likewise have no intrinsic nature and are unapprehendable. The emptiness of form has no intrinsic nature and is unapprehendable; the emptiness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness likewise has no intrinsic nature and is unapprehendable. This is because that which is unapprehendable due to the absence of intrinsic nature cannot abide anywhere.
“Subhūti! The sphere of the eye has no abiding; the spheres of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind likewise have no abiding.
The sphere of the eye is empty and has no abiding; the spheres of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are also empty and have no abiding.”
Why is this? Subhūti!

The eye-base has no intrinsic nature and is unapprehendable; the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-bases likewise have no intrinsic nature and are unapprehendable. The eye-base is empty, lacks intrinsic nature, and is unapprehendable; the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-bases are also empty, lack intrinsic nature, and are unapprehendable. This is because there is no dharma that lacks intrinsic nature and is unapprehendable which can abide anywhere.
"Subhūti! The sphere of form has no place of abiding; the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena likewise have no place of abiding.
The sphere of form is empty and has no place of abiding; the emptiness of the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena likewise has no place of abiding."
Why is this? Subhūti!

The sphere of form has no intrinsic nature and is unapprehendable; the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena likewise have no intrinsic nature and are unapprehendable. The sphere of form is empty, lacks intrinsic nature, and is unapprehendable; the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena are also empty, lack intrinsic nature, and are unapprehendable. This is because that which lacks intrinsic nature and is unapprehendable cannot have any place of abiding.
“Subhūti! The eye-element has no place of abiding; the ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-elements likewise have no place of abiding.
The eye-element is empty and has no place of abiding; the emptiness of the ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-elements likewise has no place of abiding.”
Why is this? Subhūti!

The eye-element has no intrinsic nature and is unapprehendable; the ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-elements likewise have no intrinsic nature and are unapprehendable. The eye-element is empty, lacks intrinsic nature, and is unapprehendable; the emptiness of the ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-elements likewise lacks intrinsic nature and is unapprehendable. This is because that which lacks intrinsic nature and is unapprehendable cannot abide anywhere.
“Subhūti! The realm of form has no abiding place; the realms of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena likewise have no abiding place.
The realm of form is empty and has no abiding place; the emptiness of the realms of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena likewise has no abiding place.”
Why is this? Subhūti!

The realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) has no intrinsic nature and is unapprehendable; the realms of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) likewise have no intrinsic nature and are unapprehendable. The realm of form is empty, lacks intrinsic nature, and is unapprehendable; the emptiness of the realms of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and phenomena likewise lacks intrinsic nature and is unapprehendable. This is because that which is unapprehendable due to the absence of intrinsic nature cannot abide anywhere.
“Subhūti! The eye-consciousness element has no abiding place; the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-consciousness elements likewise have no abiding place.
The eye-consciousness element is empty and has no abiding place; the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-consciousness elements are also empty and have no abiding place.”
Why is this? Subhūti!

The eye-consciousness element has no intrinsic nature and is unapprehendable; the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-consciousness elements likewise have no intrinsic nature and are unapprehendable. The eye-consciousness element is empty, lacks intrinsic nature, and is unapprehendable; the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-consciousness elements are also empty, lack intrinsic nature, and are unapprehendable. This is because that which lacks intrinsic nature and is unapprehendable cannot abide anywhere.
“Subhūti! Eye-contact has no abiding place; ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact likewise have no abiding place.
Eye-contact is empty and has no abiding place; ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact are also empty and have no abiding place.”
Why is this? Subhūti!

Eye-contact has no intrinsic nature and is unapprehendable; ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact likewise have no intrinsic nature and are unapprehendable. Eye-contact is empty, lacks intrinsic nature, and is unapprehendable; ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact are also empty, lack intrinsic nature, and are unapprehendable. This is because a dharma that lacks intrinsic nature and is unapprehendable cannot have any place of abiding.

“Subhūti! The various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition have no abiding place; the various feelings produced with ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-contact as conditions likewise have no abiding place.

The various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition are empty and have no abiding place; the various feelings produced with ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-contact as conditions are also empty and have no abiding place.”
Why is this? Subhūti!

The various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition have no intrinsic nature and cannot be apprehended; the various feelings produced with ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-contact as conditions likewise have no intrinsic nature and cannot be apprehended. The various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition are empty, lack intrinsic nature, and cannot be apprehended; the various feelings produced with ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-contact as conditions are also empty, lack intrinsic nature, and cannot be apprehended. This is because a dharma that lacks intrinsic nature and cannot be apprehended has no place to abide.
“Subhūti! The earth element has no place of abiding; the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements likewise have no place of abiding.
The emptiness of the earth element has no place of abiding; the emptiness of the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements likewise has no place of abiding.”
Why is this? Subhūti!

The earth element has no intrinsic nature and is unapprehendable; the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements likewise have no intrinsic nature and are unapprehendable. The emptiness of the earth element has no intrinsic nature and is unapprehendable; the emptiness of the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements likewise has no intrinsic nature and is unapprehendable. This is because that which is unapprehendable due to the absence of intrinsic nature cannot have any place of abiding.
“Subhūti! The causal condition has no abode; likewise, the immediately preceding condition, the object-condition, and the dominant condition also have no abode.
