one does not course in the eye-base, nor does one course in the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind-bases;
one does not course in the form-base, nor does one course in the sound, odor, taste, tangible object, or mental-object bases.
They do not course in the eye-element, nor do they course in the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind-elements;
they do not course in the eye-consciousness-element, nor do they course in the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind-consciousness-elements;
they do not course in eye-contact, nor do they course in ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind-contact.
They do not course in the various feelings produced with eye-contact as condition, nor do they course in the various feelings produced with ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind-contact as condition;
they do not course in the earth element, nor do they course in the water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness elements;

they do not course in the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), nor do they course in the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), or the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
One does not engage with phenomena produced from conditions;

one does not engage with ignorance, nor does one engage with volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, or aging, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair.
One does not engage with the perfection of generosity, nor does one engage with the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, or wisdom.
They do not practice the four dhyānas, nor do they practice the four immeasurables or the four formless attainments;

they do not practice the four foundations of mindfulness, nor do they practice the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, or the eightfold noble path;
they do not practice the liberation door of emptiness, nor do they practice the liberation doors of signlessness and wishlessness.

They do not practice inner emptiness, nor do they practice outer emptiness, inner-and-outer emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, endless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, non-alteration emptiness, essential nature emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common characteristic emptiness, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, or the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence;
they do not practice true thusness up to the inconceivable realm;
and they do not practice the noble truth of suffering, nor do they practice the noble truths of origin, cessation, or the path.
They do not practice the eight liberations, nor do they practice the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative attainments, or the ten totalities;
they do not practice any of the doors of dhāraṇī, nor do they practice any of the doors of samādhi;

they do not practice the Ground of Extreme Joy, nor do they practice the Ground of Purity, the Ground of Radiance, the Ground of Blazing Wisdom, the Ground of Difficult Victory, the Ground of Manifestation, the Ground of Far-Going, the Ground of Immovability, the Ground of Good Intelligence, or the Ground of the Dharma Cloud.
They do not practice with respect to the five eyes, nor do they practice with respect to the six supernormal powers;

they do not practice with respect to the ten powers of a Buddha, nor do they practice with respect to the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, or the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
they do not practice with respect to great loving-kindness, nor do they practice with respect to great compassion, great sympathetic joy, or great equanimity.
They do not practice in the dharma of non-forgetfulness, nor do they practice in the state of constant equanimity;
they do not practice in all-knowledge, nor do they practice in the knowledge of the paths or the knowledge of all aspects;
they do not practice in the thirty-two marks of a great man, nor do they practice in the eighty secondary signs.
One does not practice in the fruit of stream-entry, nor does one practice in the fruits of once-returner, non-returner, or arhatship; one does not practice in the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha;
one does not practice in any of the practices of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, nor does one practice in the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas;
one does not practice in internal phenomena, nor does one practice in external phenomena.
He does not engage with latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), nor does he engage with active outbursts (*paryavasthāna*);
he does not engage with worldly dharmas, nor does he engage with supramundane dharmas;
he does not engage with tainted (*sāsrava*) dharmas, nor does he engage with untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas.
"One does not practice in conditioned phenomena, nor does one practice in unconditioned phenomena;
one does not practice in the path, nor does one practice in the fruit of the path. Subhūti!..."

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, it is likewise thus: they practice nothing at all with respect to any phenomena. This is called skillfully penetrating the true mark of all phenomena, which means having no conceptual discrimination regarding the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
Then, the Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha,
saying: “World-Honored One,
how does that which is emanated by a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha manifest the cultivation of the Noble Path?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"Those emanations produced by those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas do not become defiled or purified by virtue of practicing the noble path, nor do they transmigrate through the cycle of birth and death within the five destinies."
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the profound perfection of wisdom, penetrate the fact that all phenomena lack any substantial reality?”
The Buddha said to Subhūti: “What do you think?

Do those emanations produced by the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas possess any substantial reality, such that based on that substantial reality there could be defilement or purification, or the occurrence of the five destinies of saṃsāra?”
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One!”

"No, Sugata! There is not even the slightest real entity in that which is emanated by the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas; nor is there defilement or purification based upon such an entity, nor is there saṃsāra within the five destinies."
The Buddha said, “Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, they likewise thoroughly penetrate the true mark of all phenomena; they realize that all phenomena are entirely devoid of any substantial reality.”
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
are all forms like magical illusions?”
Are all feelings, perceptions, formations, and consciousnesses also like an illusion?
Are all bases of the eye like an illusion?
Are all bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind also like an illusion?
Are all forms like a magical illusion?
Are all sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects also like a magical illusion?
Are all eye-faculties like a magical illusion?
Are all the realms of ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind also like a transformation?
Are all the realms of form also like a transformation?
Are all the realms of sound, odor, taste, touch, and mental phenomena also like a transformation?
Are all眼界 (eye-consciousness elements) like transformations?
Are all ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-consciousness elements also like transformations?
Are all eye-contact phenomena also like transformations?
Are all instances of ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-contact likewise like a magical creation?
Are all feelings produced with eye-contact as their condition likewise like a magical creation?
Are all feelings arising conditioned by ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact likewise like a magical creation?
Are all earth elements likewise like a magical creation?
Are all the elements of water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness also like a magical transformation?
Are all causes and conditions also like a magical transformation?
Are all equal-immediate conditions, object-conditions, and predominant conditions also like a magical transformation?
Are all phenomena produced from conditions like a magical illusion?
Are all instances of ignorance like a magical illusion?

Are all formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, and old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair also like a magical illusion?
Is it thus that all mundane phenomena are like a magical illusion?
Are all supramundane phenomena also like a magical illusion?
Are all contaminated phenomena likewise like a magical illusion?
Are all untainted phenomena (*anāsravadharma*) also like an illusion?
Are all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) entirely like an illusion?
Are all unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*) also like an illusion?
The Buddha told Subhūti: "So it is! So it is!"
"It is as you have said:
all phenomena are like magical illusions.

Thus ends the sixth hundred and eighty-third fascicle of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree, Part One, Chapter Sixty-nine, "The Equality of All Phenomena," Section Two. At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If all dharmas are like transformations, then all that is transformed has no real form, nor does it have real feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness;
all that is transformed has no real eye-base, nor does it have real ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind-bases.”
All transformations lack any real sphere of form; likewise, they lack any real spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, or mental objects.
All transformations lack any real eye-consciousness element; likewise, they lack any real ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-consciousness elements.
All transformations lack any real form-element; likewise, they lack any real elements of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, or mental objects.
All that is manifested through transformation lacks any real eye-consciousness element, nor does it possess any real ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind-consciousness elements;
all that is manifested through transformation lacks any real eye-contact, nor does it possess any real ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind-contact;

all that is manifested through transformation lacks any real feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition, nor does it possess any real feelings produced with ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind-contact as a condition.
All transformations lack a real earth element, nor do they possess real water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness elements;
all transformations lack real causes and conditions, nor do they possess real immediate conditions, object conditions, or dominant conditions;
all transformations lack any real phenomena produced from conditions.

All that is manifested through transformation lacks any reality; there is no real ignorance, nor are there real formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, or old age, death, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair.
All that is manifested through transformation lacks any reality as worldly dharmas, nor are there any real supramundane dharmas.
All that is manifested through transformation lacks any reality as contaminated dharmas, nor are there any real uncontaminated dharmas.
All transformations are devoid of any truly existent conditioned phenomena, nor are they devoid of any truly existent unconditioned phenomena;
all transformations are devoid of any truly existent defiled phenomena, nor are they devoid of any truly existent pure phenomena;

all transformations are devoid of any truly existent saṃsāra within the five destinies, nor are they devoid of any truly existent liberation from the five destinies. How, then, can a bodhisattva mahāsattva possess superior human efficacy toward sentient beings?
The Buddha said to Subhūti: "What do you think?

When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas were originally practicing the bodhisattva path, did they perceive any sentient beings who could be liberated from the realms of hell, animals, hungry ghosts, humans, or devas?"
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One!”
"No, Sugata! The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"So it is! So it is! When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas originally practiced the bodhisattva path, they did not perceive any sentient beings who could be liberated from the triple world."
Why is this? Subhūti!
All dharmas that bodhisattva-mahāsattvas know, see, and penetrate are like illusions and transformations; they are not at all real existents.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva knows, sees, and penetrates all phenomena as being like illusions and transformations, and that they are entirely not real, for what purpose does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice the perfections of giving, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom?”
For what purpose does one practice the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments?

For what purpose does one practice the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path?
For what purpose does one practice the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness?
For what purpose does one practice the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative attainments, and the ten universal bases?
For what purpose does one practice all the gateways of dhāraṇī and all the gateways of samādhi?

For what purpose does one practice the Ground of Utmost Joy, the Ground of Purity, the Ground of Radiance, the Ground of Blazing Wisdom, the Ground of Difficult Victory, the Ground of Presence, the Ground of Far-Going, the Ground of Immovability, the Ground of Excellent Intelligence, and the Ground of the Dharma Cloud?
For what purpose does one practice the five eyes and the six supernormal powers?

For what purpose does one practice the ten powers of a Buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha?
For what purpose does one practice the quality of non-forgetfulness and the state of constant equanimity?
For what purpose does one practice all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*)?
For what purpose do they practice all the practices of a bodhisattva mahāsattva?
For what purpose do they practice the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas?
"For what purpose does one purify a Buddha-field?
For what purpose does one bring sentient beings to maturity?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"If all sentient beings were able to know for themselves that all phenomena are like illusions and transformations, and are not at all substantially real, then Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas would not need to practice the bodhisattva path for incalculable eons for the sake of those sentient beings."

Because sentient beings themselves cannot know that all phenomena are like magical illusions and are entirely without substantial reality, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices the bodhisattva path for the sake of these sentient beings throughout incalculable eons.
Furthermore, Subhūti!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva did not know all phenomena as they truly are—namely, that they are all like illusions and transformations and are entirely without real existence—then he would not practice the bodhisattva path for countless eons to purify buddha-fields and mature sentient beings. Because a bodhisattva mahāsattva knows all phenomena as they truly are—that they are all like illusions and transformations and are entirely without real existence—he practices the bodhisattva path for countless eons to purify buddha-fields and mature sentient beings.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If all phenomena are like a dream, like an illusion, like an echo, like a reflection, like a shadow, like a mirage, like a magical creation, and like a city of Gandharvas, then in what place do those sentient beings who are to be transformed reside, such that the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, rescue and deliver them?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"Sentient beings who are to be transformed dwell in the false conceptualization of names and signs; when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they deliver them from that false conceptualization of names and signs and cause them to emerge from it."
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
what is meant by ‘name’?”
“What is meant by ‘characteristic’?
The Buddha said,
“Suvikrāntavikrāmin!

All names are adventitious, all are provisional designations, and all belong to conceptual constructs; that is to say, this is called "form," this is called "feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness";
this is called the "eye-base," these are called the "ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-bases";
this is called the "form-base," and these are called the "sound, odor, taste, tangible, and mental-object bases."
This is called the eye-element; these are called the ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-elements.
This is called the form-element; these are called the sound-, odor-, taste-, tangible-, and mental-object-elements.
This is called the eye-consciousness-element; these are called the ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-consciousness-elements.
"This is called male, this is called female;
this is called small, this is called large;
this is called hell, this is called the animal realm, this is called the realm of hungry ghosts, this is called human, and this is called deva."
This is called a worldly dharma; this is called a supramundane dharma;
this is called a contaminated dharma; this is called an uncontaminated dharma;
this is called a conditioned dharma; this is called an unconditioned dharma.
This is called the fruit of stream-entry; this is called the fruit of once-returning; this is called the fruit of non-returning; this is called the fruit of arhatship;
this is called the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha; this is called the conduct of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; this is called the unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas;
this is called an ordinary person; this is called a śrāvaka; this is called a pratyekabuddha; this is called a bodhisattva; and this is called a tathāgata.
"Subhūti! All such names as these are merely provisional designations; because names are established as conventions to express various meanings, all names lack inherent existence."

All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) also exist as mere names; for this reason, even unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) are not substantially real. Fools and ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) falsely cling to them, but when Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they skillfully employ means (*upāya-kauśalya*) to instruct them to abandon such clinging, saying:

"Names arise from conceptual discrimination and false imagination, and are also conventionally established through the conjunction of various conditions. You should not cling to them within. Names lack substantial reality; their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is entirely empty. No wise person clings to empty phenomena."
"In this way, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, they employ skillful means to teach sentient beings the dharmas that are free from names."
“Subhūti! This is called ‘name.
What is ‘characteristic’?
“Subhūti! There are two kinds of marks to which foolish common worldlings cling. What are these two?
First, the characteristic of form;
second, the characteristic of the formless.
What is meant by the characteristic of form?

"Subhūti! Whatever form there may be—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near—all such phenomena, which are empty at this very moment, are conceptually discriminated and grasped by foolish worldlings; this is called the characteristic of form."
"What is meant by 'the mark of the formless' (*arūpya-nimitta*)? Subhūti!

It refers to all those dharma-s that are formless, wherein foolish ordinary beings grasp at marks and engage in conceptual discrimination, thereby giving rise to various afflictions; this is called 'the mark of the formless.'"

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they employ skillful means to instruct all sentient beings to distance themselves from the two marks, and further instruct them to dwell securely within the signless realm (*animitta-dhātu*). Although they instruct them to dwell within the signless realm, they do not cause them to fall into the dualistic attachments of grasping, namely: "this is a mark" and "this is signless."
Thus it is, Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, through skillful means they cause all sentient beings to distance themselves from all signs, so that they abide in the signless realm without attachment.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If all dharmas are merely names and signs, and all these names and signs are established as mere designations arising from conceptual construction and lack any real intrinsic nature, how is it that when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, they are able to advance in wholesome dharmas themselves and also cause others to advance in wholesome dharmas? By virtue of their own advancement in wholesome dharmas, how can they gradually fulfill the stages (bhūmis) and establish sentient beings so that each may attain the fruits of the three vehicles according to their respective capacities?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"If there were even the slightest substantial reality among all phenomena, rather than these being merely established by way of names and signs, then when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, they would not personally advance in wholesome qualities, nor would they cause others to advance in wholesome qualities."

“Subhūti! Because among all phenomena there is not the slightest substantial reality, but only the provisional establishment of names and signs, for this reason, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), by means of signlessness as a skillful means, they are able to fulfill the perfection of wisdom;
by means of signlessness as a skillful means, they are able to fulfill the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyānapāramitā).”
By means of signlessness as a skillful method, one can fulfill the perfection of diligence;
by means of signlessness as a skillful method, one can fulfill the perfection of patience;
by means of signlessness as a skillful method, one can fulfill the perfection of ethical discipline.
By means of the signless as a skillful method, one is able to fulfill the perfection of generosity;
by means of the signless as a skillful method, one is able to fulfill the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments;

by means of the signless as a skillful method, one is able to fulfill the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right endeavors, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path.
Using the signless as a skillful means, one is able to fulfill the doors of liberation of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;

using the signless as a skillful means, one is able to fulfill internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, non-altering emptiness, essential nature emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common characteristic emptiness, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature.

Using signlessness as a skillful means, one is able to fulfill suchness, the dharma-realm, the nature of phenomena, non-falsity, immutability, equality, freedom from birth, the fixed nature of dharmas, the stability of dharmas, the limit of reality, the realm of space, and the inconceivable realm;
using signlessness as a skillful means, one is able to fulfill the noble truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path;
using signlessness as a skillful means, one is able to fulfill the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative attainments, and the ten totalities.
By means of the signless as a skillful method, one is able to fulfill all dharani-doors and all samadhi-doors;

by means of the signless as a skillful method, one is able to fulfill the Ground of Extreme Joy, the Ground of Purity, the Ground of Radiant Light, the Ground of Blazing Wisdom, the Ground of Difficult Victory, the Ground of Presence, the Ground of Far-Going, the Ground of Immovability, the Ground of Excellent Intelligence, and the Ground of the Dharma Cloud;
by means of the signless as a skillful method, one is able to fulfill the five eyes and the six supernormal powers.

Using signlessness as the means, one is able to fulfill the ten powers of a Buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
using signlessness as the means, one is able to fulfill the quality of non-forgetfulness and the nature of constant dwelling in equanimity;
using signlessness as the means, one is able to fulfill all-knowledge, the knowledge of the paths, and the knowledge of all aspects.
"By taking signlessness as the means, having personally perfected all wholesome dharmas, one is also able to cause others to perfect wholesome dharmas.
Thus it is, Subhūti!"

Because all phenomena lack even the slightest substantial reality and consist only of conventionally established names and signs, the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas do not give rise to inverted attachments therein; they are able to advance themselves in all wholesome dharmas, and are also able to cause others to advance in wholesome dharmas.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If there were any real characteristic of phenomena (dharma-lakṣaṇa) even as small as a hair-tip among all dharmas, then when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they would not—having realized that all dharmas are signless (animitta), thoughtless (amanasikāra), and of an outflow-free nature (anāsrava)—attain unexcelled, perfect enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi) and establish sentient beings in outflow-free dharmas."
Why is this? Subhūti!
All untainted phenomena (anāsrava-dharma) are without marks (animitta), without recollection (asmṛti), and without mental attention (amanasikāra).

"In this way, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, establishing sentient beings in untainted phenomena (anāsrava-dharma), this is truly called the act of benefiting others."
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If all dharmas are truly of an outflow-free nature (anāsrava), being signless (animitta), without recollection (asmṛti), and without mental engagement (amanasikāra), for what reason has the World-Honored One repeatedly stated:”
This is a mundane dharma; this is a supramundane dharma;
this is a contaminated dharma; this is an uncontaminated dharma;
this is a conditioned dharma; this is an unconditioned dharma.
"This is a blameworthy dharma; this is a blameless dharma.
This is a dharma associated with contention; this is a dharma free from contention.
This is a dharma of saṃsāra; this is a dharma of cessation."
Is this a shared dharma, or is it an unshared dharma?
Is this the dharma of the śrāvakas, or the dharma of the pratyekabuddhas?
Is this the dharma of the bodhisattvas, or the dharma of the Tathāgatas?
The Buddha said to Subhūti: "What do you think?
Are worldly phenomena different from the signless, untainted nature of phenomena?"
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One!”
"No, Sugata! The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"What do you think?
Are the dharmas of the śrāvakas and so forth different from the signless, untainted dharma-nature? Subhūti replied:
"No, World-Honored One! No!"
“Sugata! The Buddha told Subhūti:
“Are not these worldly dharmas, such as equanimity, mindfulness, and so forth, themselves the nature of the untainted dharmas that are signless?”
Subhūti replied, “So it is, World-Honored One!”
"So it is! Well-gone One!
The Buddha said to Subhūti:

"Are not the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, the fruit of arhatship, the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, the dharmas of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, and the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of a Buddha—all these indeed the signless, the recollection-less, and the uncontaminated nature of phenomena (dharmatā)?"
Subhūti replied, “So it is, World-Honored One!”
"So it is, Sugata! the Buddha said.
“Subhūti! By this causal condition, you should know that all dharmas are characterized by the markless (animitta). Subhūti!”
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva studies all dharmas as being signless, without recollection, and without mental engagement,
they are constantly able to increase the wholesome dharmas they practice— namely, the perfections of giving,
ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom; or the four dhyānas...

The four immeasurables and the four formless absorptions; the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right endeavors, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path;
as well as internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, and existence...
Whether it be emptiness, the emptiness of the unconditioned, ultimate emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, the emptiness of non-alteration,
the emptiness of intrinsic nature, the emptiness of specific characteristics, the emptiness of common characteristics, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unattainable,
the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of self-nature, or the emptiness of the self-nature of non-existence— if...

Suchness, the dharma-realm, the nature of phenomena, non-falsity, immutability, equality, the state beyond birth, the fixed nature of phenomena, the stability of phenomena, the limit of reality, the realm of space, and the inconceivable realm;
whether it be the noble truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path; or emptiness and signlessness...

the signless and wishless doors of liberation; or the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative attainments, and the ten universal bases; or all the doors of dhāraṇī and all the doors of samādhi;
or the stage of extreme joy, the stage of freedom from defilement, the stage of radiant light, the stage of blazing wisdom, and the stage of great difficulty...
The Ground of Exceeding, the Ground of Presence, the Ground of Far-Going, the Ground of Immovability, the Ground of Excellent Intelligence, and the Ground of the Dharma Cloud;

whether it be the five eyes or the six supernormal powers; whether it be the ten powers of a Buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, or the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; or whether it be great loving-kindness or great compassion.
Great joy and great equanimity; if there is the quality of non-forgetfulness and the state of constant abiding in equanimity;

if there is all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and all-aspect knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*)—all such qualities of a Buddha are increased by training in signlessness (*animitta*), non-conceptuality (*amanasikāra*), and non-mental engagement (*anabhisamskāra*).
Why is that? Subhūti!
Apart from the gateways to liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—there is no other essential dharma for a bodhisattva mahāsattva to study.
Why is this? Subhūti!
Because the three doors of liberation are able to encompass all sublime and wholesome dharmas.
Why is this so? Subhūti!

Through the gate of liberation of emptiness, one contemplates that the self-characteristics of all phenomena are empty; through the gate of liberation of signlessness, one contemplates that all phenomena are remote from all signs; through the gate of liberation of wishlessness, one contemplates that all phenomena are remote from all wishes. By means of these three gates, one can encompass all sublime wholesome dharmas, for without these three gates, the sublime wholesome dharmas that ought to be cultivated would not arise.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can train in these three doors of liberation, they can then train in the five aggregates,
and they can also train in the twelve bases, and they can also train in the eighteen elements, and they can also train in the six elements."
One can also train in the Four Noble Truths; one can also train in the four conditions;
one can also train in all phenomena arising from conditions; one can also train in the twelve links of dependent origination;

and one can also train in internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, and unconditioned emptiness.
They are able to study emptiness, ultimate emptiness, boundless emptiness, emptiness of dispersion, unchanging emptiness, essential emptiness,
emptiness of self-characteristics, emptiness of common characteristics, emptiness of all phenomena, emptiness of non-apprehensibility,
emptiness of non-existence, emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence; they are likewise able to study suchness.
Furthermore, they are able to train in the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), non-falsity, immutability, equality, the state beyond birth,
the fixedness of phenomena (*dharmaniyāmatā*), the stability of phenomena (*dharmaniyāmatā*), the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*),
the realm of space (*ākāśadhātu*), and the inconceivable realm; and they are also able to train in generosity, pure ethical discipline, patience, diligence, and meditative concentration.
...the perfection of wisdom, skillful means, sublime aspiration, power, and knowledge;
and they are also able to study the Stage of Extreme Joy, the Stage Free from Defilement, the Radiant Stage, the Blazing Wisdom Stage,
the Extremely Difficult to Conquer Stage, the Manifest Stage, the Far-Reaching Stage, the Immovable Stage, and the Stage of Excellent Intelligence.

On the Dharma-Cloud Stage (*dharmameghā-bhūmi*), one is also able to train in the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*), the four bases of power (*ṛddhipāda*), the five faculties (*indriya*), the five powers (*bala*), the seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), and the eightfold noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*);

one is also able to train in the four meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), and the four formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*); and one is also able to train in the eight liberations (*vimokṣa*) and the eight bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*).
They can also train in the bases of power, the nine successive meditative attainments, and the ten totalities;
they can also train in all doors of dhāraṇī and all doors of samādhi; they can also train in the five eyes and the six supernormal powers;
and they can also train in the Tathāgata’s ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
Regarding the common dharmas, they are also able to train in great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity;
they are also able to train in the quality of non-forgetfulness and the nature of constant abiding in equanimity;
they are also able to train in all-knowledge, the knowledge of the paths, and the knowledge of all aspects; and they are also able to train in purifying Buddha-fields and maturing sentient beings.
"One can also learn all other immeasurable and boundless Buddha-dharmas.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, train in the five aggregates?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, knows form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness as they truly are, this is called training in the five aggregates."
“Subhūti! How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, know form as it truly is? Subhūti!”

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they know the characteristic of form as it truly is, they know the arising of form as it truly is, they know the cessation of form as it truly is, and they know the suchness of form as it truly is; this is called knowing form as it truly is.
“Subhūti! How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, know the characteristic of form as it truly is? Subhūti!”

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they know form as it truly is: as ultimately having holes and ultimately having fissures, like a mass of foam, its nature being without solidity.
"Subhūti! This is called knowing the characteristic of form as it truly is. Subhūti!"
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), know the arising of form (*rūpa*) as it truly is? Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they know that form comes from nowhere and goes nowhere; although there is no coming and no going, the dharma arises in accordance with conditions.
"Subhūti! This is called knowing the arising of form as it truly is. Subhūti!"
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, know the cessation of form as it truly is?

Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they know that form comes from nowhere and goes nowhere; although there is no coming and no going, it accords with the nature of phenomena that cease.
"Subhūti! This is called knowing the cessation of form as it truly is. Subhūti!"
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, know the suchness (*tathatā*) of form as it truly is?

Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they know the suchness of form as being without arising and without cessation, without coming and without going, without defilement and without purity, and without increase and without decrease; because it is always as its own nature, non-false, and unchanging, it is called "suchness."
"Subhūti! This is called knowing the suchness of form as it truly is. Subhūti!"
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, know feeling as it truly is? Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they know the characteristic of feeling as it truly is, they know the arising of feeling as it truly is, they know the cessation of feeling as it truly is, and they know the suchness of feeling as it truly is; this is what is meant by knowing feeling as it truly is.
“Subhūti! How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, know the characteristic of feeling as it truly is? Subhūti!”

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they know feeling as it truly is: ultimately like an abscess, ultimately like an arrow, like a bubble, false and unstable, arising and ceasing swiftly.
"Subhūti! This is called knowing the characteristics of feeling as they truly are. Subhūti!"
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, know feeling as it truly is? Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they know feeling as it truly is: that it comes from nowhere and goes nowhere; yet, although there is no coming and no going, it arises in accordance with phenomena.
"Subhūti! This is called knowing the arising of feeling as it truly is. Subhūti!"
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, know the cessation of sensation as it truly is? Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they know as it truly is that sensation comes from nowhere and goes nowhere; although there is no coming or going, it is associated with the nature of cessation.
"Subhūti! This is called knowing, as it truly is, the cessation of feeling. Subhūti!"
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), know the suchness (tathatā) of feeling as it truly is? Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they know the suchness of feeling as it truly is—unborn and unceasing, neither coming nor going, neither defiled nor pure, neither increasing nor decreasing; because it is always as its own nature is, non-false, and immutable, it is called suchness.
"Subhūti! This is called knowing the suchness of feeling as it truly is. Subhūti!"
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, know perception as it truly is? Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they know the characteristic of perception as it truly is, they know the arising of perception as it truly is, they know the cessation of perception as it truly is, and they know the suchness of perception as it truly is; this is what is meant by knowing perception as it truly is.
“Subhūti! How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, know the characteristics of perception as they truly are? Subhūti!”

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they know perception as it truly is: like a mirage, water is unobtainable; this perception arises from false craving and thirst, existing only as a provisional designation, and is produced through conventional expression.
"Subhūti! This is called knowing the characteristics of perception as they truly are. Subhūti!"
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), know the arising of perception as it truly is? Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they know that perception comes from nowhere and goes nowhere; although there is no coming and no going, it arises in accordance with phenomena.
"Subhūti! This is called knowing the arising of perception as it truly is. Subhūti!"
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, know the cessation of perception as it truly is? Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they know as it truly is that perception comes from nowhere and goes nowhere; although there is no coming and no going, it accords with the nature of phenomena that cease.
"Subhūti! This is called knowing the cessation of perception as it truly is. Subhūti!"
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, know the suchness of perception as it truly is? Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they know the suchness of perception as it truly is to be without arising and without cessation, without coming and without going, without defilement and without purity, without increase and without decrease; because it is always as its own nature, non-illusory and unchanging, it is called "suchness."
"Subhūti! This is called knowing the suchness of perception as it truly is. Subhūti!"
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, know formations as they truly are? Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, knowing the characteristic of formations as it truly is, knowing the arising of formations as it truly is, knowing the cessation of formations as it truly is, and knowing the suchness of formations as it truly is—this is called knowing formations as they truly are.
"Subhūti! How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, know the characteristics of phenomena as they truly are? Subhūti!"

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they know, in accordance with reality, that formations are like a plantain tree: when analyzed leaf by leaf, no core can be found; they are produced by various conditions such as clarity and ignorance, and are conventionally designated through the conjunction of karma, afflictions, and so forth.
"Subhūti! This is called knowing the characteristics of phenomena as they truly are. Subhūti!"
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, know the arising of formations as they truly are? Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he knows as it truly is that formations come from nowhere and go nowhere; although there is no coming and no going, the production of phenomena occurs in accordance with conditions.
"Subhūti! This is called knowing the arising of formations as it really is. Subhūti!"
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, know the cessation of formations as it truly is? Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they know as it truly is that formations come from nowhere and go nowhere; although there is no coming and no going, they correspond to the nature of cessation.
"Subhūti! This is called knowing the cessation of formations as it truly is. Subhūti!"
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), know the suchness (*tathatā*) of phenomena as it truly is? Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they know the suchness of phenomena as it truly is: it is without arising and without cessation, without coming and without going, without defilement and without purity, without increase and without decrease; it is eternally according to its own nature, non-false, and immutable, and is therefore called "suchness."
"Subhūti! This is called knowing the suchness of practice as it truly is. Subhūti!"
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, know consciousness as it truly is?

Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they know the characteristic of consciousness as it truly is, they know the arising of consciousness as it truly is, they know the cessation of consciousness as it truly is, and they know the suchness of consciousness as it truly is; this is what is meant by knowing consciousness as it truly is.
“Subhūti! How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, understand the characteristics of consciousness as they truly are? Subhūti!”

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they understand consciousness as it truly is: like a magical illusion, provisionally established through the conjunction of various conditions, and ultimately unfindable. Just as a magician or his apprentice might conjure four armies at a crossroads—namely, elephant troops, cavalry, chariot troops, and infantry—or conjure other various forms and types, which appear to exist but lack any reality, so too is consciousness: it is ultimately unfindable.
"Subhūti! This is called the characteristic of knowing persons as they truly are. Subhūti!"
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, know the arising of consciousness as it truly is? Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they know that consciousness comes from nowhere and goes nowhere; although there is no coming and no going, it arises in accordance with dharmas.
"Subhūti! This is called the knowledge of reality as it is arising. Subhūti!"
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, know the cessation of consciousness as it truly is? Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they know as it truly is that consciousness comes from nowhere and goes nowhere; although there is no coming and no going, it accords with the nature of cessation.
"Subhūti! This is called knowing the cessation of consciousness as it truly is. Subhūti!"
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), know the suchness (*tathatā*) of consciousness as it truly is? Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they know the suchness of consciousness as it truly is: as neither arising nor ceasing, neither coming nor going, neither defiled nor pure, neither increasing nor decreasing; because it is always as its own nature is—non-false and unchanging—it is called suchness.
"Subhūti! This is called knowing the suchness of knowledge as it truly is. Furthermore, Subhūti!"

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they know form as it truly is: that the self-nature of form is empty; they know feeling as it truly is: that the self-nature of feeling is empty; they know perception as it truly is: that the self-nature of perception is empty; they know volitional formations as they truly are: that the self-nature of volitional formations is empty; they know consciousness as it truly is: that the self-nature of consciousness is empty.
"Subhūti! This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, is able to train in the five aggregates.
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, train in the twelve bases?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they know, as it truly is, that the sense base of the eye is empty of the intrinsic nature of the sense base of the eye; they know, as it truly is, that the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are empty of the intrinsic nature of the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.

They know, as it truly is, that the sense base of forms is empty of the intrinsic nature of the sense base of forms; they know, as it truly is, that the sense bases of sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena are empty of the intrinsic nature of the sense bases of sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena.

They know, as it truly is, that the internal sense bases are empty of the intrinsic nature of the internal sense bases; they know, as it truly is, that the external sense bases are empty of the intrinsic nature of the external sense bases.”
"Subhūti! This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, is able to train in the twelve bases.
The venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, train in the eighteen elements?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they know the eye-element as it truly is to be empty of the intrinsic nature of the eye-element; they know the form-element, the eye-consciousness-element, eye-contact, and the various feelings produced with eye-contact as conditions, up to the form-element and the various feelings produced with eye-contact as conditions, as being empty of their own intrinsic nature.

They know the ear-element as it truly is to be empty of the intrinsic nature of the ear-element; they know the sound-element, the ear-consciousness-element, ear-contact, and the various feelings produced with ear-contact as conditions, up to the sound-element and the various feelings produced with ear-contact as conditions, as being empty of their own intrinsic nature.”

One knows the nose element as it truly is: the nose element is empty of the intrinsic nature of the nose element. One knows the odor element, the nose-consciousness element, nose-contact, and all feelings produced with nose-contact as condition as they truly are: from the odor element up to all feelings produced with nose-contact as condition, they are empty of their own intrinsic nature. One knows the tongue element as it truly is: the tongue element is empty of the intrinsic nature of the tongue element.

One knows the taste element, the tongue-consciousness element, tongue-contact, and all feelings produced with tongue-contact as condition as they truly are: from the taste element up to all feelings produced with tongue-contact as condition, they are empty of their own intrinsic nature. One knows the body element as it truly is: the body element is empty of the intrinsic nature of the body element.

One knows the tangible-object element, the body-consciousness element, body-contact, and all feelings produced with body-contact as condition as they truly are: from the tangible-object element up to all feelings produced with body-contact as condition, they are empty of their own intrinsic nature.

One knows the mind-element as it truly is to be empty of the intrinsic nature of the mind-element; one knows the dharma-element, the mind-consciousness-element, and mental contact—as well as all feelings produced with mental contact as their condition—as they truly are to be empty of the intrinsic nature of the dharma-element, up to and including the intrinsic nature of all feelings produced with mental contact as their condition.
“Subhūti! This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, is able to train in the eighteen elements.
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), train in the six elements?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they know the earth element as it truly is to be empty of the intrinsic nature of the earth element; they know the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements as they truly are to be empty of the intrinsic nature of the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements."
"Subhūti! This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, is able to train in the six elements.
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, train in the four noble truths?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, knows the noble truth of suffering as it truly is, knows the noble truth of its origin as it truly is, knows the noble truth of its cessation as it truly is, and knows the noble truth of the path as it truly is, this is what is meant by being able to train in the four noble truths."
“Subhūti! How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, know the noble truth of suffering as it truly is? Subhūti!”

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they know suffering as it truly is: as a characteristic of oppression, empty by nature, and remote from dualistic phenomena; it is the noble truth. Suffering is suchness, and suchness is suffering; they are non-dual and without distinction, known only by the truly noble ones as they truly are.
"Subhūti! This is called knowing the noble truth of suffering as it truly is. Subhūti!"
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), know the noble truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*) as it truly is? Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they know that origination has the characteristic of arising, that its intrinsic nature is fundamentally empty, and that it is remote from dualistic phenomena. This is the truth of the noble ones; origination is suchness (*tathatā*), and suchness is origination. They are non-dual and without distinction, known as they truly are only by the truly noble ones.
"Subhūti! This is called knowing the noble truth of the origin as it truly is. Subhūti!"
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), know the noble truth of cessation (*nirodha-āryasatya*) as it truly is? Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they know that cessation is the characteristic of tranquility, that its intrinsic nature is fundamentally empty, and that it is far removed from dualistic phenomena. It is the truth of the noble ones; cessation is itself suchness (*tathatā*), and suchness is itself cessation. They are non-dual and without distinction, known only by true noble ones as it truly is.
"Subhūti! This is called knowing the noble truth of cessation as it truly is. Subhūti!"
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), know the noble truth of the path as it truly is?

Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they know the path as it truly is: as the characteristic of transcendence, empty of intrinsic nature by its very essence, and free from duality. This is the truth of the noble ones; the path is suchness (tathatā), and suchness is the path. They are non-dual and without distinction, known as it truly is only by the truly noble ones.
"Subhūti! This is called the noble truth of the knowledge of reality as it is. Subhūti!"
"This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, is able to train in the four noble truths.
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One!"
"How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, train in the four conditions?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, knows the causal condition as it truly is, knows the immediately preceding condition as it truly is, knows the objective condition as it truly is, and knows the dominant condition as it truly is—this is what is meant by training in the four conditions."
“Subhūti! How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, know dependent origination as it truly is? Subhūti!”

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they know, in accordance with reality, that causes and conditions have the characteristic of being seeds; their intrinsic nature is fundamentally empty, and they are far removed from dualistic phenomena.
"Subhūti! This is called knowing dependent origination as it truly is. Subhūti!"
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), know the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) as it truly is? Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they know the immediately preceding condition as it truly is: it is a characteristic of manifestation, its intrinsic nature is fundamentally empty, and it is far removed from dualistic phenomena.
"Subhūti! This is called knowing the equal-and-immediate condition as it truly is. Subhūti!"
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, know the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) as it truly is? Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they know the object-condition as it truly is: its characteristic is that of support, its intrinsic nature is fundamentally empty, and it is far removed from dualistic phenomena.
"Subhūti! This is called knowing the object-condition as it truly is. Subhūti!"
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), know the dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*) as it truly is? Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they know the dominant condition as it truly is to have the characteristic of non-obstruction, its intrinsic nature being fundamentally empty and far removed from dualistic phenomena.
"Subhūti! This is called knowing the dominant condition as it truly is. Subhūti!"
"This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, is able to train in the four conditions.
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One!"
“How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, train in all phenomena that arise from conditions?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they know all phenomena arising from conditions as they truly are: neither arising nor ceasing, neither annihilated nor eternal, neither identical nor different, neither coming nor going; they are free from all conceptual proliferation, and their fundamental nature is quiescent.”
“Subhūti! This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, is able to train in all phenomena that arise from conditions.
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, train in the twelve links of dependent origination?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they know, as it truly is, that ignorance is without arising and without cessation, without defilement and without purity, its intrinsic nature being fundamentally empty and transcending dualistic phenomena;

they know, as it truly is, that volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, and old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are without arising and without cessation, without defilement and without purity, their intrinsic nature being fundamentally empty and transcending dualistic phenomena."
“Subhūti! This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, is able to train in the twelve links of dependent origination.
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), train in internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, non-alteration emptiness, essential nature emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common characteristic emptiness, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they know as it truly is that internal emptiness is without intrinsic nature and unapprehendable, and they are able to abide therein; they know as it truly is that external emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of non-existence of intrinsic nature, is without intrinsic nature and unapprehendable, and they are able to abide therein.”
Subhūti! This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, is able to study inner emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence of intrinsic nature.
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva,

when practicing the perfection of wisdom, train in suchness, the dharma-realm, the dharma-nature, the non-erroneous nature, the unchanging nature, equality, the nature free from birth, the fixedness of dharmas, the stability of dharmas, the limit of reality, the realm of space, and the inconceivable realm?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, knows as it truly is that suchness is without conceptual proliferation and without discrimination, and is able to abide therein; and knows as it truly is that the dharma-realm, up to the inconceivable realm, is without conceptual proliferation and without discrimination, and is able to abide therein."
Subhūti! This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, is able to train in true suchness up to the inconceivable realm.

The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle 384. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Part One: Chapter Sixty-nine, Part Three, "The Equality of All Dharmas. The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, train in the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, wisdom, skillful means, sublime aspiration, power, and knowledge?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they know, in accordance with reality, that the perfection of generosity is without increase or decrease, without defilement or purity, without intrinsic nature, and unapprehendable, yet they are able to cultivate it. They know, in accordance with reality, that from the perfection of ethical discipline up to the perfection of wisdom, there is no increase or decrease, no defilement or purity, no intrinsic nature, and they are unapprehendable, yet they are able to cultivate them."
"Subhūti! This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, is able to train in the perfections from generosity up to wisdom."
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva,

when practicing the perfection of wisdom, train in the Stage of Extreme Joy, the Stage of Purity, the Stage of Radiance, the Stage of Blazing Wisdom, the Stage of Difficult Victory, the Stage of Presence, the Stage of Far-Going, the Immovable Stage, the Stage of Excellent Intelligence, and the Stage of the Dharma Cloud?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they know the Stage of Extreme Joy as it truly is—without increase or decrease, without defilement or purity, without intrinsic nature, and unapprehendable—and yet they are able to cultivate it. They know the Stages from the Stainless up to the Cloud of Dharma as they truly are—without increase or decrease, without defilement or purity, without intrinsic nature, and unapprehendable—and yet they are able to cultivate them.”
“Subhūti! This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, is able to train in the stages from the Stage of Extreme Joy up to the Cloud of Dharma.”
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva,

when practicing the perfection of wisdom, train in the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right endeavors, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they know the four foundations of mindfulness as they truly are—without increase or decrease, without defilement or purification, without intrinsic nature, and unapprehendable—and yet they are able to cultivate them. They know the four right efforts, up to and including the eightfold noble path, as they truly are—without increase or decrease, without defilement or purification, without intrinsic nature, and unapprehendable—and yet they are able to cultivate them.”
Subhūti! This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, is able to train in the four applications of mindfulness up to the eight branches of the noble path.
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha,
saying: “World-Honored One,
how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, train in the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, knows as it truly is that the four dhyānas are without increase or decrease, without defilement or purity, without intrinsic nature, and unapprehendable, yet is able to cultivate them; and knows as it truly is that the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments are without increase or decrease, without defilement or purity, without intrinsic nature, and unapprehendable, yet is able to cultivate them."
Subhūti! This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, is able to train in the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments.
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha,
saying: "World-Honored One,
how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, train in the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they know the eight liberations as they truly are—without increase or decrease, without defilement or purity, without intrinsic nature, and unapprehendable—and yet they are able to cultivate them. They know the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative attainments, and the ten totalities as they truly are—without increase or decrease, without defilement or purity, without intrinsic nature, and unapprehendable—and yet they are able to cultivate them."

Subhūti! This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, is able to train in the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative attainments, and the ten universal bases.
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,
how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, train in all the gateways of dhāraṇīs and all the gateways of samādhis?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they know all dhāraṇī-doors as they truly are—neither increasing nor decreasing, neither defiled nor pure, lacking intrinsic nature, and ungraspable—and yet they are able to cultivate them. They know all samādhi-doors as they truly are—neither increasing nor decreasing, neither defiled nor pure, lacking intrinsic nature, and ungraspable—and yet they are able to cultivate them."
"Subhūti! This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, is able to train in all dhāraṇī-doors and all samādhi-doors."
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, train in the five eyes and the six superknowledges?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they know the five eyes as they truly are—neither increasing nor decreasing, neither defiled nor pure, lacking intrinsic nature, and unapprehendable—and yet they are able to cultivate them. They know the six supernormal powers as they truly are—neither increasing nor decreasing, neither defiled nor pure, lacking intrinsic nature, and unapprehendable—and yet they are able to cultivate them."
“Subhūti! This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, is able to train in the five eyes and the six supernormal powers.
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, train in the Tathāgata’s ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four unhindered understandings, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they know the ten powers of a Tathāgata as they truly are—without increase or decrease, without defilement or purity, without intrinsic nature, and unapprehendable—and yet they are able to cultivate them. They know the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha as they truly are—without increase or decrease, without defilement or purity, without intrinsic nature, and unapprehendable—and yet they are able to cultivate them."

Subhūti! This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, is able to train in the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha,

saying: “World-Honored One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, train in great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they know great loving-kindness as it truly is—without increase or decrease, without defilement or purity, without intrinsic nature, and unapprehendable—and yet they are able to cultivate it. They know great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity as they truly are—without increase or decrease, without defilement or purity, without intrinsic nature, and unapprehendable—and yet they are able to cultivate them.”
Subhūti! This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, is able to train in great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity.
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,
how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, train in the quality of non-forgetfulness and the state of constant equanimity?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they know the quality of non-forgetfulness as it truly is—without increase or decrease, without defilement or purity, without intrinsic nature, and unapprehendable—and yet they are able to cultivate it. They know the state of constant equanimity as it truly is—without increase or decrease, without defilement or purity, without intrinsic nature, and unapprehendable—and yet they are able to cultivate it.”
"Subhūti! This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, is able to train in the quality of non-forgetfulness and the state of constant abiding in equanimity."
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha,

saying: “World-Honored One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, train in all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*)?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they know all-knowledge (sarvajñatā) as it truly is—without increase or decrease, without defilement or purity, without intrinsic nature, and unapprehendable—and yet they are able to cultivate it. They know the knowledge of the aspects of the path (mārgākārajñatā) and the knowledge of all aspects (sarvākārajñatā) as they truly are—without increase or decrease, without defilement or purity, without intrinsic nature, and unapprehendable—and yet they are able to cultivate them.”
Subhūti! This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, is able to train in all-knowledge, the knowledge of the aspects of the path, and the knowledge of all aspects.
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, train in purifying buddha-fields and maturing sentient beings?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they know, as it truly is, that the purification of buddha-fields is without increase or decrease, without defilement or purity, without intrinsic nature, and unapprehendable, yet they are able to cultivate it. They know, as it truly is, that the maturing of sentient beings is without increase or decrease, without defilement or purity, without intrinsic nature, and unapprehendable, yet they are able to cultivate it."
Subhūti! This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, is able to train in purifying buddha-fields and maturing sentient beings.
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, train in all other immeasurable and boundless buddha-dharmas?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they know all other immeasurable and boundless buddha-dharmas as they truly are—without increase or decrease, without defilement or purity, without intrinsic nature, and unapprehendable—and yet they are able to cultivate them.”
Subhūti! This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, is able to train in all other immeasurable and boundless buddha-dharmas.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One,

when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, if they understand as they truly are the mutual distinctions among the dharmas such as the five aggregates, would they not thereby destroy the dharma-realm by means of the aggregate of form, and likewise destroy the dharma-realm by means of the aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness?”
Why is this? Because the dharma-realm is non-dual and without differentiation.
"Is it not the case that one destroys the dharma-realm by means of the eye-base, and likewise destroys the dharma-realm by means of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-bases?"
