If the limit of sentient beings is identical to the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), establish sentient beings within the limit of reality without destroying the dharma of the limit of reality?”

"Bhagavān! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, were to establish sentient beings within the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), they would be establishing the limit of reality within the limit of reality."

"Bhagavān! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, were to establish the limit of reality within the limit of reality, he would be establishing self-nature within self-nature; yet, one should not establish self-nature within self-nature."

"Bhagavān, how can it be said that when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they establish sentient beings within the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) without destroying the nature of the limit of reality?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"One cannot establish the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) within the limit of reality, nor can one establish intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) within intrinsic nature. Nevertheless, when bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), through their skill in means (*upāyakauśalya*), they are able to establish sentient beings within the limit of reality; yet the limit of sentient beings is not different from the limit of reality."
"In this way, Subhūti,
the limit of sentient beings and the limit of reality are non-dual and cannot be divided.
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What is called the skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas?

When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), by the power of this skillful means, how do they establish sentient beings within the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) without destroying the characteristics of that limit of reality?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom, from their first production of the thought of enlightenment they accomplish such skillful means; by the power of these skillful means, they establish sentient beings in the practice of giving.”
Once they have been established therein, he explains to them the characteristic of non-differentiation between the prior, posterior, and middle limits of giving, saying: "Good sons!

Such giving is entirely empty across its prior, posterior, and middle limits; the giver, the recipient, and the fruit obtained from giving are likewise all empty. Thus, all these are utterly non-existent within the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) and are all unobtainable."

"You all must not cling to the idea that there is a difference between giving, the giver, the recipient, the fruit of giving, and the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*). If you can refrain from clinging to the notion that giving, the giver, the recipient, the fruit of giving, and the reality-limit each have their own distinct differences, then the merit of the giving you practice will lead toward the Deathless (*amṛta*) and attain the fruit of the Deathless; it will surely take the Deathless as its final end."
"Furthermore, he spoke these words:
'O sons of good family!
By means of this practice of giving that you have cultivated, do not grasp at form; do not grasp at feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.'"
Do not grasp at the sense-base of the eye; do not grasp at the sense-bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind.
Do not grasp at the sense-base of forms; do not grasp at the sense-bases of sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena.
Do not grasp at the eye-element; do not grasp at the elements of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind.
Do not grasp at the realm of form; do not grasp at the realms of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, or mental phenomena.
Do not grasp at the realm of eye-consciousness; do not grasp at the realms of ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-consciousness.
Do not grasp at eye-contact; do not grasp at ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-contact.
Do not grasp the various feelings produced with eye-contact as condition; do not grasp the various feelings produced with ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind-contact as condition.
Do not grasp the earth element; do not grasp the water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness elements.
Do not grasp the causal condition; do not grasp the immediately preceding condition, the object-condition, or the dominant condition.
Do not grasp at the various phenomena produced from conditions;

do not grasp at ignorance, nor at volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, existence, birth, or old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair;
do not grasp at the perfection of generosity, nor at the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, or wisdom.
Do not grasp at the four dhyānas; do not grasp at the four immeasurables or the four formless attainments.

Do not grasp at the four foundations of mindfulness; do not grasp at the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, or the eightfold noble path.
Do not grasp at the gate of liberation of emptiness; do not grasp at the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness.

Do not grasp at internal emptiness; do not grasp at external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, non-alteration emptiness, essential nature emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common characteristic emptiness, the emptiness of all dharmas, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, or the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature.

Do not grasp at suchness; do not grasp at the dharma-realm, the dharma-nature, non-falsity, non-alteration, equality, the state beyond birth, the fixed nature of dharmas, the stability of dharmas, the limit of reality, the realm of space, or the inconceivable realm.
Do not grasp at the noble truth of suffering; do not grasp at the noble truths of origin, cessation, or the path.
Do not grasp at the eight liberations; do not grasp at the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative attainments, or the ten universal bases;
do not grasp at any of the doors of dhāraṇī, nor any of the doors of samādhi;

do not grasp at the Ground of Extreme Joy, nor the Ground of Purity, the Ground of Radiant Light, the Ground of Blazing Wisdom, the Ground of Difficult to Conquer, the Ground of Manifestation, the Ground of Far-Going, the Ground of Immovability, the Ground of Excellent Intelligence, or the Ground of the Dharma Cloud.
Do not grasp at the five eyes; do not grasp at the six supernormal powers;

do not grasp at the ten powers of a Buddha; do not grasp at the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, or the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
do not grasp at the thirty-two marks of a great man, nor the eighty minor marks.
Do not grasp at the quality of non-forgetfulness; do not grasp at the state of constant abiding in equanimity.
Do not grasp at omniscience; do not grasp at the knowledge of the paths or the knowledge of all aspects.
Do not grasp at the fruit of stream-entry; do not grasp at the fruits of once-returning, non-returning, arhatship, or the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha.
Do not grasp at any of the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; do not grasp at the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas;
do not grasp at worldly dharmas, nor grasp at supramundane dharmas;
do not grasp at contaminated dharmas, nor grasp at uncontaminated dharmas.
Do not grasp at conditioned phenomena; do not grasp at unconditioned phenomena. Why is this?

All giving is empty of the nature of giving; all givers are empty of the nature of a giver; all recipients are empty of the nature of a recipient; and all fruits of giving are empty of the nature of the fruit of giving.
In emptiness, giving is unattainable; the giver is unattainable; the recipient is unattainable; and the fruit of giving is unattainable. Why is this so?
Because the intrinsic nature of these dharmas and all other dharmas is ultimately empty, and because within ultimate emptiness these dharmas cannot be apprehended.

"Furthermore, Subhūti! When Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), from the very first production of the thought of enlightenment, they achieve such skillful means (upāyakauśalya). By the power of these skillful means, they establish sentient beings in pure ethical discipline (śīla). Having established them therein, they say:
'O sons of good family!'"

You should now cultivate deep compassion for all sentient beings; abstain from taking life, abstain from taking what is not given, abstain from sexual misconduct, abstain from false speech, abstain from divisive speech, abstain from harsh speech, abstain from idle chatter, abstain from covetousness, abstain from ill will, and abstain from wrong views.
Why is this? Son of good family!
All such dharmas are entirely devoid of intrinsic nature; you should not engage in conceptual discrimination or cling to them.
You should further examine with careful scrutiny: what dharma is called "desiring to take the life of another," and for what reason does one take that life?
Furthermore, what dharma is called "desiring to take an object that has not been given"?
Furthermore, for what reason does one take those objects?
What dharma is called "engaging in improper objects" or "practicing misconduct"?
And for what reason does one practice such misconduct?
What phenomena are called "objects to be deceived" when one intends to act deceptively?
Furthermore, for what reason is "false speech" so named?
What phenomena are called "objects to be divided" when one intends to act divisively?
Furthermore, for what reason is divisive speech spoken?
What dharma is called an object fit for disparagement, such that one desires to disparage it?
Furthermore, for what reason is harsh speech spoken?
What phenomena are called "various defiled matters" and what is meant by "desiring to speak defiled words"?
Furthermore, for what reason is "defiled speech" so called?
What phenomena are called "objects of craving" and what is meant by "the arising of craving"?
Furthermore, by what conditions does sensual desire arise?
What phenomena are called the objects toward which anger should be directed, such that hatred arises?
And again, by what conditions does hatred arise?
What phenomena are called the objects of wrong view from which wrong view arises?
Furthermore, by what conditions does wrong view arise?
All such things are empty of intrinsic nature.

"Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they achieve such skillful means that they are able to skillfully bring sentient beings to maturity, teaching them that both the fruit of generosity and the fruit of pure ethical discipline are unapprehendable, causing them to know that the intrinsic nature of both the fruit of generosity and the fruit of pure ethical discipline is empty."

Having realized that the intrinsic nature of the fruits of the practiced generosity and pure ethical discipline is empty, they are able to give rise to no attachment toward them. Because their minds are free from attachment, they are undistracted; being undistracted, they are able to generate sublime wisdom. Through this sublime wisdom, having forever severed the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) and the active outbursts (*paryavasthāna*), they enter the realm of *nirvāṇa* without remainder.
"Subhūti! Thus it is spoken according to worldly convention and not according to the ultimate truth. Why is that?"

In space, there is not even the slightest dharma to be found—whether it be that which has already attained parinirvāṇa, that which will attain parinirvāṇa, that which is currently attaining parinirvāṇa, the one who attains parinirvāṇa, or that by means of which one attains parinirvāṇa. All such things are entirely non-existent and are ultimately empty. Ultimate emptiness itself is nirvāṇa; apart from this nirvāṇa, there is no other separate dharma.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom, from the very first production of the thought of enlightenment, they achieve such skillful means. By the power of these skillful means, seeing that the minds of sentient beings are full of anger and resentment, they give rise to deep compassion and provide instruction through skillful means, saying:
'O son of good family!'"
You should cultivate patience and delight in the dharma of patience; you must subdue your mind and undertake the practice of patience.
Since the nature of the phenomena toward which you feel anger is entirely empty, why do you give rise to such wrathful resentment?
You all should further examine with careful discernment: by what dharma does my anger arise?
Who is able to be angry?
Toward whom is the anger directed?
Thus, the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is empty, and that which is empty by intrinsic nature has never been anything other than empty.
This emptiness was not created by the Tathāgata, nor by the Pratyekabuddhas, nor by the Śrāvakas, nor by the Bodhisattvas;
it was also not created by devas, nāgas, various spirits, yakṣas, or gandharvas.
It was not created by asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, or non-humans;

nor was it created by the gods of the Four Great Kings, the Thirty-three Gods, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, or the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven; nor was it created by the Brahmakāyika gods.
It was not created by the gods of the Heaven of the Four Great Kings, the Heaven of the Thirty-three, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, or the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven;

nor was it created by the gods of the Brahmakāyika, Brahmapurohita, Brahmakāyika-pariṣadya, or Mahābrahmā heavens; nor was it created by the gods of the Ābhāsvara, Parīttābhā, Apramāṇābhā, or Ābhāsvara-śubha heavens;
nor was it created by the gods of the Śubhakṛtsna, Parīttaśubha, Apramāṇaśubha, or Śubhakṛtsna heavens; nor was it created by the gods of the Bṛhatphala or Parītta... [heaven].
It was not created by the Bṛhatphala devas, nor by the Apramāṇa-bṛhatphala devas, nor by the Bṛhatphala devas;
it was not created by the Asaṃjñisattva devas, nor by the Avṛha devas, the Atapa devas, the Sudṛśa devas, the Sudarśana devas, or the Akaniṣṭha devas;
nor was it created by the Ākāśānantyāyatana devas, the Vijñānānantyāyatana devas, or the Ākiṃcanyāyatana devas...
It is produced by the gods of the Sphere of Infinite Space and the gods of the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception.
You should further observe according to reality: from what does such anger and resentment arise?
To whom does it belong?
From whom does it arise?
And what fruit shall one obtain?
What benefit is gained now?
Since the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is emptiness, and within emptiness there can be no anger or resentment, one should practice patience to bring oneself benefit.

"In this way, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, through skillful means they establish sentient beings in the principle of the emptiness of nature and the causes and effects of the emptiness of nature; they gradually manifest, exhort, encourage, and gladden them with unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, causing them to dwell securely therein and swiftly attain realization."
"Subhūti! Thus it is spoken according to worldly convention and not according to the ultimate truth. Why is that?
Within the emptiness of intrinsic nature, that which attains, that which is attained, the locus of attainment, and the time of attainment—all these do not exist.
Subhūti! This is called the principle of the emptiness of intrinsic nature regarding the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).

When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, practice the perfection of wisdom by relying on this principle of the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi), they do not apprehend sentient beings, nor do they apprehend the designation of sentient beings.
Why is this? Subhūti! Because all dharmas are devoid of sentient beings.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom, from the first production of the thought of enlightenment they achieve such skillful means. By the power of these skillful means, seeing that sentient beings are physically and mentally indolent and have fallen away from diligence, they employ skillful means to exhort them, causing them to arouse physical and mental diligence to cultivate all wholesome dharmas, saying: 'Good son!'"

In the emptiness of intrinsic nature, there is no phenomenon of indolence, no indolent person, no place of indolence, no time of indolence, and nothing from which indolence arises; all these phenomena are empty by their very nature and do not transcend the principle of emptiness.
You all should arouse physical and mental diligence, abandon all laziness, and zealously cultivate wholesome dharmas— namely,
the cultivation of the perfection of generosity, or the cultivation of the perfection of ethical discipline,
or the cultivation of the perfection of patience, or the cultivation of the perfection of diligence, or the cultivation of the perfection of meditative concentration.
Maitreya, if one cultivates the perfection of wisdom; if one cultivates the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments;

if one cultivates the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of awakening, and the eightfold noble path; or if one cultivates emptiness...
the gateways of liberation of signlessness, wishlessness, and emptiness; or if they abide in internal emptiness,
external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness,
conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, non-altering emptiness, or essential nature emptiness;
The emptiness of specific characteristics, the emptiness of common characteristics, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unapprehendable,
the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence;
if one abides in suchness, the dharma-realm, the dharma-nature, non-falsity, immutability, equality, and the state beyond birth.
...the dharma-nature, the stability of phenomena, the limit of reality, the realm of space, and the inconceivable realm;
whether they abide in the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path;
or cultivate the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative attainments, and the ten totalities; or cultivate all the doors of dhāraṇī and the three...

The gateways of meditative concentration (*samādhi*): whether one cultivates the Ground of Utmost Joy, the Ground of Purity, the Ground of Radiant Light, the Ground of Blazing Wisdom, the Ground of Supreme Difficulty to Conquer, the Ground of Manifestation, the Ground of Far-Going, the Ground of Immovability, the Ground of Excellent Intelligence, or the Ground of the Dharma Cloud;
or whether one cultivates the five eyes and the six supernormal powers; or whether one cultivates the ten [powers] of a Buddha...
the powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
or if one cultivates great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity;
or if one cultivates the thirty-two marks of a Great Being and the eighty minor marks; or if one cultivates the quality of non-forgetfulness and the nature of constant equanimity; or if...
One should cultivate all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*);
if one cultivates any other of the Buddha-dharmas, one must not give rise to indolence, for if indolence arises, one will experience endless suffering.
"O sons of good family!

The intrinsic nature of all these phenomena is entirely empty and free from all obstructions. You should contemplate this principle of the emptiness of intrinsic nature: within that which is without obstruction, there is no phenomenon of indolence, nor is there anyone who is indolent; neither place, time, nor conditions can be apprehended therein."

"In this way, Subhūti, when bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom, they use skillful means to establish sentient beings in the principle that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is empty; yet, although they cause them to abide therein, they harbor no notion of duality."
Why is this? Because the principle of the emptiness of intrinsic nature is non-dual and indivisible; there is no non-dual dharma within it upon which one could form dualistic conceptions.
*The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Scroll 386, translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Order, Part One, Chapter Seventy, "The Immovable," Section Two. "Furthermore, Subhūti!"

This bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, relies on the emptiness of intrinsic nature to instruct and admonish all classes of sentient beings, urging them to apply themselves with diligence, saying:
"O noble sons!..."

You should apply yourself with diligent vigor toward wholesome dharmas. When practicing the perfections of giving, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, do not conceptualize these dharmas in terms of duality or non-duality.
When practicing the four meditative concentrations, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments, do not conceptualize these dharmas in terms of duality or non-duality.

When practicing the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path, do not conceptualize these dharmas in terms of duality or non-duality.
When practicing the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—one should not contemplate these phenomena in terms of dualistic or non-dualistic characteristics.

When abiding in internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, unchanging emptiness, essential emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common-characteristic emptiness, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature, one should not contemplate these phenomena in terms of dualistic or non-dualistic characteristics.

When abiding in suchness, the dharma-realm, the nature of phenomena, non-falsity, immutability, equality, the state beyond birth, the fixed nature of phenomena, the stability of phenomena, the limit of reality, the realm of space, and the inconceivable realm, one should not contemplate these phenomena in terms of the characteristics of duality or non-duality.
When abiding in the noble truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path, one should not contemplate these phenomena in terms of the characteristics of duality or non-duality.

When practicing the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative attainments, and the ten universal bases, one should not contemplate these phenomena in terms of the characteristics of duality or non-duality.
When practicing all the gateways of dhāraṇī and the gateways of samādhi, one should not contemplate these phenomena as having the characteristics of duality or non-duality.

When practicing the Ground of Extreme Joy, the Ground of Purity, the Ground of Radiant Light, the Ground of Blazing Wisdom, the Ground of Difficult Victory, the Ground of Presence, the Ground of Far-Going, the Ground of Immovability, the Ground of Excellent Intelligence, and the Ground of the Dharma Cloud, one should not contemplate these phenomena as having the characteristics of duality or non-duality.
When practicing the five eyes and the six supernormal powers, one should not contemplate these phenomena as having the characteristics of duality or non-duality.

When cultivating the ten powers of a Buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, one should not contemplate these dharmas in terms of dualistic or non-dualistic characteristics;
when cultivating great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity, one should not contemplate these dharmas in terms of dualistic or non-dualistic characteristics;
when cultivating the thirty-two marks of a Great Being and the eighty minor marks, one should not contemplate these dharmas in terms of dualistic or non-dualistic characteristics.
When cultivating the quality of non-forgetfulness and the state of constant equanimity, one should not contemplate these phenomena in terms of dualistic or non-dualistic characteristics;
when cultivating all-knowledge, the knowledge of the paths, and the knowledge of all aspects, one should not contemplate these phenomena in terms of dualistic or non-dualistic characteristics;
and when cultivating all other Buddha-qualities, one should not contemplate these phenomena in terms of dualistic or non-dualistic characteristics.
Why is this? Son of good family!
All such dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature; in the principle of the emptiness of intrinsic nature, one should not contemplate duality or non-duality.

"In this way, Subhūti, when bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom, they employ skillful means to perform the conduct of a bodhisattva and bring sentient beings to maturity. Once these sentient beings have matured, he gradually establishes them according to their respective capacities: either causing them to abide in the fruit of a stream-enterer, or causing them to abide in the fruit of a once-returner, or causing them to abide in the fruit of a non-returner, or causing them to abide in the fruit of arhatship, or causing them to abide in the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, or causing them to abide in the stage of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, or causing them to abide in unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), from the first generation of the mind of awakening, they accomplish such skillful means (upāyakauśalya). By the power of these skillful means, seeing that the minds of sentient beings are largely distracted and unable to find tranquility amidst the objects of desire, they employ skillful means to lead them into superior samādhi, saying: 'Come!'"
"Noble son! You should cultivate the supreme samādhi; do not give rise to thoughts of distraction or even the notion of meditative concentration. Why is this?

Good son! All these phenomena are empty by their very nature. Within this emptiness of intrinsic nature, there is no dharma that can be apprehended, nor can it be named "distraction" or "one-pointedness of mind."

If you are able to abide in this sublime samādhi, all the wholesome deeds you perform will be swiftly fulfilled, and you may likewise dwell in the emptiness of intrinsic nature according to your wish.
What are called "wholesome deeds"?
That is to say, it refers to the arising of superior and pure actions of body, speech, and mind;
whether one practices the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom;
or whether one practices the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right endeavors, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, and the seven factors of enlightenment.
The eight branches of the noble path; or if one cultivates the gates of liberation of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;

or if one dwells in internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, or...
The emptiness of change, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, the emptiness of specific characteristics, the emptiness of common characteristics,
the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of non-apprehensibility, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of self-nature, and the emptiness of the self-nature of non-existence;
or if one abides in suchness, the dharma-realm, the dharma-nature, non-falsity, and immutability.
...the nature of equality, the state of being free from birth, the fixedness of phenomena, the stability of phenomena, the limit of reality, the realm of space, and the inconceivable realm;
whether one abides in the noble truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path;
or cultivates the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments; or cultivates the eight liberations;...
The eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative attainments, and the ten universal bases;
if one cultivates all the doors of dhāraṇī and the doors of samādhi; if one enters the bodhisattva’s state of right determination and departure from birth;
if one cultivates the bodhisattva mahāsattva stages; if one cultivates the five eyes and the six supernormal powers; or if one cultivates the ten powers of a Buddha—
The four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
if one cultivates great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity; if one cultivates the thirty-two marks of a Great Being and the eighty minor marks;
if one cultivates the quality of non-forgetfulness and the nature of constant dwelling in equanimity; if one cultivates the one...
All-knowledge, the knowledge of the aspects of the path, and all-aspect knowledge;
whether one cultivates the path of the śrāvaka, the path of the pratyekabuddha, the path of the bodhisattva, or the path of the Tathāgata;

or whether one cultivates the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, the fruit of arhatship, the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, or the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of a Buddha.
Kātyāyana, whether it be the maturation of sentient beings or the purification of Buddha-fields—

all such supreme, pure, and virtuous dharmas are swiftly accomplished through the power of meditative concentration, while one abides in the emptiness of intrinsic nature according to one's aspirations.

"Thus it is, Subhūti! When bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom, through their skill in means and for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, they seek to accomplish virtuous benefits from the first generation of the mind until the ultimate end, always without interruption."

For the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, they travel from one buddha-field to another, making offerings, showing reverence, honoring, and praising the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones; in the presence of these Buddhas, they listen to and receive the true Dharma, and throughout the succession of bodies they take for countless eons until reaching unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, they never forget what they have learned during that interval.
“Subhūti! These bodhisattvas have attained dhāraṇīs, and thus their faculties of body, speech, and mind never decline. Why is this?
This bodhisattva mahāsattva constantly possesses and has well-cultivated the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*), and is able to engage in all activities with skillful reflection.

Because they possess and have well-cultivated the knowledge of all modes, and because they are able to engage in all activities with skillful reflection, they are able to cultivate all paths—namely, the path of the śrāvaka, the path of the pratyekabuddha, the path of the bodhisattva, the path of the Tathāgata, the superior path of devas, the superior path of humans, and the superior supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) of bodhisattvas. By means of these superior supernormal powers, bodhisattva mahāsattvas constantly perform what is beneficial for others, never falling back or losing their way.

Abiding in these superior supernormal powers resulting from karmic maturation, this bodhisattva mahāsattva constantly performs deeds for the benefit and happiness of sentient beings; although they undergo the cycle of birth and death across the various realms of existence, their superior supernormal powers never diminish.
Thus it is, Subhūti!

When bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom, they abide in the skillful means of the emptiness of intrinsic nature and are thus able to effectively bring benefit and happiness to all sentient beings.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom, from their first production of the thought of enlightenment they achieve such skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*). By the power of these skillful means, they abide in the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*), yet seeing that sentient beings have meager wisdom and, through delusion and inversion, commit various evil deeds, they employ skillful means to lead them into the gateway of supreme wisdom, saying:
'O son of good family!'"

"You should cultivate the perfection of wisdom by contemplating that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is empty and quiescent. If you can cultivate this wisdom and contemplate that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is entirely empty, then all the physical, verbal, and mental actions you practice will tend toward the deathless and attain the fruit of the deathless; they will surely have the deathless as their final limit."
"O sons of good family!

All these phenomena are empty by their very nature. Within this emptiness of intrinsic nature, although sentient beings and phenomena cannot be apprehended, that which is practiced does not suffer any loss or regression."
Why is this? Good son! Within the emptiness of intrinsic nature, there is no phenomenon of increase or decrease, nor is there anyone who increases or decreases.

Why is this so? Because the principle of intrinsic emptiness has neither self-nature nor absence of self-nature; it is free from all conceptual discrimination and transcends all proliferations of speech. Therefore, within this, there is neither increase nor decrease, and by virtue of this, that which is accomplished can never be lost.
"Therefore, you all should cultivate the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) and, observing intrinsic emptiness (prakṛti-śūnyatā), perform what is to be done. Thus, Subhūti,

when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom, they skillfully employ means (upāya-kauśalya) to instruct and admonish sentient beings, leading them to cultivate the perfection of wisdom, observe intrinsic emptiness, and perform all virtuous deeds.

“Subhūti! This bodhisattva mahāsattva thus instructs and exhorts sentient beings to cultivate all manner of wholesome deeds, never becoming weary or negligent. That is to say: he himself constantly practices the ten paths of wholesome action and also encourages others to constantly practice the ten paths of wholesome action;
he himself constantly upholds the five precepts and also encourages others to constantly uphold the five precepts.”
They themselves constantly observe the eight precepts and also encourage others to constantly observe the eight precepts;
they themselves constantly observe the monastic precepts and also encourage others to constantly observe the monastic precepts;
they themselves constantly cultivate the four dhyānas and also encourage others to constantly cultivate the four dhyānas.
They themselves constantly cultivate the four immeasurables and also encourage others to constantly cultivate the four immeasurables;
they themselves constantly cultivate the four formless attainments and also encourage others to constantly cultivate the four formless attainments;

they themselves constantly cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path, and also encourage others to constantly cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path.

They themselves constantly cultivate the gates of liberation of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, and they also exhort others to constantly cultivate the gates of liberation of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;

they themselves constantly cultivate the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, wisdom, skillful means, sublime aspiration, power, and knowledge, and they also exhort others to constantly cultivate the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, wisdom, skillful means, sublime aspiration, power, and knowledge.

They themselves constantly abide in internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, the emptiness of the ultimate truth, the emptiness of conditioned phenomena, the emptiness of unconditioned phenomena, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, the emptiness of dispersion, the emptiness of non-alteration, the emptiness of essential nature, the emptiness of self-characteristics, the emptiness of common characteristics, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of non-apprehensibility, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence; and they likewise exhort others to constantly abide in internal emptiness up to the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence.

They themselves abide eternally in true suchness (*tathatā*), the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), non-falsity, immutability, equality, the state beyond birth, the fixed nature of phenomena (*dharmaniyāmatā*), the stability of phenomena (*dharmaniyāmatā*), the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*), the realm of space (*ākāśadhātu*), and the inconceivable realm; they also exhort others to abide eternally in true suchness, up to the inconceivable realm.

They themselves abide eternally in the noble truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path; they also exhort others to abide eternally in the noble truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.

They themselves constantly cultivate the eight liberations (*aṣṭavimokṣa*), the eight bases of mastery (*aṣṭābhibhvāyatana*), the nine successive meditative attainments (*navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti*), and the ten totalities (*daśakṛtsnāyatana*); they also exhort others to constantly cultivate the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative attainments, and the ten totalities.
They themselves constantly cultivate all dharani-doors and samadhi-doors, and they also exhort others to constantly cultivate all dharani-doors and samadhi-doors;
they themselves constantly cultivate the various bodhisattva stages, and they also exhort others to constantly cultivate the various bodhisattva stages;
they themselves constantly study the five eyes and the six supernormal powers, and they also exhort others to constantly study the five eyes and the six supernormal powers.

I myself constantly study the ten powers of a Buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and I also encourage others to constantly study the ten powers of a Buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;

I myself constantly study great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity, and I also encourage others to constantly study great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity;

I myself constantly study the thirty-two marks of a Great Being and the eighty minor characteristics, and I also encourage others to constantly study the thirty-two marks of a Great Being and the eighty minor characteristics.

They themselves constantly study the quality of non-forgetfulness and abide perpetually in equanimity, and they also exhort others to constantly study the quality of non-forgetfulness and to abide perpetually in equanimity;
they themselves constantly study all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*),
and they also exhort others to constantly study all-knowledge, the knowledge of the aspects of the path, and the knowledge of all aspects.

They themselves constantly give rise to the knowledge of the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*) but do not abide therein; they also constantly exhort others to give rise to the knowledge of the fruit of stream-entry or cause them to dwell within it.

They themselves constantly give rise to the knowledge of the fruits of once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*), non-returner (*anāgāmin*), and arhatship (*arhat-phala*), but do not abide therein; they also constantly exhort others to give rise to the knowledge of the fruits of once-returner, non-returner, and arhatship or cause them to dwell within them.

They themselves constantly give rise to the knowledge of pratyekabuddha-enlightenment (*pratyekabodhi*) but do not abide therein; they also constantly exhort others to give rise to the knowledge of pratyekabuddha-enlightenment or cause them to dwell within it.

"I myself have constantly set out upon the path to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and I also encourage others to constantly set out upon the path to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. It is thus, Subhūti!"

When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom, they skillfully employ means to personally cultivate virtuous deeds without ever becoming weary or negligent, and they instruct and admonish all classes of sentient beings to cultivate virtuous deeds without ever becoming weary or negligent.
"Subhūti! This is called the skillful means of bodhisattva mahāsattvas when they practice the perfection of wisdom.

By the power of these skillful means, bodhisattva mahāsattvas establish sentient beings within the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), yet they are able to do so without destroying the characteristics of the limit of reality."
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If all dharmas are empty by their very nature, and within this emptiness of intrinsic nature neither sentient beings nor dharmas can be apprehended—and since there is likewise no ‘non-dharma’ therein—how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva constantly perform benefit for sentient beings while seeking to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening?”
The Buddha told Subhūti: "So it is! So it is!"
It is as you have said:

all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature. Within the emptiness of intrinsic nature, neither sentient beings nor phenomena can be apprehended; consequently, within this, there is also no such thing as non-phenomena.

Subhūti! If all phenomena were not empty by their very nature, then bodhisattva mahāsattvas, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, would not abide in the principle of the emptiness of intrinsic nature to cultivate and realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, nor would they teach the dharma of the emptiness of intrinsic nature for the benefit of sentient beings.

Subhūti! Because all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they abide in the principle that all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature, cultivate and realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and for the benefit of sentient beings, they teach the dharma of the emptiness of intrinsic nature.

“Subhūti! What are those phenomena whose intrinsic nature is entirely empty, such that when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, having realized their emptiness of intrinsic nature as it truly is, they abide in the emptiness of intrinsic nature and teach the Dharma to others?”
"Subhūti! Form is empty of intrinsic nature; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty of intrinsic nature.

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, having realized as they truly are that these aggregates are empty of intrinsic nature, they abide in the emptiness of intrinsic nature and proclaim this Dharma of the emptiness of intrinsic nature for the sake of all sentient beings."
“Subhūti! The sphere of the eye is empty of intrinsic nature; the spheres of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are empty of intrinsic nature.
The sphere of forms is empty of intrinsic nature; the spheres of sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature.”

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, having realized as they truly are that the intrinsic nature of these bases is empty, they abide in that emptiness of intrinsic nature and proclaim this Dharma of the emptiness of intrinsic nature for the sake of all sentient beings.
“Subhūti! The nature of the eye-element is empty; the nature of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-elements is empty.
The nature of the form-element is empty; the nature of the sound, odor, taste, tangible, and mental-object elements is empty.”
The element of eye-consciousness is empty of intrinsic nature; the elements of ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-consciousness are empty of intrinsic nature.
Eye-contact is empty of intrinsic nature; ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact are empty of intrinsic nature.

All feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition are empty of intrinsic nature; all feelings produced with ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact as conditions are empty of intrinsic nature.
The earth element is empty of intrinsic nature; the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements are empty of intrinsic nature.

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, having understood as they truly are that these elements are empty of intrinsic nature, they abide in this emptiness of intrinsic nature and proclaim this dharma of the emptiness of intrinsic nature for the sake of all sentient beings.
"Subhūti! The intrinsic nature of causal conditions is empty; the intrinsic nature of the immediately preceding condition, the object-condition, and the dominant condition is empty;
and the intrinsic nature of all phenomena produced from conditions is empty."

Ignorance is empty of intrinsic nature; volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, existence, birth, and old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair are empty of intrinsic nature.

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, having realized as it truly is that the nature of such dependent origination is emptiness, they abide in the emptiness of intrinsic nature and proclaim this Dharma of the emptiness of intrinsic nature for the sake of all sentient beings.

"Subhūti! The perfection of giving is empty of intrinsic nature; the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, wisdom, skillful means, sublime aspiration, power, and knowledge are empty of intrinsic nature."

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, having realized as it truly is that the intrinsic nature of all perfections is emptiness, they abide in that emptiness of intrinsic nature and proclaim this Dharma of the emptiness of intrinsic nature for the sake of all sentient beings.
“Subhūti! The four dhyānas are empty of intrinsic nature; the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments are empty of intrinsic nature.

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, having realized as they truly are that these dhyānas, immeasurables, and formless states are empty of intrinsic nature, they abide in this emptiness of intrinsic nature and proclaim this Dharma of the emptiness of intrinsic nature for the sake of all sentient beings.”

“Subhūti! The four foundations of mindfulness are empty of intrinsic nature; the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path are empty of intrinsic nature.”

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, having realized as they truly are that the intrinsic nature of the factors of enlightenment, such as the four foundations of mindfulness, is emptiness, they abide in that intrinsic emptiness and proclaim this Dharma of intrinsic emptiness for the sake of all sentient beings.
“Subhūti! The liberation door of emptiness is empty of intrinsic nature; the liberation doors of signlessness and wishlessness are empty of intrinsic nature.

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, having realized as they truly are that all liberation doors are empty of intrinsic nature, they abide in this emptiness of intrinsic nature and proclaim such dharmas of the emptiness of intrinsic nature for the sake of all sentient beings.”

“Subhūti! Internal emptiness is empty of its own intrinsic nature; external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, the emptiness of the ultimate truth, the emptiness of conditioned phenomena, the emptiness of unconditioned phenomena, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, the emptiness of dispersion, the emptiness of non-alteration, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, the emptiness of self-characteristics, the emptiness of common characteristics, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of non-apprehensibility, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence are all empty of their own intrinsic nature.”

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, having realized such emptiness as the emptiness of intrinsic nature just as it is, they abide in the emptiness of intrinsic nature and proclaim this Dharma of the emptiness of intrinsic nature for the sake of all sentient beings.
"Subhūti! The noble truth of suffering is empty of intrinsic nature; the noble truths of origin, cessation, and the path are empty of intrinsic nature.

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, having realized as they truly are that these noble truths are empty of intrinsic nature, they abide in the emptiness of intrinsic nature and proclaim this dharma of the emptiness of intrinsic nature for the sake of all sentient beings."
“Subhūti! The eight liberations are empty of intrinsic nature; the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative attainments, and the ten totalities are empty of intrinsic nature.

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, having realized as they truly are that the liberations, the bases of mastery, the meditative attainments, and the totalities are empty of intrinsic nature, they abide in the emptiness of intrinsic nature and proclaim this dharma of the emptiness of intrinsic nature for the sake of all sentient beings.”
“Subhūti! All dhāraṇī-doors are empty of intrinsic nature; all samādhi-doors are empty of intrinsic nature.

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, having realized as they truly are that the dhāraṇī-doors and samādhi-doors are empty of intrinsic nature, they abide in this emptiness of intrinsic nature and proclaim such teachings on the emptiness of intrinsic nature for the sake of all sentient beings.”

“Subhūti! The bodhisattva’s Ground of Extreme Joy is empty of its own intrinsic nature; the bodhisattva’s Ground of Freedom from Defilement, the Ground of Radiant Light, the Ground of Blazing Wisdom, the Ground of Utmost Difficulty to Conquer, the Ground of Manifestation, the Ground of Far-Going, the Ground of Immovability, the Ground of Excellent Intelligence, and the Ground of the Dharma Cloud are all empty of their own intrinsic nature.”

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, having realized as it truly is that the intrinsic nature of the bodhisattva stages is empty, they abide in that emptiness of intrinsic nature and proclaim this Dharma of the emptiness of intrinsic nature for the sake of all sentient beings.
“Subhūti! The five eyes are empty of intrinsic nature, and the six supernormal powers are empty of intrinsic nature.

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, having realized as they truly are that all eyes and supernormal powers are empty of intrinsic nature, they abide in this emptiness of intrinsic nature and proclaim such dharmas of the emptiness of intrinsic nature for the sake of all sentient beings.”

"Subhūti! The ten powers of a Buddha are empty of intrinsic nature; the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are empty of intrinsic nature."

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, having realized as they truly are that the powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, and the unique qualities are by nature empty, they abide in this emptiness of intrinsic nature and proclaim such teachings on the emptiness of intrinsic nature for the sake of all sentient beings.
“Subhūti! Great loving-kindness is empty of intrinsic nature; great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity are empty of intrinsic nature.

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, having realized as they truly are that all the great immeasurables are empty of intrinsic nature, they abide in the emptiness of intrinsic nature and proclaim this Dharma of the emptiness of intrinsic nature for the sake of all sentient beings.”
“Subhūti! The thirty-two marks of a great man are empty of intrinsic nature; the eighty secondary signs are empty of intrinsic nature.

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, having realized as they truly are that the marks and secondary signs are empty of intrinsic nature, they abide in the emptiness of intrinsic nature and proclaim this Dharma of the emptiness of intrinsic nature for the sake of all sentient beings.”
“Subhūti! The quality of non-forgetfulness is empty of intrinsic nature; the state of constant equanimity is empty of intrinsic nature.

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, having realized as they truly are that the quality of non-forgetfulness and the state of constant equanimity are empty of intrinsic nature, they abide in the emptiness of intrinsic nature and proclaim this dharma of the emptiness of intrinsic nature for the sake of all sentient beings.”
“Subhūti! The nature of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) is empty; the nature of the knowledge of the paths (*mārgākārajñatā*) and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) is empty.

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), having realized as they truly are that the nature of these various knowledges is empty, they abide in the emptiness of intrinsic nature and proclaim this Dharma of the emptiness of intrinsic nature for the sake of all sentient beings.”

“Subhūti! The fruit of stream-entry is empty of intrinsic nature; the fruits of once-returning, non-returning, and arhatship, as well as the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, are empty of intrinsic nature.”

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, having realized as it truly is that the fruits of the śrāvaka vehicle and the enlightenment of the pratyekabuddha are empty of intrinsic nature, they abide in the emptiness of intrinsic nature and proclaim this very dharma of the emptiness of intrinsic nature for the sake of all sentient beings.

“Subhūti! The intrinsic nature of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas’ practices is emptiness; the intrinsic nature of the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas is emptiness; and the intrinsic nature of the perpetual severance of the continuity of all afflictions and habitual tendencies is emptiness.”

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, having realized as they truly are that the nature of all bodhisattva practices, awakening, and nirvāṇa is emptiness, they abide in the emptiness of intrinsic nature and proclaim this Dharma of the emptiness of intrinsic nature for the sake of all sentient beings.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If the nature of internal emptiness were not empty by its very nature, and if the nature of external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, non-altering emptiness, emptiness of intrinsic nature, emptiness of self-characteristic, emptiness of common characteristic, emptiness of all phenomena, emptiness of the unapprehendable, emptiness of non-existence, emptiness of intrinsic nature, and emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence were also not empty by their very nature, then when bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom, they should not teach sentient beings that all phenomena are empty by their very nature; for to do so would be to destroy the emptiness of intrinsic nature."
However, the principle of the emptiness of intrinsic nature is indestructible; it is neither eternal nor annihilated. Why is this so?
Because the principle of the emptiness of intrinsic nature has no direction and no location; it comes from nowhere and goes nowhere.

This principle of emptiness is also called the "abiding nature of phenomena" (*dharmasthiti*). Within it, there are no phenomena; there is no aggregation and no dispersal, no decrease and no increase, no arising and no cessation, and no defilement and no purity. This is the fundamental nature in which all phenomena abide. All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas dwell within this, seeking to proceed toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; yet they do not perceive any phenomena as having a point of departure or a point of arrival. Because all phenomena fundamentally have no place of abiding, it is called the "abiding nature of phenomena."

When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas abide within this and practice the perfection of wisdom, having seen that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is empty, they will certainly attain non-retrogression from unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Why is this? Because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas do not perceive any dharma capable of acting as an obstacle; seeing that all dharmas are without obstruction, they give rise to no doubt or hesitation regarding unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and for this reason they do not regress.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

In the emptiness of intrinsic nature, a self cannot be apprehended; sentient beings cannot be apprehended; the designation of 'sentient being' cannot be apprehended. A life-principle, a living being, a nourisher, a person, an individual, a mind-born, a youth, an agent, one who causes to act, an originator, one who causes to originate, an experiencer, one who causes to experience, a knower, and a seer likewise cannot be apprehended."
“Subhūti! In the emptiness of intrinsic nature, form cannot be apprehended; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness likewise cannot be apprehended. Subhūti!”
In the emptiness of intrinsic nature, the sense-base of the eye is unapprehendable; the sense-bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are likewise unapprehendable.
"Subhūti! In the emptiness of intrinsic nature, the sense-base of form is unapprehendable; the sense-bases of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena are likewise unapprehendable."
“Subhūti! Within the emptiness of intrinsic nature, the eye constituent cannot be apprehended; nor can the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind constituents be apprehended. Subhūti!”
In the emptiness of intrinsic nature, the realm of form is unapprehendable; the realms of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena are likewise unapprehendable. "Subhūti!
In the emptiness of intrinsic nature, the realm of eye-consciousness is unapprehendable; the realms of ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-consciousness are likewise unapprehendable."
“Subhūti! Within the emptiness of intrinsic nature, eye-contact is unapprehendable; ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact are likewise unapprehendable. Subhūti!”

In the emptiness of intrinsic nature, the various sensations produced with eye-contact as a condition cannot be apprehended; likewise, the various sensations produced with ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact as conditions cannot be apprehended.
“Subhūti! In the emptiness of intrinsic nature, the earth element cannot be apprehended; nor can the water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness elements be apprehended. Subhūti!”

"In the emptiness of intrinsic nature, causal conditions cannot be apprehended; likewise, the immediately preceding condition, the object-condition, and the dominant condition cannot be apprehended. Subhūti!"
In the emptiness of intrinsic nature, all phenomena produced from conditions are unapprehendable. "Subhūti!

In the emptiness of intrinsic nature, ignorance is unapprehendable; likewise, volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, existence, birth, and old age, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are also unapprehendable."

"Subhūti! Within the emptiness of intrinsic nature, the perfection of giving cannot be apprehended; nor can the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom be apprehended."

“Subhūti! Within the emptiness of intrinsic nature, internal emptiness cannot be apprehended; nor can external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, the emptiness of the ultimate truth, the emptiness of the conditioned, the emptiness of the unconditioned, absolute emptiness, the emptiness of the limitless, the emptiness of dispersion, the emptiness of non-alteration, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, the emptiness of specific characteristics, the emptiness of common characteristics, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of non-apprehension, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of self-nature, or the emptiness of the self-nature of non-existence be apprehended.”

“Subhūti! Within the emptiness of intrinsic nature, the four foundations of mindfulness are unapprehendable; likewise, the four right endeavors, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path are also unapprehendable.”
“Subhūti! Within the emptiness of intrinsic nature, the noble truth of suffering cannot be apprehended, nor can the noble truths of origination, cessation, and the path be apprehended. Subhūti!”
In the emptiness of intrinsic nature, the four dhyānas are unattainable; the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments are likewise unattainable. "Subhūti!
In the emptiness of intrinsic nature, the eight liberations are unattainable; the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities are likewise unattainable."
“Subhūti! Within the emptiness of intrinsic nature, all dhāraṇī-doors are unapprehendable, and all samādhi-doors are likewise unapprehendable. Subhūti!”
In the emptiness of intrinsic nature, the gate of liberation of emptiness cannot be apprehended; the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness likewise cannot be apprehended. "Subhūti!

Within the emptiness of intrinsic nature, the bodhisattva’s stage of extreme joy cannot be apprehended; the stages of freedom from defilement, radiant light, blazing wisdom, extremely difficult to conquer, presence, far-reaching, immovability, excellent intelligence, and the cloud of dharma likewise cannot be apprehended."
“Subhūti! Within the emptiness of intrinsic nature, the five eyes cannot be apprehended, nor can the six supernormal powers be apprehended. Subhūti!”

In the emptiness of intrinsic nature, the ten powers of a Buddha cannot be apprehended; likewise, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha also cannot be apprehended.
“Subhūti! Within the emptiness of intrinsic nature, the quality of non-forgetfulness cannot be apprehended, nor can the state of constant abiding in equanimity be apprehended. Subhūti!”

In the emptiness of intrinsic nature, omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) is unapprehendable; the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*) and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) are likewise unapprehendable.

"Subhūti! In the emptiness of intrinsic nature, the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpattiphala*) is unapprehendable; the fruits of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmiphala*), non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*), arhatship (*arhattvaphala*), and the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha (*pratyekabodhi*) are also unapprehendable."

"Subhūti! Within the emptiness of intrinsic nature, the practices of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cannot be apprehended, nor can the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas be apprehended."

"Subhūti! Within the emptiness of intrinsic nature, form and non-form dharmas cannot be apprehended; likewise, visible and invisible, resistant and non-resistant, outflowing and non-outflowing, conditioned and unconditioned dharmas also cannot be apprehended."
“Subhūti! Within the emptiness of intrinsic nature, the thirty-two marks of a great man cannot be apprehended, nor can the eighty secondary signs be apprehended. Subhūti!”

Suppose a Buddha were to manifest fourfold assemblies—namely, bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās—and that manifested Buddha were to proclaim the essentials of the Dharma for those four assemblies for hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of kalpas. What do you think?

Among those thus transformed, is there anyone who is able to attain the fruit of stream-entry, or the fruit of once-returning, or the fruit of non-returning, or the fruit of arhatship, or the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, or unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One!”
"No, Sugata! Why is that?"
"These transformed beings have no substantial reality; yet it is not that there can be no attainment of the fruit through dharmas that lack substantial reality.
The Buddha said, "Suvikrāntavikrāmin!..."

All phenomena are likewise; they are all empty of intrinsic nature and entirely devoid of substantial reality. Within this, what bodhisattva mahāsattva could teach what dharma to what sentient beings so as to enable them to attain the fruit of a stream-enterer, or the fruit of a once-returner, or the fruit of a non-returner, or the fruit of an arhat, or the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, or even unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?

“Subhūti! Although bodhisattva mahāsattvas proclaim to sentient beings the various dharmas that are empty by nature, those sentient beings are in fact unapprehendable. Out of compassion for those who have fallen into inverted dharmas, they rescue them and cause them to abide in non-inverted dharmas.”

Non-inversion means the absence of conceptual construction; because there is no inversion where there is no conceptual construction, whereas if there were conceptual construction, there would be inversion, as it is the outflow thereof.

“Subhūti! Within that which is non-conceptual and non-erroneous, there is no self, no sentient being, no life-force, no nourisher, no spirit, no person, no individual, no mind-born, no youth, no agent, no instigator of action, no originator, no instigator of origination, no experiencer, no instigator of experience, no knower, and no seer;
nor is there form, nor feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.”
Furthermore, there is no eye-base, nor ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind-base;
there is no form-base, nor sound, odor, taste, tangible object, or mental-object base;
and there is no eye-element, nor ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind-element.
There is also no form realm, nor the realms of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, or mental phenomena;
there is also no visual consciousness realm, nor the realms of auditory, olfactory, gustatory, tactile, or mental consciousness;
there is also no visual contact, nor auditory, olfactory, gustatory, tactile, or mental contact.
Furthermore, there are no feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition, nor any feelings produced with ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind-contact as conditions;
there is no earth element, nor water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness elements;
there is no causal condition, nor immediate condition, object-condition, or dominant condition.
Furthermore, there are no phenomena produced from conditions;

nor is there ignorance, nor formative forces, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, sensation, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, or old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair.
Nor is there the perfection of generosity, nor the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, or wisdom.

Furthermore, there is no internal emptiness, no external emptiness, no internal-and-external emptiness, no emptiness of emptiness, no great emptiness, no emptiness of the ultimate truth, no emptiness of conditioned phenomena, no emptiness of unconditioned phenomena, no absolute emptiness, no emptiness of the limitless, no emptiness of dispersion, no emptiness of non-alteration, no emptiness of intrinsic nature, no emptiness of self-characteristic, no emptiness of common characteristic, no emptiness of all phenomena, no emptiness of the unapprehendable, no emptiness of non-existence, no emptiness of intrinsic nature, and no emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature;

nor are there the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, or the eightfold noble path;
nor is there the noble truth of suffering, nor the noble truths of origination, cessation, or the path.
Furthermore, there are no four dhyānas; there are no four immeasurables, nor the four formless attainments;
there are no eight liberations, no eight bases of mastery, no nine successive attainments, nor the ten totalities;
and there are no gateways of all dhāraṇīs, nor gateways of all samādhis.
There is also no gate of liberation of emptiness, nor the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness;

there is also no Ground of Extreme Joy, no Ground of Purity, Ground of Radiant Light, Ground of Blazing Wisdom, Ground of Difficult Victory, Ground of Presence, Ground of Far-Going, Ground of Immovability, Ground of Excellent Intelligence, or Ground of Dharma Clouds;
there is also no five eyes, nor the six supernormal powers.

Furthermore, there are no ten powers of a Buddha; there are no four fearlessnesses, four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, or the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
nor is there the quality of non-forgetfulness, nor the nature of constant abiding in equanimity;
nor is there omniscience, nor the knowledge of the aspects of the path, nor the knowledge of all aspects.
There is also no fruit of stream-entry, no fruit of once-returning, non-returning, or arhatship; no awakening of a pratyekabuddha;
no practices of any bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; and no unexcelled, perfect, and complete awakening of the Buddhas.
There are also no phenomena that are material or immaterial; no phenomena that are visible or invisible, resistant or non-resistant, outflowing or non-outflowing, conditioned or unconditioned.
Nor are there the thirty-two marks of a great man, nor the eighty secondary signs. "Subhūti! This non-existence is itself intrinsic emptiness.

When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom, they abide within this and see that sentient beings have fallen into perverted conceptions; through skillful means, they cause them to attain liberation—namely, liberation from the notion of 'self' regarding what is selfless, and from the notions of sentient beings, life-principles, souls, nourishers, persons, individuals, mind-born, youths, agents, instigators, originators, prompters, experiencers, feelers, knowers, and seers, up to and including the notion of a seer regarding sentient beings."

They also cause them to be liberated from the perception of form within the formless, and from the perceptions of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness within feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness;

they also cause them to be liberated from the perception of the eye-base within the absence of the eye-base, and from the perceptions of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-bases within the absence of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-bases;

they also cause them to be liberated from the perception of the form-base within the absence of the form-base, and from the perceptions of the sound, odor, taste, tangible, and mental-object bases within the absence of the sound, odor, taste, tangible, and mental-object bases.

They also cause them to be liberated from the absence of the eye-element and the notion of the eye-element; from the absence of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-elements and the notions of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-elements;

they also cause them to be liberated from the absence of the form-element and the notion of the form-element; from the absence of the sound, odor, taste, tangible-object, and mental-phenomena elements and the notions of the sound, odor, taste, tangible-object, and mental-phenomena elements;

and they also cause them to be liberated from the absence of the eye-consciousness-element and the notion of the eye-consciousness-element; from the absence of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-consciousness-elements and the notions of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-consciousness-elements.

They also cause them to be liberated from the absence of eye-contact and the absence of the perception of eye-contact; from the absence of ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact and the absence of the perception of ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact;

and they also cause them to be liberated from the absence of the various feelings produced with eye-contact as condition and the absence of the perception of those various feelings produced with eye-contact as condition;

from the absence of the various feelings produced with ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact as condition and the absence of the perception of those various feelings produced with ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact as condition.

They also cause them to be liberated from the absence of the earth element and the perception of the earth element; from the absence of the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements and the perceptions of the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements;
and they also cause them to be liberated from the absence of causes and conditions and the perception of causes and conditions;
from the absence of the immediate condition, the object-condition, and the predominant condition, and the perceptions of the immediate condition, the object-condition, and the predominant condition.
They also cause them to be liberated from the notion that phenomena produced from conditions are [inherently] produced from conditions;

they also cause them to be liberated from the absence of ignorance and the notion of ignorance, and from the absence of volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, and old age, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair, up to the absence of old age, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair and the notion thereof;

they also cause them to be liberated from the absence of the perfection of generosity and the notion of the perfection of generosity, and from the absence of the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, up to the absence of the perfection of wisdom and the notion thereof.

They also cause them to be liberated from the absence of the notion of internal emptiness regarding internal emptiness; and from the absence of the notions of external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, endless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, non-alteration emptiness, essential nature emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common characteristic emptiness, emptiness of all phenomena, unapprehendable emptiness, non-existence emptiness, intrinsic nature emptiness, and non-existence-intrinsic-nature emptiness, extending up to the absence of the notion of non-existence-intrinsic-nature emptiness regarding external emptiness;

they also cause them to be liberated from the absence of the notion of the four applications of mindfulness regarding the four applications of mindfulness; and from the absence of the notions of the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path, extending from the four right efforts up to the eightfold noble path.

They also cause them to be liberated from the notion of the Noble Truth of Suffering regarding that which is not the Noble Truth of Suffering, and from the notions of the Noble Truths of Origination, Cessation, and the Path regarding that which are not the Noble Truths of Origination, Cessation, and the Path;
