When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom through skillful means, they do not conjoin all the practices of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, nor do they disperse them;
they do not conjoin the unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas, nor do they disperse it.
Why is this? Because all such phenomena lack an intrinsic nature that could be joined or separated. "Thus it is, Śāriputra!"
"Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practicing the perfection of wisdom cultivate the path to enlightenment with courageous and correct diligence.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

If all phenomena are entirely devoid of intrinsic nature such that they could be joined or separated, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva bring forth the perfection of wisdom, and how do bodhisattva mahāsattvas train within it?
“World-Honored One!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not study the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they will ultimately be unable to attain the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi) that they seek.”
The Buddha told Śāriputra: "So it is! So it is!"
It is as you have said.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not train in the perfection of wisdom, they will ultimately be unable to attain the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment they seek.
Śāriputra! It is only by training in the perfection of wisdom that bodhisattva mahāsattvas are able to realize the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment they seek.
Śāriputra! The unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment sought by bodhisattva mahāsattvas can only be realized through skillful means; it cannot be realized without skillful means.

“Śāriputra! When bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom, if they were to perceive any dharma with an intrinsic nature that could be apprehended, then it would be something to be grasped; yet since they do not perceive any dharma with an intrinsic nature that can be apprehended, what is there to be grasped?”

That is to say, not grasping at the notion that "this is the perfection of wisdom," "this is the perfection of meditative concentration," "this is the perfection of diligence," "this is the perfection of patience," "this is the perfection of ethical discipline," or "this is the perfection of generosity";
nor grasping at the notion that "this is form," "these are feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness";
nor grasping at the notion that "this is the sense base of the eye," or "these are the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind."
"This is the sense-base of form; these are the sense-bases of sound, odor, taste, tangible objects, and mental phenomena.
This is the eye-element; these are the elements of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
This is the element of form; these are the elements of sound, odor, taste, tangible objects, and mental phenomena."
This is the eye-consciousness element; these are the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-consciousness elements.
This is eye-contact; these are ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-contact.
These are the various feelings produced with eye-contact as condition; these are the various feelings produced with ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-contact as condition.
"This is the earth element; these are the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements;
this is the causal condition; these are the immediately preceding condition, the object condition, and the dominant condition;
and these are all phenomena produced from conditions."

This is ignorance; this is volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, and old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair.

This is internal emptiness; this is external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, the emptiness of the ultimate truth, the emptiness of conditioned phenomena, the emptiness of unconditioned phenomena, absolute emptiness, the emptiness of the limitless, the emptiness of dispersion, the emptiness of non-alteration, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, the emptiness of self-characteristics, the emptiness of common characteristics, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of non-apprehensibility, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature.

"These are the four foundations of mindfulness; these are the four right endeavors, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path;
this is the noble truth of suffering, and these are the noble truths of its origin, its cessation, and the path;
these are the four dhyānas, and these are the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments."
These are the eight liberations; these are the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative attainments, and the ten totalities;
these are the doors of dhāraṇī; these are the doors of samādhi;
these are the door of liberation through emptiness, and the doors of liberation through signlessness and wishlessness.

This is the Ground of Utmost Joy; this is the Ground of Purity, the Ground of Radiant Light, the Ground of Blazing Wisdom, the Ground of Difficult to Conquer, the Ground of Presence, the Ground of Far-Going, the Ground of Immovability, the Ground of Excellent Intelligence, and the Ground of the Dharma Cloud;
these are the five eyes; these are the six supernormal powers;

these are the ten powers of a Buddha; these are the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
These are the thirty-two marks of a great man; these are the eighty minor marks;
this is the quality of non-forgetfulness; this is the state of constant abiding in equanimity;
this is omniscience; this is the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects.
"This is the fruit of stream-entry; this is the fruit of once-returning, non-returning, and arhatship;
this is the awakening of a pratyekabuddha; this is the conduct of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; this is the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening of all buddhas;
this is an ordinary person; this is a śrāvaka; this is a pratyekabuddha; this is a bodhisattva; this is a tathāgata."

“Śāriputra! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they understand, as it truly is, that the nature of all phenomena is ungraspable; that is to say, the perfection of wisdom is ungraspable, the perfection of meditative concentration is ungraspable, the perfection of diligence is ungraspable, the perfection of patience is ungraspable, the perfection of ethical discipline is ungraspable, and the perfection of generosity is ungraspable;
form is ungraspable, and feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are ungraspable.”
The eye-base is ungraspable; the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-bases are ungraspable.
The form-base is ungraspable; the sound, odor, taste, tangible-object, and mental-object bases are ungraspable.
The eye-element is ungraspable; the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-elements are ungraspable.
The realm of form is ungraspable; the realms of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena are ungraspable.
The realm of eye-consciousness is ungraspable; the realms of ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-consciousness are ungraspable.
Eye-contact is ungraspable; ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact are ungraspable.
The various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition are ungraspable; the various feelings produced with ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact as conditions are ungraspable.
The earth element is ungraspable; the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements are ungraspable.
The causal condition is ungraspable; the immediately preceding condition, the object condition, and the dominant condition are ungraspable.
All phenomena produced from conditions are ungraspable;

ignorance is ungraspable, as are volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, and old age, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair. Inner emptiness is ungraspable;

outer emptiness, inner-and-outer emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, endless emptiness, emptiness of dispersion, emptiness of non-alteration, emptiness of essential nature, emptiness of self-characteristic, emptiness of common characteristic, emptiness of all phenomena, emptiness of the unattainable, emptiness of non-existence, emptiness of intrinsic nature, and emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence are all ungraspable.

The four foundations of mindfulness are ungraspable; the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path are ungraspable;
the noble truth of suffering is ungraspable, and the noble truths of origin, cessation, and the path are ungraspable;
the four dhyānas are ungraspable, and the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments are ungraspable.
The eight liberations are ungraspable; the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative attainments, and the ten totalities are ungraspable;
the doors of dhāraṇī are ungraspable; the doors of samādhi are ungraspable;
the gate of emptiness liberation is ungraspable; and the gates of signlessness and wishlessness liberations are ungraspable.

The Ground of Utmost Joy is ungraspable; the Ground of Purity, the Ground of Radiance, the Ground of Blazing Wisdom, the Ground of Difficult Victory, the Ground of Presence, the Ground of Far-reaching Practice, the Ground of Immovability, the Ground of Excellent Intelligence, and the Ground of the Dharma Cloud are ungraspable.
The five eyes are ungraspable; the six supernormal powers are ungraspable.

The ten powers of a Buddha are ungraspable; the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are ungraspable.
The thirty-two marks of a great man cannot be grasped; the eighty minor marks cannot be grasped;
the quality of non-forgetfulness cannot be grasped; the nature of constant equanimity cannot be grasped;
omniscience cannot be grasped; the knowledge of the paths and the knowledge of all aspects cannot be grasped.
The fruit of stream-entry is ungraspable; the fruits of once-returning, non-returning, and arhatship, as well as the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, are ungraspable.
All the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are ungraspable; the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas is ungraspable.
All ordinary beings are ungraspable; all śrāvakas are ungraspable; all pratyekabuddhas are ungraspable; all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are ungraspable; and all tathāgatas are ungraspable.

“Śāriputra! This perfection of non-appropriation is itself the perfection of non-obstruction; this perfection of non-obstruction is itself the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), in which all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should train.”
Śāriputra! When Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are training in this, they do not even attain "training," much less the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment,
and much less the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā)!
How much more so for attaining the dharmas of a bodhisattva!
How much more so for attaining the dharmas of all buddhas! How much more so for attaining the dharmas of a pratyekabuddha!
How much less could they attain the Dharma of the śrāvakas!
How much less could they attain the Dharma of ordinary beings! Why is this?
Śāriputra! There is not even the slightest dharma that possesses intrinsic nature. Within these dharmas, which have non-nature as their very nature, what is the dharma of an ordinary person?
What is the dharma of a stream-enterer?
What is the dharma of the once-returner?
What is the dharma of the non-returner?
What is the dharma of the arhat?
What are the dharmas of the pratyekabuddhas?
What are the dharmas of the bodhisattvas?
What are the dharmas of the Tathāgatas?
Śāriputra! Since these dharmas are thus unapprehendable, by means of what dharma can a *pudgala* (person) be designated?

Since a *pudgala* is unapprehendable, how can it be said that "this is an ordinary person," "this is a stream-enterer," "this is a once-returner," "this is a non-returner," "this is an arhat," "this is a pratyekabuddha," "this is a bodhisattva mahāsattva," or "this is a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha"?
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!

If all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature and are not at all substantially existent, by virtue of what basis can one discern that 'this is an ordinary person' or 'these are the dharmas of an ordinary person'?"
"This is a stream-enterer; this is the dharma of a stream-enterer.
This is a once-returner; this is the dharma of a once-returner.
This is a non-returner; this is the dharma of a non-returner."
"This is an arhat; this is the dharma of an arhat.
This is a pratyekabuddha; this is the dharma of a pratyekabuddha.
This is a bodhisattva mahāsattva; this is the dharma of a bodhisattva mahāsattva."
"This is the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha; this is the Dharma of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
The Buddha said to Śāriputra: "What do you think?"
"Do those foolish, ordinary worldlings grasp at form as being truly existent, and feeling, perception, mental formations,
and consciousness as being truly existent? Śāriputra replied, "No!"
"No, World-Honored One! No, Sugata!"
"It is only because of their perversion that foolish, ordinary worldlings hold such a view.
"Śāriputra, do the sense bases of the eye, and the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, truly exist in the way that foolish, ordinary worldlings grasp them?"
"No, World-Honored One! No!"
“Sugata! It is only because of their delusions and perversions that foolish ordinary beings have such attachments. “Śāriputra!”
“Do the sense bases of form, and the sense bases of sound, odor, taste, tangibles, and mental phenomena exist as real entities, just as foolish ordinary beings cling to them? “No, they do not.”
"No, World-Honored One! No, Sugata!"
"It is only because of their perversion that foolish ordinary worldlings have such attachments.
"Śāriputra, do the eye-element,
the ear-element, the nose-element, the tongue-element, the body-element, and the mind-element truly exist in the way that foolish ordinary worldlings cling to them?"
"No, World-Honored One! No!"
“Sugata! It is only because of their perversions that foolish, ordinary worldlings have such attachments. “Śāriputra!”
“Is it as the foolish, ordinary worldlings cling to it—that there is a truly existent form-element, and truly existent sound, odor, taste, tangible-object, and mental-object elements? “No, sir!”
"No, World-Honored One! No, Sugata!"
"It is only because of the perverted views of foolish, ordinary worldlings that such attachments exist.
Śāriputra, do the eye-consciousness element and the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-consciousness elements truly exist in the way that foolish, ordinary worldlings cling to them?"
"No, World-Honored One! No!"
“Sugata! It is only because of their perversions that foolish ordinary beings have such attachments. “Śāriputra!”
"Do you hold that there is a real eye-contact, and real ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact, as do the foolish commoners? "No, sir."
“World-Honored One! No, indeed! Sugata!”
"It is only because of their inverted views that foolish, ordinary worldlings harbor such attachments. "Śāriputra,

do those feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition truly exist, and do those feelings produced with ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact as conditions truly exist, in the manner that foolish, ordinary worldlings cling to them?"
"No, World-Honored One! No!"
“Sugata! It is only because of their inversions that foolish ordinary worldlings have such attachments. “Śāriputra!”
"Do you hold that there is a truly existent earth element, and truly existent water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements, as do the foolish commoners? "No, sir!"
"No, World-Honored One! No, Sugata!"
"It is only because of their perversity that foolish, ordinary worldlings have such attachments. "Śāriputra!
Are there actually causal conditions, actually immediate conditions, objective conditions, and dominant conditions, as these foolish, ordinary worldlings cling to them?"
"No, World-Honored One! No!"
“Sugata! It is only because of their perversions that foolish ordinary beings have such attachments. “Śāriputra!”
“Are these phenomena that truly exist and arise from conditions as they are grasped by foolish ordinary beings? “No,
World-Honored One!”
"No, Sugata! It is only due to the perversions of foolish, ordinary worldlings that such an attachment exists."

“Śāriputra, do ignorance, formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, existence, birth, and old age, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair truly exist in reality, just as foolish ordinary worldlings grasp them to be?”
"No, World-Honored One! No!"
“Sugata! It is only due to the perversions of foolish, ordinary worldlings that such a grasping exists. “Śāriputra!”

Is it as the foolish, ordinary worldlings cling to them—that the perfection of generosity truly exists, and that the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom truly exist?
"No, World-Honored One! No!"
“Sugata! It is only due to the perversions of foolish, ordinary worldlings that such a grasping exists. “Śāriputra!”

Do foolish common beings cling to the idea that internal emptiness truly exists, and that external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, endless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, non-altering emptiness, essential emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common-characteristic emptiness, the emptiness of all dharmas, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence truly exist?
"No, World-Honored One! No!"
“Sugata! It is only because of their perversions that foolish ordinary beings have such attachments. “Śāriputra!”

Are there truly four foundations of mindfulness, truly four right efforts, four bases of power, five faculties, five powers, seven factors of enlightenment, and eight branches of the noble path, as they are grasped by foolish ordinary beings?
"No, World-Honored One! No!"
“Sugata! It is only because of their perversions that foolish ordinary beings have such attachments. “Śāriputra!”

"Is it as those foolish ordinary worldlings cling to them—that there truly exists the noble truth of suffering, and that there truly exist the noble truths of origin, cessation, and the path? "No, sir."
“World-Honored One! No, indeed! Sugata!”
"It is only because of the perverted views of foolish, ordinary worldlings that such attachments exist.
"Śāriputra, do the four dhyānas,
the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments actually exist in the way that foolish, ordinary worldlings grasp them?"
"No, World-Honored One! No!"
“Sugata! It is only because of their perversions that foolish ordinary worldlings have such attachments. “Śāriputra!”
Do the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities exist as real entities, just as foolish ordinary beings cling to them?
"No, World-Honored One! No!"
“Sugata! It is only because of the perversions of foolish, ordinary worldlings that such a grasping exists. “Śāriputra!”
"Are the gateways of dhāraṇī and the gateways of samādhi truly existent, as they are grasped by foolish ordinary beings? "No,
World-Honored One!"
"No, Sugata! It is only due to the perversion of foolish, ordinary worldlings that such a grasping exists."

“Śāriputra! Are the gateways to liberation of emptiness, the gateways to liberation of signlessness, and the gateways to liberation of wishlessness truly existent in the way that foolish, ordinary worldlings cling to them?”
"No, World-Honored One! No!"
“Sugata! It is only because of their perversions that foolish ordinary worldlings have such attachments. “Śāriputra!”

Do you hold that the Ground of Utmost Joy exists as a real entity, and that the Ground of Freedom from Defilement, the Ground of Radiant Light, the Ground of Blazing Wisdom, the Ground of Extreme Difficulty to Conquer, the Ground of Manifestation, the Ground of Far-Going, the Ground of Immovability, the Ground of Excellent Intelligence, and the Ground of Dharma Clouds exist as real entities, just as foolish ordinary beings do?
"No, World-Honored One! No!"
“Sugata! It is only due to the perversion of foolish, ordinary worldlings that such a grasping exists. “Śāriputra!”
“Are there truly five eyes and truly six supernormal powers, as the foolish commoners and ordinary worldlings cling to them? “No,
World-Honored One!”
"No, Sugata! It is only by reason of their perversion that foolish, ordinary worldlings have such a grasping."

“Śāriputra! Do the ten powers of a Buddha truly exist? Do the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha truly exist, in the way that foolish ordinary beings cling to them?”
"No, World-Honored One! No!"
“Sugata! It is only due to the perversions of foolish, ordinary worldlings that such a grasping exists. “Śāriputra!”
“Are the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty minor marks truly existent, as they are grasped by foolish ordinary beings? “No, sir.”
"No, World-Honored One! No, Sugata!"
"It is only because of their inverted views that foolish, ordinary worldlings hold such attachments. "Śāriputra!
Is there truly a state of non-forgetfulness, and is there truly a nature of constant equanimity, as these foolish, ordinary worldlings cling to them?"
"No, World-Honored One! No!"
“Sugata! It is only due to the perversions of foolish, ordinary worldlings that such a grasping exists. “Śāriputra!”
“Is there truly an omniscience, truly a knowledge of the paths, and truly a knowledge of all aspects, as foolish ordinary beings grasp them to be? “No, indeed!”
"No, World-Honored One! No, Sugata!"
"It is only because of the perverted views of foolish, ordinary worldlings that such attachments exist.
Śāriputra, do the fruit of stream-entry,
the fruits of once-returner, non-returner, and arhatship, as well as the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, truly exist in the way that foolish, ordinary worldlings cling to them?"
"No, World-Honored One! No!"
“Sugata! It is only due to the perversions of foolish, ordinary worldlings that such an attachment exists. “Śāriputra!”

Is there truly an existence of all the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, and is there truly an existence of the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas, as foolish ordinary beings grasp them to be?
"No, World-Honored One! No!"
“Sugata! It is only because of their perversions that foolish ordinary worldlings have such attachments. “Śāriputra!”

Do ordinary worldlings truly exist? Do stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, arhats, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, and tathāgatas, arhats, perfectly enlightened ones truly exist, as they are grasped by foolish ordinary worldlings?
"No, World-Honored One! No!"
“Sugata! It is only because of the perversity of foolish ordinary beings that such an attachment exists.
The Buddha said:

“Śāriputra! Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practicing the perfection of wisdom with skillful means, although they observe that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature and are entirely non-existent, nevertheless aspire toward unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment by relying on conventional truth. For the sake of all sentient beings, they proclaim it in various ways, enabling them to attain correct understanding and remain free from perversion.”

The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Scroll 391. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Part One: Chapter Seventy-one, "Maturing Sentient Beings," Section Three. The Venerable Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”

How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, employ skillful means such that, by the power of these skillful means, although they observe that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature and are not at all substantially real, they nevertheless set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment according to conventional truth, and extensively proclaim it to sentient beings in various ways so that they may attain correct understanding and remain free from inversion?
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

“When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom with skillful means, it means that they do not perceive even the slightest real dharma in which they might abide. Because they abide therein, there would be obstruction; because of obstruction, there would be regression; because of regression, the mind becomes weak; and because the mind is weak, laziness arises.”

“Śāriputra! Because all phenomena are entirely devoid of substantial reality, being without self or what belongs to a self, and because they take non-existence as their intrinsic nature—being by nature empty and quiescent, and empty and quiescent in their own characteristics—there are only the deluded and inverted foolish commoners who cling to the aggregate of form, and cling to the aggregates of feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness;
who cling to the sense base of the eye, and cling to the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.”
They cling to the sphere of form; they cling to the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental objects.
They cling to the eye-element; they cling to the elements of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
They cling to the element of form; they cling to the elements of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental objects.
They cling to the eye-consciousness element; they cling to the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-consciousness elements.
They cling to eye-contact; they cling to ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-contact.
They cling to the various feelings produced with eye-contact as condition; they cling to the various feelings produced with ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-contact as conditions.
They cling to the earth element, and they cling to the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements;
they cling to causes and conditions, and they cling to the immediately preceding condition, the object condition, and the dominant condition;
they cling to all phenomena that arise from conditions.

They cling to ignorance; they cling to volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, and old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair.
They cling to the perfection of generosity; they cling to the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom.

They cling to internal emptiness; they cling to external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, endless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, non-alteration emptiness, essential nature emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common characteristic emptiness, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature.

They cling to the four foundations of mindfulness; they cling to the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path.
They cling to the noble truth of suffering; they cling to the noble truths of origination, cessation, and the path.
They are attached to the four dhyānas; they are attached to the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments;
they are attached to the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities;
they are attached to the doors of dhāraṇī and the doors of samādhi.
They cling to the gate of liberation of emptiness; they cling to the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness;

they cling to the Ground of Extreme Joy; they cling to the Ground of Purity, the Ground of Radiance, the Ground of Blazing Wisdom, the Ground of Difficult Victory, the Ground of Presence, the Ground of Far-Going, the Ground of Immovability, the Ground of Excellent Intelligence, and the Ground of the Dharma Cloud;
they cling to the five eyes; and they cling to the six supernormal powers.

They cling to the ten powers of a Buddha; they cling to the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
they cling to the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, they cling to the eighty minor marks;
they cling to the quality of non-forgetfulness, and they cling to the nature of constant abiding in equanimity.
They cling to all-knowledge; they cling to the knowledge of the paths and the knowledge of all aspects;
they cling to the fruit of stream-entry, and they cling to the fruits of once-returning, non-returning, arhatship, and pratyekabuddha-enlightenment;
they cling to all the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, and they cling to the unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas.
They cling to ordinary worldlings; they cling to stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, arhats, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, and tathāgatas, arhats, samyaksaṃbuddhas.

“Śāriputra! For this reason, all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas perceive that all phenomena are entirely devoid of substantial reality; they are without self or what belongs to a self, having non-existence as their intrinsic nature, and being by nature empty and quiescent, empty and quiescent in their own characteristics. Practicing the perfection of wisdom, they establish themselves like illusionists and preach the Dharma to sentient beings: to those who are stingy and greedy, they preach giving, so that they may cultivate the perfection of giving;
to those who violate the precepts, they preach pure morality, so that they may cultivate the perfection of morality.”
To those who are angry and resentful, they preach patience, causing them to cultivate the perfection of patience;
to those who are indolent, they preach diligence, causing them to cultivate the perfection of diligence;
to those who are distracted, they preach meditative concentration, causing them to cultivate the perfection of meditative concentration.
If there are those who are deluded, he teaches them the Prajñāpāramitā, causing them to cultivate the perfection of wisdom. "Śāriputra!

Having established sentient beings in the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, that bodhisattva mahāsattva further proclaims for them the sublime, noble Dharma capable of bringing about transcendence from birth and death."

All classes of sentient beings, relying upon this to practice and train, may attain the fruit of stream-entry, or the fruit of once-returning, or the fruit of non-returning, or the fruit of arhatship; or they may attain the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, or enter the stage of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, or attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), why are they not called those who have something to apprehend?”

That is to say, although sentient beings do not truly exist, he causes them to abide in the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom; furthermore, he proclaims for them the sublime noble dharmas capable of bringing about transcendence from birth and death, causing some to attain the fruit of stream-entry, some to attain the fruits of once-returner, non-returner, or arhatship, some to attain the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, some to enter the stage of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, or some to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they do not apprehend any sentient beings as having intrinsic existence."

Why is this? Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they do not perceive even the slightest substantial reality of sentient beings; there are only sentient beings as conventional designations.
Śāriputra! When these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom, they abide in the two truths and proclaim the true Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings.
What are the two truths?
They are the conventional truth and the ultimate truth. Śāriputra!

Although within the two truths neither sentient beings nor the designation of "sentient beings" can be apprehended, yet bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practicing the perfection of wisdom employ skillful means to proclaim the essential teachings for the sake of all sentient beings. When these classes of sentient beings have heard this Dharma, they do not even apprehend a self in the present life, let alone attain the fruit of realization they seek!
In this way, Śāriputra,

when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, although they employ skillful means to proclaim the sublime Dharma for the sake of sentient beings, causing them to cultivate correct practice and attain the fruits of realization, their mind apprehends nothing at all regarding those beings.
The Venerable Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

These bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are true bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; although they do not apprehend a single nature, nor a diverse nature, nor a collective nature, nor a distinct nature among all phenomena, they nevertheless don these great armor-like robes of merit.”

By donning such armor of great merit, one does not appear in the realm of desire, does not appear in the realm of form, does not appear in the formless realm, does not appear in the conditioned realm, and does not appear in the unconditioned realm.

Although one transforms sentient beings so that they may be liberated from the three realms, yet regarding sentient beings, nothing at all is apprehended, nor is even the designation "sentient being" apprehended.

Because the designation "sentient being" cannot be apprehended, there is neither bondage nor liberation; because there is neither bondage nor liberation, there is neither defilement nor purity; because there is neither defilement nor purity, the distinctions between the various realms of existence (*gati*) cannot be discerned; because the distinctions between the various realms of existence cannot be discerned, there is neither karma nor affliction (*kleśa*); and because there is neither karma nor affliction, there is also no fruition (*vipāka-phala*). Since there is no fruition, how could there be a self or sentient beings who transmigrate through the various realms and manifest the manifold distinctions within the three worlds?
The Buddha told Śāriputra: “So it is! So it is!”
"It is as you have said, Śāriputra!

If there were any class of sentient beings that existed previously and later ceased to exist, the Bodhisattva and the Tathāgata would be at fault; likewise, if the cycle of birth and death within the various realms of existence existed previously and later ceased to exist, then the Bodhisattva and the Tathāgata would also be at fault."
The principle that what did not previously exist comes into being later is also untenable.
Therefore, Śāriputra, whether a Tathāgata appears in the world or does not appear, the nature of phenomena remains eternally abiding and never undergoes change; for...
The dharma-nature, dharma-realm, dharma-abiding, dharma-fixity, suchness, the limit of reality, non-falsity,
and non-alteration of all phenomena are like space; herein there is no self,
no sentient being, no life-principle, no born being, no nourisher, and no person.
There is no person (pudgala), no mind-born being (manuja), no youth (māṇava); there is no agent, no instigator of action;
no one who arises, no one who causes to arise; no experiencer, no one who causes to experience;
no knower, no one who causes to know; no seer, no one who causes to see.
How much more so when there is form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness!
When there is the sense-base of the eye, and the sense-bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind!
There is the sphere of visible forms; there are the spheres of sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena!
There is the eye element; there are the elements of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind!
There is the element of form; there are the elements of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental objects!
There is the element of eye-consciousness; there are the elements of ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-consciousness!
There is eye-contact; there is ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact!
There are feelings produced with eye-contact as condition; there are feelings produced with ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact as condition!
There is the earth element, and the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements!
There are the various dependent originations, there are dependently arisen phenomena, and there are the factors of dependent origination!
Since these aforementioned phenomena do not exist, how could there be the cycle of birth and death within the various realms of existence?
Since the cycle of birth and death within the various realms cannot be found, how could there be the maturing of sentient beings so as to bring them to liberation?
They exist only as conventional designations.

"Śāriputra, because the intrinsic nature of these phenomena is entirely empty, when bodhisattva mahāsattvas have heard this truth as it is from the Buddhas of the past, they set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment in order to liberate sentient beings from their inverted attachments. At the time of setting forth, they do not form such thoughts:"

"I have already attained, or shall attain, this Dharma, so as to cause those sentient beings who have already been delivered, or shall be delivered, from the manifold sufferings of birth and death to which they are attached. "Śāriputra!

This bodhisattva mahāsattva, in order to liberate sentient beings from their inverted attachments, dons the armor of merit and the great vow as adornment; with courageous and right diligence, they have no regard for self-interest or parsimony, never retreating from unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and never giving rise to hesitation regarding enlightenment, wondering:
"Shall I realize it, or shall I not realize it?"
He constantly reflects thus:

"I shall certainly realize the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment that I seek, and bring true benefit to all sentient beings; that is to say, I shall cause them to be liberated from the suffering of birth and death as they wander through the various realms of existence due to delusion, error, and inversion."

"Śāriputra! Although these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas liberate sentient beings from the delusions, perversions, and the cycle of birth and death within the various realms of existence, they do so without apprehending anything; it is only according to worldly convention that such a thing is said to exist."

“Śāriputra! Suppose a skilled illusionist or his apprentice, using the art of the Indra-net, conjures forth immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of sentient beings; he then further conjures various kinds of exquisite food and drink and causes all those conjured beings to be fully satisfied. Having performed this deed, he joyfully proclaims:
‘I have already obtained a vast accumulation of merit.’”
"Śāriputra! What do you think? Would such a magician or his disciple actually cause sentient beings to become satiated?"
Śāriputra said: “No, World-Honored One!”
"No, Sugata! The Buddha said to Śāriputra:

“Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are also like this: from the first production of the thought of enlightenment, for the sake of delivering all sentient beings, they practice the perfection of generosity; they practice the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom;

they abide in internal emptiness, and they abide in external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, non-altering emptiness, essential emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common-characteristic emptiness, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature.”

They practice the four foundations of mindfulness; they practice the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path;
they abide in the noble truth of suffering, and they abide in the noble truths of its origin, its cessation, and the path;
they practice the four dhyānas, and they practice the four immeasurables and the four formless absorptions.
They practice the eight liberations; they practice the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive concentrations, and the ten totalities;
they practice the gates of dhāraṇī, and they practice the gates of samādhi;
they practice the gate of the liberation of emptiness, and they practice the gates of the liberations of signlessness and wishlessness.

They practice the Ground of Extreme Joy; they practice the Ground of Freedom from Defilement, the Ground of Radiant Light, the Ground of Blazing Wisdom, the Ground of Supreme Difficulty to Conquer, the Ground of Presence, the Ground of Far-Going, the Ground of Immovability, the Ground of Excellent Intelligence, and the Ground of the Cloud of Dharma.
They practice the five eyes; they practice the six supernormal powers.

They practice the ten powers of a Buddha; they practice the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
They practice the thirty-two marks of a great man; they practice the eighty secondary characteristics;
they practice the quality of non-forgetfulness; they practice the constant abiding in equanimity;
they practice all-knowledge; and they practice the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects.
They bring to perfection the Great Path to Bodhi of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, maturing sentient beings and purifying Buddha-fields. "Śāriputra!
Although Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas perform these deeds, they apprehend neither sentient beings nor any phenomena whatsoever, and they do not form such thoughts:"
“I shall tame such classes of sentient beings by means of this Dharma.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying,
“World-Honored One!”
What is the great path to enlightenment of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas?
By practicing this path, how do the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas employ skillful means to bring sentient beings to maturity and purify buddha-fields?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"From the first production of the thought of awakening, all that the bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice—the perfection of generosity; the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom;

the inner emptiness they practice; and the outer emptiness, inner-and-outer emptiness, emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, endless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, non-alteration emptiness, essential nature emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common characteristic emptiness, emptiness of all phenomena, emptiness of the unapprehendable, emptiness of non-existence, emptiness of intrinsic nature, and emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature;"

The practice of the four foundations of mindfulness; the practice of the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path;
the practice of the noble truth of suffering, and the practice of the noble truths of origin, cessation, and the path;
the practice of the four dhyānas, and the practice of the four immeasurables and the four formless absorptions.
They practice the eight liberations; they practice the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative attainments, and the ten totalities;
they practice the doors of dhāraṇī, and they practice the doors of samādhi;
they practice the door of the liberation of emptiness, and they practice the doors of the liberations of signlessness and wishlessness.

The spheres of activity of the Ground of Utmost Joy; the spheres of activity of the Ground of Purity, the Ground of Radiant Light, the Ground of Blazing Wisdom, the Ground of Extreme Difficulty to Conquer, the Ground of Manifestation, the Ground of Far-Going, the Ground of Immovability, the Ground of Excellent Intelligence, and the Ground of the Cloud of Dharma;
the spheres of activity of the five eyes; the spheres of activity of the six supernormal powers;

the spheres of activity of the ten powers of a Buddha; the spheres of activity of the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
The practice of the quality of non-forgetfulness, the practice of constant abiding in equanimity;

the practice of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the practice of the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), as well as other immeasurable and boundless Buddha-dharmas—these are all the Great Path to Bodhi for the bodhisattva mahāsattva.

When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice this path, they employ skillful means to bring sentient beings to maturity and to adorn and purify buddha-fields, yet they harbor no conceptual notions of "sentient beings" or "buddha-fields."
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice the perfection of generosity and, through skillful means, bring sentient beings to maturity?”
The Buddha said to Subhūti:

"There are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, when practicing the perfection of generosity, employ skillful means; they personally practice generosity and also encourage others to practice generosity, earnestly instructing and admonishing them, saying:
'O sons of good family!'"
Do not be attached to giving; if you are attached to giving, you will undergo further rebirths, and through these successive rebirths, you will experience immeasurable, fierce, and great suffering.
"O sons of good family!

In the ultimate truth (paramārthasatya), there is no giving, no giver, no recipient, no gift, and no fruit of giving. All such phenomena are empty by their very nature (prakṛti-śūnya). Within this emptiness of intrinsic nature, there is nothing that can be grasped; even the emptiness of all phenomena cannot be grasped."

"In this way, Subhūti, when bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the perfection of generosity, although they personally practice giving toward sentient beings and also exhort others to give, they do not apprehend the gift, the giver, the recipient, the object given, or the fruit of the gift. Such a perfection of generosity is called the 'perfection of non-apprehension.'"

When this bodhisattva mahāsattva finds nothing to be apprehended among these phenomena, through skillful means he is able to transform sentient beings, causing them to attain the fruit of stream-entry, or the fruit of once-returning, or the fruit of non-returning, or the fruit of arhatship, or the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, or to proceed toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Thus it is, Subhūti!
When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of generosity, they bring sentient beings to maturity through the dharma of generosity, causing them to obtain benefit and happiness.

“Subhūti! This bodhisattva mahāsattva personally practices the perfection of generosity, encourages others to practice the perfection of generosity, correctly extols the dharma of practicing the perfection of generosity, and joyfully praises those who practice the perfection of generosity.”

"Subhūti! Having practiced such great giving as this, these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas will be born into the common lot of a great kṣatriya clan, or into the common lot of a great brāhmaṇa clan, or into the common lot of a great householder clan, or into the common lot of a great merchant clan; or they will become minor kings with sovereign wealth and power over small territories, or become great kings with sovereign wealth and power over large territories, or become universal monarchs (cakravartin) with sovereign wealth and power over the four continents."

“Subhūti! These bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, having been born in such noble and honorable states, gather in all sentient beings through the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*). What are these four?
First, giving; second, kind speech;
third, beneficial conduct.

Fourth is *samānārthatā* (common purpose). When these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas gather sentient beings through the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), they first instruct sentient beings to abide in generosity (*dāna*). Thereby, they gradually cause them to abide in ethical discipline (*śīla*), patience (*kṣānti*), diligence (*vīrya*), meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), and wisdom (*prajñā*). Furthermore, they cause them to abide in the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), and the four formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*). They further cause them to abide in the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*), the four bases of power (*ṛddhipāda*), the five faculties (*indriya*), the five powers (*bala*), the seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), and the eightfold noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*). Finally, they cause them to abide in the samādhi of emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*), the samādhi of signlessness (*animitta-samādhi*), and the samādhi of wishlessness (*apraṇihita-samādhi*).

Having established all sentient beings in such wholesome dharmas as these, this bodhisattva mahāsattva causes them either to enter the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*) and attain the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, or the fruit of arhatship;
or causes them to enter the state of right determination and gradually realize pratyekabuddha enlightenment;
or causes them to enter the state of right determination and gradually train in the stages of a bodhisattva, swiftly proceeding toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.
He further addressed them, saying:
"O noble sons! You should generate great vows to swiftly proceed toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and bring about the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings."

All phenomena to which sentient beings are attached lack any intrinsic nature; they are merely said to exist due to inverted and false conceptualization. Therefore, you should always be diligent in severing your own inversions and should likewise instruct others to sever their inversions; you should liberate yourselves from birth and death and should likewise instruct others to liberate themselves from birth and death; you should attain great benefit for yourselves and should likewise instruct others to attain great benefit.

“Subhūti! All bodhisattva mahāsattvas should constantly practice the perfection of generosity in this manner. By means of this perfection of generosity, from the first generation of the mind of awakening until the ultimate end, they do not fall into the evil destinies; rather, for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, they are frequently reborn in the human realm as universal monarchs (cakravartin).”
Why is this? Because one obtains such fruits according to the power of the seeds sown.
That is to say, when that bodhisattva was a wheel-turning monarch, upon seeing a beggar approach, he would think:

"For what purpose did I transmigrate through birth and death to become a Wheel-Turning King? Is it not that I dwell within birth and death for the sake of benefiting and bringing happiness to sentient beings, and that I have received this supreme fruit through no other cause?"
Having formed this thought, he said to the beggar:
"Whatever you require, I shall give it to you; when you take the goods, do so as if taking your own property, and harbor no other thoughts."

Why is this? It is for the sake of securing benefit and happiness for you all that I have taken up this body and accumulated these material goods; therefore, these goods belong to you. Take them as you please—whether for your own use or to bestow upon others—and do not harbor any doubt or hesitation.
When this bodhisattva mahāsattva thus feels compassion for all sentient beings, their objectless great compassion (anālambana-mahākaruṇā) is swiftly brought to fulfillment.

Because this great compassion is swiftly fulfilled, although they constantly bring benefit and happiness to immeasurable sentient beings, they apprehend no sentient beings whatsoever, nor do they apprehend any superior fruit obtained; they are able to know it as it truly is:
"It is merely by means of conceptual designations and conventional discourse that the matter of bringing benefit and happiness to sentient beings is established."
Furthermore, one knows it as it truly is:
"All things that are conceptually designated are like echoes; although they appear to exist, they lack reality.
By means of this, one grasps nothing at all regarding phenomena.

“Subhūti! All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should always practice the perfection of generosity in this way: they should have no stinginess whatsoever toward sentient beings, even to the point of being able to give their own flesh and bones, let alone external possessions which they cannot bear to relinquish!”
"This means that all requisite provisions are gathered to sustain sentient beings, enabling them to swiftly attain liberation from birth, old age, sickness, and death.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
“What are the requisites that gather in all sentient beings and cause them to swiftly attain liberation from birth, old age, sickness, and death?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“They are what are called the requisites of the perfection of giving; and the requisites of the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom.”

Whether it be the requisites of internal emptiness, or the requisites of external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, non-altering emptiness, essential emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common-characteristic emptiness, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature;

whether it be the requisites of the four foundations of mindfulness, or the requisites of the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path;
or whether it be the requisites of the noble truth of suffering, or the requisites of the noble truths of origin, cessation, and the path.
Whether it be the requisites for the four dhyānas, or the requisites for the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments;
whether it be the requisites for the eight liberations, or the requisites for the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities;
or whether it be the requisites for the doors of dhāraṇī, or the requisites for the doors of samādhi.
Whether it be the requisites for the gate of liberation of emptiness, or the requisites for the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness;

whether it be the requisites for the Stage of Extreme Joy, or the requisites for the Stages of Purity, Radiance, Blazing Wisdom, Difficult to Conquer, Presence, Far-Going, Immovability, Good Intelligence, and the Cloud of Dharma;
or whether it be the requisites for the five eyes, or the requisites for the six supernormal powers;

Whether it be the equipment of the ten powers of a Buddha; or the equipment of the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
or the equipment of the quality of non-forgetfulness, or the equipment of the nature of constant dwelling in equanimity;
or the equipment of all-knowledge, or the equipment of the knowledge of the paths and the knowledge of all aspects; [all these are ungraspable.]

Whether it be the requisites for the fruit of stream-entry, or the requisites for the fruits of once-returner, non-returner, and arhatship; or the requisites for the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha;
or the requisites for all the practices of a bodhisattva mahāsattva; or the requisites for the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas.

"Subhūti! These requisites sustain all sentient beings, enabling them to swiftly attain liberation from birth, old age, sickness, and death. Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas always sustain all sentient beings with these various kinds of requisites, causing them to achieve liberation from birth, old age, sickness, and death, thereby attaining great benefit."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When bodhisattva mahāsattvas abide in the perfection of generosity, they personally practice giving and encourage all sentient beings to practice giving. Having done so, if they see sentient beings who have violated the pure precepts, they give rise to deep compassion and say to them:

“You all should receive and uphold the pure precepts; I shall provide you with whatever food and drink, clothing, bedding, dwellings, vehicles, mani-jewels, pearls, lapis lazuli, crystal, sapphire, emerald, gold, silver, jade, conch shells, coral, and other various kinds of precious treasures of great value, as well as incense, flowers, banners, canopies, medicinal requisites for illness, and even all other various necessities of life, giving them to you so that you lack for nothing.”

"Because you lack the necessities of life, you have violated the pure precepts and committed various evil deeds; I shall provide for you whatever necessities you lack, from food and drink to medicine for the treatment of illness, as well as all other things you may be in need of."

Once you have established yourselves in the morality of restraint, you shall gradually be able to bring an end to suffering; you may attain liberation by relying on the Śrāvaka-yāna, or attain liberation by relying on the Pratyekabuddha-yāna, or attain liberation by relying on the Anuttara-yāna.

"Subhūti! This bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling securely in the perfection of generosity, personally upholds pure ethical discipline, encourages others to uphold pure ethical discipline, correctly extols the dharma of upholding pure ethical discipline, and joyfully praises those who uphold pure ethical discipline."
In this way, Subhūti,

bodhisattva mahāsattvas practicing the perfection of generosity exhort all sentient beings to abide in pure ethical discipline, thereby liberating them from birth and death and enabling them to attain supreme benefit and happiness.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
When bodhisattva mahāsattvas abide in the perfection of generosity, they see sentient beings mutually harboring anger and resentment; they give rise to deep compassion and say to them:
'For what reason do you provoke one another with such fury?'"

If you should experience such evil as arising from mutual dependence due to being destitute of anything, you should ask me for it; I shall provide for you. Whatever you require—food and drink, clothing, bedding, dwellings, vehicles, servants, precious jewels, flowers and incense, medicinal requisites for illness, music, banners and canopies, necklaces, lamps, or any other various necessary articles—I shall bestow them all upon you so that you lack nothing.
"You all should not harbor mutual anger or resentment; you should cultivate patience and together give rise to a heart of loving-kindness. Subhūti!
Having established these sentient beings in the perfection of giving and exhorted them to practice patience, that bodhisattva mahāsattva, wishing to make it firm, further addresses them, saying:
"The causes and conditions for anger and resentment have no fixed reality; they all arise from false conceptualization, for the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is empty.
For what reason do you give rise to groundless fury toward unreal matters, reviling one another and inflicting mutual harm with swords, staves, and the like?"

Do not, out of false conceptualization, give rise to groundless anger and create various evil karmas, whereby you will fall into the hells, the animal realm, the realm of hungry ghosts, or other evil states, where you will undergo intense sufferings. Those pains are bitter and poisonous, fierce and sharp, pressing upon body and mind in a way that is most extremely difficult to endure.

Do not, out of attachment to what is not a real entity, give rise to false anger and commit such karmic offenses; because of such karma, it is difficult even to obtain a human body of inferior status, let alone to be born in the time of a Buddha!
"You should all know that a human body is difficult to obtain, an encounter with a Buddha is difficult to meet, and the arising of faith is likewise difficult.

Now that you have attained these conditions, do not lose this favorable opportunity through anger; for if this opportunity is lost, it is difficult to remedy. Therefore, you should not give rise to resentment toward sentient beings, but should instead cultivate patience."

"Subhūti! This bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling securely in the perfection of generosity, personally practices patience, encourages others to practice patience, correctly extols the method of practicing patience, and joyfully praises those who practice patience."
Thus it is, Subhūti!

Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, dwelling securely in the perfection of generosity, exhort all sentient beings to practice patience. Through this, those beings gradually attain liberation by relying on the three vehicles—namely, some attain liberation by relying on the vehicle of the śrāvakas, some by relying on the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas, and some by relying on the Great Vehicle.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
When bodhisattva mahāsattvas abide in the perfection of generosity, they see sentient beings who are physically and mentally indolent; they give rise to deep compassion and address them, saying:
'For what reason do you not apply yourselves with diligence to cultivate the various wholesome dharmas, but instead give way to indolence?'"
He spoke thus: "Because I lack the necessary provisions, I am unable to practice wholesome deeds with single-minded devotion.
The Bodhisattva replied:
"I can provide you with whatever requisites you lack; you should single-mindedly cultivate the dharmas of generosity, pure ethical discipline, patience, and so forth.

At that time, those sentient beings, having obtained the requisites bestowed by this bodhisattva without any deficiency, are able to arouse physical and mental diligence to cultivate all wholesome dharmas and swiftly attain their fulfillment.

Because all wholesome dharmas are brought to fulfillment, they gradually induce the arising of all untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas. Through these untainted dharmas, one may attain the fruit of stream-entry, once-returning, non-returning, or arhatship; or one may obtain the enlightenment of a solitary realizer (*pratyekabuddha*), or enter the stages of a bodhisattva, gradually attaining unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

“Subhūti! This bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling securely in the perfection of generosity, personally practices diligence, encourages others to practice diligence, correctly extols the dharma of practicing diligence, and joyfully praises those who practice diligence.”
In this way, Subhūti, bodhisattva mahāsattvas,
dwelling securely in the perfection of generosity, cause sentient beings to distance themselves from indolence, diligently cultivate all that is wholesome, and swiftly attain liberation.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
When Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas abide in the perfection of giving, they see sentient beings who are distracted and have lost mindfulness; they give rise to deep compassion and say to them:
'For what reason do you not cultivate meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), yet remain distracted, lose mindfulness, and wallow in birth and death (*saṃsāra*)?'"
He replied, "Because I lack the necessary requisites, I am unable to practice meditative concentration.
The Bodhisattva said to him:

"I can provide you with whatever requisites you lack; from this day forward, you should no longer give rise to false discursive thoughts, nor allow yourselves to be distracted by grasping at internal or external objects."
At that time, those sentient beings, having obtained the requisites bestowed by this bodhisattva, were free from any lack;
they were thus able to suppress and sever false discursive thoughts (*vitarka* and *vicāra*) and enter the first dhyāna. Gradually, they further entered the second, third, and fourth dhyānas.
Relying upon these dhyānas, they were further able to give rise to loving-kindness (*maitrī*), compassion (*karuṇā*), and sympathetic joy (*muditā*).

Having relinquished the four divine abodes (brahmavihāra) and relying upon the meditative concentrations (dhyāna) and the immeasurables (apramāṇa), he is further able to gradually enter the four formless attainments (ārūpyasamāpatti).
Once his mind has been tamed and rendered supple through the concentrations, the immeasurables, and the formless attainments, he cultivates the four foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna),
the four right efforts (samyakprahāṇa), the four bases of power (ṛddhipāda), the five faculties (indriya), and the five powers (bala).
The seven factors of enlightenment, the eight branches of the noble path, the gateways to liberation of emptiness,
signlessness, and wishlessness, and various other wholesome dharmas— according to their respective capacities, they yield the fruits of the three vehicles:
that is, some realize the nirvāṇa of a śrāvaka, some realize the nirvāṇa of a pratyekabuddha, and others realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

The Buddha said, “Subhūti! This bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling securely in the perfection of generosity, personally cultivates meditative concentration, encourages others to cultivate meditative concentration, correctly extols the practice of meditative concentration, and joyfully praises those who cultivate meditative concentration.”
In this way, Subhūti, bodhisattva mahāsattvas,

abiding in the perfection of generosity, exhort all sentient beings to distance themselves from distraction and to cultivate the various meditative concentrations, thereby performing great benefit for them.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
When bodhisattva mahāsattvas abide in the perfection of generosity, they see sentient beings who are deluded and inverted, and out of deep compassion, they address them, saying:
'For what reason do you not cultivate wisdom, yet remain deluded and inverted, cycling through birth and death?'"
He said this: "I lack the necessary provisions and am unable to cultivate supreme wisdom.
The Bodhisattva told him:
"I can provide you with whatever requisites you lack; you may accept them.

Once you have brought to perfection the practices of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, and meditative concentration, you should carefully investigate the true nature of all phenomena and practice the perfection of wisdom."
It means that at that time, one should carefully examine whether there is even the slightest dharma that can be apprehended.

That is to say: can a self, a sentient being, a life-principle, a living being, a nourisher, a person, an individual, a mind-born, a youth, an agent, an instigator of action, an originator, an instigator of origination, an experiencer, an instigator of experience, a knower, an instigator of knowledge, a seer, or an instigator of seeing be apprehended?
Whether it be form, or feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness—can these be apprehended?
Whether it be the eye-base, or the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind-base—can these be apprehended?
Whether it be the sphere of form, or the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena—can these be apprehended?
Whether it be the eye-element, or the elements of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind—can these be apprehended?
Can the form element, or the sound, odor, taste, tangible, and mental-object elements, be apprehended?
Can the eye-consciousness element, or the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-consciousness elements, be apprehended?
Can eye-contact be apprehended? Can ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-contact be apprehended?
Can the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition be apprehended? Can the various feelings produced with ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-contact as a condition be apprehended?
Whether it be the earth element, or the water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness elements—can these be apprehended?
Whether it be the causal condition, the immediately preceding condition, the object condition, or the dominant condition—can these be apprehended?
If all phenomena that arise from conditions can be apprehended?

If ignorance, or volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, existence, birth, and old age, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair—can these be apprehended?
Whether it be the desire realm, or the form and formless realms, can they be apprehended?
Whether it be the perfection of generosity, or the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, can they be apprehended?

Whether it be internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, non-alteration emptiness, essential nature emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common characteristic emptiness, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of non-apprehensibility, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, or the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence—can these be apprehended?

Whether it be the four foundations of mindfulness, or the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, or the eightfold noble path—can these be apprehended?
Can the noble truth of suffering, or the noble truths of origin, cessation, and the path, be apprehended?
Can the four dhyānas, or the four immeasurables, or the four formless attainments, be apprehended?
Are the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative attainments, and the ten totalities obtainable?
Are the doors of dhāraṇī and the doors of samādhi obtainable?
Can the gate of liberation of emptiness, or the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness, be apprehended?

Can the Stage of Extreme Joy, or the Stage of Purity, the Radiant Stage, the Blazing Wisdom Stage, the Extremely Difficult to Conquer Stage, the Manifest Stage, the Far-Reaching Stage, the Immovable Stage, the Stage of Excellent Intelligence, or the Cloud of Dharma Stage, be apprehended?
Can the five eyes or the six supernormal powers be attained?

Can the ten powers of a Buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, or the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha be attained?
If there is the quality of non-forgetfulness, or the state of constant abiding in equanimity, can these be apprehended?
If there is omniscience, or the knowledge of the paths, or the knowledge of all aspects, can these be apprehended?
Can the fruit of stream-entry, or the fruits of once-returning, non-returning, and arhatship, or pratyekabuddha-enlightenment, be attained?
Can the conduct of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, or the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas, be attained?

“Once those sentient beings have obtained all necessary provisions without deficiency, they rely upon the Bodhisattva’s words to first cultivate generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, and meditative concentration; having brought these to perfection, they further scrutinize the true nature of all phenomena and practice the perfection of wisdom.”

When examining them closely, as previously stated, the true nature of all phenomena is found to be unapprehendable; because it is unapprehendable, there is no attachment; and because there is no attachment, one does not perceive even the slightest phenomenon as arising or ceasing, or as being defiled or purified.
When they find nothing to be apprehended among all phenomena, they give rise to no conceptual discrimination regarding anything whatsoever; that is to say, they do not discriminate:
"This is hell," "this is the animal realm," "this is the realm of hungry ghosts," "this is the asuras," "this is a human," or "this is a deva"; nor do they discriminate:
"this is the observance of precepts" or "this is the violation of precepts."
"This is an ordinary person; this is a noble one; this is a stream-enterer;
this is a once-returner; this is a non-returner; this is an arhat; this is a pratyekabuddha; this is a bodhisattva; this is a Tathāgata;
this is a conditioned phenomenon; this is an unconditioned phenomenon."
By virtue of such non-conceptuality, they gradually realize the nirvāṇa of the three vehicles as appropriate—namely, the Śrāvaka vehicle, the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, or the Unsurpassed Vehicle.

“Subhūti! This bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling securely in the perfection of generosity, personally cultivates wisdom, encourages others to cultivate wisdom, correctly extols the practice of the dharma of wisdom, and joyfully praises those who cultivate wisdom.”
In this way, Subhūti,
bodhisattva mahāsattvas, abiding in the perfection of generosity, exhort all sentient beings to practice wisdom, causing them to obtain supreme benefit and peace.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, dwelling securely in the perfection of generosity, personally practice the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom; they also encourage others to practice generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom. Having done so, they further see sentient beings wandering through the various realms of existence, undergoing immeasurable suffering without attaining liberation. Desiring to free them from the suffering of birth and death, they first benefit them with various material requisites, and subsequently gather them in through skillful means by means of the supramundane, untainted dharmas."
Once those sentient beings have obtained the necessary provisions and lack nothing, their bodies and minds become courageous and resolute, enabling them to abide in internal emptiness,
external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, the emptiness of the ultimate truth, the emptiness of conditioned phenomena,
the emptiness of unconditioned phenomena, absolute emptiness, the emptiness of the limitless, the emptiness of dispersion, and the emptiness of non-existence...
They are also able to cultivate the emptiness of change, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, the emptiness of self-characteristics,
the emptiness of common characteristics, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of non-apprehensibility, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature,
and the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence; as well as the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, and the five powers.

...the seven factors of enlightenment and the eight branches of the noble path; they are also able to abide in the noble truth of suffering, the noble truths of its origin, its cessation, and the path;
they are also able to cultivate the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments;
and they are also able to cultivate the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities.
Abiding therein, they are also able to cultivate the gateways of dhāraṇī and the gateways of samādhi;
they are also able to cultivate the gateway of liberation of emptiness, the gateway of liberation of signlessness, and the gateway of liberation of wishlessness;
and they are also able to cultivate the Ground of Utmost Joy, the Ground of Purity, the Ground of Radiance, the Ground of Blazing Wisdom, the Ground of Difficult Victory, and the Ground of Presence.
The Stage of Far-Reaching, the Immovable Stage, the Stage of Excellent Intelligence, and the Cloud of Dharma Stage;
they are also able to cultivate the five eyes and the six supernormal powers, and they are also able to cultivate the ten powers of a Buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges,
great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
