The Dharma can also cultivate the quality of non-forgetfulness and the state of constant equanimity; it can also cultivate all-knowledge (*sarvajñā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Those sentient beings, being sustained by untainted dharmas (*anāsrava-dharma*), are liberated from birth and death. "Subhūti!

This bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling securely in the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*), personally practices various sublime untainted dharmas, encourages others to practice various sublime untainted dharmas, correctly extols the practice of various sublime untainted dharmas, and joyfully praises those who practice various sublime untainted dharmas."
Thus it is, Subhūti!

All bodhisattva mahāsattvas, dwelling securely in the perfection of generosity, gather in sentient beings through untainted dharmas, causing them to escape birth and death and attain supreme benefit and happiness.

The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Scroll Three Hundred and Ninety-Two. Translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Part One: Chapter Seventy-One on Maturing Sentient Beings, Section Four. "Furthermore, Subhūti!..."

When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas abide in the perfection of generosity, they see sentient beings who are without refuge, beset by many sufferings and lacking basic necessities; they give rise to deep compassion and comfort them, saying:
"I can act as your refuge and enable you to be liberated from the things that cause you suffering."

"Whatever you require—whether food, drink, clothing, bedding, vehicles, dwellings, incense, flowers, servants, precious jewels, music, lamps, ornaments, medicine, or any other various necessary requisites—seek them all according to your wishes; do not have any doubts or difficulties. I shall grant you whatever you ask for, so that you may enjoy benefit and happiness throughout the long night."
When you receive the gifts I bestow, accept them as if they were your own property and do not harbor thoughts of them being someone else's. Why is this?
It is because throughout the long night, I have accumulated these wealth and goods solely for the sake of securing your benefit and happiness.
Now, with minds free from hesitation, you should accept these goods as you please.
Having accepted them, you should first properly utilize them yourselves to cultivate various wholesome dharmas;
subsequently, you should give these items to all sentient beings so that they too may cultivate goodness—namely, leading them to practice generosity, pure ethical discipline, patience, and diligence.
Dhyāna and the perfection of wisdom also cause one to abide in internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness,
the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness,
absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, non-alteration emptiness, and the emptiness of intrinsic nature.

They also cause them to practice emptiness, the emptiness of self-characteristics, the emptiness of common characteristics, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of non-apprehensibility, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence;
as well as the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, and the seven factors of enlightenment.
...the eight branches of the noble path; they also cause them to dwell securely in the noble truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path;
they also cause them to practice the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments;
and they also cause them to practice the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities.
They also cause them to practice the gateways of dhāraṇī and the gateways of samādhi;
they also cause them to practice the gateway of emptiness among the gates of liberation, as well as the signless and wishless gates of liberation;

and they also cause them to practice the Ground of Utmost Joy, the Ground of Purity, the Ground of Radiant Light, the Ground of Blazing Wisdom, the Ground of Difficult Victory, and the Ground of Presence.
...the Dūraṃgamā-bhūmi, the Acalā-bhūmi, the Sādhumatī-bhūmi, and the Dharmameghā-bhūmi;

they also cause them to practice the five eyes and the six supernormal powers, and they also cause them to practice the ten powers of a Buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges,
great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen [unique qualities of a Buddha].
The Buddha’s unique qualities also cause them to practice the quality of non-forgetfulness and the state of constant equanimity;
they also cause them to practice all-knowledge, the knowledge of the paths, and the knowledge of all aspects.

"Subhūti! After these bodhisattva mahāsattvas have thus instructed sentient beings, they cause them to further cultivate various untainted dharmas (*anāsrava-dharma*) according to what is appropriate for each, either causing them to realize the fruit of stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*), once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*), non-returner (*anāgāmin*), or arhat; or causing them to realize the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha; or causing them to enter the stages of a bodhisattva; or causing them to realize the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*) that they seek."

“Subhūti! This is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of generosity, employing skillful means to bring sentient beings to maturity, causing them to be liberated from the saṃsāra of evil destinies, and enabling them to realize the nirvāṇa of the three vehicles as appropriate.”
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,

how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*), as well as the Great Path to Bodhi of other bodhisattva mahāsattvas, through skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*) to bring sentient beings to maturity?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“There are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, when practicing the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*), through skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) see sentient beings lacking the necessities of life and with afflictions (*kleśa*) raging so that they cannot cultivate virtue. Out of compassion, they say to them:

‘If you are unable to cultivate virtue because you lack the necessary conditions, I shall give you various provisions such as food and drink, clothing, and bedding. You should not give rise to afflictions or evil karma; rather, you should correctly practice virtues such as generosity (*dāna*).’”

“Subhūti! This bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling securely in the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*), appropriately gathers in all classes of sentient beings: those who are stingy and greedy, he causes them to practice generosity, having no regard for body, life, or wealth;

those who violate ethical discipline, he causes them to practice pure discipline, enabling them to correctly receive and carry out the ten paths of wholesome action, abiding in the vows of restraint—unbroken, unpierced, untainted, unadulterated, and free from grasping.”
They cause those who are prone to anger and resentment to cultivate patience, remaining unchanging in mind even when reviled or harmed;
they cause those who are indolent to cultivate diligence, practicing all wholesome dharmas as if their hair were on fire;
and they cause those who are distracted to cultivate meditative concentration.
They cause those who are deluded to cultivate wisdom;
they cause those who cling to phenomena to contemplate the emptiness of phenomena;
and they cause those who lack the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment to fully practice these factors of enlightenment.
For those who have not yet contemplated the Four Noble Truths, they cause them to cultivate correct contemplation;
for those who lack the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), and the formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*), they cause them to fully practice these;

for those who lack the liberations (*vimokṣa*), the bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), the spheres of equanimity (*samāpatti*), and the spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*), they cause them to fully practice these.
May those who have not yet attained the gates of dhāraṇī and samādhi swiftly realize them;
may those who have not yet attained the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—be led to cultivate and realize them;
and may those who have not yet entered the bodhisattva stages be led to enter them and swiftly bring them to full perfection.
Those who have not yet attained the five eyes or the six supernormal powers are led to gradually cultivate and realize them;

those who have not yet attained the Buddha’s ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, or the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are led to gradually cultivate and realize them;
and those who have not yet attained the quality of non-forgetfulness or the state of constant abiding in equanimity are led to gradually cultivate and realize them.

They cause those who have not yet attained all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) to gradually cultivate and realize them. Subhūti!

These bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, abiding in the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*), employ skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*) to bring sentient beings to maturity: they cause some to be liberated from the sufferings of the evil destinies; some to realize the fruits of stream-entry (*srotāpatti*), once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmin*), non-returning (*anāgāmin*), or arhatship; some to realize the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha; and others to realize the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*) that they seek.

“Subhūti! This is called the skillful means of a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of ethical discipline (śīla-pāramitā), whereby they mature sentient beings, causing them to be liberated from the evil destinies and the cycle of birth and death, so that they may, as appropriate, realize the nirvāṇa of the three vehicles.”

“Subhūti, you should know that there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who practice the other four perfections, as well as other bodhisattva-mahāsattvas on the great path to awakening; each is able, through skillful means, to bring all beings to maturity with every kind of goodness, causing them to be liberated from the miserable realms and the cycle of birth and death, or causing them to realize the peace and bliss of śrāvaka-awakening, or causing them to realize the peace and bliss of pratyekabuddha-awakening, or causing them to realize the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening they seek, so as to constantly and uninterruptedly benefit and bring peace and happiness to all classes of sentient beings throughout the future.”
Chapter 72: Purifying the Buddha-field, Part One. At that time, the Venerable Subhūti had this thought:
"What dharma is called the path of a bodhisattva mahāsattva?"
"How do the bodhisattva mahāsattvas, dwelling securely in this path, don the various great armor of merit to benefit and bring peace and happiness to all sentient beings?
Knowing his thought, the Buddha addressed Subhūti, saying:
"Subhūti, you should know!"

The perfection of generosity is the path of all bodhisattva mahāsattvas; the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom are the paths of all bodhisattva mahāsattvas.

The four foundations of mindfulness are the path of all bodhisattva mahāsattvas; the four right endeavors, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of awakening, and the eightfold noble path are the paths of all bodhisattva mahāsattvas.

Internal emptiness is the path of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas; external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, non-alteration emptiness, essential nature emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common characteristic emptiness, emptiness of all dharmas, unapprehendable emptiness, emptiness of non-existence, emptiness of intrinsic nature, and emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence are the paths of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas;
the noble truth of suffering is the path of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas, and the noble truths of origination, cessation, and the path are the paths of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas.
The four dhyānas are the path of bodhisattva mahāsattvas; the four immeasurables and the four formless absorptions are the path of bodhisattva mahāsattvas;
the eight liberations are the path of bodhisattva mahāsattvas, as are the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive absorptions, and the ten totalities;
all doors of dhāraṇī are the path of bodhisattva mahāsattvas, and all doors of samādhi are the path of bodhisattva mahāsattvas.
The gate of liberation of emptiness is the path of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness are the path of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.

The stage of extreme joy is the path of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; the stages of freedom from defilement, radiant light, blazing wisdom, extremely difficult to conquer, manifest presence, far-reaching, immovability, excellent intelligence, and the cloud of dharma are the paths of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
The five eyes are the path of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; the six supernormal powers are the path of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.

The ten powers of a Buddha are the path of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are the path of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas;
the quality of non-forgetfulness is the path of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, and the constant abiding in equanimity is the path of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas;
omniscience is the path of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, and the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects are the path of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
Furthermore, Subhūti!
All dharmas in their entirety constitute the path of the bodhisattva mahāsattva. Subhūti!
What do you think? Is there any dharma that bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should not study?
Without studying such a dharma, can bodhisattva-mahāsattvas attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening?
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One!”
"No, Sugata! the Buddha said.
“Excellent, Subhūti! It is so, it is so!”
"It is as you have said, Subhūti!

There is certainly no dharma that bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should not study; if bodhisattva-mahāsattvas do not study this dharma, they will certainly be unable to attain the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment they seek."
Why is this? Subhūti!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not train in all dharmas, they will ultimately never be able to attain the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna).
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If the intrinsic nature of all dharmas is empty, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva train in all dharmas?”

Could it be that the Blessed One is engaging in conceptual proliferation regarding the dharma that is free from proliferation, by asserting that there are various dharmas which are "this" or "that," "from this" or "for this";
that "this is a worldly dharma" and "this is a supramundane dharma";
or that "this is a contaminated dharma" and "this is an uncontaminated dharma"?
"What are these conditioned phenomena? What are these unconditioned phenomena? What are these phenomena of ordinary beings?

What are these phenomena of stream-enterers? What are these phenomena of once-returners? What are these phenomena of non-returners? What are these phenomena of arhats? What are these phenomena of pratyekabuddhas? What are these phenomena of bodhisattvas? What are these phenomena of Tathāgatas?"
The Buddha told Subhūti: “So it is! So it is!”
"It is as you have said.
Subhūti, all phenomena whatsoever are empty of intrinsic nature."
If all phenomena were not empty of intrinsic nature, then bodhisattva mahāsattvas would not be able to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Subhūti! Because all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature, bodhisattva mahāsattvas are therefore able to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
“Subhūti! As you have said:
‘If the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is empty, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva train in all phenomena?’”

Could it be that the Blessed One is engaging in conceptual proliferation regarding the dharma that is free from proliferation— by asserting that there are various dharmas which are "this" or "that," "thereby" or "for this purpose";
that "this is a worldly dharma" and "this is a supramundane dharma," and so on,
up to "this is a bodhisattva dharma" and "this is a Tathāgata dharma"?

"Subhūti, if all sentient beings were to know that all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature, then bodhisattva mahāsattvas would not need to train in all phenomena, realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, and establish and proclaim them for the sake of sentient beings."

"Subhūti! Because sentient beings do not know that all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas study all phenomena, realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and establish and proclaim them for the sake of all sentient beings."
“Subhūti! When Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas first begin to train in the bodhisattva path, they should carefully examine: ‘The intrinsic nature of all phenomena is entirely unapprehendable;

it exists only as a fabrication produced by attachment and conjunction. I should thoroughly investigate that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is ultimately empty, and I should not have any attachment toward them—namely, one should not be attached to form, nor should one be attached to feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.’”
One should not be attached to the sense base of the eye; one should not be attached to the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind.
One should not be attached to the sense base of forms; one should not be attached to the sense bases of sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena.
One should not be attached to the element of the eye; one should not be attached to the elements of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind.
One should not be attached to the realm of form; one should not be attached to the realms of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, or mental phenomena.
One should not be attached to the realm of eye-consciousness; one should not be attached to the realms of ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-consciousness.
One should not be attached to eye-contact; one should not be attached to ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-contact.

One should not be attached to the various feelings arising with eye-contact as condition; one should not be attached to the various feelings arising with ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-contact as condition.
One should not be attached to the earth element; one should not be attached to the water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness elements.

One should not be attached to the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*); one should not be attached to the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), the object condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), or the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
One should not cling to the phenomena that arise from conditions;

one should not cling to ignorance, nor to volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, or old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair.
One should not cling to the perfection of generosity, nor should one cling to the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, or wisdom.

One should not be attached to internal emptiness; one should not be attached to external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, non-alteration emptiness, essential nature emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common characteristic emptiness, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, or the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature.

One should not be attached to the four foundations of mindfulness; one should not be attached to the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, or the eightfold noble path.
One should not be attached to the noble truth of suffering; one should not be attached to the noble truths of the origin, cessation, or the path.
One should not be attached to the four dhyānas; one should not be attached to the four immeasurables or the four formless attainments;
one should not be attached to the eight liberations, nor to the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, or the ten totalities;
one should not be attached to the doors of dhāraṇī, nor to the doors of samādhi.
One should not be attached to the gate of liberation of emptiness; one should not be attached to the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness.

One should not be attached to the Ground of Extreme Joy; one should not be attached to the Ground of Purity, the Ground of Radiance, the Ground of Blazing Wisdom, the Ground of Difficult Victory, the Ground of Presence, the Ground of Far-Going, the Ground of Immovability, the Ground of Good Intelligence, or the Ground of the Dharma Cloud.
One should not be attached to the five eyes; one should not be attached to the six supernormal powers.

One should not be attached to the ten powers of a Buddha; one should not be attached to the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, or the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
one should not be attached to the quality of non-forgetfulness, nor should one be attached to the nature of constant dwelling in equanimity;
one should not be attached to all-knowledge, nor should one be attached to the knowledge of the paths or the knowledge of all aspects.
One should not be attached to the fruit of stream-entry; one should not be attached to the fruits of once-returning, non-returning, or arhatship, nor to the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha;
one should not be attached to any of the practices of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, nor should one be attached to the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas.

Why is this? Because the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is empty; one should not cling to emptiness within emptiness. Since even emptiness cannot be apprehended within emptiness, how much less could there be an emptiness that is capable of clinging to emptiness!

"Subhūti! When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas contemplate all phenomena in this manner, although they have no attachment to the nature of phenomena, they constantly train in all phenomena without weariness."

“Subhūti! Abiding in this training, this bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates the distinctions among the mental activities of all sentient beings; that is, he carefully examines where the mental activities of these sentient beings are directed.”
Having scrutinized them thus, he understands as they truly are that those minds merely function through the grasping of what is false.
At that time, the bodhisattva thinks:
"Since those minds function through the grasping of what is false, it will certainly not be difficult for me to bring about their liberation."
"Subhūti! Having formed this thought, that bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells securely in the perfection of wisdom and, through skillful means, instructs and exhorts all sentient beings, saying:
'You all should now distance yourselves from false attachments and enter into the true Dharma to cultivate all wholesome deeds.'"
"Furthermore, he spoke thus:

'You should now practice the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā); you shall thereby obtain all necessary provisions without lack. However, do not rely on this to give rise to arrogance or negligence.'"
Why is this? Because herein there is no core of substantial reality whatsoever.
You should now practice the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom; yet, do not rely upon these to give rise to arrogance or negligence.
Why is this? Because herein there is absolutely no solid or substantial thing.
"You all should now practice internal emptiness, yet do not rely upon this to give rise to arrogance or negligence."
Why is this? Because within these there is not a single thing that is solid or substantial.

You should now practice external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, non-altering emptiness, essential nature emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common characteristic emptiness, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of non-apprehensibility, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature; yet, do not rely upon these to give rise to arrogance or negligence.
Why is this? Because herein there is absolutely no solid or substantial reality.
"You all should now practice the four foundations of mindfulness, yet do not rely upon them to give rise to arrogance or negligence."
Why is this? Because herein there is not a single thing that is solid or substantial.

You should now practice the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path; yet, do not rely upon these to give rise to arrogance or negligence.
Why is this? Because herein there is absolutely no solid or substantial reality.
"You all should now practice the Noble Truth of Suffering, yet do not rely upon it to give rise to arrogance or negligence."
Why is this? Because within these there is not a single thing that is solid or substantial.
You should now practice the noble truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path; however, do not rely on them to give rise to arrogance or negligence.
Why is this? Because herein there is absolutely no solid or substantial reality.
"You all should now practice the four dhyānas, yet do not rely upon them to give rise to arrogance or negligence."
Why is this? Because within these there is absolutely no core of substantial reality.
You should now practice the four immeasurables and the four formless absorptions, yet do not rely upon them to give rise to arrogance or negligence.
Why is this? Because herein there is not a single thing that possesses any solid substance.
"You all should now practice the eight liberations, yet do not rely upon them to give rise to arrogance or negligence."
Why is this? Because herein there is absolutely no solid or substantial reality.

You should now practice the eight bases of mastery (*aṣṭāv abhibhvāyatanāni*), the nine successive attainments (*navānupūrvavihārasamāpattayaḥ*), and the ten spheres of totality (*daśa kṛtsnāyatanāni*), yet do not rely upon these to give rise to arrogance or negligence.
Why is this? Because herein there is absolutely no solid or substantial reality.
"You all should now practice the gate of dhāraṇī, yet do not rely upon this to give rise to arrogance or negligence."
Why is this? Because herein there is absolutely no solid or substantial reality.
You should now practice the gateways of samādhi, yet do not rely upon them to give rise to arrogance or negligence.
Why is this? Because herein there is absolutely no solid or substantial thing.
"You all should now practice the gate of liberation that is emptiness, yet do not rely upon it to give rise to arrogance or negligence."
Why is this? Because herein there is absolutely no solid or substantial reality.
You should now practice the gateways of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness; however, do not rely upon these to give rise to arrogance or negligence.
Why is this? Because within this there is no core of substantial reality at all.
"You should now practice the Stage of Supreme Joy, yet do not rely upon it to give rise to arrogance or negligence."
Why is this? Because within these there is not a single thing that possesses any solid substance.

You all should now practice the Ground of Freedom from Defilement, the Ground of Radiance, the Ground of Blazing Wisdom, the Ground of Supreme Difficulty to Conquer, the Ground of Manifestation, the Ground of Far-Going, the Ground of Immovability, the Ground of Excellent Intelligence, and the Ground of the Cloud of Dharma; yet do not rely upon these to give rise to arrogance or negligence.
Why is this? Because herein there is no core of substantial reality whatsoever.
"You all should now practice the five eyes, yet do not rely upon them to give rise to arrogance or negligence."
Why is this? Because within these there is not a single thing of solid substance.
You should now practice the six supernormal powers (ṣaḍabhijñā), yet do not rely upon them to give rise to arrogance or negligence.
Why is this? Because herein there is absolutely no solid or substantial reality.
"You all should now practice the ten powers of a Buddha, yet do not rely upon them to give rise to arrogance or negligence."
Why is this? Because herein there is absolutely no core of substantial reality.

You all should now practice the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; yet you must not rely upon these to give rise to arrogance or negligence.
Why is this? Because herein there is absolutely no solid or substantial reality.
"You all should now practice the dharma of non-forgetfulness, yet do not rely upon this to give rise to arrogance or negligence."
Why is this? Because herein there is absolutely no core of substantiality.
You should now practice the state of constant equanimity (*upekṣā*), yet do not rely upon this to give rise to arrogance or negligence.
Why is this? Because herein there is absolutely no solid or substantial reality.
"You all should now practice for the sake of omniscience, yet do not rely upon this to give rise to arrogance or negligence."
Why is this? Because herein there is not the slightest thing of solid substance.
You all should now practice the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects; however, do not rely upon these to give rise to arrogance or negligence.
Why is this? Because within these there is not the slightest thing of solid substance.
"You all should now practice for the fruit of stream-entry, yet do not rely upon this to give rise to arrogance or negligence."
Why is this? Because within this there is no core of substantial reality whatsoever.

You should now practice for the sake of the fruit of once-returning, non-returning, arhatship, and pratyekabuddha enlightenment; however, do not rely on these and give rise to arrogance or negligence.
Why is this? Because herein there is absolutely no solid or substantial reality.
"You all should now practice all the deeds of Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, yet do not rely upon these to give rise to arrogance or negligence."
Why is this? Because herein there is absolutely no solid or substantial reality.
You should now practice for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, yet do not rely upon this to give rise to arrogance or negligence.
Why is this? Because within these there is no core of substantial reality whatsoever. “Subhūti!
When this bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in the perfection of wisdom and skillfully instructs and exhorts sentient beings, they practice the path to enlightenment without any attachment.

Why is this? One should not cling to the nature of all phenomena; for both that which clings and that which is clung to are devoid of intrinsic nature, because the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is empty.

“Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the path to enlightenment in this manner, they do not abide in any phenomena whatsoever. Taking non-abiding as their skillful means, although they practice the perfection of generosity, they do not abide therein;
although they practice the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, they do not abide therein.”
Why is this? Because such intrinsic nature, the practitioner, and the characteristics of practice are all empty.
Although one practices inner emptiness, one dwells nowhere within it at all.

Although they practice outer emptiness, inner-and-outer emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, the emptiness of the ultimate, the emptiness of conditioned phenomena, the emptiness of unconditioned phenomena, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, the emptiness of dispersion, the emptiness of non-alteration, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, the emptiness of self-characteristics, the emptiness of common characteristics, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of non-apprehensibility, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature, they do not abide anywhere within them.
Why is this? Because such intrinsic nature, the practitioner, and the modes of practice are all empty.
"Though one practices the four foundations of mindfulness, one abides nowhere within them."

Although they practice the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path, they abide in none of them whatsoever.
Why is this? Because such intrinsic nature, the practitioner, and the characteristics of practice are all empty.
Although one practices the Noble Truth of Suffering, one dwells nowhere within it.
Although one practices the noble truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path, one dwells nowhere within them.
Why is this? Because such intrinsic nature, the practitioner, and the characteristics of practice are all empty.
"Although they practice the four dhyānas, they do not abide in them at all;
although they practice the four immeasurables and the four formless absorptions, they do not abide in them at all."
Why is this? Because such intrinsic nature, the practitioner, and the modes of practice are all empty.
Although one practices the eight liberations, one dwells nowhere within them at all.
Although they practice the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten universal bases, they abide in none of them at all.
Why is this? Because such intrinsic nature, the practitioner, and the modes of practice are all empty.
"Although they practice the gates of dhāraṇī, they abide nowhere therein;
although they practice the gates of samādhi, they abide nowhere therein."
Why is this? Because such intrinsic nature, the practitioner, and the characteristics of practice are all empty.
"Though one practices the gate of liberation that is emptiness, one dwells nowhere within it."
Although they practice the gateways of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness, they do not dwell anywhere within them.
Why is this? Because such intrinsic nature, the practitioner, and the characteristics of the practice are all empty.
"Although they practice the Stage of Utmost Joy, they abide nowhere within it;

although they practice the Stage of Purity, the Stage of Radiance, the Stage of Blazing Wisdom, the Stage of Supreme Difficulty, the Stage of Presence, the Stage of Far-Going, the Immovable Stage, the Stage of Excellent Intelligence, and the Stage of the Dharma Cloud, they abide nowhere within them."
Why is this? Because such intrinsic nature, the practitioner, and the modes of practice are all empty.
Although one practices the five eyes, one dwells nowhere within them at all.
Although they practice the six supernormal powers, they do not dwell in them at all.
Why is this? Because such intrinsic nature, the practitioner, and the characteristics of the practice are all empty.
"Although they practice the ten powers of a Buddha, they do not dwell anywhere therein;

although they practice the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, they do not dwell anywhere therein."
Why is this? Because such intrinsic nature, the practitioner, and the modes of practice are all empty.
Although one practices the quality of non-forgetfulness, one dwells nowhere within it.
Although they practice and constantly abide in the nature of equanimity, they do not abide in anything therein.
Why is this? Because such intrinsic nature, the practitioner, and the characteristics of the practice are all empty.
"Although they practice the knowledge of all modes, they abide nowhere therein;
although they practice the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects, they abide nowhere therein."
Why is this? Because such intrinsic nature, the practitioner, and the modes of practice are all empty.
Although one practices for the fruit of stream-entry, one dwells nowhere within it at all.
Although they practice for the fruit of once-returning, non-returning, arhatship, or pratyekabuddha-enlightenment, they abide in none of these. Why is this?
Thus, because their intrinsic nature, the practitioner, and the modes of practice are all empty,
although they practice all the deeds of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, they abide nowhere therein; and although they practice the unsurpassed,
perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas, they abide nowhere therein.
Why is this? Because such intrinsic nature, the practitioner, and the characteristics of practice are all empty. "Subhūti!..."

Although this bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to attain the fruit of a stream-enterer, he does not abide therein; although he is able to attain the fruits of a once-returner, a non-returner, or an arhat, as well as the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, he does not abide therein.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha,
saying: "World-Honored One,
for what reason does this bodhisattva mahāsattva, although able to attain the fruit of a stream-enterer, not abide therein?"
"How is it that although they are able to attain the fruit of a once-returner, a non-returner, an arhat, or the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, they do not abide therein?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"This bodhisattva mahāsattva has two causes and conditions by which, although they are able to attain the fruit of a stream-enterer, they do not abide therein; and although they are able to attain the fruit of a once-returner up to the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, they do not abide therein."
What are these two?
First, that fruit is entirely devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); thus, neither the abider nor the place of abiding can be apprehended.
Second, one does not give rise to complacency regarding it; therefore, one does not abide.
That is to say, that bodhisattva constantly reflects:
"I shall certainly attain the fruit of stream-entry; it is not possible that I should not attain it, yet I should not dwell therein.

I shall certainly attain the fruits of once-returner, non-returner, and arhatship, as well as the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha; it is not possible that I should not attain them, yet I should not dwell therein."
Why is this? Since I first resolved upon unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, at all times I have had no other thought but to seek only unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
"Nevertheless, I shall certainly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; how could I dwell in any other fruit in the interim? "Subhūti!

From the first generation of the mind of awakening until entering the bodhisattva’s state of rightness and departure from birth, this bodhisattva mahāsattva never entertains any other thought, seeking only unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

"Subhūti! From the attainment of the first bhūmi up until the attainment of the tenth bhūmi, this bodhisattva mahāsattva never entertains any other thought, seeking only unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening."

"Subhūti! This bodhisattva mahāsattva single-mindedly seeks unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; at all times his mind is undistracted, and whatever physical, verbal, or mental actions he undertakes, none are not accompanied by the bodhicitta."
“Subhūti! This bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in the mind of awakening and gives rise to the path of awakening, so that his mind is not disturbed by other objects.
At that time, the venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If all dharmas are non-arising, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva give rise to the path to enlightenment?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"So it is! So it is! All dharmas are non-arising. Furthermore, how is this so? It is because those who do nothing and have no destination know that all dharmas are non-arising."
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Is it not the case that whether a Tathāgata appears in the world or does not appear, the dharma-realm of all phenomena remains eternally as it is?”
The Buddha said, “So it is, Subhūti!”

It is so! Whether a Tathāgata appears in the world or does not appear, the dharma-realm of all phenomena remains eternally as it is. Yet, sentient beings are unable to comprehend that the dharma-realm of all phenomena remains eternally as it is; therefore, the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas give rise to the path to enlightenment for their benefit, and by means of this path to enlightenment, they rescue sentient beings, causing them to be forever liberated from the manifold sufferings of birth and death.
Then, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,
do bodhisattva-mahāsattvas attain awakening by means of a path that has arisen?"
The Buddha said,
“No. [He replied,] “World-Honored One!”
"Is it by means of the path of non-arising that one attains bodhi? The Buddha said, "No!"
“World-Honored One!
Is bodhi attained by means of a path that is produced, or one that is unproduced?
The Buddha said:
"No, World-Honored One!
Is it by means of a path that is neither arising nor non-arising that one attains bodhi?"
The Buddha said, “No.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How shall a bodhisattva mahāsattva attain bodhi?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"One does not attain bodhi by means of the path, nor does one attain bodhi by means of what is not the path.
Why is this so, Subhūti?
"Bodhi is itself the path, and the path is itself bodhi.
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

If awakening is itself the path, and the path is itself awakening, then would it not be the case that all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, having already attained the path to awakening, should have already attained awakening?

If that is so, how is it that the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha further teaches them the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, the eighty secondary signs, the ten powers of a Buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and other immeasurable Buddha-dharmas, causing them to cultivate and realize them?
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"What do you think? Do you perhaps think that the Buddha has attained bodhi?"
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One!”
"No, Sugata! Why is that?"
“World-Honored One!
Since the Buddha is awakening (bodhi) and awakening is the Buddha, it should not be said that the Buddha attains awakening.
The Buddha said:
“Excellent, Subhūti! It is so, it is so!”
However, as for what you asked:
"Is it not the case that a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has already attained the path to awakening should have already attained awakening?"— Subhūti!
"How can it be said that bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have already attained awakening when they have not yet perfected the path to awakening?
"Subhūti! If bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have already perfected generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence..."
The perfections of diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, if they have already brought to fulfillment the emptiness of the internal,
the emptiness of the external, the emptiness of the internal and external, the emptiness of emptiness, the great emptiness, the emptiness of the ultimate, the emptiness of the conditioned,
the emptiness of the unconditioned, the absolute emptiness, the emptiness of the limitless, the emptiness of dispersion, and the emptiness of non-alteration;
emptiness of intrinsic nature, emptiness of specific characteristics, emptiness of common characteristics, emptiness of all phenomena, emptiness of the unapprehendable,
emptiness of non-existence, emptiness of intrinsic nature, and emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence; if one has already perfected the four foundations of mindfulness,
the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, and the seven factors of enlightenment...
The factors of enlightenment and the branches of the noble eightfold path; if one has already fulfilled the noble truth of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path;
if one has already fulfilled the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments;
and if one has already fulfilled the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities.
...abiding therein, having already perfected the gateways of dhāraṇī and the gateways of samādhi;
having already perfected the gateways of liberation of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;
and having already perfected the Stage of Extreme Joy, the Stainless Stage, the Radiant Stage, the Blazing Wisdom Stage, the Extremely Difficult to Conquer Stage, and the Manifest...
The Ground of Presence, the Ground of Far-Going, the Ground of Immovability, the Ground of Excellent Intelligence, and the Ground of Dharma-Cloud;
whether they have already perfected the five eyes and the six supernormal powers, or have already perfected the ten powers of a Buddha,
the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity—
The eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; if they have already perfected the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty secondary signs;
if they have already perfected the quality of non-forgetfulness and the nature of constant equanimity;
if they have already perfected all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*); if they have already perfected all...
The practice of a bodhisattva mahāsattva is such that they have already perfected the contemplation of the twelve links of dependent origination in both forward and reverse order;
they have already perfected all the sovereign supernormal powers of a bodhisattva;
they have already perfected sublime śamatha and vipaśyanā; and they have already perfected all the accumulations of merit and wisdom.
Having fully matured sentient beings and purified Buddha-fields, and having perfected the immeasurable, boundless,
and inconceivable sublime dharmas of all Buddhas, immediately thereafter, by means of the sublime wisdom associated with the vajra-like samādhi in a single kṣaṇa,
one forever severs the latencies (*dausthulya*) of both the afflictive and cognitive obstructions.
Through the continuity of habitual tendencies, one realizes unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; this is what is called being a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha—
one who has attained great mastery over all phenomena and brings benefit, peace, and happiness to all sentient beings until the end of the future.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva purify a buddha-field?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, from the first production of the thought of awakening until the ultimate end, constantly purifies the coarseness of body, speech, and mind in themselves, and also purifies the coarseness of body, speech, and mind in others—because this bodhisattva mahāsattva has purified the three types of coarseness in both self and others, they are then able to adorn and purify the buddha-field they seek.”
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
what are called the physical, verbal, and mental dysfunctions (dauṣṭhulya) of a bodhisattva mahāsattva?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“If one takes life, if one takes what is not given, or if one engages in sexual misconduct—if such unwholesome physical misdeeds exist, these are called the physical dysfunctions of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.”
Whether it be false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, or idle chatter—such unwholesome verbal misconduct is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s vocal *dauṣṭhulya*.
Whether it be covetousness, ill will, or wrong view—such unwholesome misdeeds of the mind are called the mental heaviness of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva’s aggregate of ethical discipline, aggregate of concentration, aggregate of wisdom, aggregate of liberation, and aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation are all impure, these are also called heavy burdens (dauṣṭhulya).
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva possesses a mind of stinginess and greed, a mind of violating the precepts, a mind of anger and resentment, a mind of laziness, a mind of distraction, or a mind of corrupted wisdom, these are also called *dausthulya* (coarse heaviness)."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva is far removed from the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of awakening, and the eightfold noble path, this is also called a 'heavy burden' (dauṣṭhulya)."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva is far removed from internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, non-alteration emptiness, essential nature emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common characteristic emptiness, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature, this is also called 'coarseness' (dauṣṭhulya)."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva is distant from the noble truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path, this is also called 'coarseness' (dausthulya)."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva is far removed from the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments, this is also called a heavy burden (dauṣṭhulya)."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva is far removed from the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities, this is also called a heavy burden (dauṣṭhulya)."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva is far removed from the gateways of dhāraṇī and the gateways of samādhi, this is also called a heavy burden of dysfunction (dausthulya)."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva distances himself from the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—that too is called a heavy burden (dauṣṭhulya)."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva is far removed from the stage of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, this is also called a heavy burden (dauṣṭhulya). Furthermore, Subhūti!"
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva is far removed from the five eyes and the six supernormal powers, this is also called a heavy burden (*dausthulya*). "Furthermore, Subhūti!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva is far removed from the Buddha’s ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha, this is also called a heavy burden."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva is far removed from the quality of non-forgetfulness and the state of constant equanimity, this is also called a heavy burden (dauṣṭhulya)."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva is far removed from all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), this is also called a heavy burden (*dauṣṭhulya*)."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva distances himself from the bodhisattva mahāsattva practice and from the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas, this is also called a heavy burden (dauṣṭhulya)."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva craves the realization of the fruit of stream-entry, or the realization of the fruit of once-returning, or the realization of the fruit of non-returning, or the realization of the fruit of arhatship, or the realization of pratyekabuddha-enlightenment, this too is called a heavy burden (dauṣṭhulya)."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives rise to the perception of form, or gives rise to the perceptions of feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness, this is also called a heavy burden (*dausthulya*).
If they give rise to the perception of the eye-base, or give rise to the perceptions of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-bases, this is also called a heavy burden."

To give rise to the perception of the sense-base of form, and to give rise to the perceptions of the sense-bases of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena, is also called "coarseness" (*dausthulya*).
To give rise to the perception of the eye-element, and to give rise to the perceptions of the elements of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, is also called "coarseness.
To give rise to the perception of the element of form, and to give rise to the perceptions of the elements of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena, is also called "coarseness."

To give rise to the perception of the eye-consciousness element, and to give rise to the perceptions of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-consciousness elements, is also called *dausthulya* (coarseness/heaviness).
To give rise to the perception of eye-contact, and to give rise to the perceptions of ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-contact, is also called *dausthulya*.

To give rise to the perceptions of all feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition, and to give rise to the perceptions of all feelings produced with ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-contact as conditions, is also called *dausthulya*.
To give rise to the perception of the earth element, and to give rise to the perceptions of the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements, is also called "coarseness" (*dausthulya*);

to give rise to the perception of causes and conditions, and to give rise to the perceptions of the immediately preceding condition, the object-condition, and the dominant condition, is also called "coarseness";
to give rise to the perception of all phenomena produced from conditions is also called "coarseness."

To give rise to the perception of ignorance, and to give rise to the perceptions of volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, and old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair—this is also called "coarseness" (*dausthulya*).

To give rise to the perception of the perfection of generosity (*dāna-pāramitā*), and to give rise to the perceptions of the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom—this is also called "coarseness."

To give rise to the perception of internal emptiness, or to give rise to the perceptions of external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, non-alteration emptiness, essential nature emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common characteristic emptiness, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature—this is also called *dausthulya* (coarseness).

To give rise to the perception of the four foundations of mindfulness, or to give rise to the perceptions of the four right endeavors, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path—this is also called *dausthulya*.
To give rise to the perception of the noble truth of suffering, or to give rise to the perceptions of the noble truths of the origin, cessation, and the path—this is also called *dausthulya*.
To give rise to the perception of the four dhyānas, or to give rise to the perception of the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments, is also called "coarseness" (dausthulya).

To give rise to the perception of the eight liberations, or to give rise to the perception of the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative concentrations, and the ten totalities, is also called "coarseness.
To give rise to the perception of the doors of dhāraṇī, or to give rise to the perception of the doors of samādhi, is also called "coarseness."

To give rise to the perception of the gate of liberation of emptiness, or to give rise to the perceptions of the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness, is also called a heavy burden (*dausthulya*).

To give rise to the perception of the Ground of Utmost Joy, or to give rise to the perceptions of the Ground of Purity, the Ground of Radiance, the Ground of Blazing Wisdom, the Ground of Difficult Victory, the Ground of Presence, the Ground of Far-Going, the Ground of Immovability, the Ground of Excellent Intelligence, and the Ground of the Cloud of Dharma, is also called a heavy burden.
To give rise to the perception of the five eyes, or to give rise to the perception of the six supernormal powers, is also called a heavy burden.

To give rise to the perception of the ten powers of a Buddha, or the perception of the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, is also called "coarseness" (*dausthulya*).
To give rise to the perception of the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, or the perception of the eighty secondary signs, is also called "coarseness.
To give rise to the perception of the quality of non-forgetfulness, or the perception of the nature of constant abiding in equanimity, is also called "coarseness."

To give rise to the notion of "all-knowledge" (sarvajñatā), or the notions of "knowledge of the aspects of the path" (mārgākārajñatā) and "knowledge of all aspects" (sarvākārajñatā), is also called a heavy burden (dausthulya).

To give rise to the notion of the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpattiphala), or the notions of the fruits of once-returning (sakṛdāgāmiphala), non-returning (anāgāmiphala), arhatship (arhattvaphala), and the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, is also called a heavy burden.
To give rise to the notion of all the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, or the notion of the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas, is also called a heavy burden.
To give rise to the notion of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), or the notion of a śrāvaka, a pratyekabuddha, a bodhisattva, or a tathāgata, is also called *dauṣṭhulya*.

To give rise to the notion of hell-beings, the notion of animals, the notion of the realm of hungry ghosts, the notion of gods, the notion of humans, the notion of male, or the notion of female, is also called *dauṣṭhulya*.

To give rise to the notion of the desire realm, the notion of the form realm, or the notion of the formless realm; to give rise to the notion of the wholesome, the unwholesome, or the indeterminate; to give rise to the notion of the mundane, the supramundane, the contaminated (*sāsrava*), the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), or the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)—these are also called *dauṣṭhulya*.

"Subhūti! All such infinite and boundless false discriminations of persons who cling to various phenomena, as well as the corresponding actions of body, speech, and mind, and their inherent nature of being unfit for abiding—all these are termed *dausthulya* (coarseness/heaviness)."

“Subhūti! This bodhisattva mahāsattva, having distanced himself from such heavy burdens as those described, personally practices the perfection of generosity and also teaches others to practice the perfection of generosity.”

If there are sentient beings who require food, one gives them food; those who require drink, one gives them drink; those who require clothing, one gives them clothing; those who require vehicles, one gives them vehicles; those who require dwellings, one gives them dwellings; those who require servants, one gives them servants; those who require attendants, one gives them attendants; those who require flowers and incense, one gives them flowers and incense; those who require ornaments, one gives them ornaments; those who require banners and parasols, one gives them banners and parasols; those who require music and performance, one gives them music and performance; those who require bedding, one gives them bedding; those who require lamps and light, one gives them lamps and light; those who require seats and thrones, one gives them seats and thrones. Whatever various requisites they may require, at all times and in all places, one bestows them all entirely. Just as one practices this oneself, one likewise instructs others to do so.

Having made such offerings, one should share these roots of virtue equally with all sentient beings and dedicate them toward the attainment of a pure Buddha-field, so that it may be swiftly perfected for the benefit and happiness of sentient beings.
“Subhūti! This bodhisattva mahāsattva personally practices the perfection of ethical discipline and also teaches others to practice the perfection of ethical discipline;
he personally practices the perfection of patience and also teaches others to practice the perfection of patience.”
They personally practice the perfection of diligence and also teach others to practice the perfection of diligence;
they personally practice the perfection of meditative concentration and also teach others to practice the perfection of meditative concentration;
they personally practice the perfection of wisdom and also teach others to practice the perfection of wisdom.

Having performed these deeds, this bodhisattva mahāsattva takes these roots of goodness and shares them equally with all sentient beings, dedicating them toward the attainment of a purified buddha-field, so that it may be swiftly perfected for the benefit and happiness of sentient beings.

The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle 393. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Part One: Chapter Seventy-Two, Part Two, "Purifying the Buddha-field. Furthermore, Subhūti:
There are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, by the power of their supernormal vows, fill the trichiliocosm with the most excellent seven treasures and offer them to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.
Having given the gift, he joyfully makes this great vow:

"By means of these roots of goodness I have planted, may I share them equally with all sentient beings and dedicate them toward the attainment of a pure Buddha-field as I seek it; may my land be adorned with the seven treasures, and may all sentient beings enjoy various precious jewels according to their wishes without any attachment."

"Furthermore, Subhūti! There are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, by the power of their supernormal vows, play and strike countless sublime musical instruments among the gods and humans, making offerings to the Triple Gem and the stūpas of the Buddhas."
Having made the offering, he joyfully made this great vow:

"By means of these roots of goodness I have planted, may I share them equally with all sentient beings and dedicate them toward the attainment of a pure Buddha-field as I seek it; may such sublime and wondrous music always be played in my land, so that when sentient beings hear it, their bodies and minds will be filled with joy and remain free from attachment."
"Furthermore, Subhūti, there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who,

by the power of their supernormal vows, fill the three-thousandfold world system with all manner of exquisite incense and flowers from among humans and devas, and make offerings to the Three Jewels and the stūpas of the Buddhas."
Having made the offering, he joyfully gave rise to this great vow:

"By means of these roots of goodness I have planted, I share them equally with all sentient beings and dedicate them toward the attainment of a pure and adorned Buddha-field. May my land always possess such exquisite fragrant flowers, so that sentient beings, upon using them, experience delight in body and mind without becoming stained by attachment."

"Furthermore, Subhūti! There are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, through the power of their supernormal vows, prepare exquisite food and drink of a hundred flavors to make offerings to the Buddhas, pratyekabuddhas, śrāvakas, and the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas."
Having made the offering, he joyfully gave rise to this great vow:

"By means of these roots of goodness I have planted, may I share them equally with all sentient beings and dedicate them toward the attainment of a pure and adorned buddha-field. When I attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, may all sentient beings within my land partake of such food of a hundred flavors, which nourishes and gladdens their bodies and minds without causing attachment."

"Furthermore, Subhūti! There are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, by the power of their supernormal vows, prepare various kinds of exquisite celestial and human unguents and fine, soft garments, and offer them to the Buddhas, pratyekabuddhas, śrāvakas, and the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; or they may offer them to the Dharma and to the stūpas of the Buddha."
Having given the gift, he joyfully made this great vow:

"By means of these roots of goodness I have planted, may I share them equally with all sentient beings and dedicate them toward the attainment of a pure Buddha-field as I seek. When I attain unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, may all sentient beings within my land always obtain such garments and fragrant ointments, enjoying them according to their wishes without any attachment."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

There are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, by the power of their supernormal vows, prepare various sublime objects of form, sound, fragrance, taste, and touch—arising at will among humans and devas—to make offerings to the Buddhas, the shrines of the Buddhas (caityas), pratyekabuddhas, śrāvakas, and all bodhisattvas, and to bestow them upon other living beings."
Rejoicing and leaping for joy, he made this great vow:

"By means of these roots of virtue I have planted, I share them equally with all sentient beings and dedicate them toward the attainment of a pure and adorned Buddha-field. When I shall attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, may all the sentient beings within my land have whatever sublime objects of form, sound, fragrance, flavor, and touch they desire appear before their minds at will; may they enjoy them with joy, yet remain free from attachment."

"Furthermore, Subhūti, there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who practice the perfection of wisdom and, having made great vows, apply themselves with diligence and valor. They themselves abide in internal emptiness (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*) and also encourage others to abide in internal emptiness;

they themselves abide in external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, non-alteration emptiness, essential nature emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common-characteristic emptiness, emptiness of all phenomena, unapprehendable emptiness, emptiness of non-existence, emptiness of intrinsic nature, and emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence—and they also encourage others to abide in external emptiness up to the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence."
Having performed this deed, he further made this vow:

"When I attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, may all sentient beings within my buddha-field never be separated from internal emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence."

"Furthermore, Subhūti, there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, practicing the perfection of wisdom, give rise to great vows and exert themselves with courageous vigor; they personally cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness and also encourage others to cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness;

they personally cultivate the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path, and also encourage others to cultivate the four right efforts up to the eightfold noble path."
Having performed this deed, he further made this aspiration:

"When I attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, may all sentient beings within my buddha-field never be separated from the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path."

"Furthermore, Subhūti, there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who practice the perfection of wisdom, having generated great vows with diligent vigor; they themselves abide in the noble truth of suffering, and also encourage others to abide in the noble truth of suffering;
they themselves abide in the noble truths of origin, cessation, and the path, and also encourage others to abide in the noble truths of origin, cessation, and the path."
Having performed this deed, he further made this aspiration:

"When I attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, may all sentient beings within my buddha-field never be separated from the Noble Truth of Suffering, the Noble Truth of the Origin, the Noble Truth of Cessation, and the Noble Truth of the Path."

"Furthermore, Subhūti! There are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, practicing the perfection of wisdom, give rise to great vows and exert themselves with courageous vigor; they personally cultivate the four dhyānas and also encourage others to cultivate the four dhyānas;
they personally cultivate the four immeasurables and the four formless absorptions, and also encourage others to cultivate the four immeasurables and the four formless absorptions."
Having performed these deeds, he further made this aspiration:

"When I attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, may all sentient beings within my buddha-field never be separated from the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless absorptions."

"Furthermore, Subhūti, there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who practice the perfection of wisdom, who give rise to great vows and apply themselves with diligence and valor; they personally cultivate the eight liberations and also encourage others to cultivate the eight liberations;

they personally cultivate the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities, and also encourage others to cultivate the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities."
Having performed this deed, he further made this vow:
"When I attain unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, may all sentient beings within my buddha-field never be separated from the eight liberations up to the ten spheres of totality."

"Furthermore, Subhūti, there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who practice the perfection of wisdom, making great vows with diligent and courageous effort; they personally cultivate the gateways of dhāraṇī and also encourage others to cultivate the gateways of dhāraṇī;
they personally cultivate the gateways of samādhi and also encourage others to cultivate the gateways of samādhi."
Having performed this deed, he further made this vow:
"When I attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, may all sentient beings within my buddha-field never be separated from the gateways of dhāraṇī and the gateways of samādhi."

"Furthermore, Subhūti, there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who practice the perfection of wisdom, giving rise to great vows and practicing with diligence and valor. They personally cultivate the gate of liberation of emptiness and also encourage others to cultivate the gate of liberation of emptiness;
they personally cultivate the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness, and also encourage others to cultivate the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness."
Having performed this deed, he further made this vow:

"When I attain unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, may all sentient beings within my land never be separated from the gate of liberation of emptiness, nor from the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness."

"Furthermore, Subhūti! There are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, practicing the perfection of wisdom, give rise to great vows and practice with diligent vigor; they personally cultivate the Stage of Extreme Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), and also encourage others to cultivate the Stage of Extreme Joy;

they personally cultivate the Stage of Freedom from Defilement (*vimalā-bhūmi*), the Stage of Radiance (*prabhākārī-bhūmi*), the Stage of Blazing Wisdom (*arciṣmatī-bhūmi*), the Stage Difficult to Conquer (*sudurjayā-bhūmi*), the Stage of Presence (*abhimukhī-bhūmi*), the Stage of Far-Going (*dūraṅgamā-bhūmi*), the Immovable Stage (*acalā-bhūmi*), the Stage of Excellent Intelligence (*sādhumatī-bhūmi*), and the Cloud of Dharma Stage (*dharmameghā-bhūmi*), and they also encourage others to cultivate the Stage of Freedom from Defilement up to the Cloud of Dharma Stage."
Having performed this deed, he further made this vow:

"When I attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, may all sentient beings within my buddha-field never be separated from the stages beginning with the Ground of Supreme Joy up to the Ground of the Cloud of Dharma."

"Furthermore, Subhūti! There are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, practicing the perfection of wisdom, give rise to great vows and practice with diligent vigor; they cultivate the five eyes for themselves and also exhort others to cultivate the five eyes;
they cultivate the six supernormal powers for themselves and also exhort others to cultivate the six supernormal powers."
Having performed this deed, he further made this vow:
"When I attain unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, may all sentient beings within my buddha-field never be separated from the five eyes and the six supernormal powers."

"Furthermore, Subhūti, there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, practicing the perfection of wisdom, give rise to great vows and practice with diligence and valor; they personally cultivate the ten powers of a buddha and also exhort others to cultivate the ten powers of a buddha;

they personally cultivate the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha, and also exhort others to cultivate these from the four fearlessnesses up to the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha."
Having performed this deed, he further made this vow:

"When I attain unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, may all sentient beings within my buddha-field never be separated from the ten powers of a Buddha, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha."

"Furthermore, Subhūti, there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, practicing the perfection of wisdom, give rise to great vows and apply themselves with diligence and valor; they personally cultivate the thirty-two marks of a great man and also exhort others to cultivate the thirty-two marks of a great man;
they personally cultivate the eighty secondary signs and also exhort others to cultivate the eighty secondary signs."
Having performed these deeds, he further made this aspiration:

"When I attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, may all sentient beings within my buddha-field never be separated from the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty secondary signs."

"Furthermore, Subhūti, there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who practice the perfection of wisdom, having made great vows and exerting themselves with heroic vigor; they personally cultivate the quality of non-forgetfulness and also encourage others to cultivate the quality of non-forgetfulness;
they personally cultivate the state of constant equanimity and also encourage others to cultivate the state of constant equanimity."
Having performed these deeds, he further made this vow:

"When I attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, may all sentient beings within my buddha-field never be separated from the quality of non-forgetfulness and may they always abide in equanimity."

"Furthermore, Subhūti, there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, practicing the perfection of wisdom, give rise to great vows and exert themselves with courageous vigor; they cultivate all-knowledge for themselves and also encourage others to cultivate all-knowledge;

they cultivate the knowledge of the aspects of the path and all-aspect-knowledge for themselves, and also encourage others to cultivate the knowledge of the aspects of the path and all-aspect-knowledge."
Having performed this deed, he further made this vow:
