"When I attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, may all sentient beings within my buddha-field never be separated from omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*)."

"Furthermore, Subhūti, there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who practice the perfection of wisdom, having made great vows with diligent vigor; they themselves cultivate all the practices of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva and also exhort others to cultivate all the practices of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva;
they themselves cultivate the unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas and also exhort others to cultivate the unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas."
Having performed these deeds, he further made this vow:

"When I attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, may all sentient beings within my buddha-field never be separated from the practices of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and from the unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas."
"Subhūti! These bodhisattva mahāsattvas, practicing the perfection of wisdom, are able to purify the buddha-fields they seek by means of these practices and vows."

"Subhūti! For as long as these bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the path to awakening, they should fulfill the practices and vows they have undertaken; for that same duration, they shall diligently train themselves."

By means of these causes and conditions, one is able to personally accomplish all wholesome dharmas and also enable others to gradually accomplish all wholesome dharmas; one is able to personally cultivate and attain a body adorned with the most excellent marks and signs, and also enable others to gradually cultivate and attain a body adorned with the most excellent marks and signs, because of being sustained by vast merit.

“Subhūti! When each of these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas realizes unexcelled, perfect, and complete awakening in their respective sought-after lands of pure buddhas, the sentient beings they have transformed will also be born in those lands together to enjoy the great Dharma-joy of the pure lands.”
“Subhūti! These bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should cultivate such purification of buddha-fields as this:
that within those fields, the three evil destinies are never heard of, nor are any evil views ever heard of, nor—”
One hears neither of the poisons of greed, hatred, and delusion; nor does one hear of the forms of male or female;
nor does one hear of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas; nor does one hear of suffering, impermanence, and so forth;
nor does one hear of the gathering of requisites; nor does one hear of the grasping at a self or what belongs to a self; nor does one hear...
They hear of neither latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), nor entanglements (*paryavasthāna*), nor fetters (*saṃyojana*);

nor do they hear of inverted attachments, nor of the establishment of the various distinctions of stages for the fruits [of practice]. They hear only the sounds of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), wishlessness (*apraṇihita*), non-arising (*anutpāda*), non-cessation (*anirodha*), and the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*).

This means that according to the diverse inclinations of sentient beings, within external and internal objects such as groves of trees, subtle winds constantly strike against one another, giving rise to various kinds of exquisite sounds.

Within those sounds it is said: "All phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature; because they lack intrinsic nature, they are empty; because they are empty, they are signless; because they are signless, they are wishless; because they are wishless, they are unarisen; because they are unarisen, they are unceasing. Therefore, all phenomena are originally quiescent and by nature in *nirvāṇa*; whether a Buddha appears in the world or does not appear, the nature of phenomena remains ever thus."
"In that buddha-field, all sentient beings—whether by day or by night, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down—constantly hear the sound of such Dharma teachings."

“Subhūti! When these bodhisattva mahāsattvas each realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment in their respective adorned and purified buddha-fields, the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the ten directions will all together praise the names of those various Buddhas. If any sentient beings hear such praised names of the Buddhas, they will certainly attain non-retrogression from unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.”

“Subhūti! When each of these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas attains unexcelled, perfect, and complete awakening within their respective adorned and purified buddha-fields, they shall proclaim the true Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings; having heard it, those beings will certainly not give rise to doubt, wondering whether it is the Dharma or non-Dharma.”

Why is this so? Because those sentient beings have realized that all phenomena are precisely suchness (*tathatā*), the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), the non-illusory nature, and the unchanging nature; that everything is the Dharma and nothing is non-Dharma.
"Subhūti! All these bodhisattva mahāsattvas are able to adorn and purify such buddha-fields.
Furthermore, Subhūti!"

These bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have sentient beings as their objects of conversion who possess unwholesome roots; they have not yet planted roots of virtue under any buddhas, bodhisattvas, pratyekabuddhas, or śrāvakas; because they are influenced by evil friends and separated from virtuous friends, they do not hear the true Dharma; they are constantly gripped and stored within by various views of a self, a sentient being, and other dogmatic positions, falling into the biased attachments of the two extremes of nihilism and eternalism.

These sentient beings give rise to false attachments on their own and also constantly teach others to give rise to false attachments; they conceive the notion of non-Buddha regarding the Buddha, and the notion of Buddha regarding those who are not Buddhas;
they conceive the notion of non-Dharma regarding the Dharma, and the notion of Dharma regarding that which is not the Dharma;
they conceive the notion of non-Saṅgha regarding the Saṅgha, and the notion of Saṅgha regarding those who are not the Saṅgha.

Due to these causes and conditions, they revile the true Dharma; because they slander the true Dharma, at the dissolution of the body after death, they fall into the various evil destinies and are born in the hells to undergo intense suffering.

Once these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have each realized unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment in their own lands, they see those sentient beings sinking and wallowing in saṃsāra, undergoing immeasurable suffering; through the power of their supernormal knowledges and skillful means, they teach and transform them, causing them to abandon evil views and abide in right view, and thus emerge from the hells to be reborn in the human realm.

Having been born into the human realm, they further employ various supernatural powers and skillful means to teach and transform them, causing them to abide within the group of those destined for right determination; by virtue of this, they ultimately never fall into the evil realms.

Furthermore, they cause them to cultivate sublime practices and vows, so that at the end of life they may be reborn in a pure and adorned buddha-field and enjoy the Mahāyāna Dharma-bliss of that pure land.
"Suvikrāntavikrāmin!
All these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are able to thus adorn and purify buddha-fields.

Because the lands they inhabit are utterly pure, the sentient beings born there do not give rise to false, hesitant conceptualizations regarding any phenomena, such as thinking, "This is a mundane dharma;
this is a supramundane dharma," or "This is a contaminated dharma; this is an uncontaminated dharma."
"This is a conditioned phenomenon; this is an unconditioned phenomenon.

Such various hesitations and conceptual discriminations will ultimately not arise. By virtue of these causes and conditions, those classes of sentient beings will certainly attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
“Subhūti! In this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva purifies a buddha-field.
Chapter Seventy-three: Expedient Means for Purifying the Buddha-land, Part One. At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Do these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas abide in the fixed category of right nature (samyaktva-niyāma), or do they abide in the indeterminate category?
The Buddha said:
“Subhūti! These bodhisattva-mahāsattvas all abide in the fixed category of rightness; they do not belong to the indeterminate category.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
In which stage of the fixed destiny of correctness (samyaktva-niyāma) do these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas abide?
Is it that of the śrāvaka vehicle, the pratyekabuddha vehicle, or the buddha vehicle?”
The Buddha said, “Suvikrāntavikrāmin!
These bodhisattva-mahāsattvas all abide in the fixed destiny of the right nature of the Buddha-vehicle; they do not abide in the fixed destiny of the right nature of the two vehicles.”
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
at what time do these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas abide in the fixed determination of the right nature?”
Is it the initial generation of the mind?
Is it the stage of non-retrogression?
Or is it the final body?
The Buddha said, “Subhūti!

Whether it be when a bodhisattva mahāsattva first generates the mind of awakening, when they reach the stage of non-retrogression, or when they are in their final body, they all abide in the fixed category of bodhisattvas.”
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
do those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who abide in the fixed determination of the right nature (samyaktvaniyāma) still fall into the various evil destinies?”
The Buddha said,
“Subhūti! Those bodhisattva mahāsattvas who abide in the fixed category of rightness will certainly never again fall into the evil destinies.”
He further addressed Subhūti: "What do you think?
Is there anyone among those who are eighth-rank practitioners, stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, arhats, or pratyekabuddhas, who would again fall into the miserable realms?"
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One!”
"No, Sugata! the Buddha said.
"Subhūti! It is likewise for all bodhisattva mahāsattvas who abide in the fixed determination of the right nature; they will certainly never again fall into the evil destinies. Why is this?

Subhūti! These bodhisattva mahāsattvas, from their first production of the thought of awakening, practice the perfection of generosity; they practice the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom.

They abide in internal emptiness, and they abide in external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersion emptiness, non-alteration emptiness, essential nature emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common characteristic emptiness, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature.

They practice the four foundations of mindfulness; they practice the four right endeavors, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path;
they abide in the noble truth of suffering, and they abide in the noble truths of its origin, its cessation, and the path;
they practice the four dhyānas, and they practice the four immeasurables and the four formless absorptions.
They practice the eight liberations; they practice the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive concentrations, and the ten totalities;
they practice the gates of dhāraṇī and the gates of samādhi;
they practice the gate of liberation through emptiness, and they practice the gates of liberation through signlessness and wishlessness.

They practice the Ground of Perfect Joy; they practice the Ground of Purity, the Ground of Radiance, the Ground of Blazing Wisdom, the Ground of Difficult Victory, the Ground of Presence, the Ground of Far-Going, the Ground of Immovability, the Ground of Excellent Intelligence, and the Ground of the Dharma Cloud.
They practice the five eyes; they practice the six supernormal powers;

they practice the ten powers of a Buddha; and they practice the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
They practice the quality of non-forgetfulness; they practice the constant abiding in equanimity;
they practice all-knowledge (*sarvajñā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*);
they practice all the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; they practice the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas, subduing and severing all evil and unwholesome dharmas.
“Subhūti! For this reason, it is impossible that these bodhisattva mahāsattvas would fall again into the evil destinies.
It is also impossible that these bodhisattva mahāsattvas would be born in the long-lived heavens, such that the various supreme wholesome dharmas could not be manifested there.”

It is impossible for these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas to be born in remote borderlands, or among the Da-xu or Mlecchas; that is to say, it is impossible for them to be in a place where they cannot practice sublime wholesome dharmas, where they frequently give rise to evil views and do not believe in cause and effect, where they constantly delight in practicing various defiled and evil deeds, and where they do not hear the names of the Buddha, the Dharma, or the Saṅgha, nor where there are the four assemblies—namely, the assembly of bhikṣus, the assembly of bhikṣuṇīs, the assembly of upāsakas, and the assembly of upāsikās.

It is impossible for these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas to be born into families that hold wrong views—that is, to be born into such families where they would cling to various evil perspectives, repudiate wholesome and unwholesome conduct as well as their results, and fail to cultivate virtues while delighting in committing evils.

"Subhūti! It is impossible that bodhisattva mahāsattvas who have first resolved upon unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and who seek to proceed toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, would—with a superior intention—undertake and practice the ten unwholesome paths of action."
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, from the first production of the thought of enlightenment, accomplishes such roots of goodness and merit as these, they will no longer take birth in the various evil realms. For what reason, then, does the World-Honored One frequently recount to the assembly his own past lives—whether numbering a hundred or a thousand—in which he was also born in the various evil realms? At those times, where were his roots of goodness?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“It is not that bodhisattva-mahāsattvas receive bodies in the evil destinies due to impure karma; rather, it is for the sake of benefiting and bringing happiness to all sentient beings that they intentionally and by vow receive such bodies.”

"Subhūti! Do the arhats and pratyekabuddhas possess such skillful means as a bodhisattva mahāsattva, who, having accomplished such skillful means, assumes the body of an animal? When a hunter comes intending to cause them harm, they give rise to unsurpassed patience and compassion; desiring to bring that person benefit and happiness, they sacrifice their own life rather than harming him."

Subhūti! By this cause and condition, you should know that because bodhisattva-mahāsattvas desire to benefit all sentient beings and to swiftly fulfill great compassion, although they manifest in various bodies among the animals, they are not defiled by the faults of animal existence.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
In which wholesome dharmas do the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas abide, such that for the sake of benefiting and bringing happiness to all sentient beings, they assume such a body?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"What wholesome dharmas are there that bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should not bring to fulfillment? Subhūti!"
All bodhisattva mahāsattvas, for the sake of attaining unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, should bring all wholesome dharmas to fulfillment. Subhūti!
From the first generation of the mind of awakening until sitting upon the seat of sublime enlightenment, there is not a single wholesome dharma that they should not fulfill during that interval.

One must fully perfect all wholesome dharmas before attaining unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; it is impossible to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment if even a single wholesome dharma has not been perfected.

Therefore, Subhūti! From the first generation of the mind of awakening until sitting upon the sublime seat of enlightenment, Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas constantly train to perfect all wholesome dharmas. Having so trained, they shall attain the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), forever sever the continuity of all habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), and realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete awakening (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha,
saying: “World-Honored One,
how is it that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having accomplished all such pure, noble, and untainted dharmas, is born in the evil destinies and receives the body of an animal?”
The Buddha said,
“Suvikrāntavikrāmin, what do you think?”
“Has the Tathāgata accomplished all pure, untainted dharmas? Subhūti replied, “It is so!”
"So it is, World-Honored One!
So it is, Sugata!"
“The Tathāgata has accomplished all pure, untainted dharmas.
The Buddha said:
“Suvikrāntavikrāmin!
"What do you think?
Would the Tathāgata, having manifested a body belonging to the animal realm, benefit sentient beings and perform the work of a Buddha? Subhūti replied:
"So it is, World-Honored One! So it is!"
“Sugata! The Tathāgata manifests a body belonging to the animal realm to benefit sentient beings and perform the various works of a Buddha.
The Buddha said:
“Subhūti, what do you think?
When a Tathāgata manifests in the form of an animal, does that animal actually experience its suffering?”
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One!”
"No, Sugata! When the Tathāgata manifests in the form of an animal, he is not actually an animal and does not undergo that suffering."
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“It is just so for all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. Although they have accomplished all pure, untainted dharmas, for the sake of bringing sentient beings to maturity, they employ skillful means to take on the bodies of animals; by taking those bodies, they bring various classes of sentient beings to maturity as appropriate.”
"Furthermore, Subhūti, what do you think?
When an Arhat whose outflows are forever exhausted manifests a transformation body to perform various activities, does that activity produce joy in others?"
Subhūti replied, “So it is, World-Honored One!”
"So it is! Well-gone One!

There are Arhats whose outflows are forever exhausted, who are able to manifest emanated bodies to perform various activities, and by means of those activities, they cause others to give rise to joy."
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"It is the same for all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. Although they have accomplished all pure, untainted dharmas, for the sake of benefiting and bringing happiness to all sentient beings, they employ skillful means to take on bodies in the evil realms. They ripen various classes of sentient beings as appropriate; though they take such bodies, they do not experience the various sufferings and afflictions like those beings, nor are they defiled by the faults of those realms."
"Furthermore, Subhūti, what do you think?

Suppose there were a skilled illusionist or his apprentice who conjured various things such as elephants and horses by means of illusion, causing people to see them and rejoice with leaping joy; would those elephants, horses, and so forth exist in reality?"
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One!”
"No, Sugata! In that place, there are truly no such things as elephants, horses, and so forth."
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"It is just so for all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. Although they have accomplished all pure, untainted dharmas, for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, they manifest by taking on various bodies such as those of animals. Though they take on such bodies, they are in reality not those [beings], nor are they defiled by the faults of those states."
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

The skillful means of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are thus vast and great; although they have accomplished pure, untainted, noble wisdom, for the sake of sentient beings they assume various bodies and manifest benefit according to what is appropriate for them.”

"Bhagavān! In what pure and sublime dharmas do the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas abide, that they are able to exercise such skillful means that, although they assume various bodies among animals and other realms, they are not defiled by their faults?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas abide in the perfection of wisdom, they are able to employ such skillful means that, although they travel to worlds as numerous as the sands of immeasurable Gaṅgā rivers in the ten directions and manifest various bodies to benefit, bring peace, and provide happiness to those sentient beings, they do not give rise to attachment therein."
Why is this? Subhūti!
This bodhisattva mahāsattva does not apprehend any phenomena at all; that is to say, they do not apprehend the defiler, the defiled, nor the causes and conditions of defilement.
Why is this? Because all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature, Subhūti!
Emptiness cannot defile emptiness, nor can emptiness defile other phenomena, nor can any other phenomenon defile emptiness. Why is this so?
Even emptiness itself cannot be apprehended within emptiness, let alone any other dharma that could be apprehended!

Subhūti, this is called the emptiness of the unapprehendable (*anupalambha-śūnyatā*); dwelling within this, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are able to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
do bodhisattva-mahāsattvas perform such skillful means by abiding solely in this perfection of wisdom, or do they also abide in other dharmas?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"Is there any other dharma that does not enter into the perfection of wisdom? Why, then, do you further doubt that one might abide in some other dharma?
Subhūti replied: "World-Honored One!"
If this *prajñāpāramitā* is empty of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnya*), how can the *prajñāpāramitā* encompass all phenomena?
Blessed One,
it cannot be said that there is the encompassing or non-encompassing of phenomena within emptiness.
“Subhūti! Is it not the case that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is empty? “It is so!”
"So it is, Blessed One! So it is, Sugata!"
“Subhūti! If all dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature, would it not be the case that all dharmas are subsumed within emptiness?
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, abide in the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena and thereby elicit the perfection of supernormal powers? How do these bodhisattva mahāsattvas, abiding in this perfection of supernormal powers, travel to immeasurable worlds in the ten directions—equal in number to the sands of the Ganges—to make offerings to the Buddhas, listen to and receive the true Dharma, and plant roots of goodness in the presence of those Buddhas?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he thoroughly contemplates that the infinite worlds of the ten directions—equal in number to the sands of the Ganges—as well as the assemblies of Buddhas and the teachings they proclaim, are all empty of intrinsic nature. There is only conventional, provisional designation by name; yet even such conventional, provisional designations by name are themselves empty of intrinsic nature.”

"Subhūti! If the worlds of the ten directions, the assemblies of Buddhas, and the teachings they proclaim were not empty of intrinsic nature (svabhāva) merely because they are designated by names, then the emptiness that has been taught would not be all-pervasive. Since the emptiness that has been taught is indeed all-pervasive, the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is empty."

“Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, by means of skillful means that universally contemplate emptiness, they are able to bring forth the sublime perfection of supernormal powers. Abiding in this perfection of supernormal powers, they further bring forth the sublime superknowledges of the divine eye, the divine ear, the power of miraculous movement, knowledge of others' minds, recollection of past lives, and the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows.”

"Subhūti! It is not apart from the perfection of supernormal powers that bodhisattva mahāsattvas are able to freely mature sentient beings, purify buddha-fields, and realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

"Subhūti! Therefore, this perfection of supernormal powers is the path to enlightenment. All bodhisattva mahāsattvas rely upon this path to seek and advance toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. While seeking and advancing, they are able to personally fulfill all wholesome dharmas and also enable others to cultivate various wholesome dharmas; yet, while performing these deeds, they do not give rise to attachment toward those wholesome dharmas."

Why is this? It is because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas know that the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all wholesome dharmas is empty; they do not have any attachment to that which is empty by its own nature. If there were attachment, there would be a relish for it; however, because there is no attachment, there is no relish, for within the emptiness of intrinsic nature there is no relish.

“Subhūti! When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he dwells in the supreme perfection of supernormal powers and brings forth the pure divine eye that transcends that of humans; with this divine eye, he perceives that all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature.”

Subhūti! Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva perceives that all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature, they do not perform any karmic actions based on the characteristics of phenomena. Although they teach such a Dharma for the sake of sentient beings, they likewise do not apprehend the characteristics of sentient beings nor the designations applied to them.

Subhūti! This bodhisattva mahāsattva, by means of non-apprehension as a skillful method, brings forth the perfection of supernormal powers; by means of this perfection of supernormal powers, they are able to perform the deeds of supernormal power through compassionate vows.

“Subhūti! By means of the extremely pure divine eye that transcends that of humans, this bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to see immeasurable worlds in the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. Having seen them, he manifests the supernormal power of the knowledge of psychic travel (ṛddhividhi-jñāna-abhijñā) and goes there to benefit sentient beings; he benefits them either by means of the perfection of generosity (dāna-pāramitā), or by means of the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom;

or he benefits them by means of the four foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna), or by means of the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path.”
They may benefit others by means of the four dhyānas; or they may benefit them by means of the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments;
or they may benefit them by means of the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, or the ten totalities;
or they may benefit them by means of the teachings of the śrāvakas, the teachings of the pratyekabuddhas, the teachings of the bodhisattvas, or the teachings of the Buddhas.

“Subhūti! If these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas see sentient beings in the worlds of the ten directions who are largely characterized by stinginess and greed, they give rise to deep compassion and preach the Dharma to them as follows:

‘You sentient beings should practice giving. Those who are stingy and greedy suffer the misery of poverty; because of poverty, they lack majesty and virtue, such that they cannot even benefit themselves, let alone others!’”

Therefore, you all should diligently practice giving; by doing so, you will bring peace and happiness to yourselves as well as to others. Do not, out of poverty, devour one another, for in that way neither of you will be liberated from the sufferings of the evil realms.

“Suvikrāntavikrāmin! If these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas see sentient beings in the worlds of the ten directions who have violated the pure precepts, they give rise to deep compassion and preach the Dharma to them in this way:

‘You sentient beings should uphold the pure precepts. Those who break the precepts undergo the suffering of the evil realms; a person who breaks the precepts possesses no majestic virtue, being unable to benefit even themselves, let alone others!’”

Due to the causes and conditions of breaking the precepts, one may be reborn in hell to undergo the ripening of suffering, or be reborn among animals to undergo the ripening of suffering, or be reborn in the realm of hungry ghosts to undergo the ripening of suffering.
If you fall into the various evil realms and must undergo the ripening of suffering there, you will not even be able to save yourselves, let alone others!
Therefore, you should maintain pure ethical discipline; you should not allow a mind of broken precepts to remain for even a single moment, much less for a long time!
"Do not give rein to your own minds, lest you later give rise to sorrow and regret. "Subhūti!

If this bodhisattva mahāsattva sees sentient beings in the worlds of the ten directions who are further incited by mutual anger and resentment, harboring grudges against one another and harming each other, he gives rise to deep compassion and teaches them the Dharma in this way:"

"You sentient beings should cultivate patience; do not harbor mutual anger, resentment, or malice toward one another. All hearts of anger and resentment are contrary to wholesome dharmas; they increase unwholesome dharmas and bring about decline and loss in the present life."

Because of this mind of hatred and resentment, when your bodies perish and your lives end, you shall fall into the realms of hell, animals, or hungry ghosts to undergo various intense sufferings; therefore, you should not allow a mind of hatred and resentment to remain for even a single moment, much less let it continue for a long duration!
"You all should now give rise to a mind of loving-kindness, and by taking one another as objects of focus, perform deeds that bring mutual benefit. "Suvīra!
If these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas see sentient beings in the worlds of the ten directions who are indolent and lazy, they will generate deep compassion and preach the Dharma to them in this way:

"You sentient beings, you should apply yourselves with diligent vigor; do not be indolent or lax regarding wholesome dharmas. Those who are indolent will be unable to accomplish any wholesome dharmas or any sublime matters."

By this, you shall fall into the realms of hell, animals, or hungry ghosts and undergo immeasurable suffering; therefore, you should not entertain this lazy mind for even a single moment, much less allow it to continue for a long duration!

“Subhūti! If this bodhisattva mahāsattva sees sentient beings in the worlds of the ten directions who have lost mindfulness, whose minds are distracted, and whose hearts are not tranquil, he gives rise to deep compassion and teaches them this Dharma:

‘You sentient beings should cultivate meditative concentration (dhyāna). Do not give rise to thoughts of lost mindfulness or distraction; such states of mind do not accord with wholesome dharmas, but increase unwholesome dharmas and bring about present decline and loss.’”

Because of this, when your bodies disintegrate and your lives end, you shall fall into the realms of hell, animals, or hungry ghosts to undergo immeasurable suffering; therefore, you should not allow a mind associated with forgetfulness and distraction to persist for even a single moment, much less for a long duration.

"Subhūti! If these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas see sentient beings in the worlds of the ten directions who are foolish and possessed of evil wisdom, they give rise to deep compassion and teach them this Dharma:

'You sentient beings should cultivate superior wisdom and not give rise to evil wisdom; for those who give rise to evil wisdom cannot even go to the various happy realms, let alone attain liberation!'"

By reason of this unwholesome wisdom, you shall fall into the realms of hell, animals, or hungry ghosts and undergo immeasurable suffering; therefore, you should not allow a mind associated with such deluded and unwholesome wisdom to endure for even a single moment, much less permit it to continue in succession for a long time.

"Subhūti! If this bodhisattva mahāsattva sees sentient beings in the worlds of the ten directions who have much greed and desire, he gives rise to deep compassion and skillfully instructs them to practice the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*).

If he sees sentient beings who have much anger and hatred, he gives rise to deep compassion and skillfully instructs them to practice the contemplation of loving-kindness and compassion (*maitrī-karuṇā-bhāvanā*)."
If he sees sentient beings who have much ignorance, he gives rise to deep compassion and provides skillful instruction, leading them to practice the contemplation of dependent origination;
if he sees sentient beings who have much pride, he gives rise to deep compassion and provides skillful instruction, leading them to practice the contemplation of the analysis of the elements;

if he sees sentient beings who have much discursive thought and investigation, he gives rise to deep compassion and provides skillful instruction, leading them to practice the contemplation of mindfulness of breathing.

If they see sentient beings practicing on deviant paths, they give rise to deep compassion and provide skillful instruction to lead them onto the right path—whether the path of the śrāvaka, the path of the pratyekabuddha, or the path of the Tathāgata—and skillfully teach them this Dharma:
"The intrinsic nature you grasp at is entirely empty; within the dharma of emptiness there can be nothing to grasp, for the characteristic of emptiness consists in the absence of anything to grasp."

"In this way, Subhūti! When bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom, they must abide in the perfection of supernormal powers (*abhijñāpāramitā*) before they can freely proclaim the true Dharma to benefit, bring peace, and happiness to all sentient beings."

"Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva remains far removed from the perfection of supernormal powers (abhijñā-pāramitā), they will be unable to freely proclaim the true Dharma and bring about the welfare of sentient beings."

"Subhūti! Just as a bird without wings cannot fly freely through the air to reach distant places, so it is with bodhisattva-mahāsattvas: if they lack the perfection of supernormal powers (*abhijñā-pāramitā*), they cannot freely proclaim the sublime Dharma or perform beneficial deeds for all sentient beings."

Therefore, Subhūti, when bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom, they should bring forth the perfection of the superknowledges (abhijñā). If they bring forth the perfection of the superknowledges, they will be able to proclaim the true Dharma at will, thereby benefiting and bringing peace and happiness to all sentient beings.

"Subhūti! This bodhisattva mahāsattva, with the most pure divine eye that transcends that of humans, surveys throughout the ten directions immeasurable worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, as well as the sentient beings born therein. Having seen them, he exercises the supernormal power of the knowledge of miraculous feats (*ṛddhividhi-jñāna-abhijñā*), arriving in those realms in a mere moment. With the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*), he understands, as they truly are, the minds and mental factors (*citta-caitasika-dharma*) of those sentient beings. According to what is appropriate for them, he expounds the essentials of the Dharma—namely, he speaks of generosity (*dāna*), or ethical discipline (*śīla*), or patience (*kṣānti*), or diligence (*vīrya*), or meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), or wisdom (*prajñā*);

or he speaks of the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), or the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*), the four bases of power (*ṛddhipāda*), the five faculties (*indriya*), the five powers (*bala*), the seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), and the eightfold noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*)."
Some speak of the four dhyānas; some speak of the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments;
some speak of the eight liberations; some speak of the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities;
some speak of the gates of dhāraṇī; and some speak of the gates of samādhi.
Sometimes he speaks of the gate of liberation of emptiness; sometimes he speaks of the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness.

Sometimes he speaks of internal emptiness; or he speaks of external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersion emptiness, non-alteration emptiness, essential nature emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common characteristic emptiness, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature.
Sometimes he speaks of the noble truth of suffering; or he speaks of the noble truths of origin, cessation, and the path.
Sometimes he speaks of causes and conditions; sometimes he speaks of the immediately preceding condition, the object-condition, and the dominant condition;
sometimes he speaks of all phenomena produced from conditions;

sometimes he speaks of ignorance; or he speaks of volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, existence, birth, and old age, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair.
Some speak of the aggregates, the sense bases, and the elements;
some speak of the path of the śrāvakas, some of the path of the pratyekabuddhas, or some of the path of the bodhisattvas;
some speak of awakening, or some speak of nirvāṇa.
"Having caused those sentient beings to hear this Dharma, they all obtain supreme benefit and peace. Subhūti!
By means of the most pure divine ear that transcends that of humans and gods, these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are able to hear the voices of all humans and non-humans."

By means of this divine ear, one is able to hear the Buddhas of the ten directions preaching the Dharma in immeasurable worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; having heard them, one is able to receive and uphold them all without error, and proclaims them to sentient beings exactly as they are—whether teaching generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, or wisdom, and so on, up to teaching nirvāṇa—so that those sentient beings, having heard these teachings, may all attain supreme benefit and peace.

“Subhūti! By means of the most pure supernormal power of knowing the minds of others, this bodhisattva mahāsattva truly understands the minds and mental factors of all sentient beings. According to what is appropriate for them, he teaches the essentials of the Dharma—whether teaching generosity, or ethical discipline, or patience, or diligence, or meditative concentration, or wisdom, and so on, up to teaching nirvāṇa. Having heard these teachings, those sentient beings all obtain supreme benefit and peace.”

“Subhūti! By means of the supernormal power of recollecting past lives with purified knowledge, this bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to remember the various events of his own and others’ previous births.

Through this supernormal power of recollecting past lives, he truly remembers and knows the names and other distinctions of the Buddhas of the past and their assemblies of disciples. If there are sentient beings who would benefit by hearing accounts of past lives, he then proclaims those accounts of past lives for them. By this skillful means, he teaches the True Dharma—whether it be speaking of generosity, or ethical discipline, or patience, or diligence, or meditative concentration, or wisdom, and so on, up to speaking of nirvāṇa—so that once those sentient beings have heard this Dharma, they all obtain supreme benefit and peace.”

“Subhūti! By means of the extremely swift supernormal power of the knowledge of the movement of the mind, these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas travel to worlds in the ten directions as numerous as the sands of immeasurable Gaṅgā rivers. There they approach and make offerings to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, and having planted various roots of virtue in the presence of those Buddhas, they return to their own lands. For the sake of sentient beings, they proclaim the various superior matters of other regions; through these skillful means, they preach the True Dharma—whether preaching on generosity, or pure ethical discipline, or patience, or diligence, or meditative concentration, or wisdom, and so on, even up to preaching on nirvāṇa. Once those sentient beings have heard this Dharma, they all attain supreme benefit and peace.”

“Subhūti! By means of the supernormal power of the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows as it has been attained, this bodhisattva mahāsattva knows, in accordance with reality, whether sentient beings have exhausted their outflows or not; he also knows, in accordance with reality, the expedient means for the exhaustion of outflows. For those who have not yet exhausted them, he proclaims the essentials of the Dharma—whether teaching generosity, or ethical discipline, or patience, or diligence, or meditative concentration, or wisdom, and so on, up to teaching nirvāṇa—so that once those sentient beings have heard this Dharma, they all obtain supreme benefit and peace.”
"In this way, Subhūti, when bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom, they should bring forth the perfection of supernormal powers."

Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva has cultivated the perfection of supernormal powers (*abhijñā-pāramitā*) to completion, they assume various bodies according to their wishes, yet are not defiled by the faults of suffering or pleasure; just as the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) of a Buddha can perform all manner of activities without being tainted by those faults of suffering or pleasure.

“Subhūti! When bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom, they should sport in the perfection of supernormal powers. If they sport in the perfection of supernormal powers, they will be able to bring sentient beings to maturity, purify buddha-fields, and swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.”

"Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not bring sentient beings to maturity and purify buddha-fields, they will ultimately be unable to attain the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment they seek."
Why is this? Subhūti!
If the bodhisattva mahāsattvas have not yet fully gathered the provisions for enlightenment, they will certainly be unable to attain the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening that they seek.

The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle 394. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Part One: The Chapter on the Expedient Means for Purifying the Buddha-field, Number Seventy-three, Part Two. At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”

What are called the provisions for enlightenment of a bodhisattva mahāsattva? By what means must bodhisattva mahāsattvas fully equip themselves with these provisions for enlightenment in order to realize the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment they seek?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"All wholesome dharmas are the provisions for enlightenment of a bodhisattva mahāsattva. Only by fully possessing such provisions for enlightenment can a bodhisattva mahāsattva realize the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment that they seek."
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What are called all wholesome dharmas, by virtue of which all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, having accomplished such wholesome dharmas, realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"From the first generation of the mind of awakening, all bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the perfection of generosity, and they practice the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, yet within these they have no conceptualization or attachment, such that they think:
'This is generosity and so forth; it is by means of this and for the sake of this that I practice generosity and the rest.'"
These three types of conceptualization and attachment are all absent, because one knows that the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena is empty.

Consequently, the *pāramitās* thus cultivated are able to benefit oneself and also benefit all sentient beings, causing them to transcend birth and death and attain *nirvāṇa*. Therefore, they are called "wholesome dharmas" (*kuśala-dharma*), are also termed the "requisites for a bodhisattva’s enlightenment" (*bodhisambhāra*), and are also termed the "path of a bodhisattva mahāsattva."

Because the assemblies of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas of the past, future, and present practice this path, they have already attained, will attain, and are now attaining unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; furthermore, they have already caused, will cause, and are now causing sentient beings to cross the great ocean of birth and death and realize the bliss of nirvāṇa.

“Subhūti! From the first production of the thought of enlightenment, bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the four foundations of mindfulness, and they practice the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path. Throughout all of this, they have no conceptualization or attachment, such that they would think:
‘These are the four foundations of mindfulness and so forth; it is by means of these and for the sake of these that I practice the four foundations of mindfulness and so forth.’”
These three types of conceptualization and attachment are all non-existent, because one knows that the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena is empty.

Consequently, the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) and other practices thus cultivated can benefit oneself and also benefit all sentient beings, causing them to transcend birth and death and attain *nirvāṇa*. Therefore, they are called "wholesome dharmas" (*kuśala-dharma*), are termed the "provisions for a bodhisattva’s enlightenment" (*bodhi-sambhāra*), and are also termed the "path of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva."

Because the assemblies of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas of the past, future, and present practice this path, they have already attained, will attain, and are now attaining unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment; furthermore, they have already, will, and are now delivering sentient beings across the great ocean of birth and death, causing them to realize the bliss of nirvāṇa.

“Subhūti! From their first production of the mind of awakening, bodhisattva mahāsattvas abide in internal emptiness; they abide in external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, non-altering emptiness, essential emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common-characteristic emptiness, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence. Within these, they have no conceptual discrimination or attachment, such that they think:
‘This is internal emptiness and so forth; it is by means of this and for the sake of this that I abide in internal emptiness and the others.’”
These three types of conceptualization and attachment are all absent, because one knows that the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena is empty.

By means of this, the internal emptiness (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*) and so forth in which one dwells can benefit oneself and also benefit all sentient beings, causing them to emerge from birth and death (*saṃsāra*) and attain *nirvāṇa*. Therefore, these are called wholesome dharmas (*kuśala-dharma*), and they are also termed the bodhisattva’s provisions for enlightenment (*bodhi-sambhāra*), as well as the path (*mārga*) of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.

Because the assemblies of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas of the past, future, and present practice this path, they have already attained, will attain, and are now attaining unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; furthermore, they have caused, will cause, and are now causing sentient beings to cross the great ocean of birth and death and realize the bliss of nirvāṇa.

"Subhūti! From the first production of the thought of enlightenment, bodhisattva mahāsattvas abide in the noble truth of suffering, and they abide in the noble truths of origination, cessation, and the path; yet within these, they have no conceptualization or attachment, such that they would think:
'This is the noble truth of suffering,' or 'For this reason and for this purpose I abide in the noble truth of suffering,' and so forth."
These three types of conceptualization and attachment are all non-existent, because one knows that the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena is empty.

By means of this, the Noble Truth of Suffering and the others in which one abides can benefit oneself and also benefit all sentient beings, causing them to transcend birth and death and attain *nirvāṇa*; therefore, they are called "wholesome dharmas" (*kuśala-dharma*), are also named the "requisites for a bodhisattva’s enlightenment" (*bodhisambhāra*), and are also named the "path of a bodhisattva mahāsattva."

Because the assemblies of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas of the past, future, and present practice this path, they have already attained, will attain, and are now attaining unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening; furthermore, they have caused, will cause, and are now causing sentient beings to cross the great ocean of birth and death and realize the bliss of nirvāṇa.

“Subhūti! From the first production of the thought of enlightenment, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the four dhyānas and practice the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments, yet they have no conceptual discrimination or attachment therein, such that they would think:
‘These are the four dhyānas and so forth; it is for this reason and for this purpose that I practice the four dhyānas and so forth.’”
These three types of conceptualization and attachment are all absent, because one knows that the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena is empty.

By means of this, the four meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) and other practices that are cultivated can benefit oneself and also benefit all sentient beings, causing them to transcend birth and death and attain *nirvāṇa*. Therefore, they are called "wholesome dharmas" (*kuśala-dharma*), are also termed the "requisites for a bodhisattva’s enlightenment" (*bodhisambhāra*), and are also termed the "path of a bodhisattva mahāsattva."

Because the assemblies of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas of the past, future, and present practice this path, they have already attained, will attain, and are now attaining unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment; furthermore, they have caused, will cause, and are now causing sentient beings to cross the great ocean of birth and death and realize the bliss of nirvāṇa.

“Subhūti! From the first production of the thought of enlightenment, bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive absorptions, and the ten totalities; yet within these they have no conceptual discrimination or attachment, such that they would think:
‘These are the eight liberations, etc.; for this reason and for this purpose I am practicing the eight liberations, etc.’”
These three types of conceptualization and attachment are all absent, because one knows that the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena is empty.

Consequently, the eight liberations and other practices thus cultivated can benefit oneself and also benefit all sentient beings by causing them to transcend birth and death and attain *nirvāṇa*. Therefore, they are called "wholesome dharmas" (*kuśala-dharma*), are also termed the "requisites for a bodhisattva’s enlightenment" (*bodhisambhāra*), and are further termed the "path of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva."

Because the assemblies of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas of the past, future, and present practice this path, they have already attained, will attain, and are now attaining unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening; furthermore, they have caused, will cause, and are now causing sentient beings to cross the great ocean of birth and death and realize the bliss of nirvāṇa.

“Subhūti! From the first generation of the mind of awakening, bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the gateways of dhāraṇī and practice the gateways of samādhi, yet within these they have no conceptual discrimination or attachment, such that they think:
‘These are the gateways of dhāraṇī and so forth; it is for this purpose and by means of this that I practice the gateways of dhāraṇī and so forth.’”
These three types of conceptualization and attachment are all non-existent, because one knows that the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena is empty.

Consequently, the *dhāraṇī* gates and other practices cultivated thereby can benefit oneself and also benefit all sentient beings, causing them to transcend birth and death and attain *nirvāṇa*. Therefore, they are called "wholesome dharmas" (*kuśala-dharma*), are also termed the "requisites for a bodhisattva’s enlightenment" (*bodhisambhāra*), and are further termed the "path of a bodhisattva mahāsattva."

Because the assemblies of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas of the past, future, and present practice this path, they have already attained, will attain, and are now attaining unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening; furthermore, they have caused, will cause, and are now causing sentient beings to cross the great ocean of birth and death and realize the bliss of nirvāṇa.

“Subhūti! From the first production of the thought of enlightenment, bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the gate of liberation of emptiness and practice the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness, yet they have no conceptualization or attachment therein, such that they think:
‘This is the gate of liberation of emptiness and so forth; for this reason and for this purpose, I am practicing the gate of liberation of emptiness and so forth.’”
These three kinds of conceptualization and attachment are all non-existent, because one knows that the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena is empty.

By means of this, the cultivation of the gate of liberation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vimokṣamukha*) and so forth can benefit oneself and also benefit all sentient beings, causing them to transcend birth and death and attain *nirvāṇa*. Therefore, these are called wholesome dharmas (*kuśala-dharma*), are also termed the provisions for a bodhisattva’s enlightenment (*bodhisambhāra*), and are also termed the path of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva.

Because the assemblies of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas of the past, future, and present practice this path, they have already attained, will attain, and are now attaining unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment; furthermore, they have already caused, will cause, and are now causing sentient beings to cross the great ocean of birth and death and realize the bliss of nirvāṇa.
“Suvikrāntavikrāmin!

From the first production of the thought of enlightenment, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the Stage of Extreme Joy, the Stage of Freedom from Defilement, the Radiant Stage, the Stage of Blazing Wisdom, the Stage Difficult to Conquer, the Manifest Stage, the Far-Reaching Stage, the Immovable Stage, the Stage of Excellent Intelligence, and the Cloud of Dharma. Throughout all these, they have no conceptual discrimination or attachment, such that they would think:
‘This is the Stage of Extreme Joy,’ or ‘For this reason and for this purpose, I am practicing the Stage of Extreme Joy and the other stages.’”
These three types of conceptualization and attachment are all non-existent, because one knows that the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena is empty.

By means of this, the stages such as the Ground of Supreme Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*) which are cultivated can benefit oneself and also benefit all sentient beings, causing them to transcend birth and death and attain *nirvāṇa*. Therefore, they are called "wholesome dharmas" (*kuśala-dharma*), are also termed the "provisions for Bodhi" (*bodhisambhāra*) of a Bodhisattva, and are also termed the "path" (*mārga*) of a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva.

Because the assemblies of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas of the past, future, and present practice this path, they have already attained, will attain, and are now attaining unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; and they have caused, will cause, and are now causing sentient beings to cross the great ocean of birth and death and realize the bliss of nirvāṇa.

“Subhūti! From the first production of the thought of enlightenment, bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the five eyes and practice the six supernormal powers, yet they have no conceptualization or attachment therein, such that they would think:
‘These are the five eyes, etc.; it is by means of these and for the sake of these that I practice the five eyes, etc.’”
These three types of conceptualization and attachment are all absent, because one knows that the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena is empty.

Consequently, the five eyes and other qualities thus cultivated can benefit oneself and also benefit all sentient beings, causing them to transcend birth and death and attain nirvāṇa; therefore, they are called "wholesome dharmas" (*kuśala-dharma*), are also termed the "provisions for bodhi" (*bodhi-sambhāra*) of a bodhisattva, and are further termed the "path" (*mārga*) of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.

Because the assemblies of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas of the past, future, and present practice this path, they have already attained, will attain, and are now attaining unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment; furthermore, they have already caused, will cause, and are now causing sentient beings to cross the great ocean of birth and death and realize the bliss of nirvāṇa.

“Subhūti! From the first production of the thought of enlightenment, bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the ten powers of a Buddha, practice the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; yet within all these, they have no conceptualization or attachment, such that they would think:
‘These are the ten powers of a Buddha and so forth; for this reason and for this purpose, I practice the ten powers of a Buddha and so forth.’”
These three types of conceptualization and attachment are all non-existent, because one knows that the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena is empty.

Consequently, the ten powers of a Buddha and other qualities thus cultivated can benefit oneself and also benefit all sentient beings, causing them to transcend birth and death and attain *nirvāṇa*. Therefore, they are called "wholesome dharmas" (*kuśala-dharma*), are also termed the "provisions for a bodhisattva’s enlightenment" (*bodhisambhāra*), and are also termed the "path of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva."

Because the assemblies of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas of the past, future, and present practice this path, they have already attained, will attain, and are now attaining unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; furthermore, they have caused, will cause, and are now causing sentient beings to cross the great ocean of birth and death and realize the bliss of nirvāṇa.

“Subhūti! From the first production of the thought of enlightenment, bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the quality of non-forgetfulness and practice the state of constant equanimity, yet within these they have no conceptualization or attachment, such that they would think:
‘This is the quality of non-forgetfulness and so forth; for this reason and for this purpose, I am practicing the quality of non-forgetfulness and so forth.’”
These three types of conceptualization and attachment are all absent, because one knows that the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena (*dharma*) is empty.

By means of this, the practice of the non-forgetfulness of the Dharma and other such qualities can benefit oneself and also benefit all sentient beings, causing them to transcend birth and death and attain *nirvāṇa*. Therefore, they are called "wholesome dharmas" (*kuśala-dharma*), are also termed the "requisites for a bodhisattva’s enlightenment" (*bodhisambhāra*), and are further termed the "path of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva."

Because the assemblies of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas of the past, future, and present practice this path, they have already attained, will attain, and are now attaining unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; furthermore, they have caused, will cause, and are now causing sentient beings to cross the great ocean of birth and death and realize the bliss of nirvāṇa.

“Subhūti! From the first generation of the mind of awakening, bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*). Within this, they have no conceptualization or attachment, such that they would think:
‘This is all-knowledge and so forth; it is by means of this and for the sake of this that I practice all-knowledge and so forth.’”
These three types of conceptualization and attachment are all non-existent, for one knows that the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena is empty.

Because of this, the cultivation of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) and so forth can benefit oneself and also benefit all sentient beings, enabling them to transcend birth and death and attain *nirvāṇa*. Therefore, these are called wholesome dharmas (*kuśala-dharma*), and they are also termed the bodhisattva’s provisions for enlightenment (*bodhi-sambhāra*) and the path of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva.

Because the multitudes of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas of the past, future, and present practice this path, they have already attained, will attain, and are now attaining unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment; furthermore, they have already caused, will cause, and are now causing sentient beings to cross the great ocean of birth and death and realize the bliss of nirvāṇa.

"Subhūti! You should know that there are further immeasurable multitudes of bodhisattvas whose cultivated merits are all called wholesome dharmas, are also called the provisions for the enlightenment of a bodhisattva, and are also called the path of a bodhisattva mahāsattva."

All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas must cultivate such sublime and virtuous dharmas until they are perfectly fulfilled before they can realize the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*); only after having realized the knowledge of all modes can they turn the wheel of the true Dharma without error, enabling all sentient beings to be liberated from birth and death and to realize the ultimate, eternal bliss of nirvāṇa.
Chapter Seventy-Four: The Nature of Non-Nature, Part One. Chapter Seventy-Four, Part One: The Nature of Non-Nature. At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"If such dharmas as these are the dharmas of a bodhisattva, then what further dharmas are the dharmas of a Buddha?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"Regarding that which you have asked:"
"If such dharmas as these are the dharmas of a bodhisattva, what other dharmas are the dharmas of a Buddha?
Subhūti, it is that very dharma of a bodhisattva which is also the dharma of a Buddha.

This refers to how Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas awaken to all aspects of all phenomena; by means of this, they shall attain the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) and forever sever the continuity of all habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).

Furthermore, when Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas have attained manifest and perfect awakening regarding all phenomena through the sublime wisdom corresponding to a single moment, they realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).

"Subhūti! Thus, there is a difference between such a bodhisattva and a Buddha, just as there is between two noble ones who, though both are noble, differ in that one is practicing toward the goal while the other abides in the fruit."
Thus it is, Subhūti!

When one is practicing within the path of uninterrupted transition regarding all phenomena, yet has not yet abandoned the obscuration of darkness, has not yet reached the further shore, has not yet attained mastery, and has not yet realized the fruit—at that time, one is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva.

When one practices within all phenomena during the path of liberation, having already abandoned the obscuration of darkness, having reached the further shore, having attained mastery, and having realized the fruit, one is called a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.
"Subhūti! This is how a bodhisattva differs from a Buddha; although their positions differ, there is no distinction in their dharmas.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:

“Bhagavān! If all phenomena are empty of their own characteristics (*svalakṣaṇaśūnya*), how can there be various distinctions within this emptiness of own-characteristics—namely, ‘this is hell,’ ‘this is the animal realm,’ ‘this is the realm of hungry ghosts,’ ‘this is a deva,’ ‘this is a human,’ ‘this is the stage of the lineage (*gotrabhūmi*),’ ‘this is the eighth stage (*aṣṭamaka*),’ ‘this is a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*),’ ‘this is a once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*),’ ‘this is a non-returner (*anāgāmin*),’ ‘this is an arhat,’ ‘this is a pratyekabuddha,’ ‘this is a bodhisattva mahāsattva,’ or ‘this is a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha’?”

"Bhagavān! Since such a person (pudgala) as you have described cannot be found, the karma they create also cannot be found; and since that karma cannot be found, its maturation fruit (vipākaphala) likewise cannot be found."
The Buddha told Subhūti: “So it is! So it is!”
It is as you have said:
all phenomena are empty of intrinsic characteristics; within the emptiness of intrinsic characteristics, there is no person, no karma performed, and no distinct ripening fruits to be found.

However, sentient beings are unable to fully comprehend the principle that all phenomena are empty of intrinsic characteristics; due to this cause and condition, they perform various karmas—namely, creating sinful karma, or creating meritorious karma, or creating immovable karma, or creating untainted karma.
Because of creating sinful karma, one may fall into the hells, or into the realm of animals, or into the realm of hungry ghosts;
because of creating meritorious karma, one may be born in the human realm, or among the gods of the desire realm;
because of creating immovable karma, one may be born in the form realm, or in the formless realm.
By performing untainted karma (*anāsrava-karman*), one may attain the fruit of a śrāvaka or the fruit of a pratyekabuddha.

If one knows that the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena are empty, one may enter the stage of a bodhisattva mahāsattva or realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).

"By means of these causes and conditions, bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the perfection of generosity, and they practice the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, wisdom, skillful means, aspiration, power, and knowledge;

they abide in internal emptiness, and they abide in external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, non-alteration emptiness, essential emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common-characteristic emptiness, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature."

They practice the four foundations of mindfulness; they practice the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path;
they abide in the noble truth of suffering, and they abide in the noble truths of origination, cessation, and the path;
they practice the four dhyānas, and they practice the four immeasurables and the four formless absorptions.
They practice the eight liberations; they practice the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive concentrations, and the ten totalities;
they practice the gates of dhāraṇī, and they practice the gates of samādhi;
they practice the gate of the liberation of emptiness, and they practice the gates of the liberations of signlessness and wishlessness.

They practice the Ground of Utmost Joy; they practice the Ground of Purity, the Ground of Radiance, the Ground of Blazing Wisdom, the Ground of Extreme Difficulty to Conquer, the Ground of Presence, the Ground of Far-Going, the Ground of Immovability, the Ground of Excellent Intelligence, and the Ground of the Dharma Cloud;
they practice the five eyes; they practice the six supernormal powers;

they practice the ten powers of a Buddha; and they practice the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
They practice the dharma of non-forgetfulness; they practice the state of constant abiding in equanimity;
they practice all-knowledge (*sarvajñā*); and they practice the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*) and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).

“Subhūti! This bodhisattva mahāsattva cultivates these factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma) without interruption or deficiency until they are perfected. Once they have attained perfection, he is able to evoke the diamond-like concentration (vajropamasamādhi) that directly assists awakening, and realizes unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. He is then designated as a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, who brings benefit, peace, and happiness to immeasurable sentient beings. Whatever he undertakes is always free from failure; because it is free from failure, he does not fall into the cycle of rebirth within the various realms of saṃsāra.”
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
Having realized unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, has the Buddha attained the dharmas of birth and death within the various realms of existence?"
"No, World-Honored One!
[It is not so], Subhūti.
"World-Honored One! [Subhūti replied.]
“After the Buddha has realized unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, does he thereby acquire black karma, white karma, both black and white karma, or neither-black-nor-white karma? “No, he does not.”
"Excellent, Subhūti!
Then, the Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

If the Buddha does not perceive the various realms of rebirth, birth and death, or the distinctions among karmas, how could he designate: "this is hell," "this is the animal realm," "this is the realm of hungry ghosts," "this is a deva," "this is a human," "this is a caste," "this is an eighth-person," "this is a stream-enterer," "this is a once-returner," "this is a non-returner," "this is an arhat," "this is a pratyekabuddha," "this is a bodhisattva mahāsattva," or "this is a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha"?
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
“Do sentient beings know for themselves that the self-characteristics of all phenomena are empty? Subhūti replied:
"No, World-Honored One! No!"
“Excellent, Sugata!
The Buddha said,
“Excellent, Subhūti!”

If all sentient beings were to know for themselves that the specific characteristics of all phenomena are empty, then it would not be necessary to say that the bodhisattva mahāsattva seeks to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and through skillful means establishes the ultimate teaching to extract sentient beings from the evil destinies and the cycle of birth and death.

"Subhūti! Because sentient beings do not know that all phenomena are empty of their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-śūnya*), they transmigrate through the various realms of existence and undergo immeasurable suffering. Therefore, after bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have heard from the Buddhas that all phenomena are empty of their own specific characteristics, they seek to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; through skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), they establish the ultimate teaching to extract sentient beings from the cycle of birth and death within the evil realms."
"Subhūti! All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas constantly maintain this thought:

'All dharmas do not possess real intrinsic characteristics as they are grasped by foolish ordinary beings; rather, through the power of their inverted conceptualization, they give rise to the perception of reality within what is not real. That is to say, they give rise to the notion of a self within what is non-self; and they give rise to the notions of a sentient being, a life-force, a nourisher, a soul, a person, an individual, a mind-born, a youth, an agent, an experiencer, a knower, and a seer, within what is devoid of a sentient being and so forth, up to a seer.'"

To give rise to the perception of form within the formless; to give rise to the perceptions of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness within that which is devoid of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness;

to give rise to the perception of the sense-base of the eye within the absence of the sense-base of the eye; to give rise to the perceptions of the sense-bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind within the absence of the sense-bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind;

to give rise to the perception of the sense-base of forms within the absence of the sense-base of forms; and to give rise to the perceptions of the sense-bases of sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects within the absence of the sense-bases of sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects.

Within the absence of the eye-element, they give rise to the perception of an eye-element; within the absence of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-elements, they give rise to the perception of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-elements.

Within the absence of the form-element, they give rise to the perception of a form-element; within the absence of the sound, odor, taste, tangible, and mental-object elements, they give rise to the perception of the sound, odor, taste, tangible, and mental-object elements.

Within the absence of the eye-consciousness-element, they give rise to the perception of an eye-consciousness-element; within the absence of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-consciousness elements, they give rise to the perception of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-consciousness elements.

One conceives the notion of eye-contact where there is no eye-contact; one conceives the notions of ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact where there is no ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-contact.
One conceives the notion of feelings produced with eye-contact as their condition where there are no feelings produced with eye-contact as their condition;

one conceives the notions of feelings produced with ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact as their conditions where there are no feelings produced with ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-contact as their conditions.

One conceives the notion of the earth element within that which is not the earth element; one conceives the notions of the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements within that which is not the water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness elements;

one conceives the notion of causal conditions within that which is not causal conditions; one conceives the notions of the immediately preceding condition, the object-condition, and the dominant condition within that which is not the immediately preceding condition, the object-condition, or the dominant condition;
and one conceives the notion of phenomena produced from conditions within that which is not phenomena produced from conditions.

To conceive the notion of ignorance where there is no ignorance; to conceive the notions of volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, becoming, birth, and old age, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair where there are no such things;
