because mundane phenomena are ungraspable, and supramundane phenomena are likewise ungraspable.
Because contaminated phenomena (*sāsravadharma*) are ungraspable, and uncontaminated phenomena (*anāsravadharma*) are also ungraspable;
because conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) are ungraspable, and unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*) are also ungraspable.
“Having realized that all phenomena are ungraspable, these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas seek to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Why is this so?

Because all phenomena are ungraspable and entirely devoid of substantial reality, they are like what is seen in a dream, like a reflection, like an echo, like a mirage, like a shadow, like a magical illusion, like a transformation body, and like a city of Gandharvas.

A dharma that cannot be grasped cannot realize a dharma that cannot be grasped; yet, because sentient beings do not know or see such dharmas, these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas seek to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment in order to deliver those sentient beings.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

From the first production of the thought of enlightenment, this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of generosity for the sake of benefiting and bringing happiness to all sentient beings; he does not do so for his own sake, nor for any other purpose.
For the sake of benefiting and bringing happiness to all sentient beings, he practices the perfection of ethical discipline; he does not do so for his own sake, nor for any other purpose."
For the sake of benefiting and bringing happiness to all sentient beings, they practice the perfection of patience, not for their own sake and not for any other purpose;
for the sake of benefiting and bringing happiness to all sentient beings, they practice the perfection of diligence, not for their own sake and not for any other purpose;
for the sake of benefiting and bringing happiness to all sentient beings, they practice the perfection of meditative concentration, not for their own sake and not for any other purpose.
For the sake of benefiting and bringing happiness to all sentient beings, one practices the perfection of wisdom, neither for one's own sake nor for any other purpose;
for the sake of benefiting and bringing happiness to all sentient beings, one seeks to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, neither for one's own sake nor for any other purpose.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he sees that foolish commoners dwell upon the notion of a self amidst what is not-self; they dwell upon the notion of a sentient being, a life-force, a living soul, a nourisher, a spirit, a person, a human, a youth, an agent, one who causes to act, an originator, one who causes to originate, an experiencer, one who causes to experience, a knower, one who causes to know, and a seer, one who causes to see—dwelling thus upon the notion of a sentient being, and so forth, up to the notion of one who causes to see."

Having seen this, these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas give rise to deep compassion and employ skillful means to teach and transform them, causing them to abandon inverted conceptualizations and attachments, and establishing them within the signless nectar-realm (*amṛta-dhātu*). Abiding in this realm, they no longer manifest the notion of a self (*ātma-saṃjñā*) up to and including the notion of a perceiver. At that time, all agitation, distraction, discursive proliferation (*prapañca*), and discrimination no longer function; their minds predominantly abide in a state of tranquility, serenity, and the signless realm free from proliferation.

"Subhūti! By means of this skillful method, the bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom; he himself has no attachment to any phenomena, and he is also able to teach others to have no attachment to all phenomena. This is based on conventional truth, not on ultimate truth."
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha,
saying: “World-Honored One,
when the Buddha realized unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, was the attainment of the Buddha-dharma said to be ‘attained’ based on conventional truth or based on ultimate truth?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“When a Buddha realizes unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, the qualities of a Buddha that are attained are said to be ‘attained’ only by way of conventional designation, not by way of ultimate truth.”
If one relies on the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), both the attainer and that which is attained are unattainable.
Why is this? Subhūti!

If one were to say that this person attains such a dharma and thereby has something attained, then having something attained entails grasping at duality; and grasping at duality prevents one from attaining the fruit and from achieving clear realization (abhisamaya).
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
if grasping at duality cannot lead to the attainment of the fruit nor to clear realization, does grasping at non-duality enable the attainment of the fruit and the occurrence of clear realization?”
The Buddha said, “Suvikrāntavikrāmin!
One who clings to duality cannot attain the fruit nor achieve clear realization; the same is true for one who clings to non-duality.”
If there is neither duality nor non-duality, this is called attaining the fruit and is also called clear realization (*abhisamaya*).
Why is this so? Subhūti!

To hold that one can attain the fruit and also possess clear realization by means of this, or to hold that one cannot attain the fruit nor possess clear realization by means of that—both are conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*). There are no such conceptual proliferations within the equality of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-samatā*); it is only when one is free from conceptual proliferation that it may be called the equality of phenomena.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If all dharmas take non-existence as their intrinsic nature, what herein is meant by the equality of dharmas?”
The Buddha said, “Sudhana!
If in a certain state there is neither existence nor non-existence, and it cannot even be described as a state of equality— this is what is called the equality of dharmas.”

Subhūti, you should know that the equality of phenomena (dharmasamatā) is neither expressible nor cognizable; apart from this equality, no phenomenon can be apprehended, and apart from all phenomena, there is no equality.
"Subhūti! You should know that the equality of dharmas cannot be traversed by either ordinary beings or noble ones, for it is not their domain.
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha again, saying:
“World-Honored One,
is the equality of dharmas not also beyond the sphere of the Buddha’s activity?
The Buddha said:

“Subhūti! The equality of phenomena (dharmasamatā) is not the domain of practice for any noble ones (ārya)—whether those who follow by faith (śraddhānusārin), those who follow by dharma (dharmānusārin), the eighth person (aṣṭamaka), stream-enterers (srotāpanna), once-returners (sakṛdāgāmin), non-returners (anāgāmin), arhats, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, or the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas; none of them can take the equality of phenomena as an object of their practice.”
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Since all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas have attained mastery over all phenomena, how can it be said that the equality of phenomena is not even within the range of the Buddhas' activity?”
The Buddha said, “Subhūti!

Although all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas have attained mastery over all phenomena, if the nature of equality were different from the Buddha, one could say it is the sphere traversed by the Buddha; however, since the nature of equality is not different from the Buddha, how can it be said that the Buddha traverses that sphere?”
"Subhūti, you should know this:
whether it be the equality of the dharmas of ordinary worldlings, the equality of the dharmas of those who follow by faith,
the equality of the dharmas of those who follow by dharma, the equality of the dharmas of the eighth-rank practitioners, or the equality of the dharmas of stream-enterers..."
The equality of phenomena (dharmasamatā): whether it be the equality of phenomena of those who have attained the stage of once-returner,
the equality of phenomena of those who have attained the stage of non-returner, the equality of phenomena of arhats, the equality of phenomena of pratyekabuddhas,
the equality of phenomena of the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, or the equality of phenomena of the Tathāgatas, Arhats...

The equality of the dharmas of the Perfectly Enlightened One, and the equality of all such dharmas, are all of one single characteristic, namely, the characteristicless (*animitta*). This is a single equality, non-dual and undifferentiated;
therefore, it cannot be said that "this is the equality of the dharmas of ordinary beings," and so on, up to "this is [the equality] of the Tathāgata, the Arhat..."
The equality of the dharmas of the Truly Perfectly Awakened One.
Within this equality of the single dharma, since no various equalities can be apprehended, the distinguishing marks between ordinary beings and noble ones are likewise unapprehendable therein.

The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Scroll Three Hundred and Ninety-Six. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Part One: The Chapter on the Yoga of Ultimate Meaning, Number Seventy-Five, Part Two. At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”

If, within the equality of all phenomena, no distinct characteristics whatsoever can be apprehended, then there would be no distinction between ordinary beings, those who follow by faith, those who follow by dharma, those who are eighth-level practitioners, stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, arhats, pratyekabuddhas, the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, or the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas—all such phenomena and sentient beings would be without differentiation.
The Buddha said,
“So it is, Subhūti! It is just so.”
"So it is! It is just as you have said.

Within the equality of all phenomena, there is no distinction between ordinary beings, noble ones, or even Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas—whether in terms of their dharmas or their sentient beings."
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If, within the equality of all phenomena, there is no distinction between the dharmas of ordinary beings and noble ones, nor between sentient beings themselves, how is it that the Three Jewels appear in the world—namely, the Jewel of the Buddha, the Jewel of the Dharma, and the Jewel of the Saṅgha?”
The Buddha said,
“Suvikrāntavikrāmin, what do you think?”
“Are the Jewels of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha distinct from the nature of equality? Subhūti replied,
“As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, the Jewels of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha are not at all different from the nature of equality.”
“World-Honored One!

Whether it be the Jewel of the Buddha, the Jewel of the Dharma, the Jewel of the Saṃgha, or the nature of equality—all such things as these are neither associated nor dissociated; they are formless, invisible, non-obstructive, and possess a single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of being without characteristics.”

Nevertheless, through skillful means within the signless, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, establishes various distinctions among phenomena, saying: "This is an ordinary person; this is one who follows by faith; this is one who follows by Dharma; this is the eighth [stage]; this is a stream-enterer; this is a once-returner; this is a non-returner; this is an arhat; this is a pratyekabuddha; this is a bodhisattva mahāsattva; and this is a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha."
The Buddha said, “So it is, Subhūti!”
"So it is! It is as you have said.
The Tathāgata is skillful in means regarding the Dharma; he is able to establish various distinctions among the dharmas within the signless."
"Furthermore, Subhūti, what do you think? If the Tathāgatas, Arhats,

and Samyaksaṃbuddhas had not realized unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, or even if they had realized unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, but did not establish the various distinct characteristics of phenomena for the sake of sentient beings, would those classes of sentient beings be able to know [them] for themselves?"
"This is the realm of hell; this is the animal realm; this is the realm of hungry ghosts; this is the human realm;

this is the Heaven of the Four Great Kings; this is the Heaven of the Thirty-three; this is the Yāma Heaven; this is the Tuṣita Heaven; this is the Nirmāṇarati Heaven; this is the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven;
this is the Brahmakāyika Heaven; this is the Brahmapurohita Heaven; this is the Brahmapārṣadya Heaven; this is the Mahābrahmā Heaven."
These are the Ābhāsvara devas; these are the Parīttābhā devas; these are the Apramāṇābhā devas; these are the Ābhāsvarābha devas; these are the Śubha devas;
these are the Parīttaśubha devas; these are the Apramāṇaśubha devas; these are the Śubhakṛtsna devas; these are the Bṛhatphala devas;
these are the Parīttabṛhatphala devas; these are the Apramāṇabṛhatphala devas; these are the Bṛhatphala devas; and these are the Asañjñisattva devas.
This is the Heaven of No Strife, this is the Heaven of No Heat, this is the Heaven of Good Manifestation, this is the Heaven of Good Vision, and this is the Heaven of the Ultimate of Form;

this is the Heaven of the Sphere of Infinite Space, this is the Heaven of the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness, this is the Heaven of the Sphere of Nothingness, and this is the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-perception;
this is form, and these are feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
This is the sense base of the eye; these are the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
This is the sense base of forms; these are the sense bases of sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena.
This is the element of the eye; these are the elements of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
"This is the realm of form; these are the realms of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena.
This is the realm of eye-consciousness; these are the realms of ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-consciousness.
This is eye-contact; these are ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact."
"These are the various feelings produced with eye-contact as condition; these are the various feelings produced with ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-contact as conditions;
this is the earth element; these are the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements; this is the causal condition (hetu-pratyaya);
this is the immediately preceding condition (samanantara-pratyaya); this is the object condition (ālambana-pratyaya); this is the dominant condition (adhipati-pratyaya)."
These are all phenomena produced from conditions;

this is ignorance, these are volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, existence, birth, and old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair;
these are mundane phenomena, and these are supramundane phenomena.
"These are contaminated phenomena; these are uncontaminated phenomena;
these are conditioned phenomena; these are unconditioned phenomena;
this is the perfection of generosity; these are the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, wisdom, skillful means, aspiration, power, and knowledge."

These are the four applications of mindfulness; these are the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path;

these are internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, the emptiness of the ultimate truth, the emptiness of conditioned phenomena, the emptiness of unconditioned phenomena, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersion emptiness, non-alteration emptiness, essential nature emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common characteristic emptiness, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature.

This is suchness; this is the dharma-realm, the nature of phenomena, the non-falsity, the non-alteration, the equality, the state beyond birth, the fixed nature of phenomena, the stability of phenomena, the limit of reality, the realm of space, and the inconceivable realm;
this is the noble truth of suffering, and these are the noble truths of the origin, cessation, and the path;
this is the four meditative concentrations, and these are the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments.
These are the eight liberations; these are the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative attainments, and the ten totalities;
these are the doors of dhāraṇī; these are the doors of samādhi;
these are the door of liberation through emptiness, and the doors of liberation through signlessness and wishlessness.

This is the Ground of Perfect Joy; this is the Ground of Purity, the Ground of Radiant Light, the Ground of Blazing Wisdom, the Ground of Difficult Victory, the Ground of Presence, the Ground of Far-Going, the Ground of Immovability, the Ground of Excellent Intelligence, and the Ground of the Dharma Cloud;
these are the five eyes; these are the six supernormal powers;

these are the ten powers of a Buddha; these are the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
These are the thirty-two marks of a great man; these are the eighty minor marks;
this is the quality of non-forgetfulness; this is the nature of constant abiding in equanimity;
this is omniscience; this is the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects.
This is the wondrous knowledge of vows regarding all marks; this is the knowledge of all-knowledge;
this is the Jewel of the Buddha, this is the Jewel of the Dharma, and this is the Jewel of the Saṅgha;
this is the Śrāvaka vehicle, this is the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, and this is the Unsurpassed Vehicle.

"Is it possible for sentient beings to know for themselves such distinctions as: 'This is one who follows by faith,' 'This is one who follows by dharma,' 'This is the eighth person,' 'This is a stream-enterer,' 'This is a once-returner,' 'This is a non-returner,' 'This is an arhat,' 'This is a pratyekabuddha,' 'This is a bodhisattva mahāsattva,' or 'This is a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha'?"
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One!”
"No, Sugata! If the Buddha did not establish such various distinctions for sentient beings, these classes of sentient beings would be unable to know for themselves such various distinctions."
The Buddha said, “Suvikrāntavikrāmin!

Therefore, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, through skillful means regarding signless phenomena, although he establishes various differentiated signs for the sake of sentient beings, remains entirely unmoved within the equal dharmatā of all phenomena.”
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha,
saying: “World-Honored One,

just as the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha does not move at all within the equal dharma-nature of all phenomena, do all these foolish common worldlings likewise not move within the equal dharma-nature of all phenomena?”

In this same way, do those who follow by faith, or those who follow by Dharma, or the eighth-rank practitioner, or a stream-enterer, or a once-returner, or a non-returner, or an arhat, or a pratyekabuddha, or a bodhisattva mahāsattva, likewise remain unmoved within the equality of the dharma-nature of all phenomena?
The Buddha said, “So it is, Subhūti!”

It is so! Because all phenomena and all sentient beings do not transcend the equality of the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), they remain entirely unmoved within that equality of the nature of all phenomena.
“Subhūti, you should know that the true suchness,
the dharma-realm, the dharma-nature, the non-falsity, the non-alteration, the equality,
the state beyond birth, and the dharma... of all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas...”
Concentration, the stability of phenomena (*dharmasthiti*), the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), the realm of space (*ākāśadhātu*), and the inconceivable realm—
these are precisely the suchness (*tathatā*), the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), the non-erroneous nature, the unchanging nature, the state of equality,
the nature free from birth, the fixedness of phenomena, the stability of phenomena, and the limit of reality for foolish ordinary beings (*bālapṛthagjana*).
The space element and the inconceivable element are likewise the suchness, the dharma-realm, the dharma-nature, the non-falsity,

and the non-alteration of those who follow by faith, those who follow by Dharma, the eighth person, stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, arhats, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
...the nature of equality, the nature of being free from birth, the fixedness of phenomena, the stability of phenomena,
the limit of reality, the realm of space, and the inconceivable realm. Why is this so?

"Subhūti! Because all phenomena and all sentient beings do not transcend suchness, the dharma-realm, the nature of phenomena, non-illusory nature, non-alteration, equality, the nature of freedom from birth, the fixedness of phenomena, the stability of phenomena, the limit of reality, the realm of space, and the inconceivable realm."
"Subhūti, you should know that from suchness up to the sphere of the inconceivable, their nature is without differentiation.
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If the equality of the dharma-nature of all dharmas is the same as the equality of the dharma-nature of ordinary beings, and likewise the equality of the dharma-nature of those who follow by faith, those who follow by dharma, the eighth-level practitioners, stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, arhats, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, and tathāgatas, arhats, samyaksaṃbuddhas—then since the characteristics of all dharmas and sentient beings are each distinct, their natures should also be distinct. If that were so, the dharma-nature would also be distinct: because the characteristic of form is distinct, its nature should also be distinct; because the characteristics of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are distinct, their natures should also be distinct; thus, the dharma-nature would also be distinct for each.”

Because the characteristic of the eye-base (*cakṣur-āyatana*) is distinct, its nature should also be distinct; because the characteristics of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-bases are distinct, their natures should also be distinct—and thus the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) would also have to be distinct for each.

Because the characteristic of the form-base (*rūpāyatana*) is distinct, its nature should also be distinct; because the characteristics of the sound, odor, taste, touch, and mental-object bases are distinct, their natures should also be distinct—and thus the nature of phenomena would also have to be distinct for each.

Because the characteristic of the eye-element (*cakṣurdhātu*) is distinct, its nature should also be distinct; because the characteristics of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-elements are distinct, their natures should also be distinct—and thus the nature of phenomena would also have to be distinct for each.

Because the characteristics of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) differ, its nature (*svabhāva*) should also differ; because the characteristics of the realms of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental objects (*dharmadhātu*) differ, their natures should also differ, and thus the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) should likewise differ for each.

Because the characteristics of the eye-consciousness realm (*cakṣurvijñānadhātu*) differ, its nature should also differ; because the characteristics of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-consciousness realms differ, their natures should also differ, and thus the nature of phenomena should likewise differ for each.

Because the characteristics of eye-contact (*cakṣuḥ-saṃsparśa*) differ, its nature should also differ; because the characteristics of ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-contact differ, their natures should also differ, and thus the nature of phenomena should likewise differ for each.

Because the sensations produced with eye-contact as a condition differ in their characteristics, they must also differ in their nature; because the sensations produced with ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact as conditions differ in their characteristics, they must also differ in their nature. Consequently, the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) would also have to be distinct for each. Because the earth element differs in its characteristics, its nature must also differ;

because the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements differ in their characteristics, their natures must also differ. Consequently, the nature of phenomena would also have to be distinct for each. Because causes and conditions differ in their characteristics, their natures must also differ;

because the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), the object condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) differ in their characteristics, their natures must also differ. Consequently, the nature of phenomena would also have to be distinct for each.
Because the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena produced from conditions are distinct, their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) should also be distinct;

thus, the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) would likewise have to be individually distinct. Because the characteristic of ignorance (*avidyā*) is distinct, its nature should also be distinct; because the characteristics of volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), consciousness (*vijñāna*), name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), contact (*sparśa*), feeling (*vedanā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), becoming (*bhava*), birth (*jāti*), and old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair are distinct, their natures should also be distinct;

thus, the nature of phenomena would likewise have to be individually distinct. Because the characteristic of greed (*rāga*) is distinct, its nature should also be distinct; because the characteristics of hatred (*dveṣa*) and delusion (*moha*) are distinct, their natures should also be distinct; thus, the nature of phenomena would likewise have to be individually distinct.
Because the views and inclinations of ordinary beings differ, their natures should also differ;

if this were so, the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) would likewise have to differ for each. Because the four dhyānas differ in character, their natures should also differ; because the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments differ in character, their natures should also differ;

if this were so, the nature of phenomena would likewise have to differ for each. Because the four foundations of mindfulness differ in character, their natures should also differ; because the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path differ in character, their natures should also differ; if this were so, the nature of phenomena would likewise have to differ for each.

Because the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of the liberation door of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vimokṣamukha*) differ, their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) should also differ; because the characteristics of the liberation doors of signlessness (*animitta*) and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*) differ, their intrinsic nature should also differ.

In that case, the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*) would also have to be distinct for each. Because the characteristic of internal emptiness (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*) differs, its nature should also differ; and because the characteristics of external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, endless emptiness, dispersion emptiness, non-alteration emptiness, essential nature emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common characteristic emptiness, the emptiness of all dharmas, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence differ, their natures should also differ. In that case, the dharma-nature would also have to be distinct for each.

Because the characteristics of the noble truth of suffering are distinct, their intrinsic nature (*dharmatā*) should also be distinct; because the characteristics of the noble truths of origin, cessation, and the path are distinct, their intrinsic nature should also be distinct—and thus the intrinsic nature of phenomena would have to be diverse for each.

Because the characteristics of the perfection of generosity (*dāna-pāramitā*) are distinct, its intrinsic nature should also be distinct; because the characteristics of the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, wisdom, skillful means, aspiration, power, and knowledge are distinct, their intrinsic natures should also be distinct—and thus the intrinsic nature of phenomena would have to be diverse for each.

Because the characteristics of the eight liberations (*aṣṭa-vimokṣa*) are distinct, their intrinsic nature should also be distinct; because the characteristics of the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities (*daśa-kṛtsnāyatana*) are distinct, their intrinsic nature should also be distinct—and thus the intrinsic nature of phenomena would have to be diverse for each.

Because the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of all *dhāraṇī* gates are different, their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) should also be different; because the characteristics of all *samādhi* gates are different, their intrinsic nature should also be different—and thus the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) should also be distinct for each.

Because the characteristics of the Ground of Extreme Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*) are different, its nature should also be different; because the characteristics of the Ground of Purity (*vimalā*), the Ground of Radiance (*prabhākārī*), the Ground of Blazing Wisdom (*arciṣmatī*), the Ground of Difficult Victory (*sudurjayā*), the Ground of Presence (*abhimukhī*), the Ground of Far-Going (*dūraṅgamā*), the Ground of Immovability (*acalā*), the Ground of Good Intelligence (*sādhumatī*), and the Ground of the Dharma Cloud (*dharmameghā*) are different, their natures should also be different—and thus the nature of phenomena should also be distinct for each.

Because the characteristics of the five eyes (*pañca-cakṣus*) are different, their nature should also be different; because the characteristics of the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍ-abhijñā*) are different, their nature should also be different—and thus the nature of phenomena should also be distinct for each.

Because the ten powers of the Tathāgata differ in their characteristics, their nature should also differ; because the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha differ in their characteristics, their nature should also differ—thus, the dharma-nature would also have to be distinct for each.

Because the thirty-two marks of a Great Man differ in their characteristics, their nature should also differ; because the eighty secondary signs differ in their characteristics, their nature should also differ—thus, the dharma-nature would also have to be distinct for each.

Because the quality of non-forgetfulness differs in its characteristic, its nature should also differ; because the nature of constant abiding in equanimity differs in its characteristic, its nature should also differ—thus, the dharma-nature would also have to be distinct for each.

Because the characteristics of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) differ, their natures should also differ; because the characteristics of the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*) and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) differ, their natures should also differ, and thus the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) should also be distinct for each.

Because the characteristics of foolish ordinary beings (*bāla-pṛthagjana*) differ, their natures should also differ; because the characteristics of those who follow by faith (*śraddhānusārin*), those who follow by dharma (*dharmānusārin*), the eighth person (*aṣṭamaka*), stream-enterers (*srotāpanna*), once-returners (*sakṛdāgāmin*), non-returners (*anāgāmin*), arhats, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, and Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas differ, their natures should also differ, and thus the nature of phenomena should also be distinct for each.

Because the characteristics of all mundane and supramundane dharmas differ, their natures should also differ; because the characteristics of all contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) dharmas, and conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) dharmas differ, their natures should also differ, and thus the nature of phenomena should also be distinct for each.
“World-Honored One!
How can one establish the single characteristic of the dharma-nature within various dharmas that possess distinct characteristics?
How is it that when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they do not discriminate between dharmas and sentient beings as having various natures?”
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not differentiate among phenomena and sentient beings as having various natures, then they would be unable to practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
If one cannot practice the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), then one will be unable to proceed from one stage (*bhūmi*) to the next.

If one cannot proceed from one stage to the next, then one will be unable to enter the bodhisattva’s state of correctness and departure from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*), thereby transcending the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.

If one cannot enter the bodhisattva’s state of rightness and departure from corruption, thereby transcending the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, then one will be unable to fulfill the perfection of supernormal powers (ṛddhipāramitā).

If one cannot fulfill the perfection of supernormal powers (*abhijñā-pāramitā*), then one will likewise be unable to fulfill the perfections of generosity (*dāna*), ethical discipline (*śīla*), patience (*kṣānti*), diligence (*vīrya*), meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), wisdom (*prajñā*), skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), sublime aspiration (*praṇidhāna*), power (*bala*), and knowledge (*jñāna*).

If one cannot fulfill the perfections from generosity up to wisdom, then one will be unable to sport with the supernormal powers, traveling from one buddha-field to another to make offerings, pay homage, show respect, and praise the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones; nor will one be able to plant roots of goodness in the presence of those Buddhas.
If one cannot plant various roots of goodness under the Buddhas, then one will be unable to mature sentient beings and purify Buddha-fields.
If one cannot mature sentient beings and purify Buddha-fields, then one will be unable to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
The Buddha told Subhūti: "Regarding what you have said:

'If the dharmatā of equality of all phenomena is the very same as the dharmatā of equality of ordinary beings, and likewise the dharmatā of equality of those who follow by faith, those who follow by dharma, the eighth-rank practitioners, stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, arhats, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, and Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas—then since the characteristics of all these phenomena and sentient beings are each distinct, their natures should also be distinct; thus, the dharmatā itself should also be distinct in each case. How, then, can one establish the single characteristic of dharmatā amidst these various distinct characteristics of phenomena?'"
How is it that when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they do not differentiate between phenomena and sentient beings as having various natures?

The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Is this nature of equality conditioned or unconditioned?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“The nature of equality is neither conditioned nor unconditioned; yet, apart from conditioned phenomena, unconditioned phenomena cannot be found, and apart from unconditioned phenomena, conditioned phenomena likewise cannot be found.”

“Subhūti! Whether it be the conditioned realm or the unconditioned realm, these two realms are neither associated nor dissociated; they are formless, invisible, non-obstructive, and possess a single characteristic—namely, the characteristic of being without characteristics. All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas speak of them based on conventional truth, not based on ultimate truth.”

Why is this? Because within the ultimate truth (paramārtha), there can be no bodily activity, vocal activity, or mental activity; nor can the ultimate truth be apprehended apart from bodily, vocal, and mental activities.

“Subhūti, you should know that the very nature of phenomena (dharmatā), which is the equality of the conditioned and the unconditioned, is called the ultimate truth (paramārtha). Therefore, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they do not waver from the ultimate truth while practicing the conduct of a bodhisattva mahāsattva; thus they bring sentient beings to maturity, purify buddha-fields, and are able to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.”
Chapter Seventy-Six: The Nature of Immovability. Part One: The Nature of Immovability. Chapter Seventy-Six. At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”

If all phenomena are equal in their dharmatā and that dharmatā is by nature empty, and this emptiness of intrinsic nature is neither an agent nor an object with respect to existence or non-existence, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, act for the sake of what a bodhisattva ought to do—benefiting sentient beings through generosity, kind words, beneficial conduct, and cooperation—without wavering from the ultimate truth?
The Buddha told Subhūti: “So it is! So it is!”
It is as you have said:
the dharmic nature of all phenomena is equal and universally equal, and this intrinsic emptiness of nature is neither an agent nor an object with respect to existence or non-existence.
“Subhūti! If all sentient beings were to know for themselves that all phenomena are by nature empty, then the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas,
and the assembly of Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas would not manifest supernatural powers or perform rare and wondrous deeds.”
This means that although there is no movement within the fundamental emptiness of all phenomena, one causes sentient beings to distance themselves from various conceptualizations and inversions,
and to abide in the emptiness of all phenomena so as to be liberated from the suffering of saṃsāra; that is, one causes sentient beings to distance themselves from the notion of a self (*ātman*),
the notion of a sentient being (*sattva*), the notion of a life-principle (*jīva*), the notion of a living being (*jantu*), and the notion of a nourisher (*poṣa*).
the notion of a self, the notion of a person, the notion of a soul, the notion of a being born of mind, the notion of a youth, the notion of an agent,
the notion of one who causes to act, the notion of an originator, the notion of one who causes to originate, the notion of an experiencer,
the notion of one who causes to experience, the notion of a knower, the notion of one who causes to know, and the notion of a seer.
It causes those who see it to conceive thoughts [of it],
yet it also causes them to distance themselves from the perception of form, as well as the perceptions of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness;
it also causes them to distance themselves from the perception of the eye-base, as well as the perceptions of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-bases.
They also cause them to distance themselves from the perception of the sense-field of form, and from the perceptions of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena;
they also cause them to distance themselves from the perception of the eye-element, and from the perceptions of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-elements;
they also cause them to distance themselves from the perception of the form-element, and from the perceptions of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental-phenomena elements.
They also cause them to distance themselves from the perception of the eye-consciousness element, and from the perceptions of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-consciousness elements;
they also cause them to distance themselves from the perception of eye-contact, and from the perceptions of ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-contact;

they also cause them to distance themselves from the perceptions of all feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition, and from the perceptions of all feelings produced with ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-contact as conditions.
They also cause one to remain far removed from the perception of the earth element, as well as the perceptions of the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements;
they also cause one to remain far removed from the perception of causes and conditions, as well as the perceptions of the immediate condition, the object-condition, and the dominant condition;
and they also cause one to remain far removed from the perception of all phenomena produced from conditions.

They also cause them to distance themselves from the perceptions of ignorance, volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, existence, birth, and old age, death, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair;

they also cause them to distance themselves from the perceptions of mundane and supramundane phenomena, of tainted and untainted phenomena, and of conditioned and unconditioned phenomena, so that they may dwell securely in the unconditioned realm and be liberated from the suffering of birth and death.
“The unconditioned realm (*asaṃskṛtadhātu*) is the emptiness of all phenomena; it is designated as the ‘unconditioned realm’ by way of conventional expression.
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"By virtue of what emptiness are all phenomena said to be empty?
The Buddha replied, "Subhūti!"
Because perception is empty, all phenomena are said to be empty. "Furthermore,
Subhūti, what do you think?
"If a transformation body further performs transformative acts, does this possess substantial reality and not emptiness? Subhūti replied, "No!"
"No, World-Honored One! No, Sugata!"
"All transformations are devoid of substantial reality; they are all empty.
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"Transformation and emptiness—these two dharmas are neither joined nor dispersed. Both are empty because they are empty of emptiness itself; one should not discriminate between what is empty and what is a transformation."
Why is this? Subhūti!
Within emptiness, neither the phenomenon of emptiness nor the phenomenon of transformation can be apprehended, because all phenomena are ultimately empty.
"Furthermore, Subhūti! Form is not a transformation;
feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are not transformations. All that is a transformation is without exception empty."
"Subhūti! There is no eye-base that is not a transformation; there is no ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind-base that is not a transformation. Whatever is a transformation is entirely empty."

“Subhūti! The sphere of formlessness is not a transformation; the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena are not transformations. All things that are transformations are without exception empty.”

“Subhūti! There is no eye-element that is not an emanation; there is no ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-element that is not an emanation. All things that are emanations are without exception empty.”

“Subhūti! The formless realm is not a transformation; the realms of sound, odor, taste, touch, and mental phenomena are not transformations. All things that are transformations are without exception empty.”

“Subhūti! There is no eye-consciousness element that is not an emanation; there is no ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-consciousness element that is not an emanation. Of all those things that are emanations, there is none that is not empty.”

“Subhūti! There is no visual contact that is not an emanation; there is no auditory, olfactory, gustatory, tactile, or mental contact that is not an emanation. Of all those things that are emanations, there is none that is not empty.”

"Subhūti! The various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition are not transformations; the various feelings produced with ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-contact as conditions are not transformations. All that are transformations are without exception empty."

"Subhūti! There is no earth element that is not a transformation; there is no water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness element that is not a transformation. Of all things that are transformations, there are none that are not empty."

“Subhūti! There is no non-emanation that lacks causes and conditions; there is no non-emanation of the equal-and-immediate condition, the object-condition, or the dominant condition. All things that are emanations are without exception empty.”
“Subhūti! Those phenomena produced from conditions are not transformations; and whatever is a transformation is entirely empty.
“Subhūti! [he continued.]

There is no ignorance that is not a transformation; there are no volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, existence, birth, or old age, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair that are not transformations. All things that are transformations are without exception empty.

“Subhūti! There is no perfection of giving that is not an emanation; there is no perfection of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, wisdom, skillful means, aspiration, power, or knowledge that is not an emanation. All things that are emanations are without exception empty.”

“Subhūti! There are no applications of mindfulness that are not transformations; there are no right efforts, bases of power, faculties, powers, factors of enlightenment, or factors of the noble path that are not transformations. Whatever is a transformation is entirely empty.”

"Subhūti! There is no gate of liberation of emptiness that is not an emanation; there is no gate of liberation of signlessness or wishlessness that is not an emanation. Of all those things that are emanations, there are none that are not empty."

“Subhūti! Internal emptiness is not an illusion; external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, endless emptiness, dispersal emptiness, non-alteration emptiness, essential emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common-characteristic emptiness, the emptiness of all dharmas, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence are not illusions. Whatever is an illusion is, without exception, empty.”

"Subhūti! The noble truth of suffering is not a transformation; the noble truths of origin, cessation, and the path are not transformations. Of all things that are transformations, there are none that are not empty."

“Subhūti! There are no four dhyānas that are not transformations; there are no four immeasurables or four formless attainments that are not transformations. Of all things that are transformations, there are none that are not empty.”

“Subhūti! There are no eight liberations that are not transformations; there are no eight bases of mastery, nine successive meditative attainments, or ten universal bases that are not transformations. All things that are transformations are without exception empty.”

“Subhūti! There are no dhāraṇī-doors that are not transformations, and there are no samādhi-doors that are not transformations; all things that are transformations are without exception empty. Subhūti!”

The Ground of Utmost Joy is not a transformation; the Ground of Freedom from Defilement, the Ground of Radiant Light, the Ground of Blazing Wisdom, the Ground of Supreme Difficulty to Conquer, the Ground of Manifestation, the Ground of Far-reaching Progress, the Ground of Immovability, the Ground of Excellent Wisdom, and the Ground of the Dharma Cloud are not transformations. Of all those that are transformations, there are none that are not empty.

“Subhūti! There are no five eyes that are not transformations, and there are no six supernormal powers that are not transformations; all things that are transformations are without exception empty. Subhūti!”

The ten powers of a Buddha are not a transformation; the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are not transformations. All things that are transformations are without exception empty.

“Subhūti! There are no thirty-two marks of a great man that are not transformations; there are no eighty secondary signs that are not transformations. All things that are transformations are without exception empty.”
“Subhūti! There is no non-illusory quality of non-forgetfulness, and there is no non-illusory nature of constant equanimity; all that is illusory is entirely empty. Subhūti!”

There is no omniscience that is not an emanation; there is no knowledge of the paths and no knowledge of all aspects that is not an emanation. All things that are emanations are without exception empty. "Subhūti!..."

The fruit of stream-entry is not an emanation; the fruits of once-returner, non-returner, and arhatship, as well as the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, are not emanations. All things that are emanations are without exception empty.

“Subhūti! There is no bodhisattva mahāsattva practice that is not a transformation; there is no unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of a Buddha that is not a transformation. All things that are transformations are without exception empty.”

“Subhūti! Based on such dharmas, various types of persons (pudgala) are designated—namely, ordinary beings; those who follow by faith; those who follow by dharma; the eighth person; stream-enterers; once-returners; non-returners; arhats; pratyekabuddhas; bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; and the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas. All of these are without exception emanations (nirmita), and whatever is an emanation is entirely empty.”
Then, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Are all the aggregates, bases, elements, dependent origination, dependently arisen phenomena, and the factors of dependent origination in the world all merely transformations?”
All supramundane perfections (pāramitās), whether they be the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (bodhipākṣika-dharmas),
the three doors of liberation (vimokṣamukha), all forms of emptiness (śūnyatā), the noble truths (āryasatya), the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables (apramāṇa),
the four formless attainments (ārūpyasamāpatti), the eight liberations (vimokṣa), the eight bases of mastery (abhibhvāyatana), or the nine successive [attainments]...
The meditative concentrations, the ten spheres of totality, the doors of dhāraṇī, the doors of samādhi,
the ten stages of a bodhisattva, the five eyes, the six supernormal powers, the ten powers of a buddha, the four fearlessnesses,
the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen [unique qualities of a buddha].
The unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*), whether they be the thirty-two marks of a great man (*dvātriṃśan-mahāpuruṣa-lakṣaṇa*) and the eighty secondary signs (*aśīty-anuvyañjana*),
or the quality of non-forgetfulness (*asaṃpramoṣadharma*) and the nature of constant equanimity (*upekṣā-pratisthita*), or omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*),
and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), or the various fruits attained through those dharmas, or the various designations established based on those dharmas— [all these are ungraspable].
"Is the *pudgala* also a transformation?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"All worldly and world-transcending phenomena (*dharmas*) are none other than transformations. Within them, there are those that are transformations of śrāvakas, those that are transformations of pratyekabuddhas, those that are transformations of bodhisattvas, those that are transformations of Tathāgatas, those that are transformations of afflictions (*kleśa*), and those that are transformations of wholesome dharmas."
"Subhūti! For this reason, it is said that all phenomena are like magical transformations, without any distinction.
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha again, saying:
“World-Honored One!

As for all the fruits of abandonment—namely, the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, or the fruit of arhatship; or the stage of a pratyekabuddha, or the stage of a Tathāgata, wherein the continuity of the habitual tendencies of afflictions is forever severed—is this too an emanation?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“In this way, all these dharmas that are conjoined with the two characteristics of arising and ceasing are also all transformations.
[Subhūti said: “World-Honored One!”
“What phenomena are not transformations? “Suvikrāntavikrāmin!
Those phenomena that do not conform to the characteristics of arising and ceasing are not transformations.”
“World-Honored One!
Which phenomena do not conjoin with the characteristics of arising and ceasing? “Suvikrāntavikrāmin!
“The dharma of non-deceptiveness is itself nirvāṇa; this dharma does not conjoin with the characteristics of arising and ceasing, and for that reason it is not a transformation.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

“As the World-Honored One has taught, the equal nature of dharmas is entirely empty; nothing can move it, no duality can be found, and there is not the slightest dharma that is not empty of its own nature. How then can it be said that nirvāṇa is not a transformation?”
The Buddha told Subhūti: "So it is! So it is!"

It is as you have said. There is not even the slightest dharma that is not empty of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnya*). This emptiness of intrinsic nature was not made by śrāvakas, nor by pratyekabuddhas, nor by bodhisattvas, nor by tathāgatas, nor was it made by anyone else. Whether a buddha appears or does not appear, its nature is eternally empty; this is itself nirvāṇa. Therefore, I say that nirvāṇa is not a transformation. There is no truly existent dharma called "nirvāṇa" that can be described as having birth or cessation, nor as a transformation. It is simply non-arising and non-ceasing, and thus not a transformation.
The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Volume Three Hundred and Ninety-seven;
The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Volume Three Hundred and Ninety-eight.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.
Chapter Seventy-Seven: Sadāprarudita Bodhisattva, Part One. Chapter Seventy-Seven, Part One: At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"How does one instruct and admonish a beginner bodhisattva so as to cause them to have faith and understanding that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is ultimately empty?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"Is it that all phenomena exist first and then cease to exist?"

However, all phenomena are neither existent nor non-existent; they possess neither intrinsic nature nor extrinsic nature. Since they were not existent in the past, they are likewise not non-existent in the future; their intrinsic nature is eternally empty, and thus there is nothing to fear.
One should instruct and admonish beginner bodhisattvas in this manner, causing them to have faith and understanding that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is ultimately and entirely empty.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!..."

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to seek the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they should seek it as the bodhisattva mahāsattva Sadāprarudita did; that bodhisattva mahāsattva is currently practicing the holy life (brahmacarya) in the presence of the Buddha Mahāmeghadundubhisvara.
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
how does the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita seek the perfection of wisdom?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"When the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita formerly sought the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), he did not spare his own body or life, nor did he regard precious wealth, nor did he pursue fame or reputation, nor did he hope for honor; rather, he sought the perfection of wisdom."
He always delighted in dwelling in forest hermitages (āraṇya), when suddenly he heard a voice from the sky saying: "Ho!
Son of good family!"
"You should travel eastward; you will certainly be able to hear the profound *prajñāpāramitā*.

As you travel, do not complain of fatigue; do not think of sleep; do not dwell on food and drink; do not be mindful of day or night; do not fear cold or heat; and let your mind not be distracted by internal or external phenomena."

While walking, one must not look left or right; do not observe what is before, behind, above, below, or in the four intermediate directions. Do not violate the rules of decorum, and do not disrupt the physical form. Do not disturb form (*rūpa*);
do not disturb feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), or consciousness (*vijñāna*).
Do not disturb the sphere of the eye (*cakṣur-āyatana*); do not disturb the spheres of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind (*manas-āyatana*).
Do not move within the sphere of forms; do not move within the spheres of sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental objects.
Do not move within the eye-element; do not move within the elements of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind.
Do not move within the element of forms; do not move within the elements of sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental objects.
Do not move the eye-consciousness element; do not move the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind-consciousness elements.
Do not move eye-contact; do not move ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind-contact.
Do not move any feelings produced with eye-contact as condition; do not move any feelings produced with ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind-contact as condition.
Do not disturb the earth element; do not disturb the water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness elements.
Do not disturb causes and conditions; do not disturb the immediately preceding condition, the object-condition, or the dominant condition;
do not disturb all phenomena that arise from conditions.

Do not move ignorance; do not move volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, or aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair.
Do not move the perfection of generosity; do not move the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom.

Do not move the four foundations of mindfulness; do not move the four right endeavors, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, or the eightfold noble path.

Do not disturb internal emptiness; do not disturb external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, the emptiness of the ultimate truth, the emptiness of conditioned phenomena, the emptiness of unconditioned phenomena, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, the emptiness of dispersion, the emptiness of non-alteration, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, the emptiness of self-characteristic, the emptiness of common characteristic, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of non-apprehensibility, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of self-nature, and the emptiness of the self-nature of non-existence.

Do not disturb suchness; do not disturb the dharma-realm, the dharma-nature, non-falsity, non-alteration, equality, the nature of transcendence from birth, the fixed nature of dharmas, the stability of dharmas, the limit of reality, the realm of space, and the inconceivable realm.
Do not disturb the noble truth of suffering; do not disturb the noble truths of origin, cessation, and the path.
Do not move from the four dhyānas; do not move from the four immeasurables or the four formless attainments;
do not move from the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, or the ten totalities;
do not move from any of the dhāraṇī-doors or any of the samādhi-doors.
Do not move from the gate of liberation of emptiness; do not move from the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness;

do not move from the Ground of Extreme Joy, nor from the Ground of Purity, the Ground of Radiant Light, the Ground of Blazing Wisdom, the Ground of Difficult to Conquer, the Ground of Presence, the Ground of Far-Going, the Ground of Immovability, the Ground of Excellent Intelligence, or the Ground of the Cloud of Dharma;
do not move from the five eyes, nor from the six supernormal powers.

Do not disturb the ten powers of a Buddha; do not disturb the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
do not disturb the quality of non-forgetfulness, do not disturb the nature of constant abiding in equanimity;
do not disturb all-knowledge, do not disturb the knowledge of the paths, and do not disturb the knowledge of all aspects.
Do not disturb the fruit of stream-entry; do not disturb the fruits of once-returning, non-returning, or arhatship; do not disturb the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha;
do not disturb the conduct of a bodhisattva mahāsattva; do not disturb unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment;
do not disturb worldly dharmas; and do not disturb supramundane dharmas.
Do not disturb the conditioned phenomena with outflows; do not disturb the phenomena without outflows;
do not disturb the conditioned phenomena; do not disturb the unconditioned phenomena. Why is this?

"Good son! If one is moved by any phenomena, one cannot dwell securely in the Buddha-dharma; if one cannot dwell securely in the Buddha-dharma, one will wander through the various realms of birth and death; and if one wanders through the various realms of birth and death, one will be unable to attain the profound *prajñāpāramitā*."

At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita, having heard the voice from the sky earnestly instructing him, was filled with joy and leaped for gladness, exclaiming in wonder at such an unprecedented occurrence. With palms joined in reverence, he replied to the voice from the sky:
"As you have just said, I shall follow your instructions."

Why is this? It is because I desire to act as a great illumination for all sentient beings; because I desire to gather the sublime teachings of all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas; and because I desire to realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Then, a voice from the air spoke again to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita, saying:
"Excellent! Excellent!"

"Noble son! You should generate faith and understanding toward the profound dharmas of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness. You should seek the profound *prajñāpāramitā* with a mind free from all signs; you should seek the profound *prajñāpāramitā* with a mind free from the signs of a self, a sentient being, a life-force, a nourisher, a spirit, a person, a soul, a human, a youth, an agent, an experiencer, a knower, or a seer."
"O son of good family, you should skillfully distance yourself from all evil friends and draw near to, and make offerings to, all virtuous friends.

Those who can skillfully explain for you the dharmas of emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, non-arising, non-ceasing, non-defilement, non-purity, and primordial quiescence; and those who can manifest, instruct, encourage, and gladden you regarding the knowledge of all modes—these are your virtuous friends."
"O son of good family, if you practice in this way, before long you will hear the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, either from a sūtra or from a bodhisattva."

Regarding the one from whom you have heard this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, you should conceive of that person as the Great Teacher; you ought to recognize their kindness and keep in mind the need to repay it with gratitude.

"O son of good family, you should reflect thus: 'The one from whom I have heard this profound *prajñāpāramitā* is my most supreme and true spiritual friend. Because I have heard this sublime Dharma from him, I shall swiftly attain non-retrogression in unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. By means of him, I have drawn near to the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas; I am constantly born in the adorned and pure lands of all Buddhas, where I reverently make offerings to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, listen to the True Dharma, and plant the roots of all virtues. I remain far removed from the states of no-leisure and am fully endowed with leisure, so that in every thought-moment my extraordinary roots of goodness increase. "

"You should reflect upon, deliberate over, and examine such merits and benefits as these; you should always serve and honor the Dharma-preacher Bodhisattva who expounds this profound Prajñāpāramitā for your sake, regarding them as you would a Buddha."

"O son of good family, do not follow the Dharma Master out of a mind seeking worldly gain or fame; rather, follow the Dharma Master solely for the sake of cherishing, respecting, and making offerings to the unsurpassed Dharma."

"O son of good family, you should recognize the work of Māra; that is to say, there may be an evil Māra who, for the sake of destroying the True Dharma and its teachers, diligently offers exquisite objects of form, sound, fragrance, taste, and touch. At such times, the Dharma teacher, through skillful means, desiring to subdue that evil Māra and to cause sentient beings to plant roots of goodness, manifests by engaging in worldly affairs. Although he accepts those offerings, he remains free from attachment; you must not harbor feelings of revulsion toward this."

One should form this thought: "I am unable to know the skillful means of this Bodhisattva who preaches the Dharma; this Dharma-preacher well understands skillful means. Desiring to subdue sentient beings who are stubborn and unruly, and wishing to cause sentient beings to plant the roots of various virtues, he conforms to worldly affairs by appearing to experience all desires. Yet this Bodhisattva does not grasp at the marks of phenomena; being without attachment and without hindrance, he has never committed any transgression."
"O son of good family, at that time you should contemplate the true principle of all phenomena.
What is the true principle of all phenomena?
It is that all phenomena are neither defiled nor pure."
Why is this? Son of good family!

Because the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is empty, they lack a self, a sentient being, a life-principle, a soul, a nourisher, a person, an individual, a mind-born, a youth, an agent, an experiencer, a knower, or a seer; they are like an illusion, like a dream, like an echo, like a reflection, like a mirage, like a shadow, like a magical creation, and like a city of Gandharvas.
"Son of good family, if you can thus observe the true principle of all phenomena and follow this Dharma Master, you will before long accomplish the profound Prajñāpāramitā."
Furthermore, son of good family!

You should recognize other demonic activities as well: namely, when a Dharma teacher, upon seeing you requesting the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, shows no regard for you and instead treats you with contempt, you should not harbor anger or resentment toward him. Rather, you should further increase your love, respect, and reverent mind for the Dharma, constantly following the Dharma teacher without ever becoming weary or disheartened.
At that time, having received the repeated instructions from the voice in the sky, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita’s joy increased all the more, and he proceeded eastward from there.
Before long, he again had this thought:
"I would rather not ask that voice in the sky about my journey to the east—how far it is, or which city or town I shall reach."
"From whom else shall I hear this profound *prajñāpāramitā*?
Having had this thought, he remained right where he was, beating his breast, lamenting with grief, and weeping in sorrow.
After a short while, he reflected thus:

"I shall remain here for one day and night, or even for seven days and seven nights; without succumbing to weariness, without thinking of sleep, without craving food or drink, without perceiving day or night, and without fearing cold or heat, my mind shall not be distracted by internal or external phenomena. Until I have ascertained the distance to the city where I heard this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, and until I have reached it, I shall never give rise to the thought of leaving this place."
“Subhūti, you should know this:
suppose, for example, that parents have an only son who is handsome, intelligent, and possesses many skills, and they love him exceedingly.”
When his son reached full maturity and suddenly passed away, the parents at that time wailed in grief and bitter anguish, remembering their son alone with no other thought in mind.
Sadāprarudita Bodhisattva was likewise; at that moment, he had no other thought but this: "When shall I hear the Prajñāpāramitā?"
Why did I not previously ask the voice in the sky to encourage me to travel east— how far it would go, to what place it would lead,
and from whom I would hear this profound *prajñāpāramitā*?

"Subhūti, you should know that while the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita was thus weeping and lamenting with self-reproach, suddenly an image of the Buddha appeared before him and praised the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita,
saying: 'Excellent!'"
Excellent, son of good family!

When the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the past were bodhisattvas, they sought the profound *prajñāpāramitā* through arduous practices, just as you now apply yourself in your quest for it.
Furthermore, son of good family!

With such a mind of courageous diligence, love, and reverence for seeking the Dharma, travel eastward from here for a distance of five hundred yojanas; there you will find a great royal city named Sugandhāvatī.

That city was high and vast, accomplished of the seven precious gems; surrounding its exterior were sevenfold walls, sevenfold watchtowers, sevenfold railings, sevenfold precious moats, and sevenfold rows of precious *tāla* trees, all made of the seven precious gems. These walls and other structures were interspersed and adorned with one another, emitting various kinds of light that were most lovely and delightful.
This great jewel city measures twelve *yojana*s on each side; it is pure, vast, teeming with people, peaceful, prosperous, and joyful.
Within it are five hundred streets, lanes, and marketplaces, all of equal proportions and as magnificent as a painting.
Along every thoroughfare flows clear water, spanned by jeweled boats that travel back and forth without congestion.
Each and every street and lane was pure and magnificently adorned; they were sprinkled with scented water and strewn with famous flowers.

The city and its walls were all equipped with defensive parapets and battlements, as well as watchtowers and pavilions, all made of purple gold and polished with various jewels that radiated brilliant light. Set amidst these battlements were jeweled trees, each and every one of them—
The roots, stems, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits were all composed of distinct jewels;
the city walls, towers, pavilions, and various jeweled trees were covered with golden nets and connected by jeweled cords, from which hung golden bells and were strung with jeweled chimes.
When stirred by a gentle breeze, they produced harmonious and elegant sounds, like the skillful performance of music consisting of five instruments. This was...
Within the precious city, immeasurable sentient beings constantly hear sounds of joy and happiness day and night.

Surrounding the city on all sides are seven tiers of precious moats, filled to the brim with water possessing the eight virtues; it is cool, warm, temperate, clear, and as limpid as a mirror. Throughout the water are boats made of the seven treasures, adorned and decorated in such a way that all who see them find them pleasing. These sentient beings, drawn by the power of their past karma, frequently board these vessels together to float and sport upon them. Within the waters of the moats grow various exquisite flowers—*utpala*, *padma*, *kumuda*, *puṇḍarīka*, and other diverse kinds of precious blossoms—vibrant in color and rich in fragrance, covering the surface of the water entirely. In short, every famous flower found within the three thousandfold world-system is present there without exception.

There were five hundred gardens surrounding the great city, adorned in various ways and most delightful. Within each garden were five hundred ponds, each one *krośa* in length and breadth, adorned with the seven precious gems and pleasing to the hearts of all. In these ponds grew four kinds of wondrous flowers—the *utpala*, the *padma*, the *kumuda*, and the *puṇḍarīka*—each as large as a chariot wheel, covering the water. These flowers were composed entirely of various jewels: those that were blue were vividly blue, casting blue reflections and emitting blue light; those that were yellow were vividly yellow, casting yellow reflections and emitting yellow light; those that were red were vividly red, casting red reflections and emitting red light; and those that were white were vividly white, casting white reflections and emitting white light.

In the various gardens and ponds there were many kinds of birds—peacocks, parrots, ducks, gulls, wild geese, yellow hawks, orioles, blue ducks, white cranes, spring warblers, herons, egrets, mandarin ducks, cormorants, kingfishers, jingwei, kunji, zhuyu, yunku, kunfeng, garudas, ospreys, kalaviṅkas, kinnaras, and śārika birds—all of which harmonized their songs as they sported therein.

These gardens and ponds belong to no one; it is because those sentient beings have practiced the profound *prajñāpāramitā* throughout the long night and have given rise to faith and joy toward the profound Dharma gates, that through the shared performance of such superior karma in past lives, they now together experience this fruit.
"Furthermore, noble son!
Within the city of Gandhavatī, there is a sublime and exalted place, the palace where the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata dwells."

The palace was one yojana in length and breadth; adorned with various jewels, it was wondrous and lovely. Surrounding the palace were sevenfold rows of walls, sevenfold towers, sevenfold railings, sevenfold jeweled moats, and sevenfold lines of precious *tāla* trees; these walls and other features were exquisitely decorated and most delightful.
There are four wonderful groves surrounding this palace: the first is named Constant Joy, the second Free from Sorrow, the third Flower Adornment, and the fourth Fragrant Ornament.

Within each grove there are eight ponds: the first is named Worthy and Good, the second Worthy Superior, the third Joyful, the fourth Joyful Superior, the fifth Peaceful and Secure, the sixth Endowed with Peace, the seventh Free from Fear, and the eighth Non-retrogression.
Each of the four sides of the ponds is composed of a single jewel: first gold, second silver, third vaidūrya, and fourth sphāṭika.

The bottom of the ponds is made of *karketa* jewels, spread over with golden sand and filled with clear, limpid water. Along each bank of the ponds are eight steps, adorned with various exquisite jewels and featuring treads of superior gold. Between the rows of steps stand plantain trees, their trunks fashioned from purple and gold. Within these ponds grow four kinds of wondrous flowers—the *utpala*, *padma*, *kumuda*, and *puṇḍarīka*—of various colors intermingled and covering the surface of the water. On all four sides of the ponds are fragrant flowering trees; when a gentle breeze blows at times, they scatter blossoms into the water. All the ponds possess the eight meritorious qualities of water, being as fragrant as sandalwood and perfect in color and taste, where ducks, geese, and other birds sport and play.

The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata dwells in this palace, constantly sporting with sixty-eight thousand handmaidens in various gardens and ponds, enjoying themselves together through the five exquisite sensual pleasures. For the sake of beholding the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata and listening to the Dharma, the men and women—both great and small—of the city of Gandhavatī sometimes gain entry into the gardens such as Nityapramudita and the ponds such as Bhadraśīla, where they likewise enjoy themselves through the five sensual pleasures.
"Furthermore, noble son!
After the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata has enjoyed exquisite pleasures with his retinue of maidens, he expounds the Prajñāpāramitā for them three times during the day and night."

Within the city of Gandhavatī, there were men and women who, upon a terrace of the seven precious gems within that city, prepared a lion throne adorned with various jewels for the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata.
The four legs of the seat were each made of a different jewel: first gold, second silver, third vaidūrya, and fourth sphatika.
