Upon the seat, cushions were layered; next, fine brocade was spread, covered with white woolen cloth and draped with silken cords. On both sides of the jeweled throne, crimson pillows were placed in pairs, while various curtains and ribbons hung down, and exquisite incense and flowers were scattered about.

The seat was high and wide, measuring half a krośa; above it, in the air, was spread a variegated canopy, within which a beaded curtain was hung to match the dimensions of the seat. Flower tassels dangled and golden bells were suspended. Out of reverence for the Dharma, five-colored flowers were scattered around the four sides of the seat, and priceless incense was burned.
Furthermore, they smeared and scattered various types of fragrant oils and powdered incense upon the ground, and arranged numerous precious banners, streamers, and canopies.
From time to time, the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata ascended this jeweled throne and proclaimed the profound *prajñāpāramitā* for the sake of the assembly.

Whenever he preached the Dharma, immeasurable devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans would all assemble together; they paid homage and made offerings to the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata and listened to the reception of the Prajñāpāramitā.

At that time, having heard the Dharma, among the great assembly there were those who memorized and upheld it, those who wrote it down, those who recited it aloud, those who contemplated it, those who practiced according to its teachings, and those who awakened others to it. By virtue of these causes and conditions, those sentient beings attained the quality of not falling into the evil realms and became forever non-retrogressive from unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

"O son of good family, you should apply yourself with diligent vigor and proceed quickly to where the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata resides; there he shall cause you to hear the Prajñāpāramitā that you seek."
"Furthermore, son of good family!

The Bodhisattva Dharmodgata has been your true, pure, and virtuous spiritual friend throughout the long night; he has shown you, instructed you, encouraged you, and gladdened you, so that you may swiftly realize the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment you seek."

In past lives, the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata sought the profound *prajñāpāramitā* through diligent ascetic practices, employing the very same skillful means that you now employ in your quest. You should go quickly to where the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata resides; do not harbor doubts or difficulties, and do not calculate days or nights, for before long you shall hear the profound *prajñāpāramitā*.
At that time, having heard these words, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita felt a surge of joy and exultant delight, and he thought to himself:
"When shall I see the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata and hear from him this profound Prajñāpāramitā?"
"Subhūti, you should know this!
For example, suppose there is a person who has been struck by a poisoned arrow; so acutely tormented by the pain that he has no other thought, he thinks only this:
'When shall I encounter a skilled physician who can extract this arrow and free me from this suffering?'"
Sadāprarudita Bodhisattva was likewise; at that time, he had no other thought, but only this reflection:

"When shall I see the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata, approach and make offerings to him so as to hear the Prajñāpāramitā? Having heard it, may I be able to forever sever all manner of false conceptualizations and views of attainment, and swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?"

“Suvikrāntavikrāmin, you should know that while the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita remained in this place and formed such a thought, he gave rise to unobstructed knowledge and vision regarding all phenomena; by means of this knowledge and vision, he was able to enter immeasurable and sublime gateways of samādhi.”
Namely: the samādhi of contemplating the intrinsic nature of all phenomena; the samādhi of non-apprehension of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena;
the samādhi of destroying ignorance regarding all phenomena; and the samādhi of attaining the non-differentiation of all phenomena.
The samādhi of seeing all phenomena as without change, the samādhi of being able to illuminate all phenomena,
the samādhi of being free from darkness regarding all phenomena, the samādhi of attaining the non-distinctive intent of all phenomena,
the samādhi of knowing that all phenomena are entirely unobtainable, and the samādhi of dispersing one...
The Samādhi of Cutting Flowers, the Samādhi that Elucidates the Selflessness of All Phenomena, the Samādhi of Departing from Illusion,
the Samādhi that Elucidates the Illumination of Mirror-Images, the Samādhi that Elucidates the Languages of All Sentient Beings,
the Samādhi that Delights All Sentient Beings, and the One that is Well-Adapted.
The samādhi of the speech of all sentient beings; the samādhi that brings forth various words and phrases;
the samādhi of fearlessness and non-interruption; the samādhi that can explain that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is ineffable;
the samādhi of attaining unimpeded liberation; and the samādhi of being far removed from all dust.
...the samādhi of skillfulness in names, phrases, syllables, and words; the samādhi that gives rise to superior insight into all phenomena;
the samādhi of attaining the unimpeded limit of all phenomena; the samādhi like space; the vajra-like samādhi;
and the samādhi which, though manifesting as form, commits no transgression. Attaining...
The Samādhi of Victory, the Samādhi of Attaining the Non-regressive Eye, the Samādhi of Emerging from the Dharmadhātu,
the Samādhi of Consoling and Subduing, the Samādhi of the Lion’s Exertion, Yawning, and Roaring,
the Samādhi of Outshining All Sentient Beings, and the Samādhi of Being Far Removed from All Defilements. Regarding...
The samādhi of attaining non-defilement in all phenomena, the lotus-adornment samādhi, the samādhi that severs all doubt,
the samādhi that accords with all that is firm, the samādhi that issues forth from all phenomena,
the samādhi of attaining the powers of supernatural knowledge and fearlessness, and the samādhi of manifest penetration into all things.
The samādhi of the Dharma, the samādhi of the seal that destroys all dharmas, the samādhi that manifests the non-differentiation of all dharmas,
the samādhi that leaves behind the dense forest of all views, the samādhi that leaves behind all darkness, the samādhi that leaves behind all marks,
the samādhi that liberates from all attachments, and the samādhi that leaves behind...
The samādhi of dispelling all indolence, the samādhi of attaining profound illumination of the Dharma,
the samādhi like Mount Sumeru, the samādhi of being unassailable, the samādhi of subduing all demonic armies,
the samādhi of non-attachment to the three realms, and the samādhi that brings forth all supreme radiance.
The ground, and so on, up to the samādhi of directly beholding all Buddhas.

While the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita dwelt in this samādhi, he directly beheld the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas in immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless worlds throughout the ten directions as they were teaching the Prajñāpāramitā to the assembly of Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas. All those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas together praised, comforted, exhorted, and instructed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita, saying:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
Excellent, son of good family!

When we formerly practiced the bodhisattva path, we also sought the profound *prajñāpāramitā* through diligent and arduous practice, just as you do now. At the time of our diligent seeking, we also attained such *samādhis* as you have now attained. Having attained these immeasurable and supreme *samādhis* at that time and having brought them to ultimate cultivation, we were able to accomplish the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and its skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*). By means of this, we were able to accomplish all Buddha-dharmas and thereby dwell in the stage of non-retrogression.

We observe that the intrinsic nature of these various samādhis is without entering or exiting; we do not see any phenomenon capable of entering or exiting, nor do we see anyone capable of practicing the conduct of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, nor do we see anyone capable of realizing unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
At that time, because we were without attachment to any phenomena, this was called the *prajñāpāramitā*.

Because we dwelt in this non-attachment, we were able to obtain a body of true golden color with a constant radiance extending one fathom, endowed with the thirty-two marks of a great man and fully adorned with the eighty secondary characteristics.

Furthermore, one is able to realize the inconceivable, unsurpassed wisdom of a Buddha, the unsurpassed ethical discipline of a Buddha, the unsurpassed meditative concentration of a Buddha, and the unsurpassed insight of a Buddha, such that all perfections of merit are fully perfected without exception.
Because he has perfected all the pāramitās of merit, even a Buddha cannot measure or fully describe them, let alone the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas!
For this reason, son of good family!

You should redouble your reverence for this Dharma, cherish it, and seek it with diligence, never abandoning it even for a moment. If you redouble your reverence for this Dharma, cherish it, and seek it with diligence such that you do not abandon it even for a moment, then unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment will be easily realized.
Furthermore, son of good family!
You should always revere spiritual friends, cherishing and diligently seeking them with the same regard as you would for the Buddhas. Why is this?
“Noble son! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva is always sustained and protected by virtuous friends, they will swiftly attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
At that time, the bodhisattva mahāsattva Sadāprarudita addressed the Buddhas of the ten directions, saying:
"What is it that you call my good friend?
Whom should I approach, revere, and make offerings to?
The Buddhas of the ten directions replied to Sadāprarudita:

“There is the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata; he is your true, pure, and virtuous friend throughout the long night. He is able to sustain and protect you, bringing you to maturity in your quest for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and he also causes you to train in the profound perfection of wisdom through skillful means. Because he has sustained and benefited you throughout the long night, he is your virtuous friend; you should draw near to him, honor him, and make offerings to him.”
Furthermore, son of good family!
Whether for one eon, or two, or three, and so on up to a hundred thousand eons, or even beyond that, you should reverently honor and uphold the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata.

Furthermore, even if one were to offer all manner of supreme and exquisite articles of pleasure, up to and including every sublime form, sound, fragrance, flavor, and tactile object existing within the entire trichiliocosm as an offering, one would still be unable to repay even a moment’s worth of that person's kindness.
Why is this? Son of good family!

It is by the power of the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata that you have now attained such immeasurable, supreme, and wondrous doors of samādhi; furthermore, it is through him that you shall obtain the profound perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) and skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), whereby you will swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
Then, the Buddhas of the ten directions, having comforted, exhorted, and instructed Sadāprarudita Bodhisattva through their skillful means and caused him to rejoice, suddenly vanished.
At that time, Sadāprarudita Bodhisattva Mahāsattva arose from the samādhi he had just realized; not seeing the Buddhas, his heart was filled with despondency, and he thought to himself:
"From where did the Buddhas of the ten directions whom I just saw previously come, and where have they now gone?"
"Who can sever such doubts for me? He further thought:

"The Bodhisattva Dharmodgata has long practiced and studied the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*); he has attained immeasurable *dhāraṇī* gates and *samādhis*; he has reached the ultimate perfection in the sovereign supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) of all bodhisattvas; he has already made offerings to immeasurable Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas; and under those Buddhas, he has made great vows and planted various roots of merit. Throughout the long night, he has been my virtuous friend, constantly sustaining me so that I may obtain benefit and happiness."

I shall go quickly to the place where the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata resides, and ask him about those Buddhas of the ten directions whom I have just seen: from where did they previously come, and where are they now going?
"He will be able to sever such doubts for me.
"Subhūti, you should know that at that time,
after the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita had formed this thought, his heart of love, respect, and pure faith toward the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata increased all the more."
Again, he thought to himself:
"I now wish to go to where the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata resides; with what should I make an offering?

However, I am poor and destitute, possessing no flowers, perfumes, unguents, powdered incense, robes, necklaces, jeweled banners, pennants, canopies, music, lamps, mani-jewels, pearls, lapis lazuli, crystal, gold, silver, coral, conch shells, jade, or any other various kinds of excellent and sublime offerings wherewith I might honor the profound Prajñāpāramitā and the Dharma-preacher, the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata."

I must certainly not go to the presence of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata in vain; if I were to go there empty-handed, no joy would arise within me. How could this demonstrate my sincere quest for the Dharma? Therefore, I should now sell myself to obtain the price, which I shall use to make offerings to the profound Prajñāpāramitā and to the Dharma-preacher, the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata.

Why is this? Throughout the long night of transmigration through various realms and births, I have pointlessly lost and destroyed infinite lifespans; for beginningless birth and death, with desire as their cause and condition, I have fallen into the various hells and endured immeasurable suffering, yet I have never sacrificed my own body and life to make offerings to such a sublime Dharma or to a teacher of the Dharma.
Therefore, I must now certainly sell my own body to obtain wealth, which I shall use to make offerings to this profound Prajñāpāramitā and to the Dharma-preacher, the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata.

At that time, after the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita had formed this thought, he gradually traveled eastward until he reached a great city, which was vast, magnificent, and pure, filled with many people living in peace, abundance, and joy.
Sadāprarudita Bodhisattva entered the marketplace and, wandering from place to place, cried out in a loud voice:
"I am now selling myself; who wishes to buy a person?
I am now selling myself; who wishes to buy a person?"
At that time, having witnessed this event, Māra the Evil One thought to himself:

"Because the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita cherishes the Dharma so deeply, he wishes to sell his own body in order to make offerings to the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and to the Dharma-preacher, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata. By means of this, he will be able to inquire correctly regarding the skillful means of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, asking:
'How should a bodhisattva practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā* through skillful means so as to swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?'"

Having asked this question, the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata shall proclaim for him the essential points of the profound Dharma so that he may attain great learning—learning as vast as the great ocean, which cannot be destroyed by Māra or his retinue—and gradually perfect all merits. By means of this, he will benefit all classes of sentient beings, enabling them to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Furthermore, he is able to cause all classes of sentient beings to realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, passing it down from one to another as they dwell within the sphere of emptiness and selflessness.
I shall employ skillful means to conceal his voice, so that the elders, householders, brahmins, and others within this city shall not hear it at all.
"Except for the daughter of an elder in the city, whose power of past roots of goodness the Māra could not obscure.
Due to these circumstances, the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita, after a long time, was unable to sell his body; filled with grief and distress, he stood in one place and said with tears:
'What sin have I committed?'"
Is it because you wish to make offerings to the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and to the Dharma-preacher, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata, that you have sold yourself yet found no buyer?
Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, having seen this, thought to himself:

"This son of good family has sold his own body out of love for the Dharma, in order to make offerings to the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and the Dharma-preacher, the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata. I shall test him:
does he truly long for the Dharma?"
"Are you harboring deceit and fraud to delude the world?
Having thought this, he immediately transformed himself into a young brahmin and went to where Sadāprarudita was, asking him: "O man!..."
"For what reason do you now stand here, weeping with grief and sorrow,
appearing unhappy? Sadāprarudita Bodhisattva replied, "O Youth!"

"I wish to make offerings to the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and to the Dharma-preacher, the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata; yet, being poor and lacking all wealth and treasures, and out of my deep love for the Dharma, I desire to sell myself. Throughout this entire city, there is no one who will inquire after me; reflecting thus upon my meager merit, I dwell here in sorrow and grief."
Then the brahmin said to Sadāprarudita:
"I am currently intending to perform a sacrifice to the gods; I do not require a human body, but only human blood, human marrow, and a human heart. Would you be able to sell these?"
Having heard this, Sadāprarudita Bodhisattva thought to himself:
"I have now certainly attained a great benefit. Why is this?..."

"Whatever that person wishes to buy, I possess it all; by means of this price, I shall be able to make offerings to the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and to the Dharma-preacher, the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata, so that I may become fully endowed with the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), and swiftly realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
When he had this thought, he was filled with joy and leaped for gladness, and with gentle words he replied to the brāhmaṇa:
"I can sell everything that you wish to buy. The brāhmaṇa said:
"How much is its price? Sadāprarudita replied,
"I shall repay you as you wish."

At that time, having spoken these words, Sadāprarudita extended his right hand, took up a sharp blade, pierced his left arm to let the blood flow out, and further cut the skin and flesh from his right thigh, placing them on the ground. He broke the bone to extract the marrow and gave it to the Brahmin; then he went toward the wall, intending to cut open his chest and take out his heart.

"A daughter of a householder was staying on an upper terrace; she first saw Sadāprarudita crying out as he sold himself, and later she saw him again as he was inflicting injury upon his own body. She thought to herself:
'For what reason or cause does this son of good family afflict his body? I shall question him.'"
Having thought thus, he descended from his chamber to where Sadāprarudita was and asked him:
"For what reason did you first announce that you would sell yourself, and now, having bled your marrow, do you wish to cut out your heart?"
Sadāprarudita replied, "Sister, do you not know?

It is for the sake of making offerings to the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and to the Dharma-preacher, the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata, that I am acting; yet, being poor and lacking all wealth and treasures, and out of my deep love for the Dharma, I first attempted to sell my own body, but found no buyer. I shall now sell these three things to the Brahmin."
The daughter of the householder said:

"If you now sell your own blood, heart, and marrow, intending to provide the proceeds as an offering to the *Prajñāpāramitā* and to the Dharma-preacher Bodhisattva Dharmodgata, what kind of meritorious benefits and advantages will you obtain?"

Sadāprarudita replied, "The Bodhisattva Dharmodgata has attained mastery over the profound Dharma; he shall explain to me the profound Prajñāpāramitā, the skillful means, that which is to be studied by a bodhisattva, that upon which a bodhisattva rides, that which is practiced by a bodhisattva, and that which is performed by a bodhisattva."
Having heard this, I shall practice according to the teaching, maturing sentient beings and purifying Buddha-fields,
so as to swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; obtaining a golden body, endowed with the thirty-two marks of a great man and fully adorned with the eighty secondary signs,
with a constant light extending one fathom and immeasurable rays of light beyond that.
Possessing the ten powers of a Buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges,
great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, the quality of non-forgetfulness,
the nature of constant abiding in equanimity, the five pure eyes, the six supernormal powers, and the inconceivable aggregate of pure ethical discipline.

the aggregate of concentration, the aggregate of wisdom, the aggregate of liberation, the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation, unobstructed knowledge and vision, and unsurpassed knowledge and vision;
having attained all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*);
and being fully endowed with all the unsurpassed jewels of the Dharma, distributing and bestowing them upon all sentient beings.
"All sentient beings rely upon them as their refuge;
I shall sacrifice my body and life to make offerings to them, and thereby I shall obtain these meritorious benefits.

At that time, having heard this sublime, inconceivable, and wondrous Dharma of the Buddha, the daughter of the elder was filled with joy and exultation such that her hair stood on end. With palms joined in reverence, she addressed Sadāprarudita, saying:

"What the Great Being has taught is foremost, vast, most excellent, subtle, and truly rare. To obtain even a single one of these Buddha-dharmas, one should be willing to sacrifice a body and life as precious as the sands of the Ganges, let alone sacrifice only one."
Why is this? If one attains such subtle and wondrous merit, one is then able to benefit and bring happiness to all sentient beings.

Even when a Great Being’s family is poor, they do not spare their own life or limb for the sake of such subtle and wondrous merit; how much less would I, whose family is wealthy and possesses abundant treasures, fail to renounce them for the sake of this merit!
"O Great Being, you should not harm yourself any further; I shall provide you with all the requisites you require.

These include gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, mani-jewels, pearls, conch shells, stone vessels, cowries, gems, sapphire, emerald, coral, amber, and other immeasurable varieties of rare treasures; as well as flowers, incense, necklaces, jeweled banners, pennants, canopies, music, lamps, vehicles, clothing, and various other exquisite offerings—by which you may make offerings to the profound Prajñāpāramitā and to the Dharma-preacher, the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata."

I only pray that the Great Being will not harm yourself again; I also wish to follow the Great Being to where the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata dwells, so that we may together behold him and plant roots of goodness for the sake of attaining all the Buddha-dharmas he has explained.

The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle 398. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Part One, Chapter Seventy-seven, Part Two: The Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita. At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, resumed his original form and stood before Sadāprarudita with his body bowed in reverence, praising him, saying:
"O Mahāsattva!..."
Excellent! Excellent!

Your sincerity and steadfastness for the Dharma are indeed such as this. When the Buddhas of the past were bodhisattvas, they were also like this Great Being; through their steadfast vows, they sought the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and skillful means, inquiring about what a bodhisattva studies, mounts, practices, and accomplishes without weariness of mind, thereby maturing sentient beings and purifying buddha-fields until they realized unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
"O Great Being, you should know!
I truly do not require human blood, heart, or marrow; I have merely come to test you.
Now, what is your wish?"
"I shall provide you with this to repay the offense of your slighting touch and your infliction of harm.
Sadāprarudita replied, "My original vow has been solely for unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment; can the Lord of Devas grant me this wish?"
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, was abashed with shame and said to Sadāprarudita:
"This is not within my power; only the Great Holy Dharma Kings, the Buddhas who possess mastery over all phenomena, can grant such a boon."
“O Great Being!
You should now set aside the aspiration for unsurpassed enlightenment and seek another vow;
I shall grant it to you. Sadāprarudita replied:
"The profound *prajñāpāramitā* is also my own aspiration; might you be able to grant it to me?
At that time, Śakra, Lord of Devas, felt even greater shame and said to Sadāprarudita:
"I cannot grant this aspiration either; however, I have the power to restore your body, Great Being, to its former state—would you accept this instead?"
Sadāprarudita replied:
"Such a vow as this can be fulfilled by myself; there is no need for the Lord of Devas. Why is that?
If I were to address the Buddhas of the ten directions with these words of solemn truth:

"I am now truly selling my own body out of a longing for the Dharma; I harbor no flattery or deceit to delude the world, and by virtue of this cause and condition, I shall certainly never regress from unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment—then may my body be restored to its former state."
Before these words were finished, he was naturally restored to his former state; what need was there for the majesty of the gods!
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, said: "It is so!"
"It is so! The spiritual power of the Buddha is inconceivable; what task could the Bodhisattva’s utmost sincerity not accomplish?
Yet, because of me, the body of the Great Being has been harmed. I only pray that, out of compassion, you will permit this matter to be settled."
Sadāprarudita Bodhisattva then said to him, "Since you are so earnest, I shall comply with your wish.

At that moment, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, manifested his celestial majesty, restoring Sadāprarudita’s body to its former state; not even the slightest trace of a wound remained, and his appearance became more dignified and handsome than it had been before. Feeling ashamed and grateful, he circumambulated him to the right and suddenly vanished.

At that time, the daughter of the elder, having witnessed the rare and marvelous deeds of the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita, her affection and reverence for him increased all the more. Joining her palms in respectful salutation, she said to Sadāprarudita:

"I pray you, out of compassion, deign to visit my home for a moment. Whatever sublime offerings are required for the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and for the Dharma-preacher, the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata, shall all be obtained through my petition to my parents."

I and my retinue shall also take leave of our parents and follow the Great Being to the city of Gandhavatī, desiring to make offerings to the profound Prajñāpāramitā and to the Dharma-preacher, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata.
At that time, Sadāprarudita, according to her wish, went with her to her house and stopped outside the door.
Then, the merchant’s daughter entered the house and said to her parents:

"I pray that you grant me all the most excellent and exquisite offerings in my home—flower garlands, scented unguents and powders, robes, necklaces, jeweled banners, pennants, canopies, musical instruments, ghee and oil, mani-jewels, pearls, lapis lazuli, crystal, coral, amber, conch shells, jade, *gṛdhra-kūṭa* stones, *śarkara-kūṭa* stones, indranīla, mahānīla, as well as gold, silver, and various other such articles. Furthermore, please permit me and my five hundred former attendants who serve me to take these offerings and follow the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita to the City of Exquisite Fragrance, in order to make offerings to the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and to the Dharma-preacher, the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata."
"He shall proclaim the essentials of the Dharma for me; having heard them, I will practice according to his instructions and will certainly attain the boundless, subtle, and wondrous Buddha-dharmas.
At that time, when her parents heard this, they were struck with alarm and immediately asked their daughter, "Where is the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita now?"
"What kind of person is this?
The woman immediately replied:

"He is currently outside the gate; he is a great being (mahāsattva) who, for the sake of liberating all sentient beings from the suffering of birth and death, diligently seeks unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

Furthermore, that Great Being, cherishing the True Dharma and not begrudging his own body or life, entered this city and wandered from place to place, proclaiming in a loud voice: "I now sell myself! This was for the sake of making offerings to the profound *prajñāpāramitā* studied by Bodhisattvas, as well as to the Dharma-preacher, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata.
"Who wishes to buy a person?
I am now selling myself!
Who wishes to buy a person?"
After a long time had passed, he was unable to sell his body; filled with grief and distress, he stood in one place and said through tears:
"What sin have I committed?"

Out of a desire to make offerings to the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and to the Dharma-preacher, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata, why is it that although he has sold himself, there is no one to buy him?
Then, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, wishing to test him, immediately transformed himself into a young brahmin and approached him, asking: "O man!..."
"Why do you remain here, sorrowful, grieving,
and unhappy? At that time, the Great Being replied, "O Youth!"

"I wish to make offerings to the profound Prajñāpāramitā and to the Dharma-preacher, the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata; yet, being poor and lacking all wealth and treasures, and out of my deep love for the Dharma, I desire to sell myself. Having searched throughout this city, I have found no one who will buy me. Reflecting upon my meager merit, I remain here in sorrow and grief."

Then the brahmin said to the Great Being, "I am currently intending to perform a sacrifice to the gods; I do not require human flesh, but only human blood, human marrow, and a human heart. Would you be willing to sell them?"
Upon hearing this, the Great Being was filled with joy and leaped for gladness;
with gentle words he replied to the brahmin, "I can sell everything that you wish to purchase. The brahmin said:
"How much do you ask for it?
The Mahāsattva replied,
"I shall accept whatever price you wish to offer."

When the Mahāsattva had spoken these words, he immediately extended his right hand and took up a sharp knife. He pierced his own left arm to let the blood flow out, then cut the skin and flesh from his right thigh, placing them on the ground; he broke the bone to extract the marrow and gave it to the brāhmaṇa, and then proceeded toward the wall, intending to cut open his chest and take out his heart.
"From atop my high pavilion, I saw this from afar and thought to myself:
'For what reason and by what causes does this good man afflict his body with such hardship?'"
"I shall question him. Having thought this, he descended from his chamber to the place where the Great Being was and asked him:
"For what reason did you first announce that you would sell yourself, and now, having bled and extracted your marrow, do you further intend to cut out your heart?"
He replied to me, saying, "Sister, do you not know?

It is for the sake of making offerings to the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and the Dharma-preacher, the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata, that I have done this. However, being poor and lacking all wealth and treasures, and out of my deep love and respect for the Dharma, I first attempted to sell my own body but found no buyer; I now sell these three things to a Brahmin."

I then asked him: "Now that you wish to sell your own blood, heart, and marrow to provide the price for making offerings to the Prajñāpāramitā and to the Dharma-preacher Bodhisattva Dharmodgata, what kind of merit and benefit will you obtain?"
He replied to me, saying:

“The Bodhisattva Dharmodgata has attained mastery over the profound Dharma; he shall explain to me the profound Prajñāpāramitā and skillful means—the training of a bodhisattva, the vehicle of a bodhisattva, the conduct of a bodhisattva, and the deeds of a bodhisattva.”
Having heard this, I shall practice according to the teaching, maturing sentient beings and purifying Buddha-fields,
so that I may swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, attain a golden body endowed with the thirty-two marks of a great man and fully adorned by the eighty secondary signs,
and possess a constant light extending one fathom with immeasurable radiance beyond it.
Possessing the ten powers of a Buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges,
great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity; the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, the quality of non-forgetfulness,
the nature of constant abiding in equanimity, the five pure eyes, the six supernormal powers, and the inconceivable aggregate of pure ethical discipline.
the aggregate of concentration, the aggregate of wisdom, the aggregate of liberation, and the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation;

possessing unobstructed knowledge and vision and unsurpassed knowledge and vision; attaining all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*);
being fully endowed with all the unsurpassed treasures of the Dharma; and distributing and bestowing them upon all sentient beings.
"All sentient beings rely upon me;
I shall sacrifice my body and life to make offerings to them, and thereby I shall obtain these meritorious benefits.

At that time, having heard such supreme, inconceivable, and subtle teachings of the Buddha-Dharma, I was filled with joy and exultation, and the hairs on my body stood on end. With palms joined in reverence, I addressed him, saying:

"What the Great Being has spoken is foremost, vast, most excellent, subtle, and truly rare. To obtain even a single one of these Buddha-dharmas, one should be willing to relinquish as many precious lives as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, let alone give up just one!"
Why is this? If one attains such subtle and wondrous merit, one is then able to benefit and bring happiness to all sentient beings.

Even when a Great Being’s family is poor, they do not begrudge their own body or life for the sake of such subtle and wondrous merit; how much more so, then, should I—not being poor but possessing abundant wealth and treasures—renounce them for the sake of this merit!

"Great Being, you should not harm yourself again. Whatever requisites you require, I shall provide them all to you—namely, gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, mani-jewels, pearls, *karketana* stones, *aśmagarbha* stones, conch shells, jade, *indranīla*, *mahānīla*, coral, amber, and other immeasurable varieties of rare treasures; as well as flowers, incense, necklaces, jeweled banners, pennants, canopies, music, lamps, vehicles, clothing, and various other kinds of supreme and wonderful offerings. You may take these to make offerings to the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and to the Dharma-preacher, the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata. I only pray that the Great Being will not harm yourself again."

I also wish that my body may follow this Great Being to where the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Dharmodgata dwells, so that we may together gaze upon him and plant roots of goodness, for the sake of attaining all the Buddha-dharmas he has described.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, immediately resumed his original form and stood before him, bowing with palms joined in reverence and praising him, saying:
"O Great Being! Excellent!"

Excellent! Your sincerity and steadfastness for the sake of the Dharma are indeed such as this. When the Buddhas of the past were bodhisattvas, they were also like this Great Being; through their steadfast vows, they sought the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and skillful means, inquiring about what a bodhisattva studies, mounts, practices, and accomplishes without weariness of mind, maturing sentient beings and purifying buddha-fields, until they had already realized unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
"O Great Being, you should know!
I truly do not require human blood, heart, or marrow; I have merely come to test you.
What is your wish now?"
"I shall provide you with a remedy to atone for the offense of your slighting touch and the harm you have caused.
He replied, "My original aspiration was solely for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; O Lord of Devas, can you grant me this wish?"
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, was struck with shame and said to him:
"This is not within my power; only the Great Holy Dharma Kings, the Buddhas who possess mastery over all phenomena, can grant such a vow."
"O Great Being!
You should now set aside the aspiration for supreme enlightenment and seek another vow;
I shall grant it to you. He then replied:
“The profound *prajñāpāramitā* is also my own wish; could you perhaps grant it to me?
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, felt even greater shame and said to him:
“I cannot grant this wish either. However, I have the power to restore your body to its former state; would you not use this instead?”
He replied again:
"Such a wish can be fulfilled by myself; there is no need for the Lord of Devas to exert himself. Why is this so?"
"If I were to address the Buddhas of the ten directions with these words of solemn truth:

'I am now truly selling my own body out of a longing for the Dharma; I harbor no flattery, deceit, or intent to delude the world. By virtue of this cause and condition, if it is certain that I shall not regress from unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, may my body be restored to its former state.'"
Before these words were finished, he was naturally restored to his former state; what need was there for the majesty of the gods!
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, said: "So it is!"

"So be it! The supernatural power of the Buddha is inconceivable, and there is nothing that a Bodhisattva’s utmost sincerity cannot accomplish; yet, because of me, the body of this Great Being has been harmed. I only pray that, out of compassion, you will grant permission for me to perform this task."
Then that Great Being said to Śakra:
"Since you are so earnest, I shall comply with your wish.

Thereupon, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, manifested his celestial majesty and restored the man's body to its former state, such that not even a trace of a scar remained; his appearance was more dignified and handsome than it had been before. Feeling ashamed and grateful, he circumambulated him to the right and suddenly vanished.
“Having witnessed those rare and marvelous events, my love and respect increased all the more, and with palms joined, I said:

‘I pray that you will deign to show compassion and visit my home for a moment; whatever offerings are required for the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and for the Dharma-preacher, the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata, shall all be obtained once I have informed my parents.’”

I and my attendants shall also take leave of our parents and follow the Great Being to the city of Gandhavatī, desiring to make offerings to the profound Prajñāpāramitā and to the Dharma-preacher, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata.

“‘Now that this Great Being has come to my door because of my utmost sincerity and has not rejected my wish, I pray only that my parents grant me abundant treasures and permit me to go with five hundred of my former attendants, all carrying various offerings, to follow the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita to the City of Excellent Fragrance. There we shall pay homage and make offerings to the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and to the Dharma-preacher, the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata, for the sake of attaining the teachings of all Buddhas as they have been expounded.’”
At that time, having heard what the daughter had said, her parents leaped for joy and marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence. They then said to her:
"As you have described, the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita is truly rare; he has donned such a great armor of merit, seeking all Buddha-dharmas with courageous diligence.
The Buddha-dharmas he seeks are subtle, supreme, vast, pure, and inconceivable; they are able to lead all sentient beings in the world to attain extraordinary benefit and peace."

Since you cherish and revere this Dharma so deeply, and wish to follow a virtuous friend to the City of Exquisite Fragrance carrying various offerings to worship the Prajñāpāramitā and the Dharma-preacher Bodhisattva Dharmodgata for the sake of realizing all Buddha-dharmas, how could we not rejoice in your resolve?
"Now we grant you leave to go; we, too, wish to accompany you—will you be pleased?
The girl immediately replied, "I am most greatly pleased!"
"I do not even obstruct the wholesome dharmas of others, much less those of my own parents!
His parents replied, "You should prepare the offerings and attendants; we must go together immediately."

At that time, the daughter of the elder immediately prepared five hundred chariots, adorned with the seven precious gems. She also ordered five hundred regular female attendants to take as many jewels as they desired to adorn their bodies. Furthermore, she took gold, silver, *vaiḍūrya* gems, *sphaṭika* gems, *maṇi* jewels, pearls, *indranīla*, *mahānīla*, conch shells, jade, coral, amber, *mudgara-kośa*, *pāṣāṇa-kośa*, and other immeasurable varieties of rare treasures; various kinds of flowers and incense, clothing, necklaces, jeweled banners, flags, canopies, musical instruments, ghee and oil, and countless types of exquisite riches, along with various other superior and wonderful offerings.

Once the daughter had completed these preparations, she respectfully requested that Sadāprarudita Bodhisattva ride in a single carriage, while she herself, her parents, and five hundred female attendants each rode in a separate carriage; surrounding and following Sadāprarudita Bodhisattva, they gradually traveled eastward until they reached the city of Gandhavatī.

He saw that the city was high and vast, accomplished of the seven treasures. Surrounding its exterior were, in every direction, sevenfold walls made of the seven treasures, sevenfold watchtowers, sevenfold railings, sevenfold jeweled moats, and sevenfold rows of jeweled *tāla* trees. These walls and other features were interspersed and adorned with one another, emitting various kinds of light that were most lovely and delightful.

This great precious city measures twelve yojanas on each side; it is pure, vast, teeming with people, peaceful, prosperous, and joyful. Within it are five hundred streets, lanes, and marketplaces, all of equal proportions and as magnificent as a painting.
In every thoroughfare and alleyway there were clear streams, spanned by precious boats that moved back and forth without congestion.
Each street and lane was pure and magnificently adorned, sprinkled with fragrant waters and strewn with famous flowers.
The city and its walls were all equipped with defensive battlements, crenellations, and towers made of purple gold, adorned with various precious gems that radiated brilliant light.
Interspersed among the battlements were jeweled trees; each tree—its roots, trunk, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits—was fashioned from distinct precious substances.

The city walls, towers, and various jeweled trees were covered with golden nets, connected by jeweled cords, hung with golden bells, and adorned with jeweled chimes; when stirred by a gentle breeze, they produced harmonious and elegant sounds, like the skillful performance of music using the five types of instruments.

Surrounding the city on all sides were seven tiers of precious moats, filled to the brim with water possessing the eight virtues—its temperature perfectly balanced and its clarity as bright as a polished mirror.
Throughout the water were boats made of the seven treasures, adorned and embellished in such a way that all who beheld them found delight.
Within the waters of the moats, various exquisite flowers of brilliant colors and fragrant scents grow in profusion, completely covering the surface of the water.
Five hundred gardens surround the great city, adorned with all manner of splendors, most delightful to behold.
Within each grove there are five hundred ponds, each measuring one krośa in length and breadth, adorned with the seven treasures and pleasing to the hearts of all.
Within these ponds are flowers of four colors, as large as chariot wheels, which reflect upon the water; these flowers are all composed of the seven treasures.
Within the various ponds and groves, there were many birds whose voices harmonized as they gathered and dispersed in their playful wanderings.

Continuing further forward, he then saw from afar the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata seated upon a lion throne within a pavilion of seven precious gems, surrounded before and behind by an immeasurable, countless multitude of hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas, as he preached the Dharma for them.

At that time, because the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita first saw the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata from afar, his body and mind were filled with joy and bliss, just as a bhikṣu who has fixed his mindfulness on a single object suddenly enters the third dhyāna.
Having seen him from afar, they thought to themselves:
"We ought not to approach the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata while riding in our carriages.
Having had this thought, they immediately alighted from their vehicles and adjusted their robes.

At that time, the daughter of the elder, her parents, and five hundred maidservants also all descended from their carriages; each adorned their bodies with various exquisite robes and many precious jewels, and carrying various offerings, they respectfully surrounded the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita and proceeded slowly toward the place where the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata was.

Beside that road stood a great Mahāprajñāpāramitā terrace constructed by the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata, adorned with red sandalwood, hung with precious bells and chimes that emitted sublime sounds, and surrounded on all sides by nets of genuine pearls.
At the four corners of the terrace, four precious jewels were suspended as lamps, providing constant illumination day and night.

On the four sides of the precious terrace were four incense burners made of white silver and adorned with various jewels; they constantly burned black aloeswood incense, and various exquisite flowers were scattered as offerings.
In the center of the hall was a throne made of the seven precious substances, upon which were spread layers of fine rugs and embroidered silks.
Upon this throne was another casket, composed of four precious materials—first gold, second silver, third lapis lazuli, and fourth sapphire—which was exquisitely adorned and magnificent.
Melted lapis lazuli juice was applied upon leaves of pure gold, upon which the *Prajñāpāramitā* was inscribed; these were placed within this casket and sealed at all times.
Throughout the pavilion, precious banners and flowers were suspended, interspersed and adorned in such a way that they were exceedingly lovely and delightful.
“The Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita, the merchant’s daughter, and the others, seeing this jewel terrace so exquisitely adorned, joined their palms in reverence and marveled at such an unprecedented sight.

They further saw Śakra, together with immeasurable hundreds of thousands of celestial hosts, standing beside the jewel terrace, scattering various kinds of sublime celestial incense powders, myriad precious gems, exquisite fragrant flowers, golden and silver blossoms, and the like upon the terrace, while celestial music resounded in the void.”
When Sadāprarudita Bodhisattva saw this, he asked Śakra:
"For what reason, Lord of Devas, do you and the host of devas make offerings to this pavilion?
Śakra, Lord of Devas, replied:

"O Great Being! Do you not know that within this pavilion there is the unsurpassed Dharma called the Profound Prajñāpāramitā? It is the mother of all Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, and of all Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas; it is able to give birth to and sustain all Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, and the assembly of all Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas."

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can diligently practice and train within this, they will swiftly reach the further shore of all merits, swiftly accomplish all Buddha-dharmas, and swiftly realize the knowledge of all-knowledge.
"For this reason, we, together with our retinues, pay respectful homage and make offerings here.
Having heard this, Sadāprarudita Bodhisattva was filled with joy; following the sound of the voice, he again asked Śakra, the Lord of Devas:
"Where is this profound Prajñāpāramitā that you have described now located?"
"I wish to make offerings; I only pray that you will show them to me!
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, said:
"Great Being, do you know?"

The profound Prajñāpāramitā is within this pavilion, inside a casket made of four jewels upon a throne of seven jewels; its pages are of pure gold and its letters are of vaidūrya gem. The Bodhisattva Dharmodgata has sealed it with a seal of the seven jewels, so we are unable to open it and show it to you at will.

At that time, when the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita, the merchant’s daughter, her parents, and the five hundred maidens heard these words, they immediately took the flowers, incense, precious jewels, garments, necklaces, jeweled banners, flags, canopies, musical instruments, lamps, and all other various articles of worship they were carrying, divided them into two portions, and first took one portion to the jeweled terrace to make offerings to the Prajñāpāramitā. Then, taking the other portion, they went together to where the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata was.

Having arrived, they all beheld the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata seated upon a lion throne, surrounded by a great assembly; they immediately scattered flowers, incense, jeweled banners, pennants, canopies, robes, necklaces, musical instruments, lamps, and various precious gems as offerings to this Dharma-preacher and to the Dharma he was teaching.

By the majestic spiritual power of the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata, the various exquisite flowers that had been scattered suddenly coalesced in the air above his crown into a single exquisite flower pedestal, adorned with myriad jewels and most delightful to behold.
Furthermore, the various exquisite incenses that were scattered suddenly coalesced in mid-air above the flower pedestal into a single wonderful incense canopy, adorned with all kinds of rare jewels.

Furthermore, the various exquisite precious robes that were scattered suddenly coalesced in mid-air above the fragrant canopy, spontaneously forming a single wondrous jeweled pavilion, likewise adorned and embellished with an array of diverse gems.

The other jeweled banners, pennants, canopies, musical instruments, lamps, and various necklaces that were scattered about spontaneously emerged at the edges of the platforms, curtains, and awnings, arranged in a surrounding display of exquisite craftsmanship and adornment.

When the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita, the daughter of the elder, and the others saw this, they were filled with joy and leaped for gladness; with one voice and in unison, they all praised the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata, saying:
"Our great teacher is truly most rare, for he is able to manifest such great majestic spiritual power."
"If he was already able to act thus even while being a bodhisattva, how much more so now that he has attained unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment!

At that time, because the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata was so deeply cherished by their hearts, Sadāprarudita, the merchant’s daughter, and all their attendants each resolved upon unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, making this vow:
"By means of these distinguished roots of goodness, may we in a future age certainly become Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas."

By virtue of these distinguished roots of goodness, we pray that in future lives, when we diligently cultivate the bodhisattva path, we may attain unimpeded mastery of the profound Dharma gates, just like the Great Master, the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata.

By virtue of these distinguished roots of goodness, we pray that in future lives, when we diligently practice the bodhisattva path, we may be able to offer the most exquisite palaces of the seven precious jewels and other articles of worship to the *prajñāpāramitā*, just as the Great Master, the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata, has done.

By virtue of these distinguished roots of goodness, we pray that in future lives, when we diligently cultivate the bodhisattva path, we may sit upon the lion throne amidst the great assembly and proclaim the profound principles of the *prajñāpāramitā* without any fear, just like the Great Master, the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata.

By virtue of these sublime roots of goodness, we pray that in future lives, when we diligently practice the bodhisattva path, we may achieve the skillful means and power of the *prajñāpāramitā*, and swiftly accomplish the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment we seek, just as our current Great Teacher, the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata.

By virtue of these sublime roots of goodness, we pray that in future lives, when we diligently cultivate the bodhisattva path, we may attain supreme supernatural powers and mastery over transformations, thereby bringing benefit, peace, and happiness to immeasurable sentient beings, just like our current Master, the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata.

“After the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita, the merchant’s daughter, and their retinue had offered all these articles of worship to the Prajñāpāramitā and to the Dharma-preacher, the Mahāsattva Dharmodgata, they prostrated at his feet, joined their palms in reverence, circumambulated him three times to the right, and withdrew to stand to one side.”
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita bowed his body and joined his palms, addressing the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata, saying:
"I have always delighted in dwelling in forest hermitages (araṇya) to seek the profound Prajñāpāramitā. Once, at one time, I suddenly heard a voice from the sky saying: 'Ho!'"
“Noble son! You should travel eastward, and you will certainly hear the profound *prajñāpāramitā*.
Having heard this instruction from the sky, I was filled with joy and leaped for gladness; I immediately set out toward the east, and before long, I had this thought:
"I would rather not ask that voice in the sky about how far east I should go,
nor to which city or town I should travel,
nor from whom I shall hear this profound *prajñāpāramitā*."

Having formed this thought, he remained in that place, beating his breast and lamenting with grief and sorrow, weeping for seven days and nights without weariness, without concern for sleep, without thought of food or drink, without reckoning day or night, and without fear of cold or heat;
his mind was undistracted regarding internal or external phenomena, and he thought only this: "When shall I hear the Prajñāpāramitā?"
Why did I not previously ask the voice in the sky that urged me to travel eastward about how far it was,
to what place I should go,
and from whom I would hear this profound *prajñāpāramitā*?
"While I was thus lamenting, weeping, and sighing in self-reproach, suddenly an image of the Buddha appeared before me and addressed me, saying:
'O son of good family!'"

With such a mind of courageous diligence, love, and reverent seeking for the Dharma, travel eastward from here for a distance of five hundred yojanas; there you will find a great royal city named Sugandhā, in which dwells a bodhisattva named Dharmodgata who constantly proclaims the Prajñāpāramitā to immeasurable hundreds of thousands of sentient beings. You shall hear the Prajñāpāramitā from him.
Furthermore, son of good family!

The Bodhisattva Dharmodgata has been your pure spiritual friend throughout the long night, instructing, teaching, encouraging, and gladdening you, so that you may swiftly realize the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment you seek.

In past lives, the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata sought the profound *prajñāpāramitā* through diligent and arduous practice, employing the very same skillful means that you now employ in your quest. You should go quickly to where the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata resides; do not give rise to doubt or hesitation, and do not calculate days or nights, for before long you shall hear the profound *prajñāpāramitā*.
“Having heard these words at that time, my heart was filled with delight, and I leaped for joy; I thought to myself:
‘When shall I behold the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata?’”

Having heard this profound *prajñāpāramitā* from him, and having heard it, how can one immediately and forever sever various false conceptualizations and views of objective attainment, and swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?

When he formed this thought, he was immediately able to give rise to unobstructed knowledge and vision regarding all phenomena; by means of this knowledge and vision, he entered directly into immeasurable and sublime gateways of samādhi.

Abiding within this samādhi, I directly perceive the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, in immeasurable, innumerable, and boundless worlds throughout the ten directions, as they proclaim the Prajñāpāramitā for the sake of the assembly of Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
"At that time, all the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas together praised and comforted me, and earnestly instructed and exhorted me, saying: 'Excellent!'"
Excellent, son of good family!

When we formerly practiced the bodhisattva path, we also sought the profound *prajñāpāramitā* through diligent and arduous practices just as you do now; and during those times of diligent effort, we also attained such samādhis as these which you have now attained.

At that time, having attained this immeasurable and supreme samādhi and having cultivated it to its ultimate conclusion, we were able to accomplish the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*); through these, we were able to fulfill all the Buddha-dharmas and thereby attained the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika-bhūmi*).
“At that time, the Buddhas of the ten directions extensively instructed and comforted me, and having caused me to rejoice, they suddenly vanished.
Rising from the samādhi I had realized, I did not see the Buddhas and felt a sense of desolation, thinking to myself:
‘From where did those Buddhas of the ten directions whom I just saw previously come?’”
"Where shall I go now?
Who is able to sever such doubts for me?
He then further thought:

“The Bodhisattva Dharmodgata has long since trained in the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*); he has attained immeasurable *dhāraṇī* gates and *samādhis*, and has reached the ultimate perfection in the sovereign supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) of all bodhisattvas. He has made offerings to immeasurable Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas; in the presence of those Buddhas, he has made great vows and planted roots of merit. Throughout the long night, he has been my good friend, constantly sustaining me so that I may obtain benefit and happiness. I shall go quickly to where the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata resides and ask from where those Buddhas of the ten directions whom I have seen previously have come.”
"Where is he going now?
He will be able to sever such doubts for me.

Having formed this thought at that time, I proceeded with courageous diligence toward the east. After a long period had passed, I entered this city and continued forward until I saw from afar the Great Teacher seated upon a lion throne within a pavilion of the seven precious gems, surrounded by a great assembly as he preached the Dharma.
In this place, I beheld the Great Teacher for the first time; my body and mind were filled with joy and bliss, just as a bhikṣu suddenly attains the third dhyāna.
I now ask the Great Teacher:
from where did the Buddhas of the ten directions whom I previously saw originally come?
Where are you now going?
I only pray that you will explain to me the destination from which those Buddhas have come, so that I may understand it; having understood it, may I see all Buddhas in every birth.

78. The Chapter on the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata, Part One: The First Section of the Chapter on the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata, Number Seventy-Eight. At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita, saying:
"O son of good family!..."

The Dharma-body of all Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, Sugatas, Knowers of the World, Unsurpassed Men, Tamer of Men, Teachers of Gods and Humans, Buddhas, Bhagavans, comes from nowhere and goes nowhere.
Why is this? Son of good family!
Because the true nature of all phenomena is entirely immovable.

“Good son! The suchness of all phenomena has neither coming nor going and cannot be conceptually established; this very suchness is the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha—and so on, as extensively explained, up to the Buddha, the Bhagavān.”

“Good son! The dharma-realm of all phenomena has neither coming nor going and cannot be conceptually established; such a dharma-realm is itself the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha—and so on, as extensively explained, up to the Buddha, the Bhagavān.”

“Good son! The dharma-nature of all phenomena neither comes nor goes and cannot be designated; such a dharma-nature is precisely the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha—and as explained at length—down to the Buddha, the Bhagavān.”

“‘Good son! The nature of non-falsity neither comes nor goes and cannot be designated; this nature of non-falsity is itself the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha—and so on, as extensively explained, up to the Buddha, the Bhagavān.’”
“O son of noble family!

The nature of non-alteration neither comes nor goes and cannot be designated; this nature of non-alteration is itself the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha—and so on, as extensively explained, up to the Buddha, the Bhagavān.”

“Good son! The equality of phenomena (dharmasamatā) neither comes nor goes and cannot be conceptually established; the equality of phenomena is itself the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha—expounded at length up to ‘the Buddha, the Bhagavat.’”

“Good son! The nature of phenomena is free from arising; it neither comes nor goes, and cannot be conceptually established. This nature of phenomena, free from arising, is itself the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha—and so on, as extensively explained, up to the Buddha, the Bhagavān.

“Good son! The fixed nature of all phenomena has neither coming nor going and cannot be conceptually established; this fixed nature of all phenomena is itself the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha—and so on, as extensively explained, up to the Buddha, the Bhagavān.”

“‘Good son! The abiding nature of all phenomena has neither coming nor going and cannot be designated; this abiding nature of all phenomena is itself the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha—and so on, as extensively explained, up to—the Buddha, the Bhagavān.’”

“Good son! The reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*) of all phenomena neither comes nor goes and cannot be conceptually established; the reality-limit of all phenomena is itself the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha—and so on, as extensively explained, up to the Buddha, the Bhagavān.”

“Good son! The dharma-realm of empty space neither comes nor goes, and it cannot be conceptually established; the dharma-realm of empty space is itself the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha—and so on, as extensively explained, up to the Buddha, the Bhagavān.”

“Good son! The inconceivable realm neither comes nor goes and cannot be designated; the inconceivable realm is itself the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha—and so on, as extensively explained, up to the Buddha, the Bhagavān.”

“‘Good son! The nature of phenomena is unborn, without coming or going, and cannot be conceptually designated. This unborn nature of phenomena is itself the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha—and so on, as extensively explained, up to the Buddha, the Bhagavān.’”

“‘Good son! The nature of phenomena is without cessation; it neither comes nor goes, and cannot be conceptually established. This nature of phenomena without cessation is itself the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha—and so on at length, up to—the Buddha, the Bhagavān.’”

“Good son! The suchness of phenomena (dharmatā) neither comes nor goes, and it cannot be conceptually designated. This suchness of phenomena is the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha—and so on, as extensively explained, up to the Buddha, the Bhagavān.”
“‘Good son! The nature of phenomena is remote;

it neither comes nor goes, and it cannot be conceptually designated. This very nature of phenomena that is remote is the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha—and so on, as extensively explained, up to the Buddha, the Bhagavān.’”

“Good son! The nature of the tranquility of phenomena neither comes nor goes, and it cannot be conceptually designated. This very nature of the tranquility of phenomena is the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha—and so on, as extensively explained, up to the Buddha, the Bhagavān.”

“‘Good son! The realm of non-defilement and non-purity neither comes nor goes, and it cannot be conceptually established. This realm of non-defilement and non-purity is itself the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha—and so on, as extensively described, up to the Buddha, the Bhagavān.’”

“Good son! The emptiness of all phenomena has neither coming nor going and cannot be conceptually established. The emptiness of all phenomena is itself the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha—and so on, as extensively explained, up to the Buddha, the Bhagavān.”
“‘Good son! All Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas— extending as far as Buddhas, Bhagavāns—
are neither identical to all phenomena, nor are they separate from all phenomena.’”
“‘O son of good family!
The suchness of all phenomena and the suchness of the Tathāgata are one and not two.
“‘O son of good family!
The suchness of all phenomena is neither conjoined nor dispersed; it has but a single characteristic, which is the so-called "characteristicless. "Good son!
The suchness of all phenomena is not one, not two, not three, not four, and so on, as extensively explained, up to not being a hundred thousand, and so forth."
Why is this? Son of good family!
Because the true suchness (*tathatā*) of all phenomena transcends number and quantity, and because it does not possess an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
"Furthermore, son of good family!
It is like a person traveling through a vast wilderness during the final period of the summer heat, who, parched with thirst at midday, sees shimmering mirages and thinks to himself:
'I shall certainly obtain water now.'"

Having formed this thought, he proceeded toward it; however, the mirage he beheld gradually receded as he went, and as he pursued it, it appeared even further away. Despite employing various means, he was unable to find water.
“Good son! What do you think? From what mountain valley, spring, or pool does this water in the mirage come?”
Where are you going now?
Are you entering the Eastern Sea,
or are you entering the Western, Southern, or Northern Seas?
Sadāprarudita replied:
"Even water in a mirage cannot be found; how much less can it be said that it comes from anywhere or goes anywhere!"
The Bodhisattva Dharmodgata said to Sadāprarudita: “So it is! So it is!”
It is as you have said.

Just as that thirsty person, foolish and lacking wisdom, being oppressed by heat, perceives a flickering mirage in waterless space and falsely conceives the notion of water; so too should it be known that if one says the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha comes or goes, such a person is likewise foolish and lacking wisdom.
Why is this? Son of good family!
All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas cannot be seen by means of their form-bodies; for the Tathāgata is, in truth, the Dharma-body.

"Good son! The Dharma-body of the Tathāgata is the suchness (tathatā) and the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) of all phenomena. Since suchness and the dharma-realm cannot be said to come or go, the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata is likewise without coming or going."

"Furthermore, good son! It is like a magician or his apprentice who conjures through illusion various elephant divisions, cavalry, chariot divisions, infantry, as well as oxen, sheep, and so forth, which suddenly vanish after a brief moment."
Good son! What do you think?
From where does that which is produced by illusion come?
"Where does it go?
Sadāprarudita replied, "An illusory phenomenon is not real; how could one speak of its coming or going?"
Dharmodgata Bodhisattva said to Sadāprarudita: "So it is! So it is!"
It is as you have said.

If one clings to the idea that illusory phenomena come and go, know that such a person is foolish and lacks wisdom; likewise, if one claims that the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha comes or goes, know that such a person is also foolish and lacks wisdom.
Why is this? Son of good family!
All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas cannot be seen by means of their form bodies; for the Tathāgata is, in truth, the Dharma-body.

"Good son! The Dharma-body of the Tathāgata is the suchness (tathatā) and the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) of all phenomena. Since suchness and the dharma-realm cannot be said to come or go, the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata is likewise without coming or going."
"Furthermore, good son! Just as various images appear within a mirror and so forth, so too these images exist for a moment and then vanish. Good son!"
What do you think?
From where does this reflection in the mirror come,
and to where does it go?
Sadāprarudita replied, “These images are not real; how can it be said that they come or go?
Bodhisattva Dharmodgata then spoke to Sadāprarudita:
"So it is! So it is! It is just as you have said."

If one holds that reflected images come and go, one should know that such a person is foolish and lacks wisdom; likewise, if one claims that the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha comes and goes, one should know that such a person is likewise foolish and lacks wisdom.
Why is this? Son of good family!
All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas cannot be seen by means of the physical body; for the Tathāgata is, in truth, the Dharma-body.

"Good son! The Dharma-body of the Tathāgata is the suchness (tathatā) and the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) of all phenomena. Since suchness and the dharma-realm cannot be said to come or go, the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata is likewise without coming or going."
"Furthermore, noble son! Just as various echoes manifest within such things as valleys, so too these echoes exist for a moment and then vanish. Noble son!"
"What do you think?
From where does this echo of the grain and so forth come?
And to where does it go?"
Sadāprarudita replied, "All echoes are unreal;
how can one speak of them having places from which they come or to which they go?
Dharmodgata Bodhisattva said to Sadāprarudita:
"So it is! So it is! It is just as you have said."

If one holds that echoes have coming and going, know that such a person is foolish and lacks wisdom; likewise, if one says that the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha has coming and going, know that such a person is also foolish and lacks wisdom.
Why is this? Son of good family!
All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas cannot be seen by means of their physical bodies; for the Tathāgata is, in truth, the Dharma-body.

"Good son! The Dharma-body of the Tathāgata is the suchness (tathatā) and the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) of all phenomena. Since suchness and the dharma-realm cannot be said to come or go, the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata is likewise without coming or going."
The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle Three Hundred and Nineteen.
The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle Four Hundred.
Translated by the Tripitaka Dharma Master Xuanzang under Imperial Decree.
The Seventy-eighth Chapter on the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata,
Part Two: "Furthermore, son of good family,
it is like shadows and reflections, which manifest various forms, shapes, movements, shifts, and distinctions."
"Good son! What do you think?
From where does such a shadow and light come?"
"Where does it go?
Sadāprarudita replied, "Light and shadow are not real; how can one speak of their coming or going?"
The Bodhisattva Dharmodgata said to Sadāprarudita: “So it is! So it is!”
It is as you have said.

If one clings to the idea that light and shadow come and go, know that such a person is foolish and lacks wisdom; likewise, if one claims that the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha comes or goes, know that such a person is also foolish and lacks wisdom.
Why is this? Son of good family!
All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas cannot be seen by means of their form-body; for the Tathāgata is, in truth, the Dharma-body.

"Good son! The Dharma-body of the Tathāgata is the suchness (tathatā) and the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) of all phenomena. Since suchness and the dharma-realm cannot be said to come or go, the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata is likewise without coming or going."
"Furthermore, good son! Just as the city of Gandharvas appears to have various kinds of objects, yet these objects exist for only a moment before vanishing;
so it is, good son!"
What do you think?
From where do all the various things belonging to this city of Gandharvas come,
and to where do they go?
Sadāprarudita replied, "All things belonging to this city of Gandhavatī are not truly existent; how can it be said that they come from anywhere or go anywhere?"
The Bodhisattva Dharmodgata said to Sadāprarudita: "So it is! So it is!"
It is as you have said.

One who clings to the idea that the various objects of a city of gandharvas come and go should be known as a person who is foolish and lacks wisdom; likewise, one who claims that the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha comes or goes should also be known as a person who is foolish and lacks wisdom.
Why is this? Son of good family!
All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas cannot be seen by means of their physical bodies; for the Tathāgata is, in truth, the Dharma-body.

"Good son! The Dharma-body of the Tathāgata is the suchness (tathatā) and the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) of all phenomena. Since suchness and the dharma-realm cannot be said to come or go, the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata is likewise without coming or going."
"Furthermore, son of good family!
Just as the emanated manifestations of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas exist for a moment and then cease to be,
so it is, son of good family!"
What do you think?
From where do these various manifested transformations come,
and to where do they go?
Sadāprarudita replied:
"All manifested phenomena are not truly existent; how can it be said that they come from anywhere or go anywhere?"
The Bodhisattva Dharmodgata said to Sadāprarudita: "So it is! So it is!"
It is as you have said.

One who clings to the idea that manifested transformations come and go should be known as a person who is foolish and lacks wisdom. Likewise, if one claims that the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha comes or goes, it should be known that such a person is likewise foolish and lacks wisdom.
Why is this? Son of good family!
All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas cannot be seen by means of their form-body; for the Tathāgata is, in truth, the Dharma-body.

"Good son! The dharmakāya of the Tathāgata is the suchness (tathatā) and the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) of all phenomena. Since suchness and the dharma-realm cannot be said to come or go, the dharmakāya of the Tathāgata is likewise without coming or going."

"Furthermore, good son! It is as if a person in a dream sees various Buddhas—whether one, ten, a hundred, a thousand, or even countless. Once that dream has awakened, all that was seen is no longer there."
"Good son! What do you think?
From where did the Buddha seen in the dream come?"
"Where does it go?
Sadāprarudita replied, "Whatever is seen in a dream is entirely illusory and not substantially real; how, then, can one speak of a place from which it comes or to which it goes?"
The Bodhisattva Dharmodgata said to Sadāprarudita: "So it is! So it is!"
It is as you have said.

One who clings to the idea that what is seen in a dream has coming and going should be known as a person who is foolish and lacking in wisdom; likewise, one who says that the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha has coming and going should also be known as a person who is foolish and lacking in wisdom.
Why is this? Son of good family!
All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas cannot be seen by means of their form bodies; for the Tathāgata is, in truth, the Dharma-body.

"Good son! The Dharma-body of the Tathāgata is the suchness (tathatā) and the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) of all phenomena. Since suchness and the dharma-realm cannot be said to come or go, the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata is likewise without coming or going."
"Furthermore, son of good family!
