All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas teach that all phenomena are like what is seen in a dream, like a magical transformation, like a city of Gandharvas, a reflection, an echo, an image, an illusion, and a mirage; they are none of them truly existent."

If one does not understand, as they truly are, the profound meaning of the Dharma taught by such Buddhas, and instead clings to the body of the Tathāgata as being name and form, or as having coming and going, you should know that such a person, because they are deluded regarding the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), is ignorant and lacks wisdom; they will wander through the various realms of existence, undergoing the suffering of birth and death, remaining far removed from the Prajñāpāramitā and likewise far removed from all the Buddha-dharmas.

If one can understand, as they truly are, the profound meanings of the Dharma taught by such Buddhas—neither grasping at the Buddha’s body as being name or form, nor asserting that the Buddha comes or goes—one should know that such a person has correctly comprehended the profound meaning of the Dharma taught by the Buddhas; they do not grasp at phenomena as coming or going, arising or ceasing, or being defiled or pure.

Because they do not grasp, they are able to practice the *prajñāpāramitā* and can also diligently cultivate all Buddha-dharmas; thus, they draw near to the sought-after unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment and are called the Tathāgata’s truly pure disciples. They never receive the faithful offerings of the people in vain, serve as excellent fields of merit for all, and are worthy of receiving the offerings of the world’s gods and humans.
"Furthermore, noble son!

Just as there are various precious jewels within the great ocean, these jewels do not come from the ten directions, nor are they produced therein by sentient beings, nor do these jewels arise without causes and conditions; rather, it is through the power of the roots of goodness of sentient beings that various jewels are produced within the great ocean."

When these jewels arise, they exist through the power of the conjunction of causes and conditions; they come from nowhere. When these jewels perish, they likewise go nowhere in the ten directions; they simply vanish because the power of the sentient beings' roots of virtue has been exhausted.

Why is this so? All conditioned phenomena arise through the conjunction of conditions and perish through the separation of conditions; within them, there is ultimately no one who arises and no one who perishes. Therefore, all phenomena neither come nor go.

The bodies of all Tathāgatas are likewise thus: they do not come from anywhere in the ten directions, nor is there any creator therein; yet it cannot be said that they arise without causes and conditions. Rather, because the cultivation of fundamental pure conduct has reached perfection as a cause and condition, and because the karma of sentient beings having previously cultivated the vision of a Buddha has matured, the body of a Tathāgata appears in the world. When the Buddha-body ceases, it likewise does not go anywhere in the ten directions; it simply vanishes when the power of the harmony of causes and conditions is exhausted. Therefore, all Buddhas neither come nor go.
"Furthermore, good son! It is like a *vīṇā* (lute), which produces sound based on the conjunction of various causes and conditions.

The causes and conditions for this sound are the body, the neck, the strings, the plectrum, and the human effort and attention; yet each of these individually cannot produce sound. Only when they are in conjunction does the sound arise. At the moment this sound arises, it comes from nowhere; when it ceases, it goes nowhere."
"Good son! The bodies of all Tathāgatas are likewise so; they arise depending upon various causes and conditions. The causes and conditions for these bodies are as follows:

immeasurable merit and wisdom, as well as the ripening of the roots of goodness cultivated by sentient beings through the vision of the Buddha. Individually, none of these can produce the body; it is only when they harmoniously combine that the body arises. At the stage of its arising, the body comes from nowhere; at the time of its passing away, it goes nowhere."

"Good son! You should understand that for the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, there is no coming or going; following this principle, you should likewise understand that all phenomena are characterized by neither coming nor going."

“Good son! If one can, with respect to the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, and all phenomena, know them as they truly are—neither coming nor going, neither arising nor ceasing, neither defiled nor pure—one will certainly be able to practice the profound perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) through skillful means (upāyakauśalya), and will surely attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi).”

When the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata explained to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita the characteristic of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas—extending even to the Buddhas, Bhagavāns—having neither coming nor going, the entire great earth of this trichiliocosm, including its mountains, great oceans, and celestial palaces, shook in six ways; all the palaces of the Māras lost their majestic splendor, and the Māras and their armies were utterly terrified.

At that time, all the grasses, trees, and forests throughout this great trichiliocosm produced flowers out of season; they all leaned toward the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata, while various kinds of fragrant flowers also rained down from the sky.

At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, the Four Great Kings, and the hosts of devas, immediately scattered various kinds of exquisite celestial fragrant flowers from the midst of the sky as an offering to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata. Having done so, they further took various kinds of exquisite celestial fragrant flowers and scattered them as an offering to the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita, saying:

"Because of this Great Being, we have been able to hear such teachings on the ultimate meaning; all those in the world who dwell in the view of a self, having heard this Dharma, will be able to abandon their attachments and all come to abide in the stage that is difficult to subdue."
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata, saying:

"For what cause and for what reason does the entire great earth, the mountains, and the great oceans of this world undergo the six kinds of movement, and manifest these various rare and wondrous signs?"
The Bodhisattva Dharmodgata addressed Sadāprarudita, saying:

“Because I have answered your question regarding how the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha is without the characteristics of coming or going, eight thousand sentient beings in this assembly have all realized the patience of the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti); furthermore, eighty nayutas of sentient beings have all resolved to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening; and furthermore, eighty-four thousand sentient beings have become free from dust and removed from defilement, giving rise to the pure Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena.”
By reason of these causes and conditions, the entire great earth, all the mountains, and the great oceans of this world undergo six kinds of movement, and various rare and marvelous signs appear.
When Sadāprarudita Bodhisattva heard these words, he leaped for joy and thought to himself:

"I have now attained a great and excellent benefit; namely, because of my questioning of Dharmodgata Bodhisattva, all sentient beings have been enabled to hear this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, which explains that all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas possess neither coming nor going, thereby bringing great benefit to so many beings."
"By means of such supreme roots of virtue, I shall certainly accomplish the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment that I seek.

I have no further doubt regarding this unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; in a future life, I shall certainly become a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, bringing benefit, peace, and happiness to immeasurable sentient beings."
Having formed this thought, he leaped for joy and ascended into the air to the height of seven *tāla* trees.
He then further thought:
"With what should I make an offering to the Great Master, the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata, to repay his kindness in preaching the Dharma for me?"
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, knowing his thoughts, manifested immeasurable and exquisite fragrant flowers and, wishing to offer them to the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita, spoke these words:
"O Mahāsattva!..."
"Now, out of compassion for us, you should accept these flowers and take them to make an offering to the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata. Great Being!
You should accept our offering; we now assist you in accomplishing your merit."

Why is this? Because of this Great Being, we immeasurable hundreds of thousands of sentient beings have obtained great benefit; that is to say, we shall certainly realize the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment that we seek.
"O Great Being!

You should know that it is extremely rare to find anyone who, for the sake of all sentient beings, undergoes such diligent toil and suffering throughout immeasurable and incalculable great eons as you do. Therefore, you should now accept what I offer."

At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita accepted the exquisite fragrant flowers from Śakra, the Lord of Devas, and having scattered them as an offering to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata, he descended from the sky, prostrated at his feet, and with palms joined in reverence, addressed him, saying:
"O Great Teacher!
"From this day forward, I vow to offer my very body and life to the Great Master to serve as his attendant.
Having spoken these words, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata stood before him with palms joined in reverence.
Then the daughter of the elder and her retinue, with palms joined in reverence, said to Sadāprarudita:
"From this day forth, we also offer our own bodies and lives to serve you; we pray that you will graciously accept us!"

By these roots of goodness, may I obtain such sublime dharmas as those realized by the Honored One; may I always remain in close proximity to the Honored One in future lives, constantly following the Honored One to make offerings to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, and together cultivate the holy life.
Sadāprarudita Bodhisattva then replied to them:
"If you are sincerely subject to me, you must follow my instructions; then I shall accept you."
The daughters of the elder and their attendants said to Sadāprarudita, "We truly devote ourselves to you; we shall follow your instructions.

Thereupon, Sadāprarudita Bodhisattva had the daughters of the elder and all their retinues adorn themselves with various exquisite ornaments. He then took five hundred magnificent chariots made of the seven precious gems, along with various articles of offering, and presented them all at once to Dharmodgata Bodhisattva, saying:
“‘Great Master!
I offer these daughters of householders and others to you, Great Master; I pray that out of compassion you will graciously accept them for me.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, praised Sadāprarudita, saying:”
“Excellent! Excellent!
Great Being, you are indeed able to practice such relinquishment and generosity.”

It is the natural law for all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas to relinquish and give away everything they possess; if a bodhisattva-mahāsattva can train in such total relinquishment, they will swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
If one can thus respectfully honor and make offerings to the Dharma-preacher without any stinginess, one will certainly hear the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*).

When the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the past were diligently training in the bodhisattva path, they also inquired about the profound perfection of wisdom and skillful means for relinquishing all that one possesses; by this, they realized the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment they sought.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata, desiring to bring to fulfillment the roots of goodness planted by the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita, accepted the five hundred precious chariots along with all the offerings and the daughter of the elder and her retinue; having accepted them, he then bestowed them back upon the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita.

After the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata had taught the Dharma for a long time, as the sun was about to set, he perceived that the assembly was weary; he descended from his lion throne and returned to his palace.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita, seeing the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata enter the palace, thought to himself:

"I have come here for the sake of the Dharma; until I have heard the True Dharma, I ought not to sit or lie down. I should maintain only the postures of walking and standing, waiting for the Great Master, the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata, to emerge from the palace and proclaim the essentials of the Dharma."

"After the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata had entered the palace, seven years passed while he remained with a single-minded focus and without distraction, sporting in immeasurable and innumerable bodhisattva samādhi-doors, and dwelling securely in immeasurable and innumerable profound prajñāpāramitās and skillful means."

For seven years, the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita neither sat nor lay down; he did nothing but walk and stand. He did not think of sleep, did not distinguish day from night, did not complain of fatigue, did not crave food or drink, did not fear cold or heat, and did not attend to anything internal or external. He never gave rise to thoughts of desire, malice, or harm, nor any other afflictions, fetters, or impurities.
He thought only this: "When will the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata arise from his samādhi?"

"We, as your retinue, shall prepare the Dharma seat, sweep and sprinkle this ground, and scatter various fragrant flowers; may the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata ascend this seat to proclaim the Prajñāpāramitā, skillful means, and other essential points of the Dharma."

At that time, the daughter of the elder and her retinue also spent seven years walking and standing alone; in all they relinquished and all they contemplated, they followed the example of Sadāprarudita, following his every movement without ever departing from him for even a moment.
"At that time, after the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita had practiced with such diligence for seven years, he suddenly heard a voice from the sky saying: 'Ho!'"
“Good son! Seven days from now, the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata shall arise from his meditative concentration and proclaim the True Dharma within this city.
Having heard the voice from the sky, the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita leaped for joy and thought to himself:

"I shall now prepare and adorn a lion throne for the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata, sweep and sprinkle this ground, and scatter exquisite fragrant flowers, so that my Great Teacher may ascend this seat and proclaim for the assembly the profound Prajñāpāramitā, skillful means, and other essential teachings."
After the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita had formed this thought, he, together with the merchant’s daughter and her retinue, prepared lion thrones made of the seven precious substances.
Then, the merchant’s daughter and her retinue each removed a pure and exquisite robe from their bodies and spread them over the thrones as an offering for the Dharma teacher.
"Once the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita had spread his seat, he sought water to sprinkle upon the ground but was unable to find any.
Why was this? Because the evil Māra had concealed all the water within and outside the city, causing it to disappear from view."
Māra thought to himself:

"If the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita fails to find water, he will become distressed, sorrowful, and afflicted; he will grow weary and physically debilitated, and his mind may undergo a change. Consequently, his roots of goodness for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment will not increase, his wisdom will not shine forth, and he will be delayed in attaining omniscience. Thus, he will be unable to empty my realm."
Sadāprarudita Bodhisattva, having sought water through various skillful means without success, thought to himself:
"I should pierce my own body to draw blood and sprinkle it upon the ground, lest dust rise up and soil my Great Teacher."
"Now this body of mine must inevitably perish; what use is such a false and deceptive body?

Since beginningless time, I have wandered through birth and death, repeatedly losing my life for the sake of the five desires, yet I have never sacrificed my body for the sake of the True Dharma. Therefore, I should now pierce my body to draw blood."
Having formed this thought, he immediately took up a sharp knife and pierced his body all over until blood flowed out, which he sprinkled upon the ground.
At that time, the daughter of the elder and her attendants also followed the example of Sadāprarudita, piercing their own bodies with blood to sprinkle upon the ground.

The Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita, the daughter of the elder, and the others, for the sake of the Dharma, pierced their own bodies to draw blood, never giving rise to even a single thought of a contrary mind.

At that time, the various evil Māras were unable to find an opportunity, nor could they obstruct the wholesome qualities being cultivated, because the minds of Sadāprarudita and the others were courageous and resolute.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, having witnessed this event, thought to himself:

"The Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita, the daughter of the elder, and the others are truly most rare. Because of their love for the Dharma and their reverence for the Dharma, they have even pierced their entire bodies to draw blood and sprinkled it over the ground for the sake of the Dharma-preacher; yet they never gave rise to a single thought of distraction, so that the evil Māras could find no opportunity and were unable to obstruct the wholesome qualities they were cultivating."
How marvelous!

That you, Great Being, are able to don such firm armor of vast vows, desiring to bring benefit and happiness to all sentient beings; that with a pure mind, disregarding even body and life, you seek unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and constantly make this vow:

"I seek unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment in order to rescue all sentient beings submerged in the cycle of birth and death from their immeasurable and boundless physical and mental suffering, and until this task is accomplished, I shall never grow weary or abandon it."

Then, having formed this thought, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, transformed all the blood shed by Sadāprarudita and the others into sandalwood-scented water. He caused it to be sprinkled upon the ground surrounding the seat on all four sides, each side measuring a full hundred yojanas, so that there was the inconceivable, most supreme, and most marvelous fragrance of celestial sandalwood throughout.
Then, having performed these deeds, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, praised Sadāprarudita, saying:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
The Great Being’s vow is firm and difficult to shake; his diligence and valor are inconceivable, and his cherishing of the quest for the Dharma is supreme.

Past Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas likewise, through such firm vows, valorous diligence, and cherishing of the quest for the Dharma, practiced the pure brahmacarya of a bodhisattva and realized unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

"Great Being, since your aspiration is now so diligent and you cherish the seeking of the Dharma so deeply, you shall certainly realize the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment that you seek.
At that time, Sadāprarudita thought to himself:

"I have now prepared a lion throne of the seven precious gems for the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata and swept and sprinkled this ground until it is exceedingly fragrant and pure. How shall I obtain various exquisite incense and flowers to adorn the ground on all four sides of the throne? When the Great Master ascends the throne and is about to preach the Dharma, we should also hold them out to scatter as an offering."

At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, knowing his thoughts, immediately manifested a subtle and exquisite fragrant flower in a quantity equal to a thousand *dronas* of Magadha measure, which he reverently offered to the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita, so that he and his retinue might take it to make offerings.

Thereupon, Sadāprarudita, having accepted the flowers bestowed by Śakra, Lord of the Devas, divided them into two portions. He first took one portion and, together with his retinue, circumambulated the four sides of the seat, scattering them to adorn the ground; he reserved the remaining portion to be offered as a scattering when the Great Master ascended the Dharma-seat.

At that time, after seven days had passed, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata arose calmly from the samādhi-door of his playful sport. Surrounded by an entourage of immeasurable hundreds of thousands, he emerged from the inner palace to preach the Prajñāpāramitā; ascending the lion throne, he sat solemnly amidst the great assembly.

When Sadāprarudita Bodhisattva beheld the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata once more, he leaped for joy with a heart full of delight, his body and mind filled with bliss, just as a bhikṣu who has fixed his mindfulness on a single object suddenly enters the third dhyāna.

He then, together with his retinue, took the exquisite incense and flowers previously set aside and scattered them as an offering. Having completed the offering, he prostrated at [the Buddha’s] feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and withdrew to sit at one side.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita, saying:
"Son of good family,
listen attentively!
Listen attentively!
Reflect upon it well!
I shall proclaim for you the Prajñāpāramitā.
Sadāprarudita said: "Indeed, please speak; we long to hear it!
Bodhisattva Dharmodgata addressed Sadāprarudita, saying:
“Good son! Because all dharmas are equal, you should know that the prajñāpāramitā is also equal.
Because all dharmas are detached, you should know that the prajñāpāramitā is also detached.”
Because all phenomena are immovable, one should know that the perfection of wisdom is also immovable.
Because all phenomena are without mentation, one should know that the perfection of wisdom is also without mentation.
Because all phenomena are fearless, one should know that the perfection of wisdom is also fearless.
Because all phenomena are without dread, one should know that the perfection of wisdom is also without dread.
Because all phenomena are of one taste, one should know that the *prajñāpāramitā* is also of one taste.
Because all phenomena are without limit, one should know that the *prajñāpāramitā* is also without limit.
Because all phenomena are without arising, one should know that the perfection of wisdom is also without arising.
Because all phenomena are without cessation, one should know that the perfection of wisdom is also without cessation.
Because great empty space is boundless, one should know that the Prajñāpāramitā is also boundless.
Because the waters of the great ocean are boundless, one should know that the Prajñāpāramitā is also boundless.
Because Mount Sumeru is boundless, one should know that the Prajñāpāramitā is also boundless.
Because Mount Sumeru is magnificent and beautiful, one should know that the Prajñāpāramitā is also magnificent and beautiful.
Just as the great void is without discrimination, one should know that the Prajñāpāramitā is also without discrimination.
"O son of good family!
Because form is boundless, one should know that the Prajñāpāramitā is also boundless;..."
Because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are boundless, one should know that the perfection of wisdom is also boundless.
Because the sense base of the eye is boundless, one should know that the perfection of wisdom is also boundless;
because the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are boundless, one should know that the perfection of wisdom is also boundless.
Because the sphere of form is boundless, one should know that the perfection of wisdom is also boundless;
because the spheres of sound, odor, taste, touch, and mental phenomena are boundless, one should know that the perfection of wisdom is also boundless.
Because the eye-element is boundless, one should know that the perfection of wisdom is also boundless;
because the ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-elements are boundless, one should know that the perfection of wisdom is also boundless.
Because the realm of form is infinite, one should know that the perfection of wisdom is also infinite;
because the realms of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena are infinite, one should know that the perfection of wisdom is also infinite.
Because the visual consciousness element is boundless, one should know that the perfection of wisdom is also boundless;
because the auditory, olfactory, gustatory, tactile, and mental consciousness elements are boundless, one should know that the perfection of wisdom is also boundless.
Because eye-contact is boundless, one should know that the perfection of wisdom is also boundless;
because ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact are boundless, one should know that the perfection of wisdom is also boundless.
Because the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition are boundless, one should know that the perfection of wisdom is also boundless;
because the various feelings produced with ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact as conditions are boundless, one should know that the perfection of wisdom is also boundless.
Because the earth element is boundless, one should know that the perfection of wisdom is also boundless;
because the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements are boundless, one should know that the perfection of wisdom is also boundless.
Because causes and conditions are boundless, one should know that the perfection of wisdom is also boundless;
because the immediately preceding condition, the object condition, and the dominant condition are boundless, one should know that the perfection of wisdom is also boundless.
Because all phenomena produced from conditions are boundless, one should know that the *prajñāpāramitā* is also boundless.
Because ignorance is boundless, one should know that the *prajñāpāramitā* is also boundless;

because volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, existence, birth, and old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are boundless, one should know that the *prajñāpāramitā* is also boundless.
“‘O son of noble family!
Because the perfection of generosity is limitless, you should know that the perfection of wisdom is also limitless;

because the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, skillful means, sublime aspiration, power, and knowledge are limitless, you should know that the perfection of wisdom is also limitless.’”
Because internal emptiness is limitless, one should know that the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) is also limitless;

because external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, non-altering emptiness, essential emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common-characteristic emptiness, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence are limitless, one should know that the perfection of wisdom is also limitless.
Because suchness is boundless, one should know that the perfection of wisdom is also boundless;

because the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), non-erroneousness, immutability, equality, the state beyond birth, the fixed nature of phenomena (*dharmaniyāmatā*), the stability of phenomena (*dharmaniyāmatā*), the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), the realm of space (*ākāśadhātu*), and the inconceivable realm are boundless, one should know that the perfection of wisdom is also boundless.
Because the four foundations of mindfulness are boundless, one should know that the perfection of wisdom is also boundless;

because the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path are boundless, one should know that the perfection of wisdom is also boundless.
Because the Noble Truth of Suffering is boundless, one should know that the Prajñāpāramitā is also boundless;
because the Noble Truths of Origination, Cessation, and the Path are boundless, one should know that the Prajñāpāramitā is also boundless.
Because the ten paths of wholesome action are boundless, one should know that the perfection of wisdom is also boundless;
because generosity, ethical discipline, and cultivation are boundless, one should know that the perfection of wisdom is also boundless.
Because the four dhyānas are boundless, one should know that the perfection of wisdom is also boundless;
because the four immeasurables and the four formless absorptions are boundless, one should know that the perfection of wisdom is also boundless.
Because the eight liberations are boundless, one should know that the perfection of wisdom is also boundless;
because the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative attainments, and the ten totalities are boundless, one should know that the perfection of wisdom is also boundless.
Because the gate of liberation of emptiness is boundless, one should know that the perfection of wisdom is also boundless;
because the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness are boundless, one should know that the perfection of wisdom is also boundless.
Because the gateways of dhāraṇī are boundless, one should know that the perfection of wisdom is also boundless;
because the gateways of samādhi are boundless, one should know that the perfection of wisdom is also boundless.
Because the ten stages of the bodhisattva are boundless, one should know that the perfection of wisdom is also boundless. "Good son!
Because the five eyes are boundless, one should know that the perfection of wisdom is also boundless;
Because the six supernormal powers are boundless, one should know that the perfection of wisdom is also boundless.
Because the ten powers of a Buddha are boundless, one should know that the perfection of wisdom is also boundless;

because the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are boundless, one should know that the perfection of wisdom is also boundless.
Because the quality of non-forgetfulness is boundless, one should know that the perfection of wisdom is also boundless;
because the nature of constant equanimity is boundless, one should know that the perfection of wisdom is also boundless.
Because omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) is boundless, one should know that the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) is also boundless;
because the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*) and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) are boundless, one should know that the perfection of wisdom is also boundless.
Because the thirty-two marks of a great man are boundless, one should know that the Prajñāpāramitā is also boundless;
because the eighty secondary signs are boundless, one should know that the Prajñāpāramitā is also boundless.
Because the fruit of stream-entry is boundless, one should know that the perfection of wisdom is also boundless;
because the fruits of once-returning, non-returning, arhatship, and the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha are boundless, one should know that the perfection of wisdom is also boundless.
Because the practices of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are boundless, one should know that the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) is also boundless;
because the unexcelled, perfect enlightenment of all buddhas is boundless, one should know that the perfection of wisdom is also boundless.
Because all contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) are boundless, one should know that the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) is also boundless;
because all uncontaminated phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*) are boundless, one should know that the perfection of wisdom is also boundless.
Because all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) are boundless, one should know that the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) is also boundless;
because all unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*) are boundless, one should know that the perfection of wisdom is also boundless.
Because the diamond-like [samādhi] is equal, one should know that the Prajñāpāramitā is also equal.
Because all dharmas are indestructible, one should know that the Prajñāpāramitā is also indestructible;
because all dharmas are unmixed, one should know that the Prajñāpāramitā is also unmixed.
Because all dharmas are without differentiation, one should know that the *prajñāpāramitā* is also without differentiation.
Because the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all dharmas cannot be apprehended, one should know that the intrinsic nature of the *prajñāpāramitā* also cannot be apprehended;
because all dharmas are equal in their non-existence, one should know that the *prajñāpāramitā* is also equal in its non-existence.
Because all phenomena are without activity, one should know that the perfection of wisdom is also without activity;
because all phenomena are inconceivable, one should know that the perfection of wisdom is also inconceivable.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita, having heard the exposition of the distinct meanings of the phrases of the Prajñāpāramitā,
immediately attained sixty billion samādhi-doors before his seat, namely: the samādhi of the equality of all dharmas,
the samādhi of the detachment of all dharmas, and the samādhi of the immovability of all dharmas.
The samādhi of all phenomena being without recollection, the samādhi of all phenomena being fearless, the samādhi of all phenomena being without dread,
the samādhi of all phenomena having a single flavor, the samādhi of all phenomena being without limit,
the samādhi of all phenomena being unarisen, and the samādhi of all phenomena being unceasing.
The samādhi of the boundlessness of space, the samādhi of the boundlessness of the great ocean, the samādhi of the boundlessness of Mount Sumeru,
the samādhi of the exquisite adornment of Mount Sumeru, the samādhi of non-discrimination like space,
the samādhi of the boundlessness of the aggregates such as form, and the samādhi of the boundlessness of the sense bases such as the eye.
The samādhi of [the limitlessness of] form and other sense bases; the samādhi of the limitlessness of the eye and other elements;
the samādhi of the limitlessness of the element of form and others; the samādhi of the limitlessness of the element of eye-consciousness and others;
the samādhi of the limitlessness of eye-contact and others; and that which is produced with eye-contact as its condition.
The samādhi of the boundlessness of all feelings and so forth; the samādhi of the boundlessness of the earth element and so forth;
the samādhi of the boundlessness of causes and conditions; the samādhi of the boundlessness of all phenomena produced from conditions;
the samādhi of the boundlessness of all members of dependent origination; and the samādhi of the boundlessness of all pāramitās.
The samādhi of the boundlessness of all emptiness; the samādhi of the boundlessness of the suchness of all phenomena;
the samādhi of the boundlessness of the factors of enlightenment; the samādhi of the boundlessness of the noble truths;
the samādhi of the boundlessness of the paths of wholesome action; the samādhi of the boundlessness of generosity, ethical discipline, and cultivation; and the samādhi of meditative concentration.
The boundless samādhis of the formless and the infinite; the boundless samādhis of the liberations, the spheres of mastery, the meditative attainments, and the spheres of totality;
the boundless samādhis of the gateways to liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;
the boundless samādhis of the gateways to dhāraṇīs and meditative concentrations; and the boundless samādhis of the bodhisattva stages. The five...
The infinite samādhi of the six supernormal powers; the infinite samādhi of the powers, fearlessnesses, analytical knowledges, great compassion, joy, equanimity, and the unique qualities of a Buddha;
the infinite samādhi of the quality of non-forgetfulness and the constant abiding in equanimity;
and the infinite samādhis of all-knowledge, the knowledge of the paths, and the knowledge of all aspects.
The samādhi of the earth and its infinite marks and secondary characteristics; the samādhi of the infinite Śrāvaka vehicle;
the samādhi of the infinite Pratyekabuddha vehicle; the samādhi of the infinite Unsurpassed Vehicle;
the samādhi of the infinite contaminated and uncontaminated phenomena; and the samādhi of the infinite conditioned and unconditioned phenomena.
...the vajra-like samādhi of equality, the samādhi of the indestructibility of all phenomena, the samādhi of the non-confusion of all phenomena,
the samādhi of the non-differentiation of all phenomena, the samādhi of the unapprehendability of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena,
the samādhi of the equality of the non-existence of all phenomena, and the samādhi of the non-substantiality of all phenomena...
He attained the samādhi of "Acting" and the samādhi of "The Inconceivability of All Dharmas," as well as sixty hundred thousand such gateways to samādhi.
As soon as Sadāprarudita Bodhisattva had attained these sixty hundred thousand gateways to samādhi, immediately—
I clearly see, in each of the ten directions— east, west, south, north, the four intermediate points, above, and below—
as many trichiliocosm great thousandfold world systems as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas currently residing therein,
surrounded by assemblies of śrāvakas and bodhisattvas, [teaching] by means of such names, such phrases, such syllables, and such principles.
Gone to that realm, he taught the *prajñāpāramitā* to the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas,
using such names, such phrases, such syllables, and such principles, just as I do now in this trichiliocosm, surrounded by a great assembly of śrāvakas and bodhisattvas.
He proclaimed the *Prajñāpāramitā* and its equalities without distinction for the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.

From that time forward, the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita’s vast learning and wisdom became inconceivable, like a great ocean. In whatever place he was born, he constantly beheld the Buddhas; he was always reborn in the pure and wondrous lands of the Buddhas. Even in his dreams, he constantly saw the Buddhas preaching the *Prajñāpāramitā* to him. He drew near to and made offerings to them without ever ceasing for a moment, thereby leaving behind the states of no-leisure and becoming fully endowed with leisure.
Chapter 79: The Section on the Exhortation to Practice.

"Subhūti, you should know that by virtue of this profound principle, the majestic power of the *prajñāpāramitā* is so preeminent that it enables all bodhisattvas to swiftly attain the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñājñāna*)."
Therefore, Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to study the six perfections so that they may be swiftly fulfilled;
wishes to fully penetrate and master the realm of all buddhas; wishes to attain the sovereign supernormal powers of all buddhas; and wishes to quickly realize—
One who wishes to attain the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna) and desires to ultimately bring benefit, peace,
and happiness to all sentient beings should study this profound perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā);
they should respectfully hear, receive, uphold, read, recite, and master this profound perfection of wisdom.
...practicing according to the teaching, reflecting upon the profound meaning and intent as they truly are,
transcribing and disseminating them, and explaining them to others; one should offer various kinds of exquisite flower garlands,
powdered and scattered incenses, robes, necklaces, precious banners, pennants, canopies, music, lamps, and other such items.
They shall offer various rare and precious items as an act of worship, reverence, respect, and praise. Why is this so?

Because this profound *prajñāpāramitā* is the true birth-mother who nurtures all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas; it is the true preceptor for the assembly of Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas. All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas collectively respect, revere, and praise it; there are no Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas among the entire assembly who do not make offerings to it and diligently study it. This constitutes the true instruction of the Tathāgata.
At that time, the Buddha said to Ānanda:
"Do you have love and reverence for the Tathāgata? Ānanda replied:
"So it is, World-Honored One! So it is!"
“Sugata! I truly have love and reverence for the Buddha; the Tathāgata knows this himself.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:

"So it is! So it is! You truly possess love and reverence for me. From the past until now, you have always honored and made offerings to me with wholesome actions of body, speech, and mind, attending upon me without ever failing."

"Ānanda! Just as you now honor my body with true love and respect, so too, after my parinirvāṇa, should you honor, revere, and pay homage to this profound *prajñāpāramitā* with such love and respect. A second and a third time the Buddha instructed Ānanda in this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, causing him to develop a love, respect, and veneration for it that surpassed even that for the Tathāgata’s own person.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"I entrust this profound Prajñāpāramitā to you before this great assembly; you should receive and uphold it."
After my parinirvāṇa, do not allow even a single word of this to be forgotten or lost.

To whatever extent this Prajñāpāramitā circulates in the world, you should know that the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are currently dwelling in the world, teaching the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings.

Ānanda! You should know that if there are those who, regarding this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, respectfully listen to it, receive and uphold it, read and recite it, master it thoroughly, practice according to its teachings, contemplate its profound meaning and intent as it truly is, copy it and disseminate it, and explain it to others; and furthermore, if they honor, respect, revere, and praise it with various kinds of exquisite flower garlands, powdered and scattered incenses, robes, necklaces, precious banners, streamers and canopies, music, lamps, and other various rare and wonderful objects—then you should know that such persons will constantly see all Buddhas, perpetually hear the True Dharma, and cultivate the holy life (*brahmacarya*).

When the Bhagavān had finished speaking this sutra, the immeasurable assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, with the Bodhisattva Maitreya as their leader; the great śrāvakas such as Mahākāśyapa, Śāriputra, and Ānanda; and the rest of the entire assembly—including devas, nāgas, humans, and non-humans—having heard what the Buddha taught, were all greatly rejoiced, and they faithfully accepted and practiced it.
